pages.text: Wednesday, December 31, 2025 29 Gray Cathrall Continued from page 28 March 2, 2016 issue of the Post During Gray’s 20th birthday celebration, Sgt. Catherine Carr does what many have only dreamed of and slapped some cuffs on knowntroublemaker Gray Cathrall, threatening to haul him into the station. Local media can help the community understand what is working as well as what needs improving. During election season, I know a lot of residents like to read interviews and op-eds to better understand the issues and the candidates.” Piedmont is not only the town’s watchdog: it’s also its mirror, and a kind of collective scrapbook for many parents of Piedmont. At home, I have thick albums of newspaper clippings that track my daughters’ milestones, the high moments of tennis tournaments, poetry slams, and graduation speeches. I also love seeing neighbors and friends (and, occasionally, my own family) in the “Where in the World Are We?”, the wildly popular column where residents pose with the paper on their travels. “It’s about connection,” Gray says. “About people recognizing themselves and each other in these pages.” Gray’s commitment to Piedmont didn’t stop at the newsroom; it carried into nearly every corner of the city’s cultural and civic life. In 2011, he became one of the founding members of what would become the Piedmont Center for the Arts (PCA), a project he viewed as a natural extension of the Post’s mission to uphold the town’s cultural and civic vibrancy. Over the fourteen years since its founding, PCA has hosted everything from chamber music to student recitals, providing a stage not only for visiting performers but for Piedmont’s own artists, writers, and musicians—including Cathrall himself, a devoted musician who occasionally takes the piano bench with his jazz ensemble, Shades of Gray. Among his contributions to PCA is launching the Berkeley Symphony’s Chamber Series. As PCA president Sue Malick recalls, “Gray was instrumental in forming the relationship with Berkeley Symphony’s René Mandel that brought all of their chamber concerts to the Center, where he has remained one of the series’ chief sponsors.” His commitment to Piedmont’s young people has been equally steady. Gray serves on the Advisory Board of the Piedmont Council of the Boy Scouts of America and led youth groups when his children were growing March 2, 2016 issue of the Post Post Production Manager Paul Fairchild (left), Sports Editor Kate Fratar, News Editor Paisley Strellis, and Editorial Cartoonist Brian Kelly presented Cathrall with a personalized Where in the World? (Strellis tried to discreetly remind Cathrall where he might have seen the house in the background before.) March 2, 2016 issue of the Post Five former Piedmont mayors wish Cathrall well on his 20th birthday, including Dean Barbieri (left), Margaret Fujioka, Patty White, John Chiang, and Skip Rhodes. up. In recognition of his decades of service, Cathrall was named Grand Marshal of Piedmont’s Fourth of July Parade in 2024—a fitting tribute to a man whose tireless commitment to his city has helped bring the community together. Having built a model of sustainable local journalism and enhanced the vibrancy of the local art scene, Gray has recently tapped Misha Edel, a former journalist and a longtime Piedmont resident, as the Post’s new Executive Editor. Edel will work closely with Gray on setting the paper’s editorial calendar and coverage priorities and will also focus on growing subscriptions and advertising revenue, streamlining operations, and developing a digital edition that complements the print paper. “The paper has always belonged to Piedmont,” Gray says. “Our job is to make sure it keeps serving this town for generations to come.” While Edel takes the helm of day-to-day publishing, Gray will turn more of his attention to philanthropy, a new chapter that he promises to unveil at his milestone birthday celebration in February 2026. Yet even as his focus widens, his imprint will remain on every page—the headlines, the stories, and the civic pride they reflect. As he looks ahead, Cathrall remains what he’s always been: the steady presence at the center of Piedmont’s civic life, an engaged and truly compassionate public servant whom many town residents consider a dear friend. The Post he built continues to bind us together—and to prove that when a community believes in local journalism, its spirit thrives. Nearly three decades later, the Post endures as Gray envisioned it: an honest, lively reflection of the town it serves. articles.text: As Dylan gains creative control, his music begins to rise to mainstream attention, writing songs about the growing political and social unrest at the time. This resonated with listeners, especially Joan Baez (Monica Barbaro). The two would become close friends and eventually go on tour together. Through his tour with Baez and playing at large festivals, Dylan became a cultural icon, but with the newfound fame comes increasing frustration with the expectations of both the music industry and the folk community. His lack of creative freedom frustrates Dylan, and he lashes out, taking his music in a new direction that frustrates the folk community. The climax comes during his performance at the 1965 Newport Folk Festival. I won’t reveal what happens at the festival, but it encapsulates how Bob Dylan lived his life. A man fighting not to conform to everyone’s expectations of who he should be but pushing to be the artist that he desired and write songs about topics he cared about. A Complete Unknown delivers a fantastic representation of Bob Dylan from Chalamet, in one of his best films. The movie leaves audiences with the message of individuality. A Complete Unknown. Directed by James Mangold. Starring Timothée Chalamet, Elle Fanning, Edward Norton, and Monica Barbaro. Duration 2 hr. 21 min. Rated R. Released 2024. Genre: Docudrama, music. articles.text: For more than a century, Piedmont Church has been a church of open doors - welcoming and affirming all who wish to gather, worship and serve. This history of acceptance provides a powerful atmosphere where our faith in God, combined with the love for our neighbor, creates the perfect ‘church home’ for many. Some say they attend Piedmont Church to rest, to find shelter from many of life’s challenges. Others find spiritual strength by participating in worship, preparing them for the week ahead. Those who enjoy serving their community explore ways to give back through our local and international Mission Partners. And, fellowship brings vivid life to it all. For the many reasons we give thanks during this season, we are most grateful for our church and for you - the friends we’ve known, and those we’ve yet to meet. Come and see Piedmont Church, where everyone is welcome. WORSHIP IN PERSON OR ONLINE SUNDAYS, 10AM

articles.text: Wildwood Elementary School families gathered last Friday, December 12, for Wildwood Winterfest, transforming the campus into a festive winter celebration. With twinkling lights, falling snow, live music, and holiday cheer the event brought together the Wildwood school community for an evening of connection and fun. Families enjoyed a community potluck alongside macaroni and cheese from Homeroom, while the Wildwood Dad’s Club, led by Mike Hagerty and Jake Strzelecki, hosted a popular hot cocoa station. Highlights included a Photo Booth sponsored by Jomiography (contact: JonMichael@jomiography.com), the debut of the Wildwood Wreath Walk, and live music from the PHS Jazz Trio led by Eric Anderssel-Venner. articles.text: As the commissioning process for the new pool continues, Aquatics staff are preparing for future operations and aquatics programming, including swim lessons. Community feedback will help the City better understand community interest levels for swim lessons, including age groups, general skill levels, and preferred days and times. Survey responses will be used by Recreation Department staff to support planning and prioritization of swim lessons offerings once the pool is operational and aquatics programming begins. The survey, available at piedmont.ca.gov/SwimLessonsSurvey, invites residents to share: • The age ranges and approximate skill level of likely participants in their household • Preferred days and times for lessons • Seasons of interest • Factors that could make participation difficult The activity pool Photo courtesy of the city of Piedmont

Oakland’s strength has always come from our diversity and our unwavering commitment to all residents from hate and violence. articles.text: The Alameda County Women’s Hall of Fame (WHOF) is now accepting nominations for its 2026 inductees and applications for its Mary V. King/Wilma Chan Youth Scholarship Program. The event will take place on Saturday, March 28, 2026, at The Club at Castlewood in Pleasanton. The deadline for inductee nominations is December 12, 2025. Since 1993, the WHOF has honored women whose leadership, innovation, and service have strengthened Alameda County’s diverse communities. “For more than three decades, the Alameda County Women’s Hall of Fame has celebrated the achievements of remarkable women who are shaping our communities for the better,” said Susan S. Muranishi, Alameda County Administrator and Co-Chair of the Women’s Hall of Fame. “We invite residents to help us honor these changemakers by nominating women who exemplify leadership, compassion, and service.” Through the Mary V. King/ Wilma Chan Youth Scholarship Fund, WHOF will also award up to six $5,000 scholarships to outstanding high school seniors who demonstrate academic excellence, community involvement, leadership, and perseverance in overcoming challenges. Up to twelve inductees and six youth scholarship recipients will be honored at the Alameda County Women’s Hall of Fame Luncheon and Awards Ceremony. Proceeds from the event and related activities help fund programs that support women and families across Alameda County. Community members are invited to nominate inspiring women in the following categories: Business & Professions, Culture & Art, Community Service, Education, Emerging Leaders, Environmental, Health, Justice, Non-Traditional, Philanthropy, Science/Technology/Engineering, and Sports & Athletics. For nomination and scholarship details, visit www.acgov. org/whof
articles.title: Nominations and scholarship applications now open for Alameda County Women’s Hall of Fame 2026

articles.text: Sweet Gianna is small but spunky. She weighs only 9 pounds and was extremely shy when she arrived at Oakland Animal Services. She is now living in a foster home with several other small dogs who are teaching her that humans aren’t scary and how to live in a home. Three-year-old Gianna is taking her cues from her foster siblings and is working on her potty training, leash, walking and socialization. She would benefit from being adopted by a household with a resident dog who is patient and playful. Giana enjoys playing outside and has figured out how to use the dog door in her foster home. To see more photos of her and a video of one of her recent outings, visit Oakland Animal Services’ website. If you would enjoy helping Miss Gianna build her confidence Gianna is small but spunky and come out of her shell, she may be the dog for you. articles.text: Piedmont voters appear poised to renew the Measure G parcel tax, according to results presented at the Dec. 10 school board meeting. Consultant Dr. Tim McLarney of True North reported that a recent survey showed strong support for continuing the tax, which provides about $12 million a year for local schools, roughly 20 percent of the district’s budget. Based on the findings, the district plans to place the Measure G renewal on the June ballot. The survey reached 342 likely voters by phone, email and text. An initial ballot test projected 84% support, well above the twothirds threshold required for passage. Of those surveyed, 51.5% said they would “definitely” vote yes, while 32.8% said they would “probably” vote yes. “I can say that in my career I struggle to think of examples, other than in Piedmont, where we have had initial ballot tests in the 80s,” McLarney said. He joined the meeting remotely, along with district consultant Larry Tramatola, who was present in person. At its next meeting on January 7, the board plans to adopt a resolution formally placing the measure on the June ballot. Board members also discussed adding language to “evergreen” the tax, allowing it to continue without a set expiration date, with an annual 3% increase to keep pace with inflation. “Could that resolution include language to keep this Measure G parcel tax at the same base rate structure, an annual increase for inflation, probably 3 percent, and language to evergreen this parcel tax?” Superintendent Jennifer Hawn asked. All five board members supported including that language. “The fact it’s an evergreen proposal is a huge relief, because our district can’t function without that. That’s wonderful,” said APT President Elise Marks. Board members, students and teachers expressed appreciation for the community’s ongoing support of local schools. Following the January 7 resolution, the district plans to begin its campaign for the June election, with Ted Kinch and Rebecca Pelle serving as campaign co-chairs.
articles.title: Parcel Tax survey says: Yes!

articles.text: During the December 10 Piedmont School Board meeting Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT) President Elise Marks brought up a recent negotiation session with the district that she deemed unsuccessful and disheartening. District negotiation sessions between labor groups, like the teachers and CSEA workers, are held in closed session. Currently, working conditions, but not salaries, are up for discussion. “We came out of this round feeling that district leadership was not willing to move meaningfully on anything,” said Marks. Marks reported that teachers filled out surveys, necessary so the school can obtain its WACS accreditation and recertification, of how well current district structures are supporting student success and student well-being. Marks said the scores were not good. At the end of her statement, with union members in mass behind her, Marks concluded that the Association of Piedmont Teacher will not threaten a strike, they will take their offers off the table, and will prepare for negotiations in the spring. “APT is choosing not to go to impasse. We will agree to mutually withdraw all proposals on both sides, and focus on a return to the bargaining table as early as possible in the spring as our entire contract is open again,” said Marks. An overarching concern was raised that teachers are not having their voices heard. “In the last few years we have experienced a profound shift: teachers are being left out of major conversations. We learn about many decisions only as they are announced to the public, not before,” said Marks. In response to the Mark’s quote immediately above, School Board President Ruchi Medhekar responded to the Post with “We respectfully disagree with this characterization. We’ve significantly expanded teacher voice in decision-making.” Medhekar and the board pointed to five examples of teacher involvement including engagement via district-level meetings, and programs initiated by the district teachers like the new 6th and 7th grade language programs and the Fishtank curriculum for elementary language arts. “We reversed course on sophomore honors English and history based directly on teacher and community feedback,” Medhekar said. President Medhekar added that the board now shares all policy changes with labor partners at least ten days before Board discussion to ensure meaningful input. In their current round of negotiations teachers were asking for hard caps to class sizes to formally prohibit enormous classes. “Our contract language is very soft on class size,” said Marks. Sometimes the text of their contract says “every effort will be made” by the district. APT wants clear and unambiguous contract language on this to prevent teachers from being saddled with up to 37 students. The district sees the progress of their negotiations in a significantly different light. “Although we did not reach formal agreement on any items, we identified common ground, including our mutual desire to reopen negotiations early in the spring and our shared commitment to ensuring balanced and manageable class sizes across all grades, which we look forward to revisiting after we return from winter break,” said Superintendent Jennifer Hawn in an email to the Post. “Teachers are with students, boots on the ground, all day long, making school happen. We see things that administrators and parents just don’t have the opportunity to see,” said Marks. What voices will be heard and at what volume remains to be seen, but both sides have work to be done to repair their relationships. Maybe the holiday spirit and a little break can help return hope.
articles.title: Teachers ask for their voices to be heard

articles.text: The instructional calendar for the 2026-27 school year proffered by Piedmont teachers was approved by the school district via the consent calendar at the December 10 school board meeting. Next year’s school schedule, which mirrors this year’s, was approved, but the board chose not to approve it for two years, as has been custom. The district did not approve the calendar for its second year because the schedule the Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT) offered did not reflect any changes the district wanted based on a parent survey. “The APT contract provides language that describes what teachers will do, including presenting calendars for two years to the Board. That contract language was met at the November Board meeting. However, the Board decided to approve only one year, which occurred at the December Board meeting,” explains Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. APT did not want to shorten the first semester to achieve a midweek start to the first week or a later first day of school. The current schedule, which will be in effect for next year, starts the school year on a Monday, and keeps first semester finals before Winter Break.
articles.title: Next year’s school instructional calendar approved

An initial ballot test projected 84% support, well above the twothirds threshold required for pasParcel Tax survey says: Yes! sage. Of those surveyed, 51.5% said they would “definitely” vote yes, while 32.8% said they would “probably” vote yes. “I can say that in my career I struggle to think of examples, other than in Piedmont, where we have had initial ballot tests in the 80s,” McLarney said. He joined the meeting remotely, along with district consultant Larry Tramatola, who was present in person. At its next meeting on January 7, the board plans to adopt a resolution formally placing the measure on the June ballot. Board members also discussed adding language to “evergreen” the tax, allowing it to continue without a set expiration date, with an annual 3% increase to keep pace with inflation. “Could that resolution include language to keep this Measure G parcel tax at the same base rate structure, an annual increase for inflation, probably 3 percent, and language to evergreen this parcel tax?” Superintendent Jennifer Hawn asked. All five board members supported including that language. “The fact it’s an evergreen proposal is a huge relief, because our district can’t function without that. That’s wonderful,” said APT President Elise Marks. Board members, students and teachers expressed appreciation for the community’s ongoing support of local schools. Following the January 7 resolution, the district plans to begin its campaign for the June election, with Ted Kinch and Rebecca Pelle serving as campaign co-chairs. E v e n t C a l e n d a r By Jay Russell During the December 10 Piedmont School Board meeting Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT) President Elise Marks brought up a recent negotiation session with the district that she deemed unsuccessful and disheartening. District negotiation sessions between labor groups, like the teachers and CSEA workers, are held in closed session. Currently, working conditions, but not salaries, are up for discussion. “We came out of this round feeling that district leadership was not willing to move meaningfully on anything,” said Marks. Marks reported that teachers filled out surveys, necessary so the school can obtain its WACS accreditation and recertification, of how well current district structures are supporting student success and student well-being. Marks said the scores were not good. At the end of her statement, with union members in mass behind her, Marks concluded that the Association of Piedmont Teacher will not threaten a strike, they will take their offers off the table, and will prepare for negotiations in the spring. “APT is choosing not to go to impasse. We will agree to mutually withdraw all proposals on both sides, and focus on a return to the bargaining table as early Teachers ask for their voices to be heard as possible in the spring as our entire contract is open again,” said Marks. An overarching concern was raised that teachers are not having their voices heard. “In the last few years we have experienced a profound shift: teachers are being left out of major conversations. We learn about many decisions only as they are announced to the public, not before,” said Marks. In response to the Mark’s quote immediately above, School Board President Ruchi Medhekar responded to the Post with “We respectfully disagree with this characterization. We’ve significantly expanded teacher voice in decision-making.” Medhekar and the board pointed to five examples of teacher involvement including engagement via district-level meetings, and programs initiated by the district teachers like the new 6th and 7th grade language programs and the Fishtank curriculum for elementary language arts. “We reversed course on sophomore honors English and history based directly on teacher and community feedback,” Medhekar said. President Medhekar added that the board now shares all policy changes with labor partners at least ten days before Board discussion to ensure meaningful input. In their current round of negotiations teachers were asking for hard caps to class sizes to formally prohibit enormous classes. “Our contract language is very soft on class size,” said Marks. Sometimes the text of their contract says “every effort will be made” by the district. APT wants clear and unambiguous contract language on this to prevent teachers from being saddled with up to 37 students. The district sees the progress of their negotiations in a significantly different light. “Although we did not reach formal agreement on any items, we identified common ground, including our mutual desire to reopen negotiations early in the spring and our shared commitment to ensuring balanced and manageable class sizes across all grades, which we look forward to revisiting after we return from winter break,” said Superintendent Jennifer Hawn in an email to the Post. “Teachers are with students, boots on the ground, all day long, making school happen. We see things that administrators and parents just don’t have the opportunity to see,” said Marks. What voices will be heard and at what volume remains to be seen, but both sides have work to be done to repair their relationships. Maybe the holiday spirit and a little break can help return hope. Next year’s school instructional calendar approved By Jay Russell The instructional calendar for the 2026-27 school year proffered by Piedmont teachers was approved by the school district via the consent calendar at the December 10 school board meeting. Next year’s school schedule, which mirrors this year’s, was approved, but the board chose not to approve it for two years, as has been custom. The district did not approve the calendar for its second year because the schedule the Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT) offered did not reflect any changes the district wanted based on a parent survey. “The APT contract provides language that describes what teachers will do, including presenting calendars for two years to the Board. That contract language was met at the November Board meeting. However, the Board decided to approve only one year, which occurred at the December Board meeting,” explains Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. APT did not want to shorten the first semester to achieve a midweek start to the first week or a later first day of school. The current schedule, which will be in effect for next year, starts the school year on a Monday, and keeps first semester finals before Winter Break. Exploration of the Ice Giants and Beyond The harsh conditions of Uranus and Neptune, combined with their distance from Earth, have made exploration challenging. To date, NASA’s Voyager 2 remains the only spacecraft to have visited both planets, flying by Uranus in 1986 and Neptune in 1989. Still, tools such as the Hubble Space Telescope and the James Webb Space Telescope continue to provide scientists with new insights into these distant worlds. Beyond the Ice Giants, our solar system contains many other icy worlds. The dwarf planet Pluto, several of Saturn’s moons, and Jupiter’s moon Europa are just a few examples. Unlike Uranus and Neptune, scientists believe some of these icy bodies may contain the building blocks necessary for life, making them promising targets in the search beyond Earth. Experience Icy Worlds in Oakland This year, Chabot Space & Science Center’s annual WinterFest explores what it might be like to experience an icy world firsthand. On Saturday, Dec. 20, and Sunday, Dec. 21, visitors can immerse themselves in a winter atmosphere while learning about some of the coldest and most fascinating worlds in our solar system. Guests can begin their journey at the Chabot Space Station, exploring Jupiter’s glacial moon, “skating” across the icy plains of Pluto during the Sock Skate experience, discovering an icy exoplanet orbiting a distant star, and attending the premiere of the new planetarium show, SPACETIME. articles.text: Part 6.3: Surviving the 2019 ascent of Everest (29,028’) in spite of “traffic jam” Previously printed in the May 13, 2020 edition of the Piedmont Post. In last week’s saga of Bill Baringer’s attempt to reach the summit of Mt. Everest, the world’s tallest peak at 29,028 feet, a cyclone over India created fierce weather on the mountain that delayed plans for the climbing team. “No one actually ‘conquers’ Everest; one can only possibly The strong, cold winds along summit ridge proved to be very challenging for many of the climbers. Bill Baringer climbed up fixed ropes with an ascender, on the very steep slope between camps Two and Three. After cresting the top of the Geneva Spur ridge, Bill Baringer traverses the long granite slate before Camp Four at 26,300.’ The narrow paths on Summit Ridge have fixed rope lines installed by Sherpas every May. Each line is held by ice screws, at times holding thousands of pounds of climbers. survive Everest,” explained Baringer. On May 5, 2019 they received the green light for their third rotation up the mountain. They stayed at Camp One for a night, Camp Two for a night, then used their ascenders to clip onto the fixed lines for the ascent up the steep ice wall to “touch” Camp Three and descend the same day. When coming back down from Camp Three a cluster of ice and rock chunks cascaded down from above. A rock projectile hit the leg of climbing guide Pemba and tore through his pants and socks, gashing a hole in his leg. Baringer helped Pemba bandage his leg, offered his ski poles and helped him down to camp. Pemba was flown down the mountain by helicopter to get stitched back up. Three days later Pemba flew back up to help the team summit Everest. Another high wind weather delay turned Everest Base Camp into a waiting room. Many climbing teams were held up there, so nearly everyone eyed May 21 as the window of opportunity to reach the top. “No one knew if there was going to be another window after that, and the season closed on May 30. We weren’t going to wait for the 28,” said Baringer. Finally, they got the call to start the final rotation on May 17. The now familiar, 2:00 a.m. alarm clock commenced the move to Camp One at 19,500’ for a one-night stay. Here the Sherpas served Baringer spicy ramen soup, also known as “Sherpa Down Jacket.” The trip up to Camp Two at 21,500’ took three hours on May 18. The next day took them up to Camp Three at 23,500’, their first overnight at this height. Oxygen bottles were brought out to be used for the rest of the trip. May 20 marked new territory for Baringer on the way up to Camp Four at 26,300’. The route featured the infamous “Yellow Band” section of rock to be managed with crampons designed for snow. Baringer recalled the uneasy memory of balancing on the tips of his crampons. “Front-pointing on granite just seemed wrong,” he recalled. After Yellow Band, Baringer faced the first bad traffic jam on a steep rocky segment called “Geneva Spur.” In trying to get past a boulder on the slope Baringer pulled on two separate fixed lines. When one broke, he swayed and fell, but his ascender on the other rope held fast – another close call. After Geneva Spur, the group sighted the rocky Camp Four, the area known as the “Death Zone” where the ambient oxygen is 30 percent of the value at sea level. Baringer describes the camp five miles above sea level. “It was a disaster. All the lower camps were pristine, super clean. I’m sure they did some cleaning there, but you were still left with canisters, tent poles, and shrapnel everywhere. It looked like a bomb went off,” he said. The guides planned for a few hours of rest before attempting the summit that night. But the winds were howling, so an extra day was spent at Camp Four. The next day Baringer’s guides decided they were not going to start at the usual 10 p.m., but at 5:30 p.m. to climb all night and summit before sunrise on Wednesday, May 22. They started early because of the anticipated crowds. Photos that became famous throughout the world showed a long, congested queue to summit. “It wasn’t because there were so many mountaineers on the mountain itself. It’s that they were all attempting their summit bids on the same day,” explained Baringer. Climbing Everest in the dark turned out to be very prudent. The historic traffic jam on Everest in 2019 resulted in the deaths of a number of climbers who were stuck in place. A total of 11 people died on that mountain in May 2019. Many died of hypothermia while stuck in line, unable to go up or down. For the final push the climbers turned up their oxygen flow four liters per minute – the maximum flow. Lack of oxygen at this elevation made everyone foggy. “I don’t know how many bottles I went through. It could have

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, free compostable bags are available at City Hall to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. Compostable bags are also available from Republic Services (1-800-320-8077) for a fee. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ basketball team got its season started in a big way, winning its own Paris Twins Classic for the first time since the 2022. The Highlanders opened with a 91-35 win over Oakland High on Thursday, December 11, beat Vanden in the semifinals 85-43 the following day, and won 64-50 over Cardinal Newman on Saturday, December 13. Their win over the Cardinals was a match of two top-10 Bay Area teams. Before the game, Cal-Hi Sports had Cardinal Newman ranked No. 4 in its top-10 list and Piedmont as No. 5. Just three games into the season, beating Cardinal Newman was important to help build Piedmont’s candidacy for a North Coast Section Open Division bid at the end of the regular season. The game was a rematch of last year’s Open Division first-round, which Cardinal Newman won 51-45. Piedmont trailed through the first half before finally taking the lead in the third quarter with 4:22 remaining. “We could both be in the NCS Open (Division), so it was a big win,” said coach Bryan Gardere. “In the second half we really tightend up and figured it out. We ended up getting the 50-50 balls and it changed the tone of the game,”. Staff Photos Freshman Alexa Ba made her debut on the team. Andrea Martin led with 28 points in Piedmont’s tournament victory over Cardinal Newman. It was a big tournament for Andrea Martin, who was The Post’s honorable mention for 2025 Athlete of the Year. She recorded 28 points against the Cardinals. “When we played them in last year’s playoffs, it was their home game and we ended up taking the loss. Today, we really showed them who we are at our home base,” Martin said. The three-day tournament was also the debut of freshman Alexa Ba, who looks to be a key player. Her addition is important after the team lost Briana Webb from last year’s team. “The past two years, I’ve just been watching the team and practicing with them, so it’s nice to contribute. Last year, I was unhappy that we lost to Cardinal Newman, and now I get to help get the win,” Ba said. 64-50 over Cardinal Newman Piedmont trailed 17-10 through the first quarter and clipped away at Cardinal Newman’s lead in the second quarter to make it threepoint deficit at 33-30. In the third quarter, Taylor White turned a rebound into an assist to Savannah Dennig to give PHS a 37-35 lead with 5:10 left. The Cardinals hit a 3-pointer to go up 38-37, but it led to Dennig recording a steal, turning it up court. Jenelle Solis then whipped in a pass to Martin, scoring at the basket to give PHS a 39-38 lead with 4:22 left. Solis hit a 3-pointer in the final seconds to give her team a 46-42 lead to start the fourth. In the fourth, PHS went on a 10-3 run to establish a 58-47 lead and scored six of the last eight points to win 64-50. Final stats: Martin led with 28 points, White and Solis had 10 points, White had nine, and Ba had seven. 85-43 win over Vanden Piedmont led 21-13 by the end of the first quarter and extended the gap to 39-23 by halftime. PHS outscored Vanden 22-12 in the third quarter to build a 61-35 lead, adding 24 more points in the final going while only allowing nine. PHS finished with five players in double-figures. Final stats: Martin led with 25 points, Ba had 17 points, both Solis and Dennig had 16 points, White had 10 points, while Saniyah Johnson had one. 92-35 victory vs. Oakland High Piedmont took a commanding 25-6 lead in the first quarter and led 45-15 by halftime. The Highlanders scored 23 points in both the third and fourth quarters, conceding just eight and 10 points respectively. Once again, PHS had five players in double-figures. Final stats: Martin had 21 points, 11 rebounds, and four assists. Ba had 19 points, eight rebounds, and one assist. Dennig had 19 points, eight rebounds, and to assists. Solis had 14 points, four rebounds, and eight assists. White had 11 points, six rebounds, and five assists. Johnson had four points and six rebounds. Jaden Jones had three points and one rebound. NEXT UP Piedmont (3-0 overall) hosts Sacred Heart College Prep on Friday, December 19 at 6:30 p.m. They also play Archbishop Riordan the following day on Saturday, December 20 in San Francisco at the Simply Basketball Showcase at 12:00 p.m. Jenelle Solis scored 10 points against Cardinal Newman, 16 on Vanden, and 14 against Oakland.

articles.text: Highlanders go 1-2 at Chris Huber Classic Piedmont High’s boys’ basketball team came away with one win at the Chris Huber Classic at Acalanes in Lafayette last weekend. The Highlanders opened the tournament with an 80-77 overtime loss to the host team, then rebounded with a 54-43 win over Northgate. They lost by four points, 51-47, to Campolindo in their third game. Against Acalanes, Piedmont led for most of the game but allowed a 12-point advantage slip away late. “We blew a 12-point lead with 3:30 to go after leading for 31 minutes,” said coach Ben Spencer. “Costly turnovers down the stretch killed us. We played good defense against Northgate, but Campolindo was another heartbreaker.” The recent games bring Piedmont’s record to 5-3. The Highlanders will have a rematch with Campo this Saturday, December 20, and will close out the year with a home game against Emerald High of Dublin. 51-47 loss to Campolindo Campolindo led 17-13 after the first quarter, but Piedmont closed the gap to trail just 28-27 at halftime. Campo outscored the Highlanders 16-13 in the third quarter to extend the margin to 44-40. Piedmont struggled offensively in the fourth, scoring seven points in the loss. Final stats: P.J. Brayer led Piedmont with 19 points, Dillon Casey scored 14, Beach Lorin added nine, Lucian Fang-Ring had three, and Yoseph Baskin finished with two. 54-43 victory over Northgate The teams were tied 10-10 after the first quarter, before Piedmont outscored Northgate 18-10 in the second to take a 28-20 halftime lead. The Highlanders’ defense held the Broncos to just five points in the third quarter, stretching the lead to 42-25. Piedmont scored 12 points in the fourth while allowing 18. Lorin sparked the offense in the second quarter with 11 points, while Fang-Ring knocked down Staff Photos Beach Lorin had a tournament high 22 points in Piedmont’s win against Northgate. P.J. Brayer led with 19 points in PHS’ loss to Campolindo. Lucian Fang-Ring had 19 points in Piedmont’s overtime loss to Acalanes. two 3-pointers. Lorin continued the push in the third quarter with seven more points. Final stats: Lorin led all scorers with 22 points. Brayer had 13 points, Fang-Ring scored nine, and Casey and Cash Panico each added five. 80-77 loss to Acalanes Piedmont jumped out to a 21-14 lead after the first quarter and carried a 41-35 advantage into halftime. Acalanes cut into the lead in the third quarter, trailing 57-52, before outscoring Piedmont 17-12 in the fourth to force overtime at 69-69. The Dons edged the Highlanders 11-8 in the extra period. Piedmont had a balanced first quarter with four players scoring, including six points each from Casey, Fang-Ring and Lorin. Fang-Ring connected on two 3-pointers in the opening frame. The offense continued in the second quarter, with Casey and Fang-Ring each scoring six more points, as Fang-Ring hit two additional 3-pointers. Final stats: Fang-Ring led Piedmont with 19 points, Lorin had 18, Casey scored 16, Brayer added 14, Ollie Dougan had seven, and Akash Bornstein finished with three. Next up Piedmont (5-3 overall) visits Campolindo in Moraga on Saturday, December 20, and hosts Emerald High on Monday, December 22. Both games are scheduled for 4 p.m.

articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team earned its first win of the season with an emphatic 8-0 victory over San Lorenzo on Friday, December 12 at Witter Field. Two days earlier they lost 2-0 to Arroyo in San Lorenzo without several key attackers, Roman Ahearn, Evan Yamanaka and Robert Piniella. They struggled to break through the Dons’ pressure. The dynamic shifted against San Lorenzo, however, as the Highlanders played on the front foot, forcing turnovers high up the field and repeatedly won possession in the “We tried something a little bit different against Arroyo and it will be a building block for us,” said first-year coach Ben Russell. “We’re trying to create different ways to create opportunities, whether it’s off the press or out of Piedmont wasted no time getting on the scoreboard, with Henry Devan scoring in the first minute. The goal began with Eli Dao-Hoang making a tackle in San Lorenzo’s defensive half. Devan took control, dribbled to the top of the box and rocketed a right-footed shot into the net. The Highlanders doubled the Roman Ahearn scored a brace against San Lorenzo. Matias Shahid helped create two goals against San Lorenzo. Staff Photos Henry Devan scored two goals in Piedmont’s 8-0 shutout of San Lorenzo. lead four minutes later. Defender Matias Shahid sent a long, low pass to Dao-Hoang, who slipped a through ball to Roman Ahearn running past the back line. Ahearn took one touch around the keeper and finished into the open net. Piedmont added its third goal early in the second half. In the 45th minute, Shahid intercepted an errant pass near midfield, pushed forward through contact along the left side and sent a long cross to Travers Kemp at the far post. Kemp finished with a firsttouch volley. Ahearn scored again in the 47th minute after Russell Pan volleyed a long pass between two defenders. Ahearn carried the ball from midfield into the box and sent a low shot past the keeper. Devan added his second goal in the 59th, dribbling around two defenders before unleashing a long shot from outside the box. Piedmont made it 6-0 in the 62nd when a long cross from the right corner by Ben Gerber found Van-Kleeck unmarked near the six-yard box for a header. Gerber scored in the 66th, sending a shot from the right side of the box past the keeper. articles.text: Staff Photos Miranda Liu scored the game-winning goal against Marin Academy Piedmont High’s girls’ soccer team captured its first win of the season with a 1-nil victory over Marin Academy in San Rafael on Saturday, December 13. The result brings PHS’ record to 1-1-2 (W-T-L) through its first four games. Piedmont’s goal came from Miranda Liu in the 54th minute when she scored on a penalty kick. The foul came after a handball by a Marin Academy player in the penalty area. Piedmont goalkeeper Rachel Young also had one of the most critical plays in the game in the first half to preserve a 0-0 tie through the first 40 minutes. The Highlanders were penalized for a back pass in their own box in the 22nd minute, leading to an awkward in-direct free kick near the penalty spot. Marin Academy played a low shot through the defense, but Young quickly blocked the shot with her foot. Piedmont has two matches left before the New Year. They are set to host Oakland Tech today, December 17, and will play neighboring Head-Royce in Oakland on Friday, December 19. Match Recap Piedmont had the game’s first shot attempt in the fifth minute, when Ayla Blanford sent a shot wide of the net. Liu also had a shot trail wide in the 10th minute. PHS’ next chance came in the 20th minute, when a long pass from a corner fell to Blanford, who tried to chip a shot to the far post. However, her shot was cleared away. Marin Academy had a critical scoring chance in the 22nd when Piedmont was penalized for a back pass in its own box. That’s what led to Young making her instinctive kick save to keep the game deadlocked at 0-0. The second half started with back-and-forth action without either side having overtly dangerous chances. Marin Academy had a shot blocked by Darcy McKee in the 41st minute, then had a shot trail wide two minutes later. In the 53rd minute, Piedmont was awarded its penalty kick when a Marin Academy defender failed to clear a ball, kicking it high into the sky instead of out her own box. Another Wildcat’s defender missed on a header clearance, leading to the ball back spinning off the turf and into her hand. Liu stepped to the spot, sending her shot to the left of the keeper to give PHS a 1-nil lead. That was the only shot Piedmont needed from then on. Marin Academy had a slow shot handled by Young in the 55th, then had a long shot from about 30 yards easily saved by Young. Young came up with another critical save in the 68th minute at the end of a corner. The Wildcats sent a high looping cross, leading to a header attempt that skipped off the ground and toward net. Young was ranging to her right, and reached back to her left to get a hand on the shot, pouncing on it to regain possession. Both teams traded possession for the remaining 12 minutes of regulation. NEXT UP Piedmont (1-1-2) hosts Oakland Tech tonight, December 17, at 7:00 p.m. They also visit Head-Royce in Oakland on Friday, afternoon, December 19 at 3:15 p.m. Ayla Blanford handles the ball as new head coach Matt SpencerHarty watches. Freshman Olivia Kan-Miller looks to make a play.

articles.text: With basketball being the only overlapping winter sport between high school and college, we take a look at former basketball stars still active in college: Natalia Martinez at San Diego State, A.J. Harris at Emory University, and Eva Levingston at Robert Morris University. NATALIA MARTINEZ San Diego State Natalia Martinez, PHS Class of 2024, in currently in her sophomore season at San Diego State and is close to being the Aztecs’ leading scorer. She was the Post’s only back-to-back Athlete of the Year award winner (2023 and 2024). This year, San Diego State is 6-3 through a 29-game regular season schedule. Martinez is second on the team in scoring and minutes with 113 points and 239 minutes. She’s currently hitting 34 percent of her 3-pointers. She scored a season-high of 24 points on November 24 against Penn State, and this week was named the Mountain West Conference Player of the Week. Martinez was impressive as a freshman last season, making the MWC All-Freshman team. They won the conference title as the No. 4 seed and earned the No. 14 ranking in the NCAA’s March Madness tournament. The Aztecs went up against No. 2 LSU, which made it to the Elite Eight. Martinez was in the starting five, playing 27 minutes for seven points, and had one rebound and one assist. She set a MWC record in an 85-66 win over Utah State, where she became the first player to ever sink six 3-pointers in a conference game. In her record-setting performance, Martinez finished with 22 points, converting 7/8 from the field and 6/7 for 3-pointers. She hit one of her 3-pointers from around seven feet behind the 3-point line. Photo courtesy of San Diego State Natalia Martinez, PHS Class of 2024, is a sophomore at San Diego State and is challenging to lead the team in scoring. Harris appeared in all 29 games for 825 minutes, scoring 336 points by shooting 45 percent from the field and 33 percent from 3-pointers, to go along with 149 rebounds, 43 assists, 42 steals and seven blocks. Harris notched a career-high of 28 points in a 77-71 win over Union College. He finished his illustrious Piedmont High career as the school’s All-Time leading scorer with 1,570 points after playing in just two full varsity seasons and an abbreviated 2021 season due to COVID-19. We named Harris the Posts’ 2023 honorable mention for Athlete of the Year. team in Pittsburgh after playing the first two years of her collegiate career at Cal State Fullerton. So far this season, Robert Morris is 8-2 with Levingston as a starter. In seven appearances, Levingston is averaging 27.7 minutes per game, scoring 59 points. She’s second on the team with 50 rebounds and third on steals with eight. Levingston departed from Fullerton after becoming the Titans’ most active player as a sophomore. She finished last year with 928 minutes and 231 rebounds to lead the team, while she second in scoring with 233 points. As a freshman, she appeared in 29 games and recorded 139 points, 107 rebounds, five blocks, and 29 steals. Levingston was a key player in Piedmont High’s 2023 NCS and WACC titles. She came up big, once again in the 68th minute by making a one-handed save on a header attempt by the Wildcats to preserve the shutout win. Henry Devan gets an honorable mention for scoring two goals in Piedmont’s 8-nil rout of San Lorenzo. Both goals were a product of some individual brilliance. He scored in the first minute of action, making a dribble to dodge a tackle then sending in a shot to the far post from the top the box. His second goal came in the 59th, taking possession around the midfield line before dribbling around two defenders before taking an inch-perfect shot for a goal. articles.text: To celebrate the season, the Post has reprinted Clement Clarke Moore’s classic poem so that parents may read it to their children in advance of Christmas Eve.
articles.title: The Night Before Christmas

articles.text: With a sleigh full of toys – and Saint Nicholas, too. And then in a twinkling, I heard on the roof ’Twas the night before Christmas, when all through the house Not a creature was stirring, not even a mouse. The stockings were hung by the chimney with care, In hopes that Saint Nicholas soon would be there. The children were nestled all snug in their beds, While visions of sugar plums danced in their heads; And mama in her kerchief, and I in my cap Had just settled our brains for a long winter’s nap. When out on the lawn there arose such a clatter I sprang from my bed to see what was the matter. Away to the window I flew like a flash, Tore open the shutter and threw open the sash. The moon on the breast of the new-fallen snow Gave a luster of midday to objects below; When to my wondering eyes should appear But a miniature sleigh and eight tiny reindeer. With a little old driver, so lively and quick, I knew in a moment it must be Saint Nick! More rapid than eagles his coursers they came, And he whistled and shouted and called them by name: “Now, Dasher! Now, Dancer! Now, Prancer! Now, Vixen! On, Comet! On, Cupid! On Donder and Blitzen! To the top of the porch, to the top of the wall, Now dash away, dash away, dash away all.” As dry leaves that before the wild hurricane fly, When they meet with an obstacle mount to the sky. articles.text: The true history of Silent Night Can a crisis evoke from us a one-shot pinnacle of creativity? In the case of two Austrian villagers in 1818, the answer was an emphatic yes. It was in the small church of Oberndorf, Austria, near Salzburg, readying for the gala Christmas Eve service. The all-important pipe organ had broken with no chance for repairs being done in time. To compensate for the crisis, the young priest Josef Mohr pulled out his poetic text now known as the sacred lullaby “Silent Night,” calming words for the Christ child in the manger, “Sleep in heavenly peace.” He passed these along to the village school teacher Franz Gruber, who was suddenly the superfluous church organist. The very same day Gruber (1787-1863) produced the music to fit the voices – equally straightforward, but uniquely memorable. He scored it for a pair of soloists, chorus and the best substitute instrument available, the guitar. Gruber called his effort “a simple composition.” The parishioners crowded in that night were treated to the world premiere of a work with singers who had barely had time to rehearse. Later, the work was taken up by the Strasser Sisters singing group specializing in Tyrolean music, as well as the Rainers. It became a hit all over the touring itineraries, eventually attributed to the eminent composer Michael Haydn (brother of Franz Josef Haydn). Who, after all, would believe that two village nobodies could create great music? After 15 years, it was finally published, and another six years later was already being heard in New York City. For decades, uncertainty reigned about the carol’s creators. It took a courtroom trial 26 years after the premiere to establish the truth, when Gruber’s son brought in a copy of the original manuscript to prove the true authorship before a governmental investigation committee. Case closed. Any thoughts that Gruber-Mohr could become the Austrian Rodgers and Hammerstein, or Lerner-Loewe, would be sheer fantasy. After 1818, they went their separate ways, given the usual moves and transfers, and never produced other significant works. It was sheer coincidence that the two were together at all; Mohr (1792-1848) had been sent to Oberndorf from his earlier posting because his delicate health could not cope with a harsh climate. Shortly before the Millennium, the sole manuscript regarding the carol’s origins was discovered, written in Mohr’s handwriting, dating back to 1820 or thereabouts. He attested that he had written the texts in 1816, with the music composed by Gruber in 1818. The lesson here is profound and invaluable: The Mozarts and Leonardos of our world could be brilliant every single day. As for the rest of us, however mediocre in the greater scale of things, we can still rise up once in full flower, like a century plant. We can create something uniquely masterful, provided we possess the will, the faith and the motivation. From adversity comes the flowering of inspiration. And a catalytic pairing doesn’t hurt, either. Silent Night, Holy Night Mohr; English trans. by John Freeman Young. Silent, night, holy night, All is calm, all is bright. ’Round yon virgin, mother and child Holy infant so tender and mild, Sleep in heavenly peace, Sleep in heavenly peace. Silent night, holy night, Shepherds quake at the sight. Glories stream from heaven afar, Heavenly hosts sing Alleluia; Christ the Savior is born, Christ the Savior is born. Silent night, holy night, Son of God, love’s pure light. Radiant beams from Thy holy face, With the dawn of redeeming grace, Jesus, Lord at Thy birth; Jesus, Lord at Thy birth.

articles.text: The song “The 12 days of Christmas” has its origins as a teaching tool to instruct young people in the meaning and content of the Christian faith. From 1558 to 1829 Roman Catholics in England were not able to practice their faith openly, so they had to find other ways to pass on their beliefs. The song is an allegory. Each of the items in the song represents something of religious significance. The hidden meaning of each gift was designed to help young Christians learn their faith. ✝ In the song “On the first day of Christmas my true love gave to me” true love represents God, and “me” is the Christian. ✝ The “partridge in a pear tree” represents Jesus Christ who died on a tree. ✝ Two turtle doves represent the Old and New Testaments. ✝ Three French hens are faith, hope and love – the three gifts of the Spirit. ✝ Four calling birds are the four Gospels. ✝ Five golden rings are the first five books of the Bible, also known as the Books of Moses. ✝ Six geese a-laying are the six days of creation. ✝ Seven swans a-swimming are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. ✝ Eight maids a milking are the eight beatitudes. ✝ Nine ladies dancing are the nine fruits of the Holy Spirit. ✝ Ten lords a-leaping are the Ten Commandments. ✝ Eleven pipers piping are the eleven faithful disciples. ✝ Twelve drummers drumming are the twelve points of the Apostles’ Creed. On the first day of Christmas my true love gave to me: A partridge in a pear tree. On the second day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Two turtle doves, and a partridge in a pear tree. On the third day of Christmas my true love gave to me Three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. articles.text: Played and narrated by all-star jazz trio On December 9, 1965, nearly half of U.S. TV sets were tuned to one unlikely show: “A Charlie Brown Christmas.” With its jazz score by Vince Guaraldi and using amateur voice actors, it was predicted to be a flop. Instead, it has become a beloved annual tradition. The show, based on Charles Schulz’s Peanuts cartoon series, was premiered that day by a major TV network, and subsequently became available everywhere to watch around the holidays. Piedmont Center for the Arts this year celebrates the program’s 60th anniversary with a live concert version of “A Charlie Brown Christmas,” with Vince Guaraldi’s classic score played by the jazz trio of Larry Dunlap, piano, Akira Tana, drums, and Ken Miller on bass – plus live narration by the performers. Dress your family in Peanuts-inspired costumes and bring them to a show that will spark nostalgia for you, delight your children and bring holiday spirit to everyone. Two performances back to back on the Sunday before Christmas, December 21. Performance times are 12 noon and 1:30 p.m. Advance tickets are highly recommended as space is limited. Buy tickets at https://www.brownpapertickets.com/e/6756087.
articles.title: Live Charlie Brown Christmas comes to Piedmont

articles.text: Center Repertory Company, in partnership with AXIS Dance Company, premiered a new adaptation of Charles Dickens’ holiday classic “A Christmas Carol,” bringing together an award-winning creative team for what the company calls its most ambitious seasonal production to date. The all-new staging reimagines the familiar story through the eyes of young Tim Cratchit, who makes a wish on a candle that summons a series of ghostly visitors to the bedside of the famously miserly Ebenezer Scrooge. The adaptation is written by playwright Harrison David Rivers, whose retelling emphasizes compassion and responsibility toward society’s most vulnerable. While remaining faithful to Dickens’ original narrative, the production frames the story as a contemporary meditation on empathy, generosity and the human cost of valuing profit over people. The production is described as Center REP’s grandest interpretation of the Dickens classic and marks a premiere for the company. Center REP is the resident professional theater company of the Lesher Center for the Arts in Walnut Creek. Led by Artistic Director Matt M. Morrow and Managing Director Carolyn Jackson, the company was founded in 1968 and is among the oldest professional theaters in the Bay Area. “Our West Coast premiere of this new holiday tradition is the cornerstone of the Lesher Center’s 35th Anniversary. This milestone for our beloved home is all about shaping the future, and Harrison’s adaptation is nothing if not forward facing,” said Center Rep Artistic Director Matt Murrow. Director Jared Mezzocchi, who previously introduced Center REP’s “FROGGY,” leads the production. Mezzocchi employs an immersive digital design to bring Victorian London and its supernatural netherworld vividly to life, blending traditional storytelling with modern theatrical technology. A Christmas Carol is showing onstage this Thursday through Sunday. Runtime is approximately two hours including one 15-minute intermission. Lesher Center for the Arts is located at 1601 Civic Drive in Walnut Creek, California, in downtown Walnut Creek’s arts district. Visit https://www.centerrep.org/whats-on/25-26-season/a-christmascarol to purchase tickets or call the box office at (925) 943-7469. Photo by Kevin Berne Brayden K. Sinkay as “Tim”, and Danny J. Gomez as “Man” in Center REP’s A Christmas Carol.
articles.title: Center Rep presents reimagined Christmas Carol at Lesher Center for the Arts

articles.text: Berkeley City Ballet, the East Bay’s premiere training school for classical ballet, presents its 51st annual Nutcracker at the Alan Harvey Theater on the Piedmont High School campus on Saturday, December 20. Following a sold out run of its debut at the Alan Harvey Theater at Piedmont High School last year, the ballet company is returning to Piedmont to showcase the holiday classic, featuring dancers from the company’s pre-professional program as well as professional guests artists from ballet companies including Boulder Ballet and Ballet Memphis. Berkeley City Ballet, founded in 1974, presents one of the East Bay’s few traditional, full-length productions of the Nutcracker, complete with classic characters Clara and the Nutcracker Prince, with traditional settings like the enchanting Land of the Sweets. Two performances are held at 1:00 p.m. and 5:00 p.m. General admission tickets are $35. Purchase tickets at https://berkeleycityballet.org/nutcracker/.

articles.text: The San Francisco Ballet presents a special matinee performance of Nutcracker geared toward neurodivergent audience members on Sunday, December 28. The company introduced its first-ever sensory friendly performance of Nutcracker on December 21, 2022. The event is presented in collaboration with Autism Society San Francisco Bay Area. Special accommodations have been made to the Nutcracker for the performance that are friendly to those who experience sensory processing disorders, autism, post traumatic stress disorder, and all neurodiverse audiences. It takes place in a relaxed and “shushfree” setting and is appropriate for all ages, and designated quiet areas will be available for guests. “As a musician, and parent of an autistic son, I’m especially sensitive to how much music and dance can touch the hearts of people with autism and special needs,” Stephen Prutsman, President of Autism Society San Francisco Bay Area, said in 2022. “The holiday season can be stressful and isolating for autism and special needs families, so for a world-class company like San Francisco Ballet to open its doors and welcome our community is a landmark for the entire ballet world, and a tremendous gift for us.” This family-friendly performance also serves as an opportunity for first-time balletgoers and young children to experience ballet in a more informal setting. This special version of Nutcracker is open to all audience members; but because it is adapted specifically to accommodate individuals with sensory sensitivities, guests are encouraged to familiarize themselves with the adjustments of the Sensory Friendly Performance. The performance begins at 11 a.m. Visit www.sfballet.org to purchase tickets and to learn more about sensory friendly performances. The ballet company partners with the Autism Society San Francisco Bay Area to deliver a sensory-friendly performance of Nutcracker appropriate for all ages.

articles.text: The Oakland Museum of California is hosting an afternoon of live performances and celebrating the Persian holiday of Yalda this Sunday, December 21. The event coincides with the Winter Solstice and features performances by internationally-acclaimed Iranian Bay Areabased singers Mahsa Vahdat and Marjan Vahdat, accompanied by musician and writer Atabak Elyasi. Yalda, also known as Shab-e Yalda, is an ancient Persian holiday marking the winter solstice, the longest night of the year. Observed on the evening of December 21, the celebration has roots stretching back more than 2,000 years to pre-Islamic Iran, where it symbolized the triumph of light over darkness and the promise of longer days ahead. Families and friends traditionally gather after sunset and remain together until midnight or later, sharing food, poetry and conversation. Seasonal fruits such as pomegranates and watermelon are staples of the night, their red color representing life and renewal. Reading from the works of the 14th-century poet Hafez is a common custom, with verses interpreted as reflections on the year ahead. Yalda is celebrated by Iranians of all backgrounds, as well as Persian-speaking communities in countries including Afghanistan and Tajikistan, and among the Iranian diaspora worldwide. The event begins at 1 p.m. Visit https://museumca.org/event/spotlight-sundays-a-yalda-night-ofsong-and-poetry/ for more information and to purchase tickets. Seasonal, red-colored fruits such as pomegranates and watermelon are staples of the holiday. pages.text: 20 Wednesday, December 17, 2025 The Musical Gourmet Setting the record straight By Joseph Gold Last week’s article on the tall tales told by Freddie Potter (real name: Fritz Kreisler) opened a large can of worms. Crazy tales have been told generation after generation. This is especially true in the world of classical music. It’s now time to set the record straight. Let’s start with the great Czechoslovakian violinist Jan Kubelik. He was probably the biggest classical music star at the beginning of the 20th century. His first tour of the United States earned him a ton of money. He was a very disciplined artist and spent many hours each day practicing. In 1935–1936 the Kubelik family lived in Los Gatos. He was invited to the Bohemian Grove in the summer of 1935. I met a man who was a waiter during the encampment of 1935. He told me that he listened to Kubelik practice scales and arpeggios every day for about one hour. This story was corroborated by the noted San Francisco Symphony bass player, Phil Karp. He knew the entire Kubelik The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet family intimately. Kubelik’s son Raphael, who became an internationally noted conductor, told me that this information was absolutely correct. But that doesn’t make good press, does it? The accepted story is that Kubelik practiced so many hours a day that his fingers bled. What rubbish. But it makes a good news story. I forgot to tell you that he was so famous that he was dubbed the “reincarnation of Paganini.” Speaking of Paganini, he exploited every form of publicity. There was a story that he was thrown into jail because he murdered his wife. He was in jail for one or two days and was arrested by mistake. You need to know is that it was impossible for Paganini to have murdered his wife; he was never married. Many historians have repeated that Paganini was at least 6 feet tall. The truth is that he was no taller than 5’5”. Proof is offered in the photograph which shows the death cast hand of Paganini in comparison with the hand of a virtuoso violinist who is 5’4” tall. Much of the “fantastic” publicity of the past was pure baloney and it remains baloney today. It’s always a good idea to ask yourself if something is possible. Bloody fingers from practicing the violin? No way! In contrast, many stories which seem incredible are actually true. One of these stories concerns the famous opera tenor Enrico Caruso during a 1915 performance with the noted opera bass singer Andres de Segurola. The story goes that Segurola lost his voice during a performance of La Boheme. articles.title: Pawsitive Touch: Essential Handling Exercises for Your New Puppy

pages.text: Wednesday, December 17, 2025 21 Features Pawsitive Touch: Essential Handling Exercises for Your New Puppy By Sierra Berrick Bringing home a new puppy can be overwhelming, and prioritizing trust and respect is key. Teaching your puppy to accept handling and restraint is crucial for their safety and is even more important than obedience or socialization. It is essential to teach your puppy to respect your right to examine them and restrain them, as this could save their life in an emergency. The following handling exercises will help strengthen your bond and increase your puppy’s comfort with handling and restraint. Cradling: Hold your puppy like a baby, cupping one hand around their chest and under their chin so they do not have access to your hand with their mouth. Give the command “settle” and examine them closely, using your other hand to spread out their toes, check inside their ears or mouth, and rub their belly. If they struggle or vocalize, hug them firmly and give a verbal negative marker (“uh uh”) before repeating the “settle” command. Be sure to release puppies only when they are calm. Side Exam and Flipping Over: Lay your puppy on their side and place your arm along their body to keep their head and shoulders down. Continue the body examination, using your A collie puppy modeling the cradling exercise during a puppy class forearm to keep them in place if needed. When calm, grab the puppy’s front legs in one hand and rear legs in the other, then flip them over to their other side gently but swiftly. Repeat the exam. Stand, Sit, Down: Take one hand under their chin and one hand under their belly to place them in a standing position. Then, scoop under their rear legs to sit them down (don’t push down on their hips!), and finally, take their front legs and place them in a down position. Troubleshooting: If your puppy bites, firmly wrap your hand around their muzzle and say “no bite!” Repeat if necessary as they may think this a game at first. Also, be prepared for the occasional temper tantrum when your puppy is still getting used to extensive handling. They may vocalize excessively or attempt to squirm. Respond by giving a verbal negative marker and reinforce the “settle“ command by holding your puppy more firmly until they relax. It is essential to only release puppies from handling when they are calm. These exercises (originally from Mike Wombacher’s Puppy One course), will help build a strong bond and prepare your puppy for life’s challenges. By prioritizing these trust and respect through handling, you will not only strengthen your bond but also help your puppy develop essential life skills. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland, California. She helped to launch the service dog and facility dog training organization Alpha Dog Assist in Mill Valley in 2021 and currently offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, December 17, 2025 Walking on Wednesday Walking on Wednesday visits Piedmont’s new police dispatch center By Dick Cartner The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group had a oncein-a-lifetime opportunity last week when Piedmont Police Chief Frederick Shavies invited them to tour the city’s new police dispatch center. Once the center becomes operational, it will be closed to the public, making the visit a rare chance to see a critical piece of the city’s public safety infrastructure up close. More than 60 walkers, along with at least five well-behaved K-9 companions, gathered at the Exedra for the walk. Chief Shavies joined them for the short trip to the Piedmont Police Department, located on the lower level of the Veterans Memorial Building. Also on hand were Director of Public Works Daniel Gonzales, Police Commander Brandy Marvin-Morris, and administrative assistant to the chief April Fitzgerald. Because of the group’s size, it was not possible to pass through the police department entrance to view the new soundproof interview room. Instead, everyone made their way around the side of the building and into the expanded dispatch center itself. The room was nearly at capacity, and the group noted with some relief that Fire Chief Dave Brannigan was unable to attend due to another commitment. Inside, Chief Shavies and Gonzales pointed out key features of the new facility, beginning with the bulletproof window overlooking the police department lobby. They explained that the project relocates and modernizes dispatch operations within the existing police department footprint. The former dispatch room was cramped and outdated, placing significant strain on dispatchers who routinely work 12-hour shifts. The upgrade also ensured that Piedmont’s 911 services remain local. Prior to the project, the city had considered outsourcing dispatch services to Oakland or Berkeley. The new center allows Piedmont to retain local control while significantly improving working conditions and service capabilities. Renovating the dispatch center was a high priority of retired Police Chief Jeremy Bowers and was identified by the City Council as the best use of American Rescue Plan Act funding in October 2021. Design work began in 2022, construction started in June 2024, and the center is scheduled to go live on December 19. The total project cost was $3.1 million. City officials described the project as a major public safety investment. The new dispatch center features state-of-the-art equipment, including improved cell phone location accuracy and real-time, on-screen translation in multiple languages. The center handles more than 13,000 calls each year for the Piedmont Police and Fire departments. The former dispatch space relied on a 200-amp electrical panel and could not support modern technology. It also lacked seismic retrofitting, creating a risk of service disruption during a major earthquake. The new center is seismically reinforced and includes a secure, independent electrical system and a backup generator capable of powering the entire Veterans Memorial Building, ensuring uninterrupted 911 service. The upgraded facility includes a new monitoring system capable of accessing images from multiple sources across the city. Infrastructure improvements benefit the entire police department, and the center also supports the Fire Department’s fire protection and medical response services. Staffing improvements accompany the physical upgrades. For the first time since 1978, the city increased dispatch staffing, adding two new dispatcher positions made possible by Piedmont voters’ approval of Measure F in March 2024. Chief Shavies said dispatch workloads have increased significantly over the past decade and are expected to continue rising with the implementation of next-generation 911 technology. The new center is designed to expand the capabilities of both police and fire personnel. Dispatchers will use advanced call-answering systems that improve geolocation of cell phone calls and provide realtime language translation. Large, wall-mounted displays allow dispatchers to monitor public safety cameras and automated license plate readers. Chief Shavies and Gonzales described the facility as a “public intelligence center,” where incoming information can be rapidly analyzed and translated into effective responses to community safety issues. After thanking Chief Shavies and Gonzales for the tour, the group continued their weekly walk through nearby neighborhoods. They first headed down Magnolia Avenue for another look at the new Community Pool, which remains closed and is now expected to open in the spring due to equipment delays. From there, the walkers visited several “one-block wonder” streets known for their charm and history. On Carmel Avenue, they revisited landscaping and stonework highlighted during a 2023 walk by architect, urban designer, and Piedmont Post columnist Will Adams, who died last year after a stroke. The walk continued up Blair Avenue to Dracena Avenue and along Park Way, where recent cold, wet weather had produced a striking bloom of large mushrooms. The group’s final stop was Waldo Avenue, tied to Piedmont’s early history as the former rear boundary of Walter Blair’s 19th-century home. The walkers returned to the Exedra past the now-quiet police station. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 AM. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration is at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu to register or call (510) 420-3070 for more information. articles.text: If old foundation needs replacement A significant number of older homes are experiencing settlement problems, cracking, sloping floors, drainage issues and other infrastructure concerns related to 100-year-old foundations that may need replacement. A common question from homeowners facing this work is whether this is the right time to add more space in the basement. Many people consider expanding their homes to accommodate additional family members, create a second unit, or add a bedroom, workshop, office, utility or media room, storage space, or some combination of these uses. The pros of a new basement renovation If significant foundation work is already planned, this may be the only practical opportunity to add usable space beneath your home. A new foundation design is typically more substantial than the original and can accommodate increased ceiling heights. Because basement work requires comprehensive drainage solutions and addresses underlying structural issues, combining the projects can allow you to tackle multiple problems at once. Basement jobs are big projects These projects begin with excavating more soil than most homeowners anticipate. From there, contractors build tall retaining foundation walls with extensive rebar, install wholehouse drainage systems, pour new reinforced concrete floors, and add new walls, beams and seismic upgrades. This phase typically takes about three months. The remodel itself is a larger undertaking, often lasting six months. It frequently requires reworking plumbing, electrical and mechanical systems that are outdated or need to be relocated. Does this make sense to do These jobs are far more expensive than many people expect, so the decision often comes down to budget and necessity. Homeowners can expect to spend about $600 per square foot or more for the project from start to finish, with roughly half of the cost going toward the dig-out and half toward the remodel. One common cost-saving strategy, if time allows, is to divide the work into two phases. Phase one completes the digout and prepares the space for remodeling. Phase two proceeds later, as budget and timing permit, sometimes with homeowners hiring carpenters and individual trades rather than a general contractor for the entire scope. Adding habitable space increases a home’s square footage and can raise its value, often exceeding the cost of the work itself. Jim Gardner of Jim Gardner Construction Inc. Jim is a longtime Piedmont resident and has been doing foundation replacement, drainage work, structural repair and basement dig outs in your neighborhood since 1983.
