articles.text: Robert Hendrickson of Piedmont passed away unexpectedly on November 12, 2025. Rob came into this world with a great zest for life and his enthusiasm was exhibited in all of his endeavors, relationships, and achievements. He was a man of routine and schedules, and believed in being generous, honest, and accountable. His family and community were very strongly impacted by his life force true to his wishes and his loss is felt deeply. He was born in 1952 to veteran parents from the Midwest and grew up in Sacramento next to a creek. From there he ventured to the nearby American River on his bicycle and the Sierra mountains working for the US Forest Service. He was a high academic achiever in his district, took an early interest in engineering, and developed lifelong friendships. Rob graduated from the University of California, Berkeley with bachelor’s and master’s degrees in civil engineering, and a law degree. There he met his fellow law school student and future wife Carola Ingram of Los Angeles, with whom he had three children. He got his pilot’s license and went sky diving, loved the Grateful Dead and photography, and researched earthquakes at the Pacific Earthquake Engineering Center. Working as an attorney in San Francisco in civil engineering and construction cases, Rob found accomplishment in commercial litigation through his understanding of both engineering and legal aspects. He traveled across the country and internationally for work, most recently for the Duane Morris law firm. He said he liked solving problems and helping people solve theirs. He also worked as an arbitrator and was involved in many industry construction forums. A tendency towards identifying right and wrong in law translated to Rob’s interest in sports. He was a coach and referee in his kids’ soccer games, and later switched to rugby as he and his Piedmont resident Rob Hendrickson died on November 12, 2025 sons played the sport. He was a referee or touch judge in most of his younger son’s high school and Cal rugby games. He was a dedicated member of the Northern California Rugby Football Union Referee Society (Pelican Refs) and helped bring on new refs. Rob had a passion for backpacking, skiing, rafting, and scuba diving, often centering vacations around these activities. He loved spending time in Calaveras County, frequently visiting his mountain cabin with his family, friends, and pets. He collected local art and had a personal library of history books about the surrounding areas and the Gold Rush. At home Rob was also interested in gardening, cooking, wine making, reading about geology and evolution (often multiple books at the same time), and the comics. Rob is predeceased by his wife Carola in 2017, and is survived by his sons David and Carl, daughter Katherine, granddaughter Jannah, sister Elisabeth Belle, and brother Lief. Donations to the Northern California Rugby Football Union Referee Society (Pelican Refs) can be made in his honor. A celebration of his life will be held at Piedmont Community Hall.
articles.title: Rob Hendrickson dies on November 12

articles.text: For years I have driven past the huge imposing chateau of Ledson Winery and wondered what the wines were like. Nestled in the heart of Sonoma Valley near Kenwood, Ledson Winery & Vineyards is one of Northern California’s most distinctive and inviting wine destinations. Known to locals and visitors alike as “The Castle,” the winery’s 16,000-square-foot French Normandy–style estate was designed and built by founder Steve Ledson, originally intended as a family residence but ultimately becoming an iconic winery and tasting venue. The Ledson family has deep roots in Sonoma agriculture that stretch back to the 1860s, and that legacy of land stewardship and winemaking is woven into every bottle. Ledson produces over 70 handcrafted wines annually, encompassing more than 20 varietals and blends sourced from estate vineyards and select appellations throughout Sonoma County. Visitors can enjoy a variety of tasting experiences — from classic walk-in tastings at several beautifully appointed bars to private, appointment-only sessions. Ledson places great emphasis on hospitality and education, with knowledgeable staff guiding guests through the breadth of Ledson’s portfolio. The Ledson family’s agricultural roots strongly influence the winery’s culture. Founder Steve Ledson came from a farming background, and that practical, hands-on mindset carries through today in vineyard management and production. Nestled in the heart of Sonoma Valley near Kenwood, Ledson Winery & Vineyards is one of Northern California’s most distinctive and inviting wine destinations. The Ledson family’s agricultural roots strongly influence the winery’s culture. The estate owns and farms several vineyards across Sonoma County, giving the winery greater control over fruit quality and stylistic consistency while still allowing for experimentation with different terroirs. Beyond wine, the estate features a gourmet marketplace stocked with local cheeses, artisan foods, and picnic provisions, making it a perfect stop for a summer picnic under majestic oak trees. Ledson Winery in Sonoma Valley The Caudalies is a blend of Zinfandel and Petite Sirah. • 2019 Ledson Syrah Moon Mountain $48 Layers of fresh, dark fruit show surprising complexity on the nose. Full-bodied, it is focused and balanced, with a firm structure and good acidity. The wine is bold-without being overly ripe – and maintains a dense and chewy character perfect for a hearty beef stew. Specializing in Italian varietals, VJB stands apart from many Sonoma producers by focusing on grapes rarely seen in California. Wines such as Barbera, Nebbiolo, Sangiovese, Dolcetto, and Montepulciano form the core of the portfolio, crafted in a style that emphasizes balance, acidity, and food-friendliness rather than sheer power. These wines reflect both California sunshine and Italian sensibility, bridging two winemaking traditions with authenticity and charm. The winery experience is as memorable as the wines themselves. Guests are welcomed into a lively, Tuscan-inspired setting featuring an Italian marketplace stocked with imported olive oils, balsamic vinegars, pastas, and gourmet foods. A wood-fired pizza kitchen serves rustic Italian fare that pairs naturally with the wines, making VJB a favorite destination for relaxed, social tasting experiences. VJB remains a true family enterprise, with the Belmonte family actively involved in every aspect of the business, from winemaking and hospitality to culinary offerings. Their commitment to warmth, generosity, and tradition creates an atmosphere that feels less like a formal tasting room and more like a visit to an Italian country estate. For visitors seeking something different from the typical Sonoma itinerary, VJB Winery offers an inviting, flavorful journey into Italian-inspired winemaking— where wine, food, and family are inseparable. articles.text: On Friday, December 5, the Piedmont Police Department hosted a holiday gift drive in front of the police station in an effort to fill the Community Service Officer’s (CSO) truck bed for those in need. Officers in Santa hats collected donations of new, unwrapped gifts benefiting children and adults served by Building Futures’ shelters, housing programs, and domestic violence services. Piedmont Police Support Services Commander Brandi Marin-Morris oversaw the event. “Our department has gifted household items to Building Futures once before; however, this was our first time hosting an event of this kind,” said Marin-Morris. Children walked up to the CSO truck to drop in their donations and chat with Officer Hugo Diaz, who was outfitted with a Santa hat and a generous holiday grin. articles.text: Piedmont’s annual tree lighting ceremony, now in its 56th year, celebrated the winter holidays in glowing style on Wednesday, December 3. Now, in its fourth year with the name “Lights Up,” the event featured a menorah lighting, latkes, cider and hot cocoa in addition to the grand illumination of the Community Center’s 80-foot redwood tree. articles.text: With AC Transit’s elimination of bus line 33 cutting off service to much of Piedmont, many families have looked for alternative ways for their children to get to school. In response, the community group Piedmont Unplugged is launching a “bike bus” on Friday, January 9, offering students a supervised group ride from Bear Park to Havens Elementary. The “bike bus” will be meeting at 8 am and leaving at 8:10 am. The bike bus will be led by experienced parents and accompanied by a Piedmont Police Department officer on its first day, helping students learn street safety and the rules of the road as they ride together. Helmets and bikes are required, and students can park their bikes on the Havens campus without needing a lock. AC Transit’s recent service redesign replaced line 33 with line 88, which now stops at Highland Avenue but no longer reaches deeper into Piedmont. For many families, the reduced access has made it difficult for students to take the bus to school. Line 18 now serves the corridor between downtown Oakland and Montclair. For resident Danielle Horowitz, founder of Piedmont Unplugged, the loss of line 33 was a turning point. Her family had been preparing for their children to ride the bus to school this year. articles.text: Piedmont’s new 9-1-1 dispatch center on Highland Avenue is on track to open on Friday, December 19. The new center replaces an undersized facility that was unable to accommodate modern technology. The upgraded space aims to increase efficiency and reliable responses for callers in emergencies. The new dispatch center is the city’s largest public safety investment in decades, costing $3.1 million. The majority of funding for this project comes from the American Rescue Plan Act. articles.text: Each year, the school calendar shapes the rhythm of learning, family life, and teacher workload across our district. With that in mind, many parents — myself included — were hopeful that the newly proposed calendars for the next two school years might reflect adjustments the community has expressed interest in: a slightly later August start, a midweek first day, and a less fragmented spring schedule. Instead, the new calendars reflect minimal positive change from previous versions. Under our current system, the calendar is negotiated entirely within the teachers’ union contract, with the School Board’s role limited to approving the final product rather than helping shape it. There has also been recent community discussion on this topic, including thoughtful perspectives shared by both parents and APT. My intention is not to revisit disagreements, but to focus on how we might approach this process more collaboratively in the future. I understand that APT enters calendar negotiations with real needs: predictability, equitable teaching assignments, and stability. At the same time, families and students have needs as well - smoother pacing, more cohesive semesters, and a gentler transition from summer into the school year. Our current approach makes it difficult to balance these needs in a holistic way. Many nearby high-performing districts — including Palo Alto, Orinda, and Acalanes — have found ways to balance these interests more effectively. Their Boards maintain oversight of the academic calendar while still centering teacher voice. As a result, they have adopted more sensible semester splits, with 84-86 instructional days in the fall and 94-96 in the spring, while still scheduling finals before winter break. This demonstrates that teacher priorities and community priorities can coexist within a collaborative process. articles.text: Piedmont is in the final phase of the repaving portion of its 2025 street rehabilitation project. Work began last week on five roads, which are expected to be finished by the end of this week. The final phase includes repaving 10 streets and restriping an additional 32 to improve road quality across the city. The $1.5 million project is funded primarily by Alameda County transportation sales tax revenue and state transportation funds. Repaving has been split into two phases, one in October and the other in early November. The first phase focused on streets in better condition, which received chip and slurry sealing treatments to repair cracks and other surface-level issues. Phase two includes streets needing more extensive work. These roads are receiving a combination of grind-and-pave treatment, in which the top layer of asphalt is removed and replaced, as well as full reconstruction on sections where both the pavement and underlying base material must be rebuilt. The remaining steps in the project include completing paving on streets that were dug out last week and adding striping to the newly paved roads. articles.text: Linda Park As Piedmont begins work on a new Sustainable Park Management Plan, the City is gathering community input to understand how residents use local parks and which qualities they most want preserved. Piedmont Park bushy dell creek The effort focuses on long-term stewardship of Piedmont’s existing parks and open spaces. Unlike a Parks Master Plan, this project is not about new facilities or added amenities. Instead, it will guide maintenance practices, sustainability standards, and priorities for caring for the parks residents already rely on every day. Community feedback will help the City identify what matters most to park users and what should be protected as longterm management guidelines are developed. Two ways to participate: online survey or park pop-ups The survey, available at piedmont.ca.gov/ParkSurvey, invites residents to share: • How they use Piedmont’s parks • What they value most about • these spaces What they want to ensure is preserved for the future Residents can also talk with the project team during a series of park pop-up events the week of December 8: • Linda Park: Monday, December 8, 4–5 p.m., west side lawn area • Crocker Park: Wednesday, December 10, 4–5 p.m., at the bottle-filling station • Piedmont Park: Friday, December 12, 3–5 p.m., behind the Exedra foundation • Dracena Park: Saturday, December 13, 10 a.m.–12 p.m., tables in the upper and lower park More information is available at piedmont.ca.gov/SustainableParks. articles.text: Ansel is a 4-year-old Lynx point with striking blue eyes and an expressive face that has earned him the nickname of “the least mysterious cat ever” from his foster. Although shy at first, he warms quickly, gaining confidence from gentle affection. Once settled, he becomes a sweet, chatty, companion who offers soft trills, chirpy meows, and the sweetest paw pokes to let you know he would like some attention. He enjoys soft petting, cuddles, and being held, often melting into your arms. At night, he loves sleeping beside his person, and during the day he alternates between cozy naps and playful bursts of activity. His favorite way to play is wrestling with stuffed toys, and he enjoys the company of other cats — he’ll thrive with a friendly feline buddy in a calm home with older kids. Ansel is on a simple special diet that helps support his digestion, and he’ll need to remain indoors because he Come meet Ansel at Cat Town in downtown Oakland. has feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV), which is easily managed and doesn’t shorten his lifespan. What matters most to him is a loving adopter who appreciates his sensitive nature and gentle, affectionate personality. Ansel is neutered, vaccinated, microchipped, and negative for FeLV. Learn more at www.cattownoakland.org or email adopt@cattownoakland. org.

articles.text: Meet Squirtle, an 11-pound Miniature Pinscher Mix with superstar potential. This young guy starts off cautious and prefers slow, gentle handling while he settles in. His foster says it took a couple days, but that he warms up beautifully with patience (and snacks!) According to his foster, once Squirtle trusts you he’s a super cuddly shadow. Affectionate and easy to take care of, he loves nothing more than curling up with his person. He’s done well with other small dogs in the foster’s home and would enjoy calm canine friends. The new working stations for dispatchers information in front of them on several new screens,” Brannigan said. The new technology will improve response times. “The new alerting system is going to reduce the amount of time it takes for them to get a call and then send us out on a call from there,” he added. The project includes a new independent electrical system, a backup generator, and IT infrastructure for the Police Department. The new space is now seismically designed to remain functional in the case of a severe earthquake. This ensures the dispatch center can work through potential outages and environmental emergencies. The previous facility was a cramped space unfit for the demands of a modern dispatch center. The old center has been repurposed into two new rooms: a conference room for meetings and presentations, and an interview room to speak with suspects or victims in a private area. Previously, the department did not have a dedicated space to conduct interviews, and now the repurposed space provides an exclusive area for questioning. Chief Brannigan is excited that their dispatchers will be able to work in a modern environment to serve the city of Piedmont. “It’s great, the chance to have our dispatchers working in an ergonomically fit and modern space is going to be excellent,” Brannigan said. PEF will celebrate Piedmont Education Foundation Day and its 50th anniversary by hosting an open house at 401 Highland Avenue on December 10 from 10:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. with a special all-ages “happy hour” from 2 to 4 p.m. The community is invited to stop by, learn about PEF’s history, meet the staff and board members, purchase See’s Candies for the holidays, and make their Giving Campaign donation at PiedmontEdFoundation.org/donate. Below is the text of this proclamation.
articles.title: December 10 proclaimed Piedmont Education Foundation Day

articles.text: WHEREAS, The Piedmont Educational Foundation (PEF) was officially established on December 10, 1975 with the mission to “Provide new and improved educational opportunities” for students in the Piedmont Unified School District; and WHEREAS, the vision of a sustained funding stream for Piedmont schools led the District to place the first parcel tax measure on the ballot in 1985, and with PEF at the helm of the campaign, the measure passed by an impressive 76 percent; and WHEREAS, in 1989, PEF further strengthened its commitment to the long-term future of Piedmont schools by establishing an endowment to provide additional sustained funding; WHEREAS, PEF has demonstrated its dedication to the broader community by assisting 20 other school support organizations with fundraising and marketing efforts; and WHEREAS, PEF fosters a sense of community engagement through annual events, including the beloved Harvest Festival carnival and the Spring Fling gala; and WHEREAS, for half a century, the Piedmont Educational Foundation has provided sustained financial support to Piedmont schools through fundraising and community engagement, granting over $60 million to enrich the educational experiences of thousands of students; and WHEREAS, we honor the countless volunteers, donors, and community members who have contributed to PEF’s success and encourage all citizens to join in celebrating this significant milestone. NOW, THEREFORE, I, Betsy Smegal Andersen, Mayor of the City of Piedmont, do hereby recognize and proclaim December 10, 2025, as PIEDMONT EDUCATION FOUNDATION DAY in honor of its 50th Anniversary, and express deep appreciation for its outstanding contributions to education and to the betterment of our community. Signed this 5th day of November, 2025 Betsy Smegal Anderson, Mayor
articles.title: CITY OF PIEDMONT PROCLAMATION

articles.text: While the University of California and California State University systems do not include SAT or ACT scores as part of their application, there are schools across the country that are reinstating the once-ubiquitous standardized tests as a college admissions requirement. From Caltech to MIT, and at many other campuses nationwide, standardized testing is back. For students intending to apply to schools that are test-blind, like the UCs and CSUs, or test-required, the decision to prepare for and take standardized tests is easy. But for students who have colleges that are test-optional on their lists, deciding whether or not to take the SAT and/or ACT is more nuanced. When a college is test-optional for admissions, it means that the test is one part of the application that admissions officers evaluate. Like the student’s essay, extracurricular activities, course rigor, leadership, and AP test scores, SAT or ACT test scores can strengthen the overall application. Even at schools that are officially test-optional, there are some colleges whose admission data (as reported in the Common Data Set) indicates that students who submit scores are admitted at a much higher rate than those who do not. Standardized test scores also may be required for university-based merit scholarship consideration. If your student’s college application strategy includes chasing merit money, a solid test score can quite literally pay off. Some schools, like University of Chicago and Drexel University, have a no-harm test policy. The admissions officers at schools with this policy indicate that SAT or ACT scores will be considered only if they are an asset to a student’s application. Admissions officers at test-required schools like Brown University and University of Texas at Austin have been outspoken regarding how standardized tests help demonstrate readiness for college level work. Furthermore, for students interested in pursuing STEM disciplines, these tests quantify preparatory math skills on which admissions decisions may be based. Understanding the state of standardized testing can help families shape a test preparation plan that allows the student to submit the strongest application possible. Karen Shopoff Rooff is Director of College Consulting at Study Smarter. Study Smarter has been providing individualized academic tutoring, test preparation, and college counseling to Piedmont families since 1997. For more information please visit www.studysmarter.com, email info@studysmarter.com, or call (510) 350-8444.
articles.title: The state of standardized testing

Thinking Outside the Classroom The state of standardized testing By Karen Shopoff Rooff While the University of California and California State University systems do not include SAT or ACT scores as part of their application, there are schools across the country that are reinstating the once-ubiquitous standardized tests as a college admissions requirement. From Caltech to MIT, and at many other campuses nationwide, standardized testing is back. For students intending to apply to schools that are test-blind, like the UCs and CSUs, or test-required, the decision to prepare for and take standardized tests is easy. But for students who have colleges that are test-optional on their lists, deciding whether or not to take the SAT and/or ACT is more nuanced. When a college is test-optional for admissions, it means that the test is one part of the application that admissions officers evaluate. Like the student’s essay, extracurricular activities, course rigor, leadership, and AP test scores, SAT or ACT test scores can strengthen the overall application. Even at schools that are officially test-optional, there are some colleges whose admission data (as reported in the Common Data Set) indicates that students who submit scores are admitted at a much higher rate than those who do not. Standardized test scores also may be required for university-based merit scholarship consideration. If your student’s college application strategy includes chasing merit money, a solid test score can quite literally pay off. Some schools, like University of Chicago and Drexel University, have a no-harm test policy. The admissions officers at schools with this policy indicate that SAT or ACT scores will be considered only if they are an asset to a student’s application. Admissions officers at test-required schools like Brown University and University of Texas at Austin have been outspoken regarding how standardized tests help demonstrate readiness for college level work. Furthermore, for students interested in pursuing STEM disciplines, these tests quantify preparatory math skills on which admissions decisions may be based. Understanding the state of standardized testing can help families shape a test preparation plan that allows the student to submit the strongest application possible. Karen Shopoff Rooff is Director of College Consulting at Study Smarter. Study Smarter has been providing individualized academic tutoring, test preparation, and college counseling to Piedmont families since 1997. For more information please visit www.studysmarter.com, email info@studysmarter.com, or call (510) 350-8444. CITY OF PIEDMONT PROCLAMATION WHEREAS, The Piedmont Educational Foundation (PEF) was officially established on December 10, 1975 with the mission to “Provide new and improved educational opportunities” for students in the Piedmont Unified School District; and WHEREAS, the vision of a sustained funding stream for Piedmont schools led the District to place the first parcel tax measure on the ballot in 1985, and with PEF at the helm of the campaign, the measure passed by an impressive 76 percent; and WHEREAS, in 1989, PEF further strengthened its commitment to the long-term future of Piedmont schools by establishing an endowment to provide additional sustained funding; WHEREAS, PEF has demonstrated its dedication to the broader community by assisting 20 other school support organizations with fundraising and marketing efforts; and WHEREAS, PEF fosters a sense of community engagement through annual events, including the beloved Harvest Festival carnival and the Spring Fling gala; and WHEREAS, for half a century, the Piedmont Educational Foundation has provided sustained financial support to Piedmont schools through fundraising and community engagement, granting over $60 million to enrich the educational experiences of thousands of students; and WHEREAS, we honor the countless volunteers, donors, and community members who have contributed to PEF’s success and encourage all citizens to join in celebrating this significant milestone. NOW, THEREFORE, I, Betsy Smegal Andersen, Mayor of the City of Piedmont, do hereby recognize and proclaim December 10, 2025, as PIEDMONT EDUCATION FOUNDATION DAY in honor of its 50th Anniversary, and express deep appreciation for its outstanding contributions to education and to the betterment of our community. articles.text: Girl Scout Troop 32125 shops for their adopted family, a single mom with a toddler and a baby, at Target. Girl Scout Troop 32125, a group of 2nd graders from Wildwood Elementary, went shopping on Wednesday, December 3 for an adopted family. The Adopt-aFamily program is organized by Brighter Beginnings, an East Bay non-profit providing families in resource-poor communities with the support and help needed to raise children with healthy and happy futures. Troop 32125 visited the Target store in Emeryville and broke into teams of two or three Girl Scouts and an adult. Each team shopped for a member of the family: a single mom, her two year-old daughter, and a newborn baby. First names and ages are included in the family bios, but the interaction is otherwise anonymous. Seven-year-old Girl Scout Siena Paley described her experience: “I felt like I was doing the right thing. I felt good. I thought the family needed more than what we were able to give them and I feel bad that they don’t have everything they need. But it’s a good start! And I can’t wait to hear what the baby’s name is!” “On the surface, this is a nice, hands-on way for our troop to give back to less fortunate members of our community,” said Troop Leader Maggie Pickavance. “Each team had a budget to shop with and had to calculate the prices of their gifts. They had to make some choices between buying a coat or buying a toy and had to weigh the difference between a want and a need.” After shopping, the troop wrapped all the gifts, which was an exciting project in and of itself. Items were then dropped off at Brighter Beginnings, where they’re distributed to families. Girl Scout cookie season will begin online on January 12 and booths will start appearing on February 4. Proceeds from cookie sales provide the funds for Girl Scout troops to operate, but also to support community service efforts throughout the year.
articles.title: Girl Scout Troop adopts family for holidays

articles.text: Piedmont Play School (PPS) is partnering with Alameda County Toys for Tots to help bring holiday cheer to local children in need. Community members are invited to drop off new, unwrapped toys in the barrels in front of the school Monday-Friday from 8 a.m. to 12 p.m. through December 12. PPS is located at 401 Hampton Road on Hampton Field beside the tennis courts. “Tangible giving opportunities like this help our children learn, in a hands-on way, what it means to care for others. Those are the values that have always guided PPS,” said PPS board member Sandy Fedor. “All donations will go directly to Toys for Tots, which distributes gifts to families who might otherwise go without.” The City of Piedmont is ending PPS’s residency in the building that Piedmont residents built for the school, making this year’s tradition of giving back especially meaningful. “Even though the future of Piedmont Play School is uncertain, we feel strongly about contributing to the community,” added Fedor. Piedmont Play School welcomes donations from all members of the community. Together, families, neighbors and friends can help make the season brighter for children across the East Bay. articles.text: On October 10, Piedmont Scouts in Troop 11 embarked on a fantastic adventure in Yosemite Valley. Although arriving in the dark, Scouts found their campsites, set up their tents and enjoyed one another’s company. In the morning patrols prepared breakfast, and snacks or a sack lunch, ate together and set out on their various activities. Some explored Yosemite Falls, others hiked to Mirror Lake and took in the beautiful views of Half Dome. Other Scouts climbed the steep path up to Vernal Falls. Taking in the view of the waterfall and Merced River from an iconic bridge, the Scouts rested from the intense incline. Those who journeyed on witnessed Yosemite’s stunning beauty from a higher altitude. The trees and boulders gave way to stone steps glimpsed from below. As they climbed, the fresh air felt more rewarding and the rocks changed color, becoming a paler granite. At multiple points on the way, rainbows were spotted shimmering in the mist generated by the Vernal Falls cascade eternally watering the forest Once the steepest, most precarious steps were climbed, and the top of the waterfall attained, the Scouts took in the stunning view. They enjoyed the sounds of water crashing against the rocks below and breathed the fresh air. In order to take the switchback trail down to the valley floor, they climbed more steep rock paths, and accidentally found a higher viewpoint. The warm glow of the sun filtered through the leaves above, giving atmosphere to their Once back at camp, the hungry Scouts enjoyed warm meals with their patrols. One patrol made Ahi Tuna, and curly fries, and Seven Eleven Patrol made tikka masala and enjoyed many sugary treats together. As the stars began to come out, the Troop assembled They sang call and response songs with silly wordplay, repeated a tongue twister radio test culminating in the line “Ten Andrew Lavin (left) and Colby Lavin on the climb to the summit of Vernal Falls The 7-11 and Curly Fries patrols cooking dinner. One such question was “Who was the first President to protect Yosemite?” The answer? “Abraham Lincoln.” Scouts enjoyed another night sleeping under the trees and stars despite the chilly temperatures. That night the moon shined as bright as a floodlight, and lit up the forest with a beautiful glow. On Sunday morning a concern was raised about their schedule to leave. The troop planned to leave the next morning, but it was scheduled for snow and rain as the Scouts would be packing up their tents. In an effort to avoid this, Troop 11 decided to leave that night after dinner. The whole day was still ahead, and Scouts embarked on adventures, including biking along the Merced River and around Curry Village, climbing, and hiking to new locations. Along the way, they were instructed to collect any trash they spotted on or off the trails. When everyone had their fill of exercise, Scouts played card games, relaxed in hammocks, and chatted in their campsites. All throughout, from the moment of arrival to the moment of departure, National Park staff were present and actively attending to their duties despite the government shutdown. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. articles.text: Dillon Casey eclipses 1,000 career points Piedmont High’s boys’ basketball team advanced to the finals but had to settle for second-place in the school’s annual Winter Classic tournament. The Highlanders fell 58-48 to Archie Williams in the finals on Saturday, December 6 at Binks Rawlings Gym. To get there, PHS beat Arroyo 58-34 in the first round on Thursday, December 4 and won 70-55 over neighbor Head-Royce on Friday, December 5. Against Archie Williams, Piedmont got many of the looks they wanted, but struggled with the finish through the first three quarters. “I thought we got great looks and the energy came out good. We just couldn’t make the shots; that’s been the story of the tournament. Against Head-Royce, if we finished a little better, we could have put up 90,” said coach Ben Spencer. Dillon Casey became the latest Highlander to join the 1,000 career points club when hitting a 3-pointer with 2:32 left in the game. Piedmont High has now had a player eclipse a thousand career points every year since 2020. Luke Barrett reached the mark in 2019/2020, Luke Harris in the 2021 pandemic season, JoJo Murphy in 2021/2022, A.J. Harris in 2022/2023, Brit Burden in 2023/2024, Ravi Silverberg 2024/2025, and now Casey. “It means a lot to me. There’s Staff Photos Dillon Casey notched his 1,000th career point in Purple and White against Archie Williams. Piedmont fell in the finals of its Winter Classic tournament to Archie Williams. They have established a 4-1 record through five games. been a lot of players before me who have scored 1,000 points, so it’s cool to follow in their footsteps. Hopefully, I can create my own path,” Casey said. Piedmont is off to a 4-1 record. “I love the heart of our guys. 4-1 is a great start, we can score in bunches but I’m not sure if we were ready for the physicality of Archie Williams. These types of games get us ready for the rest of the season,” Spencer said. Piedmont looks ahead to the Huber Classic at Acalanes in Lafayette on December 11-13. 58-48 loss to Archie Williams It was a close first quarter with four lead changes before Archie Williams took the lead for good late in the quarter. PHS opened strongly when leading 9-6, but AWHS took over at 13-11 to end the first quarter. In the second, A rchie Williams started scoring in bunches, establishing a 33-18 by halftime. Piedmont trailed by as many as 21 in the third, 45-24, but started landing its shots in the fourth. Casey landed a 3-pointer in the final going with 2:23 left in the game to surpass the 1,000 point mark—which made the score 57-45. Beach Lorin hit a 3-pointer as time expired to make it 58-48. Final stats: Casey had 22 points, two rebounds, two steals, and three assists. Lorin had 15 points and six rebounds. P.J. Brayer had six points, three rebounds, three assists, and one steal. Lucian Fang-Ring had three points, and Yoseph Baskin had two.
articles.title: Piedmont falls in Winter Classic final to Archie Williams

articles.text: Another fall season has come and gone for Piedmont High. An overarching theme across nearly every sport this fall was young stars emerging on varsity rosters. Here is taking a look at some of the key highlights from the 2025 fall season. Football’s NCS Championship appearance The football team made history this fall season, achieving their first berth in a North Coast Section championship since the 1976 title winning team that was elected into the Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame. Piedmont finished 8-5 with the No. 2 seed in the Division 7 NCS postseason. They bashed No. 7 St. Patrick 49-7 and followed up with a 28-10 win over No. 3 Willits in the semifinals. PHS faced No. 1 seed Middletown in the title game, falling 37-23. The team featured six juniors, eight sophomores, and one freshman. Many were earning their first starting role on varsity. The team could have a healthy cast for years to come with playPiedmont’s football team made its first NCS Championship appearance since 1976. ers like sophomore QB Jimmy Lagios, sophomore LB George Saunders, sophomores WR/DBs Max Fujimoto and Mateo Long, sophomore DE John Bunje, sophomore OL/DL Jax Thayer, and freshman DT Jared Lavaka. Girls’ Cross-Country reaches State Championship Piedmont’s girls’ cross country team achieved their first berth in the CIF State Championship as a team since 2019, placing 18th of 25 schools in the D4 race. PHS’ seven varsity runners at State included Leighton Mand, Skylar Best, Viviane Oesterer, Cora Chun, Amalia Gray, Cora Borzowski Schrader, and Nikita Gorelik. The 2019 team that reached State included former Post Athletes of the Year Sophia Zalewski and Ellie Black. Sophia went on to run at Carnegie Mellon, while Ellie ran for the University of California—which shows the talent level of this year’s team to reach the hallowed ground. Both the girls’ and boys’ cross-country teams look ahead to 2026 with healthy rosters. For the girls’ team, Mand, Gray and Borzowski Schrader will be seniors, Oesterer and Gorelik will Staff Photos be juniors, while Kelsey Coleman made her varsity debut this year as a freshman. Over to the boys, sophomores Aaron Bennett and Dresden Schulte-Sasse burst onto the scene, while freshman Dylan Wallway also left his mark. Alex Schleuning will be a senior leader next year, and a healthy Sebastien Swain back in the mix could pose a strong team. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team opened the season with a 2-2 tie against Granada and a 2-nil loss to Miramonte. Piedmont High’s girls’ soccer team opened its season with a 2-2 tie with Granada at Witter Field on Wednesday, December 3, and a 2-0 loss to Miramonte on a cold and foggy night in Orinda two days later. The games marked the debut of new head coach Matt Against Granada, Piedmont carried a 2-0 lead until late in the action before the visitors got on the board with five minutes left in the game and landed the equal- “First game, I think we struggled with the build and getting the girls to play how we want to play. I told them we need to be braver in possession, braver in the buildup, and braver in the aggressive press. It’s just getting them to believe in what we’re doing. Once they did tonight, things looked much better,” Spencer-Harty said. In the game with North Coast Section rival Miramonte, PHS held a 0-0 tie into the second half but the Matadors’ experienced quality eventually took control. It’s not an easy early schedule for the Highlanders who will face defending Division 2 NCS Champions Cardinal Newman tonight in Santa Rosa. Then, they will face the NCS Div. 2 runners up Marin Academy on Friday. Granada reached last year’s Div, 2 postseason playoffs and Miramonte reached the quarterfinals of last year’s Div. 1 playoffs. “It’s four really tough games to begin with, which I’m happy about. We’ll get tested against top opposition,” Spencer-Harty said. 2-2 tie with Granada Miranda Liu scored Piedmont’s first goal of the season in the 31st minute on what may have been a cross. Along the right wing near the end line, Liu ripped a ball toward the near post. The ball was mishandled by Granada’s keeper, hitting off her hands and into the net. Right before halftime in the 40th minute, Teah Suhr scored for the Highlanders to give them a 2-nil lead. This time, freshman Olivia Nealon dribbled down the left side into the box before sending a ball across the face of the net for the assist. The ball skipped through to Suhr on the right side, looping in a left footed shot to the far post. Piedmont had a couple of chances in the second half before Granada scored both its goals. Liu had a long shot on target from about eight yards above the box in the 47th minute. She had a big chance in the 55th minute when Piedmont had a counter attack off a Granada corner, where Liu wheeled in behind the back line from midfield into the box. However, her shot skipped narrowly wide of the far post. Miranda Liu scored Piedmont’s first goal of the season against Granada.
articles.title: Girls’ soccer team opens season with tie and loss

articles.text: Staff Photos Henry DeVan scored Piedmont’s first goal of the season against Skyline. Piedmont High’s boys’ soccer team had a rough start of the season with a 3-2 loss to Skyline in Oakland on Wednesday, December 3. Two days later they suffered a one-sided 5-nil loss at Newark Memorial. Against Skyline, the Highlanders conceded two goals by way of set pieces. The Titans scored from a corner in the 23rd minute to take a 2-nil lead, then made it 3-1 in the 62nd from a nicely placed free kick from just outside the penalty box. “One of things we said coming into the game is our build-out is something we’re [working on]. We have options A, B, C, and worked down to option Z. We have a scale intention, behavior, habit, excellence. The intention wasn’t quite there, and therefore the behavior led to the goals,” explained coach Ben Russell. Russell faces the task of replacing former forwards Gianluca Bini and Bosco Lorin. With a young team including 10 sophomores and three freshmen, Russell used a combination of different players in the attacking roles, including Gerber, Piniella, sophomore Eli Dao-Hoang, and freshman Evan Yamanaka. “We’re figuring out where the pieces fall. We know we have speed with Evan and Ben, but now it’s how we understand that as a group. Can we get the ball in behind? When teams defend that, can we play underneath?” Russell said. Piedmont got both of its goals in the second half. Midfielder Henry DeVan got the first score on a nice dribble with possession before slotting in a shot from atop the box in the 57th minute. “He’s stepping into the central defensive midfield role. We know he’s a strong driver with the ball. He’s sometime takes one too many touches, but there’s more to come from him for sure,” Russell said of DeVan. PHS’ next goal came from Robert Piniella in the 75th. This time, sophomore forward Ben Gerber took an initial shot that rebounded off a diving save by Skyline’s keeper, allowing to Piniella to charge toward for a goal. 3-2 loss to Skyline Skyline struck first in the 19th minute when a low shot was saved by Tobias Tsai, but it rebounded to a forward in the box. By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s boys’ soccer team had a rough start of the season with a 3-2 loss to Skyline in Oakland on Wednesday, December 3. Two days later they suffered a one-sided 5-nil loss at Newark Memorial. Against Skyline, the Highlanders conceded two goals by way of set pieces. The Titans scored from a corner in the 23rd minute to take a 2-nil lead, then made it 3-1 in the 62nd from a nicely placed free kick from just outside the penalty box. “One of things we said coming into the game is our build-out is something we’re [working on]. We have options A, B, C, and worked down to option Z. We have a scale intention, behavior, habit, excellence. The intention wasn’t quite there, and therefore the behavior led to the goals,” explained coach Ben Russell. Russell faces the task of replacing former forwards Gianluca Bini and Bosco Lorin. With a young team including 10 sophomores and three freshmen, Russell used a combination of different players in the attacking roles, including Gerber, Piniella, sophomore Eli Dao-Hoang, and freshman Evan Yamanaka. “We’re figuring out where the pieces fall. We know we have speed with Evan and Ben, but now it’s how we understand that as a group. Can we get the ball in behind? When teams defend that, can we play underneath?” Russell said. Piedmont got both of its goals in the second half. Midfielder Henry DeVan got the first score on a nice dribble with possession before slotting in a shot from atop the box in the 57th minute. “He’s stepping into the central defensive midfield role. We know he’s a strong driver with the ball. He’s sometime takes one too many touches, but there’s more to come from him for sure,” Russell said of DeVan. articles.text: Within the Piedmont High School community, English teacher Beth Black is known for her ability to lift students up. She can turn a hesitant ninth grader into a confident writer, she brings a steady, calm authority to seniors preparing for their next steps, and as the inaugural head coach of the Girls Flag Football team, she has become a defining presence in one of the fastest growing sports in the country. Coach Black has spent more than 24 years teaching English and journalism at Piedmont High School. She guides students through literature, analysis, revision, and the work of finding their own voice. Many return years later to share that something they learned from her stayed with them, moments that reflect the care and intention she brings to her teaching. Sports have always played an important role in her life. She grew up in Ohio in a family where football was part of everyday conversation. At the University of Toledo, she became a competitive dancer, honing the discipline and focus that now guide her coaching style. She also played recreational flag football in college and discovered just how strategic and engaging the sport can be. When girls f lag football became an official high school sport in California in 2023, Coach Black stepped forward to establish the program at Piedmont. She partnered with teacher and assistant coach Haley Adams to build the program from the ground up, creating a welcoming space for experienced athletes and newcomers alike. Their work resonated immediately. Interest surged, tryouts filled quickly, and the program became one of the most popular and inclusive teams on campus. Piedmont now fields three full levels. The varsity team brings experience and competitive skill. The JV team supports developing athletes. The frosh team gives newcomers a place to learn the game and grow with confidence. This structure has produced allleague players and created opportunities that did not exist even a few years ago. For Coach Black, the most rewarding moments are the ones when a player suddenly sees the game differently. A route comes together, a read makes sense, or a young athlete trusts her ability for the first time. These breakthroughs reflect the confidence and growth she works to build. Whether she is guiding a student through a college essay, helping a reporter refine a story for The Piedmont Highlander, or supporting her players during practice, Coach Black brings steady commitment and genuine care. Her influence reaches from the classroom to the newsroom to the field, and many students discover new confidence because she helps them see what they can achieve. Coach Black reflected further on her coaching journey and the rise of girls’ flag football. girls like me who grew up playing football with boys but had no real opportunity to join a team, this is a long-awaited change. For many years, girls had to become the sideline supporters instead of the players. Now the door is open, and the message is clear: of course you can do this. Q: What core values do you instill in your players? A: One value is to try something new, even in high school. Many of our players come from soccer, volleyball, water polo, and other sports, and they are discovering they can be good at something completely new. Another key value is teamwork. Football requires teamwork in a way that few other sports do. And finally, football teaches you to own your space. You have a right to that space on the field, and if you get there first, it is yours. That awareness and confidence are important lessons. Q: What has been the most rewarding or exciting moment so far, on or off the field? A: Watching the growth of players over three years has been incredibly rewarding. Some of our seniors began with no understanding of football at all. Early on I would give very simple instructions like rush the quarterback, and they would do it without much awareness. Now they understand angles, leverage, how the quarterback might roll out, and how to adjust. They think and react like football players, and I no longer need to teach those basics. Seeing that transformation has been amazing. Q: With colleges adding women’s flag football, how do you see Piedmont fitting into that pipeline of opportunity? A: So this is where we now have to start shifting from the very beginning of the program which was introducing football to as many girls as possible, to now becoming two approaches. If you still want to learn football, I will coach you, but if you expect to be on the varsity squad, you have to know football. You already have football awareness. We need to become competitive. Now, girls can start earlier if they want. They can find outside organizations to get involved in to continue their football knowledge. That’s how I can help them have football opportunities in the future. Q: When future players look back at that first season three years ago, what do you hope they remember about being part of Piedmont’s first flag football team? A: Even if they did not consider themselves a football player at the beginning of that first year, I hope they know that they became a football player. So, in the future if anyone ever asks them what sports they played, they will never think twice about saying “I played football in high school.” Q: What inspired you to become the inaugural head coach of Piedmont’s first Girls Flag Football team? I was truly excited about the opportunity and ready for the challenge. Q: Can you share a little about your background in athletics or coaching and how it prepared you for this role? A: I had coached cross country and track as an assistant at a former school, and I have been involved in several other sports and sports organizations over the years. In terms of my own athletic background, I grew up playing soccer and later played intramural flag football in college, which gave me basic knowledge of the game. The sport has changed since then, but it gave me a foundation. I also have strong knowledge of many sports through sports journalism and years of watching and studying different games. My coaching experience also includes cheerleading and informal coaching in volleyball and freshman-level football. Q: How did you feel when you learned you would be leading the program, and what does it mean to you personally to be the first? A: Being the first meant approaching the program with a clear purpose. My goal from the beginning was that by the time I finished coaching, girls would never again see football as something closed to them. I wanted them to see it as accessible from a young age. My mindset was to teach as many girls as possible the skills of the sport and show them they belong in football. We taught what a football team is, what offense looks like, what defense looks like, and how different the sport is from anything they had played before. articles.text: With Piedmont High soccer getting underway and the fall season officially over, we take a look at Louisa Symkowick of Carleton College’s soccer team, Enzo Bernales of Occidental College’s soccer team, and Sadie Town of Santa Monica City College’s volleyball team. Photo courtesy of Occidental College Athletics Enzo Bernales, PHS Class of 2025, just finished his freshman season on Occidental College’s soccer team. ENZO BERNALES Occidental College Photo courtesy of Carleton College Athletics Louisa Symkowick, PHS Class of 2025, is a freshman on Carleton College’s soccer team. LOUISA SYMKOWICK Carleton College Bernales, PHS Class of 2025, is a freshman on Occidental College’s soccer team. He was a leader of Piedmont High’s Division 4 NCS title in 2023, when we named him The Posts’ Sophomore of the Year. This year, Occidental went 10-4-6 (W-T-L) and won the Southern California Intercollegiate Athletic Conference championship with a 1-nil win over Redlands on November 8. They reached the Division 3 NCAA Tournament, losing 3-1 in the first round to No. 2 Augsburg on November 15. Bernales appeared in 11 games this season for 205 total minutes, recording one assist to go along with three shots with one on target. Louisa Symkowick, PHS Class of 2025, just finished her freshman season on Carleton College’s soccer team. She was a member of Piedmont’s 2023 Div. 4 North Coast Section championship team. Carleton College went 18-3-3 this season to win the Minnesota Intercollegiate Athletic Conference title with a 1-nil win over St. Catherine University on November 8. The Knights proved to be one of the best Division 3 schools in the country, reaching the Elite 8 before falling 2-1 to No. 7 University of Chicago on November 23. To get there, No. 16 seeded Carleton beat John Carroll University 1-0 I the first round on November 15, beat Lake Forest College 2-nil the next day, and beat No. 13 Swarthmore College in penalty kicks 4-2 on November 22. Symkowick appeared in 19 matches this season for 475 total minutes. She scored once, recording six shots with three on target in the process. Photo courtesy of Santa Monica City College Athletics Sadie Town, PHS Class of 2024, helped Santa Monica City College achieve its first State Championship Tournament berth in 31 years. SADIE TOWN Santa Monica City College Sadie Town, PHS Class of 2024, just finished her sophomore season on Santa Monica College’s volleyball team. She was a fouryear starter at Piedmont. Santa Monica CC recently finished its season with a five-set 3-2 loss to San Diego Mesa in the 3C2A State Championship Semifinals on December 6, concluding with a 27-5 overall record, winning the SoCal Regional title in the process. Their State Championship berth marked the school’s first in 31 years. Town appeared in 24 matches throughout the fall season, recording highs of 12 kills against Ventura on September 5 and Irvine Valley on August 29.
articles.title: Three former PHS athletes in college

articles.text: Oakland Zoo’s popular “Glowfari” festival is underway, featuring hundreds of life-sized glowing animal lanterns and all-new light fixtures this year. Running through January 25, 2026, the family-friendly lantern festival invites guests to stroll among larger-than-life illuminated animal sculptures during festival hours from 4:30 to 9 p.m. “Glowfari” joins dozens of holiday-themed light festivals across the Bay Area, but this long standing event, previously named “Zoolights,” focuses on wildlife, sustainability and animal conservation. The reinvented event features larger light displays, longer hours of admission, and more available dates and has been a wildly successful fundraiser for the Zoo since its inception. Each handcrafted lantern creates a colorful journey through Oakland Zoo’s themed zones, including the savanna, the ocean, and a whimsical bug tunnel. Seasonal treats will be available for purchase. While animal displays are closed for late night events, “Glowfari” ticketholders can still take a gondola ride to the California Trail for panoramic views of the illuminated exhibits spread across the zoo’s hillsides. Timed-entry tickets are required and often sell out early. Admission prices vary by date, and parking is included with each reservation. Children under two are free. Proceeds from Glowfari help support the Oakland Zoo’s wildlife conservation programs and animal care initiatives. More information is available at www.oaklandzoo.org. Tickets are available online for Oakland Zoo’s annual light festival. The festival focuses on wildlife, sustainability and animal conservation. 4400 Piedmont Avenue, Oakland • 547-5507 Value of $125.70 Value of $203.70

articles.text: Photo by Gary Sexton Installation view of Contemporary Painting in Papua New Guinea: Mathias Kauage and His Family A rare and unique exhibition featuring artwork by contemporary Papuan artist Mathias Kauage is on display at the de Young, one of the fine arts museums of San Francisco, now through March 2026. Kauage is regarded as the leading figure of contemporary art in Papua New Guinea and exhibited internationally in Europe, America and Australia regularly before he died in 2003. The exhibition features four paintings from the de Young’s permanent collection by Mathias Kauage and his family, on view for the first time. Born in 1944 in a remote village in Papua New Guinea’s remote highlands, the artist moved to Port Moreseby, the country’s capital, as a teenager. He began drawing at a young age when he was inspired by the work of Timothy Akis, the first Papuan artist to hold a western-style exhibition. Under the mentorship of German artist Gerogina Beier at the National Arts School in Port Moresby, Kauage began to develop his own distinctive style and find his preferred medium of acrylic on canvas. He also learned and mastered printmaking techniques, woodcuts and copper-beating. Kauage is most famous for his acrylic on canvas paintings and murals, which are highlighted in this exhibit. His works famously focused on how technology has impacted life in remote Papua New Guinea, and his later works addressed societal issues such as the onset of the HIV/AIDS epidemic. In the late 1970s, Kauage and his wife Elisabet led the contemporary arts movement in the newly independent Papua New Guinea. His works are currently held in the National Gallery of Australia, the National Gallery of Papua New Guinea, the British Museum and the Gallery of Modern Art, Glasgow, but are less often on display in western museums, making the de Young’s exhibition a rarity. To learn more, visit https:// www.famsf.org/exhibitions/papua-new-guinea-mathias-kauage.
articles.title: Mathias Kauage exhibition on display at de Young now through March

articles.text: Alameda art exhibition organized by PHS alum Rhythmix Cultural Center will open a new group exhibition next month showcasing artwork created by frontline staff of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. Art Comes From Art, Comes From Art runs January 17 through February 22 and features seven artists who work at the Legion of Honor and the de Young while maintaining active creative practices of their own. The exhibition is organized by Natalie Jeng, PHS class of 2019, and highlights new pieces inspired directly by the museums’ collections, architecture and visitors. Works range from beadwork and painting to digital illustration, cartooning and brush-and-ink comics, reflecting the varied perspectives found within the museum community. The exhibition’s title nods to Art Comes from Art, the 2025 Wayne Thiebaud exhibition at the Legion of Honor, Jeng said. “[The exhibition title] echoes Thiebaud’s belief that all art exists in dialogue with what has come before,” she said. “In a moment when cultural institutions everywhere are navigating challenges, this show focuses on something uplifting: how much inspiration museum staff draw from the art they help steward, and how that influence flows back into the Bay Area’s artistic community.” The Rhythmix exhibition aims to celebrate that “circular exchange of inspiration” by presenting artwork shaped by daily encounters with masterpieces and with colleagues who share a passion for art, she added. Mathias Kauage exhibition on display at de Young now through March Photo by Gary Sexton Installation view of Contemporary Painting in Papua New Guinea: Mathias Kauage and His Family By Allyson Aleksey A rare and unique exhibition featuring artwork by contemporary Papuan artist Mathias Kauage is on display at the de Young, one of the fine arts museums of San Francisco, now through March 2026. Kauage is regarded as the leading figure of contemporary art in Papua New Guinea and exhibited internationally in Europe, America and Australia regularly before he died in 2003. The exhibition features four paintings from the de Young’s permanent collection by Mathias Kauage and his family, on view for the first time. Born in 1944 in a remote village in Papua New Guinea’s remote highlands, the artist moved to Port Moreseby, the country’s capital, as a teenager. He began drawing at a young age when he was inspired by the work of Timothy Akis, the first Papuan artist to hold a western-style exhibition. Under the mentorship of German artist Gerogina Beier at the National Arts School in Port Moresby, Kauage began to develop his own distinctive style and find his preferred medium of acrylic on canvas. He also learned and mastered printmaking techniques, woodcuts and copper-beating. Kauage is most famous for his acrylic on canvas paintings and murals, which are highlighted in this exhibit. His works famously focused on how technology has impacted life in remote Papua New Guinea, and his later works addressed societal issues such as the onset of the HIV/AIDS epidemic. In the late 1970s, Kauage and his wife Elisabet led the contemporary arts movement in the newly independent Papua New Guinea. His works are currently held in the National Gallery of Australia, the National Gallery of Papua New Guinea, the British Museum and the Gallery of Modern Art, Glasgow, but are less often on display in western museums, making the de Young’s exhibition a rarity. articles.text: Play runs through Dec. 21 Berkeley Repertory Theatre presents Jessica Huang’s newest play Mother of Exiles, following one American family across 150 years of migration and reinvention. The play is showing onstage now through December 21. Mother of Exiles, developed through Berkeley Rep’s Ground Floor new-work program, blends historical drama, supernatural encounters and unexpected humor. The story begins in 1898 on Angel Island, where a pregnant Eddie Loi faces deportation amid increasingly restrictive federal immigration laws. A century later, her great-grandson Braulio, working as a Miami border patrol officer, conjures Eddie’s outspoken spirit unknowingly, forcing him to confront the family history he Playwright Jessica Huang never knew. The story then jumps to the year 2063, where their descendants, living in a climate-ravaged future, undertake a perilous ocean journey in search of sanctuary. Huang said the inspiration for the play emerged from a personal realization about America’s unevenly taught immigration history. “When I was in history class, the immigration pathway I learned about was through Ellis Island,” she said. “I didn’t learn very much about the West Coast immigration pathway, which is wild because that’s where half of my identity comes from. And so when I first learned about Angel Island after college, I was fascinated by its history and by that journey. I began doing research into Angel Island… and it became an American landmark for me. When I started to write Mother of Exiles, which tells the story of multiple generations of one American family from the moment they immigrate to the moment they emigrate, it made sense to start this story at Angel Island.” Performances details and tickets are available at https://www. berkeleyrep.org/shows/motherof-exiles-sb2l.

articles.text: Grammy award-winning violinist Mads Tolling returns to SFJAZZ this Saturday and Sunday, December 14 and 15, to perform four concerts featuring ‘jazzified’ traditional carols from Nordic countries. Tolling is a Danish-American violinist and composer and twotime Grammy award-winner, best known for his work with the Turtle Island Quartet, Stanley Clarke, Bob Weir, and local groups including the all-star San Francisco String Trio. After about nine years with Turtle Island Quartet and several years touring with bassist Stanley Clarke’s band, Tolling branched out to lead his own groups. He is a regular performer at the SFJAZZ Center, having first performed at the center in 2010 in a double bill with Regina Carter. He collaborated with the Grateful Dead’s Bob Weir and the Wolf Bros. on projects more recently. This weekend, Tolling celebrates the season with reimagined Mads Tolling versions of carols from Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Finland and Iceland, blending the mysticism, customs and sounds of the Nordic countries along with the joy and soul of American jazz. Two concerts are held on Saturday, December 13, at 7 p.m. and 8:30 p.m. Mads Tolling will perform two concerts the following day, Sunday, December 14, at 6 p.m. and 7:30 p.m. Visit https://www.sfjazz.org/ tickets/productions/25-26/madstolling-cool-yule/ to purchase tickets.

articles.text: Revered maestro Riccardo Muti Revered maestro Riccardo Muti and his beloved Chicago Symphony Orchestra will reconvene in Berkeley for a program of popular orchestra gems on Saturday, January 17. Muti, who turns 84 this year, stepped down as the Orchestra’s music director to assume the role of Music Director Emeritus for Life in 2023, but rejoins the musicians for this special evening performance on UC Berkeley’s campus. The New York Times hails Muti’s legacy, calling the orchestra “all power and finesse” under his tenure, saying “he barely had to move for the players to unleash torrents of stupendous, beautifully balanced sound.” Muti excels at Brahms and will conduct the composer’s majestic Fourth Symphony; Stravinsky’s delightful suite from the ballet The Fairy’s Kiss; and Ravel’s magnificent Boléro, which builds the concert to a volcanic climax. A full program book will be available approximately one week before the performance. The concert, organized by Cal Performances, begins at 8 p.m. Visit https://calperformances.org/ to purchase tickets.

After winning first prize at the Vienna Conservatory, he won first prize at the Paris Conservatory. pages.text: 18 18 Wednesday, December 10, 2025 The Musical Gourmet Famous Freddy By Joseph Gold You probably don’t recognize his name, but Freddie Potter really was the most popular violinist of all time. The piano world had Paderewski and the violin world had Freddie Potter. That wasn’t his real name, however. It is a translation. Freddie was born in Vienna on February 2, 1875. Quite coincidentally another contender for greatest violinist of all time was born on the same date. His name was Joseph Heifetz who later changed his last name to Heifitz. And now to Freddie. In addition to being the most popular violinist of all time, Freddie was a fantastic composer. He was also a prevaricator – a very charming liar. He simply made up stories and related them with conviction. As is the case with many musicians, he was a child genius. After winning first prize at the Vienna Conservatory, he won first prize at the Paris Conservatory. Soon after, he was engaged to concertize in America, but the concert tour was not an overwhelming success. Despite the early promise of this gifted musician, his career did not materialize. He decided to audition for a violin position with the Vienna Philharmonic but it was a failure in every aspect. He liked to tell people that he The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet studied art in an art academy. He was very good at drawing stick figures. Then he enrolled in medical school but probably didn’t graduate because he never became a doctor. At some time he actually became an officer in the Austrian army and got married. His career blossom and he composed countless popular violin pieces. His wife took 100% of the credit for his success. Freddie decided to move to the United States. W hen Aust r ia became involved in World War I, Freddie decided he’d better return to his army unit. He was an officer, after all. He claimed that he was wounded in the battle of Tannenburg, and even wrote a book about his adventures describing his leg injury. It was impossible to ascertain if he actually was injured. Freddie was great at saying whatever was good at the time. Both of his parents were Jewish. His wife, however, was a bigot. She denied Freddie’s Jewish background and often said: “My husband does not have one drop of Jewish blood”. A famous response to this statement was: “He must be anemic.” Mrs. Potter often stated that she insisted that Freddie practice. She was, after all, responsible for his concert success. It was known that Freddie did not practice while on tour. The truth is, he didn’t need to practice. His concert schedule was 13 concerts in a row with one day off. Along the way, he composed countless popular pieces but denied that he was the composer. A suspicious music critic demanded to see the original manuscripts, and Freddie was forced to admit that he composed all of them. An international scandal ensued. But the public loved Freddie so much they embraced him even more. His career continued at the highest level until he was severely injured in a traffic accident. That was just about the end of his career. He was lucky to be alive. When he died in 1962 all the newspaper headlines read: “greatest violinist of all time dies.” Have you figured out who Freddie Potter was? His original first name was Friedrich. That’s Frederick in English. The diminutive is Freddie and in German, it’s Fritz. Potter is an English version of Kreisler. That’s it… Fritz Kreisler… the most popular violinist of all time. Caricature of a famous violinist by another famous musician, Enrico Caruso. Democracy is not a spectator sport! articles.text: Ethel Smyth’s Op. 6 (1886) (1798) Tracing the evolution of the string trio: Beethoven was one of the first to establish it as a serious chamber music form, challenging each player with intricate interplay and individual virtuosity. Nearly a century later, Smyth engages with Beethoven’s tradition and expands it with her Romantic voice, inventive textures, and a charming nod to Scottish folk music.

articles.text: Noomi Rapace in The Girl Who Kicked the Hornet’s Nest More than a decade after the Millennium trilogy first electrified readers and audiences, The Girl Who Kicked the Hornet’s Nest remains a reminder of just how indelible Noomi Rapace’s Lisbeth Salander truly is. For many who discovered Stieg Larsson’s novels in the summer of 2010, curiosity about the films centered on a single question: who could possibly play Salander? The answer, as it turned out, was an actress who would go on to build an extraordinary global career. Long before her recent psychological-sci-fi turn in Constellation, Rapace’s breakout performance in The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo set a standard that has rarely been matched. Her Lisbeth is fierce and fragile, wounded and impenetrable, a character who communicates more with a single glance than with a page of dialogue. Rapace gives her a coiled, electric stillness, masking a history of trauma with razor intelligence and a silent, unyielding will. All three films unfold in Sweden, and though the first can be watched on its own as a taut murder mystery, the second and third chapters lock together. To fully appreciate Hornet’s Nest, it is essential to start at the beginning. The trilogy’s world is dense with intrigue and shadowy institutions, threaded through with violence, corruption, and a constant sense of danger. At the center, always, is Salander: hacker, survivor, and a counterforce to the institutional rot that has defined her life. Her gift for navigating the digital underworld, her alliances with fellow hackers with names like Plague, and her relentless pursuit of the truth give the films a propulsive urgency. The battle she wages against a system determined to erase her is as harrowing as anything in contemporary thrillers. When the trilogy ends—on the page or on screen—what lingers is a wish for more: one more book, one more film, one more glimpse into the mind of a character who reshaped the modern thriller. There were rumors, once, of a fourth manuscript left on Larsson’s laptop, but his sudden passing, before the first novel was even published, left that hope unresolved. Hollywood eventually tried its hand at the series, with David Fincher directing an English-language remake of The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo. But Rapace’s interpretation remains singular. Watching Hornet’s Nest today, especially in light of her recent work, you see how this role launched one of the most intriguing actresses of her generation— one still drawn to stories of identity, resilience, and the dark edges of human experience. The Girl Who Kicked the Hornet’s Nest endures because Lisbeth Salander endures. And with Rapace, it never feels over. The Girl Who Kicked the Hornet’s Nest. Directed by Daniel Alfredson. Starring Noomi Rapace, Michael Nyqvist, Annika Hallin, Erika Berger and Micke Spreitz. Released in 2010. 2 hrs., 35 min. Rated R. Streaming on Prime

articles.text: Tangled is a bright, buoyant retelling of the Brothers Grimm story of Rapunzel, shaped into a Disney fantasy-musical perfect for tween audiences. Mandy Moore voices the “lost princess,” stolen as an infant from the King and Queen of Corona by the vain and manipulative Gothel (Donna Murphy). Posing as Rapunzel’s mother, Gothel has kept her hidden in a tower for 18 years, guarded only by a chameleon companion whose shifting colors mirror the girl’s moods. Gothel’s motive is simple: Rapunzel’s impossibly long, golden hair possesses a magical healing power that keeps the old crone forever young. As long as the girl stays isolated, Gothel remains ageless. Everything changes when Flynn Ryder (Zachary Levi), a charming rogue on the run after stealing a tiara, climbs through Rapunzel’s window while looking for a hiding place. She promptly knocks him out with a frying pan, but soon strikes a bargain with him. For years, Rapunzel has watched lanterns rise in the distance on her birthday, unaware they are sent skyward by her grieving parents. She convinces Flynn to guide her to the kingdom of Corona so she can finally see the world beyond her tower walls. The adventure that follows is filled with Disney verve: chase scenes, a flooding cave, run-ins with palace guards, the formidable Gothel, and a scene-stealing horse named Maximus. Through it all, Rapunzel discovers her courage, her identity, and her long-buried connection to the royal family. The ending delivers precisely what a fairy tale promises: Rapunzel’s return, a joyful reunion with her parents, and a royal wedding that brings the story full circle. With its humor, heart, and memorable music, Tangled remains one of Disney’s modern animated standouts. Tangled. Directed by Nathan Greno and Byron Howard. Voices of Mandy Moore, Zachary Levi and Donna Murphy. Released in 2010. 1 hr., 41 min. Rated PG. Streaming on Prime, Disney+, Fandango and Apple. A scene from Disney’s Tangled A scene from The Iron Giant The Iron Giant, directed by Brad Bird, adapts Ted Hughes’ 1968 children’s book, originally set in the U.K., and reimagines it in Rockwell, a nostalgic 1950s Maine town. What follows is one of the most tender, visually striking, and thematically rich animated films of the last quarter-century. During a violent storm, a blazing object crashes into the ocean off the Maine coast. Soon after, nine-year-old Hogarth Hughes (Eli Marienthal), a bright, lonely kid whose single mother Annie (Jennifer Aniston) works nights at a diner, wanders into the woods and discovers the source: a towering, metal-eating robot, voiced by Vin Diesel. Nearly electrocuted while feeding on a power station, the self-sacrifice that cements the film’s enduring message: “You are who you choose to be.” Yet the closing moments offer a hint that this may not be the end after all. Beautifully animated—handdrawn characters paired with CGI for the robot—The Iron Giant evokes the warmth and artistic ambition of Studio Ghibli while delivering an unmistakably American story about fear, friendship, and moral choice. It remains a landmark in family animation, heartfelt and unforgettable. The Iron Giant. Directed by Brad Bird. Voices of Vin Diesel, Harry Connick Jr., Jennifer Aniston, Eli Marienthal. Released in 1999. 1 hr., 26 min. Rated PG. Streaming on Fandango, Prime, Apple and YouTube

articles.text: The Indie Next List has fresh reading recommendations every month. Check out this newest list of hot off the press books that should come in handy during holiday shopping. The Indie Next List of new releases is curated by independent bookstore owners and staff of only new releases. November’s supply has an extra helpings of thrillers and romance novels fit to be read more and more voraciously, as the days grow shorter. The American Booksellers Association fights to keep independently owned bookstores alive and thriving. At the start of each month ABA publishes a list of 25 inspired recommendations from independent booksellers called the “Indie Next List.” The titles below received praise from independent bookstore owners from across the country. Go to Indiebound.org/indienext-list for archives of recommendations, more information and ways to order that will support the small book store culture. Every Day I Read: 53 Ways to Get Closer to Books Tan (Transl.), Bloomsbury Publishing, Memoir “If you’re feeling burnt out with your TBR, this is a great book to stop and smell the roses (or pages). The Mating Game is exactly what it should be: hilarious, heartwarming and freaking sexy.” —Mekhala Villegas, Fountain Bookstore, Richmond, VA Second Chance Romance: A Harlot’s Bay Novel “Olivia Dade takes us back to Harlot’s Bay. This book will give you so much to think about.” —Brandy Herr, Arts & Letters Bookstore, Granbury, TX Tender Cruelty (Dark Olympus #9) Casablanca, Romance “Okay, this is 100% my favorite book of the series. The animosity that they (I say they, but I mean Callisto) had for each other at the beginning made their love at the end that much sweeter. The WORST part of this book is that it’s OVER.” —Amelia Yasuda, Queen Takes Book, Columbia, MD Supersaurio Square Press, Fiction “This book lets you know you’re not the only one that’s cried in the bathroom at work.
