Even though I knew Medusa’s ultimate fate, I wanted to go on this journey with her.” —Ginger Young, WordsWorth Books, Little Rock, AR Canticle & Grau, Historical Fiction “As a young woman in the 13th century, facing a future being married off to a man she doesn’t love, Aleys joins a group of women, beguines, who live a life of prayer and service. A most original tale of faith and power!” —Pat Rudebusch, Orinda Books, Orinda, CA The Bookshop Below Fantasy “Chiron’s Bookshop is where Cassandra grew up, but sinister forces are at play. An ode to bookshops and a somewhat cozy and paradoxically dark magical fantasy. An exciting read!” —Aerie Brown, Blue Willow Bookshop, Houston, TX House of Day, House of Night Lloyd-Jones (Transl.), Riverhead Books, Fiction “House of Day, House of Night is further proof of Olga Tokarczuk’s genius. Each fragment of this book creates a fablelike tapestry that illuminates deeper truths. articles.text: There was a large turnout of 26 readers on the patio at the Piedmont Community Hall on a cool November 3 for the monthly First Mondays Reading Group discussion. The group was there to talk about their December book, Differ We Must: How Lincoln Succeeded in a Divided America written by NPR’s Morning Edition host Steve Inskeep. The 2023 book examines Abraham Lincoln’s leadership through his interactions with 16 different people, many with whom he had disagreements. Some are wellknown people, but others are obscure. They range from William Seward to Cheyenne Chief Lean Bear. Inskeep uses these people to describe how Lincoln navigated a deeply divided nation. The book’s title comes from a letter that Lincoln wrote to his friend Joshua Speed. In it, Lincoln rebuked Speed for not opposing slavery. He wrote, “If, for this, we must differ, differ we must.” The book tells how Lincoln’s willingness to engage with those with whom he disagreed was crucial to his success. Additionally, Lincoln was a politician. Inskeep shows that because Lincoln was willing to engage in politics, meeting and working with critics, that he was able to keep the union united and lead the social revolution that ended slavery in our country. The acoustics inside the Community Hall can sometimes create hearing issues for the large group and they decided to try an experiment. Ivy Sandoval from the Recreation Department provided a wireless microphone and the readers passed it around during the discussion for them to share their views. The group thought that with the countless books that have been written about Lincoln it was hard to image this book would provide something new. However, for some, it was a totally different Lincoln story and very satisfying. This history was not only based on Lincoln’s actions, but also on others’ lives and voices too. The politics were fascinating and there was so much going on that Lincoln had to contend with. The readers liked that Lincoln was a “people person” as well as a “political creature.” He tempered his idealism and tailored his communications and actions for his audiences to accomplish what he needed to get done. He listened to everyone and then made his discissions. Additionally, the other people that Inskeep profiles had their own stories and they provided the readers with a better understanding of the times. Readers enjoyed some of these people as much as Lincoln. While most readers enjoyed the book, some had to differ. They felt there was too much detail and the “minutia” was more than they wanted. They were disappointed with the book and felt its introduction promised more than Inskeep delivered regarding solutions to our country’s current issues. Some readers didn’t see the relevance of minor characters. They wondered why Lincoln’s Illinois barber, the Native American chief, and some others were included, but the readers found it interesting that the barber was originally from Haiti. The narrative may have been interesting, but it could also be confusing at times. It seemed inevitable that the discussion would move to our nation’s current situation and political divide. Today seems to be another time when history is repeating itself. How can we hold conflicting, contradictory views and somehow reconcile them within ourselves? How could Jefferson proclaim that all men are created equal and be a slave owner? How can we be a “nation of immigrants” and treat immigrants so harshly? Is there a solution other than civil war to keep the country together? That was Lincoln’s primary goal, but it was voiced that Trump is no Lincoln. Politicians are putting self-interest over the country’s needs. Every generation has its own challenges, but ignorance and bigotry haven’t gone away. Inskeep implied that we need to have conversations and work together to resolve our differences, but neither he nor the readers seemed to have answers for making it really happen. The group did have a solution regarding the use of the wireless microphone for improving their conversation. Next month they will start the discussion by passing the microphone around the readers’ circle for each person to express their thoughts about the book and then let the conversation have a free flowing back and forth to understand their different perspectives more fully. Maybe that’s what our country needs, too. The readers had previously selected Cry, the Beloved County by Alan Paton for their January book and The Wide Wide Sea: Imperial Ambition, First Contact and the Fateful Final Voyage of Captain James Cook by Hampton Sides for their February read. After Darby Gregg’s presentation of three fiction candidates the group selected Harlem Shuffle by Colson Whitehead for their March book. It was a chilly day, so the readers took a group photo inside the Community Hall. The group will meet at the Community Hall for their next discussion on January 5th at 1:30 p.m. New readers are welcome and there is no fee to participate, Register at https://bit.ly/3R86PP4. Among those participating in the First Monday Reading Group’s discussion were Heidi Schmidt, Sarah Johnson, Bella Almanzan, Ken Young, Adrienne Hamlin, Martin Levy, Lisa Euphrat, Darby Gregg, Rich Siegel, Orrel Lanter, Mary Carter, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Alicia Rivera, Dick Carter, and discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus. The group was pleased that Rob White, Marj Blackwell, and Evie Stilwell were with them for the first time.
articles.title: First Monday Readers discuss Abraham Lincoln

articles.text: Beloved award-winning American Rom-Com comes to Piedmont How could the upcoming movie possibly be a success? It was to be filmed by Columbia, a second-class studio. MGM loaned Clark Gable out to star in the production, though he didn’t want to do it. His co-star, Claudette Colbert, didn’t want to do it either, and when filming was completed, she called it “the worst picture ever made.” Columbia had low expectations when they released it—but guess what? It went on to win all five major Academy Awards: Best Picture, Best Director, Best Writer, Best Actor, Best Actress. It was 1934’s It Happened One Night, often ranked high among the best American movies ever. Who can resist It Happened One Night? One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends and then chatting about it when the lights come up. That’s just what the Piedmont Flix Fest, which meets on the second Thursday of each month, offers: a great movie in a comfortable setting, and then a lively discussion of it afterward. The next film in the series is, indeed 1934’s It Happened One Night. Directed by Frank Capra, its plot is similar to that of Roman Holiday, which imitated it 30 years later. In the Capra film, spoiled heiress Ellie Andrews (Claudette Colbert) impetuously marries the gold-digging King Westley, leading her gruff tycoon father (Walter Connolly) to spirit her away on his yacht. After jumping ship, Ellie falls in with cynical newspaper reporter Peter Warne (Clark Gable), who offers to help her reunite with her new husband in exchange for an exclusive story. But during their travels, the reporter finds himself falling for the feisty young heiress. This is a pre-moral-code film, so the sexual innuendos are amusingly frank. It Happened One Night will be screened on Thursday, December 11 at 1:00 p.m. at the Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue. Doors will open at 12:45 p.m. The movie is free and available to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis. Everyone is welcome to bring snacks or lunch. The next movie in the Piedmont series is the 1992 comedy/ mystery My Cousin Vinny, starring Joe Pesci and Marissa Tomei, who won an Academy Award for her role. It will be shown on January 14th.
articles.title: It Happened One Night shown at Center for the Arts on Dec. 11

articles.text: There was a strong turnout of 45 walkers and three K-9 best friends at the Exedra last Wednesday for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group. Two special first-time walkers joined them as well: Piedmont Police Chief Frederick W. Shavies II and his assistant, April Fitzgerald. Before setting out, Chief Shavies was introduced to the group. He grew up in Oakland and attended Fremont High School, where he was an AllCity football player. He went on to Washington State University, played defensive end, and appeared in the Rose Bowl. After graduating, he joined the Oakland Police Department in 2006 and rose to deputy chief. He was appointed Piedmont’s police chief in July and has children in Piedmont schools. He has already registered for Walking on Wednesdays and hopes to join when his schedule allows. The morning’s route combined familiar paths with a few rarely visited corners of the city. The group wanted to see a unique home on Lexford Road, just off Hampton Road, a street they had not walked in two years. To begin with some beauty, the walkers moved behind the Exedra, past the Community Hall and Tea House, and up the Highland– Guilford steps in upper Piedmont Park. Completed in 2023 with support from the Piedmont Beautification Foundation, the $155,000 project replaced old wooden ties with concrete steps, landings, and handrails. It now offers a handsome entrance into the park. The group emerged on Highland Avenue and crossed to Sierra Avenue. Chief Shavies provided safe crossing for the large group throughout the morning. On Sierra, a Julia Morgan–designed home was undergoing extensive foundation and structural work. From there the walkers continued up Sheridan Avenue to Wildwood Avenue, through the Hall Fenway, and along Crocker Avenue to Hampton Road. They paused for a group photo with Chief Shavies at the park’s edge on King Avenue. The route continued along Hampton to Hampton Park and Field. Everyone made the climb up Hampton to Lexford and Huntleigh Roads. After crossing LaSalle Avenue, the group passed between two white pillars marking an entrance to the early twentieth-century St. James Woods Terrace neighborhood. Each sidewalk section in the development contains four distinctive terracotta tiles set into the concrete. At the Hampton Triangle on Lexford stands the first of two Piedmont Heritage Tree Southern magnolias within a long block of one another. The group continued uphill to the second magnolia at Huntleigh. Though native to the southeastern United States, Southern magnolias thrive in Piedmont, where many striking specimens can be found. The City Council Chief Shavies Walking with Dick Carter on Walking on Wednesday Walking on Wednesday in motion Among those participating were Jack Fischrup with K-9 best friend Kojak, Albert Chen, Dan Scdoris, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Mark Davis, Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Jim Kuo, Jim Kellogg, Cathy Laymon, Lisa Leonard, Chuck Oraftik, Priscilla Wanerus, Camille Scribner, Helen Dong, Mary Ann Barnes, Noemi Alvarado, Ragina O’Connor, Peggy Shultz, Stella Houston, Tina Shum, Garrett Clifford, Quincy Dong, Sherry Jacobs, Kat Lang, Ken Moy, Alissa Quan, Irene Thompson, Karin Fetherston, Lois Price, Phil Witte, Lori Austin, Pat Nicholas, Mary Carter, Sean Brient with K-9 best friend Pip, Caskey Mason, Rick Eigenbrode, Judy Love, Bonnie Sherwood with K-9 best friend Zippy, Claudine Bach, Laurie Leonard, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased that Neve Cohen was with them for the first time, walking with her mother, Sheila Leunig, and grandmother, Margaret Leunig. It was also extra special to have Chief Shavies and April Fitzgerald on the walk.

After crossing LaSalle Avenue, the group passed between two white pillars marking an entrance to the early twentieth-century St. James Woods Terrace neighborhood. Each sidewalk section in the development contains four distinctive terracotta tiles set into the concrete. At the Hampton Triangle on Lexford stands the first of two Piedmont Heritage Tree Southern magnolias within a long block of one another. The group continued uphill to the second magnolia at Huntleigh. Though native to the southeastern United States, Southern magnolias thrive in Piedmont, where many striking specimens can be found. The City Council created the Piedmont Heritage Tree Program in 2018 based on a Park Commission recommendation, and twenty-eight trees have been designated to date. The walkers then crossed Huntleigh to return to Lexford. Near Hampton they reached a 1939 brick storybook-style home, one of the highlights of the morning. Designed by architect and engineer Carr Jones, one of the Bay Area’s noted storybook builders, the home features a circular brick chimney, a wavy brick wall, a terracotta tile and slate roof, and a maze of bricks arranged in the front yard. A turret at the center gives it a small-castle look. A sign at the front door reads, “The Rooster Crows, but the Hen Delivers.” Architect and walker Jim Kellogg shared background from his time on the Piedmont Planning Commission. The home includes a distinctive brick garage addition to the right and a swimming pool in back. At one time there was a proposal for a two-story pool house, Jim said, but it was never approved. As the group admired the house, owner Eric Tupper stepped outside. He told the walkers that the home had been his wife’s childhood house and that their children built the brick maze as a Covid project using leftover materials from the property. He added that the radiant heating is his favorite feature. After visiting with Eric and taking in the unusual home, the group began its return trip. They followed Hampton, La Salle, and St. James Drive back toward Hampton Road, then retraced their earlier steps to the center of town. It was a slightly longer walk than usual, but the group enjoyed every minute of it, especially the chance to walk with Chief Shavies and Fitzgerald, who provided a gracious and steady police escort throughout the morning. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited. There is no charge, and new walkers and friendly K-9 best friends are always welcome. Registration is required. To sign up, visit https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu or call 510-420-3070 for more information. Chief Shavies Walking with Dick Carter on Walking on Wednesday Walking on Wednesday in motion Among those participating were Jack Fischrup with K-9 best friend Kojak, Albert Chen, Dan Scdoris, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Mark Davis, Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Jim Kuo, Jim Kellogg, Cathy Laymon, Lisa Leonard, Chuck Oraftik, Priscilla Wanerus, Camille Scribner, Helen Dong, Mary Ann Barnes, Noemi Alvarado, Ragina O’Connor, Peggy Shultz, Stella Houston, Tina Shum, Garrett Clifford, Quincy Dong, Sherry Jacobs, Kat Lang, Ken Moy, Alissa Quan, Irene Thompson, Karin Fetherston, Lois Price, Phil Witte, Lori Austin, Pat Nicholas, Mary Carter, Sean Brient with K-9 best friend Pip, Caskey Mason, Rick Eigenbrode, Judy Love, Bonnie Sherwood with K-9 best friend Zippy, Claudine Bach, Laurie Leonard, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased that Neve Cohen was with them for the first time, walking with her mother, Sheila Leunig, and grandmother, Margaret Leunig. It was also extra special to have Chief Shavies and April Fitzgerald on the walk.

Everest Base Camp’s accommodations were staggering, with large dining tents, cooking tents and hundreds of client tents with 5” thick mattresses. The team spent a day of “puja” or worship at a handcrafted stone altar and brought their mountaineering gear for blessing by the Sherpa high priest in a four-hour joyous ceremony. On Everest, “ice-falls” are some of the most treacherous features. The ice flows rapidly down steep portions of glaciers creating uneven crevassed surfaces amidst 100’ tall ice towers known as seracs. To prepare, guides had the team practice walking across metal ladders with crampons and boots while fully geared up. April 22 marked three weeks into the trip and the first ascent to Camp One, the start of the “rotations” up Everest itself. At 19,500’ the change in elevation caused Baringer to have a sleepless night and a mental battle over concerns he might have developed High-Altitude Pulmonary Edema and sleep apnea. Through that long night, BarBill Baringer crossing a crevasse on a sunny day near Base Camp. inger have serious consideration of canceling his trip. But by the next morning he shook off the night’s doubts with new resolve. On April 24 the team moved up to Camp Two at 21,500’. That day the temperature reached the 90s and required the arduous tasks of removing layers of clothing while climbing. While still suffering from a chest cough and trying to sleep at high elevation, Baringer said he felt his breath through two audible pathways as if he had a hole in his lungs, ear canal or throat. Combined with a gurgle in his lungs and chest pain, he further suspected High-Altitude Pulmonary Edema. The trip’s rotation called for a return to Everest Base camp and Baringer took the opportunity to go to the Himalayan Rescue Association health clinic, where he was diagnosed with pneumonia. Of this development Baringer said, “I was in trouble. Pneumonia and elevation are not a good combination.” The doctor prescribed four medications of steroids and antibiotics in an attempt to purge the pneumonia.The climbing company’s owner Mike Hamill recommended that Baringer rest for four days at Base Camp. Other climbers at Base Camp were battling sinusitis, coughing induced cartilage tears and broken ribs, bronchitis and hallucinations. Six of the original 24 climbers called off their trip at that point. But Baringer maintained his resolve and his teammates took notice. By Jay Russell Article originally published in the May 6, 2020 issue of the Piedmont Post. In April 2019 Piedmont climber Bill Baringer was at Lobuche base camp in the Himalayan mountain range, elevation 17,000’. He was recovering from a flu virus and had just twisted an ankle – and he was still 12,000’ away from the Everest summit. On April 14 he attempted to get back on schedule with the rest of the climbing group. Baringer and fellow climber Jay, who was also sick, arose at 2:00 a.m. for a bid at the Lobuche summit with guides Peema and Pemba. Baringer recalled, “It was unreasonably cold, requiring me to wear several layers inside my winter-rated sleeping bag.” Lobuche, a nondescript peak at 20,000’, is similar to Alaska’s Denali in height. It served as the first serious training ground for everyone to test their equipment, technique and feelings. Two hours into the climb Jay’s crampon suddenly detached from his mountaineering boot. This was unprecedented for him, having used the same mountaineering gear in many previous climbs without issue. When the crampon fell off again 10 minutes later, Pemba and Peema made adjustments to secure it. Then, to Baringer and the guides’ dismay, Jay suddenly stopped, and let them know that he wasn’t feeling it and was done. Baringer said, “What do you mean,you’re just quitting this peak right?” Jay replied, “Nope. I’m calling off my trip.” It was Jay’s third attempt at Everest, and he had a two-page resume of climbs around the world. Despite Baringer’s encouragement and support, his new ally and friend waved the white flag to the beast called Everest. articles.text: Montclair Village will shine bright on Thursday, December 11, when the Montclair Village Association welcomes the community to its 23rd annual Holiday Stroll from 4 to 8 p.m. More than 40 Village businesses will offer seasonal treats, shopping and dining promotions, live music, and plenty of holiday cheer. Families can stop by the F&M Bank Family Fun Zone for music and hands-on activities. Santa will be available for Winter Wonderland photos by Leah Marie Studio for $35. Kids can enjoy crafting tables and glowin-the-dark face painting. Entertainment will fill the Village throughout the evening, with performances by The Tap Dancing Christmas Trees, Edna Brewer Jazz Band, The Back Dimples Band, The Zesty Lemons Jazz Combo, and the Jazz Education Ensemble. Shops and restaurants will feature festive sweets, hot beverages, dining specials, unique gifts, and special offers. Vendor Lane returns with more than twenty local artisan vendors. In the spirit of giving, the Oakland Fire Department’s Random Acts Toy Drive and Parade Rig will be stationed outside Montclair Toyhouse, which is offering 20 percent off toy-drive purchases. Visitors can also warm up at the Stroll’s Hospitality Hut, serving cocoa, cocktails, and seasonal beverages. Proceeds support the Montclair Village Association, a nonprofit serving the community for more than seventy-five years. “The Holiday Stroll is a festive time shared with families, small businesses, local artists, and schools where we all come out to support our community. Come kick off the holiday season with shopping, food, and entertainment in our charming Montclair Village district,” said MVA board president Virginia Davis, co-owner of Yellow Door. Sponsors of this year’s Holiday Stroll include Flair Travel, Sliver Pizzeria, F&M Bank, Montclair Cares Club, Village Chiropractic and Wellness Center, and Supervisor Nate Miley. Thursday, December 11, 2025 4-8pm | Free | All Ages Montclair Village, 6235 La Salle Ave, Oakland CA 94611 The Tap Dancing Christmas Trees performing at the 2024 Holiday Stroll Photo by Peter Marcus. Early December snapped alert in near-Arctic blasts, when seemingly, merry villages materialized. Next Sunday a curious market, Le Hasard Ludique (The Playful Chance), promises crafted goods made in the district and held at the community hall (previously an old railroad station), and now serving as a bar and restaurant. At other markets, the merch takes second chair to the Christmas production, itself the experience. A few booths stocking carny merch, named for trinkets sold at old-timey carnivals, underperform in sales. But at Paris City Hall, snow gently drifts in a thick forest of fir trees twinkling with stars, and music and fragrance are in the air. All is well in the world, though the snow is a clever lighting illusion, and the music surrounds masterfully, kudos to a good quality sound system. Merci beaucoup. It was also a historic season for the doubles team of Samantha Huynh and Emma Chan, winning the school’s first WACC Doubles title at the individual tournament. With the girls’ tennis team, the singles order was led by freshman Ella Ruthven, while Chan jolted up the ranks to No. 1 doubles as a junior. Staff Photos Piedmont’s girls’ volleyball team achieved its first NCS berth since 2018 with a young roster. Resurgence of girls’ volleyball The girls’ volleyball team returned to form in 2025, accomplishing the school’s first berth in NCS since 2018 and finished with a 9-12 overall record. As the No. 8 seed, Piedmont lost to No. 9 Urban in the first round of the D4 playoffs in a heated fiveset match, 25-23, 15-25, 26-24, 24-26, 16-14. The emerging talent featured eight sophomores, including key players like Maika Ting, Allyson Huynh, Olivia Stevens, Mia Bechtel, Izara Dando, and Sophia Meyer. Freshman Carina Vora also turned out to be an important setter. Boys’ Water Polo back in NCS The boys’ water polo squad reached the Div, 2 NCS Quarterfinals as the No. 1 seed, falling in a heated overtime win with No. 9 Marin Academy, 10-9. To get there, they beat No. 16 St. Patrick 19-8 in the opening round. They finished with an 16-9 overall record with a cast that is poised for success in the future. Sophomores like Rylan Patty and Henry Stein lead the charge going into 2026, along with freshmen Ben Kappes and Wilson Walker. Photo by Jenni Tsoi Best The cross-country girls’ team reached the CIF State championship race in Woodward Park. Pictured are Nikita Gorelik (left), Viviane Oesterer, Skylar Best, Leighton Mand, Amalia Gray, Cora Chun, and Cora Brozowski Schrader. The Matadors scored the equalizer in the first minute of stoppage time at 80+1’. This time, they played a long pass from around midfield in behind. Granada’s forward took a shot on her first touch, rolling it in. Senior midfielder Elia Kwong during a foggy night at Miramonte. 2-nil loss to Miramonte Miramonte controlled the action through the opening 40 minutes without PHS recording any shot attempts. Piedmont goalkeeper Rachel Young recorded saves in the 15th and 30th minutes. PHS came out of the break with some renewed energy in the second half, recording its only shot on target in the 43rd minute when Liu lined up an attempt. However, Miramonte broke the deadlock in the 57th when a giveaway in the back allowed an easy goal. Miramonte made it 2-0 just six minutes later on a play in front of the net. articles.text: Editor: I am writing to express my concern about the City’s decision to end Piedmont Play School’s lease in the building that the Piedmont community built for it, effectively abandoning an institution that has served this community for decades. Nearly 25 years ago, Piedmont families — including my wife and me — partnered with the City to design, fund, and build a permanent home for PPS. Our design firm donated roughly onethird of the design and development costs. Parents fundraised and donated to cover another third, and the City contributed the remainder. The project was publicly described as PPS’s permanent home by city officials, in the press, and by the Piedmont families who contributed so generously to build it. Given that history, the City’s refusal to even discuss a lease extension feels like a profound breach of trust. Piedmont families invested time, money, and labor, believing they were building a permanent home for PPS — not a temporary rental to be reclaimed when convenient. After learning of the City’s decision, I met with the PPS Board and offered my help. I also spoke with councilmembers and administrators. Mark Delventhal, the retired Recreation Director who led the PPS discussions, called me personally to express his displeasure and confirmed to me that the building we built was intended as a permanent home for PPS as long as the school was in operation. Current City Council members and administrators have described the PPS cooperative model as “outdated,” noting that most parents are dual-income working families. They also said that PPS is “not at full capacity” and “out of step with the needs of the community,” and pointed to a waitlist of 41 children for full-time care. In response, I met with the PPS board and suggested offering full-time care while maintaining the cooperative elements that

articles.text: Photos by Dayle Ross Volunteers Ellen Reed, Randi Voorhies (former Piedmont Middle School teacher librarian), Helen Dittmer, Neil Ouye, and Ann Katz stand behind a fraction of the donated books. Community members yet again spearheaded a successful book donation drive during this year’s Turkey Trot Bib Pickup at the Piedmont Veterans’ Memorial Building. The final tally of books donated to the East Bay Children’s Book Project (EBCBP) was 4534, a haul requiring five “We are so grateful for the support we continue to receive from Piedmont!” said Ellen Reed, former Wildwood librarian. Reed is one of the active volunteers at the East Bay Children’s Book Project. She and her husband, Bill, helped unload all of the books. Ellen’s librarian’s patience aided her during the final count of books on Tuesday. City Council and School Board members founded this effort more than ten years ago. The book drive has now become a staple of the Turkey Trot Bib pickup. Combined with Dress-Best for Less also accepting donations during the bib pickup event residents can A couple of pugs proudly pose at the Thanksgiving Children’s Book Drive donation booth at the Turkey Trot Bib pickup. now count on the option to multitask seasonal donations and pre-Thanksgiving errands. The mission of EBCBP is to help build literacy by putting books into the hands of children who have little or no access to them. articles.text: The planning permit counter. New Planning & Building permit fees will go into effect on January 1 in Piedmont. The adjustments are designed to better align each permit’s fee structure with the true cost of processing the permit. Most permit fees will increase to reflect the actual staff time spent on the permit. In some cases, fees will decrease. A complete list of new fees is available on the City’s website at piedmont.ca.gov/permits. Key changes • New and expanded categories: New permit types have been added to reflect recent changes in State law. Certain existing fees, such as solar permits, will be expanded into separate categories for residential and commercial projects. • Added valuation tiers: The new fee schedule adds two new valuation tiers for very large construction projects ($10 million and $25 million), scaling fees proportionally with the complexity of review. • Flat-fee conversions: Many common building permits (such as water heaters, HVAC systems, and EV chargers) will be converted from valuation-based to flat Photo courtesy of the city fees, making costs more predictable and aligned with the service provided. The goal is not to raise revenue, but to ensure each permit type is charged fairly and in proportion to the staff time and resources required to process it. The fee updates were adopted by City Council in September, following a comprehensive study. Considered a best practice in municipal operations, fee studies compare the cost of providing services to the fees charged to ensure they are fair, transparent, and based on data. Piedmont’s fee study found that the fees were only recovering 73% of the cost of permit services, resulting in a loss of revenue of more than $400,000 per year. The fee study was initiated by the City Council during the FY24-25 budget process, along with an organizational assessment. Together, these reviews aim to strengthen the Planning & Building Department’s capacity to provide timely, high-quality service to the community. The fee updates are the next step in aligning operations with best practices, ensuring services are delivered efficiently, equitably, and sustainably.
articles.title: New Planning & Building permit fees take effect Jan. 1

articles.text: The City of Piedmont has completed its storm drain improvement project. The city has upgraded the drainage infrastructure at eight locations and is in the process of repairing or replacing 20 sewer or storm drain maintenance holes (“manholes”). The total budget for the project is $632,008, funded from the City’s Facilities Capital Fund. Storm drain improvements consist of replacing drainage inlets, replacing outdated grates, and, in some cases, upsizing sections of storm drain pipe at problem areas throughout Piedmont. Each location prioritized for upgrades is considered a “hotspot” that routinely experiences flooding during storm events. These locations previously required ongoing monitoring and maintenance from Public Works crews. According to Piedmont’s communications manager, Echa Schneider, there are three main reasons for these upgrades. “First, some of these inlets have always been undersized – New Inlet on St James Trenching for new pipe at Sharon Avenue they were inadequate for their location even when they were first installed. Second, in some locations, infrastructure has simply deteriorated over time. Finally, infrastructure that was previously adequate is no longer sufficient as we experience more intense storms, more often due to climate change,” Schneider said. During the upsizing process of the inlets, Piedmont has decided to oversize these inlets to include a detention area to hold excess water and properly deal with peak storm conditions. “Providing that extra holding capacity is an efficient way to adapt our infrastructure to accommodate these more intense storms – allowing us to get water underground and prevent flooding during peak flow,” said Schneider. For the manhole repairs, these are being performed at locations Photos courtesy of the City where the city has identified groundwater leaking into the sanitary sewer system during storms. Where the city can do so economically, they’re replacing the maintenance hole. Where replacement is not economical, the city will rehabilitate them with a new lining. In both cases, the goal is to make them watertight. All storm drain upgrades have been completed. There are a few maintenance holes repairs left to do. The city says it should be wrapped up within the next couple of weeks. The eight locations are: Monticello Avenue Artuna Avenue St. James Drive Dracena Avenue Park Way Oakland Avenue Dracena Park trail Sharon Avenue Storm drain work underway at St James

articles.text: Piedmont resident and former syndicated journalist William Gee Wong has won a PEN America Literary Award for his memoir Sons of Chinatown. PEN awards promote writers of all cultural and racial backgrounds and educate the public and media about the nature of multicultural work. The winners will be recognized at the 36th annual PEN Oakland award event on Saturday, December 6, from 2-5 p.m. at the Black Repertory Group Theater. Wong said he was honored to receive the award, “I was very pleased to get the award because at least PEN Oakland and Ishmael recognize the value of the story that I’m telling,“ he said. Sons of Chinatown is a memoir about the impact of the Chinese Exclusion Act on one immigrant family that connects China to America through Oakland’s Chinatown. The book discusses the relationship and differences in the lives of Wong and his father. Wong first thought of writing the book in 2011 during a New Year’s party hosted at his residence. “2012, would be the centennial of my father’s arrival from China to America. I wanted to tell my father’s story to my family, because we are four generations now in America, and many of the younger people in our family don’t know his story,” Wong said. Wong spent 13 years researching and writing his memoir and eventually having it published it in 2024. “It was a search for who my father was and a search for who I am,” Wong said. Sons of Chinatown carries themes of identity and the pursuit of the American dream – how his father immigrated to America during the Chinese exclusion era of America, and how he found a home in Oakland’s Chinatown. Wong grew up trying to discover who he was as a first-generation Sons of Chinatown bookxover American. “Sons of Chinatown is really almost a testimonial to the good America. And by good America, I mean the America that welcomes immigrants from all over the world, that gives us, the descendants, many opportunities to try to achieve the American dream,” Wong said. The Wong’s family restaurant in Oakland Chinatown from 1943 to 1961. Photo courtesy of Oakland Public Library

articles.text: Kim and I are true believers in the magic of Piedmont. Returning from a weekend away, my first thought while driving down Moraga was, “There is no place I’d rather raise my children.” I think about this each year while racing in the Turkey Trot, watching the Fourth of July parade, volunteering at Harvest Festival, and enjoying the tree lighting ceremony. Can you believe that the Piedmont Beautification Foundation is 61 years old? PEF just celebrated 50 years of community members supporting our schools. Dress Best for Less has been finding a new home for our clothes for 40 years. And, as a cancer survivor, I’m proud to say this community has supported research through the Cancer League for more than 52 years. This is our community and this is why we are here. At the heart of it all are our schools, and it’s up to us to keep them vibrant. As parents, we lead our robotics teams, we coach soccer, softball, and basketball, and we volunteer in the libraries, serving lunch, and at career fairs. And Kim and I are completing our third year as Giving Campaign chairs. We are thankful for all the time parents put into volunteering, and so very thankful for the financial support that your families provide our schools. Together, our contributions make up nearly 7% of our schools budget. That might not seem like a large number, but believe us it makes all the difference. Imagine what our schools would like without those funds. Larger class sizes, less qualified teachers, fewer counselors, and the list goes on.

articles.text: The Piedmont School Board recently added a Modern World History Honors course for sophomores, another weighted class in the growing list of courses available to PHS students next year. Like many high-performing Bay Area communities, PHS students increasingly feel pressure to take harder classes earlier, leaving them tracked into pathways long before they understand their interests. Early honors tracks push PHS toward narrow college prep, locking students into rigid pathways instead of fostering curiosity and exploration. Moder n World Histor y teacher Hayley Adams recalled first hearing about the proposal for the honors course from an email survey sent to students. She explained that she “had no idea” the course was being considered until she stumbled upon the notice and shared it with colleagues. Adams and fellow teacher Melanie McCauley designed the class using the strengths of the existing College Prep course and resources Adams had already developed. Although proud of the final curriculum, Adams said she is “saddened that sophomores will now be split up even more… in a kind of tracked system,” which she believes undermines diverse peer groups and shared learning experiences. Academic tracking separates students into standard, honors, or AP classes early, and those choices shape nearly everything they take later. Honors students are expected to continue on advanced paths, while others struggle to catch up, leading over time to different teachers, peers, and academic identities all based on a decision made at fourteen. The board had initially planned to adopt AP World History, which many felt would increase pressure, but Adams and McCauley’s month-long effort to create the honors alternative stopped that proposal. Unlike AP World History, which spans nearly twice the time period and focuses on a high-stakes exam, the honors class covers 1500 to the present with more flexibility and depth, emphasizing analytical reading, historiographical writing, interdisciplinary projects, activities like Model UN, and Harkness-style discussions. The history department works with English to align themes and texts across subjects. As English teacher Beth Black explained, Harkness discussions let students “pull from English texts, real world events, and historical perspectives” to deepen learning. She added that the method “takes time and dedication… to use effectively” and creates a “very intense history class” experienced only by honors students, widening the gap between sophomores. While many see the course as a valuable opportunity for students who want more challenge, others worry about its effect on school culture. AP U.S. History teacher David Keller noted that Modern World History does not fully prepare students for the junior weighted history class, but adding honors could push tracking even earlier, raising the question of how students will ever be adequately prepared. He asked, “How will 10th grade students get prepared for Honors Modern World History? The answer seems to be to make an honors ninth grade history class, which will necessitate an eighth grade class…” He also cautioned that APUSH could become more difficult for students who skip honors in sophomore year, as teachers may assume they already possess skills taught in the honors course. Student experiences with the current Modern World History class vary, but many seniors who took the standard course feel it prepared them well without the added pressure of a weighted grade. Senior Quincy Antaya explained that a weighted class might have shifted her focus toward grades instead of analytical thinking. Donovan Sar-Garza felt the current course already teaches essential skills. “The school doesn’t do a great job between the jump between freshman year and sophomore year” said sophomore Diego Branneria. Meanwhile, students like Lucia Dorsey, who enjoy history, welcomed the idea of greater depth. Even supporters of an honors option recognize its cultural impact. Catie Osborn and Kim Hunter are Co-Chairs of Piedmont School District’s’ annual Giving Campaign E v e n t C a l e n d a r By Evolette Mak The Piedmont School Board recently added a Modern World History Honors course for sophomores, another weighted class in the growing list of courses available to PHS students next year. Like many high-performing Bay Area communities, PHS students increasingly feel pressure to take harder classes earlier, leaving them tracked into pathways long before they understand their interests. Early honors tracks push PHS toward narrow college prep, locking students into rigid pathways instead of fostering curiosity and exploration. Moder n World Histor y teacher Hayley Adams recalled first hearing about the proposal for the honors course from an email survey sent to students. She explained that she “had no idea” the course was being considered until she stumbled upon the notice and shared it with colleagues. Adams and fellow teacher Melanie McCauley designed the class using the strengths of the existing College Prep course and resources Adams had already developed. Although proud of the final curriculum, Adams said she is “saddened that sophomores will now be split up even more… in a kind of tracked system,” which she believes undermines diverse peer groups and shared learning experiences. Academic tracking separates students into standard, honors, or AP classes early, and those choices shape nearly everything they take later. Honors students are expected to continue on advanced paths, while others struggle to catch up, leading over time to different teachers, peers, and academic identities all based on a decision made at fourteen. The board had initially planned to adopt AP World History, which many felt would increase pressure, but Adams and McCauley’s month-long effort to create the honors alternative Modern World History Honors class added for next year stopped that proposal. Unlike AP World History, which spans nearly twice the time period and focuses on a high-stakes exam, the honors class covers 1500 to the present with more flexibility and depth, emphasizing analytical reading, historiographical writing, interdisciplinary projects, activities like Model UN, and Harkness-style discussions. The history department works with English to align themes and texts across subjects. As English teacher Beth Black explained, Harkness discussions let students “pull from English texts, real world events, and historical perspectives” to deepen learning. She added that the method “takes time and dedication… to use effectively” and creates a “very intense history class” experienced only by honors students, widening the gap between sophomores. While many see the course as a valuable opportunity for students who want more challenge, others worry about its effect on school culture. AP U.S. History teacher David Keller noted that Modern World History does not fully prepare students for the junior weighted history class, but adding honors could push tracking even earlier, raising the question of how students will ever be adequately prepared. He asked, “How will 10th grade students get prepared for Honors Modern World History? The answer seems to be to make an honors ninth grade history class, which will necessitate an eighth grade class…” He also cautioned that APUSH could become more difficult for students who skip honors in sophomore year, as teachers may assume they already possess skills taught in the honors course. Student experiences with the current Modern World History class vary, but many seniors who took the standard course feel it prepared them well without the added pressure of a weighted grade. Senior Quincy Antaya explained that a weighted class might have shifted her focus toward grades instead of analytical thinking. Donovan Sar-Garza felt the current course already teaches essential skills. “The school doesn’t do a great job between the jump between freshman year and sophomore year” said sophomore Diego Branneria. Meanwhile, students like Lucia Dorsey, who enjoy history, welcomed the idea of greater depth. Even supporters of an honors option recognize its cultural impact. As weighted classes expand into 10th and potentially 9th grade, taking them can feel less like a choice and more like an unspoken requirement. At PHS, this academic arms race pressures students to “keep up” rather than explore interests or form new relationships. Sophomores, still adjusting to high school, may take on heavier loads, increasing stress and reducing community. The more students are divided into rigid pathways, the harder it is to meet new peers, discover unexpected interests, or experience high school beyond competition. Now that Honors Modern World History is permanent, the challenge is to ensure that it does not deepen segmentation or narrow students’ experiences. The school must prioritize balance: rigor without needless acceleration, opportunity without stratification, and learning that preserves shared experiences. In light of upcoming course registration, students should remember to choose classes not just for weighted GPA or perceived college advantage, but for genuine interest and growth. Colleges care less about how many advanced courses you take and more about how those classes have shaped your thinking, curiosity, and character. Evolette Mak is a senior at Piedmont High School and an intern with the Piedmont Post. articles.text: More than 20 students from Piedmont High School and Piedmont Middle School spent the Saturday before Thanksgiving volunteering at CityTeam Oakland. They helped prepare and serve a community meal for people experiencing homelessness. The event, organized annually through Piedmont Community Church, is a long-standing tradition that brings local families CityTeam Oakland provides meals, groceries and shelter services throughout the year. The Saturday meal is one of its regular community gatherings and offers guests a warm place to share food. Students and parent volunteers prepared pot roast, baked ziti, vegetables and apple crisp. Wearing white shirts and black pants, students greeted guests, served meals and cleared tables. Nearly two hundred meals were served, and extra portions were packaged for the next day. “These students spent countless hours planning, preparing and serving a nutritious meal at CityTeam Oakland for those experiencing homelessness. Seeing young people lead with such humility, strength and love gives me immense hope for the world they are shaping,” said Kerry Perschitte of Piedmont Community Church. Her comments matched the atmosphere in the dining room, where students stayed busy throughout the evening and guests expressed appreciation for the meal and the volunteers. Students said meeting guests was a meaningful part of the evening. Piedmont High School junior Jordan Palsa said, “I really enjoyed cooking and meeting all of those wonderful people and seeing the smiles on their faces.” The event reflected Piedmont Community Church’s ongoing commitment to service and offered students, families and CityTeam guests a thoughtful start to the holiday season. Organizers with the church’s NextGen program hope to build on this momentum through future service projects at CityTeam and the Alameda Food Bank and encourage local families to join them. Piedmont students and parent volunteers serving at CityTeam Oakland included Thomas Moison, Leyton Poole, Colin Amen, Cora and Willa Brozowski Schrader, Anna Benson, Arndt Schrader, Jane Saunders, Jordan Palsa, Mehrad Malekpour, Ben Mittan, Andre Stolicny, Clara Shum, Paula Rios, Orna Brodie, Mia Borsodi, Evan Jahn, Eva Stolicny, Saya Presley, Marta Stolicny, Evodio Kaltenecker, and other adult volunteers.

articles.text: When it comes to building a child’s vocabulary, parents often imagine flashcards, worksheets, or structured lessons. While these tools have their place, the most powerful vocabulary lessons often happen naturally—during daily routines and ordinary moments at home. As a speech-language pathologist, I’ve seen how simple, everyday activities can provide rich opportunities for language growth and comprehension, helping children develop the words they need to communicate effectively. Everyday Conversations Matter Vocabulary grows when children are exposed to new words in meaningful contexts. Mealtime, cooking, laundry, or grocery shopping can all become language lessons. Describing what’s happening, labeling objects, and talking about actions encourages children to connect words with real experiences. For example, asking a child to help “measure the flour” or “fold the towels” introduces verbs and nouns in a practical context. Ask Questions That Invite Thinking Instead of yes/no questions, try open-ended prompts that encourage children to explain, predict, or compare. Questions like “Why do you think the cake needs to bake?” or “Which shirt should we wear today and why?” encourage children to articulate ideas, use descriptive language, and practice reasoning. This not only expands vocabulary but also strengthens critical thinking skills. Read Together—Interactively Reading remains one of the best ways to grow vocabulary. Make it interactive: pause to discuss new words, ask your child to predict what will happen next, or connect the story to real-life experiences. Picture books, nonfiction texts, or even comic strips can all introduce new concepts and language in fun, engaging ways. Use Play and Hands-On Activities Play is a natural way to build language. Pretend play, building blocks, art projects, or even outdoor exploration offer opportunities to describe actions, colors, shapes, and materials. Encourage children to narrate what they are doing or explain their choices. This not only reinforces vocabulary but also strengthens narrative skills—an important foundation for reading comprehension. Model Rich Language Yourself Children learn by imitation. Use descriptive words, varied sentence structures, and expressive language in your own speech. Instead of “Put your shoes on,” try “Can you carefully tie your blue sneakers so they don’t come undone?” Small changes in everyday language expose children to more words naturally, without pressure or drills. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of SPEECH Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language, reading and writing. She can be reached at kathryn.pengilly@speechinc. com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com. Christmas Trees are here Open Wednesday to Sunday • 8:30 am - 5:00 pm

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, free compostable bags are available at City Hall to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. Compostable bags are also available from Republic Services (1-800-320-8077) for a fee. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: Piedmont’s quest for its first NCS title since 1976 came up short, falling 37-23 to Middletown. Staff Photos Piedmont High’s quest for a North Coast Section title came to an end on Friday, November 28, losing in the Div. 7 championship 37-23 to No. 1 seed Middletown under the lights of Justin-Siena’s Dodd Stadium in Napa As the No. 2 seed, the game marked a moment of triumph for the football program which nearly became extinct a few years ago. It was the school’s first NCS Final appearance since its 1976 win. This year’s team put itself in rarified air as the only other team to do so in the school’s 104-yearold history. “This was a meaningful game. We’re building character, we’re going to learn from it and grow. We’re looking forward to the future,” said PHS coach Jordan Seiden. The loss was similar to Piedmont’s early-season 32-17 loss to the same school on September 5. The Mustangs leaned on running backs Tyler Galamay and Trenton Griffith in September and did it again on Friday night in Napa. “All season I’ve been yelling about tackling. We weren’t great at it tonight and it showed its ugly head. We had some opportuniXavier Henderson pictured here during his long 73-yard run in the second quarter. ties, and had a chance to take the lead in the third quarter, but the second half started ugly,” Seiden said. Piedmont finishes its season 8-5 overall, including a six-game winning streak after being 2-4 at one point. “After we lost 63-7 to Hayward we got back on our feet. Our team really bonded, and now I hope the guys next year can do it. That game against Hayward really was a switch for us. We decided that we had to stop blaming each other and work as a group,” senior lineman Adrian Kondakov said. Despite the defeat, the titleberth is a one-game improvement over last year’s NCS loss in the semifinals. Remarkably, Piedmont got to the championship game this year after a change of starters from the 2024 team at nearly every position. It was a close game going into halftime with Piedmont trailing by just two points, 16-14. Xavier Henderson had a huge run less than a minute before halftime when he switched the field on a screen pass, broke several tackles and took the ball 73 yards to Middletown’s one-yard line. It enabled Colby Hong to score a touchdown, but Henderson was tackled hard at the end of the run and was forced to play sparingly in the second half. “He got shaken up. When your best player goes out, it forces you to scramble. It hurts to lose your best player,” Seiden said. articles.text: Photos by Jenni Tsoi Best Piedmont’s girls’ cross country reached State for the first time since 2019. Pictured are Nikita Gorelik (left), Viviane Oesterer, Skylar Best, Leighton Mand, Amalia Gray, Cora Chun, and Cora Brozowski Schrader. Piedmont High’s girls’ cross country team made its way to Woodward Park for the 2025 CIF State Cross Country Championship on Saturday, November 29. With 438 points, the Highlanders finished the day in 18th of 25 schools in the Division 4 category. It marked the first Piedmont’s team qualified for State since 2019, while continuing the school’s 37-year tradition of having at least one athlete qualify for the state championships. “The PHS Varsity girls team culminated their season with a trip to the state meet, the first since 2019. The girls ran for each other all season and they ran as a pack – that was their strength,” said coach Steve Zirkelbach.. Leading the charge for the Highlanders was junior Leighton Mand, who placed 96th in a field of 205 runners with a time of 19:52.3 on the 5,000-meter course. Mand finished as Piedmont’s top runner in eight meets this season, including the De La Salle Nike Invitational on September 20, the WACC Championship on November 8, and the North Coast Section Championship on November 22. “It’s not easy to get to the State meet,” Zirkelbach said. “There are so many obstacles to endure, from the long season which can result in fatigue or injuries.” Behind Mand was senior Skylar Best in 112th, with a time of 20:13.8. It marked her second CIF State appearance after last competing at State as a freshman in 2022. “It’s great to bookend my high school career in this way. It’s so much more meaningful for me to qualify as a team instead of just as an individual. It’s really special,” Best said. Viviane Oesterer was next in for Piedmont, finishing 118th in 20:19.7, while Amalia Gray was behind her 11 spots in 129th in 20:35.2. Rounding out Piedmont’s best five runners was senior Cora Chun, clocking a 20:44.5 to finish 133rd. Chun had to persevere through an early-season injury and came on strong late in the season. “Cora Chun’s return from an early season injury really helped the team, as did the steady performances of the rest of the team,” Zirkelbach said. Looking ahead to next year’s team, the Highlanders could bring back a strong group poised to push for another State berth. Of PHS’ top eight runners on the varsity roster, only Best and Chun are set to graduate. That means lead runners like Mand, Gray, and Oesterer could be back in the fold, while junior Cora Brozowski Schrader, sophomore Nikita Gorelik, and freshman Kelsey Coleman provide considerable talent. “Our third runner, Viviane, and Cora Brozowki Schrader continued to get faster and show their racing grit. That’s something that I look forward to using as the foundation for next year’s team,” Zirkelbach said. Skylar Best ran the final race of her Piedmont cross country career. She was a four-year starter and last qualified for State as an individual in 2022. Leighton Mand led the way for Piedmont, placing 96th of 205 runners.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ basketball team got its season started in a strong way on Saturday, November 29. The Highlanders visited Gateway in San Francisco and returned with a one-sided 84-50 victory. It was a big game for senior leader Dillon Casey, logging a team-high 22 points. He scored half of his points in the third quarter, where he scored eight points from the field and another three at the free throw line. “Dillon is an unbelievable ball handler and has an ability to get to the basket. He’s able to make plays and also dump off passes to people around the 3-point line,” coach Ben Spencer said. PHS also had two other scorers in double figures, senior P.J. Brayer with 17 and junior Lucian Fang-Ring with 16. Brayer lit up the scoreboard in the first quarter with 12 points, including two 3-pointers. “P.J. grew as a player last year. He cleans up the boards, can get to the basket, and can also shoot, Spencer said. Fang-Ring, meanwhile, hit four 3-pointers on the night. He had 10 of his points in the third quarter, where he knocked down a pair of threes and converted all four of his free throw attempts. “He’s really worked on his ball-handling and kept up with his shooting. He’s a knockdown shooter, and we’re hoping he can hit 40 to 50 percent. He’ll get good looks with teams having to send a second defender over to other players,” Spencer said. Piedmont looks ahead to their annual Winter Classic tournament at Binks Rawlings Gym, opening with Arroyo on Thursday, December 4. Game Recap Piedmont led 22-9 through the first quarter and took a 36-22 lead into halftime. They nearly P.J. Brayer scored 17 points against Gateway. Staff Photos Dillon Casey led Piedmont with 22 points in Piedmont’s seasonopening win over Gateway. doubled their score with a huge 35-point performance in the third quarter while only allowing 13 points, extending the gap to 71-35 lead. PHS added 13 more points in the fourth while allowing 15—84-50. Brayer scored 12 of Piedmont’s 22 points in the first quarter, while Casey added seven and Fang-Ring scored a three. Gateway got four of its nine points at the free throw line. In the second quarter, Casey and Beach Lorin led the way with four points apiece. Fang-Ring hit another three, while junior Ollie Dougan scored his first varsity point in purple and white with a 3-pointer of his own. The Highlanders’ huge 35-point third quarter featured Casey scoring 11 points and Fang-Ring scoring 10. Fang-Ring hit two 3-pointers in the quarter, while both Casey and Lucian did well at the stripe—scoring seven points by way of free throws. With the game well in-hand, PHS added 13 in the fourth, including 3-pointers by Nicholas Riordan, Cash Panico, and Dougan. Sophomore Yoseph Baskin scored four points for his first varsity baskets. Final stats: Casey had 22 points, Brayer scored 17, FangRing had 16, Lorin scored nine, Dougan had eight, Panico and Riordan had three, while Ruben Cohen had two. Tuesday vs. Envision Academy Piedmont hosted Envision on Tuesday, December 2. See next week’s Post for game details. NEXT UP Piedmont (1-0 overall) hosts Arroyo for the first round of the Piedmont Winter Classic on Thursday, December 4 at 7 p.m. They are also set to play on Friday and Saturday, December 5-6. Lucian Fang-Ring had 16 points in Piedmont’s season opening game.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ basketball team isn’t sneaking up on anyone this year. Matter of fact, there’s now a target on their backs. The Highlanders return to Binks Rawlings Gym for the 2025-26 season after finishing last year with a 25-6 record. Piedmont reached the North Coast Section Open Division as the No. 5 seed and fought their way to the Division 1 CIF State Regional Semifinals as the No. 8 seed. They did all that with a roster that featured three freshmen, Jenelle Solis, Andrea Martin, and Savannah Dennig, and one sophomore Taylor White. Now with an added year of experience, coach Bryan Gardere knows that everyone in the basketball community has their eyes on Piedmont. “Our schedule is tougher and there’s no sneaking up on anybody. We’re going to get the best of the teams we’re going against. No one truly knows your expectations your freshman year, but now can you match those expectations? Our whole thing is we’re trying to compete and work hard every day, you have to hold that bar really high,” Gardere said. Martin, Solis, Dennig and White burst onto the scene last year. Martin was the first freshman to be named honorable mention for Athlete of the Year by the Post. “Andrea is a big guard, but she can play one through five. We expect her to do a little bit of everything. We’re excited for her and think she can handle all those responsibilities,” Gardere said. Solis was the Post’s Freshman of the Year, showing her quality and savvy as Piedmont’s primary ball handler. She was named the Western Alameda County Conference Player of the Year. “Jenelle is looking to build off her MVP year. She’s a big part of what we do. We really leaned on her to be the primary ball handler. Her shooting and finishing has gotten even better during the offseason,” Gardere said. Dennig was honorable mention for Freshman of the Year and very much embodied the heart and soul of the team. articles.text: Soccer team promoted to National Premier League The Piedmont Soccer Club (PSC) 2014 Girls Purple capped off a landmark season with a 2–0 win over Revolution FC, closing Fall 2025 with both strong results and a place in club history. The team finished second in Pre-National Premier League and, in the process, became the first team in Piedmont Soccer Club history to compete at the NPL 1 level — the highest statewide competitive tier for their age group. For a team that has focused on steady development over several years, the achievement represents a significant milestone. The group’s upward trajectory began last year, when they captured the Fall League Gold title, earning advancement into the East Bay Premier bracket. Their performance validated the team’s potential and led to promotion into Pre-NPL, where they spent this season competing against some of the strongest U12 female teams in Northern California. Their second-place finish not only secured an NPL 1 placement for Spring 2026 but also boosted their standing heading into State Cup. The team enters the final stages of the competition seeded #6 in NorCal, with an opportunity to reach the top 16 for the second consecutive year. Piedmont SC Director of Coaching Dan Chubbock praised the group’s achievements. “The 2014 Girls Purple under Coach Matt have had another outstanding season,” he said. “They stepped up a division, which they knew was going to be a challenge, and not only did they compete — they ended up second! The girls are extremely hard workers and play some excellent soccer. They demonstrate what it means to be a Highlander, and we are so proud of their continued success.” The roster draws players from several schools across Piedmont, Alameda, Berkeley, Oakland, and San Leandro yet the group’s chemistry has become one of its defining strengths. The 11-member PSC 2014 Girls Purple team features a balanced mix of talent across the field: Anna Khrabrova (Forward); Arianna Algarate (Defense); Athena Lee (Defense); Audrey Frantz (Midfield); Clara Tran (Midfield/Forward); Eloise McDowell (Midfield/Defense); Fia Sims (Forward); Zoe Tang (Midfield/Defense); Livia Bennett (Goalkeeper); and Team Captains Ava Gonzales (Midfield) & Saya Lal (Midfield/Defense). Coach Matt Spencer-Harty credited the team’s success to their collective mindset and their willingness to embrace a demanding style of play. “I’m incredibly proud of this 2014 group. Finishing 2nd in NPL and earning promotion to NPL 1 is an exceptional accomplishment, especially for a team that, on paper, isn’t always the most physically imposing or naturally standout team. What has always set these girls apart is their collective commitment, the hours of work they’ve put in, their willingness to be coached, and their belief in a true possession-based, intelligent style of football.” “We’ve built our success on structure, teamwork, and identity. These players bought into a demanding game model that requires bravery on the ball, patience, movement, and complete trust in one another. They’ve embraced building through the thirds, understanding positional rotations, and controlling games through disciplined possession.” With the State Cup entering its decisive rounds, the team’s focus now turns to building on their momentum. A second straight appearance in the top 16 remains within reach, and the team is eager for the opportunity. Regardless of the final result, the season stands as a historic one for PSC — and for a young team that continues to set new standards for itself. Spencer-Harty will soon step into a new role at Piedmont High School (PHS) as head coach. “My goal is to bring that same tactical clarity, attention to detail, and footballing identity to the program,” he said. “If we can bring the same mentality, unity, and commitment that this 2014 group has modeled so consistently, I truly believe we can build something special at PHS as well.” Piedmont Soccer Club’s 2014 Girls qualified for the National Premier League’s top division. articles.text: The San Francisco Symphony will perform George Frideric Handel’s Messiah, a musical meditation on Christ’s birth, life, and resurrection, this Friday, December 5 and Saturday, December 6. Conductor Jane Glover leads the symphony and chorus in this classic holiday favorite. Glover is a fellow of the Royal College of Music and was the artistic director of opera at the Royal Academy of Music between 2009 and 2016. In December 2013, she became the third woman ever to conduct at the Metropolitan Opera of New York, leading Mozart’s The Magic Flute. Performances include Susanna Phillips as soprano, Jennifer Johnson Cano as mezzo-soprano, Josh Lovell as tenor, and Will Liverman as baritone. Davies Symphony Hall will be decked out for the holidays during these performances, filled with lit evergreen trees, wreaths and garlands. The hall’s lobby bar will feature festive winter cocktails, including a Gingerbread Old Fashioned, limited-time sparkling wine and holiday-themed desserts throughout December. The Friday and Saturday performances both begin at 7:30 p.m. A preconcert talk by San Francisco Symphony’s resident lecturer Laura Stanfield Prichard will be presented onstage at 6:30 p.m. before both performances. The preconcert talk is free to all ticketholders. Tickets are on sale now. Visit https://www.sfsymphony.org/ Buy-Tickets/2025-26/ H ANDEL-MESSIAH or call the box office at (415) 864-6000 to purchase tickets. Jennifer Johnson Cano

articles.text: Cast of Sunday in the Park with George Shotgun Players closes out its 2025 season with a new production of Sunday in the Park with George, the Pulitzer Prize–winning musical by Stephen Sondheim and James Lapine, showing now through December 30 at the Ashby Stage in Berkeley. Directed by Susannah Martin with music direction by David Möschler, the show is inspired by Georges Seurat’s pointillist painting A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte. The musical explores the artist’s obsessive creative process and its impact on his relationships. The production features immersive on-stage seating and an expanded bar menu. “This musical captures the questioning, fear, joy, and obsession that go into making art and the toll it takes on the people we love,” Director Susannah Martin said in a press release. “I’ve never experienced a musical which gets so deeply into the experience of being an artist and the process of making art.” “The sound-world of the show is just as daring, provocative, interesting, and non-traditional as the type of art that the character of George Seurat was striving to create,” added Möschler. “It’s not book scenes followed by songs belted out ad nauseum; it’s a score that is interwoven through dialogue and comes together more like a film score that helps create a strong sense of narrative and dramatic continuity from beginning to end.” Kevin Singer stars as George, with Marah Sotelo as Dot. The cast includes Alex Rodriguez, Laura Domingo, Jill Slyter and a 16-member ensemble. Artistic Director Patrick Dooley called the work a “legitimate masterpiece,” adding, “Sondheim captures the tension between artist and muse, beautifully and tragically.” Tickets and performance details are available at shotgunplayers.org.
articles.title: Sunday in the Park with George playing at Ashby Stage now through Dec. 30

articles.text: Piedmont resident and jewelry appraiser Sacha Grippando will share highlights from her recent jewelry trip to London at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Thursday, December 11. Doors open at 6 p.m., and beverages and festive snacks will be provided. Her talk will explore London’s history as a global center for jewelry manufacturing from the nineteenth century to today. Grippando will also walk attendees through current exhibitions at the Victoria and Albert Museum, Buckingham Palace, the Tower of London and the noted jewelry dealer Wartski. The program includes a look at contemporary work from London designers such as Solange Azagury-Partridge and Jessica McCormack, along with pieces showcased at the annual Noted London jewelry dealer Wartski Goldsmith’s Fair. The presentation will feature photographs of extraordinary jewelry and stories gathered during her visit.
articles.title: Piedmont appraiser presents discoveries from London’s jewelry scene

articles.text: Alejandro Cartagena The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) is exhibiting Alejandro Cartagena: Ground Rules now through April 2026, marking the first retrospective of the acclaimed photographer’s career. The exhibition features two decades of Cartagena’s work and more than 20 major projects exploring themes of urban development, migration, and environmental change in Mexico. Known for his inventive use of landscape photography and portraiture, Cartagena employs the camera as a tool for examining social and ecological shifts in contemporary life. Born in Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic, in 1977, Cartagena has lived and worked in Monterrey, Mexico, since his youth. His photographs have been featured in more than 50 solo and group exhibitions worldwide, including the Centre de Cultura Contemporània de Barcelona in Spain and the Fondation Cartier pour l’Art Contemporain in Paris. His work is held in the permanent collections of institutions such as the J. Paul Getty Museum, the Museum of Fine Arts in Houston, the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, and the Museum of Contemporary Photography in Chicago. Cartagena’s early projects, including Identidad Nuevo León (2005) and Espacios Habitables (2004–05), reflect on belonging and identity, while later series such as Between Borders (2009– 10), Americanos (2012–14), and Without Walls (2017) explored U.S.-Mexico relations and gained him international recognition. Works like Suburbia Mexicana (2005–10) and Carpoolers (2011– 12) examine the effects of rapid suburban growth, highlighting economic disparities and environmental transformation. In recent years, Cartagena has expanded his practice to include collage, video, and AI-generated imagery, as seen in Photo Structures (2018–19) and his latest video series, We Are Things (2025). “Photography changed our world two centuries ago; the way we see it, and the way we think about it has never been the same since we started using it,” Cartagena said in a press release. “I want to be part of that history of how the medium transformed our understanding of social, political and environmental issues through images.” SFMOMA Director Christopher Bedford said Cartagena’s photographs “open up broad conversations that transcend geography.” “Cartagena’s work invites reflection and probing questions that serve to complicate our understanding of important social and environmental topics. I believe this exhibition will resonate deeply with our audiences,” he added. The exhibition will be on view through April 19, 2026. Visit sfmoma.org or call (415) 357- 4000 for more information.
articles.title: Alejandro Cartagena exhibit now on view at SFMOMA

articles.text: Holiday light shows ends Jan. 11 Ruth Bancroft Garden’s annual holiday fundraiser and festival, Garden of D’Lights, is open now through January 11. Garden of D’Lights is a selfguided light festival that is suitable for all ages. Thousands of lights and lasers transform the Garden’s cacti, succulents and trees into magical, multicolored botanical sculptures, unlike anything else in the East Bay. The holiday light and laser experience dresses the three-acre garden and its many succulents, cacti, and native flora. The gardens house plants from various hemispheres, so there is always something in bloom at Ruth Bancroft. Tickets are available online at https://www.ruthbancroftgarden. org/garden-of-dlights/ and must be purchased in advance. Entry times are 5:30 p.m., 6:30 p.m. and 7:30 p.m. Capacity for each entrance time is limited to accommodate onsite parking.The event is dog-friendly. Dogs must be on a leash at all times. Each ticket order includes two free daytime guest passes, allowing Garden of D’Lights guests to return during regular hours and explore the garden. Passes will be given at check-in and are valid for six months. Photo courtesy of Ruth Bancroft Gardens The light festival is the Garden’s annual holiday fundraiser.
articles.title: Garden of D’Lights continues at Ruth Bancroft

articles.text: Good Fire: Tending Native Lands and Students on Strike on view now The Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) is inviting all East Bay residents to take advantage of its monthly “First Sundays,” a regular day of increased access and community connection. This Sunday, December 7, and every first Sunday of the month, general admission to OMCA’s galleries of California art, history, and natural sciences is free. “First Sundays” run from 11:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., giving ample time to explore exhibits, relax in the newly updated garden, or browse locally-made goods at the museum shop. Whether you’re curious about California’s history, local art, or natural science, “First Sundays” at OMCA offer a great chance to engage with Oakland and the local community’s culture and to bring friends, family, or neighbors along for a relaxed Sunday outing. Visitors are encouraged to reserve tickets online in advance to secure a preferred entry time and reduce wait times. While general admission is free, time slots can fill up on busy days. For those interested in special exhibitions in OMCA’s Great Hall, discounted tickets are offered on First Sundays. Special exhibitions open now include Good Fire: Tending Native Lands and Students on Strike. OMCA’s newest exhibition, Good Fire: Tending Native Lands explores cultural and historical significance of Northern California’s native communities’ use of fire and presents the significance of intentional fire use by local tribes whose practices predate state and federal fire management systems. Students on Strike highlights the 1968 student-led strike at San Francisco State University (SFSU) and other noteworthy movements that established the nation’s first Black Studies Department and first College of Ethnic Studies at the university. Visit https://museumca.org/ to learn more. OMCA offers free admission every first Sunday of the month.
articles.title: Enjoy free admission to OMCA this Sunday
