articles.text: Until December 15 Love at First Sight Art Exhibit Piedmont native Michael Stehr’s art exhibit will remain on the walls at PCA into mid-December for you to enjoy while attending other events at the venue. Please visit the Fine Art 2025 section of his website at mstehr.com for more information on the exhibit and write to the artist at mstehrart@gmail.com. Thursday, December 4, 4:00 p.m. US Premiere Screening — Monastir Monastir is a haunting and poetic film whose imaginative premise has earned Francesco Paolo Paladino outstanding praise in Italian film circles. This is a rare opportunity to witness a truly international collaboration. Paladino creates his collages in Piacenza. The introductory and closing texts are by his long-term collaborator Luca Chino Ferrari, za respected author and lyricist from Cremona. The narration is by London’s Edward Ka Spel, soloist and composer of the Legendary Pink Dots. The melodies and lyrical adaptations are crafted by Dorothy Moskowitz Falarski in Piedmont. Paladino, Ferrari and Falarski have been working together since 2022 as The United States of Alchemy, their name inspired by the United States of America rock band in which Dorothy made her debut in 1968. Monastir is a follow-up to their highly acclaimed Under an Endless Sky, released by Tompkins Square Records in 2023. Free event. Saturday, December 6, 7:30 p.m. Boon Hiker Band Concert The Boon Hiker Band returns to Piedmont for a performance by John Bidwell, Clare Broussard, J.T. Devine, Robin Eschner, Natasha Haugnes, Dennis Hysom, Chris Smith, and John Tuttle. The songs lean toward Americana/Folk/Indie traditions. Advance tickets at https://www. brownpapertickets.com/e/6749696. Sunday, December 7, 4:30 p.m. In the Tradition Jazz & Pop Piano Trio In the Tradition Piano Trio – Bill Jackman, Michael Jones, and Albert Brooks – will kick off the holiday season with a program that includes all your favorite holiday music, from 16th Century traditional songs to O Tannenbaum (1824), and thence to mid-20th Century holiday songs. Don’t miss the relaxed pleasure of a Sunday late afternoon in the Classic Jazz Club with the trio. Doors open at 4:15 PM. Tickets $30, cash/check ONLY, at the door, or $25 at https://www.brownpapertickets.com/e/6214927. Thursday, December 11, 6:30 p.m. Sacha Grippando Jewelry Lecture A Jewelry Tour of London will be an enchanting evening of wine and festive cookies as Sacha Grippando shares highlights from her jewelry trip to London this past September. This lecture will delve into London’s rich history as a global center for jewelry manufacturing from the 19th century to present day. Sacha will guide you through current exhibitions at prestigious venues including the Victoria & Albert Museum, Buckingham Palace, the Tower of London, and the renowned jewelry dealer Wartski. Discover contemporary jewelry as well as creations featured at the annual Goldsmith’s Fair. articles.text: The World’s Fair in Paris in 1889 opened the European world to the rest of the world. The Eiffel Tower is the only example that physically remains of that extraordinary fair. But the world changed in many ways. The exhibitions included the cultures of diverse peoples and the people themselves. The souvenirs of that fair were almost as diverse as the exhibitions. Many important European composers attended in 1889. Is it a coincidence that their music changed… literally overnight? They became aware of the beauties beyond their borders. Far flung European empires became all the more encompassing. French composer Maurice Ravel is an excellent example of this transformation. This was the case, exemplified by the first piece on the program on Sunday afternoon in Piedmont’s Center for the Arts. Ravel was inspired by the “exotic” aspect of the Orient. (We use the word Asia now instead of Orient.) His music added new flavors in music which resonated with his listeners. The music allowed the listeners’ imagination to take flight. The gas-filled dirigibles were around, but airplanes were a generation away. The important name of the time was Nadar. The Wright Brothers had to wait. Ravel offered his musical perspective. Soprano Jennifer Lien explained her standpoint from a different perspective. Her’s is an authentically Asian one. Some might think that the difference of opinion was a combat instead of a basic conundrum. Fortunately, music forces us to think in a wider perspective. Ravel was the only historical composer on Sunday’s program. What came next were compositions by Melissa Dunphy, Kamala Sankaram, and Justine F. Chen. All of these composers are contemporary, and the music was co-commissioned by soprano Jennifer Lien. The whole concert was like going to an art exhibition. Each artist sees things from an original and unique perspective. As a result, all of us grow in underSunday’s concert in the Piedmont center for the arts featured two excellent performers in an thoughtprovoking, program. The performers were pianist Gwendolyn Mok ( second from the left) and soprano Jennifer Lien (third from the left). They were flanked by board members of the PiedmontCenter for the Arts. Say something...anything.” Mick, a hello caught in his throat, his right hand beginning an upward extension, heard a voice just behind him. “Monica.” Both Mick and Anthony turned as one, glancing over their shoulders. After a tentative embrace, arms encircling each other, they walked toward the slowing Concord train, the doors sliding open with a whisper. “Whoa, dude,” Anthony said. “Close call, man. But I think she looked at me. Felt we had a moment. We totally made a connection. Too bad Larry showed. Coulda gone another way, man. Mick sat across from him, his board on his lap. “I‘m feeling some pressure here, Mick. If the head at Concord is locked, I’m toast.” Mick stared absently out the window at the people on the platform. articles.text: A scene brom Disney’s Bolt Bolt is a lively, family-friendly Disney adventure that young viewers will happily settle into. The story opens with sevenyear-old Penny, voiced by Miley Cyrus, who adopts a White Swiss Shepherd puppy she names Bolt, played by John Travolta. Five years later, the two are stars of a hit action TV series, battling the schemes of the villainous Dr. Calico. To keep Bolt’s performance sharp, the show’s director works hard to convince him that his superpowers — including his trademark “super bark” — are real. Penny is uneasy with the ruse, knowing Bolt can never leave the set without the truth becoming clear. During one cliffhanger episode, Penny’s character is kidnapped. Bolt believes the danger is real, escapes the studio, and accidentally ends up inside a packing crate of peanuts. Knocked unconscious and shipped across the country, he lands in New York City. Lost and confused, Bolt meets Mittens, a wary, streetwise cat voiced by Susie Essman, and insists they must return to Hollywood to rescue Penny. Back at the studio, producers quickly replace Bolt with another White Swiss Shepherd so the show can go on, despite Penny’s reluctance. Meanwhile, Bolt and Mittens begin an eventful cross-country journey. In Ohio, they tangle with animal control and pick up an unlikely ally: Rhino, an exuberant hamster and Bolt super-fan, voiced by Mark Walton. The trio presses on toward California, forging an unexpected bond along the way. Once they reach Hollywood, one final crisis strikes on the studio lot. But this is Disney, and the film brings things home with a warm, satisfying ending. Bolt and Penny are reunited, and Penny adopts both Mittens and Rhino, giving the trio a real home at last. Bolt is earnest, energetic, and sweet-natured — a gentle reminder that sometimes the greatest superpower is loyalty. Bolt. Directed by Chris Williams and Byron Howard. Walt Disney Animation. Voiced by John Travolta, Miley Cyrus, Susie Essman. Genre adventure. Duration 1 hr., 36 min. Rated PG. Released 2016. Streaming on Disney+, Fandango, Apple, Prime. Nearly a century later, Smyth engages with Beethoven’s tradition and expands it with her Romantic voice, inventive textures, and a charming nod to Scottish folk music. articles.text: It was a cool, sunny Thanksgiving Eve morning, and members of the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group gathered in front of the Exedra at their usual 10:30 a.m. meeting time. The group was smaller than usual for a holiday week, with about thirty walkers and one K-9 best friend ready to set out. They were there to work up appetites for their Thanksgiving dinners, but for another reason too. More than 2,400 runners and walkers would be standing on this same spot the next morning for the annual Piedmont Turkey Trot, and the Wednesday group planned to get a head start. They would walk the entire Turkey Trot course the day before Thanksgiving and be the first to cross the race’s finish line. With activity leader Dick Carter away, Matt Gerhardt took the lead. Matt and Harriette Louie had recently represented the group at the Piedmont Adult Recreation EXPO on November 16, and Matt began the morning by reading a few comments people had shared about what they liked most about the weekly activity. Then, he treated everyone to “A Turkey Trot Story.” According to Matt, “Like all Walking on Wednesday stories, this one starts with Frank C. Havens. Frank was somewhat of an athlete, and every Wednesday he liked to go jogging around town with his publicist, a young man by the name of Dick Carter. They’d run up and down the streets while Dick made up heroic stories about Frank, and they had a good laugh together. “Over time, their friends started running with them all over town, up La Salle and Seaview, down Mountain, and the group became known as the Wednesday Runners. This went on for many years, but eventually they all got too old to run, so they became the Wednesday Walkers. “Now, there was an interim period, in between the Wednesday Runners and the Wednesday Walkers, when they were the Wednesday Trotters. And one year during that period, due to some kind of mix-up related to Leap Year, Thanksgiving fell on a Wednesday. All November of that year they called themselves the Turkey Trotters. Now, Frank C. Havens – that guy was always trying to make a buck – thought, ‘Just about everybody in Piedmont has the day off on Thanksgiving. I bet I could get them to pay to run with us and be Turkey Trotters.’ “Sure enough, it was wildly successful, and the Turkey Trot has continued to this day. Frank made a boatload of money off the deal and was able to buy the naming rights to the local elementary school. As for Dick Carter and the Wednesday Walkers, well, they all lived happily ever after.” Matt made clear that this tale was pure fiction. pages.text: 24 24 Wednesday, December 3, 2025 Features Walking on Wednesday Walking on Wednesdays group traces the Turkey Trot route By Dick Carter It was a cool, sunny Thanksgiving Eve morning, and members of the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group gathered in front of the Exedra at their usual 10:30 a.m. meeting time. The group was smaller than usual for a holiday week, with about thirty walkers and one K-9 best friend ready to set out. Matt and Harriette Louie had recently represented the group at the Piedmont Adult Recreation EXPO on November 16, and Matt began the morning by reading a few comments people had shared about what they liked most about the weekly activity. Then, he treated everyone to “A Turkey Trot Story.” According to Matt, “Like all Walking on Wednesday stories, this one starts with Frank C. Havens. Frank was somewhat of an athlete, and every Wednesday he liked to go jogging around town with his publicist, a young man by the name of Dick Carter. They’d run up and down the streets while Dick made up heroic stories about Frank, and they had a good laugh together. “Over time, their friends started running with them all over town, up La Salle and Seaview, down Mountain, and the group became known as the Wednesday Runners. This went on for many years, but eventually they all got too old to run, so they became the Wednesday Walkers. “Now, there was an interim period, in between the Wednesday Runners and the Wednesday Walkers, when they were the Wednesday Trotters. And one year during that period, due to some kind of mix-up related to Leap Year, Thanksgiving fell on a Wednesday. All November of that year they called themselves the Turkey Trotters. Now, Frank C. Havens – that guy was always trying to make a buck – thought, ‘Just about everybody in Piedmont has the day off on Thanksgiving. I bet I could get them to pay to run with us and be Turkey Trotters.’ “Sure enough, it was wildly successful, and the Turkey Trot has continued to this day. Frank made a boatload of money off the deal and was able to buy the naming rights to the local elementary school. As for Dick Carter and the Wednesday Walkers, well, they all lived happily ever after.” Matt made clear that this tale was pure fiction. Names, characters, places and incidents, he assured everyone, were products of the author’s imagination or used fictitiously. Any resemblance to real people or events was entirely coincidental. With story hour concluded, Matt was ready to lead the group on the official Piedmont Turkey Trot 5K course. Before setting out, he shared a few statistics. According to Google, in 2024 approximately 1.1 million people participated in Thanksgiving Turkey Trot races across the United States, with 936 races held nationwide. Participation was up 21 percent from the previous year, and these events collectively raised more than $3.6 million for charities, making Thanksgiving the biggest running day of the year. The Piedmont Turkey Trot is conducted by a nonprofit that supports local charities, the Piedmont High School Cross Country and Track and Field teams, and the PHS Athletic Boosters. This year marked the event’s twenty-fourth running. The first Turkey Trot was held in 2001 with about 300 participants. In one peak year, participation topped 3,100, but that size was eventually deemed unsafe and the number of runners was capped. Last year’s top three overall finishers were Jack Stein (15:40), Xander Schulte-Sasse (16:17) and Robert Schutz (16:31). Eightyyear-old Len Goldman completed the course in 27:21. The Wednesday Walkers did not expect to match Jack’s or Len’s times, but they intended to complete every step of the Turkey Trot’s 5K, which is 3.1 miles. The group took off from the Exedra, just steps from the race start and finish line on Magnolia Avenue. It was not a fast-paced trot, but a steady walk and stroll. The route followed Highland Avenue, then left on Wildwood Avenue, right on Crocker and Lafayette Avenues, and east on La Salle Avenue all the way to Hampton Road. From there, the group turned right on Sea View Avenue and began the long climb known affectionately as “Heartbreak Hill.” Walkers continued at their own pace, chatting with friends, enjoying the fall weather and making their way up the hill before floating down Mountain Avenue. They finished the loop on Craig, Highland, Vista and back onto Magnolia to complete the course. It was great exercise, with good conversations and much to be thankful for. The group expects to repeat the Turkey Trot walk next Thanksgiving Eve. Walking on Wednesdays meets each Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland and Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join. There is no charge, and new walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are always welcome. Registration is required. To sign up, go to https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu or contact at (510) 420-3070 for more information. articles.text: The Altenheim, located at 1720 MacArthur Blvd. in Oakland, will host the East Bay Weihnachtsmarkt on Saturday, Dec. 6, from 1 to 7 p.m. The annual outdoor market brings a touch of German Christmas tradition to the East Bay with music, food, crafts and holiday shopping. Visitors can enjoy classic seasonal treats including Glühwein, bratwurst, spaetzle and candied almonds, along with children’s arts and crafts and a wide range of vendor booths offering holiday gifts. Admission is free. Food and beverages may be purchased with tickets sold on-site, with proceeds supporting the Bay Area Kinderstube in Albany and the East Bay German International School in Emeryville. Organizers invite families and neighbors to stop by, enjoy the festive atmosphere and celebrate the start of the holiday season. “We look forward to seeing you at the Weihnachtsmarkt. Frohe Weihnachten and happy holidays,” said Petra Specht of the Excelsior German Center at the Altenheim and a Piedmont resident. Join Us

articles.text: Part 6.1: From Kathmandu 4,593’ to Lobuche High Camp at 17,000’ The Nepalese know 29,029- foot Mt. Everest – the world’s highest peak – as Sagarmatha (Goddess of the Sky). The Tibetans call her Chomolungma (Goddess Mother of the World). On April 1, 2019 Piedmont’s Bill Baringer embarked on an eightweek dance with the goddess in cold weather and long days. His trip started in Kathmandu, Nepal, elevation 4,593 ft., where the peril ramped up immediately with a flight to the most dangerous airport in the world, Lukla, at 9,330 ft. The runway at Lukla is very short and not level; it is on an incline. “Planes don’t glide into it, they kind of just smack into it, like a fly on a wall,” recalled Baringer. There were problems with the runway at the time, so he and his climbing group took helicopters, a little more expensive, but a lot safer. Bill chose the company “Climbing The Seven Summits,” owned by legendary mountain guide Mike Hamill, and found himself part of a group of 24 climbers. This would be a twomonth program in Nepal to give the group the best chance of acclimatizing, and to account for weather setbacks, which turned out to be very much needed. After having climbed the highest peak on five other continents, he prepared for Everest with months of training at home with a heavy backpack. Each climber was allowed to bring two 50-pound duffel bags, one to be taken directly to Everest base camp and the other carried to sleeping accommodations each evening by porters. Bill thought each porter was going to carry one 50 lb. bag, but they tied two bags together and went up the mountain. Bill was amazed at their strength and endurance. ”I’m not going anywhere with 100 pounds on my back. They took amazing loads,” he said of the porters. Bill’s journey commenced through the Khumbu Valley along the glacier melt of the Dudh Kosi River. On April 4 the trek from Phakding to Namche Bazaar required a significant elevation change of 2,727’ up the steep Namche Hill. Namche Bazaar had upgraded and expanded significantly since Bill’s paragliding trip to the region with his wife in 1995. The hotel now had water heatLukla airport at 9,330 feet is considered the most dangerous airport in the world, with frequent weather cancellations, and a pitched, short runway. A suspension bridge over the Dudh Kosi river near Phakding has recently been upgraded to metal from wood and rope. Namche was littered with mountaineering stores, including “The North Face” (or “The North Fake” as it’s called) with Chinese knock-offs of original goods. On April 6th they left Namche Bazaar and headed to Deboche. But 20 minutes into the hike, it started to rain, and as they climbed it turned to snow. On the trail they were forced to yield to some heavy traffic as trains of yak were coming down the mountain. It was advised to stay on the uphill side of the trail to prevent a yak’s headturn from sending you spinning down the mountain. Once in Deboche they warmed up at a teahouse with a wood-burning stove in the center, stoked with yak dung. After a rest day, the group headed on a frozen ice trail to Pheriche at 14,300. He tried to take it slow because he caught a minor flu virus which resulted in a sore throat. Baringer focused on taking shallow breaths while trekking, hoping to avoid the “Khumbu Cough.” On April 9th he was still feeling the effects of the virus, and found it was difficult to regulate his temperature and painful to swallow. He managed to stay with the team for the climb of 1,100 feet. The next day he decided to check himself into the Himalayan Rescue Center medical clinic. The doctors confirmed he had a flu virus and gave him medication to battle the symptoms, but said it would just have to work its course. It could be a couple of days or two weeks. Baringer chose to take a fourth day of rest in Pheriche, considering there would be no more medical centers until they reached Everest Base Camp in six or seven days. Determined to reduce his symptoms, he napped between meals, took hot showers and enjoyed the comforts of a bed before spending 5-7 weeks in a one- or two-person tent. Most of his group had already arrived at the Lobuche base camp, and Baringer was beginning to fear he would not be able to stay on the schedule to acclimatize at base camp and summit A prayer wheel and rock in Chheplung inscribed with a Tibetan Buddhist prayer “om mani padme hum”, which translates to “Praise to the Jewel in the Lotus.”

articles.text: Piedmont’s Commercial Center, 1912-1970 The Piedmont Commercial Center was built in 1913 and housed the first stores in Piedmont. This 1970 photo shows Wells Fargo Bank on the left, Hamby’s Market, Springman’s Pharmacy and the Highland Sweet Shop. design the commercial building. Farr did not design a square box for Piedmont’s stores. He designed three storefronts that gracefully followed the curve of Highland Avenue. A mission tile pent roof spanned the three stores, and tall transom windows and bold columns framed the storefronts. Farr claimed his design would “rival in tone and architecture, the enormous mansions which are to surround it on every side.” The building was completed in 1913. Over time, Farr’s building would fondly be called “The Stores.” Hamby’s Market The first grocery store opened in 1915 and was run by the Ainsworth Brothers. By 1921, Walter Hamby was running the grocery that became the popular Hamby’s Market. For decades, Piedmont shoppers often met and caught up on local news while they bought their groceries. Hamby’s was a full service grocery and later offered delivery service. After school, high school boys delivered groceries in collapsible wood crates to homes throughout Piedmont. One of those wood crates is in the Piedmont Historical Society collection. Hamby’s thrived for almost 50 years until the building was sold and slated to be demolished in 1970. Before closing, then owners Mary and Harry Sund, threw a ”Goodbye to Hamby’s party” with champagne, cake, and coffee for their customers. Piedmont’s Drug Store In 1921, W. L. Ferard opened the first drug store in Piedmont, the Piedmont Drug Company. From at least 1931 to the late 1960s, Gustav Springman operated the successful Springman’s Pharmacy. Also, a full service store, the pharmacy delivered prescriptions and goods to their customers. Highland Sweet Shop In 1921, Joseph H. Cheatham opened the Highland Sweet Shop with a candy store, soda fountain, and tea room. Originally, this candy store was to have housed George Merra’s candy shop in Piedmont Park before his untimely death in 1920. The Sweet Shop was popular with old and young alike. Piedmont matrons enjoyed lunch and tea in the small tea room at the back of the shop, and students often stopped for candy or a soda on the way home after school. Also, in 1921, the Standard Oil Company built the first serCrowds of Piedmont shoppers attended the Hamby’s Market closing party in 1969. vice station on Highland Avenue, opposite Vista Avenue. American Trust Bank In 1928, Albert Farr added the American Trust Bank building to the original three stores. His design included a deeply arched entrance with Churrigueresque relief and a decorative niche to the left. American Trust operated this branch until the 1960s when it became part of Wells Fargo Bank. A small office building behind the bank was the Alexander Allen realty office and later the Robert F. Atkinson realty company. Later, it became the local barber shop, which served generations of Piedmonters. Piedmont’s beloved stores were demolished in 1970 to make way for the current Wells Fargo Bank Building.

pages.text: Wednesday, December 3, 2025 27 The History of Piedmont Piedmont’s Commercial Center, 1912-1970 By Gail G. Lombardi Previously published in the Piedmont Post on February 27, 2019. Until 1912, Piedmont was known as the “store-less” city. With just over 1700 residents and 700-plus houses, the closest grocery store was the H. F. Sacks grocery on Piedmont Avenue, now the Piedmont Grocery. While residents enjoyed living in a completely residential city, they began to feel the need for a commercial center. To protect the city from what the Oakland Tribune called “an invasion of cheap and unsightly stores,” a group of residents, headed by Wallace Alexander, formed the Piedmont Commercial Association. The Association purchased 2 acres from Frank C. Havens directly across from Piedmont Park, and Alexander hired Albert Farr to A eucalyptus believed to have been planted by Walter Blair in 1878 once grew in the intersection of Highland and Magnolia. articles.text: Last spring, four new youth board members joined the board of Piedmont Council Scouting America. They serve as a voice for the youth the council supports, and each is responsible for completing at least one project. They will lead a team during the second weekend of the tree lot, December 6–7, from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. They have kicked off their project with a “design an ornament” activity that kids can complete before they arrive. After that, young participants can enjoy a cup of hot chocolate and make a paracord bracelet. Stephanie Lee and Tai March-Cunningham have been very active in Piedmont Community Service Crew. Theo Ferguson and Evan Friedman have both been active in their respective troops and have earned their Eagle rank. Although they are only halfway through their term, they have already learned a great deal. Evan said, “It’s been eye opening recognizing the number of gears turning at the council level, and the level of detail in the council budget.” “Seeing how strong the scouting community is,” said Stephanie, “and how people look out for each other.” Tai shared that she learned that the council even exists to support the packs, troops, crews and post in Piedmont. “I’ve learned about the people and the roles that they fill on the council board, and how that all connects.” “I’ve had a chance to practice collaboration skills and teamwork,” shared Theo. “Coming together to present a project that we’re proud of.” All four youth were selected because of their deep involvement in their respective units. None of these projects would have been possible without Piedmont residents donating their funds, expertise, and time. The citizens of Piedmont contribute generously to city projects because we believe in this community and trust that our efforts will have a lasting impact. To see what has happened to the home built for Piedmont Play School — a project funded and built by parents, volunteers, and local professionals — is a breach of that trust. It’s hard to imagine giving more to Piedmont when the City appears willing to disregard the commitments made when Piedmont citizens donate to civic projects. Piedmont Play School is more than a tenant. It is a valued, community-built institution, one the City once proudly supported. To dismiss it without meaningful dialogue undermines the civic partnership that has made the City of Piedmont a model of community engagement. We urge the City Council to reconsider its decision, or at a minimum, to engage openly and respectfully with the PPS community to find a path forward that honors the history, investment, and values that created this school. PHS drove to inside the 10 on its next drive, including a long 39-yard catch and run by Mumtaz to convert a 4th-and-2. However, Piedmont settled with a 23-yard field goal by Matias Seelenberger at the 9:34 mark of the fourth quarter—bringing Piedmont within one score down 24-17. Middletown went on to score two consecutive touchdowns. They made it 30-17 with 4:53 left, and then recorded an interception on the first play of Piedmont’s next drive. It led to the Mustangs’ next score with 2:19 left, making it 37-17. Piedmont scored the game’s final touchdown with 30 seconds left in the game. This time, they took it 68 yards on 10 plays, capping off with a four-yard touchdown catch by Meyjes. Official game stats were not provided. Turkey Trot Continued from page 17 Proctor. “It was great, it was a beautiful morning, everyone was in great spirits, we did not hear any complaints.” Proctor noted that the event draws visitors for many reasons: the scenery, the cheerful atmosphere and the challenge of the course, which is at least 60% uphill. “It says a lot about people that they come out in extended families, pick up 10 shirts at a time, for 18 people sometimes,” said Proctor. “We are one of the few trots that allow strollers and allow dogs. We have something for everyone, the upfront corral for the fast turkeys, and it is also tailored to walkers.” Two days before the race, signs reading “Run for Them!” appeared along the course in memory of Soren Dixon, Jack Nelson and Krysta Tsukahara, the three Piedmont teens killed in a car crash the day before Thanksgiving in 2024. A total of 125 volunteers helped make the event a success, including Scouts, Piedmont Community Service Crew, the Mountain Bike Team and members of the Piedmont Police Department. In its 24th year, the Turkey Trot once again set the tone for a beautiful Thanksgiving holiday. Runners got their blood pumping early and warmed up their smiles before turning their attention to dinner, family and giving thanks. At that time, he teamed up with another climber, Jay, from Colorado. Like Baringer, he also was dealing with altitude induced respiratory issues. They quarantined themselves off in a separate dining tent to reduce the chance of infecting other climbers. On April 13 Baringer, Jay and sherpa guides Pemba and Peema roped together and began the ascent to Lobuche High Camp. When walking through the snow, Baringer’s boot went through a thin layer of snow and he fell to the rocky surface below, resulting in a twisted ankle. “None of us can afford any such injuries. One small mistake could eliminate our chance of summiting Everest,” he wrote in his journal. Tune in next week. Will Baringer overcome the ankle injury and the flu virus to conquer the next 12,000’ to reach the pinnacle peak of the world? NEXT WEEK: Part 2 of the Everest climb: A cyclone strikes India and the weather on Everest changes everyone’s plans. Namche Bazaar at 12,500 feet has many culinary and lodging options, including bakeries, mountaineering shops and even an Irish pub. Rising Sun Continued from page 22 woman, Sophie Willis. She lost her husband in WWI, and now supports herself by fishing lobsters just off the coast during the week, and on Sundays with her easel and paints, captures on canvas the ocean and the surrounding wildlife. Slowly Mr. Ohta begins to mend and reveals not only his quiet decency, but his skills as a gardener, a talent that surprises and pleases Mrs. Morrison for she too finds refuge in simply caring for her plants. Of course, Sophie and Mr. Ohta meet and she discovers that he shares her love of painting and their paths cross each Sunday morning. What changes the warm, heartfelt arc of the narrative is December 7, 1941. Mr. Ohta tells Ann that he is not Chinese but Japanese and was born in America. The townspeople of Salty Creek initially react to the presence of Mr. Ohta with curiosity and even suspicion, with the attack on Pearl Harbor to emerge as gossipy, racist and xenophobic with the exception of Ann, her newly hired maid Salomé (Lorraine Toussaint), and Sophie. These women soon begin to comprehend the risk involved for Mr. Ohta if he remains in Salty Creek. Sophie and the rising Sun is not only an exceptionally fine film, with strong performances (look for Margo Martindale), it is also timely in this moment in America. Sophie and the Rising Sun. articles.text: In the summer of 2010, Stephen Main, Director of Music at Piedmont Community Church, had the wonderful idea of pulling the special Christmas music with choir and five instruments out of a Sunday service and presenting it in the evening. First, it would not be limited to twenty minutes; it could run a full hour and include a full symphony orchestra. Second, it would recognize that many people in Piedmont and surrounding communities love beautiful Christmas music standing on its own. Third, the concert could be followed by a festive holiday reception. And so the Overture to Christmas tradition was born. Every year, Stephen conducts a concert with full orchestra, 45 voice choir and soloists. Each one has a unique theme related to the Christmas story. These have included angels, shepherds, the animals around the manger, Mary, Joseph, love, instruments used in Christmas music and more. This year, Stephen has chosen the theme of Christmas – Through the Eyes of a Child. Until the second half of the 19th century children were not included in the religious observation. As childhood became viewed as a separate life stage, the privileged connection between innocent children and God coming to earth as a helpless baby grew. The pieces included in this year’s concert explore this idea and range from medieval to contemporary. The audience is invited to sing four traditional carols with the orchestra, which is great fun. Following the concert join us for a joyful reception. Mingle with your neighbors and the musicians. Enjoy a buffet of sweets and savories, wine, coffee, punch and lots of good fellowship. articles.text: As Piedmont Play School searches for options with its lease set to expire with the City, the school’s architect, Mark Becker, reflects on its impact and legacy on the community. The City of Piedmont is not entertaining an extension to its lease agreement with Piedmont Play School, a private daycare that has served families for nearly 75 years, and ousting the school from its current location at Hampton Field. Mark Becker, who also designed Havens Elementary, was frustrated with the city’s decision, “you see your hard work go into something like Piedmont Play School and see that the council has no desire to negotiate, it’s a closed-door session, they’re stripping this from us as a donor, it feels horrible, and it makes me not want to do anything in this town,” said Becker. The Becker family has been living in Piedmont for over 30 years, moving to the city after the tragic Oakland Hills fires. They moved just two doors down from Marcia Nybakken, who was the director of Piedmont Play School at the time, and they became close friends. As the Beckers’ children attended Piedmont Play School, the Witter Field renovations were voted on and approved. articles.text: Today, Wednesday, November 26, from 3:00 to 6:00 p.m., runners in this year’s Piedmont Turkey Trot can pick up their bibs and t-shirts for tomorrow’s race. Bib pickup is in the Veterans’ Hall, 401 Highland Avenue. Runners who cannot make it to Veterans’ Hall during this time frame may have family or friends pick up their items using their registration number (bib number). Dog Bandanas will be available for $6. The 24th annual Turkey Trot will take place tomorrow, Thanksgiving day at 8:30 a.m., located at the Piedmont Exedra on Highland and Magnolia avenues. The 5K race will have more than 2,100 registered participants, and organizers expect the event to reach the registered cap of 2,400 runners. The Top male and female finishers will receive a turkey from Village Market, a gift card for Transports, a pie from Piedmont Grocery, flowers from J. Miller Flowers and a 2025 Turkey Trot hat. The top finisher in each age group also will receive a pie. The top 3 finishers in each age group will receive flowers, a hat, and a gift card from one of the Turkey Trot sponsors. Proceeds from the race benefit the Piedmont High School cross-country and track and field teams, and also the middle school running program. Don’t forget the Tiny Trot The Tiny Trot returns for its 2nd year. The Tiny Trot is a free event for ages 3-6 at Witter Field on Wednesday, November 26. Registration opens at 3:45 p.m. and the race will begin at 4:15 p.m. The Tiny Trot will be one lap around the quarter-mile track. The Turkey Trot receives help during the race from members of the Piedmont Service Crew, which is part of the Piedmont Scout Council. “We are perfect as a family event, whether it’s young families who are walking and pushing strollers or slightly older families who are running. We have families that are comprised of locals and those visiting from out of town,” said race director Sydney Proctor. articles.text: The next two years of Instructional Calendars for Piedmont Unified School District were discussed in a first reading but not approved during the last school board meeting on November 12. After teachers voted on four calendar options, a majority put forth a calendar that mirrors the current calendar. “The greatest challenge that we faced was to find enough days in the fall to create balanced semesters, without having to start the school year the first week of August,” said teacher Allison Cota, Chair of the Calendar Committee. There are sticking points and disagreements between district leadership, parents and teachers about the calendar teachers have put forth. An opinion piece published in last week’s Piedmont Post by April Gruber outlined some desired changes expressed by 455 responses to a parents survey. Gruber, a Piedmont parent, stated that parent groups were hoping for the following changes: 1. Start school 1-3 days later in August. 2. Avoid Monday as the first day of school. 3. Shorten Winter break from 16 days to 14 days to resume Monday, January 4 instead of January 6. How long will you hide your face from me?” Psalm 13:1 Trying to remember the psalm in which I could find the prayer of complaint “How long, Lord?” I typed “Psalm of Ingratitude” into my search engine and received a rather testy response. “There is no single ‘Psalm of Ingratitude,” but several psalms illustrate the dangers and consequences of ingratitude.” Further on in the AI generated response informed me that “Ingratitude is a sin” and “It leads to negative outcomes.” Duly chastened by the heresy hunting watchdog that is my search engine, let me be clear, I love Thanksgiving. I see great value in counting one’s blessings. I affirm the spiritual practice of daily putting into writing three things that I am grateful for. I love the hymn “Now Thank We All Our God.” I have Diana Butler Bass’ book “Grateful: The Subversive Practice of Giving Thanks” on my Kindle and refer to it frequently. I honor the teaching of Maya Angelou, “Let gratitude be the pillow upon which you kneel to say your nightly prayer. And let faith be the bridge you build to overcome evil and welcome good.” Yet, I also assert that there is also a time and place for ingratitude, a time and place to acknowledge there is much in our world is wrong, a time and place to pray “Dear God, This sucks.” Noting that Psalm 13 was not excluded from the Bible, I would argue that there is a spirituality to naming our ingratitudes along with our blessings; a living faith to naming our pain, our hurt, our grief and our guilt along with our praises and celebrations. articles.text: Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. Subscribe to the Post and we’ll deliver Editor: I want to strongly second what Alli Cota shared in her letter this week. I joined the Calendar Committee towards the end of their process and served on APT’s negotiations team. Both groups focused closely on the parent survey and spent hours examining every possible alternative that would let us start later without moving finals back to mid-January. In the end, we rejected all options that would have started school the first week of August, though that had been our solution for several years. Of course, we also talked with students about their preferences and needs. And as teachers, we have our own understanding of how even small changes to the calendar impact curricula and student success. Teachers’ calendar votes aren’t based on personal preference– teachers aren’t eager to start school in early or mid-August, and find a five-day first week of school exhausting. In fact, the traditional fall semester calendar ending in January was actually easier on secondary teachers: with mid-December finals, we spend much of the holiday “break” feverishly grading. But again and again, we vote for calendars we believe are overall best for the kids. Shortening fall semester doesn’t just impact semester classes–though those are most intensely impacted, with Civics teachers saying they can scarcely cover legally-required state standards in the current semester split, and couldn’t reasonably do so if even more fall classes are cut. Currently, I only teach yearlong courses, but given the critical importance of fall semester grades for college admissions, I feel a deep obligation to ensure my students are truly ready for summative assessments before Winter Break. To really learn, students need adequate time to absorb and reflect on new information, they need iterative prac-

pages.text: Wednesday, November 26, 2025 3 LETTERS - MAIN Careful school calendar considerations By Allison Cota Editor: As Chair of the Calendar Committee, I’d like to respond to the suggestion that the results of the recent vote didn’t account for the interests of families. In truth, the Committee closely examined the Parent Survey results twice. And, since every teacher and CSEA member on the Committee has sent their kids through Piedmont schools, we had the lens not only of educators, but of fellow parents in the district. Building possible calendars is simultaneously straightforward and complex – a shift of just one day creates a domino effect that impacts the rest. The parameters are strict: proposed calendars must include 180 student and 185 staff days, prevent the loss of Average Daily Attendance (ADA), abide by Federal holidays and have semesters of approximately equal length. Additionally, all stakeholder groups clearly indicated that Fall semester should end before Winter Break, including 71.5% of parents on the survey. The Committee also considered calendars of many nearby districts before drafting and weighing the merits and challenges of 9+ different options of our own. We were required to propose one model mirroring our current calendar, plus at least three others. Negotiating teams then evaluated our recommendations; ultimately district leadership asked to replace two with their own. One mirrored 2025-2026, two started one day later by moving a day from Fall to Spring, and the fourth started a full week later, but at the cost of pushing the end of first semester to mid-January. Teachers then voted based on what they believed would best serve the interests of our students. The “cur rent” calendar received 80 of 158 votes, as compared to 35, 24, and 19 respectively for the others. While the winning calendar received “only” just over 50%, it received more than twice as many as the next runner up, and won by a landslide 34 to 6 at the high schools. According to the feedback we’ve received, the main reason for that choice was avoiding further unbalancing the semesters. Two years ago, when asked to move the start of school later than the first week of August, teachers agreed to move from an 88/92 to an 87/93 semester split. For those not in the classroom, moving one day still farther, to an 86/94 split, might seem minor. However, the combined loss of two 90-minute periods in the Fall, nearly a week of instruction, (and an 8-day difference from Spring), while having to cover the same content and skills with less time, forces teachers to make difficult decisions: do we cut out essential topics/standards? push more assignments into homework? remove engaging activities that reinforce key concepts? eliminate opportunities for in-class feedback? While returning to school on a Monday is not ideal, many felt the cost of further truncating Fall semester would have been considerably worse for our classes. Additionally, there’s a strong argument to support student days-off throughout the school year. These days provide muchneeded opportunities to catch up with coursework, allow time with family/friends, and help protect student social-emotional health at a time when they may need it substantially more than at the close of ten weeks of summer. And interestingly, it’s not true that “feedback strongly favored a mid-week start”; 53.1% of parents indicated that was “not at all important”; only 13.9% responded it was “very important”. While I understand that some are frustrated that APT did not vote the way they preferred, it is my hope that my comments will help to clarify how we got here. By Elise Marks Editor: I want to strongly second what Alli Cota shared in her letter this week. I joined the Calendar Committee towards the end of their process and served on APT’s negotiations team. Both groups focused closely on the parent survey and spent hours examining every possible alternative that would let us start later without moving finals back to mid-January. In the end, we rejected all options that would have started school the first week of August, though that had been our solution for several years. Of course, we also talked with students about their preferences and needs. And as teachers, we have our own understanding of how even small changes to the calendar impact curricula and student success. Teachers’ calendar votes aren’t based on personal preference– teachers aren’t eager to start school in early or mid-August, and find a five-day first week of school exhausting. In fact, the traditional fall semester calendar ending in January was actually easier on secondary teachers: with mid-December finals, we spend much of the holiday “break” feverishly grading. But again and again, we vote for calendars we believe are overall best for the kids. Shortening fall semester doesn’t just impact semester classes–though those are most intensely impacted, with Civics teachers saying they can scarcely cover legally-required state standards in the current semester split, and couldn’t reasonably do so if even more fall classes are cut. Currently, I only teach yearlong courses, but given the critical importance of fall semester grades for college admissions, I feel a deep obligation to ensure my students are truly ready for summative assessments before Winter Break. articles.text: Community volunteers will host a book drive for the East Bay Children’s Book Project (EBCBP) at the Piedmont Turkey Trot Pre-Race Packet Pick-Up on Wednesday, November 26, from 3:00-5:00 p.m. at the Piedmont Veterans’ Memorial Building, 401 Highland Avenue. Weather permitting, the table for book drop offs will be outside. Volunteers will collect new and gently used children’s books, including board books through high school books. Books should be clean with no marks or stains. Please bring donated books in boxes for easy transport to the East Bay Children’s Book Project (EBCBP). No textbooks, religious books, encyclopedias, magazines, adult books, or library discards. The mission of EBCBP is to help build literacy by putting books into the hands of children who have little or no access to them. Working through individuals and organizations who help children in need, the organization has given out more than two million free books since opening their doors in May 2005. School Board and City Council members started this tradition more than ten years ago. EBCBP volunteer and former Wildwood Elementary School librarian Ellen Reed notes that 4,022 books were donated last year during this event. “We are so grateful for the community’s contribution to our children’s literacy project year after year,” says Reed. Individuals available to help collect or drive books on Wednesday, November 26 from 3:00-6:00 p.m., are asked to please email Sarah Pearson at srpear@gmail. com. Anyone that misses this opportunity to donate books, may drop off books at EBCBP on Tuesdays 3:30-5:30 p.m. Children’s books may also be donated in the EBCBP box at the Piedmont Middle School library at 740 Magnolia during school hours. Monetary donations to EBCBP can be accepted by mail at 2501 Harrison St., Oakland, CA 94612 or online at Eastbaychildrensbookproject.org/donate-now/ About EBCBP Too many children in the Bay Area live in homes without books, and attend schools and programs where books are in short supply. Encouraging reading is not enough when families and schools do not have books. East Bay Children’s Book Project’s books are given directly to children in need by teachers, social workers, health care professionals, community outreach groups, housing authority employees, and police officers. Some are used by schools, daycare and community centers, homeless shelters, and hospitals to create libraries at their sites. EBCBP clients determine how best to meet the needs of the children with whom they work. Eastbaychildrensbookproject.org/about/ Last year volunteers delivered 4,022 books to East Bay Children’s Book Project. articles.text: Izzy is a beautiful fouryear-old, 41-pound Shepherd mix with striking ice blue eyes. Izzy is house-trained, sleeps soundly through the night, and is super food-motivated facilitating training. Her fosters say she has a playful, silly side and enjoys a good romp. She’s always up for an energizing walk, snoozing on the couch, or just watching the world go by from the window. On walks, she can pull when excited, but she responds well to calm, consistent guidance. Izzy gets along well with other gentle dogs and could thrive as a solo pup or with a wellmatched dog buddy. With her alert, people-loving personality and eager-to-please nature, Izzy’s ready to be someone’s best friend. Follow her in foster with @fosteredbyapril on Instagram. To meet Izzy, submit your adoption questionnaire online (https://www. oaklandanimalservices.org/ Come meet Izzy at Oakland Animal Services. adopt/dogs/foster-dog-adoption-questionnaire/) at the shelter’s website and you will be contacted by her foster to arrange a meet-and-greet. For more information on fostering or adoption, contact Piedmont resident Jessica McDevitt at jessicamcdev@gmail.com. open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm

articles.text: A warm welcome with a sweet treat, Lisa Chan Carnazzo, Broker Associate with The Grubb Company, hosted multiple neighborhood celebrations to introduce her clients to their new community. One gathering took place on Harvard Road, complete with a soft-serve ice cream truck and a visit from Piedmont Police Chief Frederick Shavies. Longtime neighbors, newer neighbors, and friends stopped by to say hello and share an ice cream cone in honor of the city’s newest homeowners. Chief Shavies praised the event’s community-building spirit, saying, “This is an absolutely incredible event. You have soft serve out here, you have children from the elementary school, middle school, and high school, and you get to know new families. It’s a great opportunity, and I’m happy my team and I were actually invited.” Also in attendance was Officer Tyler Petit, who echoed the department’s support of neighborhood engagement. “I love coming to these because it’s a great opportunity for the new owners to understand the level of service they’ll receive in Piedmont. We respond to every call and provide the best level of service possible,” said Petit. These events are part of a growing tradition Carnazzo has created, using her “Local with Lisa” platform and real estate expertise to not only secure homes for her clients but to instantly connect them with the community they are joining. As neighbors mingled along the sidewalk, children enjoyed swirls of vanilla and chocolate ice cream, and new homeowners were greeted with warm handshakes and friendly conversation. The gatherings showcased what Piedmont is known for: a close-knit community that welcomes with intention and a little extra sweetness. Photo courtesy of Lisa Chan Carnazzo Party on Harvard Rd. With Officer Tyler Petit, Lisa Chan Carnazzo, Chief Fredrick Shavies, Jenny Kan, and Harvard Rd. neighbor.

articles.text: The City of Piedmont and the Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF) are partnering to install new swings in the Tot Lot at the Main Park. This project comes closely on the heels of their collaboration to do a spectacular renovation of the Linda Beach Tot Lot, to which PBF contributed $100,000. Last year, the swings at the Main Park were removed for safety reasons, and Piedmont grandmothers, parents, and nannies have been lamenting their absence ever since. Swings bring a special kind of joy to a tot lot, and PBF has agreed to raise funds to return this joy to the Main Park. Residents should watch for their LIGHTS UP PIEDMONT brochures, which will arrive in mailboxes soon. In addition to announcing that this year’s Lights Up Ceremony will take place at 6 p.m. on Wednesday, December 3, the brochure highlights the Main Park Swings Project as this fall’s primary campaign focus. The redesigned swing area will feature: • State-of-the-art materials for durability and safety • Safety matting to replace the existing sand • An expanded play area providing a secure perimeter for enthusiastic swing lovers This year’s PBF brochure offers plenty of alternative opportunities for the community to support its ongoing work. Funds are still needed for the Sydney Dearing Memorial, and the “reforest Piedmont” project has become a long-term effort of great significance. PBF’s two endowment funds, the Sports Facilities Maintenance Endowment and its general Endowment, are both worthy of support. Donors can return their gifts in the envelope accompanying the brochure or by visiting the PBF website: piedmontbeautificationfoundation.org. The brochure’s most important function is to invite all residents to this year’s Lights Up Piedmont ceremony at 6 p.m. on Wednesday, December 3. PBF hopes for a huge turnout for this celebratory kickoff to the Holiday Season. For 25 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmont-post.com, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken.

articles.text: From bedtime questions to Sunday pancakes, the patterns that hold us together My daughters were twelve when they casually mentioned that Thursday nights were their favorite. Not because anything extraordinary happened . . . we simply made quesadillas together, the same way we had since they were six. They’d grate the cheese while I diced peppers, and we’d talk about nothing in particular. “It’s just ours,” as if that explained everything. And of course, it did. In the blur of school runs, work deadlines, and weekend sports schedules, family life can sometimes feel less like a story and more like a logistics operation. We connect, but it’s often about what’s next: “Did you finish your homework?” “Who’s driving to soccer?” We crave connection, but the “how” gets lost. What if the “how” isn’t a grand, week-long vacation, but something we already have, hidden in plain sight? What if it’s in the way we say good morning, the specific board game we pull out on a rainy day, or the one question we ask at the dinner table? You’re Already a Ritual-Maker Most households already have rituals . . . they just don’t notice them. The way you greet each other in the morning, the bedtime rhythm, the micro-conversations in the car, the joke you repeat so often your kids pretend to hate it . . . those are rituals. They’re the background music of childhood. And once you see them, you can shape them. This is good news because rituals don’t need to be elaborate or time-consuming. They don’t require themed tablescapes, color-coded calendars, or anything Pinterest would applaud. They just need to be intentional, recurring, and meaningful to the people involved. How do you spot them? Ask yourself: • What do your kids complain about when it doesn’t happen? • What small thing would feel wrong to skip, even when you’re exhausted? • What phrase, gesture, or moment happens the same way every time—a particular goodbye, a weekend breakfast routine, the way you always end the day? • What would a visitor to your home notice that you do “your way”? Maybe it’s the knock-knock joke your seven-year-old insists you tell every morning on the drive to school. Perhaps it’s how your teenager still lets you play “your song” when you pick her up from practice. It might be the way everyone gravitates to the kitchen on Sunday mornings, knowing pancakes are coming, or how Friday night means pizza and a family movie. Your Ritual Shopping List: From Micro-Moments to Milestones Some are tiny (10 seconds). Some take a bit more effort. Some happen daily, while others yearly. And yes, holidays already give us rituals. The goal isn’t to do them all; it’s to find a handful that feel like your family. Check out the table of rituals like going shopping or visiting a store for inspiration. The rituals that stick are the ones that feel easy, that fit your family’s particular rhythm and humor and needs. Don’t force it. But don’t underestimate the quiet power of showing up, in the same small way, again and again. The Invitation You don’t need to adopt a dozen new rituals this month. Start with one. Or start by simply naming and cherishing the ones you already have. Tell your kids: “I love our Thursday quesadillas.” They’re surprisingly easy to start. Pick something your family genuinely enjoys, tie it to a time or trigger, repeat it, and watch it grow. In the end, rituals are how we become the kind of family we like being—one pancake, car-ride playlist, or bedtime question at a time. And years from now, when your child casually mentions that Thursday nights were their favorite, you’ll know exactly why. Randall Grayson Ph.D. (psychology) has been Camp Augusta’s director for over twenty years. The camp, nestled in the Sierra Nevada foothills outside Nevada City, has been beloved by many families since 1931. Information about summer programs, family camps, and two-week sessions can be found at www. campaugusta.org. Dr. Grayson is also the founder and director of the nonprofit AMeaningOfLife.org: from a scientific lens, it helps you consider your life more deeply and broadly, so you can live it more meaningfully and richly.

Beach Elementary also held its own celebration. This year marks the 65th anniversary of Ruby Bridges’ historic walk into William Frantz Elementary School, when she became the first Black student to integrate an allwhite school in New Orleans. Her courage inspires students to stand up for equity and belonging. What began as a small parent-organized event has grown into a district-wide tradition. Organizers Sarah Eisemon and Laura Edeen partnered with Ms. Jean Takazawa, Director of DEIB and leader of the Affinity Mentorship Program, to expand middle and high school involvement. PHS Affinity Mentors led the program, sharing the story of Ruby Bridges’ courage. Kids and families covered the walkways with chalk art filled with messages of love, inclusion, and belonging. Tables offered bags, beanies, and flags, which students waved proudly as This is the time of year when the requests for donation are widespread, and given the challenges families face in our world today, I feel fortunate to serve our Piedmont school community. Thank you to all those who have already given. I am sometimes asked if Piedmont USD is a “Basic Aid” school district, which is loosely translated a district whose local property tax revenue exceeds the amount of funding the district would receive under the state’s Local Control Funding Formula (LCFF) “guaranteed” level. Piedmont is not a Basic Aid district, and will not likely become one in the foreseeable future. And yet, Basic Aid districts are also sometimes referred to as “community funded” districts, and this description is certainly accurate for Piedmont in other ways. Our community’s support has sent a clear message about the high value of education in Piedmont. PEF’s Giving Campaign is a remarkable force in preserving our outstanding educational programs. articles.text: Jon Reining, the head coach of the Piedmont Mountain Bike team, spoke at the City Council’s public comment period to discuss a recent break-in of the team’s trailer. The team is seeking a new location to store their bikes and equipment. Reining and the volunteer coaches have set up a petition to allow the team to park their trailer in Piedmont. The team’s equipment currently is kept in a storage facility in Richmond. They are currently paying $125 a month in rent to store their gear. Recently, the facility was broken into, and a loaner bike was stolen from their trailer. Reining has a growing concerned about the safety of their gear. “It strikes a blow. Anytime anything is stolen it kind of hits your sense of security,” said Reining. “Our loaner bikes are primarily used to recruit more girls to the team. The team prides itself on its female representation, so the loss of a bike can harm recruitment. The mountain biking team includes 23 athletes from Piedmont High School and 25 members from the middle school. For every race, the team brings a trailer stocked with the equipment and supplies needed to compete. Not only is the trailer a functional part of the team, but an important part of their publicity efforts. The team utilizes the trailer to raise awareness and support recruiting efforts through participating in local community events. Most notably they were visible as an entry in Piedmont’s Fourth of July Parade. Reining believes moving the storage location to Piedmont would make things easier for their volunteer coaching staff. “It can take around 45 minutes to an hour to take the trailer out of storage and back,” Reining added. “It’d be really great to find a parking space somewhere inside the city of Piedmont. We’d love to have this trailer in town, closer to home.” According to the mountain biking team’s petition, “We are asking the broader city, school district and various facilities management organizations within the City of Piedmont to provide one parking space for the trailer. The team is happy to pay market-rate rent for the parking space.” The petition launched on October 20 has more than 150 signatures supporting the team’s goal to find parking in Piedmont. To sign the petition, see: change. org/p/allow-piedmont-highschool-mountain-bike-team-topark-a-trailer-in-piedmont. Piedmont middle and high school mountain biking team. Move one or two school days from the first semester to the second semester After teachers considered nine different calendars, four were advanced by teachers, then district negotiators replaced two of the four calendars, one had to be the current calendar. Cota and Marks provided their rationale for why teachers voted in a majority for the next two years instructional calendars to remain the same as the current calendar. “If you want to have finals before winter break, it’s just impossible to start much later. Why not begin with a virtual journey with Federica Bressan, author of “In the Heart of Tuscia”? This event is a book talk and an open conversation about the search for meaning, meaningful encounters, and the drive to keep exploring the world. The beauty of nature as a catalyst for inner transformation and the quiet power of gratitude are other themes recurring in the book. Federica is currently visiting from Italy—more precisely from an area between Tuscany and Rome called Tuscia (pronounced too-shah), where the novel is set. The story’s main character has recently settled in Tuscia, and she discovers the territory guided by a local friend and—lacking a better word—her “angel.” As if the landscape weren’t stunning enough, their friendship-turned-romance adds emotional depth, as she recounts the journey in retrospect, inviting us into her memories. During the talk, Federica will share stories, history, and cultural insights about Central Italy, along with photos she took herself. She also looks forward to hearing about your own trips to Italy—or your plans to go someday. She is an independent author and speaks out of love for her homeland; she is not affiliated with any agency or organization. (510) 327-1325 | GRANDLAKEVET.COM 3331 GRAND AVE, OAKLAND, CA 94610 After break-in, mountain bike team needs location to store its trailer By Jake Lannon Jon Reining, the head coach of the Piedmont Mountain Bike team, spoke at the City Council’s public comment period to discuss a recent break-in of the team’s trailer. The team is seeking a new location to store their bikes and equipment. Reining and the volunteer coaches have set up a petition to allow the team to park their trailer in Piedmont. The team’s equipment currently is kept in a storage facility in Richmond. They are currently paying $125 a month in rent to store their gear. Recently, the facility was broken into, and a loaner bike was stolen from their trailer. Reining has a growing concerned about the safety of their gear. “It strikes a blow. Anytime anything is stolen it kind of hits your sense of security,” said Reining. “Our loaner bikes are primarily used to recruit more girls to the team. The team prides itself on its female representation, so the loss of a bike can harm recruitment. The mountain biking team includes 23 athletes from Piedmont High School and 25 members from the middle school. For every race, the team brings a trailer stocked with the equipment and supplies needed to compete. Not only is the trailer a functional part of the team, but an important part of their publicity efforts. The team utilizes the trailer to raise awareness and support recruiting efforts through participating in local community events. Most notably they were visible as an entry in Piedmont’s Fourth of July Parade. Reining believes moving the storage location to Piedmont would make things easier for their volunteer coaching staff. “It can take around 45 minutes to an hour to take the trailer out of storage and back,” Reining added. “It’d be really great to find a parking space somewhere inside the city of Piedmont. We’d love to have this trailer in town, closer to home.” According to the mountain biking team’s petition, “We are asking the broader city, school district and various facilities management organizations within the City of Piedmont to provide one parking space for the trailer. The team is happy to pay market-rate rent for the parking space.” The petition launched on October 20 has more than 150 signatures supporting the team’s goal to find parking in Piedmont. To sign the petition, see: change. org/p/allow-piedmont-highschool-mountain-bike-team-topark-a-trailer-in-piedmont. Piedmont middle and high school mountain biking team. Move one or two school days from the first semester to the second semester After teachers considered nine different calendars, four were advanced by teachers, then district negotiators replaced two of the four calendars, one had to be the current calendar. Cota and Marks provided their rationale for why teachers voted in a majority for the next two years instructional calendars to remain the same as the current calendar. “If you want to have finals before winter break, it’s just impossible to start much later. You’re trying to compress a semester into not enough time, you’ve got to choose one,” said Marks. Parent survey results were discussed with the calendar committee. “I am not thrilled with this calendar with the simple reason that the feedback from the survey strongly indicated that folks wanted to start later,” said school board Vice President Ruchi Medkehar. As the clock neared midnight in the five-hour meeting, Medhekar proposed approving only next year’s calendar. “It would be a violation of contract to simply do one year at a time,” said Marks. “The contract says it’s a two-year cycle.” “The implication of [Medhekar’s] comments is that we haven’t taken time and the Calendar Committee has been working on this since last March,” said Cota. “It’s not a function of time, it’s a function of [for] every choice that is made, for what you gain, you lose something else.” Cota explained they considered but couldn’t shorten Thanksgiving Break or Winter Break because Average Daily Attendance (ADA) would decrease because many parents will take their kids out of school anyway. ”Obviously trying to schedule family vacations is important, but it just can’t be the main driver of what we do,” said Marks. Cota said she personally spent 40-50 hours drafting the nine calendars. Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich advocated for shortening the first semester, and moving those days to the second semester to affect the desired changes from parents. Marks and Cota were adamant that moving even one day from the fall to the spring would have undesirable educational effects for students. Teacher-Librarian, Tiffany Cothran, spoke at the end of the meeting around midnight, confused as to how the district was rationalizing their efforts to not accept the teachers vote to keep the calendar the same. “My understanding was that we got four calendars that we agree would be voted on, and then they were voted on, and now we are saying that the one that was voted on wasn’t acceptable,” said Cothran. “I don’t understand how we follow certain process and procedure and then it can just be completely set aside.” READ IT IN THE POST

The trip began at Heart’s Desire Beach near the small town of Inverness, where 19 scouts and 15 parents mounted their kayaks to start a journey of nature and beauty through the waters of the bay. After two hours of kayaking and sightseeing, the troop finally landed on the campsite. It was a small, quiet beach with a view of the golden hills, surrounded by trees and the sounds of birds. The next day, we embarked on our journey back to Hearts Desire Beach where we encountered choppy waves and harsh winds, which managed to steer many of our kayaks off course. Even on the way back with the harsh climate on our backs, we still managed to enjoy the beauty of Tomales Bay State Park. A lenticular cloud is a rare lens-shaped cloud that occurs when stable, moist air flows over a mountain, creating a series of oscillating waves. On the climb, each mountaineer carried 110 pounds of gear, 60 pounds in a backpack and 50 pounds on a sled. Article originally published in the April 22, 2020 issue of the In May of 2018 Bill Baringer, Piedmont’s tenacious mountaineer, headed to Alaska to climb Denali, North America’s highest Denali is a fierce climb; only 25% of those who attempt it have success. In Baringer’s group of five climbers and three guides, three individuals had to turn In Talkeetna, the climbers selected their own lunches and snack food to carry for the next 22 days, including a nine-day supply for possible days of being trapped From Talkeetna an air taxi flew them to Denali National Park, home of the majestic mounThe expedition involved no porters. Each person carried 110 pounds of gear, including white gas and food, with a 60-pound backpack and 50 pounds on a sled towed behind. Mountain Trip, the guide company, took both fresh and dehydrated food, resulting in larger loads than customary. Baringer, a lifelong mountain skier, was disappointed that he couldn’t ski on Denali. “I badly wanted to ski this mountain,” Baringer recalled, “I called all six guide companies and got the same answer from all six.” He was told that no skis are allowed in guided groups. The first day involved 4 1⁄2 hours of travel at a reasonable pace from Base Camp at 7,605 feet. Day two took them to Kahiltna Pass at 9,990 feet. The Denali trip involved multiple trips on each leg of the journey. On “carry days” the climbers took gear up to the next higher camp, buried everything under ice and snow to keep them from ravens and bears, before taking a trip back down to sleep at lower elevation. On that first night when the wind died down, Baringer heard the roar of three avalanches ricocheting across the mountain side in horrifying fashion. On day four Baringer developed a mild headache, so he aimed to double or triple his water intake. Heavy breathing of cold, dry air in altitude for days can lead to “climber’s cough,” a frequent sound on such trips. Hand sanitizer was essential, as was proper food handling. For mountaineers, the food was luxurious – cream of broccoli soup, veggie burgers on buns, French fries and melted brie. All this and no French chef in sight. Day six was a move day from Camp Two at 11,230 feet to Camp Three at 14,235 feet. During the day’s ascent Baringer felt a burning twinge on the outside of his right ankle, and a minor case of plantar fascia from the rigid sole of his triple-layer mountaineering boots. In addition, his right knee began to express its displeasure, causing Baringer to make a mental note to increase his NSAIDs. Fellow climber Jochen Diedrichs from Germany noted that Baringer was a “silent sufferer” who always tried not to bother others during such dark periods. But later that night Baringer developed stomach pains that kept him up most of the night (though the sun never set), which raised questions about whether he would be able to complete the climb. Day eight was a carry day from Camp Three up the headwall to the ridge above. It was a climb that would end the trip for two of the five climbers. An experienced mountaineer of the group, Jill from Colorado, had recently purchased new mountaineering gloves, but they proved to be too stiff to manipulate the ascender or “jumar” on the fixed lines. Jill removed her gloves at each anchor point to make the transition to the next rope. “That is very dangerous; you cannot be gloveless at that elevaOn summit day, Bill Baringer pushed up the slow “Autobahn” section of slope. On a ridge at the summit, Bill Baringer is shown roped to the lead guide, Dan Starr. tion and at those temperatures, especially when holding onto metal ascenders,” Baringer said. Jill slowed her ascent and her fingers began to stiffen. She had to be turned around and taken down the mountain by a guide. Danger on the ice Later that day while tied together, Fernando Yanez, of Chile, slipped on a steep section and started to slide down the ice. Baringer was yanked off of his feet, so he immediately yelled “falling” and punched his ice axe into the slope with his chest. Jochen above did the same and the team held on. Yanez had a second dangerous accident that day which ended his ascent. He fell when crossing a crevasse, twisted his ankle, and like Jill, had to be taken down back to camp. At Camp Three there was a ranger station with a rescue helicopter, but it was not available for hire. Only a broken leg, High Altitude Pulmonary/Cerebral Edema, or another life-threatening condition warranted an emergency airlift, the group was told. At Camp Three the weather turned nasty and the crew went through some of their emergency rations waiting in tents to make the push to Camp Four and then on to the summit. Bill Baringer stands at a cliff aptly named “The Edge of the World.”

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, free compostable bags are available at City Hall to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. Compostable bags are also available from Republic Services (1-800-320-8077) for a fee.
