articles.text: Piedmont High’s No. 2 seeded football team made school history on Friday, November 21. It is the second team in school history to qualify for the North Coast Section Championship game after beating No. 3 Willits 28-10 in the NCS semifinals at Witter Field. They are now set to square off in the Division 7 title game against No. 1 Middletown this Friday, November 28 at Justin Siena High School in Napa. The 1976 NCS title-winning Hall of Fame squad and this year’s team are the only Championship game appearances in Piedmont High’s 100-plus year history. “I was just three years old. I’ve said before, not a lot of people thought we’d be here. The guys stuck with it through my ranting and raving. They never wanted to quit and they never lay down,” said Piedmont head coach Jordan Seiden. It’s a miraculous moment for the football program, considering it lost eight seniors from last year’s team and fell in the Dov. 8 NCS semifinals on Ferndale’s swampy playing surface. This is the first time Piedmont has reached the semifinals in two consecutive years. It has appeared in the semifinals in 1976, 1981, 2014, 2016, 2024, and now 2025. “We’re in the history books. It’s amazing; we couldn’t get it done last year. We had the talent, but had to play in tough field conditions,:” said running back and linebacker Xavier Henderson. “I don’t even know what to say; so many words come to mind. We’re making history and hopefully we can get that win to make history next Friday,” added quarterback Jimmy Lagios. Piedmont had to lean on its defense to keep Willits out of the end zone. The HighlandStaff Photos Piedmont football players stand proudly after beating Willits 28-10 in the D7 NCS Semifinals. Their championship game this Friday marks the school’s first since 1976. ers didn’t score the game’s first touchdown until 3:43 remained in the first quarter, and the Wolverines stayed just one possession back of the lead through three quarters of the game. But once PHS figured out Willits’ rushing attack, Ferndale struggled to finish drives. “To start the game, they were chipping off small plays, and their big drive came from some big plays. We knew if we did our jobs, we’d be fine. Once our offense started going, it forced them to pass. Our coverage is really good, and their throws were all screens, so we just had to focus on tackling,” middle linebacker Colby Hong said. Henderson, the team’s star running back, made his presence felt on defense as a linebacker. On offense he led the team with three rushing touchdowns. “I give all credit to my offensive line, as always. I couldn’t do anything without them,” Henderson said. “Defensively, I haven’t played in a few weeks because of a concussion. I had to step up and play for the team. There’s a lot to correct still, but that’s football; we live to fight another day.” Game Recap After trading possessions to start the game, Piedmont struck first with 3:34 remaining in the first quarter when Rehan Mumtaz punched across a two-yard carry. The previous play, Henderson broke a tackle to take a carry 26 yards to the two. Willits answered on its next possession, scoring on a 12-play series at the 10:56 mark of the second quarter, which capped off with a 31-yard touchdown carry on a 4th-and-4 situation. PHS wound up punting on its next possession, but thwarted Willits on 4th-and-1 at the Highlanders’ 16, where linebacker George Saunders burst through the line to stop a fullback carry. PHS then scored on a nineplay series with 32 seconds left in the half. The drive featured a 23 yard carry my Mumtaz, a 47-yard reception by Diego Hurwitz down to the three, and capped by a touchdown by Henderson. In the third quarter, more back-and-forth possessions led to a 34-yard field goal by Willits with 2:20 left, cutting Piedmont’s lead to 14-10. But PHS’ offense came alive with two touchdowns in the fourth quarter. The Highlanders scored on its next possession, taking it 64 yards on eight plays, finishing with a two-yard score by Henderson with 10:39 left. During the series, PHS had chunk plays of 16 and 15 yards by Henderson, and 18 and 12-yard receptions by Cash Panico. Piedmont then forced another turnover on downs at Willits’ 45 with 6:25 left, leading to a 12-play touchdown series with 1:44 remaining in the game. Jack Meyjes had a 12 yard reception, Henderson had a 14-yard run where he stiff-armed a defender to the floor, while Henderson scored on a six-yard carry. Final game stats were not provided. Mateo Long jumps on a fumble that was forced by Colby Hong (left). George Saunders (right) celebrates.

articles.text: First time since 2019 for Highlanders Photos by Jenni Tsoi Best Piedmont’s girls’ cross-country team placed third at the North Coast Section championships last Saturday to qualify for the State Championship on November 29. Pictured with their medals are Cora Chun (left), Cora Brozowski Schrader, Viviane Oesterer, Leighton Mand, Skylar Best, Amalia Gray, and Nikita Gorelik. Piedmont High’s cross country team traveled back to Hayward High for the 2025 North Coast Section Cross Country Championship on Saturday, November 22. As a result, the school extended its streak of sending at least one student athlete to the CIF State Championship to 37 years, this time with the entire girls’ team making the trip to Woodward Park after finishing third of 15 schools in the Division 4 race. For an entire team qualifying for the CIF State Championship on Saturday, November 29 marks the school’s first time doing so since 2019. “Pack Running. They ran together and pushed each other. It was the strength of the team that made the difference again. It is the strength and consistency of the depth of all of the seven runners that continues to propel them to such good outcomes,” said coach Steve Zirkelbach. “The last time the girls team advanced to the state meet was 2019.” Piedmont’s top-five finishers all finished within 57 seconds of each other. Junior runner Leighton Mand led the way in 17th of 111 runners with a time of 19:52.42; senior Skylar Best was 24th in 20:23.06, and right behind her was sophomore Viviane Oesterer in 25th in 20:23.26. Senior Cora Chun placed 30th in 20:46.84, and sophomore Nikita Gorelik rounded things out in 33rd, 20:49.18. Best qualified for State individually as a freshman in 2022, making Saturday’s result a unique full-circle moment for her. “It’s great to bookend my high school career in this way. Our team is very tight-knit, and the goal was working together to qualify. It’s so much more meaningful for me to qualify as a team instead of just an individual. It’s really special,” Best said. All five finishers coming across the line in less than one minute apart was imperative towards the third-place run. It’s also a testament to the importance of having all seven varsity runners pushing each other throughout the 2025 campaign. “We were all so close together. For NCS, our coach told is it would come down to the fourth, fifth, and sixth runners. Everyone on this team is so important. Cora Chun and Nikita Gorelik passed a lot of people during the race. What makes our team so special is that we’re stronger together and we all push each other,” Best said. “I’m really excited to go to State, it’ll be my first time,” added Oesterer. “What got us there is our teamwork and everyone racing for each other. All of us are pretty close in time. That allows us to race with each other and push each other to be better. We found that having a strong team overall will help you win meets, instead of just having one or two insanely fast runners like other teams,” Senior Skylar Best helped the team qualify for CIF State by finishing 24th of 111 runners. It marks her second time to reach State after individually qualifying as a freshman.

articles.text: With Piedmont High reaching the CIF State Cross Country Championship and both soccer programs beginning their seasons this week, we highlight Jack Stein of Pomona-Pitzer’s cross country and track teams, Audrey Lam of Brown University’s women’s soccer team and Julien Lee of Colorado College’s cross country and track and field teams. Photo courtesy of Pomona-Pitzer Athletics Jack Stein, PHS Class of 2022, recently set Pomona-Pitzer’s school record in the 8,000 meter run. Jack Stein, Pomona-Pitzer Jack Stein, PHS Class of 2022, was the Post’s Co-Athlete of the Year in 2022 and is now a senior on Pomona-Pitzer’s cross country and track teams. This fall, Stein ran his way into Pitzer’s record books on September 27 at the UC Riverside Invitational, where he set the program’s all-time record in the 8,000-meter run. He clocked a time of 23:45.4, breaking the previous record by seven seconds. Pomona-Pitzer finished eighth out of 32 schools at this year’s Division 3 NCAA Championship on November 22, where Stein placed 11th out of 291 runners in 24:10.3. Stein also helped the Sagehens place third out of 32 schools at the 2024 Division 3 NCAA Championship, finishing 28th out of 294 athletes with a time of 24:34.3 on the 8k course. In the 2025 track season, Stein competed in the 5k and 10k events at the SCIAC Track and Field Championship. He placed seventh out of 44 in the 5k in 14:57.80, and second out of 16 in the 10k with a time of 30:57.88. Stein and Pomona-Pitzer won the 2023 Division 3 NCAA Championship, edging Wisconsin-La Crosse by a single point, 158-159. Stein finished as the Sagehens’ fifth scorer, with his time of 25:49.3 ultimately determining the national title. Stein graduated from Piedmont High as the school’s all-time record holder in the 1600 and 3200, with times of 4:14.77 and 9:12.62. He also won the WACC cross country championship in 15:34.76, finished second out of 144 runners at the NCS Championship in 15:29.4 and placed 12th out of 209 at the CIF Championship in 15:43.4. Audrey Lam, Brown University Audrey Lam, PHS Class of 2023, was the Post’s Honorable Mention Athlete of the Year as a senior. She is now a junior on Brown University’s women’s soccer team, which just completed its 2025 season. Brown finished 9-4-4 and Staff Photo Audrey Lam, PHS Class of 2023, is a junior at Brown University. She’s pictured here competing with Oakland Soul’s USL W-League team. fell 3-0 to Princeton in the Ivy League tournament semifinals on November 6. Lam started all 17 matches and was among the team’s most active players, logging 1,328 minutes and recording four assists. Lam also played for the Oakland Soul pre-professional W League team over the summer, starting nearly every match and contributing one assist. In 2023, Lam helped Brown go 12-2-3 and earn the No. 3 seed in its NCAA Tournament bracket. The Bears beat Quinnipiac 3-0 in the opening round before falling 2-1 to No. 6 Mississippi State in the second round. Lam earned the Post’s Honorable Mention Athlete of the Year award after helping lead Piedmont High’s girls soccer team to a 13-1-6 record and its first Division 4 NCS championship in 20 years. She also earned WACC Player of the Year honors. Photo courtesy of Colorado College Athletics Julien Lee, PHS Class of 2024, is set to be a sophomore on Colorado College’s cross country and track teams. Julien Lee, Colorado College Julien Lee, PHS Class of 2024, is a sophomore on Colorado College’s cross country and track and field teams. This fall, Lee competed in four meets. At the Southern Collegiate Athletic Conference Cross Country Championship on November 1, he finished 46th out of 109 runners in 27:25.2. He was among the reserves as Colorado College won the team title over a field of 11 schools. His best time of the 2024 season came at the Roadrunner Invitational in Denver, where he clocked 28:15.3 to place 136th out of 187 runners. He also finished 96th out of 130 runners at the Colorado Springs Open in 28:29.4. In track and field, Lee competed in the SCAC Track and Field Championship in April, placing 21st out of 35 runners in the 5k with a time of 16:20.77.

articles.text: Staff Photos Ben Russell and the defending D5 CIF NorCal champion boys’ soccer team returns to the pitch on December 3 at Skyline in Oakland. Piedmont High’s boys soccer team opens its regular season on Wednesday, December 3, with a visit to Skyline High in Oakland. The Highlanders return to the pitch after winning last year’s Division 5 CIF NorCal title and finishing as runners-up in the Division 4 North Coast Section tournament. The Highlanders will have big shoes to fill with nine seniors from the Class of 2025 having graduated. Up top, Piedmont will have to replace lead striker Gianluca Bini, who scored a hat trick in the team’s 4-1 NorCal title win over Williams. Several younger players are stepping into key roles. Sophomore Ben Gerber and freshman Evan Yamanaka are already making an impact, while sophomore Robert Piniella returns as a starter from last season. “It’s going to be quite different to go from a 6’5” senior to younger players. It’s a slightly younger team, but we’re not just setting the standard for this season, but for years to come. That’s why it’s important to get these young guys in and get them prepared,” coach Ben Russell said. The attack could get a late-season boost from junior Derin Sabuncuoglu once he returns from his club’s MLS Next schedule. Sabuncuoglu scored in Piedmont’s 2-0 win over Colusa in last year’s NorCal semifinals and is currently on trial with USL Championship side Sacramento Republic, which is the second division of U.S. professional soccer. “He’s on trial at Sacramento Republic, but we will try to get him involved at the right time of the season again. He’ll practice when available and join when there’s a gap in his MLS Next season,” Russell said. The departure of Harper Mand opens a spot in the midfield, but senior Henry DeVan returns and has been named a team captain. Roman Ahearn looks set to take over the central attacking midfield role. Ahearn proved to be a vital playmaker and set-piece specialist last season. “Roman Ahearn is gonna be a crucial part of it, as well as Henry DeVan, who is going to be a captain. Henry plays as a six, and Roman as a ten,” Russell said. Piedmont’s backline will also feature new faces following the graduations of Max Goldfarb and Jacques Saldanha. Freshman Cole Venner is stepping in as the starting right back, while sophomore Maxwell Rodriguez is a player to watch at center back. “We have a very young back line. Cole Venner is a freshman and did a really great job in a scrimmage. Maxwell Rodriguez is a brother of Jacob Rodriguez, who graduated. He’ll be at the heart of our back line,” Russell said. In goal, Tobias Tsai takes over as starting goalkeeper, replacing Lucas Malecki. Colt Hitchcock

articles.text: Piedmont High’s junior varsity girls’ tennis team finished its 2025 fall season with a 9-8 record with impressive wins over Head Royce, Lick Wilmerding, and Bishop O’Dowd. The strength comes from team depth with 10 returning players who provided leadership and guidance to the six new team members. Team captains included Nuala Price and Chloe Hong, who helped create and nurture a positive environment where the girls showcased their dedication to both academics and tennis. In a little over two months, the players did drills and match play to improve their shots and especially mental toughness. Each match brought on challenges, but the constant was our players’ energy, enthusiasm and support of their teammates. The season culminated with the WACC Next Gen Tournament on November 1 at Castro Valley. The team represented PHS well with Layla Reed-Miguel winning the Singles Consolation bracket, and Lauren Udovch and Charlotte Phung winning the Doubles Consolation. Piedmont High’s JV girls’ tennis team finished its season with a 9-8 record. articles.text: The City of Piedmont and the Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF) will host the annual tree lighting ceremony at Community Hall on December 3. PBF will keep last year’s earlier start time of 6 p.m. to make the event easier for younger guests. The celebration will feature the illumination of an 80-foot redwood tree and a menorah, along with activities for both children and adults. Santa will be available in Community Hall starting at 5:30 p.m. for photos. Piedmont Girl Scouts and the Recreation Department will host an activity table where children can create a light-themed art project and play games. Inside Community Hall, children can write letters to Santa using the provided supplies, including colored pencils, paper and envelopes. Volunteer “elves” will be on hand to help, and a special mailbox with express delivery to the North Pole will be available for drop-off. Food and drinks have been donated by local groups eager to contribute to the holiday celebration. Piedmont Boy Scouts will serve hot cider donated by Piedmont Grocery and hot cocoa supplied by the Heafey-Baum Group. Recreation Department staff will offer latkes, gifted by the Chabad Jewish Center. Music will be performed by the Piedmont High School Troubadours, the student-run a cappella group. After brief remarks from Piedmont mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen, a Make-AWish Foundation recipient will flip the switch to light the 80-foot redwood, the menorah and the surrounding greenery throughout the park. Attendees will receive a fiber-optic light wand so everyone can take part in lighting up Piedmont together. This community tradition began in 1969 as Piedmont’s tree lighting ceremony. Now in its fourth year under the name Lights Up Piedmont, the event has grown to include symbols of winter light celebrations from around the world. The 80-foot Redwood tree lit up Staff photo

articles.text: The Asian Art Museum’s newest exhibition, Rave into the Future: Art in Motion, is on view now through January 26, 2026. The exhibition spotlights women and queer artists from the West Asia diaspora currently based in the United States and Europe and is inspired by West Asian rave and underground music culture. Oakland-based Arab Persian American artist Sahar Khoury contributes a multimedia sculpture equipped with a functioning DJ deck that will be activated by local Asian and Asian diaspora DJs. Los Angeles–based Yemeni American artist Yasmine Nasser Diaz’s installation For Your Eyes Only recreates an intimate bedroom where projections of dancers, archival clips, and protest materials form a layered portrait of generational expression and activism. Disguise as Dancefloor, a nearly 100-square-foot copper dancefloor by London-based Lebanese American artist Joe Namy, is designed to record the footsteps of visitors while symbolizing the healing properties associated with the material across cultures. Other featured pieces bring humor, futurism, and fantastical narrative into the mix, including Meriem Bennani’s Party on the CAPS, Sophia al Maria and Fatima al Qadiri’s bass-driven Spiral, and Farah Al Qasimi’s horror-comedy Um Al Naar. The exhibition culminates in a glitter-filled “after-party” animated by robotic vacuum cleaners in Puff Out by the Brussels-based duo :mentalKLINIK. Curated by Naz Cuguoğlu, Assistant Curator of Contemporary Art, the exhibition has already earned significant recognition. Cuguoğlu received a curatorial research fellowship from The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts last year, and the museum was recently awarded an additional foundation grant to bring the project to fruition. “I wanted to create a space for narratives that build solidarity through joy, pleasure, and laughter,” Cuguoğlu said, noting the need to counter dominant Western portrayals of West Asia rooted in Orientalism and suffering. “This exhibition asks what we can learn from the autonomy, healing, and bliss that unfold on the dancefloor,” Cuguoğlu said. Museum Director and CEO Soyoung Lee added that the show offers a timely opportunity to broaden public understanding of West Asia while celebrating the universal joy of collective dance.
articles.title: Rave into the Future on view now at Asian Art Museum

articles.text: Eight performances presented in SF, Berkeley and Sonoma State University The beloved, annual holiday concert series returns next month. The San Francisco Gay Men’s Chorus ushers in the holiday season this December with its annual Holiday Spectacular concert series, presenting eight performances across the Bay Area and continuing a decades-long tradition of music, community and festive flair. Led by Artistic Director Jacob Stensberg, the 2025 program blends classic seasonal arrangements with the chorus’s signature camp, humor and theatrical energy. Event organizers said audiences can expect heartfelt choral harmonies, showstopping production numbers and a celebratory atmosphere designed to bring “joy, laughter and glitter” to the holidays. Chorus leaders said this year’s program is designed to offer a sense of unity and celebration for audiences of all ages, including families and “chosen families” throughout the region. The long-running holiday event remains one of the Bay Area’s most anticipated seasonal traditions, drawing thousands each year for a blend of musical artistry, community spirit and holiday exuberance. The series opens in San Francisco at the Golden Gate Theatre, located at One Taylor St., with performances scheduled for December 12 at 7:30 p.m. and December 13 at 1 p.m. and 7:30 p.m. Tickets start at $35. The following weekend, the chorus travels to the East Bay for two shows at Zellerbach Hall in Berkeley organized by Cal Performances. Those concerts take place December 20 at 2 p.m. and 8 p.m., with tickets ranging from $43 to $98. The Holiday Spectacular continues on December 21 at 5 p.m. at the Green Music Center’s Weill Hall at Sonoma State University in Rohnert Park. Tickets for that performance range from $31 to $118. The series concludes Christmas Eve with “Home for the Holidays – Special Christmas Eve Edition” at Davies Symphony Hall in San Francisco. Performances are scheduled for December 24 at 4 p.m. and 7 p.m., with tickets starting at $35. Tickets for all performances are available online at https:// www.sfgmc.org/welcome/.
articles.title: San Francisco Gay Men’s Chorus launches “Holiday Spectacular” performances on Dec. 12

Los Angeles–based Yemeni American artist Yasmine Nasser Diaz’s installation For Your Eyes Only recreates an intimate bedroom where projections of dancers, archival clips, and protest materials form a layered portrait of generational expression and activism. Disguise as Dancefloor, a nearly 100-square-foot copper dancefloor by London-based Lebanese American artist Joe Namy, is designed to record the footsteps of visitors while symbolizing the healing properties associated with the material across cultures. Other featured pieces bring humor, futurism, and fantastical narrative into the mix, including Meriem Bennani’s Party on the CAPS, Sophia al Maria and Fatima al Qadiri’s bass-driven Spiral, and Farah Al Qasimi’s horror-comedy Um Al Naar. The exhibition culminates in a glitter-filled “after-party” animated by robotic vacuum cleaners in Puff Out by the Brussels-based duo :mentalKLINIK. Curated by Naz Cuguoğlu, Assistant Curator of Contemporary Art, the exhibition has already earned significant recognition. Cuguoğlu received a curatorial research fellowship from The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts last year, and the museum was recently awarded an additional foundation grant to bring the project to fruition. “I wanted to create a space for narratives that build solidarity through joy, pleasure, and laughter,” Cuguoğlu said, noting the need to counter dominant Western portrayals of West Asia rooted in Orientalism and suffering. “This exhibition asks what we can learn from the autonomy, healing, and bliss that unfold on the dancefloor,” Cuguoğlu said. Museum Director and CEO Soyoung Lee added that the show offers a timely opportunity to broaden public understanding of West Asia while celebrating the universal joy of collective dance. San Francisco Gay Men’s Chorus launches “Holiday Spectacular” performances on Dec. 12 Eight performances presented in SF, Berkeley and Sonoma State University The beloved, annual holiday concert series returns next month. By Allyson Aleksey The San Francisco Gay Men’s Chorus ushers in the holiday season this December with its annual Holiday Spectacular concert series, presenting eight performances across the Bay Area and continuing a decades-long tradition of music, community and festive flair. Led by Artistic Director Jacob Stensberg, the 2025 program blends classic seasonal arrangements with the chorus’s signature camp, humor and theatrical energy. Event organizers said audiences can expect heartfelt choral harmonies, showstopping production numbers and a celebratory atmosphere designed to bring “joy, laughter and glitter” to the holidays. Chorus leaders said this year’s program is designed to offer a sense of unity and celebration for audiences of all ages, including families and “chosen families” throughout the region. The long-running holiday event remains one of the Bay Area’s most anticipated seasonal traditions, drawing thousands each year for a blend of musical artistry, community spirit and holiday exuberance. The series opens in San Francisco at the Golden Gate Theatre, located at One Taylor St., with performances scheduled for December 12 at 7:30 p.m. and December 13 at 1 p.m. and 7:30 p.m. Tickets start at $35. The following weekend, the chorus travels to the East Bay for two shows at Zellerbach Hall in Berkeley organized by Cal Performances. Those concerts take place December 20 at 2 p.m. and 8 p.m., with tickets ranging from $43 to $98. The Holiday Spectacular continues on December 21 at 5 p.m. at the Green Music Center’s Weill Hall at Sonoma State University in Rohnert Park. Tickets for that performance range from $31 to $118. The series concludes Christmas Eve with “Home for the Holidays – Special Christmas Eve Edition” at Davies Symphony Hall in San Francisco. Performances are scheduled for December 24 at 4 p.m. and 7 p.m., with tickets starting at $35. Tickets for all performances are available online at https:// www.sfgmc.org/welcome/.

articles.text: American Conser vator y Theater (A.C.T.) presents the acclaimed holiday tribute musical Judy Garland: We Need a Little Christmas, showing at Strand Theatre in San Francisco December 6 and 7. London native Debbie Wileman marks her San Francisco debut with A.C.T.’s production of We Need a Little Christmas fresh off the release of her new holiday album A Christmas Garland. Wileman impersonates a range of classic female singers of Hollywood’s Golden Age, including Shirley Bassey, Marilyn Monroe, Julie Andrews and Billie Holiday, but her uncanny recreation of Judy Garland’s famous vocals garnered her a massive online following and worldwide recognition. She teams up with producer Scott Stander to perform a touring concert of Garland’s famous holiday hits including “Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas,” which Garland introduced in the 1944 movie Meet Me in St. Louis, and “The Christmas Song,” which she performed with Mel Tormé on The Judy Garland Show. A.C.T.’s Strand Theater is located at 1127 Market Street in San Francisco. Judy Garland: We Need a Little Christmas is showing on Saturday, December 6 at 7:30 p.m. and Sunday, December 7 at 2 p.m. Tickets are on-sale now at www.act-sf.org. articles.title: A.C.T. presents Judy Garland: We Need a Little Christmas Dec. 6 & 7

articles.text: Dancers in Rex Wheeler’s “Snow Day!” Smuin Contemporary Ballet’s annual holiday production “The Christmas Ballet” is touring the Bay Area with performances in Carmel, Mountain View and San Francisco next month. “The Christmas Ballet” is a popular ensemble of 31 short dance pieces, ranging from classical to swing to step dance and Broadway and featuring holiday classics like “Santa Baby,” “Joy to the World” and “Silver Bells.” Showtimes for the 2025 production tour vary. “The Christmas Ballet” will be presented at Sunset Center in Carmel December 5 and 6; at Mountain View Center for the Performing Arts in Mountain View December 11 through 14; and at Blue Shield of California Theater at Yerba Buena Center for the Arts in San Francisco December 18 through 28. Visit https://www.smuinballet. org/ for more information and to purchase tickets. Most of the choreography is by the dance company’s founder, Michael Smuin, who died in 2007. Along with a return to Smuin’s original pieces, the company will also reveal new works this year by Smuin Ballet’s Dance Director Julia Adam, Artistic Director Amy Seiwert, and San Francisco Ballet Soloist Myles Thatcher. Smuin’s beloved “Santa Baby,” featuring the “world’s longest feather boa” rounds out the two-act performance. After the concert, I spoke with pianist Amy Zanrosso and asked her who made the arrangement. She responded that everything came together, and that the musicians did not need to make any adjustments. It was fun watching the individual players. In one particular piece, bass player Ken Miller dazzled the audience with his harmonics. Carnival of the Animals served as an appetizer for what came next. This was the variation movement from Schubert’s “Trout” quintet. Perhaps they will play the entire quintet next time. The all-too-brief concert came to an end with Sacha Jacobsen’s arrangement of Gershwin’s Rhapsody in Blue. It is quite amazing how adaptable this composition is. Exactly one week ago there was a solo piano version of Rhapsody. That version was fabulous and so was the yesterday’s version for piano and string quintet. Bravo to all of the performers and to arranger Sasha Jacobsen. Sending all of you warmest regards for a beautiful Thanksgiving…
articles.title: Smuin Ballet presents “The Christmas Ballet” in San Francisco Dec.18 - 28

articles.text: ‘Twas the week before Thanksgiving Ogden Nash was preparing his animal parade in Piedmont’s Center for the Arts last week as six musicians served up a memorable concert on Sunday afternoon: violinists Beni Shinohara and Karen Shinozaki, viola Paul Ehrlich, cello Victoria Ehrlich, bass Ken Miller, piano Amy Zanrosso and narrator Danny Slomoff. Entitled “Carnival, Trout, and Blue,” the concert was a success from beginning to end. St.-Saens’ composition, Carnival of the Animals, opened the program. Curiously, the composer had some misgivings about his masterpiece and forbade its publication. If he had witnessed Sunday’s performance, he would have been overjoyed. Narrator Danny Slomoff delivered the delightfully clever poems by Ogden Nash with appropriate relish. So did the six musicians. It was obvious that they had fun at every turn, including subtle sarcasm alongside understated virtuosity. Those of us in the audience who were watching noticed smiles on the faces of the musicians. Ogden Nash’s poems always produce laughter from the audience. It was obvious that they understood everything perfectly. Piedmont’s Center for the arts concert on Sunday featured violinists Beni Shinohara and Karen Shinozaki, pianist Amy Zanrosso, violist Paul Ehrlich, cellist Victoria Ehrlich, bassist Ken Miller, and narrator Danny Slomoff. The concert had all the right ingredients.
articles.title: The right ingredients

articles.text: From ornament-making at Randall Museum in San Francisco to evening hot cocoa strolls in Downtown Alameda, the Bay Area has a lot to offer to families with kids of all ages throughout December. articles.text: Until December 15 Love at First Sight Art Exhibit Piedmont native Michael Stehr’s art exhibit will remain on the walls at PCA into mid-December for you to enjoy while attending other events at the venue. Please visit the Fine Art 2025 section of his website at mstehr.com for more information on the exhibit or write to at mstehrart@gmail.com. Sunday, November 30, 5:30 p.m. mOthertongue: Lived Experience in Asian America Now, in the 21st century, old stereotypes persist, affecting how Asian-Americans continue to be viewed to this day. Soprano Jennifer Lien attempts to challenge outdated cultural ideas by sharing new art with fresh cultural ideas. The new songs on this program, accompanied by Dr. Gwendolyn Mok on piano, express the joys, pains, contradictions, and pride experienced by Asians living in this land we call home. She is grateful to composers Justine Chen, Melissa Dunphy, and Kamala Sankaram and the others who made this project possible. The stories are all American stories: all of us belong here. Advance tickets are at https://www.brownpapertickets. com/e/6743616. Thursday, December 4, 4:00 p.m. US Premiere Screening — Monastir Monastir is a haunting and poetic film whose imaginative premise has earned Francesco Paolo Paladino outstanding praise in Italian film circles. This is a rare opportunity to witness a truly international collaboration. The introductory and closing texts are by his long-term collaborator Luca Chino Ferrari, a respected author and lyricist from Cremona. The narration is by London’s Edward Ka Spel, a soloist and composer of the Legendary Pink Dots. The melodies and lyrical adaptations are crafted by Dorothy Moskowitz Falarski of Piedmont. Paladino, Ferrari and Falarski have been working together since 2022 as The United States of Alchemy, their name inspired by the United States of America rock band in which Dorothy made her debut in 1968. Monastir is a follow-up to their highly acclaimed Under the Sky, released by Tompkins Square Records in 2023. Free event. Saturday, December 6, 7:30 p.m. Boon Hiker Band Concert The Boon Hiker Band returns once more to sing in the resonant and lovely Piedmont Center for the Arts. The songs lean toward Americana/Folk/Indie traditions, with energetic musicianship provided by three East Bay members. The five North Bay members bring additional mayhem on instruments and enhance the vocal textures and harmonies. Advance tickets at https://www.brownpapertickets.com/e/6749696. Sunday, December 7, 4:30 p.m. In the Tradition Jazz & Pop Piano Trio In the Tradition Piano Trio – Bill Jackman, Michael Jones, and Albert Brooks – will kick off the holiday season with a program that includes all your favorite holiday music, from 16th Century traditional songs to O Tannenbaum (1824), and thence to mid-20th Century holiday songs! Don’t miss the relaxed pleasure of a Sunday late afternoon in the Classic Jazz Club with the trio. Doors open at 4:15 PM. Tickets $30, cash/ check ONLY, at the door, or $25 at https://www.brownpapertickets.com/e/6214927. Thursday, December 11, 6:30 p.m. Sacha Grippando Jewelry Lecture A Jewelry Tour of London will be an enchanting evening of wine and festive cookies as Sacha Grippando shares highlights from her spectacular jewelry trip to London. This captivating lecture will delve into London’s rich history as a global center for jewelry manufacturing from the 19th century to present day. Sacha will guide you through current exhibitions at the Victoria & Albert Museum, Buckingham Palace, the Tower of London, and the renowned jewelry dealer Wartski. The presentation will be filled with stunning photographs of exquisite jewelry and with anecdotes about this incredible city. No fee, but donations will be accepted at the door for entry and refreshments.

articles.text: have passed. We see a Victorian farmhouse that has been turned into a survivalist island. It is inviting, cozy even, surrounded by crops and powered by a generator. A necklace of lights glows at night, strung from the house to the outbuildings. A wide path of sand leads to the front porch. Through what we see, we understand the family has endured. In fact, they have thrived, for Evelyn is now pregnant. In the basement, Lee’s workshop is filled with gear, electronics and screens monitoring the property. Newspaper clippings warn people to avoid all sound. A shortwave radio sits on a workbench. The house is filled with light, for whatever “they” are, they cannot see, only hear. Even the faintest crunch of a leaf can bring danger. Over and over, the universal gesture appears, an index finger held in front of the lips, telling the children that silence is their only defense. Remain still, wait, listen, their lives depend on it. Even a family game of Monopoly is played with soft, covered pieces. I am hesitant to reveal more than what is evident in the first act. This is a film that should be experienced fresh. Knowing too much would diminish the trepidation and uncertainty that build as the plot unfolds, silently and step by step. pages.text: Wednesday, November 26, 2025 21 MOVIES FOR ADULTS By Chris Honoré A Quiet Place is almost totally without dialogue but still conveys a sense of dread more loudly than the familiar horror trope so common to this genre. It is a film of faces and close ups, capturing a spectrum from deep familial affection to unequivocal terror. Its premise is brilliant in its simplicity and elegance. The opening scene tells us it is DAY 89. Immediately it is evident that something terrible has taken place, an apocalypse of a kind. The what and how are unclear. The setting is a small, bucolic town in upstate New York. A family, three children and their mother and father, scavenges the pillaged shelves of a grocery and drug store searching for supplies and medicine. They walk slowly, carefully. Each is barefoot. No A Quiet Place one speaks. They communicate in sign language. Within minutes, the tension that will haunt the film throughout is palpable. What is the source of their fear? When they leave the store, they walk on a ribbon of sand that cushions their footsteps. The parents, Lee and Evelyn Abbott (John Krasinski and Emily Blunt), are hyper vigilant, pausing often to listen. Whatever is out there represents an existential threat in the extreme, and the audience is not given even a hint of what it might be, until a sudden, shocking moment of movement results in their youngest child being taken. Lee’s face twists in anguish as he runs toward his son, realizing he is too late to save him. What was a blindingly quick reveal is followed by a title card telling us that more than 400 days Amistad Emily Blunt and Millicent Simmonds in A Quiet Place have passed. We see a Victorian farmhouse that has been turned into a survivalist island. It is inviting, cozy even, surrounded by crops and powered by a generator. A necklace of lights glows at night, strung from the house to the outbuildings. A wide path of sand leads to the front porch. Through what we see, we understand the family has endured. In fact, they have thrived, for Evelyn is now pregnant. In the basement, Lee’s workshop is filled with gear, electronics and screens monitoring the property. Newspaper clippings warn people to avoid all sound. A shortwave radio sits on a workbench. The house is filled with light, for whatever “they” are, they cannot see, only hear. Even the faintest crunch of a leaf can bring danger. Over and over, the universal gesture appears, an index finger held in front of the lips, telling the children that silence is their only defense. Remain still, wait, listen, their lives depend on it. Even a family game of Monopoly is played with soft, covered pieces. I am hesitant to reveal more than what is evident in the first act. This is a film that should be experienced fresh. Knowing too much would diminish the trepidation and uncertainty that build as the plot unfolds, silently and step by step. All of it feels authentic and believable, though a certain suspension of disbelief is required. articles.text: by Wanda Sykes. excitement. A scene from How to Train Your Dragon: The Hidden World How to Train Your Dragon: The Hidden World is the final installment of what has been a very successful franchise, the first released in 2010. This last chapter may lack the punch and freshness of the earlier films, but it is beautifully animated, with glorious scenes of dragons in flight circling the island refuge of Berk. This medieval village, home to a cohort of Vikings now led by the aspirational chief Hiccup (Jay Baruchel) and supported by his girlfriend Astrid (America Ferrera), is filled with memorable characters both young and old. And of course Hiccup’s best friend Toothless, a rare alpha dragon, is alive and well, and the two still ride the skies as one. Again, the computer graphics are breathtaking. This is no longer your grandfather’s painstaking, Disneyesque animation. There is, naturally, a villain, a malevolent dragon hunter named Grimmel (F. Murray Abraham) who speaks with a curious accent. His mission is to kill Toothless and control the dragons who live peacefully in Berk. Fortunately, he is a bit of a klutz, good at plotting, less so at carrying out his schemes. Unexpectedly, there are two budding love stories in this film. One, telegraphed in the previous installments, is between Hiccup and Astrid, who are now talking about marriage. The other involves Toothless and a kindred female dragon who, unlike his obsidian scales, is white as snow. It is hard not to wonder how these romantic threads will play for an audience still well below tween age. Still, the dialogue is charming and lightly contemporized, though Hiccup never quite ventures into “Dude!” territory. The final act, which takes Hiccup and Astrid to the Hidden World, is remarkable, a feast of color. Having found this sanctuary at the edge of the world, Hiccup understands that Toothless and his new companion finally have a true home. Separation is inevitable. Or perhaps not. In the end, there is more than enough here for young viewers to fully say goodbye to a delightful crew of dragon riders and their dragons. How to Train Your Dragon: The Hidden World. Directed by Dean DeBois. Starring Jay Baruchel, Gerard Butler and America Ferrera. Duration 1 hr., 44 min. Rated PG. Released 2019. Genre: animated adventure. Streaming on Prime Video, Netflix, Apple TV, Fandango and YouTube. Tickets: $27.99 advance, $30 at the door. Doors open 7:00 p.m. ~ refreshments available! pages.text: 24 24 Wednesday, November 26, 2025 Features Walking on Wednesday A Visit to the nearly finished Linda Beach tot lot By Dick Carter The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group kept its good weather streak alive last week. Rain was forecast for the nigh before, but once again the morning offered nothing more than a blanket of clouds. A lively crowd of 52 walkers and four K-9 best friends gathered at the Exedra. Before heading out, the group heard that the following week’s Thanksgiving Eve walk would feature something special: Matt Gerhardt will lead a gentle tour, not a run, of the Piedmont Turkey Tot 5K route. Several walkers had also read in the previous week’s Post that the redesigned Linda Beach Tot Lot had opened the Friday before. Back in February the group had visited the old tot lot and discussed the City’s “Linda Beach Tot Lot Equipment Replacement Project.” Now that the work was done, they wanted to see the new version for themselves. The route up Linda Avenue would also take them to a few streets they had not visited yet this year. The walkers headed down Magnolia Avenue and paused to admire the new Community Pool. It is beautiful, though they knew the opening had been delayed because of equipment issues. Walker and Post cartoonist Phil Witte refers to it as “the pool of the future,” and the group agreed that the name fits. From there they continued along Magnolia, then down lower San Carlos Avenue to Oakland Avenue. After crossing Oakland, they reached Howard Avenue and the edge of Beach Playfield. It was unclear whether the tot lot’s upper gate was open, so the group cut through the lower playfield and joined Linda Avenue from there. As they walked up Linda toward the gate, they spotted a SIDEWALK CLOSED sign. When they arrived, they discovered a torn up sidewalk and a friendly worker who told them construction was still underway and the tot lot was closed. The group took the news gracefully, though not everyone on the street felt the same. A preschooler with her instructors voiced her disappointment with an impressive display of volume and persistence. Even without entering, the walkers were able to see the new tot lot through the gate and get a sense of the changes. Some background details were shared. The $400,000 project was funded 75% by the City’s Facilities Capital Fund, with the remaining 25% coming from a $100,000 donation from the Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF). The PBF has a long history of supporting play areas in every major park in town, including Dracena, Main Park and Hampton Field. The redesigned tot lot reflects months of outreach and surveys with parents, caregivers and young users who offered feedback on their favorite features. The new play area includes updated equipment, a bright and welcoming theme, swings, low climbing structures sized for ages two to five, an enclosed layout and classic elements like slides and steps. Interactive panels and balance features encourage imagination and movement. The new rubber matting surface is ADA compliant and provides additional safety. A new water fountain is also in place. The group could not go inside, but the sidewalk offered enough space for a group photo to mark their reconnaissance mission. With the morning still young, the walkers continued up Linda past Beach School and on to the 900 block of Kingston Avenue. The street, repaved this year, looked terrific. The group admired the many older homes built in the early decades of the 1900s. Some began life as modest bungalows and have been thoughtfully remodeled over the years. A house at 934 Kingston featured a 100-year medallion, and a quick Zillow search confirmed it was built in 1907, just one year after Piedmont was incorporated. Kingston also offered its share of small curiosities. There was an eye catching red orange trimmed house, a very old and very large jade plant pruned into a front yard hedge and, on the car strip in front of one home, a padded piece of porch furniture. The walkers admired it but did not test its comfort. Their return route took them down Greenbank Avenue, across Grand Avenue to Cambridge Way and up Jerome Avenue to Oakland Avenue. They climbed the upper portion of San Carlos Avenue and made their way back up Magnolia for an on time, noon return to the Exedra. The group agreed it had been a good outing, even without the long awaited tour of the new tot lot. They know there will be another Wednesday. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join. There is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration is at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu or contact (510) 420-3070 for more information. articles.text: The culinary cognoscenti have proclaimed flavors of the Eastern Mediterranean are all the rage, and for good reason. These tasty spice and herb combinations are familiar, but with an exotic twist. The good news for us is there are numerous options to procure them for your home’s kitchen. I find it is easier to try out a few prepared spice blends when venturing into new flavor territory to learn what suits my taste buds. Inevitably after a few uses I start “doctoring” the blend – adding here, subtracting there, until I start making my own concoctions. Such is the case for ras el hanout, a spice blend originating in North Africa. It translates from Arabic to “top of the shop,” implying the best spices available go into the mix. While there are many versions (some with dozens of ingredients), most include cumin, ginger, cinnamon, cardamom, coriander, turmeric, cayenne, allspice, cloves, salt and pepper – spices found in most well-stocked pantries. You might notice these are also very warming spices – perfect for cold winter days. Starting with a prepared blend, this soup comes together very quickly, under 30 minutes. This recipe is perfect for adapting according to your tastes and what you have available. After all, it’s soup – so there’s a wide range to navigate! Experiment by switching out the kale for any winter green, and adding some shredded cooked chicken for a hearty meal-in-a-bowl.

Your Neighborhood Garage Door Store for Over 50 Years RESIDENTIAL GARAGE DOORS AUTOMATIC GATES & ACCESS CONTROLS COMMERCIAL DOORS RSDOORS.COM 510-483-9700 RSDOORS.COM 510-483-9700 35 years of experience in architectural design www.kaplanarchitects.com (510) 361-0223 Ingredients • 1 tablespoon olive oil • 2 cups butternut squash, diced into ½-inch cubes • ½ cup onion, diced • 2 cloves garlic, minced • 1-2 teaspoons ras el hanout spice blend to taste • ½ teaspoon ground cumin • ⅛ teaspoon cayenne pepper, or to taste • Salt and freshly ground black pepper to taste • 32 ounces chicken or vegetable broth, homemade or low sodium • 1½ cups cooked chickpeas, rinsed and drained (equals one 15-ounce can) • 3 cups kale leaves, remove the tough center stem and slice into ¼-inch ribbons • Greek yogurt and fresh cilantro leaves to serve, optional Instructions Heat the olive oil in a large saucepan over medium heat until shimmering. Add the butternut squash, stirring occasionally, until the edges begin to brown and the squash begins to soften; about 4 minutes. Add the onions and stir frequently until they start to become translucent; about 2 minutes. Add the garlic and spices, stirring constantly to evenly coat the squash and onions. Be careful to avoid scorching the garlic and spices. Add the chickpeas and broth. Bring to a low boil. Add the kale and simmer until it is tender but retains its bright green color; about 3-4 minutes. Taste and adjust seasoning, salt and pepper. Garnish with yogurt and freshly chopped cilantro and serve. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok at PiedmontPantry.com

pages.text: 26 26 Wednesday, November 26, 2025 WINE CORNER The Wine Corner Napa Valley Wine Tasting Featuring Lewis Cellars and Elyse Winery By Pierre DuMont For anyone who has tried to go wine tasting in Napa Valley recently you know that it is not exactly an easy task. Not that there is any scarcity of wineries; Napa now hosts over 500 wineries. It’s just that prices for tastings have increased so much in recent years that the cost becomes prohibitive. Also, some of the better wineries are booked out weeks in advance. So, I was delighted on a recent trip to Napa to have the opportunity to taste at two totally different wineries. On the luxurious end of the spectrum, I visited Lewis Cellars who just opened an opulent new tasting room on Silverado Trail 5 days before my visit. On the other end of the scale representing an old school winery was Elyse Winery who offered a casual down-home tasting experience that was simple and perfect. Here is a run-down on some of the current releases of each winery. Lewis Cellars Lewis Cellars was started in 1992 by former Indy racer Randy Lewis and his wife Debbie and later joined by their son Dennis. Over the years the Oak Knoll area winery gained notoriety for producing outstanding Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon, and Syrah. The little winery won outstanding accolades from the wine press including a “Wine of the Year” from Wine Spectator magazine. In 2021 the Resnick family bought Lewis Cellars along with the Robert Sinskey Winery on Silverado Trail. They decided to turn the Sinskey property into a luxurious world class wine tasting showroom. Randy Lewis and Dennis Bell remain involved with leadership under the new structure. When I approached the tasting room last month three attendants in black suits, white shirts and bolo ties greeted us with a glass of Sauvignon Blanc and nonstop patter about the new tasting room. It was obvious no expense had been spared. The furniture was luxurious, the fabrics ornate, the walls adorned by beautiful custom designed art and the wall to ceiling glass windows offered a stunning view of Napa Valley. In addition to the wines, they served delicious culinary tidbits created by their on-site chef and designed to pair specifically with the wines. It was one of the most luxurious tastings I have experienced anywhere. • 2023 Lewis Sauvignon Blanc Matured in oak and stainless steel the Lewis Sauvignon Blanc features subtle toast and lees notes and a hint of hazelnut to go along with guava, pear and fig. It’s on the ripe side flavor wise while being medium bodied with a softly, creamy feel on the palate and a long silky finish. Excellent aperitif. • 2023 Lewis Chardonnay Russian River Valley Two Chardonnays to us at the tasting. One was a big buttery old style Napa Valley Chard which was just a bit over the top. Then there was this wine from the Russian River Valley which was leaner with much less oak on the nose. It has lemon citrus flavors that were refreshing in the mouth with great acid and fine balance. Both wines were well made but we preferred this style. • 2022 Lewis Cabernet Sauvignon This wine is blended with some Merlot and Cabernet Franc and aged in 75% new French oak. The wine begins with aromas of cherries and currants with some herbal notes. In the mouth, the wine is medium to full-bodied, The view of Napa Valley from Lewis Cellars. The Elyse tasting room is a throwback to simpler days in Napa Valley. silky textured and elegant, with hints of toasty oak and red berries lingering on the finish. Not particularly tannic, it should be approachable within a few years and drink well for at least 15. • 2022 Lewis Big Blend This is a mélange of Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Petite Sirah. It unwinds in the glass with notes of cassis, plums, violets and black pepper. On the palate, the wine is bold, velvety and full-bodied, with lots of crunchy fruit and good juicy acidity, as well as excellent concentration and length. This saw 65% new oak, but it is not obtrusive and provides great structure and a hint of vanilla. • 2023 Lewis Full Circle This is Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah and Petite Sirah. It used to be considered an anathema to combine a Bordeaux grape like Cabernet and a Rhone grape like Syrah. This wine proves how silly that rule was. It combines the best of both worlds with an ebullient nose that bounds out of the glass followed by blackberry, plum and black cherry flavors on the palate. It is big bodied with a round mouthfeel, extremely complex, it has just the right amount on tannins on the satisfying finish. Elyse Winery Our next tasting was at the opposite end of the Napa Valley luxury continuum. Elyse Winery is about as far as you can get from the opulence of Lewis. The tasting room is housed in a humble wood building and our tasting was outdoors under a trellis on a wooden picnic table. It was very old school and like the Napa I visited 20 years ago. Nestled in the heart of Napa Valley on Hoffman Lane just south of Yountville, Elyse Winery is a beloved, small-producThe knowledgeable Garett Lyon directs the Elyse tasting room. tion estate known for crafting deeply expressive, vineyard-designate red wines. Founded in the mid-1980s by Ray and Nancy Coursen, Elyse started in 1987 with just 286 cases of Zinfandel sourced from the historic Morisoli Vineyard. Over the decades, the winery has built a reputation for fruit-forward authenticity, focusing especially on Zinfandel, Cabernet Sauvignon, and Petite Sirah. In 1997, the Coursens purchased their own hilltop property with a rustic barn-turned-tasting room, anchored by just 1.5 acres of estate vines and set among quiet Napa vineyards. Elyse is celebrated for its commitment to expressing “sense of place”: each wine reflects the unique soils, climate, and farming of its source vineyards. In 2018, the winery passed to new owners Josh Peeples and Cheryl Foil but retained its traditional ethos under talented winemaker Russell Bevan. The new ownership under the name HQ also added additional brands Addax and Institution. pages.text: Wednesday, November 26, 2025 31 Bill Baringer Continued from page 10 Permission from Denali Gabriel, a mountain guide from Chile, told the group, “The mountain will grant, or deny, permission to reach its summit, and you need to honor that decision.” While they were waiting for the weather to clear, the rescue helicopter retrieved a badly frostbitten guide and climber high on the mountain above. Additionally, a pair of climbers in another party nearly suffered asphyxia by using a camp stove in their tent without sufficient ventilation. After two weather days, Baringer and the group ventured to Camp Four at 17,255 feet, despite forecasts of 60+ mph winds. In the words of singer David Lee Roth, “I guarantee, you will find no reasonable men on top of big mountains.” They woke up the next morning and found no new snow from the night and relatively light winds. The guides told them if they couldn’t summit in eight hours, they were turning around regardless. Baringer headed up the “autobahn” section, an ironically named extremely steep and slow slope. The weather turned out to be great and they summited in 6 ½ hours, giving them extra time at the summit. Having conquered another behemoth of a mountain, Baringer checked off number five on his list of the world’s highest peaks on each of the seven continents. Weeks later back home in Piedmont, Baringer reflected on the trip warmly. “Denali, I have to say, is my favorite. It is such a beautiful mountain and I had a great time. I’d love to go back and ski it from the top.” Some people never give up. NEXT: Part 1 of Baringer’s Mt. Everest climb, the world’s tallest peak. • 2021 Elyse Zinfandel Morisoli Vineyard $75 The Morisoli Family has been growing grapes in the Rutherford area for many years and have recently started producing their own wines. articles.text: For many, Thanksgiving is their very favorite holiday. It doesn’t involve presents, chocolate, fireworks or barbeques. articles.text: Highlands Preschool has enjoyed remarkable consistency with the same beautiful home and only four directors in 70 years of playtime. Their space has all the intangibles preschool age kids desire, a beautiful classroom full of light, a craft room to create, an outdoor space on the Piedmont Community Church campus and even a pet tortoise named Tortellini. In charge of the fun is Angela Livermore, the fourth director of Highlands Preschool who took over in 2024 when Deanna Johnson retired. The lineage of leadership starts with Mary Wood as the first director when Highlands opened in 1955. She passed the torch to her daughter, Joanna Wood, who led the program until Johnson succeeded her started in 1999. The longevity enjoyed in the chief position of the school is a testament to the culture there. Highlands Preschool is run daily by Livermore, Head Teacher Danielle Biondi, Art & Movement Teacher Tracy Herrera and volunteer parents. The space has a magical clubhouse feel and the institution believes wholehearted in learning through play. “You can learn everything through play, kids retain information better that way. We call it sneaky learning,” said Livermore. Danielle Biondi (left), Deanna Johnson, Angela Livermore, and Tracy Herrera at Deanna’s retirement party in 2024.
articles.title: Highlands Preschool celebrates 70 years and new Director

articles.text: On the crisp morning of Friday, November 14, Piedmont students, families, and community members gathered for the annual Ruby Bridges Walk. This district-wide event honors the courage of Ruby Bridges, the first Black child to integrate an all-white Southern elementary school. What began as a simple walk of solidarity has become a powerful tradition that invites participants to reflect, learn, and take action. The event commemorates Ruby’s historic 1960 walk into William Frantz Elementary School, a moment that helped challenge segregation nationwide and reminds today’s students that history is carried forward through their own choices and commitment to equity. This year’s event was co-sponsored by SERVES, led by Sarah Eisemon and Laura Edeen, and the Affinity Mentorship Program under the guidance of teacher and Director of Diversity Jean Takazawa. Together, they coordinated the event and brought the community together for a morning grounded in togetherness, education, and belonging. “This celebration not only honors the courage of one young girl, but also signals the collective commitment of the Piedmont community to being a place that is welcoming, inclusive, and rooted in Belonging for all,” said Takazawa. Like previous years, the walk began at Piedmont Park, where students proudly waved purple flags provided by Affinity Mentors at a welcoming booth. Parents and guardians joined along-

RELIGION CORNER A Soccer Sunday By Pastor Jim Hopkins “Children are a gift from the Lord.” Psalm 127:3a Instead of going to church this past Sunday morning I went to the soccer field. Specifically, as the Assistant Coach of the FC Clippers U-10 Boys Titan Turtles, I went to be on the sideline for our final game in the 2025 Jack London Youth Soccer League Recreational Tournament. After losing our two games on Saturday we concluded the season with a well-played victory over the FC Clipper Knights. The tournament itself was a beautiful sight with hundreds of adults and children from hundreds of households gathered on a resplendent fall day to play, coach, cheer, create memories and enjoy time together in the outdoors. Every church I know of would be overjoyed to have such a diverse throng of families gathered for worship and service. I do not intend to lift the long standing lament on the part of churches which runs “Youth ______ (fill in the sport or activity) is hurting us. Those families used to be in church. Now they are at _____________ (fill in the venue).” I do want to acknowledge that almost every household with children in it faces unrelenting demands of time and schedule. They have to make choices. Many try to balance commitment to congregation and to team. Most importantly, what I desire to recognize is that though there is something of a rift between church and sport based on the narrative that they are competing for participation, support, time and energy; they also have much in common and are committed to the same goals. They are unified in their desire for healthy children, healthy households and healthy communities. The methods and practices may be slightly different, yet both intend to bring adults and children together to experience beauty, share laughter, share tears, honor effort, encourage teamwork, cultivate joy, learn from disappointment, acknowledge loss and create a context in which the generations can connect. The Christian Bible tells of Jesus growing in wisdom and stature and in favor with God and the human family. Youth sports, such as soccer, are about children growing physically, mentally and even spiritually. Experts in the field teach us that children have four main spiritual needs. articles.text: The weekend my family moved to Piedmont, the COVID- 19 pandemic had just begun. I didn’t know where or how we would find our community. Our first year in Piedmont was a wash, with our kids still enrolled in Berkeley schools. The second year, my son was starting TK at Havens, and my middle daughter landed in a Piedmont preschool while we were on the waitlist for Piedmont Play School (PPS). While both schools offer a great education, it wasn’t until we walked through the doors of PPS that I finally felt it: This is our community. This is where we belong. Two of my three children have now attended PPS. I can say without hesitation it is the best preschool in Piedmont. Its magic lies not in a fancy curriculum, but in its whole-child approach and its welcoming of parents as collaborators. As a working parent, the co-op model was transformative. Each month, I stepped into the classroom, experiencing my child’s world alongside them. I watched PPS teachers gently navigate conflicts and set up activities that empowered every child. I took those practices home. PPS didn’t just prepare my kids for elementary school; it made me a better parent. Unlike other preschools we attended, where all art was preprinted and uniform, PPS lets kids create from their own imaginations. pages.text: Wednesday, November 19, 2025 3 The quiet magic of Piedmont Play School By June Groboske The weekend my family moved to Piedmont, the COVID- 19 pandemic had just begun. I didn’t know where or how we would find our community. Our first year in Piedmont was a wash, with our kids still enrolled in Berkeley schools. The second year, my son was starting TK at Havens, and my middle daughter landed in a Piedmont preschool while we were on the waitlist for Piedmont Play School (PPS). While both schools offer a great education, it wasn’t until we walked through the doors of PPS that I finally felt it: This is our community. This is where we belong. Two of my three children have now attended PPS. I can say without hesitation it is the best preschool in Piedmont. Its magic lies not in a fancy curriculum, but in its whole-child approach and its welcoming of parents as collaborators. As a working parent, the co-op model was transformative. Each month, I stepped into the classroom, experiencing my child’s world alongside them. I watched PPS teachers gently navigate conflicts and set up activities that empowered every child. I took those practices home. PPS didn’t just prepare my kids for elementary school; it made me a better parent. Unlike other preschools we attended, where all art was preprinted and uniform, PPS lets kids create from their own imaginations. Children decide how to engage, what to explore, and how to express themselves, supported by expert and caring teachers. The thoughtful curriculum at PPS fulfills the true purpose of preschool, supporting each child’s full potential: social, emotional, and academic. The indoor-outdoor flow is key. The yard is a classroom, too, where children develop motor skills, negotiate turn-taking, and build the social-emotional muscles that matter so much later on. My youngest, who spent two years at PPS, entered kindergarten with an ease I hadn’t seen in her older siblings: she knew how to ask questions and advocate for herself. PPS also quietly builds community for parents. Director Michelle used our parent meetings to bring in child development experts – from child psychologists to nutritionists – whose advice I still share with other parents today. Most importantly, PPS is a place where every child truly belongs. The teachers meet each student exactly where they are, giving them a clear, consistent message: This is your school. You have a place here. That deep sense of belonging stays with them. My daughter, who still plays “school” at home, talks about being a teacher, a seed planted firmly at PPS. In a town that prides itself on educational excellence, Piedmont Play School is one of our greatest assets. It prepares children not just for school, but to become curious, confident, and kind humans. That is the kind of magic a community can’t afford to lose. articles.text: Community volunteers will host a book drive for the East Bay Children’s Book Project at the Piedmont Turkey Trot Pre-Race Packet Pick-Up on Wednesday, November 26, from 3:00 - 5:00 p.m. at the Piedmont Veterans’ Memorial Building. Weather permitting, the table for book drop offs will be outside. Volunteers will collect new and gently used children’s books, including board books through high school books. Books should be clean with no marks or stains. Please bring donated books in boxes for easy transport to the East Bay Children’s Book Project (EBCBP). No textbooks, religious books, encyclopedias, magazines, adult books, or library discards. The mission of EBCBP is to help build literacy by putting books into the hands of children who have little or no access to them. Working through individuals and organizations who help children in need, the organization has given out more than two million free books since opening their doors in May 2005. School Board and City Council members started this tradition more than 10 years ago. EBCBP volunteer and former Wildwood Elementary School librarian Ellen Reed notes that 4022 books were donated last year during this event. “We are so grateful for the community’s contribution to our children’s literacy project year after year,” said Reed. If you are available to help collect/drive books on Wednesday, November 26 from 3:00-6:00 p.m. and have interest in maintaining this tradition going forward, please email Sarah Pearson at srpear@gmail.com. If you miss this opportunity to donate books, drop off books at EBCBP on Tuesdays 3:30 - 5:30 p.m. Children’s books may also be donated in the EBCBP box at the Piedmont Middle School library, 740 Magnolia Avenue during school hours. Monetary donations to EBCBP may be sent to: EBCBP, 2501 Harrison St., Oakland, CA 94612 or online at https://www.eastbaychildrensbookproject.org/donate-now/ About EBCBP Too many children in the Bay Area live in homes without books, and attend schools and programs where books are in short supply. Encouraging reading is not enough when families and schools do not have books. East Bay Children’s Book Project’s books are given directly to children in need by teachers, social workers, health care professionals, community outreach groups, housing authority employees, and police officers. Some are used by schools, daycare and community centers, homeless shelters, and hospitals to create libraries at their sites. Our clients determine how best to meet the needs of the children with whom they work. For more information see https://www.eastbaychildrensbookproject.org/about/. Last year volunteers delivered 4022 books to East Bay Children’s Book Project. Not pictured: Sarah Pearson (former School Board Trustee).

articles.text: Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan and a resident are pictured at a wildfire-resistant construction planning open house. Piedmont City Council will consider proposed updates to Piedmont’s energy efficiency “Reach Codes” and fire-resistant construction, or “home hardening,” requirements at their regular meeting on Monday, November 17, at 6:00 pm. The proposed changes are part of a larger update to Building and Fire Codes, driven by the State of California, which updates statewide building standards every three years. Cities are required to adopt the new codes and may include local amendments that address community priorities and local conditions. Expanded fire-resistant construction In 2020, the City Council voluntarily designated all of Piedmont as a Wildland-Urban Interface (WUI) based on topography, geography, and built environment – steep terrain, mature vegetation, and homes built close together – that make the city susceptible to wildfires. The proposed updates would reaffirm that commitment and ensure that consistent, research-based standards apply across the entire city. Proposed updates would adopt a newly developed State “Wildland-Urban Interface” code, replacing previous Piedmont-specific rules with a comprehensive statewide standard that: • Maintains strict home-hardening requirements for new construction • Expands fire-resistant construction requirements for major renovation projects The choice to continue incorporating these measures into City code – though Piedmont is not required to do so – reflects a clear community value: wildfire resilience matters here. Over the past nine months, extensive community outreach on home hardening found that residents broadly supported keeping Piedmont’s existing protections and expanding them to major renovations. The long-term aim is to make Piedmont’s overall housing stock more wildfire resistant through steady progress over time as new homes are built and existing homes are renovated. Making energy-efficiency Reach Codes easier to achieve Piedmont’s “Reach Codes” are local energy efficiency requirements that go beyond state minimums for certain types of home renovation projects. Proposed updates aim to make these requirements more flexible, easier to meet, and better aligned with current construction costs, while encouraging high-impact measures that advance the City’s climate goals. Proposed updates would: • Add four new compliance options, giving homeowners more ways to meet Reach Code requirements. New items on a “menu” of energy efficiency measures residents can choose from include installing an induction cooktop, a heat pump dryer, or solar panels. • Increase the project value thresholds that trigger Reach Code requirements, reflecting updated construction pricing and reducing impacts on smaller projects. • Strengthen incentives for higher-impact energy upgrades, encouraging actions that will deliver the greatest long-term benefits. If adopted, the updates would take effect on January 1, 2026, in alignment with the statewide Building Standards Code cycle. Community members may watch and participate in Monday’s meeting in-person or via Zoom at piedmont-ca-gov.zoom. us/j/82500567382 For 25 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmont-post.com, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of city of Piedmont. Open house Objective Design Standards A year and a half in development, Piedmont’s Draft Objective Design Standards aim to create clear, measurable, and enforceable rules governing design for homeowners and developers, with clear and consistent expectations for what new housing in Piedmont will look like. While not dictating specific architectural styles, the draft standards are designed to result in housing consistent with existing housing in the city. State law now requires cities to approve certain new housing proposals, including accessory dwelling units and SB9 applications, based on “objective” standards. Unlike the traditional design review process, these state-mandated “ministerial” permits cannot take into account public comments and do not come to the Planning Commission for approval at a public meeting. When developing the Objective Design Standards, the project team started with Piedmont’s existing Design Review guidelines and looked at how they could be translated into objective, measurable rules. The draft Objective Design Standards were also informed by community feedback received at two open house events, an online survey, and two Planning Commission study sessions. Community members may submit comments by email to kjackson@piedmont.ca.gov or by mail to Kevin Jackson, Planning & Building Director, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611. The comment period closes December 7. Learn more about this initiative and see materials and video from previous discussions at piedmont.ca.gov/ObjectiveDesignStandards open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm

From dolls and action figures to books and board games, the drive accepts all types of toys. All toys collected will be distributed to families in Oakland and Alameda County. Toys dropped off before December 10 will be distributed through the Marine Toys for Tots Foundation. Community members in attendance are welcome to participate in this tradition. A donation of any kind helps provide a brighter holiday for children and families in need. Piedmont firefighters Brandon Clupny (left), Lt. Zach Heliker, Capt. Justin McNulty FF. Nadder Shehadeh, FF. Kevin Sauder with organizers of the Three Wise Men toy drive.

articles.text: Editor: I’m writing to share my disappointment that the proposed 2026–27 PUSD calendar is essentially a repeat of the past two years and is unchanged despite the district’s efforts to gather community feedback. A total of 455 families participated in the calendar survey, yet the results are nowhere reflected in the outcome. Families even developed and submitted thoughtful alternate calendars, but the proposal again mirrors prior years. Community feedback — and the preferences of Piedmont families — should inform the school calendar, yet under the current structure they hold little weight. The APT-approved calendar passed by only a narrow margin (just above the 50% threshold), suggesting limited consensus even among teachers. Parent groups proposed modest, broadly supported adjustments that would have benefited students, teachers, and families, but they were not considered or implemented. For example: 1. Start school later in August, aligning with instructional pacing and regional family schedules. The request was simply to start 1–3 days later — a small change with big meaning for families wishing to attend summer camps or visit relatives. With the proposed first day on Monday, August 11, PMS and PHS students must return by Thursday, August 6, for walkthroughs on Friday, August 7 — effectively ending summer one week early. 2. Avoid Monday as the first day of school. It creates an unnecessarily long first week for staff and families. Survey feedback favored a mid-week start, yet this was ignored. 3. Shorten Winter Break to a standard two weeks. The proposed schedule extends it to two weeks plus two days, forcing families to find childcare as most working parents return to work on Monday, January 4, while PUSD resumes on January 6. 4 Align with nearby high-performing districts such as Palo Alto and Orinda, which use an 85/95 (or 86/94) semester balance. PUSD’s 87/93 structure remains unnecessarily rigid, especially when “semester classes” make up less than 2% of high school offerings. It’s disappointing to see our district remain tied to an outdated model that no longer reflects the needs of our students, teachers, and families. PUSD can — and should — evolve to better serve the entire Piedmont community. –April Gruber Piedmont parent
articles.title: School district calendar disappoints

articles.text: On December 10, 1975 Articles of Incorporation for the Piedmont Educational Foundation were filed with the Secretary of State. Fifty years later, on November 5, 2025, PEF’s 50th Board and Co-Chairs Rich Thompson and Cameron Wolfe, Jr. hosted a celebration at Piedmont’s Community Hall to commemorate this milestone and to thank PEF’s many heroes. Invitees included current and former Board members, City and School District officials, former employees and Lifetime Donors. Wolfe, an early president of PEF, recounted PEF’s beginnings, noting that the list of signers of the Articles, 12 in all, reads like a list of who was who in Piedmont in the mid-1970s.
