School district calendar disappoints Editor: I’m writing to share my disappointment that the proposed 2026–27 PUSD calendar is essentially a repeat of the past two years and is unchanged despite the district’s efforts to gather community feedback. A total of 455 families participated in the calendar survey, yet the results are nowhere reflected in the outcome. Families even developed and submitted thoughtful alternate calendars, but the proposal again mirrors prior years. Community feedback — and the preferences of Piedmont families — should inform the school calendar, yet under the current structure they hold little weight. The APT-approved calendar passed by only a narrow margin (just above the 50% threshold), suggesting limited consensus even among teachers. Parent groups proposed modest, broadly supported adjustments that would have benefited students, teachers, and families, but they were not considered or implemented. For example: 1. Start school later in August, aligning with instructional pacing and regional family schedules. The request was simply to start 1–3 days later — a small change with big meaning for families wishing to attend summer camps or visit relatives. With the proposed first day on Monday, August 11, PMS and PHS students must return by Thursday, August 6, for walkthroughs on Friday, August 7 — effectively ending summer one week early. 2. Avoid Monday as the first day of school. It creates an unnecessarily long first week for staff and families. Survey feedback favored a mid-week start, yet this was ignored. 3. Shorten Winter Break to a standard two weeks. The proposed schedule extends it to two weeks plus two days, forcing families to find childcare as most working parents return to work on Monday, January 4, while PUSD resumes on January 6. 4 Align with nearby high-performing districts such as Palo Alto and Orinda, which use an 85/95 (or 86/94) semester balance. PUSD’s 87/93 structure remains unnecessarily rigid, especially when “semester classes” make up less than 2% of high school offerings. It’s disappointing to see our district remain tied to an outdated model that no longer reflects the needs of our students, teachers, and families. PUSD can — and should — evolve to better serve the entire Piedmont community. –April Gruber Piedmont parent Piedmont Education Foundation celebrates 50 years By Cameron Wolfe, Jr. On December 10, 1975 Articles of Incorporation for the Piedmont Educational Foundation were filed with the Secretary of State. articles.text: On November 9, Piedmont student Ivan Tam won the Chess 7th Grade California State Championship in Milpitas. He’s now a back-to-back champion after winning the state’s 2024 tournament for 6th graders. Tam was undefeated in all six matches over the two-day Swiss-system tournament with 280 other middle school chess players from the state. This past year, Tam has spent a lot of effort mastering the Scotch Gambit opening, which he employed successfully in this tournament. “Ivan played very aggressively and used the Scotch Gambit opening. Ivan pretty much dominated the field, none of his matches were competitive,” said his father, Tim Tam. “He had the initiative throughout all his matches. His opponents just tried to defend.” The State Championship tournament coincided with the LA Open in Irvine which attracted some of Tam’s stiffest competition. The LA Open offered kids the chance to compete and earn a title against National Masters and Grandmasters; Tam chose the local tournament instead. For Tam, the State Championship tournament was less about hoisting the trophy at the end and more about getting the chance to bond with teammates from Kings Land Chess (KLC) school. Ivan Tam holds his latest 1st Place Chess trophy after winning the California State Championship for 7th graders. KLC was recently awarded the 2025 FIDE World Gold School award by the International Chess Federation KLC. This honor means KLC is one of the world’s top chess schools and the first institution in the United States to receive this highest international honor. Next month Tam will travel to Spokane, Washington with his KLC chess teammates to compete in the K-12 National Championship.
articles.title: Ivan Tam wins 7th grade State Chess Tournament

articles.text: For 142 years, Chabot Space & Science Center has been dedicated to educating learners of all ages about the Universe and our home planet. From early days as a public observatory in downtown Oakland to its current home on Skyline Boulevard, Chabot has served as a hub for discovery, curiosity, and lifelong learning. That mission continues today through the Oakland Space Academy, an initiative designed to help students build career readiness and technical skills for future success in STEM fields. The Academy builds upon the success of Galaxy Explorers, Chabot’s long-standing teen volunteer and education program. Galaxy Explorers play a central role at the Center—guiding visitors through exhibits, leading science demonstrations, and engaging in hands-on inquiry projects. The program provides an opportunity for high school students to explore real-world science topics, from aerodynamics to environmental monitoring, while developing key workforce competencies like teamwork, communication, and critical thinking. This balance of technical training and durable skill-building lays the foundation for the Oakland Space Academy. Students can progress from Galaxy Explorers to more advanced Career Technical Intensives that focus on high-demand STEM skills. These programs go beyond volunteerism, offering applied, project-based experiences that bridge the gap between classroom learning and professional practice. The Academy’s goal is to help young people – and increasingly, adult learners – gain both confidence and capability in science, engineering, and technology. “I’m most excited about creating an informal learning environment where students can develop both creativity and engineering skills,” says Ben Tagami, Engineering Lead at the Oakland Space Academy. “There’s something valuable about stepping away from traditional classroom structure and giving students time and space to explore and tinker.” That philosophy of exploration is at the heart of Chabot’s approach. The Academy offers a range of technical and science intensives designed to engage students through doing. Upcoming workshops include an Astrophotography Workshop, where participants learn to capture images of the night sky, and a Drone Challenge, where students aged 15–25 will design, build, and code their own object-tracking drones. These experiences emphasize problem-solving, collaboration, and applied technical skills—qualities essential in today’s evolving workforce. The Academy’s programs are also informed by strong local roots. By anchoring STEM education in Oakland, Chabot aims to make space- and science-related careers visible and accessible to local students. Participants have opportunities to work with Chabot’s staff, collaborate with peers, and connect their learning to real-world applications. In an era when much learning happens within rigid classroom structures, the Oakland Space Academy demonstrates the value of learning outside the classroom. Through hands-on exploration, mentorship, and skill development, it empowers students to see themselves not just as learners, but as emerging scientists, engineers, and innovators. As Chabot continues its 142- year legacy of curiosity and education, the Oakland Space Academy represents a forward-looking chapter. One where the next generation of Oakland’s thinkers and makers can discover their place among the stars. For more information about the Oakland Space Academy or upcoming workshops, visit chabotspace.org/education/oakland-space-academy/ Students from the Oakland Space Academy are taking part in a Coding Intensive at Chabot Space and Science Center. pages.text: 10 10 Wednesday, November 19, 2025 Bill Baringer summits Antarctica’s Mt. Vinson Part 4: Ascent of 16,070-foot peak in January 2018 No commercial flights fly to Antarctica, so mountaineering companies charter Ilyushin-76 Russian cargo planes. By Jay Russell Article originally published in the April 15, 2020 issue of the Piedmont Post. In January 2018 Bill Baringer traveled to the southernmost region of the world, the barren landscape of Antarctica, to tackle the top of the bottom of the world, Mt. Vinson. At 16,070 feet it is the highest peak on the continent. From Chile, Baringer and his new climbing posse bordered an Ilyushin-76 Russian cargo plane, bundling up for a cold 4-hour flight to an ice runway on Union Glacier. There is an extreme effort to keep Antarctica pristine and free from bacteria. Climbers conformed to strict pack-in, pack-out mandates and give their boots bleach baths. Baringer received dark glacier glasses, new permanent headwear to combat a never setting sun’s ultra bright glare off the endless reaches of white snow. After the plane landed, the climbing party boarded a twin Otter plane on skis to get to the Vinson base camp at 6,900 feet. As they climbed up, the temperatures would go down, battling the cold would be the number one challenge. Hikers geared up with double layers of everything. “The effort expended in putting on all these clothes is usually enough to warm up,” Baringer said with a smile. The trek from Vinson Base Camp to Low Camp involved a gentle climb of 2,100 vertical feet over a 5.5-mile distance. In addition to not letting his fingers freeze, Baringer had to keep his food warm like a penguin standing with an egg. “If you didn’t want something transformed into an unusable frozen brick, then it would have to be worn against your body. Food quickly became inedible if not kept at least a few degrees above freezing,” he explained. His party of climbers reached Low Camp after a five-hour ascent, and had a one day rest while acclimating to 9,100 feet. Baringer’s GPS watch, which normally tells sunrise and sunset time, merely showed “--:--” in Antarctica, where the sun menacingly circles 24 hours a day. On the way to High Camp the pitch of the climb increased dramatically to nearly 45 degrees. The climbers latched onto fixed ropes and slowly chewed their crampons into the glacier for a grueling ascent. The path tapered off to 25 degrees as they made it to High Camp at 12,400 feet. Since the atmosphere is thinner at the South and North Pole, the Antarctic altitude felt as it would 2,000 feet higher elsewhere in the world. At High Camp the guides chose to take another rest day. But for Baringer, a perpetual hiker, the “rest” part was optional. On the day off he set his sights on Mt. Shinn, the 3rd highest peak on Antarctica at 15,289 feet, visible from High Camp. After strategic nudging, their mountaineering guide Vern Tejas, a legend among mountain climbers, agreed to take Baringer and fellow climber Steve Plain, up Mt. Shinn. The crew of three took the side quest. Near the top Baringer made his first mistake. Everyone left their trekking poles in the snow as they approached a rock and ice section. Thinking the peak of Shinn was right above, Baringer left his ice axe there too. Some moments later it became apparent that a knife edge of ice and snow required an ice axe. Tejas gave his axe to Baringer, and they continued. Shortly after, Baringer fell and using the axe tried to self-arrest, but slid downhill a few yards in a frightful moment. Although within sight and possibly 20 minutes from the summit, Baringer’s slide was enough for Vern to call off the trip. They headed back down, The ascent to High Camp required conquering this steep incline on a fixed rope. Bill Baringer stands on the eastern peak of Mt. Shinn. High Camp is nestled beneath Antarctica’s 3rd highest peak, Mt. Shinn. without the summit of Shinn, but with everyone safe. The climb to Shinn was quite taxing and Baringer was glad that the Vinson summit trip was postponed one more day giving him some recuperation time. At “night,” with the sun still high and only momentarily behind Mt. Vinson, the cold of Antarctica flashed its teeth. Baringer recalled, “The cold can be described as how many layers of thermals must be worn inside the -40°C sleeping bag. It may be so cold that you have to do a few sit-ups in the sleeping bag to generate enough heat in order to get back to sleep.” As dinner time rolled around, climber Pavol of their team told everyone he had to bow out of the summit push, due to a debilitating toothache affected by the altitude. The next day the climbers had relatively favorable weather – little wind and the temperature warmer at -32°C (-25°F). Tied together the crew trekked upwards, using ice axes for the final push. The lack of wind made the summit glorious. Tejas said it was probably the second best weather he’d seen in his 40 summits of Mt. Vinson. On top of the southernmost part of the world, Bill Baringer stood tall at the summit of 16,070- foot Mt. Vinson. Having completed the summit with time to spare, the team got to spend 45 minutes at the top. Baringer took some photos of friend Steve Plain, who was attempting to break the record for time taken to conquer all seven summits. It was Plain’s first of the seven summits. He later went on to complete all seven in 117 days to become the world record holder. Baringer continued to accomplish his goals and acquire friendships along the way. Fellow hiker Chris Newton said, “Bill will be very hard to forget. He was an exemplary team player and a great example of how training, passion and commitment can conquer age.” With this summit, Baringer had climbed to the top of the highest peak on four continents. After trekking to the end of the world, sunny Piedmont awaited his tales of conquest. NEXT WEEK: Part 5 of Bill Baringer’s quest to climb the highest peak on each continent. In May 2018 he attempted an ascent of 20,308-foot Mt. Denali in Alaska. Climbers ascended Mt. Vinson with a white-on-white view of the placid sky, snow and glacial expanse. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, free compostable bags are available at City Hall to place with your green cart on garbage day. articles.text: Piedmont High’s football team, seeded No. 2, started off its Division 7 North Coast Section playoffs in a big way, dominating No. 7 St. Patrick 49-7 in Vallejo on Friday, November 14. With the victory, the Highlanders are now set to host No. 3 Willits this Friday, November 21 at Witter It is the second straight year for PHS to reach the semis. Friday’s game against Willits will be the first time Piedmont has hosted an NCS Semifinal since 2014, when the No. 2 Highlanders fell to eventual NCS champion No. 3 Justin Siena. Piedmont will be favored in Friday’s game against Willits. With a win, the school could make history by reaching the NCS Championship game. According to available online records, it appears PHS has not made a championship appearance since its storied 1976 title-winning program. Since the 1976 Hall of Fame team, Piedmont High has reached the semifinals four times, including in 1981, 2014, 2016, and 2024. Now, the championship game is truly feeling in reach. “It’s looming. We have a great opportunity to be there. Considering what we lost from last year and the group that graduated, we have a group of scrappy guys who really put things together,” coach Jordan Seiden said. It was a big night for senior running back and linebacker Xavier Henderson who recorded 215 rushing yards on 15 carries for two touchdowns, averaging an eye-popping 14.3 yards per carry. Henderson, he had to miss a couple of games this season due to injury, making the performance that much more special to him. “Just coming off an injury was tough. I had to fight back for my spot, nothing is given and it’s always the next man up. The team trusts me enough to run the ball, and I trust my offensive line all the way,” Henderson said. Cash Panico also had a big night with three touchdown receptions on four receptions for 51 yards. Panico has shown skill in snatching the ball at its high point. He did so for his second touchdown, leaping in a one-onone situation to get the ball. “Most of them, we set up in a run, then we check to coach. Jimmy makes the throw and I got up to get it. I always try to highpoint the ball where the defender can’t get it. A lot of defenders I go up against aren’t too tall, so I try to take advantage,” Panico said. Game Recap Piedmont opened the game by recovering an onside kick at the 50. They scored in five plays, capping off with a one-yard punch by Henderson, making it 7-0 just one minute and 40 seconds into the game. Both teams traded possession before St. Patrick scored its Staff Photos Xavier Henderson had 215 rushing yards in Piedmont’s 49-7 win over No. 7 St. Patrick. articles.text: Reflections by PHS football coaches It was a tragic week for Oakland and the Bay Area football community. A senseless act of violence took the life of legendary Laney College athletic director and former football coach John Beam. He was shot and killed at Laney College on November 13. Beam’s death made national news after the former Laney College and Skyline HS coach became a star in the Netflix film, Last Chance U, in 2020. But he was much more than a reality TV personality. For countless athletes and coaches, Beam was a mentor, friend, father-figure, and a community pillar. Piedmont head football coach Jordan Seiden has been a in the East Bay for nearly 30 years and has had his run-ins with Beam, but Seiden’s coaching staff has largely been filled by former Laney College Eagles, like Bo Photo courtesy of Netflix Oakland football legend John Beam was killed at Laney College on November 13 in a senseless act of violence. and Oski Tauaho, Mo Glenn, and Vaha Mafi. Seiden pointed out following Piedmont’s 49-7 win over St. Patrick that the Highlanders played their game with a mission in Staff Photo Piedmont coaches Bo Tauaho (left), Jordan Seiden, and Mo Glenn reflect on the death of John Beam. mind: win it for their coaches. “They played this game for the twins [Bo and Oski, Vaha, and Mo. They lost a very important person in life; coach Beam was a huge mentor and role model for them. They’ll probably tell you that Beam saved their lives in a lot of ways. Everybody was out here with very heavy hearts,” Seiden said after the playoff game with St. Patrick. “I’ve known Beam since I was a kid. I didn’t play for him, but I coached against him. As long as I’ve been around football, I’ve known who John Beam was. Having an impact on thousands of people would be an understatement, I could only dream to have that kind of effect on people,” Seiden added. Bo and Oski Tauaho both played for Laney in 2008 and 2009. The two credit Beam for influencing them to become coaches. “He took care of a lot of families, on and off the field. He’s probably one of the reasons why I coach. He coached me, and it makes me want to give back just like him. He’s seen things in us John Beam (middle) pictured here with former players, including Bo Tauaho (left), Oski Tauaho (back, green shirt), and Mo Glenn (second from right).
articles.title: Oakland football legend John Beam killed at Laney College

Piedmont head football coach Jordan Seiden has been a in the East Bay for nearly 30 years and has had his run-ins with Beam, but Seiden’s coaching staff has largely been filled by former Laney College Eagles, like Bo Photo courtesy of Netflix Oakland football legend John Beam was killed at Laney College on November 13 in a senseless act of violence. and Oski Tauaho, Mo Glenn, and Vaha Mafi. Seiden pointed out following Piedmont’s 49-7 win over St. Patrick that the Highlanders played their game with a mission in Staff Photo Piedmont coaches Bo Tauaho (left), Jordan Seiden, and Mo Glenn reflect on the death of John Beam. mind: win it for their coaches. “They played this game for the twins [Bo and Oski, Vaha, and Mo. They lost a very important person in life; coach Beam was a huge mentor and role model for them. They’ll probably tell you that Beam saved their lives in a lot of ways. Everybody was out here with very heavy hearts,” Seiden said after the playoff game with St. Patrick. “I’ve known Beam since I was a kid. I didn’t play for him, but I coached against him. As long as I’ve been around football, I’ve known who John Beam was. Having an impact on thousands of people would be an understatement, I could only dream to have that kind of effect on people,” Seiden added. Bo and Oski Tauaho both played for Laney in 2008 and 2009. The two credit Beam for influencing them to become coaches. “He took care of a lot of families, on and off the field. He’s probably one of the reasons why I coach. He coached me, and it makes me want to give back just like him. He’s seen things in us See John Beam on page 31 No. 2 Highlanders dominate St. Patrick in NCS Quarterfinals By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s football team, seeded No. 2, started off its Division 7 North Coast Section playoffs in a big way, dominating No. 7 St. Patrick 49-7 in Vallejo on Friday, November 14. With the victory, the Highlanders are now set to host No. 3 Willits this Friday, November 21 at Witter It is the second straight year for PHS to reach the semis. Friday’s game against Willits will be the first time Piedmont has hosted an NCS Semifinal since 2014, when the No. 2 Highlanders fell to eventual NCS champion No. 3 Justin Siena. Piedmont will be favored in Friday’s game against Willits. With a win, the school could make history by reaching the NCS Championship game. According to available online records, it appears PHS has not made a championship appearance since its storied 1976 title-winning program. Since the 1976 Hall of Fame team, Piedmont High has reached the semifinals four times, including in 1981, 2014, 2016, and 2024. Now, the championship game is truly feeling in reach. “It’s looming. We have a great opportunity to be there. Considering what we lost from last year and the group that graduated, we have a group of scrappy guys who really put things together,” coach Jordan Seiden said. It was a big night for senior running back and linebacker Xavier Henderson who recorded 215 rushing yards on 15 carries for two touchdowns, averaging an eye-popping 14.3 yards per carry. Henderson, he had to miss a couple of games this season due to injury, making the performance that much more special to him. “Just coming off an injury was tough. I had to fight back for my spot, nothing is given and it’s always the next man up. The team trusts me enough to run the ball, and I trust my offensive line all the way,” Henderson said. Cash Panico also had a big night with three touchdown receptions on four receptions for 51 yards. Panico has shown skill in snatching the ball at its high point. He did so for his second touchdown, leaping in a one-onone situation to get the ball. “Most of them, we set up in a run, then we check to coach. Jimmy makes the throw and I got up to get it. I always try to highpoint the ball where the defender can’t get it. A lot of defenders I go up against aren’t too tall, so I try to take advantage,” Panico said. Game Recap Piedmont opened the game by recovering an onside kick at the 50. They scored in five plays, capping off with a one-yard punch by Henderson, making it 7-0 just one minute and 40 seconds into the game. articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis season came to an end over the past week. The Highlanders lost 5-2 to No. 5 Northgate in the first round of the Division 1 North Coast Section Team Tournament. For the first time Piedmont was the No. 12 seed. The match was pkayed at home at the Corey Reich Tennis Center on Tuesday, November 11. PHS also had three players in the Division 2 NCS Individual Tournament on Monday, November 17. Ella Ruthven competed in the singles bracket, losing 6-4, 6-2 to Justin Siena’s Lyla Hogan. In the doubles bracket was Samantha Huynh and Emma Chan, losing 6-1, 6-2 to No. 1 seed Jane McDermott and Ann McDermott of Marin Academy. Despite the losses, Piedmont ends the season as this year’s league champion in the Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division. Also Chan and Huynh won the team’s first-ever WACC Doubles title. “It was a great season. We were League Champions and played a lot of really good tennis. In the NCS Individual yesterday, Ella Ruthven lost in first round to Lila Hogan, a really tough player for Justin Sienna. Sam and Emma ran into the McDermott sisters, who were the tournament’s top seed from Marin Academy,” coach Jim Landes said. Against Northgate, the Highlanders won at No. 3 singles and No. 2 doubles. Faith Chin won her singles match in straight sets, 6-4, 6-2. At doubles, Inara Mehta and Chiara Silvio dominated their match 6-3, 6-1. At singles, Ella Ruthven lost 6-3, 6-3 at the No. 1 spot, while Kate Jumper lost 6-4, 6-0 at No. 2. Arianna Kortum took her No. 4 singles match to three sets, but lost 3-6, 6-2, 6-2. Huynh and Chan also kept things competitive at the No. 1 doubles spot, losing in a narrow three-set battle by scores of 6-4, 4-6, 10-4. Piedmont’s No. 3 doubles team of Leela Sivakumar and Ella Thomasson also fell in a heated three-set battle, 6-4, 1-6, 6-2. The Highlanders end their season with a 13-9 overall record. articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ basketball team gets back into action on Saturday, November 29 at Gateway School in San Francisco for its first official opening game of the 2025-26 season. The Highlanders return after going 15-16 and falling 75-70 to St. Patrick in the Division 4 North Coast Section championship game, marking the school’s second consecutive championship game appearance. The Highlanders watched their leading scorer, Ravi Silverberg, graduate with the Class of 2025, but bring back an experienced group with six seniors, five juniors, and just one sophomore. Four returning players will lead the way; Dillon Casey, P.J. Brayer, Lucian Fang Ring, and Beach Lorin. “Returners are so important in high school athletics, bringing back six seniors is huge. I think this year is our deepest group of guards that I’ve ever had,” said coach Ben Spencer. Casey enters his third year as a starter and will likely eclipse the 1,000-career point mark early in the season. “Dillon will be the best player on the floor most nights. He’s at 925 points and is really close to breaking 1,000. He’s been starting at us for three years and I can’t say enough about what he does. He handles the ball 99 percent of the time, gets us into our offense, is a great off-ball defender, and is a great team leader,” Spencer said. Brayer is another captain and was an every-game starter last season. He’ll provide presence on the boards, while he’s shown a propensity to knock down a 3-pointer. “P.J. cleans up the boards, he’s an animal. He’s skilled and fast, get to the basket, and he also can shoot. We’ll be able to spread out the floor with him,” Spencer said. Fang Ring is another player who proved to be dependable from beyond the arc. He gained minutes as a starter last year during his sophomore season, and will have an increased role as a junior. “He’s really improved his ball-handling. There were a couple of games last year where Dillon got in foul trouble and Ravi was hurt, so we had Lucian play the one. Getting to the rim was difficult for him, but he’s really worked on his ball-handling and kept at his shooting. We’ll get good looks this season,” Spencer said. One player Spencer has been mightily impressed with throughout the offseason is junior Beach Lorin. He made his mark last year as a rotational player but is already drawing comparisons to former Athlete of the Year Luke Harris. “Beach Lorin could be our best player. He finishes like Luke Harris and is about 6 feet 4 inches now. He’s crafty around the basStaff Photos Dillon Casey returns as a three-year starter. He’s close to eclipsing the 1,000-point mark for Piedmont High. P.J. Brayer is another returning starter and among the team captains. Coach Ben Spencer has been impressed with Beach Lorin, who steps into the starting lineup as a junior. ket. When you see him this year and he’ll remind you of Luke Harris with how he finishes. We’ll get a lot of scoring from him,” Spencer said. As for the fifth spot in Spencer’s starting rotation, Cash Panico is poised for minutes when he returns from the football team, while first-year varsity players junior Ollie Dougan and sophomore Yoseph Baskin have caught the coach’s attention. “Cash Panico is a tough defender. Ollie Dougan is around 6’2”, 6’3” and is strong. Yoseph is a sophomore who is extremely athletic, he’s skilled around the rim and great offensively,” Spencer said. Piedmont will hosts its annual Winter Classic from Thursday through Saturday, December 4-6. The Highlanders will open competition against Arroyo on the opening day.

articles.text: It’s a new day for Piedmont High’s girls’ soccer team as it enters the 2025-26 season. The team will have a new head coach. Matt Spencer-Harty, who succeeds Dan Chubbock after 17-years at the helm. Spencer-Harty joins the Highlanders, but already has a connection to the community as a coach at Piedmont Soccer Club and the 24-7 UK Soccer Academy. “Dan [Chubbock] is my Director of Coaching at Piedmont Soccer Club; he’s someone I have immense respect for both on and off the field. I have a lot of respect for the work he put into Piedmont High. At the same time, every coach brings their own identity and vision, and I’m looking forward to putting my own stamp on the program,” Spencer-Harty said. “My focus is on building the team in a way that reflects my philosophy, a clear structure, a modern style of play, and a strong, positive culture. I want to create an environment where players are challenged, supported, and able to grow both individually and collectively. Stepping into this role is an opportunity to shape the program in a direction I believe will push us forward, and I’m excited to take on that responsibility,” he added. Spencer-Harty is a native of England and attended high school in Vietnam. One of his first coaching jobs was at Fox Football Vietnam in Ho Chi Minh City from 2016 to 2021. “Coaching abroad teaches you adaptability, different styles of play, different cultures, different approaches to development. Coming to the United States was a result of wanting a new challenge and wanting to be part of a country where the women’s game Elia Kwong is a returning starter from last season. Staff Photo Staff Photo Miranda Liu is listed on this year’s roster. She missed most of last season due to her club schedule. Photo courtesy of Piedmont Soccer Club Matt Spencer-Harty joins Piedmont High as the girls’ soccer team’s new head coach. in particular has such a rich history and enormous potential. The level of passion here, from youth soccer all the way to the professional game, has been incredible to be a part of. That’s what ultimately led me here, and to Piedmont,” Spencer-Harty said. The Highlanders open their season on December 3 when hosting Granada. PHS finished last year with a 7-2-10 (W-T-L) record and reached the Division 4 NCS Quarterfinals as the No. 1 seed. The 2025 team lost 10 players to graduation, including key midfield starters Louisa Symkowick and Juliana Thornborrow. Elia Kwong, Arden Sorensen-Wald, Teah Suhr, and Ayla Blanford made an impact as midfielders last season and look ahead to increased roles. “We did lose some important players, but I’m very confident in the group we have. We’ve added some exciting talent, and we have returning players who are ready to take on bigger roles. A number of players have shown real quality in the midfield during preseason, players who are comfortable on the ball, brave in tight spaces, and capable of controlling the tempo,” Spencer-Harty said. In the attack, Piedmont will have to replace Ryo Woltag as one of last year’s leading scorers. Stephanie Lee is a returner who will pick up minutes, while Miranda Liu is back as a senior. Spencer-Harty also points out that he’ll need “versatility” in his lineup. “Up top, we have pace and creativity, and a few players who I think will surprise people with how quickly they adapt to having more responsibility. One thing I’m emphasizing is versatility; many of our players can operate across multiple roles, which gives us flexibility in how we set up based on the opponent,” Spencer-Harty said. As for the back line, defenders like Darcy McKee, Daniela Luccaccini, Chloe Toyama, Chloe Koh, and Erica Smith will hold down the fort. PHS will also have a new goal keeper after Friedie Schickedanz graduates, meaning Rachel Young is set to start. “Our goalkeeper this season is Rachel Young. She’s an immensely talented athlete, and her background in water polo gives her a natural advantage in areas like reaction speed, handeye coordination, and reading play under pressure. Rachel played outfield for JV last year, but she’s embraced the challenge of stepping into a new position for the team this season,” Spencer-Harty said.

articles.text: Remembering Jack Nelson, Soren Dixon through the game they loved Soren Dixon and Jack Nelson, two remarkable young men whose love for lacrosse and strong leadership on and off the field, will continue to inspire and support rising student-athletes in the Bay Area. Approaching the one year anniversary of their tragic passing, Oakland Lacrosse Club is honored to announce the creation of the Purple One ScholSharing their love of lacrosse Soren and Jack were standout four-year varsity players at Piedmont High School, helping lead their team to league titles in 2021, 2022, and 2023. In their senior season, they advanced to the 2023 Division 2 NCS Final as the No. 3 seed, falling just short in double overtime to top-seeded Tamalpais. articles.text: Guest conductor Jane Glover The San Francisco Symphony will present George Frideric Handel’s Messiah, a musical meditation on Christ’s birth, life, and resurrection, on December 5 and 6. Guest conductor Jane Glover leads the symphony and chorus in this classic holiday favorite. Glover is a fellow of the Royal College of Music and was the artistic director of opera at the Royal Academy of Music between 2009 and 2016. In December 2013, she became the third woman ever to conduct at the Metropolitan Opera of New York, leading Mozart’s The Magic Flute. Performers include Susanna Phillips as soprano, Jennifer Johnson Cano as mezzo-soprano, Josh Lovell as tenor, and Will Liverman as baritone. Davies Symphony Hall will be decked out for the holidays during these performances, filled with lit evergreen trees, wreaths and garlands. The hall’s lobby bar will feature festive winter cocktails, including a Gingerbread Old Fashioned, limited-time sparkling wine and holiday-themed desserts throughout December. The Friday and Saturday performances both begin at 7:30 p.m. A preconcert talk by San Francisco Symphony’s resident lecturer Laura Stanfield Prichard will be presented onstage at 6:30 p.m. before both performances. The preconcert talk is free to all ticketholders. Tickets are on sale at https:// www.sfsymphony.org/Buy-Tickets/2025-26/HANDEL-MESSIAH or call the box office at (415) 864-6000 to purchase tickets. ®

articles.text: The Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco unveiled a major reinstallation of Native American art at the de Young museum, highlighting the deep ties between Indigenous peoples and the Bay Area and beyond. The new presentation spans more than a millennium of artistic expression in North, South and Central America, developed with a group of Native America co-curators. The refreshed Arts of Indigenous America galleries at de Young feature both ancestral works and contemporary pieces, including new acquisitions and specially commissioned artworks. The four-gallery suite features two newly developed spaces for Native American art, alongside updated galleries of Ancestral Maya works and mural fragments from Teotihuacan. Native American art has been central to the Fine Arts Museums’ collections since the museum’s founding in 1895, but this reinstallation represents a transformational approach to curation and community engagement. Indigenous scholars and community advisors participated from the project’s inception, shaping the selection of works and interpretive strategies, said Hillary Olcott, Curator of Arts of the Americas at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “We consult with communities of origin to determine how to care for the artworks and cultural items in the collection, and which are appropriate to share with the public,”Olcott said in a press release. “The curatorial team has chosen to frame these items through neither an art historical nor an anthropological lens, but rather a blend of the two. We have also opted for a multivocal interpretative framework instead of a single curatorial perspective. Our hope is that this will bring a liveliness to the galleries and will re-center people within the stories of this art.” “The reconceived Arts of Indigenous America galleries embody our ongoing commitment to building lasting collaborative partnerships with Indigenous communities,” added Thomas Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums. “This spirit of collaboration has had a transformational effect in our newly reinstalled galleries, where visitors may find their understanding of Native art expanded.” Visit https://www.famsf.org/ to learn more and plan your visit. Installation view at the de Young Photo by Gary Sexton
articles.title: de Young Museum’s reimagined Native American art galleries now on display

articles.text: Visit Filoli Historic House and Garden in Woodside beginning November 22 to see the 16-acre estate lit up for holidays. Every year in November, Filoli’s decorating team installs and decorates 22 trees, 3,600 light strands that stretch more than 18 miles, over 7,000 luminescent ornaments, and 1,000 feet of festive garlands. The Reception Room’s 18-foot ceilings create an appropriate adobe for “The Grand Tree,” the tallest of those on display. The two-story historic mansion contains 56 rooms, including a large ballroom and reception room designed to host concerts and debut balls. Each room in the mansion is adorned with holiday decorations that complement the room’s original hues and aesthetics. The design team carefully recreates the original holiday placement that is indicative of Agnes and William Bourn, the house’s first residents. More original artifacts can be viewed throughout the home. Lurline Roth, who lived with her family in the mansion after the Bourns, was an avid collector of religious icons. Her Italian Murano glass nativity scene, one of her favorites, is displayed in the study. Winter-themed cocktails and treats are available for purchase throughout the holiday season at Filoli’s Quail Cafe and Chalet bars. This year, guests can upgrade their tickets for an exclusive reception in Filoli’s grand ballroom. Tickets include a glass of Moet champagne, or uninterrupted pours of Dom Perignon for an extra fee. Non-alcoholic options are available. While holiday evenings at Filoli are truly a sight to see, the lighting enhancements glow just as festively in the daylight. Daytime admission gains you access to explore the estate trail before sundown and admire the garden’s autumnal colors. Daytime hours are 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. The estate is open until 9 p.m. beginning November 22. Last tickets for Filoli’s holiday festivities are sold at the door at 7 p.m. To learn more about “Holidays at Filoli” and to purchase tickets, visit https://filoli.org/holiday-lights/. Photo courtesy of Filoli House Filoli Historic House and Garden is dressing up for the holidays.

articles.text: Good Fire: Tending Native Lands installation at Oakland Museum of California. Oakland Museum of CaliGood Fire presents the signifBrittani Orona, co-curator of “From the very beginning, Museum officials said the text for cultural burning amid a period of increasingly intense wildfires in the region. Cultural burning, sometimes referred to as “good fire,” has historically supported biodiversity, improved habitat conditions, and maintained access to plants essential for food, medicine, basketry and ceremonial traditions. The exhibition begins with an immersive environment designed to replicate aspects of a cultural burn through sound, imagery and interpretive material. A map of California tribal territories is featured to emphasize Native sovereignty and the place-based knowledge that shapes these practices. The first gallery section, “Working with Fire,” outlines the tools, ecological functions and cultural applications of cultural burning. It includes artworks by Harry Fonseca, a recorded fire story by Rumsen Ohlone artist Linda Yamane, and regalia by Tiśina Parker. Additional displays highlight fire-adapted plants and cultural items that rely on fire-managed landscapes. A second section, “Good Fire, Interrupted,” examines the consequences of colonial fire suppression policies that restricted or criminalized cultural burning. Archival photographs, firescarred tree samples and works by artists Brian D. Tripp and Saif Azzuz address the resulting ecological decline and the emergence of large-scale wildfires linked to decades of fuel buildup. The final section, “The Future of Fire,” focuses on current efforts to restore cultural burning and expand tribal leadership in land management. Short films and artworks by Native creators, as well as baskets from Pomo artists and the California Indian Basketweavers Association, document initiatives including prairie restoration, Land Back movements and collaborative cultural burns. “This exhibition centers Native fire practitioners and culture bearers, whose knowledge is grounded in the specific ecologies of their homelands and thousands of years of experimentation,” Ryder Diaz, OMCA Curator of Natural Sciences, said in a press release. “Good Fire invites visitors to expand their view of fire in Northern California and to respect and support the sovereignty of Native peoples, who have never ceded their right to care for their lands with fire,” he added. articles.text: Rami Bar-Niv The piano concert in our Piedmont Center for the Arts Sunday afternoon was inspiring from beginning to end. The pianist was Rami Bar-Niv. His biography states that he is one of Israel’s most acclaimed and sought after pianists. He deserves this acclaim. Perhaps I am stating the obvious: good musicians always play well. Their performances are always inspired. Throughout the concert, a backdrop sign on the wall was emblazoned with the words: “considering the nature of inspiration”. This is the stated philosophy of artist Michael Stehr and his words were prophetic. It is my habit to arrive early and listen to the musicians warming up. Rami Bar-Niv has an easy-going manner. But as soon as he sits down at the piano, he is ready to play. In reality, he doesn’t need to warm up. In every aspect, he is serious about his art. It is quite obvious that music comes first. Bar-Niv’s accomplishments are all-encompassing. He has a commanding tone and technique which he modulates in a most artistic way. He knows how to emphasize a phrase and how to offer the appropriate contrasts. As was the case for the great pianists in the past, the music speaks for itself, and the performer presents it to the audience in the most appropriate manner. There is no need for gimmicks; lofty, artistic playing speaks for itself. As the concert progressed, it became obvious that we were listening to an outstanding pianist. Every composition was interpreted with intelligence. The speed of each piece, which we musicians refer to as tempo, was in keeping with the composer’s intentions. There was no mindless speed, which seems to be the main ingredient of the young generation. Sunday’s program was playing on the grand scale. The program itself was well thought out and well balanced. A few well-chosen words by the pianist were very appropriate. And then he was ready to go. The program opened with the Bach-Busoni adagio from the Toccata in C Major. Bar-Niv’s artistry is such that he can create the sound of a grand organ while he plays the piano. It was a supersmooth and expressive legato, hinting at outstanding singing. Second on the program was the Mozart Sonata in F major. The mood changed. So did the performer’s persona. He literally became a classic-period musician. No sooner had the Mozart ended then the pianist introduced the composer JJ Hollingsworth. The San Francisco composer was present and sitting in the front row. Her composition: “Cobalt Moon and Stars“ from the Glass Suite was all too brief. The pianist explained that there were certain very special piano techniques. Interesting? Absolutely. He concluded the first half of the program with his own composition entitled “Rhapsody in Blue and White“ which is based on three Hebrew songs. Nothing beats a composer playing his own music, and it was performed with an expansive and virtuoso approach. What is amazing is that the playing was so expressive in the simplest way. After a brief intermission, the audience was treated to a very characteristic performance of Polonaise in A flat major by Chopin and his introspective and expressive Nocturne in C-sharp minor, a work of Chopin’s youth. The pianist explained the nature of a Polonaise, a processional dance of noble character. It must be stately. It is, after all, of noble character and nobility never rushes. The program concluded with Bar-Niv’s arrangement of Rhapsody in Blue by Gershwin. This excellent arrangement featured some mind-boggling finger work. Throughout the program we experienced expansive playing on the grand scale. All of the ingredients were present. Despite the bright acoustics of the hall, the soloist was able to evoke sensitive dynamics. I had a delightful conversation with Bar-Niv following the concert. He told me that he is 80 years old. It’s hard to believe. He has perfectly timed humor in addition to a youthful manner of playing which gives no hint to his age. How fortunate the Piedmont audience was on Sunday.
articles.title: Considering the nature of inspiration – Piano concert

articles.text: Dog Man: The Musical, based on Dav Pilkey’s best-selling children’s book series, will make its East Bay debut at the Henry J. Kaiser Center for the Arts on January 3. The production is scheduled for three performances: Saturday, January 3, 2026, at 11 a.m. and 4 p.m., and Sunday, January 4, 2026, at 1 p.m. Pilkey, author and illustrator of the children’s popular series books Dog Man, Captain Underpants, and Cat Kid Comic Club, called the musical adaption “the perfect mash-up of memorable music, humor, and love.” The touring production brings Dog Man’s adventures to life, starring a crime-fighting hero with the head of a dog and the body of a police officer as he battles Flippy the cyborg fish, an army of Beasty Buildings, and the villainous Petey the cat. The story also follows young creators George and Harold as they rush to finish their show before lunchtime. O r ig i n a l ly p r e m ie r i ng off-Broadway in 2019 and returning in 2023, Dog Man: The Musical has been celebrated by critics for its humor and energy. The cast features Mundo Ballejos as Harold, Nick Manna as Dog Man, Sadie Jayne Kennedy as Li’l Petey, Troi Lennoxx Gaines as George, Anthony Rodriguez as Petey, and Diamond Destiny as Flippy. Swings include Zack Abbey, Jeremiah Rosado, and Emerese Noel. The musical includes book and lyrics by Emmy Award winner Kevin Del Aguila and music by Brad Alexander, with original direction and choreography by Jen Wineman. The creative team also includes scenic designer Timothy R. Mackabee, costume designer Heidi Leigh Hanson, lighting designer David Lander, sound designer Emma Wilk, orchestrator Lloyd Kikoler, and music director Miriam Daly. Tickets, priced from $25 to $68, are now available at hjkarts. com. Originally premiering off-Broadway in 2019, Dog Man: The Musical has been celebrated by critics for its humor, energy, and broad appeal to audiences of all ages.
articles.title: Dog Man: The Musical makes East Bay Debut

Oakland Ballet dancers bring Artistic Director Lustig’s classic holiday ensemble to life with magnificent scenery and costumes. The production features more than 40 dancers aged 7 to 17, in the roles of snowballs, mice, soldiers and candies, performing alongside Oakland Ballet dancers. The Oakland Symphony with Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir will deliver Tchaikovsky’s magnificent score, marking the 54th year that Oakland Ballet has presented a production of The Nutcracker in the East Bay. This year’s production coincides with Oakland Ballet’s 60th anniversary. Running time is approximately two hours including intermission, and doors open one hour before showtime. Both performances begin at 1 p.m. Performances are family-friendly and all ages require a ticket. Guests may add on a ticket for the “Sweet Considering the nature of inspiration – Piano concert by Rami Bar-Niv ickets to Oakland Ballet’s popular holiday performance The Nutcracker are limited. Dreams Party” on December 20, where ticket-holders of all ages will meet the cast and characters of The Nutcracker, pose for photographs, collect autographs, and enjoy treats and refreshments. Tickets are available online now at https://oaklandballet.org/ or call the Paramount box office number 510-465-6400. Dog Man: The Musical makes East Bay Debut By Allyson Aleksey Dog Man: The Musical, based on Dav Pilkey’s best-selling children’s book series, will make its East Bay debut at the Henry J. Kaiser Center for the Arts on January 3. The production is scheduled for three performances: Saturday, January 3, 2026, at 11 a.m. and 4 p.m., and Sunday, January 4, 2026, at 1 p.m. Pilkey, author and illustrator of the children’s popular series books Dog Man, Captain Underpants, and Cat Kid Comic Club, called the musical adaption “the perfect mash-up of memorable music, humor, and love.” The touring production brings Dog Man’s adventures to life, starring a crime-fighting hero with the head of a dog and the body of a police officer as he battles Flippy the cyborg fish, an army of Beasty Buildings, and the villainous Petey the cat. The story also follows young creators George and Harold as they rush to finish their show before lunchtime. O r ig i n a l ly p r e m ie r i ng off-Broadway in 2019 and returning in 2023, Dog Man: The Musical has been celebrated by critics for its humor and energy. The cast features Mundo Ballejos as Harold, Nick Manna as Dog Man, Sadie Jayne Kennedy as Li’l Petey, Troi Lennoxx Gaines as George, Anthony Rodriguez as Petey, and Diamond Destiny as Flippy. Swings include Zack Abbey, Jeremiah Rosado, and Emerese Noel. The musical includes book and lyrics by Emmy Award winner Kevin Del Aguila and music by Brad Alexander, with original direction and choreography by Jen Wineman. The creative team also includes scenic designer Timothy R. Mackabee, costume designer Heidi Leigh Hanson, lighting designer David Lander, sound designer Emma Wilk, orchestrator Lloyd Kikoler, and music director Miriam Daly. Tickets, priced from $25 to $68, are now available at hjkarts. com. Originally premiering off-Broadway in 2019, Dog Man: The Musical has been celebrated by critics for its humor, energy, and broad appeal to audiences of all ages. READ IT IN THE POST Rami Bar-Niv By Joseph Gold The piano concert in our Piedmont Center for the Arts Sunday afternoon was inspiring from beginning to end. The pianist was Rami Bar-Niv. His biography states that he is one of Israel’s most acclaimed and sought after pianists. He deserves this acclaim. Perhaps I am stating the obvious: good musicians always play well. Their performances are always inspired. Throughout the concert, a backdrop sign on the wall was emblazoned with the words: “considering the nature of inspiration”. This is the stated philosophy of artist Michael Stehr and his words were prophetic. It is my habit to arrive early and listen to the musicians warming up. Rami Bar-Niv has an easy-going manner. But as soon as he sits down at the piano, he is ready to play. In reality, he doesn’t need to warm up. In every aspect, he is serious about his art. It is quite obvious that music comes first. Bar-Niv’s accomplishments are all-encompassing. He has a commanding tone and technique which he modulates in a most artistic way. He knows how to emphasize a phrase and how to offer the appropriate contrasts. As was the case for the great pianists in the past, the music speaks for itself, and the performer presents it to the audience in the most appropriate manner. There is no need for gimmicks; lofty, artistic playing speaks for itself. As the concert progressed, it became obvious that we were listening to an outstanding pianist. Every composition was interpreted with intelligence. The speed of each piece, which we musicians refer to as tempo, was in keeping with the composer’s intentions. There was no mindless speed, which seems to be the main ingredient of the young generation. Sunday’s program was playing on the grand scale. The program itself was well thought out and well balanced. A few well-chosen words by the pianist were very appropriate. And then he was ready to go. The program opened with the Bach-Busoni adagio from the Toccata in C Major. Bar-Niv’s artistry is such that he can create the sound of a grand organ while he plays the piano. It was a supersmooth and expressive legato, hinting at outstanding singing. Second on the program was the Mozart Sonata in F major. The mood changed. So did the performer’s persona. He literally became a classic-period musician. No sooner had the Mozart ended then the pianist introduced the composer JJ Hollingsworth. The San Francisco composer was present and sitting in the front row. Her composition: “Cobalt Moon and Stars“ from the Glass Suite was all too brief. The pianist explained that there were certain very special piano techniques. Interesting? Absolutely. He concluded the first half of the program with his own composition entitled “Rhapsody in Blue and White“ which is based on three Hebrew songs. Nothing beats a composer playing his own music, and it was performed with an expansive and virtuoso approach. What is amazing is that the playing was so expressive in the simplest way. After a brief intermission, the audience was treated to a very characteristic performance of Polonaise in A flat major by Chopin and his introspective and expressive Nocturne in C-sharp minor, a work of Chopin’s youth. The pianist explained the nature of a Polonaise, a processional dance of noble character. It must be stately. It is, after all, of noble character and nobility never rushes. The program concluded with Bar-Niv’s arrangement of Rhapsody in Blue by Gershwin. This excellent arrangement featured some mind-boggling finger work. Throughout the program we experienced expansive playing on the grand scale. All of the ingredients were present. Despite the bright acoustics of the hall, the soloist was able to evoke sensitive dynamics. I had a delightful conversation with Bar-Niv following the concert. He told me that he is 80 years old. It’s hard to believe. He has perfectly timed humor in addition to a youthful manner of playing which gives no hint to his age. How fortunate the Piedmont audience was on Sunday.

articles.text: It’s an interesting experience to approach a film with one set of expectations and realize, as the story evolves, that it is something else entirely. That’s the case with Mr. Holmes. Going in I assumed that the setting would be London, during those nascent years of the 20th century, not long after the end of WWI. Mr. Holmes is at the top of his deductive game and often takes intricate cases with subtle clues to be cleverly unraveled. Buttressing my assumption is the fact that Ian McKellen, a gifted character actor, is portraying Holmes, sans deerstalker cap and oversized Meerschaum pipe (something Watson added), but in all ways a perfectly cast Holmes. But Mr. Holmes is a decidedly different movie. Based on the novel A Slight Trick of the Mind, by Mitch Cullin, the narrative is set in 1947. Sherlock Holmes, now in his 90s, is living on his bucolic Sussex farm. He has been retired for some 30 years and has used this time to raise bees and study botany. He lives a solitary life, with the exception of his housekeeper, Mrs. Munro (Laura Linney), and her precocious 10-yearold son, Roger (Milo Parker). articles.text: Current until December 15 Love at First Sight Art Exhibit Piedmont native Michael Stehr’s art exhibit will remain on the walls at PCA into mid-December for you to enjoy while attending other events at the venue. Please visit the Fine Art section of his website at www.mstehr.com for more information on the exhibit, and write to the artist at mstehrart@gmail.com. Thursday, November 20, 7:00 p.m. Miss Maybell & her Ragtime Romeos Concert Get your vintage groove on for this light-hearted, entertaining evening of vintage Jazz, Blues, and Ragtime music! Miss Maybell and her husband Charlie Judkins give new life to songs created over 100 years ago and rescued from dusty old 78 rpm records and antique sheet music! The concert will also feature Marty Eggers on bass and Don Neely, founder of SF’s Royal Society Jazz Orchestra, on clarinet & saxophone. Please be sure to buy advance tickets at http:// www.brownpapertickets.com/e/6728377 in case this concert sells out! Performers will follow this show with appearances at Sacramento’s West Coast Ragtime Festival, November 21-23, 2025. Sunday, November 23, 4:00 p.m. Carnival, Trout, & Blue Concert This local quintet of expert string players led by renowned pianist Amy Zanrosso will take us on a whimsical exploration beginning in Camille Saint-Saëns’ Carnaval des Animaux, after which we will float downstream to visit Franz Schubert’s Trout Quintet, finally moving to George Gershwin’s mid-1920s cityscape to enjoy his Rhapsody in Blue, arranged for piano and string quintet. Musicians are two violinists, Beni Shinohara and Karen Shinozaki Sor, violist Paul Ehrlich and cellist Victoria Ehrlich, and bassist Ken Miller, all of whom have extensive experience with San Francisco’s Ballet, Symphony, and Opera Orchestras, among others. Please visit https://www.brownpapertickets. com/e/6726700 for advance tickets, half-price for patrons under 18! Sunday, November 30, 5:30 p.m. mOthertongue: Lived Experience in Asian America Now in the 21st century old stereotypes persist, affecting how Asian-Americans continue to be viewed to this day. Soprano Jennifer Lien attempts to challenge outdated cultural ideas by sharing new art with fresh cultural ideas. Wanting to perform songs that assert the Asian-American lived experience from the perspective of those who live it, she reached out to three Asian-American women composers in their prime who also write beautifully for the voice. The new songs on this program, accompanied by Dr. Gwendolyn Mok on the piano, express the joys, pains, contradictions, and pride experienced by Asians living in this land we call home. Their stories are all American stories where everyone belong. Advance tickets are at https://www.brownpapertickets.com/e/6743616. Thursday, December 4, 4:00 p.m. US Premiere Screening — Monastir Monatir is a haunting and poetic film whose imaginative premise has earned Francesco Paolo Paladino outstanding praise in Italian film circles. This is a rare opportunity to witness a truly international collaboration. The narration is by London’s Edward Ka Spel, soloist and composer of the Legendary Pink Dots. The melodies and lyrical adaptations were created by Piedmont native Dorothy Moskowitz Falarski. Paladino, Ferrari and Falarski have been working together since 2022 as The United States of Alchemy, their name inspired by the United States of America rock band in which Dorothy made her debut in 1968. Mpnastir is a follow-up to their highly acclaimed Under an Endless Sky, released by Tompkins Square Records in 2023. Free event. Support the programming of Piedmont Center for the Arts by donating generously to the Tip Jar at these events.

articles.text: A scene from Disney’s Zootopia Zootopia is not your typical animated talking animals movie; rather, Disney created a family-friendly buddy cop comedy with a raft of subtle messages and teachable moments. The film is set in a world where predator and prey identities have been abolished, hence Zootopia (utopia). The story focuses on Judy Hopp (Ginnifer Goodwin), the first metropolitan bunny cop ever hired. She’s a perky go-getter. Determined to prove herself. But officer Hopps, on her first day on the force, to her surprise, confronts some discouraging prejudices. Given her size, and given some thickheaded assumptions, officer Hopps is assigned parking ticket duty by her Cape Buffalo police chief, Bogo (Idris Elba). But then Judy learns that a family man Otter has disappeared and his wife, Mrs. Otter, is frantic, and appeals to Judy to find him. Judy rises to the challenge and so bets her career that she can. The problem is that in order to track Mr. Otter down, she will have to partner up with slick and sly fox, Nick Wilde (Jason Bateman), which forces her to rethink her assumptions about foxes in general. The team’s search for the missing Mr. O. takes the pair in unexpected directions, while encountering the most extraordinary cast of characters, examples being an adorable lamb; a mafiatype polar bear; and a wonderful sloth who works for the Department of Motor Vehicles, which means extremely slow service and long, exasperating lines. Judy and Nick must also unravel an unanticipated conspiracy, one that tests their teamwork, and tucks nicely into that thread of prejudice that stitches the narrative together at every turn. But there are also moments of silly slapstick, exciting chases, all while taking them into fascinating enclaves of Zootopia known as Tundra Town, Sahara Square, and little Rodentia. For all of the film’s asides, and not too subtle references to Disney’s Frozen, the most significant are the scenes, however nuanced, that touch on racism in everyday Zootopian life. Hopps, for example, makes the point that “cute” is a word used only by bunnies and considered offensive if used by other denizens of Zootopia. What Disney points out, often with the lightest of touches, is that we are all tempted to prejudge one another, even by the most benign Judy Hopps. However, when Judy is confronted by her blind spots regarding Zootopians, she willingly steps up and apologizes to those she has offended and promises to do better. All of this takes place in the context of a fun, exiting movie with lots of laughs and energetic, fastpaced animation that pays close attention to detail and texture. Zootopia, Disney animation. Directed by Byron Howard, Rich Moore. With voices of Ginnifer Goodwin, Jason Bateman, Idris Elba. 1 hr., 48 min. Rated PG. Streaming on Disney+/Apple tv/ Prime/HBO MAX/Roku.

articles.text: Last Wednesday the Walking on Wednesdays group got lucky again with the weather. There was very heavy rain the following day, but the walkers’ Wednesday morning was just cloudy. The group was not surprised. They say it never rains during their walks and are almost always right. There was large turnout of 49 walkers and three K-9 best friends at the Exedra ready to enjoy their usually dry, weekly time together. The group tries to walk every traffic-safe Piedmont street during the year, but one set of streets they hadn’t gotten to this year was the Glen Alpine Road/ Sotelo Avenue loop. It has many beautiful homes and lots of Piedmont history. It’s a steep climb, but the group was ready for the challenge. On the way they stopped in front of 395 Hampton Road at the foot of Glen Alpine. This elegant Mediterranean, 11,870 square foot home, known as the Hampton House, was designed by Albert Farr in 1927 and has eight bedrooms and nine baths in 11,870 square foot home on 1+ acres with space for eight cars. Before the Hampton House was built, Louis Titus, a successful Berkeley real estate developer, bought 50 acres in these Piedmont hills in 1911. He intended to build a Spanish Italian mansion that he was going to call “Greenacres.” However, in 1912 the Piedmont’s Board of Trustees, now called the City Council, decided new property taxes were needed to pay for the new City’s public services. They passed taxes based on the amount of land owned, and Titus’ taxes were increased to a reported $200,000. He decided Piedmont was not such a great place for this mansion and Greenacres was never built. James Tyson was a wealthy lumber and shipping businessman. In 1914 he purchased 30 acres from Titus’ tract to build his estate, “Oakmont,” at what is now 70 Sotelo. He also built a carriage house as a garage and servant quarters where he and his wife lived temporarily while supervising the construction of their home. pages.text: Wednesday, November 19, 2025 21 Features Walking on Wednesday Wed. Walkers head to Glen Alpine and Sotelo Last Wednesday the Walking on Wednesdays group got lucky again with the weather. There was very heavy rain the following day, but the walkers’ Wednesday morning was just cloudy. The group was not surprised. They say it never rains during their walks and are almost always right. There was large turnout of 49 walkers and three K-9 best friends at the Exedra ready to enjoy their usually dry, weekly time together. The group tries to walk every traffic-safe Piedmont street during the year, but one set of streets they hadn’t gotten to this year was the Glen Alpine Road/ Sotelo Avenue loop. It has many beautiful homes and lots of Piedmont history. It’s a steep climb, but the group was ready for the challenge. On the way they stopped in front of 395 Hampton Road at the foot of Glen Alpine. This elegant Mediterranean, 11,870 square foot home, known as the Hampton House, was designed by Albert Farr in 1927 and has eight bedrooms and nine baths in 11,870 square foot home on 1+ acres with space for eight cars. Before the Hampton House was built, Louis Titus, a successful Berkeley real estate developer, bought 50 acres in these Piedmont hills in 1911. He intended to build a Spanish Italian mansion that he was going to call “Greenacres.” However, in 1912 the Piedmont’s Board of Trustees, now called the City Council, decided new property taxes were needed to pay for the new City’s public services. They passed taxes based on the amount of land owned, and Titus’ taxes were increased to a reported $200,000. He decided Piedmont was not such a great place for this mansion and Greenacres was never built. James Tyson was a wealthy lumber and shipping businessman. In 1914 he purchased 30 acres from Titus’ tract to build his estate, “Oakmont,” at what is now 70 Sotelo. He also built a carriage house as a garage and servant quarters where he and his wife lived temporarily while supervising the construction of their home. This carriage house, which was built in 1913, is now a lovely home at 45 Glen Alpine with eight bedrooms and six and a half baths in 8,692 square feet. When the group got to the house they were surprised to see a FOR SALE sign and a take-one box full of flyers. The flyer had pictures of the home’s beautiful interior and a lengthy house description. One bit of new information was that it was once a hunting lodge owned by Stanford University. One Cal alum was not surprised because he said everyone knows “This is Bear Territory!” At the very top of Glen Alpine is another very large, beautiful mansion. 75 Glen Alpine is a five bedroom/eight bath, 11,938 square foot, French revival chateau built in 1926 on 1.62 acres. Just to its right are Tyson’s original, two sandstone pillars with the words, “Oakmont” and “70 Sotelo.” However, Oakmont, which was completed in 1916, no longer exists. It was demolished in 1964. The pillars mark the entrance and long driveway to Tyson’s now-gone home. A gated driveway now leads to new homes built on the former Oakmont site. It was a great spot for a group photo. The walkers turned down Sotelo, and passed a front yard with a lovely succulent, drought-tolerant garden and were able to get a peak of Tyson Lake through the side of one of the homes. This lake was another Tyson creation. After he constructed Oakmont he dammed the creek that ran through his property and built a reservoir for his sons to swim. The lake is now owned and managed by a neighborhood association. As the group completed the loop at the foot of Sotelo was a very large, inflatable Rudolph the Red Nosed Reindeer in a front yard to wish the walkers an early Merry Christmas. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Raising a socially confident puppy Many will agree that watching puppy play is one of the most joyful things one can witness. The joyful yips, comical play bows, and the inevitable chaos can result in owners roaring with laughter. But did you know that encouraging your puppy to engage in play, thereby building social skills, is actually essential for healthy development? Similar to people, puppies must also learn social skills at a young age to live successful lifestyles. Confidence is part of it, yes, but so is learning to read the physical body language of other dogs. An adult dog with good social skills has the ability to engage in play without fear, but also understands when another dog is signaling they are not interested or even fearful. This well-socialized adult dog will also be able to set their own boundaries without starting fights. All of these skills are learned in a critical socialization age for puppies between 3 and 14 weeks old, and much of this is learned with their littermates. Once a puppy goes to their forever home at around 8 weeks old, it’s essential for the new pet parents to continue to find opportunities for the puppy to further build their social skills. What happens if a puppy is not well socialized? They can become fearful, which is the number one cause of aggression. Not every nervous dog presents an immediate bite risk, but the most common reason people and dogs are bitten is because they fail to read a dog’s clear signs that they are afraid and saying “no thank you” to being touched. Having a multitude of social interactions, the majority of them being positive, will give your puppy the confidence to know when a situation is safe as well as the ability to comfortably set their own boundaries. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, November 19, 2025 Social Puppy Butterflies Raising a socially confident puppy By Sierra Berrick Many will agree that watching puppy play is one of the most joyful things one can witness. The joyful yips, comical play bows, and the inevitable chaos can result in owners roaring with laughter. But did you know that encouraging your puppy to engage in play, thereby building social skills, is actually essential for healthy development? Similar to people, puppies must also learn social skills at a young age to live successful lifestyles. Confidence is part of it, yes, but so is learning to read the physical body language of other dogs. An adult dog with good social skills has the ability to engage in play without fear, but also understands when another dog is signaling they are not interested or even fearful. This well-socialized adult dog will also be able to set their own boundaries without starting fights. All of these skills are learned in a critical socialization age for puppies between 3 and 14 weeks old, and much of this is learned with their littermates. Once a puppy goes to their forever home at around 8 weeks old, it’s essential for the new pet parents to continue to find opportunities for the puppy to further build their social skills. What happens if a puppy is not well socialized? They can become fearful, which is the number one cause of aggression. Not every nervous dog presents an immediate bite risk, but the most common reason people and dogs are bitten is because they fail to read a dog’s clear signs that they are afraid and saying “no thank you” to being touched. Having a multitude of social interactions, the majority of them being positive, will give your puppy the confidence to know when a situation is safe as well as the ability to comfortably set their own boundaries. So how does a new pet parent find ways to socialize their dog? A good way to start is by joining a puppy training class. A competent trainer who understands that socialization is equally as important as obedience will provide time during their puppy class for play. This will simultaneously increase your dog’s social skills and provide much-needed brain breaks. An example of a class structured this way is the one taught by Mike Wombacher. During his classes, puppies and owners learn new skills, as well as getting significant play time. Owners receive feedback from the trainer about puppy socialization and play to build their understanding of healthy canine interactions. And of course, your pup will have the time of their lives testing out their budding social skills in play. By prioritizing socialization, you will set your puppy up for a successful life of wail wagging and joy. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland. She helped launch the service dog and facility dog training organization Alpha Dog Assist in Mill Valley in 2021 and currently offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. Call 510–507– 2017, email Sierra109@gmail. com, or visit her website at www. oakhillsdogtraining.weebly.com. articles.text: One of my favorite things to do when on vacation in France is to visit the local charcuterie shop. I am always amazed by the wonderful variety of products available, many of which are unknown in the US. There will often be 10 types of pate, goose, duck and pork rillettes, tons of different types of salami, confit of goose and duck, foie gras of various sorts – an amazing panoply of meaty goodness. Over the years of travel to France, I realized you did not even have to find a charcuterie shop to locate these products. Any good French Supermarche like Leclerc, Casino, Intermarche, or Carrefour will have a long charcuterie counter where you can purchase the same quality of products that you find in the small shops. After years of smuggling home pate and rillettes in my suitcase I was amazed and delighted to discover the wonderful Fabrique Delices. It was a dream come true – a company started by French entrepreneurs to create French style charcuterie in America. On top of that it was right here in the East Bay in Hayward. The company began in 1920 in Meaux, France and was called SAPAR. It became the leading producer of pates in Europe – its products carried by Fauchon in Paris as well as gourmet stores all over Europe. In 1985 Jean Claude Auge decided to establish Fabrique Delices and bring French charcuterie to the American market. The idea was to offer products of outstanding and consistent quality with unique and eye-catching presentations. In 1996 Marc Poinsignon and Antonio Pinheiro were brought from France to oversee the U.S. subsidiary. In 2002 Fabrique Delices moved into a newly built plant in Hayward, California and today is the largest producer of French charcuterie in America. We cooked up a box of penne pasta and basted it with the tub of truffle butter, I chose white because it is rarer. It was more than enough for that amount of pasta. Hit it with a ton of coarse ground Tellicherry black pepper and you have a simple, delicious hit on your hands. We also excitedly tried out the duck leg confit. FD sells these in packages of 1, 3 and 6 legs. Confit is the leg of a duck or goose cooked and then preserved in its own fat. In rural France this was a way of ensuring the family had meat during the lean winter months. For us today it is a way of serving duck with absolutely no hassle. Having been cooked for you, all you do is heat up the legs under the broiler in the oven. After about 20 minutes the skin becomes crisp while the meat stays tender. You can use the duck legs in cassoulet, tear the meat off for use in pasta or salad or do what we did – eat it plain. There is something especially delicious about the meat of a duck that you just don’t get from chicken. I am so glad Fabrique Delices is here in the East Bay to give us access to products which I had previously had to travel to France to enjoy. He loved the idea, so I recruited the Kensington Road Dinner Club: a bunch of neighbors in Kensington and El Cerrito who like to eat to be my guinea pigs. Mike, Drennen, Fernanado, NIcoletta, Megan and Kodie, Ittai, Maureen, and Margaret all brought their discerning palates to evaluate the products. We started with the duck and pork rillettes. Most Americans know about pate but not many know rillettes, which are very popular in France. Every charcuterie place has big bowls of duck, goose and pork rillettes which they scoop out for you. It is basically moist meat mixed with extra fat which gives it an incredibly rich taste. You spread it on crusty French bread and finish with a tart cornichon pickle to cut the fat. Both types of rillettes were good but the nod went to the duck. There was something almost decadent about spreading this essence of duck on bread. We progressed to the salumi course which featured something truly rare – black truffle salami. Considering how expensive truffles are I did not expect it to really have that much truffle flavor. Boy, was I wrong. This salami was heavily flecked with black truffles which gave off the distinctive, enchanting, almost indescribable aroma that makes truffles so highly coveted. This stuff is addictive, and the slices flew off the platter. Back to duck land with the smoked duck breast and the dried cured duck breast. Each was thinly sliced so it had both dark meat and white fat. They both melted in your mouth with unctuous deliciousness. Voters at the Kensington Road Dinner Club were split as to which was preferred – both incredibly savory. Next, we were on to the sausage course. Mike had grilled a large coil of Lamb Merguez sausage along with some fat, juicy Duck and Fig sausages. The lamb Merguez was reminiscent of eating at a Middle Eastern restaurant and the duck sausage with figs was a wonderful contrast of savory and sweet and a truly interesting combination. Yes, we did also have a salad and some cheese to balance out the meats. We started with a delicious dish of moules frites Margaret and Ittai cooked that took us all to Paris in our minds. The wines of the evening were bottles of 2015 Bordeaux, Muscadet from the Loire Valley and Cotes du Rhone - simple basic wines they drink in France with this kind of food.
