articles.text: The 2nd annual Piedmont Adult Recreation Expo was held on November 16, from 2:00 to 4:00 p.m. at the Veterans Memorial Building. The event featured 25 recreation providers and was attended by approximately 200 people. The event was co-chaired by Recreation Commission members Dick Carter and Lisa Gardner. Their subcommittee reviewed existing activities throughout Piedmont and the general Bay Area. They conducted a community survey that reached nearly 500 responses. It identified a lack of knowledge about existing opportunities as the primary reason more people weren’t participating. “A lot of our adults and seniors are not all tech savvy, so a lot of them weren’t aware of things that were being offered online. As a result of the survey, we made a recommendation that we do an in-person event, which we called the Expo,” said Gardner. The Expo offered a chance to learn about available programs and discuss details with the organizers, including Piedmont Adult School. “The things the survey found were that people want to be involved. They just didn’t know how… We looked at what we had offering in Piedmont and pulled them all together in one house, in one day,” said Gardner The Expo provided a place for adults to learn about the activities that interested them. “We know that loneliness and isolation are serious problems for older adults. [It was a compelling motivation],” added Carter. The Expo was made possible through the efforts of Piedmont volunteers and in collaboration with the Recreation Department, the Piedmont Adult School, and the non-profit Piedmont Center for the Arts. articles.text: Picture my client, a wildly successful entrepreneur whose innovation and drive propelled him into the top half-percent. His life was one of luxury: yachts, private planes, global travel, and a beautiful mansion on one of the most distinguished streets in the East Bay. I’ve known him my entire life. To me, he was strong, charismatic, and absolutely a force to be reckoned with. But as time went on, subtle changes began to surface. The brightness in his eyes dulled. His sharpness softened. His longtime companion, overwhelmed by what she believed was controlling and irritable behavior, eventually had to move on. She didn’t realize he wasn’t being difficult — he was changing. Slipping. Losing control. When I visited him, I found a man I barely recognized — surrounded by a lifetime of belongings and memories, growing thinner, sadder, and more frustrated by the day. This wasn’t just the stress of a move. This was the unraveling of independence, identity, and the confidence he once carried with ease. Sadly, this wasn’t the first time I’d witnessed such a decline. More recently, I’ve spent the last decade helping another dear friend — a once vibrant traveler, respected and admired, supported for years by a loving husband who has since passed. I’ve watched as she, too, has begun to slowly unravel with age. Strength turning to fear. Confidence slipping into confusion. Even the simplest decisions become overwhelming. Is it dementia? Is it aging? Or is it the disorienting experience of life suddenly spinning beyond one’s control? It’s hard to know. But one truth remains: no one should have to navigate this alone. These experiences have reinforced something profoundly important: we must plan ahead. For ourselves, for our aging parents, and for the people we love — long before the need becomes urgent, and before a crisis makes the decisions for us. It’s not just about choosing a community with pretty surroundings or a full social calendar. It’s about understanding the depth of care, the consistency of support, and the human connection that actually exists. Ask: Will someone check in daily? Will they notice changes? Will they help you settle in, feel safe, and feel truly seen? For decades, I’ve helped families through life’s most emotional and complex transitions — downsizing, relocating aging parents, navigating estates, and finding communities that offer dignity, compassion, and real care. I don’t just sell homes. I walk with families through seasons of uncertainty, overwhelm, and change. If you or someone you love is facing a major life transition, I’m here to help — with compassion, clarity, and experience. Let’s begin the conversation now, before the storm hits. articles.text: Stagebridge, the nation’s first performing arts organization for adults 50+, is stepping confidently into a new chapter with the appointment of Michelle Taylor Lagunas as its next Executive Director. A seasoned nonprofit leader with deep roots in senior services, Lagunas brings more than two decades of experience in program development, community engagement, and organizational leadership. Her career includes senior roles at the Lions Center for the Blind, Center for Elders’ Independence, and Sisters of the Presentation SF, where she led multimillion-dollar budgets, strengthened partnerships, and championed creative aging. Her arrival marks an exciting moment as Stagebridge continues expanding its impact across the Bay Area. This leadership transition follows a joyful, art-filled season for the organization. In late October, Stagebridge partnered with The Marsh to present a special edition of Tell It On Tuesday, blending music, storytelling, and intergenerational creativity. Beloved instructor Scrumbly Koldewyn opened the evening with The Dreamers, whose spirited harmonies from the 1920s–1950s set a vibrant tone. Emceed by the charismatic Wayne Harris, the event featured an impressive lineup of storytellers, including Anthony Michael Jefferson, Debi Mason, Doug McKechnie, Monica Ten Eyck, and Linda Yemoto, who filled the room with humor, reflection, folklore, and unforgettable personal narratives. Just weeks earlier, the community gathered for Scrumbly Koldewyn’s 80th Birthday Salon, an uplifting celebration of music, stories, and decades of creative Beloved instructor and musical legend Scrumbly Koldewyn celebrates his 80th in true Stagebridge style – surrounded by community, creativity, and plenty of cake. Michelle Taylor Lagunas, Stagebridge’s new Executive Director, brings decades of nonprofit leadership and a passion for creative aging to her new role. legacy. Held at Reidenbach Hall, the event doubled as a fundraiser supporting Stagebridge’s programs. Friends, students, and fellow artists honored Scrumbly’s influence with performances and tributes that perfectly reflected his joyful, inventive spirit. Stagebridge performers also shone at Kaiser Permanente’s Aging Well Summit, showcasing the power of creative aging through music and storytelling. Their performance underscored what Stagebridge demonstrates every day: aging well is rooted in connection, expression, and community. As Lagunas steps into her role, she joins a thriving, multigenerational community fueled by artistry and belonging. With fresh leadership, energized programming, and a vibrant season behind them, Stagebridge is poised for its next inspiring act— one where older adults continue to learn, perform, and thrive through the transformative power of the performing arts.
articles.title: Stagebridge welcomes new Executive Director

Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. By Cookie Segelstein Dear MacMama: I have an iMac that I bought in 2023. My son keeps telling me to upgrade to the new operating system, Tahoe. Is there any reason to do that? I have not upgraded anything since I bought it. He said something about easier organization with the new one, as I am trying to write my memoir. Jayne, Oakland Dear Jayne: Although I often caution clients to wait for the .2 release of a new operating system (e.g. OS Tahoe 26.2), I have found Tahoe to be very stable, even though at this writing we are on OS Tahoe 26.1. The reasons for keeping your operating system up to date mostly have to do with security but sometimes upgrades contain exciting new features. One misconception is that the updates that happen automatically will keep things current. But those are updates, not upgrades, and only apply to the operating system that is already on your computer. For instance, if you have Sequoia installed on your Mac, the updates that happen automatically only pertain to Sequoia. So, an update applies to your current operating system and an upgrade is a new one. The actual operating system upgrade will only happen when you initiate it. Another reason to update your OS, is that in the eventual act of getting a new computer, keeping up with the changes will prevent you from feeling like a stranger in a strange land, as often the interface changes with each upgrade. Now, since you are writing your memoir, I think that Tahoe (OS 26) could be very helpful in helping you organize your files. Let me list a few of my favorite features. 1. CUSTOMIZE FOLDERS: Many years ago, there was some third party software that allowed you to color code your folders, not just apply colored dots next to the folder title. Tahoe allows for a real customization of each folder. If you want all your folders to be a different color, you can do that in System Settings/Appearance. There you can change all your folders to a different color than the default blue. But what I like to do is to change each folder or group of folders to a different color. To do this, right-click (or hold the control key and click) on a folder and choose the Customize Folder option in the contextual menu. You can even apply and emoji or symbol. This is very helpful if you have many folders and feel like you are wading through an ever-expanding sea of blue to find the ones you need. 2. FOLDER ICON CHANGES: Speaking of folders, I know many times we have folders that are empty. Now you can tell by looking whether a folder has items inside. You will see a bit of virtual paper sticking out. This makes it much easier to clean out unwanted empty folders without having to open each one. 3. SYSTEM THEMES: In System Settings/Appearance, you can even change the theme of your whole interface. You can change the highlight color, the way the dock looks, whether it’s more or less transparent, among other things. 4. HOLD ASSIST: Many of us use our computers to make and receive phone calls. In the phone app, when you are waiting to speak to a person, you can activate Hold Assist. Your mac will let you know when an agent is on the line and inform the person on the other end that you will be right with them. 5. LIVE TR ANSLATION: This is perhaps my favorite. Facetime now supports live translation. If you are talking to someone who speaks another language, FaceTime can display captions in your language. This feature utilizes Apple Intelligence and you must have an Apple silicon Mac (all of the computers with M1-M5 chips). These are just a handful of the new features on OS Tahoe, with new ones being added with each update. To initiate an operating system upgrade, go to: System Settings/General/Software Update. Before doing any major upgrade make sure you have a current back up to Time Machine, and that any third-party software that you use is compatible. You can usually find that information on the developer’s website. Also, make sure your Mac is new enough to handle the upgrade. For Tahoe, Apple provides this site to check if your machine is compatible: https://support.apple. com/en-us/122867. Cookie Segelstein is the MacMama, an Apple Certified Service Professional that provides Apple computer consultation and trouble-shooting in your home and office. For more information, call 510-520-7760, email cookie@themacmama.com, or visit her website at www.themacmama.com READ IT IN THE POST

articles.text: The Piedmont Seniors enjoyed a beautiful fall day during pumpkin season visiting Half Moon Bay, home of the 53rd Annual Art & Pumpkin Festival. First, the group visited the fabulous Ritz Carlton Hotel, where they. were given a private tour. The Ritz Carlton opened in March 2001 and this luxury hotel which sits atop a dramatic bluff, and overlooks the Pacific Ocean, features 261 guest rooms, oceanview dining areas, a spa, and two championship golf courses. The resort’s architectural style is inspired by a 19th-century seaside lodge. From one’s first glimpse of the expansive sea vista from the hotel’s foyer, one is immediately ensconced by its elegance. Once the tour was completed the group was allowed time to meander around the grounds and take in the beautiful scenery. Afterwards, the Seniors ventured downtown, home to the world-famous Half Moon Bay Art & Pumpkin Festival, which celebrates the beauty, bounty, and creativity of the autumn season. This is the season’s signature event, drawing visitors to the “World Pumpkin Capital” on historic Main Street. The Seniors had the opportunity to walk through the downtown area, The Piedmont Seniors group enjoy a wonderful lunch at the Half Moon Bay Brewing Company. Pictured are Sue Getreuer (left), Mary Buller, Lois Horwitz, Maddie Katoa, Jan Yager, Greg Jurin, Sandra Ponce, Jim Ayotte, Fred Pemberton, Yorkman Lowe, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, Edith Hereso, and Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein. Members of the Piedmont Seniors in front of this year’s Half Moon Bay Art & Pumpkin Festival winner from Santa Rosa, CA. This award-winning pumpkin weighed 2,346 pounds! Pictured are Mary Buller (left), Sandra Ponce, Janet Epstein, Lois Horwitz, and Maddie Katoa. including a visit to where the Half Moon Bay Art & Pumpkin Festival was recently staged, to see the first-place award-winning pumpkin on display. Then it was time for lunch as the Piedmont Seniors visited the Half Moon Bay Brewing Company, a restaurant, brewery and pillar of the community. Celebrating its 25th anniversary makes it Half Moon Bay’s oldest brewery still in operation. Along with its brewery, this restaurant is also known for the freshness of the seafood. Everything is made in house from raw ingredients. After lunch the group headed back home, taking a ride along the coast, on highway 1, absorbing the spectacular coastal scenic views. In all, it was a beautiful, leisurely day enjoyed by all. The Piedmont Seniors at the Ritz Carlton’s festive fall harvest display in Half Moon Bay: (standing) Ritz Carlton tour guide Stacy (left), Sandra Ponce, Edith Hereso, Fred Pemberton, Jim Ayotte, Mary Buller, Greg Jurin, Lois Horwitz, Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein, Jan Yager, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, and Maddie Katoa. Seated are Sue Getreuer and Yorkman Lowe.
articles.title: Piedmont Seniors visit Half Moon Bay

articles.text: Daley Mae Sarver Humphries, a beloved wife, mother, grandmother, cousin and friend, passed away at home in Piedmont surrounded by family and so much love on Sunday, November 2, 2025, shortly after her 77th birthday. Daley is survived by her husband, Mike Humphries; daughters Alisa Sarver Latvala (Rich) and Amy Sarver Engler (Jeremy); step-children, Steven Humphries (Amy) and Mary Jane Rogers (Chris); and grandchildren, Thomas, Henry, Maia, Sydney, Olivia, Eva, Aubrey, and Ella. Born on October 13, 1948, in Oakland, she was the daughter of Anne and Marvin Blankstein. She attended Crocker Highlands Elementary School, and graduated from Oakland High. She was a 3rd generation alumni of UC Berkeley where she earned a Bachelor of Arts degree in History. Earlier in her career she managed dental offices before completing her Society for Human Resources Management (SHRM) certification. She spent many years working for Levi Strauss & Company in Human Resources before completing her professional career at Abbott Laboratories, after which she retired to be a full time Grandma, helping to raise her grandchildren. She was an incredibly engaged and nurturing grandmother who helped with everything from caring for her grandchildren as infants, to driving them to all of their activities and showering them with love, always. Her grandchildren adored their “Maea”. Daley loved many things in life, but nothing compared to the love she had for her daughters, grandchildren, husband and family. Daley was a mom to all and a devoted partner to Mikey, her heartthrob. Together they created a warm and loving home that became the hub for lively dinner parties with an abundance of shared laughter, sleepovers, holiday gatherings and a myriad of celebrations. Daley created a positive, warm, accepting environment where people felt comfortable being their authentic selves. Her home became a place of comfort to many. Daley was most happy when surrounded by her family and friends, and made a point to tell her loved ones just how much she loved, cherished, and appreciated them, always finishing a conversation by saying, “I love you,” Daley Mae Humphries died on November 2, 2025. She was 77. and then, “I love you more.” She enjoyed cooking, reading, music, happy hours, game days, family gatherings, holidays and celebrations, vacations in Hawaii and traveling internationally with Mike and their lifelong friends. As a child and younger adult, she enjoyed time spent in Tahoe skiing, waterskiing, and being outdoors. She was an avid Cal fan, known for displaying her Go Bears spirit at Cal games and throughout the many years spent camping at the Lair of the Bear. She was the best mother to her daughters - unconditionally loving, empathetic, caring and encouraging. She was known as the fun and cool mom, always welcoming and hosting many in her home with open arms. She was an animal lover through and through – many compared her to Snow White. With a magnetic personality and vibrant sense of humor, Daley was always up for a good time, often being the last one to leave a party. Goodbyes took hours. She is known for her kindness, compassion, vibrance, sense of humor, smile, laughter, welcoming nature, and pristine skin. She will be remembered for sharing her light, love, sparkle, wit and warmth with all who knew her. A celebration of life and memorial service will be held on Sunday, November 23, at 11 a.m. at Piedmont Community Hall. The family requests that attendees wear something sparkly or colorful in honor of her vibrant and radiant personality and her love of sparkles. In lieu of flowers, please consider donating to your local animal shelter or food bank in honor of Daley.
articles.title: Daley Mae Sarver Humphries dies on November 2

The Piedmont Seniors at the Ritz Carlton’s festive fall harvest display in Half Moon Bay: (standing) Ritz Carlton tour guide Stacy (left), Sandra Ponce, Edith Hereso, Fred Pemberton, Jim Ayotte, Mary Buller, Greg Jurin, Lois Horwitz, Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein, Jan Yager, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, and Maddie Katoa. Seated are Sue Getreuer and Yorkman Lowe. Obituary Daley Mae Sarver Humphries dies on November 2 Daley Mae Sarver Humphries, a beloved wife, mother, grandmother, cousin and friend, passed away at home in Piedmont surrounded by family and so much love on Sunday, November 2, 2025, shortly after her 77th birthday. Daley is survived by her husband, Mike Humphries; daughters Alisa Sarver Latvala (Rich) and Amy Sarver Engler (Jeremy); step-children, Steven Humphries (Amy) and Mary Jane Rogers (Chris); and grandchildren, Thomas, Henry, Maia, Sydney, Olivia, Eva, Aubrey, and Ella. Born on October 13, 1948, in Oakland, she was the daughter of Anne and Marvin Blankstein. She attended Crocker Highlands Elementary School, and graduated from Oakland High. She was a 3rd generation alumni of UC Berkeley where she earned a Bachelor of Arts degree in History. Earlier in her career she managed dental offices before completing her Society for Human Resources Management (SHRM) certification. She spent many years working for Levi Strauss & Company in Human Resources before completing her professional career at Abbott Laboratories, after which she retired to be a full time Grandma, helping to raise her grandchildren. She was an incredibly engaged and nurturing grandmother who helped with everything from caring for her grandchildren as infants, to driving them to all of their activities and showering them with love, always. Her grandchildren adored their “Maea”. Daley loved many things in life, but nothing compared to the love she had for her daughters, grandchildren, husband and family. Daley was a mom to all and a devoted partner to Mikey, her heartthrob. Together they created a warm and loving home that became the hub for lively dinner parties with an abundance of shared laughter, sleepovers, holiday gatherings and a myriad of celebrations. Daley created a positive, warm, accepting environment where people felt comfortable being their authentic selves. Her home became a place of comfort to many. Daley was most happy when surrounded by her family and friends, and made a point to tell her loved ones just how much she loved, cherished, and appreciated them, always finishing a conversation by saying, “I love you,” Daley Mae Humphries died on November 2, 2025. She was 77. and then, “I love you more.” She enjoyed cooking, reading, music, happy hours, game days, family gatherings, holidays and celebrations, vacations in Hawaii and traveling internationally with Mike and their lifelong friends. As a child and younger adult, she enjoyed time spent in Tahoe skiing, waterskiing, and being outdoors. She was an avid Cal fan, known for displaying her Go Bears spirit at Cal games and throughout the many years spent camping at the Lair of the Bear. She was the best mother to her daughters - unconditionally loving, empathetic, caring and encouraging. She was known as the fun and cool mom, always welcoming and hosting many in her home with open arms. She was an animal lover through and through – many compared her to Snow White. With a magnetic personality and vibrant sense of humor, Daley was always up for a good time, often being the last one to leave a party. Goodbyes took hours. She is known for her kindness, compassion, vibrance, sense of humor, smile, laughter, welcoming nature, and pristine skin. She will be remembered for sharing her light, love, sparkle, wit and warmth with all who knew her. A celebration of life and memorial service will be held on Sunday, November 23, at 11 a.m. at Piedmont Community Hall. The family requests that attendees wear something sparkly or colorful in honor of her vibrant and radiant personality and her love of sparkles. In lieu of flowers, please consider donating to your local animal shelter or food bank in honor of Daley.

articles.text: Staff Photos Soren Dixon (left) and Jack Nelson celebrate a goal on the lacrosse field. Both won league titles each season they played at Piedmont High. community. Friend and teammate Nate Carter Fredericks shared: “Jack and Soren are two of the most positive and driven people I’ve ever played with. They always brought light and laughter to every situation, even when things were tough. Their energy and determination were contagious. You could feel it in every huddle and play.” In memory of Jack and Soren, friends and family have gifted over $130,000 to Oakland Lacrosse Club. These contributions will carry forward the values these young men exemplified—teamwork, perseverance, and joy in the game—through the Purple One Scholarship and the Helmets Rising Initiative, our new endeavor to expand boys high school lacrosse in Oakland Unified School District. Purple One Scholarship Jack and Soren’s bond was rooted in their shared love of sports and the joy they found in playing together. The name of the scholarship, “Purple One,” comes from a play the Piedmont team ran, one that always ended with Soren passing to Jack for the goal. Even when opposing teams had seen it before and tried to stop it, it still worked. The play captured everything about their friendship and teamwork: trust, connection, and the pure joy of competing side by side. Teammate Henry Brayer believes that the Purple One scholarship “an amazing way to honor their legacy while encouraging others to adopt the qualities that made Soren and Jack such amazing teammates and people.” Launching Spring 2026, this annual scholarship will award two $2,500 scholarships to graduating senior boys’ players from Oakland Lacrosse Club. The scholarship will support the educational pursuits of club participants as they continue their academic journeys. The Purple One Scholarship celebrates the qualities that defined Jack and Soren on and off the field—qualities Brayer, a teammate for eight years through youth and high school lacrosse, will always appreciate: “Jack was a fearless leader that prioritized the well being of his teammates. Soren was a very selfless player. He chased assists rather than goals and was the first guy to praise his teammates.” Each year, two graduating senior boys from Oakland Lacrosse Club will be selected who embody the same spirit that made Jack and Soren such beloved teammates. These Oakland players will be recognized for their leadership, the quiet kind that lifts others up and strengthens the whole team. The selection committee will be looking for student-athletes who have heart and hustle, the ones who show up to every practice ready to work hard and inspire those around them. Moreover, recipients will be chosen not for their statistics or records, but for how they show up for their team, school, and community. Like Soren and Jack, awardees will be great teammates, the kind who earn respect not through words, but through actions, effort, and unwavering positivity. And they’ll be enthusiastic ambassadors of the game, sharing their love of lacrosse with others and helping to grow access and opportunity for the next generation. Through Purple One, Jack and Soren’s legacy lives on in every player who leads with compassion, plays with joy, and builds community through the game they loved. The scholarship recipients will be chosen by a panel that includes members of Soren’s and Jack’s families, Piedmont teammates Nate Fredericks, Henry Brayer, and Noah Lindenbaum, and a representative from Oakland Lacrosse. Recipients will be recognized at the Oakland Athletic League (OAL) Championships, celebrating their achievements both on and off the field. Teammate Noah Lindenbaum sees the scholarships as a passing of the torch, an inheritance of a legacy of excellence, from Soren and Jack: “For lacrosse, this means playing hard, practicing harder, emphasizing teamwork, and being grateful for every second they’re on the field. Off the field, this means emphasizing academic achievement, serving as a role model for your peers, and living a life that fulfills your passion. Soren and Jack were irreplaceable, and I know they’d be

Soren and Jack were irreplaceable, and I know they’d be 43 55 56 57 58 62 65 68 beyond honored to be a part of the Purple One scholarship.” Helmets Rising Initiative Through the Helmets Rising Initiative, Oakland Lacrosse is growing from two boys high school programs with twenty players to six schools and 150 players. Jack and Soren’s joy for the game was infectious and they believed deeply in the power of team sports to bring people together. Supporting Oakland Lacrosse in their honor helps open that same world of opportunity to young players who might never otherwise get the chance to pick up a stick. This initiative aims to establish and expand boys’ lacrosse programming at six Oakland high schools by Spring 2029. Inspired by the teamwork, leadership, and inclusivity Jack and Soren embodied, this initiative ensures that cost and access are never barriers to play. Through Helmets Rising, Oakland Lacrosse expands holistic programing, combining free access to lacrosse with leadership development, mentoring, college counseling, and a curriculum to strengthen mental health and wellness. By removing financial barriers and providing consistent guidance on and off the field, the program helps young men from Oakland build confidence, resilience, and leadership skills. Each participant gains access to a caring community of teammates, coaches, mentors, and a powerful network of resources that includes job and networking opportunities, college counseling, and mental wellness resources. We aim to create a safe, structured environment for personal growth. Together, with your support, we can continue what Jack and Soren started, sharing the game they loved and expanding its reach to the next generation of players who will learn, lead, and play with the same heart. Thank you, Jack and Soren Soren and Jack remind us why sports matter. “They gave everything they had for the good of the team, always putting others before themselves. I’ll always remember how much heart they played with and how deeply they cared about the people around them” Nathan Fredericks shared. Beyond wins and losses, athletics teach resilience, teamwork, and community building. Lacrosse creates supportive places where young people learn to lead, lift one another up, and find purpose and community. Oakland Lacrosse is proud to carry forward a shared belief that every young person deserves the chance to play, to thrive, and to belong. Their light, enthusiasm, and passion for the game will forever inspire us to play, teach, and give back—just as they did. The Purple One Scholarship and the Helmets Rising Initiative ensure that Jack and Soren’s love for lacrosse continues to open doors for future generations. To learn more about Oakland Lacrosse Club, visit its website at oaklandlacrosseclub.org. Kevin Kelley is a former lacrosse coach at Piedmont High School. articles.text: Seven mayors of the 12th Congressional District gathered in Oakland to discuss the Federal Government’s shutdown. Starting on October 1st, this marks the longest government shutdown in history and is still ongoing. Residents of the district are already feeling the impact of the federal shutdown. “We have federal employees who live in Piedmont, and we have folks with businesses that have federal contracts. Although we sleep in Piedmont, we live beyond our borders. We go to hospitals, we travel, we have entertainment, and we go shopping. We’re affected by what happens regionally,” said Piedmont Vice Mayor Conna McCarthy, who spoke at the meeting in place of Mayor Betsy Andersen, who could not attend. One of the biggest problems the shutdown has created is healthcare. Piedmont Vice Mayor Conna McCarthy speaks in front of six other mayors, including Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee and Rep. Lateefah Simons of District 12.

articles.text: In 1960, six-year-old Ruby Bridges became the first Black student to integrate an all-white elementary school in the South. Escorted by U.S. Marshals through angry crowds, Ruby became a national symbol of bravery and hope during the Civil Rights Movement. Her courage has inspired generations to stand up for equality and access to education for all. This Friday, November 14, students, families, and community members are invited to join the Ruby Bridges Walk, led by the Affinity Mentorship Program at Piedmont High School. Participants are encouraged to arrive at 8:00 a.m. in front of Piedmont High School. Affinity Mentorship speakers will begin at 8:05 a.m. before the walk starts. The event celebrates courage, inclusion, and the power of young people to make a difference in their community. The Ruby Bridges Walk honors Ruby’s legacy by inviting students across the country to walk in her name, promoting kindness, inclusion, and the continued fight for justice in education. At Piedmont High, the Affinity Mentorship Program aims to strengthen community connection and emphasize the value of mentorship, representation, and shared action. The program’s student mentors will speak about Ruby’s impact and how her story continues to inspire young leaders today. In May 2018, fifth graders from Martin Elementary School in South San Francisco learned about Ruby and asked their school board to pass a resolution making November 14 Ruby Bridges Day. The annual tradition has expanded since then and Piedmont’s participation began in 2023. All are encouraged to join the Affinity Mentorship team this Friday to honor Ruby Bridges’ courage and walk together toward a more inclusive, compassionate future, one step at a time. Evolette Mak is a student intern with the Piedmont Post. Piedmont students participate in the Ruby Bridges Walk to School event in 2023. Photo by Jean Takazawa
articles.title: Join the Ruby Bridges Walk this Friday, November 14

articles.text: Editor: This week, PUSD’s School Board will vote on a plan to bring 60 minutes of Latin instruction to the 5th grade schedule next year. As the parent of a current 4th grader, I’ll admit I was surprised when I first heard about this plan. Is a “dead language” really something today’s 11-year-olds need to spend time learning? But after learning more about the district’s rationale for bringing Latin to the 5th grade curriculum, I am impressed and grateful that our district is making this change. Up until this school year, the earliest that PUSD students could start learning a foreign language was 8th grade – putting us behind our peer districts like Orinda and Albany, who begin foreign language in 7th and sometimes 6th grade, and well past the age when young brains are the most plastic and receptive to foreign language acquisition. I was thrilled when Dr. Hawn and the School Board announced last year that they were exploring ways to bring foreign language instruction to the lower grades – and that they worked so quickly to make that priority a reality. Thanks to their efforts, this year’s 7th graders at PMS are now able to take Spanish, Mandarin, or French as an elective – and next year 6th graders will have the same opportunity. Offering foreign language instruction at the elementary level, however, has proven to be a bit more complicated. While most parents expressed interest in Spanish instruction in 5th grade, offering only Spanish in the elementary schools would have a negative impact on French and Mandarin enrollment in secondary school. And logistically the elementary schools are unable to offer all three world languages. Given those constraints, the School Board started exploring Latin instruction for PUSD’s 5th graders. While Latin will only be offered for 60 minutes per week, the district has made a strong case for the potential benefits including improving vocabulary and fostering literacy skills, academic confidence, and cultural awareness. I also really appreciate that our 5th graders will have the shared experience of confronting an entirely new language as their first classroom exposure to a foreign language – especially a language that serves as the foundation for so many other languages they may study in the future. I am thrilled that my daughter will be one of the first PUSD students to receive Latin instruction next year, and I am grateful that our district has continued to find a way to bring foreign language to our younger students. At a time when much of America’s current leadership wants to isolate us from the international community, how wonderful that our district is working to create the next generation of global citizens. — Laura Maestrelli Parent of Havens 4th grader and PMS 7th grader

articles.text: After years of planning and a month of construction, the Linda Beach Tot Lot will open at 10 a.m. Friday, November 14. Mayor Betsy Andersen along with other city staff will host a ribbon-cutting ceremony to celebrate the opening of the Tot Lot. The project cost $400,000, with 75% funded by the City’s Facilities Capital Fund, and the remaining 25% from a donation by the Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF). Members of the foundation will be in attendance for the ceremony and will present their $100,000 donation. Patty Dunlap, president of PBF, said she is excited for the opening of the Tot Lot. “PBF is committed to enhancing public spaces throughout Piedmont, including projects that serve children. Safe and friendly play spaces have never been more crucial, as many children are drawn to screens beginning at an early age. Piedmont parks provide a gentle antidote by encouraging connection and creativity outdoors. And it’s not just the kids who benefit – adults need outdoor play time, too.” Dunlap believes tot lots have a positive impact on the community. “The first word that comes to mind is joy,” said Dunlap. “Most people – children for sure – come to a park full of anticipation and energy, knowing they are in for a good time. There is no greater joy than watching a child fully immersed in imaginative play - coasting down a slide, climbing a tree, or trying to touch the sky from a swing. PBF wants to ensure that our parks help create that priceless joy.” The PBF has an extensive history of donating to the creation of tot lots. “PBF has financially contributed to play areas within every major park in the City of Piedmont, including Dracena, the Main Park, and Hampton Field,” said Dunlap. Depending on the upcoming weather for Friday, the grand opening is set for the Linda Beach Tot Lot. Soon, kids will play until their hearts’ content. Linda Beach Tot Lot Staff photo from left to right.
articles.title: Linda Beach Tot Lot opens on Friday

articles.text: Come meet Baldwin at Oakland Animal Services. Baldwin is a calm and confident 6-year-old German Shepherd Mix. He currently lives in a foster home with cats and kittens and enjoys watching them play. Baldwin’s foster says he is well-mannered, house and crate trained, knows his basic cues, and takes treats gently. He enjoys car rides, walks calmly on leash and is friendly towards people and other dogs when approached. Baldwin, 65-pounds, is a great match for someone looking for an even-keeled, loyal companion. He likes to lean in for pets when people kneel beside him and is happy to hang out without demanding attention, content to just be by someone’s side. You can see more of him in foster on Instagram @catpeoplefosterdogs and on the Oakland Animal Services website. To meet Baldwin, submit your adoption questionnaire online at the shelter’s website and you will be contacted by his foster to arrange a meet-andgreet. For more information on fostering or adoption, contact Piedmont resident Jessica McDevitt at jessicamcdev@ gmail.com. open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm

articles.text: Dr. Breakfast is a gray, one-year-old cat with a big personality and an even bigger heart. Friendly, playful, and full of charm, she loves to be in the middle of the action — whether that’s chasing toys, following you from room to room, or flopping down dramatically for belly rubs. This confident girl is happiest when she has plenty of enrichment and time with her people. She’ll proudly parade her toys around after a good “hunt,” as if to ask for applause. She enjoys being carried, loves attention, and will happily tell you what she’s thinking. Dr. Breakfast can get a little overstimulated during play or petting, so she’ll do best with adopters who can read her cues and give her short breaks when she needs them. She could enjoy a calm home with older kids and may appreciate Adopt Dr. Breakfast through Cat Town. having another playful cat as a companion. If you’re looking for a social affectionate cat who brings both energy and affection into your home, Dr. Breakfast might be the perfect match. She is spayed, vaccinated, microchipped, and tested positive for FIV and negative for FeLV. Learn more at www. cattownoakland.org or email adopt@cattownoakland.org. articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont is pleased to host mediator, author, and peacemaker Larry Rosen for its holiday luncheon and talk on Friday, December 5, with the theme “The Enemies Project: Finding Connection in a Time of Division.” This fundraiser will be held at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue, at 11:30-1pm. The League invites guests to socialize with friends old and new, enjoy a catered holiday lunch, learn more about the League, and explore peace and understanding with the local speaker. Larry Rosen is a Piedmont High School father to Sadie (class of 2023) and Lila (currently a senior), and is founder of the mediation law practice Through Understanding, and the visionary behind his nonprofit, The Enemies Project. His wife Shelley Seto-Rosen is a PHS science teacher. Over his career, he has guided thousands toward lasting conflict resolution, and his widely-viewed TEDx talk, The Secret to Understanding Humans, has inspired audiences to reconsider how we relate to one another. Rosen will invite attendees to envision how individuals in community can serve as microcosms for what is possible on a broader scale, in our everyday interactions and in our willingLarry Rosen ness to engage across differences. Rosen’s talk promises to spark conversation, challenge assumptions, and inspire action around how ordinary people can become peacemakers. articles.text: At the November 3 meeting, the City Council voted to reinvest $2.6 million from Fiscal Year 2024-2025 into long-term capital and maintenance needs, augmenting dedicated funds that have been significantly drawn down over the past two years as the City undertakes an unprecedented number of concurrent facility, park, and infrastructure improvements. The action followed a review of FY2024-25 financial results by Finance Director Kiran Bawa. At year-end, City revenues were 2% above budget and expenditures 3% below budget, leaving a General Fund balance of $9.9 million. Consistent with City policy, $7.3 million will remain in reserve. The remaining $2.6 million will be transferred into special funds that support the City’s ongoing capital, facility, and infrastructure needs: • $1.5 million to the Facilities Capital Fund, which finances major building projects and renovations • $850,000 to the Equipment Replacement Fund for future vehicle and equipment purchases • $250,000 to the Facilities Maintenance Fund for preventative maintenance and facility preservation These transfers reflect the City’s ongoing commitments to creating healthy, vibrant pubStorm Drain Upgrades lic spaces and addressing aging infrastructure, while continuing to budget conservatively and maintain a healthy reserve. More capital projects are underway throughout Piedmont now than at any point in memory. articles.text: The People of Faith photo show and reception will be held at St. Paul’s Episcopal Church, 114 Montecito Avenue in Oakland, on Saturday, November 22, from 4:00-5:30 pm. The show is a project by award-winning photographers Nicolò Sertorio and J Michael Tucker. People of Faith is a collection of photographs of Oakland faith leaders and will be on view at St. Paul’s Episcopal Church from November 16 to January 18, 2026. The exhibit explores the stories, transformative potential, and roles in the community of Oakland faith leaders, who stand as both anchors and mirrors of their communities, reflecting the struggles, hopes, and transformations taking place around them. People of Faith is a photographic exploration of these individuals, capturing them in the spaces where they serve. The portraits invite viewers to consider the evolving nature of faith in an urban landscape marked by gentrification, inequality, and cultural flux. ‘People of Faith’ aims to question what it means to be a spiritual leader today. The ‘People of Faith’ exhibit will run simultaneously with ‘House of Worship’ at Oakland City Hall which explores visually the coalescence of faiths and cultures within the diverse landscape of Oakland. articles.text: When the school board voted to remove Health as a required class, the decision seemed straightforward on paper: give students more flexibility and open up space for electives and academic courses. Combined with new AP and honors options at Piedmont High School, students can now take advanced classes earlier than ever. But for many students and teachers, the change signals a shift in what our school values most. At PHS, Health Science fulfills California’s health education requirement through a one-semester course taken in sophomore year. The class goes beyond textbooks and tests, covering topics often overlooked in traditional academics: mental health, stress management, sexual education, healthy relationships, and substance abuse prevention. Health class is the only time in high school where students are explicitly taught how to care for themselves and make informed, real-world decisions. Some sophomores say the class has already had a lasting impact. “I’ve learned things that will carry on with me for a lifetime,” said Quinn Wagener. “The lessons on opioids and drug awareness were eye-opening. I don’t think I’d understand the full picture of drugs and alcohol if I hadn’t taken this class.” “There are so many risks that come with alcohol. At our age, it’s even more likely for someone to be taken advantage of in an intoxicated state,” said sophomore Noah Baldwin. For Health teacher Lael McAuliffe, who works closely with students when they are most vulnerable, removing the requirement is about far more than just scheduling. “This is a significant loss for our students,” she said. “Health education builds a foundation in mental wellness, relationships, and decision-making, skills that research links to better academic and life outcomes.” McAuliffe also warns of the social consequences. “In small Sophomores Andson Zhou, Olivia Bailey, and Diego Branneria present the effects of tobacco usage to the Health Class. Photos by Lael McAuliffe Sophomores George Saunders, Rafeal Rajan, Dahlia Sar-Garza, and Quinn Wagener work with mannequin models to learn about anatomy in Health Science. schools, this can divide students into tracks: those who take accelerated courses and those who don’t. When you take away Health, you take away shared experiences that build empathy and balance,” she said. According to McAuliffe, Health Science functioned as its own department, with a budget of zero dollars. All the models and supplies the students used were either donated by McAuliffe or borrowed from her nonprofit. Even after the class was moved under the Science Department, no funding was added. A small grant from Piedmont Makers covered dissection materials, but only after Health Science applied for it independently. Nonetheless, not all students see the change as a loss. “I would rather take an in-person class that really impacts my future and is something I enjoy,” said Zoya Schulze. “Although Health is important, an online class should suffice for learning the necessary topics.” Senior Mira Sachs chose to skip Health to take Journalism. “They were the same period, and I had no other option,” she said. Though she stands by her choice, Sachs admits missing out on some lessons. “I’m disappointed I didn’t get to take it, but it was the right decision for me at the time.” Flexibility matters, and students deserve choices, but there is a difference between choice and neglect. Every student should have not only the opportunity but the expectation to learn how to manage stress, make healthy decisions, and understand their well-being. Removing Health may open space for electives, but it also strips away structured time to learn how to live well. Even though Health remains technically available, few students are likely to take it once it becomes optional. Under pressure to build “impressive” schedules filled with AP and honors classes, many see Health as expendable. Students may think they’re gaining an academic edge by skipping it, but the cost is steep. Without structured health education, future students risk entering adulthood unprepared to manage stress, navigate relationships, or make informed decisions about their bodies and minds. In a world dominated by social media, misinformation spreads faster than guidance, and peer pressure can easily lead to risky behaviors. Many students also lack the home environment or parental support to fill these gaps, leaving them vulnerable to mistakes with lasting consequences. Neglecting to invest in students’ well-being creates a gap not only in practical knowledge but in confidence, resilience, and the ability to navigate adulthood: advantages no GPA can measure. class, the school board is failing students, prioritizing academics over essential life skills and leaving them unprepared for the realities of college and beyond. As senior Samantha Huynh said, “Some of the topics taught in Health, like Sex-Ed, might not be relevant to all of us right now, but these life skills will become crucial for every one of us in the future.”

articles.text: Piedmont High School’s Advanced Acting class will present four showings of the comedy Noises Off at the Alan Harvey Theatre this weekend. Four-time nominee of best play, Noises Off, written by Michael Frayn, is considered one of the best farces ever written. The shows are set for Thursday, November 13 through Sunday, November 16. Noises Off is a hilarious backstage comedy about a small theater company struggling to put on a play. The chaotic play-within-aplay gives the audience a glimpse of what putting on a show is like, from a shaky tech rehearsal to performances on a tour that completely fall apart. Forgotten lines, misplaced props, slamming doors and messy relationships ultimately lead to total chaos. Prior to leaving for college, recent PHS graduate Noah Bruggeman built the set with longtime construction coach and director, Bob Moorhead. The pair, along with PHS stagecraft students, spent hours crafting the elaborate two-story set for Noises Off, which features numerous stairways, doors and passageways that the cast runs, walks, and falls through during the show. The set is practically a character in the play, as it features seven doors, three staircases, and it turns 180 degrees to allow the audience to see the play onstage as well as backstage. Sparrow Lieu, who plays Poppy Norton-Taylor, the anxious assistant, says “Noises Off is ridiculously funny and complicated. The tangled relationships between characters combined with slapstick comedy shows the audience the true value of resilience.” Sacha Andrews, who plays Brooke Ashton, the ditzy and clueless cast member, says that everyone should come see the show. “It has super cool sets, costumes, and character choices. It’s a really fun show, especially for people who have any interest in theatre.” Noises Off contains humor about sexual innuendos, and is a slapstick comedy that is appropriate for ages 10 and up. For more information or questions. contact director Kimberly Taylor at ktaylor@piedmont.k12.ca.us. All shows are at the Alan Harvey Theatre at Piedmont High School, 800 Magnolia Avenue. Tickets are available at phsacting.ludus.com. Tickets are $10 for Students and $18 for General Admission online. “Sardines” Cast photo for the Thursday and Saturday nights of Noises Off this week. Back row: Mattias Seelenberger (left), Kirstin Fedor, Collin Cameron, Dinar Kidane, Trenton Downing, Ali Atanasio, and Theo Ferguson. “Doors” Cast for Friday at 7 p.m. and Sunday at 5:30 p.m. Front row: Declan Murphy (left), Ben Wakefield, Chaz Amit-Guite, and Lila Schwab. pages.text: Wednesday, November 12, 2025 9 By Theodore Cost One foggy weekend in September, Troop 1 Scouts enjoyed a multiday surfing trip to Santa Cruz, learning to surf, picking up surfing slang, and enjoying the famous Santa Cruz Boardwalk. They set out on Friday evening, to be able to get the ideal early morning surfing conditions the next day. The Scouts camped out for two nights at a local private home in Bonny Doon, near Santa Cruz, thanks to the generosity of one of the Scout’s relatives. Waking up early the next morning, the Scouts divided up into small groups for lessons with a surf instructor. The early Troop 1 Surfing Trip to Santa Cruz morning conditions were glassy (i.e., smooth clean water perfect for surfing), with a light wind and some good a-frames (perfect waves that break cleanly down the middle to catch.) The surf instructors were divided into groups and led the Scouts out into the surf, picking the ideal waves for them to catch and giving them feedback and laughing with the Scouts when their wave did not work out. The groms (i.e., young surfers) and adults alike were stoked, and enjoyed a solid few hours at the beach surfing and playing in the swells and waves. Despite some wipeouts, the groms had a good time and a few even caught some bombs (large Eleanor Hawthorne and her father pose for a photo before entering the water. After surfing, Scouts headed to the downtown Cowell beach where they enjoyed boogie boarding, playing volleyball and frisbee, and riding the rollercoasters at the famous Santa Cruz Boardwalk. articles.text: Everywhere I turn lately, I hear the same thing: “I just want to feel connected again.” It’s there in conversations with friends, at work, and even in the media. People miss being together. We miss laughing in the same room, sharing real moments, feeling part of something bigger than ourselves. But connection doesn’t just appear out of nowhere. Someone has to start it, and that takes courage. It takes courage to send the text. It takes courage to invite people over (even if you don’t have time to clean your house). It takes courage to be the one who says, “Hey, want to get together?” without knowing who will say yes. Sure, you could wait for someone else to make the first move, but connection only grows when someone chooses to go first. And that person might need to be you. So what does that look like in real life? Here are three simple ways to start: 1. Keep it simple. Connection doesn’t need a theme or a color palette. It just needs an opening. Invite a couple of friends for tea. Meet at the park. Send the message that says, “Want to catch up?” The less complicated it is, the more likely it will actually happen. Simplicity makes connection possible. 2. Don’t let setbacks stop you. Sometimes people won’t respond. Sometimes plans fall through. That’s okay. It’s not a reflection of your worth or your effort. Keep trying. Keep inviting. Keep showing up. Courage isn’t about never feeling awkward—it’s about choosing to keep reaching out even though you know it might feel awkward. 3. Look for novelty. New experiences spark connection. Invite someone to try a pottery class, take a spontaneous day trip somewhere new, or explore a new walking path. Novelty wakes up the brain and gives people something to share, laugh about, and remember. It doesn’t have to be big, just different enough to feel fresh. So if you’ve been waiting for a sign to reach out, this is it. Don’t wait for perfect—just start. That one small act of courage might be exactly what someone else has been waiting for, too. Nina Meehan is a coach, speaker and workshop facilitator with expertise in creativity, connection and communication. https://ninameehan.com/

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, free compostable bags are available at City Hall to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. Compostable bags are also available from Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) for a fee. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. articles.text: Piedmont High’s doubles team of Samantha Huynh and Emma Chan made school history at the Western Alameda County Conference on Friday and Saturday, November 7-8 at Chabot College in Hayward. The duo battled their way to win the Foothill Division’s doubles bracket, the first girls’ team in school history to win the doubles title since the league’s inception in 2012. Piedmont has reached the WACC doubles final four times – 2016 (Hannah Marcus/Sophia Landes), 2018 (Kiana Kasrovi/ Audrey Call), 2019 (Call/Marlowe McEffee), and in 2024 with Kate Jumper and Arianna Kortum – but never won it. That came to an end on Saturday. “I had no clue that we’re the first. It’s funny because I’m writing the five things I wanted to accomplish for our senior yearbook, and winning the WACC was at the top of my list. It’s just so meaningful for me as a senior to have this. I’m really proud of it,” Huynh said. “Going into the tournament, I didn’t really have any expectations. Going in unseeded, I didn’t want to get my hopes up for something that wasn’t guaranteed to happen. I tried to take things match by match,” Chan added. The pair defeated Alameda’s No. 2 seed Natalie Wong and Sophie Featherstone in the finals, 4-6, 6-3, 6-3. To get there, they defeated Naomi Lin and Caroline Sue of Alameda 6-4, 6-4 in the semifinals, won 7-6 (7-2), 6-3 over No. 4 seed Fiona Wood and Sloane Kau of Bishop O’Dowd in the quarterfinals, and opened the tournament with a heated 4-6, 6-2, 14-12 win over Berkeley’s Esra Abarbanel and Vera Ertel. Despite being Piedmont’s No. 1 doubles team throughout the season, Chan and Huynh entered the bracket as an unranked team. Perhaps the chemistry they established this year was a catalyst to their performance in the tournament, where doubles teams like Alameda’s are filled with the team’s best singles players. “It’s really special. In the finals, we played two singles players. It was obviously very challenging and it demonstrates how it’s a common strategy for the tournament. Sam and I were already in-synch this season, and this tournament showed how connected our play is. Sam knew when to switch sides every single time, I didn’t even have to say anything,” Chan said. “I knew it has been a while since an unseeded team has won. We were a little surprised we were unseeded. Once we beat the No. 4 seed, we really gained a lot of momentum,” Huynh added. The Highlanders received the No. 12 seed in the Division 1 North Coast Section Team Championship and hosted No. 5 Northgate on Tuesday, November 11. Tournament Results Freshman Ella Ruthven, who played No. 1 singles for Piedmont throughout the season. finished in fourth place in the playoffs. articles.text: Lagios, Henderson lead Highlanders in offensive outburst Staff Photos Jimmy Lagios completed 10 of 13 passes for 219 yards and four touchdowns against Newark Memorial. Piedmont’s football team ended its regular season on Friday, November 7 with a commanding 42-28 win over Newark Memorial at the Cougars’ home field. The Highlanders go into North Coast Section with a 6-4 overall record. Piedmont received a berth in the Division 7 NCS bracket as the No. 3 seed for the second straight season. They are set to visit No. 7 St. Patrick in Vallejo on Friday, November 14. The Bruins earned home field advantage after winning the Tri-County League title. Piedmont had a slow start against Newark and trailed 14-0 before coming to life. They scored 28 straight points before the Cougars’ next score. It was a big game for quarterback Jimmy Lagios and running back Xavier Henderson. Lagios had just three incomplete passes, recording 219 passing yards and four touchdowns, average 21.9 yards per completion. Henderson, meanwhile, was back in the lineup after missing the last game due to an injury. He recorded 142 yards and two touchdowns on 10 carries. Game Recap Newark Memorial struck first on its first drive of the game with a six-yard touchdown carry. After a turnover on downs at Piedmont’s own 30, the Cougars scored again in four plays to go up 14-0, but the comeback was on from there. PHS scored on a seven-play series, which started with a 45-yard run by Henderson to the Newark 25. Henderson capped off the drive with a one-yard dive after coming in motion to take the snap, making it a 14-7 deficit near the end of the first quarter. On the ensuing drive, Piedmont’s Henry Brennan forced a fumble that was recovered by Rehan Mumtaz at NMHS’ 44 early in the second. PHS scored on just three plays, where Lagios found Jack Meyjes on a 25-yard seam down the middle, making it 14-13 after a blocked extra point. Newark went three-and-out, leading to a 51-yard touchdown pass from Lagios to Cash Panico on their very first play to give Piedmont a 20-14 lead. On the play, Panico made an athletic catch to high-point the football, leading to a catch and run to the end zone. After trading possession to end the first half, PHS started the third quarter with a 55-yard, fourplay touchdown drive. Henderson scored on a 20-yard carry, breaking a tackle and dragging another defender into the end zone, while he converted a two-point run to make it 28-14. Newark got one back in the third quarter on a four-play, 68 yard drive to put itself behind one possession at 29-21. articles.text: Photos by Jenni Tsoi Best Piedmont’s girls’ team placed second at the WACC Championship. Pictured are Leighton Mand (left), Skylar Best, Amalia Gray, Kelsey Coleman, Cora Chun, Viviane Oesterer, and Cora Brozowski Schrader. Piedmont High’s cross-country team returned to Hayward High on Saturday, November 8, for the 2025 Western Alameda County Conference Championships. The girls’ team placed second among six schools, while the boys’ team placed fifth. The girls’ team trailed Berkeley High in scoring by five points. “Only Berkeley beat us, a school with over 3000 students. It showed the strength of the girls’ team, especially in the Division 4 category. I’ve got to say, even though many of the varsity girls did not run distance personal best times, they sure raced hard, especially in the latter part of the race,” coach Steve Zirkelbach said. Leighton Mand led Piedmont’s team, placing sixth among 41 runners with a time of 19:25.92 on the three-mile course. “In this race, I used a similar strategy of taking the first mile more conservatively, then trying to push the second. I really wanted to focus on positioning for the team and being among the top seven runners. I thought I raced well but will focus on keeping the pace during the third mile,” Mand said. Skylar Best finished ninth in 19:38.88, and Amalia Gray followed 20 seconds later, placing 14th in 19:58.07. “I had a race plan to stay conservative the first mile, which I stuck to pretty well. During the last mile, I was behind two Castro Valley girls and I knew I Leighton Mand led for Piedmont, finishing sixth of 41 runners. Aaron Bennett led Piedmont’s boys’ team, finishing eighth of 42. could catch them, so I sat on their shoulder until I felt good enough to pass them. I’m really proud of how the race went and I really pushed myself to execute the plan,” Best said. “I went out a bit more conservatively than in prior races, which I think helped me stay more even with my splits. I also tried to focus on staying with my teammates and tried to stay focused when things started to hurt,” Gray recalled. Viviane Oesterer placed 17th in 20:22.21, and Cora Chun finished 19th in 20:30.94 to round out Piedmont’s top five. Boys’ Varsity For the boys it was another strong race for sophomore Aaron Bennett, who led the team by finishing eighth of 42 athletes in 16:28.56. Bennett has been a standout runner for the team finishing as their top runner in his last four events. “I was nervous going into the race. What allowed me to succeed was my patience through the first half mile. I knew the first couple of runners were going to go out too fast to try to chase, so I made sure to stick with my plan. In the second mile, I started passing a lot of kids. I knew I had energy left going into the last mile, and I was able to push past a lot of people. My progression throughout the season is due to the help and guidance from my coaches,” Bennett said. Alex Schleuning was next in for the boys, placing 10th in 16:40.22. Dresden Schulte-Sasse followed in 19th with 17:03.22, while Devon Thai finished 26th in 17:14.09, and Dylan Wallway rounded out the scoring five in 30th, 17:24.79. Next up: Piedmont has a two-week break before the North Coast Section Championships at Hayward High on Saturday, November 22. The Division 4 boys’ race starts at 10:30 a.m., and the girls’ race starts at noon.

articles.text: Michael Aikawa, PHS Class of 2023, was recently named to the Pacific International League’s All-League team. RBIs, one triple, and four home Michael Aikawa, PHS Class of 2023, is currently a junior at Lewis & Clark College in Portland, Oregon, where he is the baseball team’s third baseman. Over the summer, Aikawa kept his skills sharp with the DubSea Fish Sticks of the Pacific International League, a premier summer collegiate baseball league in the Northwest. The Pacific International League recently named Aikawa to its All-League Team for his performance last summer. The Fish Sticks captured the PIL Championship on August 2 with a dominant 18–1 win over the Gumberoos; their first title since the team’s founding in 2015. The 33-year-old Pacific International League typically attracts college players from across the Pacific Northwest. It is a semi-professional league, with most participants unpaid to preserve NCAA eligibility. The league also offers a unique mix, with former Major League players competing alongside recent college graduates. As a sophomore at Lewis & Clark, Aikawa earned All-Northwest Conference honors last season. The Pioneers finished 20–19, with Aikawa leading the team in several categories. articles.text: Derin Sabuncuoglu (left), Nathan Bekele and Aidan Patty at their October 25th Equipment Drive at the Oakland Roots game at the Oakland Coliseum Piedmont High School students from Next Gen Soccer are extending their mission to make the game more accessible and sustainable for kids across the East Bay. After a successful drive collecting gear earlier this fall, the youth-led nonprofit set up a booth at the Oakland Roots Family Appreciation Night at the Oakland Coliseum on October 25, collecting more gently used soccer gear and spreading awareness about their cause. This season, Next Gen Soccer is expanding its efforts to include pinnies from recreation clubs throughout the East Bay that have only seen one or two seasons of use. Many clubs replace uniforms every two years, leaving plenty of good-quality gear ready for a second life. By recirculating these items, the group hopes to ease the financial burden on families and reduce textile waste, keeping still-useful gear in play rather than in storage or landfills. Families in Piedmont may schedule a free home pickup throughout November and December. Learn more by visiting www.thenextgensoccer.org or emailing info@thenextgensoccer.org. Accepted items include: • Cleats • Shin guards • Soccer balls • Gently used pinnies • Portable pop-up soccer goals • New pinnies and recreation team uniforms GIRLS & BOYS * K-8 * ALL SKILL LEVELS

articles.text: Vienna Boys Choir The world-renowned Vienna Boys Choir returns to UC Berkeley for a special performance celebrating the 200th birthday of composer Johann Strauss Jr. The concert, titled “Strauss For Ever,” takes place this Sunday, November 16 at 3 p.m. at Zellerbach Hall. Presented by Cal Performances as part of its “Vocal Celebration / Family” series, the event showcases Strauss Jr.’s timeless compositions through the pure, soaring voices of one of the world’s oldest and most prestigious boys’ choirs. The program includes familiar favorites such as The Blue Danube, Tales from the Vienna Woods, and a lively mix of polkas. Founded in 1498, the Vienna Boys Choir has performed across the globe, preserving Austria’s rich musical heritage. The group, made up of boys aged 9 to 14 from various countries, is known for its crystal-clear tone, precision, and spirited performances. The choir has been singing choral arrangements of Strauss’s music since the 1920s. “Strauss For Ever” offers audiences a unique opportunity to hear the signature waltz and polka sounds of Vienna reimagined through youthful voices, serving as an homage to a composer who helped define his city’s cultural identity. Tickets are available at calperformances.org, by phone at (510) 642-9988, or in person at the Ticket Office at Zellerbach Hall, Tuesday through Friday, 12 p.m. to 5:30 p.m. and Saturday through Sunday, 1 p.m. to 5 p.m.
articles.title: Vienna Boys Choir perform at Zellerback Hall this Sunday

articles.text: Oakland Zoo’s popular “Glowfari” festival is underway, featuring hundreds of life-sized glowing animal lanterns and all-new light fixtures this year. Running through January 25, 2026, the family-friendly lantern festival invites guests to stroll among larger-than-life illuminated animal sculptures during festival hours from 4:30 to 9 p.m. “Glowfari” joins dozens of holiday-themed light festivals across the Bay Area, but this long standing event, previously named “Zoolights,” focuses on wildlife, sustainability and animal conservation. The reinvented event features larger light displays, longer hours of admission, and more available dates and has been a wildly successful fundraiser for the Zoo since its inception. Each handcrafted lantern creates a colorful journey through Oakland Zoo’s themed zones, including the savanna, the ocean, and a whimsical bug tunnel. Seasonal treats will be available for purchase. While animal displays are closed for late night events, “Glowfari” ticketholders can still take a gondola ride to the California Trail for panoramic views of the illuminated exhibits spread across the zoo’s hillsides. Timed-entry tickets are required and often sell out early. Admission prices vary by date, and parking is included with each reservation. Children under two are free. Proceeds from Glowfari help support the Oakland Zoo’s wildlife conservation programs and animal care initiatives. More information is available at www.oaklandzoo.org. articles.text: Museo Italo Americano, the first museum in the United States devoted exclusively to Italian and Italian-American art and culture, is hosting a holiday artisan market at San Francisco’s historic Fort Mason Saturday, December 6 and Sunday, December 7. The Mercatino di Natale, or Italian Christmas Market, welcomes local vendors and artists selling Italian food, fashion, jewelry, art and one-of-a-kind crafts. Proceeds from the Mercatino benefit the Museo’s historical and cultural programs as well as participating Italian and Italian-American artists, and serves as a unique holiday shopping experience. The two-day event is held in the museum from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. on December 6, and 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. on December 7. Museo Italo Americano was founded in 1978 above a café in the city’s North Beach neighborhood, San Francisco’s Italian-American enclave. The museum’s mission is to research, collect and display works by Italian and Italian-American artists, and to promote language courses, lectures and educational programs. Through its permanent collection, historical archive and community programs like Mercatino, the museum aims to preserve and share the rich heritage of Italian-Americans for Bay Area residents. For more information, visit https://museoitaloamericano.org.
articles.title: Museo Italo Americano at Fort Mason hosts artisan market Dec. 6 & 7

articles.text: Saturdays/Sundays through Nov. 16 Michael Stehr art exhibit Piedmont native Michael Stehr has opened his annual exhibition of new work at PCA. This year’s exhibit is entitled Love at First Sight: Considering the Nature of Inspiration. The exhibition will include 40 new works framed in gilt moldings hand-crafted by the artist. When visiting, ask about his annual art history tours to Italy and France, along with mural and decorative arts work. Please visit the Fine Art section of his website at www.mstehr.com for an online preview of the exhibit, which will be open for viewing on Saturdays and Sundays November 8–16, 11 a.m.– 2 p.m. Saturday, November 15, 3:00 p.m. Friends of Ethnic Art Lecture San Francisco Friends of Ethnic Art present an illustrated talk on African Beads by Herbert M. (Skip) Cole, professor emeritus, UCSB. African beads are Sacred and Secular, Symbolic and Sexy: and are used as money, medicine, clothing and to show power. They are about Identity, Status, Health, and certainly Beauty. The illustrated talk will explore varied types of beads, their contexts, uses, meanings and aesthetic quality among many African people in different parts of the continent. S. Bach, W. A. Mozart, JJ Hollingsworth, Frédéric Chopin, George Gershwin, and a composition of his own based on three Hebrew songs. articles.text: The Young Peoples’ Symphony Orchestra is celebrating its 89th season. The programs are always well balanced and well played. Under maestro David Ramadanoff, the concert Saturday evening in the first Church of Berkeley scaled the heights. I always come away from their programs feeling delighted musically and educated. As always, the concert began with a few chosen words by management and conductor David Ramadanoff. The concert began with one of the greatest luminary composers in the history of music – Hector Berlioz, who did for orchestras what Niccolo Paganini did for the violin. Truthfully speaking, Berlioz did it all and brought a new dawn to music. Many of the miracles he created were on display in his Le Corsaire Overture. The music itself is brilliant, but it helped that the YPSO musicians played it so brilliantly. In many ways, the interpretation was a miracle. Our imagination was encouraged to take flight and it scaled the heights. Conductor Ramadanoff, despite his many years, was inspiring – as he always is. Another thing that is always a pleasure is speaking with the parents whose kids play in the Orchestra. They are supportive in all manner. As a result, the concerts are inspiring. The second piece on the program was Rhapsody Espanol by Maurice Ravel. He was another icon of musical inspiration and continued many of Berlioz’s innovations. But he did it in his own way. The colorful romanticism of Berlioz becomes the very Every concert by the young peoples’ Symphony Orchestra is delightful as well as educational. That was the case Saturday evening in first church of Berkeley. Conductor David Ramadanoff is the inspiration… season after season.

It was their style of playing as well as their tone quality. In my opinion, their conductor is responsible for this interpretation. Give credit where credit is due. In addition to being a pillar of central European musical romanticism, Dvorak must be considered a “creator” of American music. Thanks to him, American music developed. Dvořák’s melodies to flow like a river. He hardly had time to write them down. His music has drama, as well as memorable melodies and always a sweetness. That’s part of what makes Czech music unique: Dvorak’s melodies always keep us guessing. Where is he going? The concert ended on a high note and everyone had fun. articles.text: Kate Winslet and Idris Elba in The Mountain Between Us The Mountain Between Us is an apt title that neatly captures the film’s essence—from its opening setup to the final frame. It follows a familiar survival-and-romance template, but remains solidly entertaining thanks to two superb performances. Dr. Ben Bass (Idris Elba) and Alex Martin (Kate Winslet) meet by chance at the Boise, Idaho airport after their respective flights are canceled. Ben, a neurosurgeon, must reach Baltimore via Denver to perform a lifesaving operation, while Alex, a photojournalist, is trying to get to her own wedding. They decide to charter a private plane piloted by an old-timer (Beau Bridges) who brings along his golden Labrador. Everything goes according to plan—until it doesn’t. When their small aircraft crashes on a snow-covered mountain range in the dead of winter, survival becomes the only priority. The story unfolds on two levels. The first is a gripping tale of endurance reminiscent of The Revenant: the cold is punishing, the terrain treacherous, and their chances slim. With Alex’s leg badly injured, Ben must decide whether to stay with the wreckage and hope for rescue or attempt a desperate trek through the wilderness. The second thread, equally compelling, explores the growing bond between Alex and Ben. Amid exhaustion, injury and isolation, attraction simmers beneath their shared determination to survive. articles.text: The Disney animated feature James and the Giant Peach is based on Roald Dahl’s beloved 1961 children’s book. Like most well-crafted films made for young audiences, it casts a spell—even when it turns a bit scary. But then, kids like a touch of fright if it’s wrapped in fairy-tale fantasy. The story, both outlandish and humorous, centers on a British orphan, James (Paul Terry), who has lost his once-doting parents and now lives on a mountaintop with two sadistic aunts, Spiker and Sponge (Joanna Lumley and Miriam Margolyes). They’ve turned the boy into a chore servant, callously ignoring his grief and loneliness. One day, a strange old man (Pete Postlethwaite) gives James a bag of magical crocodile tongues, which he accidentally spills on the ground. The mixture fertilizes a barren peach tree, producing a single enormous fruit. Inside the giant peach, James finds sanctuary—and a family of human-sized insects, including a brash centipede, an aristocratic caterpillar, a sultry spider, a matronly ladybug, a wise green grasshopper, a glowworm, and an earthworm. When the aunts come looking for James, the centipede cuts the peach’s stem in panic, sending it rolling down the hill and into the ocean. There, the peach transforms into a floating airship, carrying James and his insect companions across the sea toward New York City. What follows is a classic children’s adventure filled with chases, escapes, a mechanical shark, ghostly pirates, and magical flights—all leading to a climactic arrival at the Empire State Building and a daring rescue by the fire department. As in any good fairy tale, the ending is sweetly satisfying. James, surrounded by his new family of friends, settles into a cozy cottage in Central Park— finally home. James and the Giant Peach. Directed by Henry Selick. Based on the book by Roald Dahl. Voices of Paul Terry, Miriam Margolyes, Joanna Lumley. Duration 1 hr., 20 min. Rated PG. Released 1996 / 2014.
