articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, free compostable bags are available at City Hall to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. Compostable bags are also available from Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) for a fee. articles.text: Piedmont High’s football team came away with a big 39-35 victory of Western Alameda County Conference foes Washington at Tak Fudenna Stadium in Fremont on Friday, October 24. It was a thrilling game with six total lead changes before the Highlanders scored the winning touchdown with 1:40 left in the game. Piedmont had to play the entire second half without star running back and linebacker Xavier Henderson who suffered an injury. It enabled backup running back Rehan Mumtaz to take control of the first-team offense, recording several big plays in the second half. “Six heart attacks for coach,” noted PHS coach Jordan Seiden. “We’ve been working on our tackling. It wasn’t great tonight but showed up when we needed it to. We were without several starting linebackers, but this is a proStaff Photos Rehan Mumtaz had a huge 162-yard performance in Piedmont’s 39-35 win over Washington. gram where kids step up. Rehan had a huge performance. He’s had his moments. He likes to use his speed and get outside, but we want him to stay inside” Xavier Henderson scored two touchdowns before leaving the game with an injury. Cash Panico scoring one of his two touchdown receptions against Washington. Mumtaz finished with two touchdowns, including an 18-yard carry in the third quarter and the game-winning score on a nineyard carry. During the final drive, he also broke open for a critical 35-yard gain. Capping off his big night, Mumtaz recorded an interception on Washington’s last-second Hail Mary pass. “I was scared coming up, but as soon as I got my first play, all the nerves washed away,” Mumtaz said. “Everything started coming together; I slowed down and watched the field. I had a good night blocking.” A sprinter on the track team he is learning how to use his speed in football. “Patience is really key. I noticed that every time I ran inside I would be more patient and wait for the defenders to move inside, then bounce around them. It was open every time,” Mumtaz said. Game Recap Piedmont scored on its opening drive of the game, where Henderson scored on a 40-yard run on 4th-and-1. A blocked extra point made it 6-0 with 8:51 left in the first quarter. Washington punted on its first series, leading to an eight-yard touchdown drive for PHS where Henderson took a 29-yard screen down to the three before scoring on a carry. A failed 2-point conversion made it 12-0 with 2:33 left. Washington scored to open the second quarter on a six-play drive, making it 12-7 eight seconds into the second. But Piedmont answered with a quick score a minute later, opening with a 57-yard carry by Mumtaz, which setup a 22-yard touchdown pass from Jimmy Lagios to Cash Panico bringing the score to 19-7. Both teams traded possession before Washington scored on a 10-play drive with 3:53 left, cutting Piedmont’s lead to 19-14 by halftime. But coming out of the break, the Huskies took its first lead on a kickoff return for a touchdown, putting them up 21-19. Piedmont scored on the ensuing drive, which started with a 37-yard completion to Panico. Five plays later, Mumtaz scored his 18-yard touchdown with 8:07 left in the third. articles.text: Staff Photos Samantha Huyhn (left) and Emma Chan clinched Piedmont’s 4-3 win over Alameda at No. 1 doubles. They were the last match of the day. Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis team captured the 2025 Western Alameda County Conference’s title in a dramatic way. Playing league rival Alameda on Wednesday, October 22 at home, they won 4-3 capped by a remarkable victory by the No. 1 doubles team of Samantha Huyhn and Emma Chan. In the last match of the day and the teams tied at 3-3, the PHS tandem lost the first set 6-2 and trailed 3-0 in the second set. Mounting a remarkable comeback, they won the second set in a 7-6 (7-2) tiebreak, then won the third set 10-5 for the team victory. They won 5-2 over Berkeley the next day, October 23, at the Berkeley Tennis Club and clinched the title by beating Bishop O’Dowd at home 5-2 on Tuesday, October 28. (Final scores were not reported by press time.)It marks the school’s first title banner since 2022. Against Alameda, it all came down to No. 1 doubles team Samantha Huyhn and Emma Chan with the match deadlocked at 3-3. After losing the first set 6-2 and trailing 3-0 in the second set, the duo mounted a huge comeback to win the second set in a 7-6 (7-2) tiebreak, then winning the third set 10-5 for the team victory. “We were down 3-0 and brought it up to 4-3, then 5-all and 6-all. In the tiebreaker, we just tried to keep consistent and be aggressive, especially at the net,” Huyhn said. “Coming back really motivated us. When we got to the tiebreaker, we just stepped it up a notch. We really pulled off our shots at the net,” Chan added. articles.text: Piedmont enters the WACC Tournament as the No. 2 seed. Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team closed its regular season by beating Bishop O’Dowd 18-13 on Tuesday, October 21. The result improves the Highlanders’ record to 13-7 overall and 6-1 against league competition. PHS enters the Western Alameda County Conference tournament as the No. 2 seed behind Alameda, which is currently undefeated at 24-0. The Highlanders played their first-round match on Tuesday, October 28, and will play in the semifinals on Thursday, October 30. The championship is set for Saturday, November 1. Against the Dragons, Piedmont responded to a 5-3 deficit at the end of the first quarter before taking a 9-8 lead before halftime. Rylan Patty and Elles Kreickhaus had big offensive performances, recording seven goals and six goals respectively. Patty had a pair of goals in both the second and fourth quarters, while scoring three goals in the third. Match Recap Piedmont trailed 5-3 in the first quarter and took a 9-8 lead going into halftime. They took control in the third quarter, scoring six while allowing just one to go up 15-9 to start the fourth. They added three more goals in the final going. In the first period, Kreickhaus scored the game’s first goal with 4:47 left, but O’Dowd answered on its next possession. The Dragons went ahead 3-1 before Kreickhaus netted another with 1:13 left. In a scoring flurry, BOD scored quickly after just 12 seconds, followed by Henry Stein after 14 seconds, while O’Dowd scored once more with 37 seconds left. BOD extended its lead to 6-3 at the 4:49 mark in the second. Kreickhaus scored after just 11 seconds, but the Dragons made it 7-4 a minute later, but the comeback was on. Zach Dupree scored with 3:14 left, Patty scored 25 seconds later and again with 2:16 left, while Stein gave PHS a 8-7 lead with 1:57 remaining. O’Dowd tied it up at 8-8 with 25 seconds left, but Kreickhaus made it 9-8 as time expired. In the third, Patty extended the lead to 10-8 a minute and 10 Staff Photos seconds in, while goals by Stein and Patty made it 12-8 before O’Dowd’s next goal. PHS went on a three-goal scoring run to end the quarter with goals by Kreickhaus, Ben Kappas and Patty. O’Dowd scored two straight to start the fourth, down 15-11 with 5:36 left. Patty and Kreickhaus netted two to put PHS up 17-11 with 4:30 remaining. Patty scored the Highlanders’ final goal with 2:08 left. Final stats: Patty had seven goals, Kreickhaus had six, Stein had three, while Dupree and Kappas had individual goals. The semis and finals are both hosted by Encinal in Alameda. Rylan Patty scored seven goals against Bishop O’Dowd, including three in the third quarter. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont’s girls’ volleyball team qualified for North Coast Section for the first time since 2018. Piedmont High’s girls’ volleyball team closed its regular season with a 3-0 loss to Castro Valley at Binks Rawlings Gym on Wednesday, October 22 and a 3-1 loss at Bishop O’Dowd on Friday, October 24. However, though finishing its season with a 9-11 overall record, the Highlanders qualified for the Division 4 North Coast Section for the first time since 2018. PHS enters the playoffs as the No. 8 seed and will play No. 9 Urban of San Francisco today, October 29. Piedmont beat the Blues 3-1 earlier this season on September 9. Wednesday’s postseason match marks the school’s first time hosting a playoff game since 2017 when the Highlanders were the No. 7 seed, but lost to No. 10 St. Patrick 3-2. If Piedmont beats Urban, it will mark the school’s first NCS win since 2015, when the school upset No. 8 St. Helena 3-0. “We qualified for NCS, it’s the first time in I don’t even know how long. We are getting good talent coming in. Volleyball is really becoming a staple kind of sport and everyone is interested in it,” coach Mariah Cardenas said. Although Piedmont’s losses brought their league record to 2-8, each set against Castro Valley was separated by fewer than seven points. “The underclassmen are ready for it. They just need another club season and they’ll be ready for next year. It’s been a long time. We knew we’d have rocky moments, but the program is building, we should be even better next year,” Cardenas said. Piedmont celebrated its two members from the Class of 2026 for Senior Night prior to the match, Stella Wilk and Mira Sachs. “I’ve been with Stella and Mira since they were freshmen,” Cardenas explained. I coached them on JV all the way through varsity. Stella has been a really good leader on and off the court. Mira has always been really, really kind. They both show their leadership in different ways, “ 3-0 to Castro Valley Piedmont lost by narrow scores of 25-23, 25-18, 25-19. In the first set, both teams traded the early points before Piedmont scored four straight to take an 8-7 lead. However, CV got back to the front at 9-8 and never relinquished. Piedmont tied the set at 14-14 after two straight kills by Maika Ting, while PHS trailed 22-21. CV closed the set with a winning kill. Castro Valley controlled the second set, opening with a 10-2 lead. Piedmont clawed back late, scoring seven of nine points to put them back 24-18, but a service error won it for the Trojans. It was similar in the third set with the Trojans going up 17-7 at one point. PHS fought to keep itself within distance at 23-18, but Stella Wilk goes up for a spike. Piedmont honored her on Senior Night before playing Castro Valley.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Thoughtsicle.com Tyson Lake is the only surface body of water in Piedmont. It is estimated to have 3 million gallons of water, and is the site of drowning victims in 1951 and 1952. Now that it’s Halloween week, what better time to awaken some spooky history of the city? Tyson Lake is a small reservoir located between private residences between La Salle and Sotelo Avenues, tucked quietly behind Hampton Field. The location is not public property, but is the only body of water in Piedmont. In the 1950s Tyson Lake was the sight of two separate drowning incidents which led to the site nearly being forgotten in history. On July 20, 1951, the Oakland Tribune published a story stating that the Alameda County coroner’s office recommended that Tyson Lake be either drained or properly fenced to prevent further accidents following the drowning of 17-year old James Richards. But nearly one year later to the day, a second victim drowned, 19-year old Donald Stracner, who Another clipping from 1952. A clipping of a 1952 Oakland Tribune article of Piedmont PD’s search for Donald Stracner. had been swimming with two other companions. World War 2 Navy diver John Haubner, who was a former Piedmont Police Officer, was called in to retrieve Stacner’s body. “As search for the body continued, Police Chief William Pflaum said he will “definitely recommend that some action be taken to alleviate this menace to life.” He said that in view of the fact there have been two drownings in the lake within a year, “something must be done.”,” wrote the Oakland Tribune. Later on August 8 of 1952, the City of Piedmont sought out to determine the owner of Tyson Lake following the drowning of Stracner. City Council urged the 20 home owners surrounding the lake to erect a fence Tyson Lake now sits quietly behind the well landscaped homes of Sotelo and La Salle. articles.text: Piedmont High’s cross country team competed in two different events over the past week. They recently ran at the Haystack Tune-Up Invitational at Hayward High on Saturday, October 25 and the Mid-Season Mania 3200 Invitational at Campolindo in Moraga three days earlier on Wednesday, October 22. At the event in Hayward, Piedmont’s girls’ team placed second of nine schools while the boys’ team was fifth of 14 teams. PHS brought eight athletes to the 3200 invitational at Campolindo. “The varsity girls’ team raced well on Saturday, besting every team except for College Preparatory, who scored just 56 points. Each of the girls ran a solid race. Again, the boys keep getting better and stronger with each passing week. While not everyone was at the top of their game on Saturday, they are still fit and strong and can race well, and we are getting them ready to compete at their best and be ready for the showdown at NCS on November 22,” coach Steve Zirkelbach said. Photos by Jenni Tsoi Best Leighton Mand placed eighth of 71 runners at the Haystack Tune-Up and 42nd at the MidSeason Mania. Piedmont’s boys’ cross-country team placed fifth out of 14 schools at the Haystack Tune-Up. Pictured are Devon Thai (left), Alex Schleuning, Noah Sohn, Dresden Schulte-Sasse, Ian Chung, Aaron Bennett, and Dylan Wallway. Leighton Mand led the girls’ team in Hayward, placing eighth of 71 runners in 19:06.87 on the three-mile course. She was also 42nd of 127 at the Mid-Season Mania. “I wanted to start the race not pushing the first mile, but keeping decent positioning, and focusing on what I can do throughout the entire race instead of just getting out hard. articles.text: The Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO), the oldest independent youth orchestra in California, opens its 89th season with a fall concert on Saturday, Nov. 8, at 7:30 p.m. at First Church Berkeley. The performance features a dynamic program that includes Hector Berlioz’s Le Corsaire Overture, Maurice Ravel’s Rapsodie Espagnole, and Antonín Dvořák’s Symphony No. 8. “This concert highlights the talents of our young musicians and introduces YPSO’s new season,” said Executive Director Nadia Liu. “As we look ahead to our international tour, we are excited to share these performances with our community.” The evening opens with Berlioz’s Le Corsaire, an energetic overture known for its dramatic flair and vivid orchestration. Ravel’s Rapsodie Espagnole follows, showcasing Spanish-inspired rhythms and textures. The concert concludes with Dvořák’s Symphony No. 8, celebrated for its pastoral warmth and expressive melodies. The orchestra, composed of musicians aged 12 to 22, continues its tradition of offering professional-level performance opportunities while fostering musical education and growth. YPSO enters the new season with a focus on musical excellence and community engagement. The 2025-26 season includes a celebration of the upcoming 250th anniversary of the United States and culminates in an international tour scheduled for June 2026. Music Director David Ramadanoff has led YPSO for over three decades. He studied at the Cleveland Institute of Music and The Juilliard School, before serving as Assistant Conductor of the San Francisco Symphony. Maestro Ramadanoff chooses programs that “highlight diverse eras and composers while fostering each student’s musical growth.” Tickets for the Nov. 8 concert are available through YPSO’s website and at the door. For more information, visit ypso.org. The Young People’s Symphony Orchestra is composed of talented musicians aged 12 to 22.
articles.title: YPSO opens season on Nov. 8 featuring Berlioz, Ravel and Dvořák

articles.text: San Francisco Opera will present the world premiere of The Monkey King, a new opera by composer Huang Ruo and librettist David Henry Hwang. Performances will be from November 14 to 30 at the War Memorial Opera House. The production is an adaptation of Journey to the West, the 16th-century Chinese novel attributed to Wu Cheng’en. The opera follows Sun Wukong, the mythical Monkey King, on his quest for immortality and enlightenment, blending elements of opera, dance and puppetry. The Monkey King is “Asia’s supreme superhero, loved and adored not only by Chinese people throughout the centuries but increasingly by people throughout the world,” Ruo said in a press release. “The Monkey King’s adventures awaken in him an understanding of true power which leads to his self-enlightenment,” he said. “In our new opera, which blends cultural traditions with a spectacular multidisciplinary production, I hope to bring this Eastern superhero to life and shine a positive light that will always appear in any turbulent time.” Conductor Carolyn Kuan, music director of the Hartford Symphony Orchestra, makes her San Francisco Opera debut leading the new work. The production is directed by Diane Paulus, artistic director of the American Repertory Theater, with puppetry by Basil Twist, choreography by Composer Huang Ruo Ann Yee, and designs by Anita Yavich, Ayumu “Poe” Saegusa, and Hana S. Kim. Australian-Chinese tenor Kang Wang debuts with the company as the titular Monkey King. The cast also includes soprano Mei Gui Zhang as Guanyin, tenor Konu Kim as the Jade Emperor, bass Peixin Chen as Supreme Sage Laojun, and baritone Joo Won Kang in dual roles as Dragon King Ao Guang and Lord Erlang. Opera General Director Matthew Shilvock said the production continues the company’s tradition of “building cultural bridges across the Pacific Ocean.” He called The Monkey King “a stunning and magical undertaking” and said the company hopes it will “become a beloved and lasting opera for the world.” The Monkey King will be performed in English and Mandarin with English and Chinese supertitles. Eight performances are scheduled between Nov. 14 and 30. Tickets and information are available at www.sfopera.com.
articles.title: San Francisco Opera premieres The Monkey King Nov. 14

articles.text: Tickets are on sale now for San Francisco Ballet’s holiday favorite Nutcracker. The production runs from December 5 to 28. This special production is set in San Francisco’s post-1906 earthquake era, with opening scenes featuring famous landmarks like the Painted Ladies by Alamo Square. Nutcracker is the longest-running production in the company’s history. San Francisco Ballet premieres the production every year and features “a kaleidoscope” of more than 150 dancers within the company to tell the story of the Sugarplum Fairy. The company’s former artistic director and principal choreographer Helgi Tomasson’s production is inspired by the city of San Francisco, accompanied by a live orchestra that performs Tchaikovsky’s familiar score. The San Francisco Chronicle named Nutcracker one of Tomasson’s “finest achievements.” A diverse array of instruments are played during performances, including the glockenspiel, triangle, suspended cymbal, crash cymbal, tambourine, snare drum, bass drum, castanets, tam tam, ratchet, and timpani – all played by only three musicians. Nutcracker is appropriate for children aged five and older, no children under the age of three will be permitted. Nutcracker runs two hours with one intermission. A sensory-friendly performance will be held on December 28. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfballet.org/productions/nutcracker/. Helgi Tomasson’s production of Nutcracker begins December 5. Photo by Erik Tomasson
articles.title: Tickets on sale now for SF Ballet’s Nutcracker

articles.text: Exhibition leaves Nov. 30 The Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) presents Routed West: Twentieth-Century African American Quilts in California, an exhibition of more than one hundred quilts by approximately eighty artists, on view now through November 30. African American Quilts is the most expansive presentation to date of a transformative bequest of African American quilts that BAMPFA received in 2019, and highlights the history of the Second Great Migration where African Americans emigrated from the south fleeing economic and racial oppression. Many families settled in California, bringing quiltmaking traditions from the communities they had left behind. Approximately one fourth of the quilts displayed were completed in the South prior to 1950, while others were created in California during the postwar era. Also featured in the exhibition are nearly a dozen recent artworks by Black quilt artists in the Bay Area, including members of the African American Quilt Guild of Oakland. Curator Elaine Yau, a distinguished folk art specialist who has overseen the collection since 2019, said the exhibition highlights BAMPFA’s multi-year initiative to research, catalog, and conserve the nearly three thousand African American quilts and several hundred unattributed quilts in its care. The exhibition is believed to comprise the largest collection of its kind, according to museum officials. “With Routed West, we’re activating the extraordinary collection of African American quilts at BAMPFA to honor the stories of the individuals and communities whose vibrant artistic traditions are indispensable to, but too often omitted from, the larger narrative of American art history, and of our own history here in California,” Yau said in a press release. “These magnificent quilts carry within them stories of resilience, creativity, self-determination, and ingenuity, [including] narratives that not only define a distinctive period of artistic production but also inform a deeper understanding of the intergenerational ties that continue to sustain Black life in the United States,” she added. The exhibition is on view through November 30, Wednesdays through Sundays, 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. For more information about this exhibition and BAMPFA’s summer season, visit bampfa.org.
articles.title: Last chance to see African American Quilts at BAMPFA

articles.text: Black Gold: Stories Untold leaves Fort Point National Historic Site in the Presidio this Sunday, November 2. The exhibition highlights the transformative impact of Black communities on California’s cultural, social, and political worlds, and features artwork by 17 conCheryl Derricotte is one of over a dozen artists featured. temporary artists and collectives who lived in California from the Gold Rush to the Reconstruction period following the Civil War. Black Gold includes never-before-seen commissions by Akea Brionne, Demetri Broxton, Adrian L. Burrell, Adam Davis, Cheryl Derricotte, Mildred Howard, Tiff Massey, Umar Rashid, Trina Michelle Robinson, Bryan Keith Thomas, and Cosmo Whyte. New commissions explore themes of African American resilience during a pivotal era in the American West, including the fight for legal rights within the “free” state of California, the successes of early Black entrepreneurs and the experiences of African American Army regiments known as the Buffalo Soldiers. The exhibition also features recent works by Carla Edwards, Isaac Julien, Alison Saar, and Hank Willis Thomas. The exhibition is presented by FOR-SITE, a nonprofit organization dedicated to the cultural arts, and curated by Cheryl Haines, the nonprofit’s founding executive director. “Black Gold is a collaborative effort that brings together the work of an array of artists, thinkers, and community leaders to reveal narratives that are historically significant and continue to resonate today,” Haines said in a press release. “I am thrilled to shed light on this important part of California’s story.” The exhibition remains on view through November 2. Admission is free. Fort Point National Historic Site is located 201 Marine Drive in San Francisco. For more information, visit www.for-site.org.
articles.title: Black Gold: Stories Untold exhibition leaves Fort Point this Sunday

articles.text: Oakland Zoo’s popular “Glowfari” festival returns on November 7, featuring hundreds of life-sized glowing animal lanterns and all-new light fixtures this year. Running through January 25, 2026, the family-friendly lantern festival invites guests to stroll among larger-than-life illuminated animal sculptures during festival hours from 4:30 to 9 p.m. “Glowfari” joins dozens of holiday-themed light festivals across the Bay Area, but this long standing event, previously named “Zoolights,” focuses on wildlife, sustainability and animal conservation. The reinvented event features larger light displays, longer hours of admission, and more available dates and has been a wildly successful fundraiser for the Zoo since its inception. Each handcrafted lantern creates a colorful journey through Oakland Zoo’s themed zones, including the savanna, the ocean, and a whimsical bug tunnel. Seasonal treats will be available for purchase. While animal displays are closed for late night events, “Glowfari” ticketholders can still take a gondola ride to the California Trail for panoramic views of the illuminated exhibits spread across the zoo’s hillsides. Timed-entry tickets are required and often sell out early. Admission prices vary by date, and parking is included with each reservation. Children under two are free. Proceeds from Glowfari help support the Oakland Zoo’s wildlife conservation programs and animal care initiatives. More information is available at www.oaklandzoo.org. “Glowfari” displays at Oakland Zoo.
articles.title: Glowfari returns to Oakland Zoo Nov. 7

articles.text: Conjure up visions of the comedy of Monty Python and the Holy Grail. Combine that with the high adventure of Indiana Jones in quest of the Holy Grail. Add the religious visions of the Good Friday spell with its magic, and the exquisite architecture of Santa Chappelle in Paris. All of these are present in Richard Wagner’s opera Parsifal. This all-encompassing opera was the feature of San Francisco Opera performance on Saturday The name Richard Wagner arouses a mass of contradictions. He was, himself a man of immense contradiction. So is his music. Both provoked fist fights and physical confrontations, controversy and genetic debate. His very ethnicity has been debated. All of these things are ongoing since his mysterious death in 1883. But the controversy of the subject of Parsifal began much In literature, it goes back to around 1180 with a romance written by Chretien de Troyes. In legend, it is a central part of King Arthur and his Knights of the round table. The quest for eternal life and effective healing powers have always been elusive. The Nazis thrust these principles to the very forefront of their regime. The story of Parsifal has many detours. Wagner’s operatic version of this story takes five hours and has more turns than the Prix de Monte Carlo. Each listener is welcomed to make a personal interpretation as wished. That’s how elusive the story is. The San Francisco Opera presentation was multifaceted. From the outset I thought that the performance was going to be a dreadful bore of five hours. Despite the strange configurations of the music, the prelude that opens the opera had no magic. The acting was as if in slow motion. I began to think: how is it possible to move so slowly? Things got much better in the second act. All of the singers were in good voice, and they had smooth, rich voices. As is the case these days, the diction was poor, but the spectacle began to unfold. pages.text: 18 18 Wednesday, October 29, 2025 The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet Wagner’s mass of contradictions By Joseph Gold Conjure up visions of the comedy of Monty Python and the Holy Grail. Combine that with the high adventure of Indiana Jones in quest of the Holy Grail. Add the religious visions of the Good Friday spell with its magic, and the exquisite architecture of Santa Chappelle in Paris. All of these are present in Richard Wagner’s opera Parsifal. This all-encompassing opera was the feature of San Francisco Opera performance on Saturday afternoon. The name Richard Wagner arouses a mass of contradictions. He was, himself a man of immense contradiction. So is his music. Both provoked fist fights and physical confrontations, controversy and genetic debate. His very ethnicity has been debated. All of these things are ongoing since his mysterious death in 1883. But the controversy of the subject of Parsifal began much earlier. In literature, it goes back to around 1180 with a romance written by Chretien de Troyes. In legend, it is a central part of King Arthur and his Knights of the round table. The quest for eternal life and effective healing powers have always been elusive. The Nazis thrust these principles to the very forefront of their regime. The story of Parsifal has many detours. Wagner’s operatic version of this story takes five hours and has more turns than the Prix de Monte Carlo. Each listener is welcomed to make a personal interpretation as wished. That’s how elusive the story is. The San Francisco Opera presentation was multifaceted. From the outset I thought that the performance was going to be a dreadful bore of five hours. Despite the strange configurations of the music, the prelude that opens the opera had no magic. The acting was as if in slow motion. I began to think: how is it possible to move so slowly? Things got much better in the second act. All of the singers were in good voice, and they had smooth, rich voices. As is the case these days, the diction was poor, but the spectacle began to unfold. The audience was encouraged to watch and to experience the events. Wagner’s music by itself is a thing of wonder. Oktoberfest in Piedmont Piedmont celebrated its popular Oktoberfest at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Friday. It was a splendid event. Dave Larson, owner of Piedmont Grocery, generously donated all the food for the German dinner served outside on the lawn. Inside the center were countless tables featuring locally produced beer. The revelers were encouraged to vote for their favorites. There were many varieties of beer and all were excellent. Throughout the entire event, a young jazz trio from Piedmont High School entertained with music that was inspired, energetic and tireless. Their Jazz Trio was composed of pianist Maximo Miller, guitarist Eric Venner, and drummer Deniz Radzik. I want to emphasize emphatically that they were absolutely outstanding in every way and I am not alone with this opinion. The nationally-known music critic Richard Ginell was equally enthusiastic about their music. When the trio took a very short break, Ginell sat down at the piano and began to perform. Drummer Deniz Rodzik joined in the music making, and then the pianist Maximo Miller joined Ginell and they played some fourhand jazz. What a delight it was. articles.text: Empire of the Sun, directed by Steven Spielberg, is extraordinary. It was faithfully adapted by screenwriter Tom Stoppard from the autobiographical novel by J.G. Ballard, and earned six Oscar nominations at the 60th Academy Awards ceremony. It is a mustsee classic that will appeal to a wide audience, from older kids to adults. Its moving score is by John Williams with a recurring thematic leitmotif solo by James Rainbird, backed by the Ambrosian Junior Choir. The story focuses on a young, privileged British boy, Jamie Graham (Christian Bale), who lives with his parents in a cloistered expat Shanghai community that is convinced it is immune from the gathering storm of WWII; until it isn’t. The Japanese invade Shanghai, and in a remarkable, panic-driven, surging scene Jamie is separated from his parents and suddenly finds himself surrounded by crowds of crowds of fleeing Chinese. The last words he hears his mother yell at him as she is swept away by a surge of humanity, are to go home and wait. Which he does. His parents never return, and Jamie soon runs out of food. Desperate, he decides to bicycle to the urban center of Shanghai. Through a series of circumstances, involving two American expats, Basie and Frank (John Malkovich and Joe Pantolino), the three are captured and sent to a British prisoner of war camp where they are interned by the Japanese for the duration. Jamie (called Jim by Basie) soon learns that if he is to survive the harsh conditions of the camp he must emulate Basie who has an array of side-hustles. He also learns that nothing in his previous affluent, sheltered life prepared him for what he is now confronting. His former insulated life has not prepared him for what he is about to endure. articles.text: Saturday, November 1, 4:00 – 6:00 p.m. Artist’s Opening Reception Piedmont native Michael Stehr opens his annual exhibition of new work at PCA with a curated wine and cheese reception. This year’s exhibit is entitled Love at First Sight: Considering the Nature of Inspiration. The exhibition includes 40 new works framed in gilt moldings made by the artist. Please visit the Fine Art section of his website at www.mstehr.com for an online preview of the exhibit, which will be open for viewing in person from 11 a.m.–2 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays November 2-16. E-mail Michael at mstehrart@gmail.com to RSVP for the reception Sunday, November 2, 4:00 p.m. Piedmont Chamber Orchestra Piedmont’s popular local chamber orchestra returns with an intriguing program of smaller works featuring soloists Kate Juliana, soprano, Susanne Rublein, flute, and pianist Hadley McCarroll, in popular works by W.A. Mozart. Conductors Martha Stoddard and Andrew O’Donnell will lead the orchestra in Bay Area Artists’ Showcase … Mostly Mozart, with selections from Don Giovanni, the Rondo from Piano Concerto No. 20 in D minor, and Andante for Flute in C Major. The program also includes movements from Mozart’s Symphony No. 39 and Joachim Raff’s Sinfonietta for winds and horns. Admission is free, but reservations are strongly recommended, at https:// www.eventbrite.com/e/1758819669979. Saturday, November 8, 3:00 p.m. Ravel’s Complete Solo Piano Works To celebrate the 150th birthday of French composer Maurice Ravel, renowned pianist Dr. Gwendolyn Mok has gathered a group of pianists to perform the complete repertoire of Ravel’s solo piano works at Piedmont Center for the Arts. The 13 pianists come mostly from the Bay Area, with guests from Toronto and Tokyo. They include Silicon Valley engineers, public relations professionals, lawyers, etc. Many have competed in prestigious international piano competitions for amateur pianists and are top prize winners. Note that the organizer will donate proceeds from the event to a major international charity. Get tickets at https://www.brownpapertickets.com/e/6716987. Saturday, November 15, 3:00 p.m. Friends of Ethnic Art Lecture San Francisco Friends of Ethnic Art present an illustrated talk on African Beads by Herbert M. (Skip) Cole, professor emeritus, UCSB. African beads are Sacred and Secular, Symbolic and Sexy: also used as money, medicine, clothing and to show power. Illustrated by slides of people and their beadwork, the talk will explore varied types of beads, their contexts, uses, meanings and aesthetic quality among many African people in different parts of the continent. Bead collectors are encouraged to bring examples to share/discuss. Admission is free and the talk will be followed by a brief wine and snacks reception. Sunday, November 16, 4:00 p.m. Rami Bar-Niv Piano-Solo Recital Internationally renowned Israeli concert pianist, Mr. BarNiv will offer a unique program entitled Rhapsody in Blue and White, to include works by J. S. Bach, W. A. Mozart, JJ Hollingsworth, Frédéric Chopin, George Gershwin, and one composition of his own, based on three Hebrew songs, which gives the solo concert its name. The concert will conclude with BarNiv’s arrangement of Gershwin’s Rhapsody in Blue, and light refreshments will be available. Advance tickets are at https:// ww.brownpapertickets.com/e/6725302. Thursday, November 20, 7:00 p.m. Miss Maybell & her Ragtime Romeos Get your vintage groove on for this light-hearted, entertaining evening of vintage Jazz, Blues, and Ragtime music. Miss Maybell and her husband Charlie Judkins give new life to songs created over 100 years ago and rescued from old 78 rpm records and antique sheet music. The concert will also feature Marty Eggers on bass and Don Neely, founder of SF’s Royal Society Jazz Orchestra, on clarinet & saxophone. Buy advance tickets at http://www.brownpapertickets.com/e/6728377 before the concert sells out.

articles.text: The group usually tours Mountain View Cemetery the week of Halloween, and this year’s cemetery walk was planned for October 29. But last Wednesday wasn’t too soon to get in the spirit. With so many “spooktacular” decorations around central Piedmont, the walkers decided to make this week’s route a Halloween house tour. Forty-six walkers, plus one loyal K-9 friend, gathered at the Exedra for the start. Before setting out, they heard a short history of Halloween. The holiday traces back more than 2,000 years to the Celtic festival of Samhain (pronounced sow-in), celebrated in what is now Ireland, the United Kingdom and northern France. The Celts marked Nov. 1 as the new year, the end of harvest, and the beginning of the dark winter season associated with death. They believed that on the night before, Oct. 31, the boundary between the living and the dead blurred and spirits could return to earth. To protect themselves, they lit bonfires and wore costumes made of animal heads and skins. When the Romans conquered Celtic lands, they blended their traditions with Samhain. By the eighth century, Pope Gregory III had declared Nov. 1 All Saints Day, and the evening before became All Hallows Eve—later Halloween. In America, the holiday grew after 19th-century Irish and Scottish immigration, evolving into trick-or-treating, carved pumpkins and costumes. At Highland and Sierra Avenue they spotted their first ghostly figure in a front yard. Down and back up Hazel Lane, a giant spider clung to a house, and on Requa Road they came to a Universal Studios-worthy scene filled with skeletons and lights. It was worthy of a group photo— and a few Halloween facts. Halloween is now the second-largest commercial holiday in the U.S., trailing only Christmas. Americans spent about $950 billion on Christmas in 2023, while 2025 Halloween spending is projected at $13.1 billion—$4.3 billion on costumes, $3.9 billion on candy, and $4.2 billion on decorations. pages.text: Wednesday, October 29, 2025 21 Features Walking on Wednesday Wed. Walkers have Halloween on their minds By Dick Carter The group usually tours Mountain View Cemetery the week of Halloween, and this year’s cemetery walk was planned for October 29. But last Wednesday wasn’t too soon to get in the spirit. With so many “spooktacular” decorations around central Piedmont, the walkers decided to make this week’s route a Halloween house tour. Forty-six walkers, plus one loyal K-9 friend, gathered at the Exedra for the start. Before setting out, they heard a short history of Halloween. The holiday traces back more than 2,000 years to the Celtic festival of Samhain (pronounced sow-in), celebrated in what is now Ireland, the United Kingdom and northern France. The Celts marked Nov. 1 as the new year, the end of harvest, and the beginning of the dark winter season associated with death. They believed that on the night before, Oct. 31, the boundary between the living and the dead blurred and spirits could return to earth. To protect themselves, they lit bonfires and wore costumes made of animal heads and skins. When the Romans conquered Celtic lands, they blended their traditions with Samhain. By the eighth century, Pope Gregory III had declared Nov. 1 All Saints Day, and the evening before became All Hallows Eve—later Halloween. In America, the holiday grew after 19th-century Irish and Scottish immigration, evolving into trick-or-treating, carved pumpkins and costumes. At Highland and Sierra Avenue they spotted their first ghostly figure in a front yard. Down and back up Hazel Lane, a giant spider clung to a house, and on Requa Road they came to a Universal Studios-worthy scene filled with skeletons and lights. It was worthy of a group photo— and a few Halloween facts. Halloween is now the second-largest commercial holiday in the U.S., trailing only Christmas. Americans spent about $950 billion on Christmas in 2023, while 2025 Halloween spending is projected at $13.1 billion—$4.3 billion on costumes, $3.9 billion on candy, and $4.2 billion on decorations. A good share of that seemed to be displayed right there on Requa. From Requa the group retraced its steps to Highland and continued to Wildwood Avenue. Burgundy leaves still clung to the maples lining the street, giving it a warm autumn glow. Ghosts hung from balconies, and a tower of skulls guarded one yard. Everyone was glad no small children were along for this stretch—all the walkers this week were comfortably over six. A real squirrel added comic relief, happily chewing a pile of miniature pumpkins. On Crocker Avenue, just before Lincoln, another highlight appeared: a human skeleton walking a skeleton dog. They continued down Lincoln, passing Piedmont Mayor Betsy Andersen’s festively decorated home. Marigolds in her yard prompted a note that these bright flowers are symbols of Día de Muertos—their color and scent said to guide spirits home. At Sheridan and Caperton Avenues, a lone skeleton rested peacefully against a tree. From there the group began its return to the city center. But at longtime walker June Yee’s suggestion, they detoured up Mountain and Craig Avenues to see one of the morning’s most creative displays: six small witches standing in a circle around a steaming cauldron. Water vapor rose in curls, evoking Auguste Rodin’s sculpture The Burghers of Calais. After that stop, the walkers returned down Highland and continued along Vista Avenue past City Hall and the Corey Reich Tennis Center to Hillside and Magnolia Avenues. Outside the Recreation Center they admired another towering skeleton and a front yard full of Halloween decorations. The Rec Department will host its “Trick or Tasty Treat” event there on Halloween. Before wrapping up, the group peeked at the nearly completed community pool—a final treat at the end of a walk that mixed local color, holiday lore and good company. Walking on Wednesdays meets each week at 10:30 a.m. at the Exedra, at Highland and Magnolia Avenues. All are welcome and there is no cost. New walkers and friendly dogs are encouraged. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. Among those participating in last week’s Wednesday Walk were Jim Kuo, Denny McGee, Karin Fetherston, Joyce Ahern, Jasmine Cai, Debbie Powell, Tom Lehrkind, Sanghi Wagner, June Yee, Priscilla Wanerus, Maricella Contreras, Mark Davis, Albert Chen, Alicia Rivera, Deborha Curtin, Gary Laymon, Cathy Laymon, Gloria DaSilva, Claudine Bach, Matt Gerhardt, Noemi Alvarado, Liz Dalyrmple, Brian Henderson, Caskey Weston, Judy Sokoloff, Mary Henderson, Phil Witte, Jack Fischrup with K-9 best friend Kojak, Tina Shum, Stella Houston, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Lori Austin, Irene Thompson, Peggy Shultz, Jim Kellogg, Chuck Oraftik, Bill Ahern, Kat Lang, Lisa Euphrat, Laura Dudell-Foley, Mary Carter, and Dick Carter. The walkers were pleased to have Ann Cheng and Scott Brumburgh in from Bend, Oregon visiting family. articles.text: Portugal, though small in size, is one of the world’s most diverse and distinctive wine-producing countries. With more than 250 indigenous grape varieties—many found nowhere else on earth—Portugal offers an extraordinary range of styles, from crisp, mineral-driven whites to rich, complex reds and world-famous fortified wines. Its winemaking tradition dates back over two millennia, shaped by Roman settlers, monastic orders, and generations of families who continue to craft wines deeply rooted in their regions. Portugal’s geography and climate create a natural tapestry for viticulture. The cool, green northwest is home to Vinho Verde, a refreshing, lightly effervescent white that captures the Atlantic’s maritime influence. Moving inland, the Douro Valley, one of the oldest demarcated wine regions in the world, produces powerful red table wines and the iconic Port—a fortified wine known for its depth, sweetness, and aging potential. To the south, the Alentejo region contrasts with rolling plains and hot, dry summers that yield bold, fruit-forward reds and smooth, approachable whites. Beyond these famous regions, Portugal’s charm lies in its variety. The Dão offers elegant, structured reds from the Touriga Nacional grape, while the Bairrada region is known for its robust wines made from the Baga variety. Even the volcanic Azores and Madeira islands contribute unique expressions—Madeira itself being another legendary fortified wine prized for its longevity and complexity. Modern Portuguese winemakers have skillfully blended innovation with respect for tradition. Today, Portugal stands at the intersection of authenticity and contemporary appeal, producing wines that combine old-world character with exceptional value. Whether enjoyed as an introduction to Europe’s lesser-known treasures or as a study in terroir and heritage, the wines of Portugal offer a captivating journey through history, landscape, and culture—one glass at a time. I recently had the opportunity to attend a master class and large general tasting of Portuguese wines and ports at the Port Wine Fest in San Francisco on Sept. 30. The range of excellent wines was impressive and I was astounded by the number of grape varieties I had never heard of. The world of Portuguese wine is largely unexplored by the American consumer. My colleagues and I made our way through the tasting searching for the hidden gems. The following wines were the most memorable and deserve the effort to search them out. They are the cream of the crop. The Port wine Fest in San Francisco

The Port wine Fest in San Francisco Table Wines Quinta da Gricha is from the Douro Valley • 2021 Quinta da Gricha $46 This dry red table wine from the Churchill group comes from the Douro Valley. it is dark, dense and perfumed without excess, not exuberant, with serious plum and cassis fruit and a little earth. The oak feels quite integrated, and it has abundant, slightly dusty tannins that would welcome food. Should last in the cellar for a decade or more. but will also last for 5 or 6 years in the cellar. • 2019 Duorum Field Blend $55 A product of the J. Portugal Ramos winery this interesting field blend from the Duoro Valley. this dark purple wine is explosive, exuberantly fruity with abundant berry fruit and a core of violets. It’s showy and a bit smoky with a juicy palate, balanced with good freshness and abundant smooth tannins and a long finish. This finely crafted wine is delicious now yet will certainly improve with time in the cellar. • 2023 Bathoreu Trincadeira $19 A wine from the little seen (in the US) Tejo region of Portugal from the obscure Trincadeira grape. It reveals a smoky rustic, earth and tar-scented nose, to go along with its saturated purple color. The wine reveals excellent extraction, a clean, rich style with good length and moderate tannins. This would be the perfect partner to grilled ribs or burgers. • 2020 Rapariga da Quinta Reserva $28 This wine contains a majority of Alicante Bouchet the star of the Alentejo with some Aragonez and Touriga Nacional. The wine is dark and opaque and feels young and lively. The palate is fresh seamless and still pretty underdeveloped. It’s a textbook, old style Alentejo red with notes of wild berries, herbs and spices and earthy and rustic touch and plenty of character. Built to last this wine will improve with time in the cellar. Lovely. Ports unheard of in America. They often serve it over ice as an aperitif. This smoothly textured wine is ripe, generous and rich. It has delicious honey and lemon flavors that are enhanced by the baked apple flavors. It would make the perfect aperitif. Montaria was the best value wine • 2020 Montaria $15 (Best Value) Hailing from one of my favorite regions in Portugal – the Alentejo this wine is crafted from Syrah, Trincadeira and Aragonez. It is sensually textured and shows exceptional mid-palate finesse, a dry and serious finish and ripe tannins. It is approachable now • 2009 Nierpoort Colheita 2009 Port $46 A Colheita port is a single-vintage Tawny Port, meaning that all the grapes come from one harvest year. It is aged in wooden casks for seven years. It is young and lively, keeping the red fruit character, some bittersweet notes, serious, balanced, juicy and tasty with a velvet texture. • Ramos Pinto Adriano White Port Reserva $24 One of the surprises when I visited Portugal was how much white port they drink. It is almost White port is delicious as an aperitif or on its own • 2005 Kopke White Colheita Port $66 This is a weightier and more complex white port that would be more suitable on its own rather than in a cocktail. This smooth ripe wine is poised between honey and bright acidity. It is complex and concentrated touched with spirit and gifted with an attractively rich aftertaste. • 2021 Boeira Late Bottled Vintage Port $45 This is a beautifully focused LBV with a real backbone, fine concentration and intense flavors on the finish. The texture is particularly seductive and velvety. Full-bodied and lingering on that finish, it should drink well for the next 15-20 years or so. • Pocas 20 Year Old Tawny Port $48 For a lot of folks a 20 Year is the sweet spot in the lineup for Tawnies. Its fresh, and reasonable complex, so its old enough to be serious; and most of all it is actually affordable compared to some of the really old ones. This is lovely showing a grace of caramel and darker chocolate flavors this is still dominated by freshness. articles.text: PART 1: MT. KILIMANJARO, October 2016 In honor of Piedmonter Bill Baringer climbing to the top of the highest mountain on each continent, the Post is re-running the articles about each of his climbs, originally published in 2020. The list of the top spots on each continent is called the Seven Summits, which Baringer completed on October 3, 2025 when he submitted Carstensz Pyramid Piedmont’s Bill Baringer, has quietly has climbed the highest mountain peak on each of the seven continents. In late 2016 he embarked on a three-year quest to reach the top of the highest mountain on each of the world’s seven continents before his 60th birthday. His quest clearly was not for the faint-hearted. First on his list of major peaks was Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania; at 19,340 feet, it is Africa’s Local Tanzanian law dictates the only way to summit Kilimanjaro is with a guided travel group. Known throughout the world, the majestic mountain is a popular destination for as many as 30,000 people in any given year. On his first climb, Baringer talked his wife, Cynthia, into joining him. And although it is an easier ascent than some of other major peaks, something can always go wrong. An experienced climber they met on the climb developed optic edema while at the summit, in which her optic nerve became swollen due to altitude pressure. She lost her sight for 24 hours until the swelling went down. The Baringers chose an eightday route from Lemosho, involving 43 miles of hiking and time to acclimatize on the climb. Kilimanjaro is the largest free-standing mountain in the world, making it visually dramatic by land and by air. The trip traverses through alpine desert, moorland, rainforest, lava fields and finally into arctic zones. The ascent of Kilimanjaro began at Lemosho Gate. In the photo Cynthia Baringer is shown surrounded by porters and guides. This mountain creates its own weather, and despite being just three degrees latitude south of the equator, has glaciers on the upper parts of the mountain. Baringer confirmed that due to global warming, the glaciers are melting rapidly, but are still there for the moment. Becoming acclimated to altitude is the main battle with climbing. Thus, hiking slowly to a new height is better than racing up and then resting. The guides constantly told the hikers to slow down, “polepole” (pronounced “POH-lay”), meaning “slowly” in Swahili. But their exhortations didn’t sit well with Baringer. “It is truly challenging for me to walk at what was likely 1 mph. So, I tried juggling rocks while walking, to keep myself entertained,” he said with a grin. The day of reaching the summit is usually the hardest climb, Cynthia and Bill Baringer, still in his hiking shorts, stop for a photo at a base camp at an elevation of 12,600 feet. Most of the trip is a gradual incline, but the trail does get steep at times. articles.text: With bags strapped onto the front and back of dual kayaks and food and tents piled into a small motorboat, they pushed off into the cold water for a long paddle. When they finally reached the campsite, they set up their tents and changed into their swimwear, spending the rest of the day together exploring the shore, building sand castles, wading in the water, and playing Uno. The Scouts waited for darkness to fall so that they could see the famed bioluminescence of Tomales Bay. The bioluminescence comes from single-celled organisms called dinoflagellates. This phenomenon occurs during the summer, becoming visible to the human eye when agitated in the dark of the night. At first it was difficult to see the bioluminescence, but sounds of excitement filled the air as the water around their paddles lit up with sparkles and swirls. articles.text: The Piedmont Seniors marked their 29th anniversary in lively style on Sept. 24, gathering more than 60 members and guests at the Piedmont Community Hall for a day filled with learning, laughter, and local connection. The celebration began with the group’s regular monthly business meeting, followed by a special presentation from Clars Auctions. Senior Vice President Deric Torres and Director of Marketing Talesa Eugenio shared insights into what makes items most valuable at auction. The talk turned into a local version of “Antiques Roadshow” as six members took the stage to showcase family treasures — from antique paintings and pottery to a pair of silver swords and even a photo of a stately grandfather clock. Lunches from Joaquin Deli in San Leandro added to the festivities, and attendees enjoyed a presentation on white-collar crime by FBI Agent Michael Rolden, introduced by Piedmont’s new Police Chief Frederick Shavies. Rolden offered practical advice for preventing fraud and encouraged residents to report online scams at www.ic3.gov. Chief Shavies also shared his own story and reasons for joining Featured at the Piedmont Seniors 29th Anniversary luncheon were: guest speaker FBI Agent Michael Rolden (left), Piedmont Police Chief Frederick Shavies, Police Captain Chris Monahan, and Police Officer Tyler Petit. the Piedmont Police Department in July. A veteran of law enforcement, he spoke warmly about the community spirit that drew him to the city. City staff joined in the celebration, including Recreation Director Chelle Putzer, Fire Chief Dave Brannigan, Mayor Betsy Anderson, Communications Director Echa Schneider, and Aquatics Director Paula Tipton. As the event wrapped up, the mood was joyful — a fitting tribute to nearly three decades of camaraderie and civic pride. The Piedmont Seniors meet monthly on Wednesdays from 10 a.m. to noon at the Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Ave., and enjoy monthly excursions throughout the Bay Area. For more information, contact coordinator Janet Epstein at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. Attending the Piedmont Seniors 29th Anniversary luncheon were: Elene Manolis (left), Beverly Becker, Barbara Friede, City of Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan, Aquatics Director Paula Tipton, and Madeleine Moore. Also attending the Piedmont Seniors luncheon were: Fred Pemberton (left), Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein, Jim Ayotte, Gloria Wilmer, Nancy Hinsch, and Carole Jones.

articles.text: You don’t have to wait until selling to make the most of your home. Your spare room is an opportunity to elevate your home’s function and appeal. With a little creativity—and a yearly declutter—it can shift from forgotten storage to a space that improve your space. While it is easy to let spare rooms become storage spaces, a yearly declutter can breathe new life into your home. Instead of filling unused rooms with forgotten belongings, clear the clutter and give the space a purpose. You can sell, consign, or donate items to make the process simpler. Once you’ve cleared out the excess, here are five creative ideas to inspire your transformation: 1. Build a Home Library For book lovers, nothing compares to having a dedicated reading retreat. Line the walls with shelves, add a cozy armchair or loveseat, and soften the atmosphere with warm lighting, pillows, and a throw blanket. This creates a quiet corner perfect for escaping into your favorite stories. 2. Create a Multi-Use Room If you can’t decide on one purpose, make the room adaptable. A Murphy bed, wall-mounted desk, or modular furniture can transform the space throughout the day—guest room by night, office by day, and even a small home gym when needed. Hidden storage and collapsible bins keep it tidy and functional. 3. Design a Music Lounge Turn your extra room into a sanctuary for sound. Add a quality speaker system or vintage record player, cozy seating, and personal touches like instruments, framed album covers, or posters. Whether you’re winding down with mellow tunes or enjoying a lively jam session, this room will radiate personality. 4. Arrange an Entertainment Space Make your spare room the ultimate hangout zone. A projector or large screen sets the stage for movie nights, while bean bags or a sectional keep things comfortable. Add shelving for games, a snack cart, or colorful lighting to create a fun, welcoming atmosphere for family and friends. 5. Create a Relaxation Escape Sometimes, the most valuable transformation is into a serene retreat. Keep the space clutter-free and soothing with simple décor, soft lighting, a diffuser, and comfortable seating. This can be your go-to spot for meditation, journaling, or simply recharging away from the bustle of everyday life. A few of the local resources to help you declutter: Consign: The Home Consignment Center, Danville — (925) 794-8229 Donate: Bambino Thrift Store, College Ave, Oakland — (510) 658-7473 Sell: Half Price Books, Shattuck Ave, Berkeley — (they buy books, music, collectibles, Legos, and more) Don’t hesitate to call upon us anytime for a referral to one of our trusted service providers aswell as for all other lifestyle needs you may have. Transform your spare room: from storage to stylish living You don’t have to wait until selling to make the most of your home. By Debbi DiMaggio Your spare room is an opportunity to elevate your home’s function and appeal. With a little creativity—and a yearly declutter—it can shift from forgotten storage to a space that improve your space. While it is easy to let spare rooms become storage spaces, a yearly declutter can breathe new life into your home. Instead of filling unused rooms with forgotten belongings, clear the clutter and give the space a purpose. You can sell, consign, or donate items to make the process simpler. Once you’ve cleared out the excess, here are five creative ideas to inspire your transformation: 1. Build a Home Library For book lovers, nothing compares to having a dedicated reading retreat. Line the walls with shelves, add a cozy armchair or loveseat, and soften the atmosphere with warm lighting, pillows, and a throw blanket. This creates a quiet corner perfect for escaping into your favorite stories. 2. Create a Multi-Use Room If you can’t decide on one purpose, make the room adaptable. A Murphy bed, wall-mounted desk, or modular furniture can transform the space throughout the day—guest room by night, office by day, and even a small home gym when needed. Hidden storage and collapsible bins keep it tidy and functional. 3. Design a Music Lounge Turn your extra room into a sanctuary for sound. Add a quality speaker system or vintage record player, cozy seating, and personal touches like instruments, framed album covers, or posters. Whether you’re winding down with mellow tunes or enjoying a lively jam session, this room will radiate personality. 4. Arrange an Entertainment Space Make your spare room the ultimate hangout zone. A projector or large screen sets the stage for movie nights, while bean bags or a sectional keep things comfortable. Add shelving for games, a snack cart, or colorful lighting to create a fun, welcoming atmosphere for family and friends. 5. Create a Relaxation Escape Sometimes, the most valuable transformation is into a serene retreat. Keep the space clutter-free and soothing with simple décor, soft lighting, a diffuser, and comfortable seating. This can be your go-to spot for meditation, journaling, or simply recharging away from the bustle of everyday life. A few of the local resources to help you declutter: Consign: The Home Consignment Center, Danville — (925) 794-8229 Donate: Bambino Thrift Store, College Ave, Oakland — (510) 658-7473 Sell: Half Price Books, Shattuck Ave, Berkeley — (they buy books, music, collectibles, Legos, and more) Don’t hesitate to call upon us anytime for a referral to one of our trusted service providers aswell as for all other lifestyle needs you may have. articles.text: Programs like Stagebridge show that education after midlife is less about achievement and more about staying connected, creative, and curious. In the Bay Area, education isn’t just for the young. More adults over 50 are joining creative learning communities to stay sharp, connected, and purposeful. Research shows that continued learning later in life boosts cognitive health, reduces isolation, and can even extend longevity. For many, though, the classroom now looks a bit different — filled not with textbooks and tests, but with laughter, storytelling, and the rhythm of tap shoes. At Oakland’s Stagebridge, one of the nation’s first performing arts programs for older adults, students meet weekly to study acting, music, and movement. The focus isn’t applause, but growth. “We learn lines, we forget them, we laugh, and we try again,” says one participant. “That’s life practice, not just acting practice.” Experts point to neuroplasticity, the brain’s ability to form new connections at any age, as the key to staying mentally agile and emotionally resilient. Creative learning also builds social bonds, offering a sense of belonging that can fade in later years. “Learning something new in the community keeps you both humble and hopeful,” says one Stagebridge instructor. “It reminds us that we’re still evolving.” Programs like Stagebridge reflect a growing regional trend as community colleges, arts collectives, and continuing-education centers welcome students well past retirement age. The motivation isn’t career advancement — it’s curiosity, connection, and joy. As winter approaches, many lifelong learners are already signing up for the next session. They’re not returning to school because they have to — but because they want to. Curiosity, after all, never retires. Stagebridge is America’s oldest performing arts nonprofit for older adults. articles.text: Former Piedmont resident Patty Brown passed away peacefully at home on September 13, 2025. Born Patricia DeWitt Brown on July 22, 1933 in Oakland, she was the daughter of Mae Louise Coolidge and James Quinne DeWitt Sr. Patty spent most of her life residing in the Bay Area and Piedmont except for the last 15 years when she moved to San Diego to be close to her daughters and their families. A beacon of kindness, she touched the lives of all who knew her. Patty spent several years in Hawaii where she learned to surf and discovered a lifelong passion for the islands. Her adventurous spirit led her to water-ski, snowski, and travel the world. Patty enjoyed an early career as a dental assistant before raising her family and eventually teaching Preschool. She was an enthusiastic reader, active member of her community, member of the Town & Gown Club of Berkeley, and a devoted family member and loyal friend. Patricia is survived by her daughters Victoria Moats (Thomas) and Elizabeth Brown (Samisoni) and five grandchildren, Jessica Moats, Ryan Moats, Kenny Moats, Noah Molimoli and Olivia Molimoli, who will forever carry her memory in their hearts. She will be deeply missed, but her legacy of love and kindness will continue to inspire and touch all who had the privilege of knowing her. In lieu of flowers, the family requests that donations be made to Alzheimer’s Association: https:// donorservices.alz.org/page/FUNZRKELQMQ?utm_source=- Patty Brown was a resident of Piedmont for many years. google&utm_medium=paidsearch&utm_campaign=giving_ google_SL&gad_source=1&gad_ campaignid=1707986387&gbraid= 0A A A A AD8n X1pxzvgSS9-u3U93kG52uh9Zd.

articles.text: Jim Smith, a longtime Piedmont resident, passed away peacefully in Oakland on September 19, 2025. He was 82. Jim was an accomplished businessman with unparalleled wit and a heart of gold. He was “the last of the lion kings,” as a dear friend reflected, “and a person who had an enormous impact on everyone with whom he came into contact, consistently adding humor and nuance to our lives.” He loved Henny Youngman, the British-born American comedian and musician famous for his mastery of the “one-liner” – and that was Jim! Born James Richard Smith in 1943 to Robert and Mildred Smith in Portland, Oregon, he grew up there with his sister Barbara. He did well academically and excelled at basketball from an early age. He was a star at Wilson High School where his team won the all-city and state championships. Jim’s basketball ability benefitted from his height of 6’8” and a rigorous practice schedule that grew into the steadfast and tenacious work ethic for which he was later known. Smith was the focal point of Southern Methodist University’s offense where he was a forward, becoming Co-Captain of the team in his third varsity season. With Smith in tow, the Mustangs captured the 1965 Southwest Conference Championship and reached the NCAA Tournament Sweet 16. Jim was inducted into the Portland Interscholastic League Hall of Fame in 2022. In 1960, he met his high school sweetheart, Sharon. Together, they went on to SMU where he had a full basketball scholarship and studied marketing and finance. Upon graduation from college, the two were married in Lake Oswego, Oregon. They then drove across the country in he was able to coach them in basketball and little league baseball. This enthusiasm found him spearheading the Piedmont Baseball and Softball Foundation. Jim was endlessly proud of the good men his sons have become and the wonderful families they have created. He loved being ‘Poppy’ to his grandchildren, never failing to let each one of them know how much they meant to him - in between ribbing them with a good joke, that ultimately served to shape their sensibilities in navigating life’s adventures. One of the great landscapes of Jim’s life was Claremont Country Club. He revered every aspect of the Club’s traditions, though it was the members and the staff that he treasured most. Jim was President during a critical period of historic preservation that helped to define the experience and beauty of the Club today. When not at the Club he enjoyed entertaining at their bungalow in St. Helena, CA. He had a full circle of friendships, keeping up with people from all over the world. This truly was his joy. His memory will live on in the hearts of all those who knew and loved him. Jim is survived by his wife of 60 years, Sharon Smith, children Jeff (AnnMarie) Smith, and Jamie (Melinda) Smith, and seven grandchildren: Carter, Brady, Alyssa, Andrew, Ashley, Charlie and Caroline. He also played an important role in many extended family member’s lives, including Brian and Noah Berry and all of his dear nieces and nephews, and great nieces and nephews. Friends and Family are invited to the Celebration of Life for Jim on November 2, 2025 at 2:00 pm. Donations to the Claremont Country Club Oak Tree Foundation, Dumbarton Oaks Park Conservancy, or a charity of your choice, are greatly appreciated. Longtime Piedmont resident Jim Smith passed away on September 19. He was 82. a VW “bug” to Pittsburgh where Jim began his steel career with Jones & Laughlin Steel Corporation. His career took them to many places including Baltimore, Greensboro, and St. Louis. When he left J&L in 1980, they moved to Piedmont, CA where Jim continued in the steel business with Davis Walker Corp as VP and later VP at Franco Steel. As the steel industry was winding down in the U.S. he shifted careers taking on BTS Group as president and co-owner. In 1998, while living in Lake Tahoe, Jim sold BTS and went on to purchase Custom Logo, a promotional products company, for one dollar. He built it from the ground up and took great pride in describing himself as a “golf ball salesman!” Throughout the years, he employed many young people who, to this day, cherish having worked under his mentorship. He was always interested in the energy and ideas of the younger generations. Jim and Sharon’s two sons, Jeff and Jamie, were their greatest life’s work. Jim especially enjoyed the boys’ youth when

He dreams of airplanes (the camp borders a Japanese airfield where he bonds with a Japanese boy about to become a Kamikaze pilot). There are more than a few compelling scenes where Jim views the Japanese Zero through romantic eyes and not as instruments of death and destruction. There is also an extraordinary scene when, with the war concluding, a squadron of American P-51s bomb and strafe the airfield, the attack watched by Jim from the rooftop of a crumbling building. It is a long, breathtaking moment asking a boy to comprehend the reality of war and inevitable destruction. Empire of the Sun is episodic with magical, wonderfully created moments that can border on the surreal. The conclusion is compelling beyond expectation. A work of art. Empire of the Sun. articles.text: find a place to hide. In the dark of night he finds his way back to Bird Street, and it is there, amid the wreckage of what was once an elegant threestory apartment building, Alex begins his struggle to prevail. As the days and weeks pass, he demonstrates an extraordinary ability to adapt to his isolation and potentially lethal circumstances. He searches the many damaged hallways and crumbling rooms and with found binoculars watches the street below for the soldiers who are relentlessly searching for those Jews who are still hidden in the devastation. The Island on Bird Street is compelling, with harrowing and breathtaking moments wherein Alex narrowly escapes being discovered. A suggestion: The story, despite the age of Alex, is suited for mature tweens/teens and certainly for adults. It’s a remarkable film with exceptional portrayals, most especially by Jordan Kiziuk as Alex. He carries the narrative with exceptional verisimilitude. The Island on Bird Street. Their group of hikers and guides began climbing at midnight. Climbing in the dark with headlamps, they passed other groups that had stopped due to the altitude. Bill bragged about his hiking mate. The long climb to the summit of Mt. Kilimanjaro includes large stretches of barren land. Bill and Cynthia Baringer celebrate reaching the summit of Mt. Kilimanjaro, at 19,341 feet, the highest point on the African continent. On the way to the summit, the Baringers were surprised to see a large succulent, nearly three feet in circumference. “Cynthia made it to the peak first and passed other groups that set out one or two hours earlier,” he said. The group setting of a hike tends to create lifelong friends with people from literally all over the world. Baringer made an impression on a fellow hiker from Denmark, Sofie Dyhr Meister, the mother of two boys, Marcus and Nicklas, all of whom made it to the summit. When he saw her two sons at the top, he said, “Wow, there are my two heroes.” “I was very proud that a stranger had taken notice of their accomplishment,” she recently told the Post. “I will never forget those kind words.” Baringer admitted that he has gotten hooked on what he describes as “Type 2 Fun,” a cycle of climbing. He describes it in chronological order. “First you show up to base camp, you survive miserable conditions, then you summit, and swear off climbing again. But then you recover, tell type-2 fun stories and plan your next trip, shop for gear and find yourself at base camp again,” he said. articles.text: Dear PUSD Families & Staff, [On] Wednesday, [October 8], at our Regular Board Meeting the School Board voted to approve five new courses. These courses were brought to us in response to one of the primary concerns the Board has heard from parents and students for years — that students have access to advanced STEM courses earlier in high school than they do to comparable humanities courses. This imbalance deprives students who are stronger in humanities of the same opportunities while pushing them into advanced or accelerated STEM courses they may not otherwise choose. Our objective in approving these advanced courses was to provide balanced course offerings. The administration researched comparable high schools and available AP courses to determine which ones may be most suitable for our students. PHS Principal Dr. Yoshihara sent around a survey to students asking which of the courses under consideration they would be most likely to take; he noted in his Friday newsletter to parents that this survey would be going out to ensure parents were engaged in the conversation. This survey data was important in our decision making process. DANTE JIMENEZ, 9th grade Piedmont Park, it’s a nice spot to sit in the shade on the benches while eating lunch. VALERIE LIU, Wildwood Avenue Beach Field is my favorite. We just had a 3rd birthday party there. The bulldozers tearing up the Tot Lot provided free entertainment for all the kids. LETTERS - MAIN City Council enters blind curve on Moraga Canyon housing Editor: Piedmont’s City Council has invited developers to choose either Blair Park or around Coaches Field as the location for 200 new homes. The Council justified this delegation of authority with the argument that the city’s constitutional obligation to protect the health and safety of residents would be equally discharged by housing families at either location. But the staff report that supposedly informed the Council’s decision acknowledged that a large section of Moraga Avenue, centered at the Red Rock intersection, does not meet Caltrans standards for safe stopping distances. This means that an estimated 2,500 drivers who daily travel the blind curves of Moraga Avenue at speeds exceeding 40 MPH will not see pedestrians crossing the roadway until it’s too late to stop safely. Recognizing this hazard, earlier Councils protected children walking to and from Coaches Field with a fence along the north side of the Moraga Avenue right of way. The fence keeps pedestrians from wandering onto the blind curve between Monte and Red Rock. Children living in Blair Park will have to cross the same blind curve to attend school or enjoy Coaches Field. The Council claimed it protected them by adding a signalized intersection at Red Rock. When reminded that drivers will not see this intersection in time to stop safely, the Council “fixed” the problem by requiring signs warning drivers of the blind curve. Research on such signs finds, however, that they reduce fatal accidents by only 10%. Piedmont’s Council therefore has created two classes of Piedmont children -- those precluded from crossing Moraga Avenue on a dangerous blind curve, and those required to cross Moraga Avenue on the same curve. The citizens committee appointed by Council to identify sites for new housing chose the area around Coaches Field as the best location in Moraga Canyon for housing families. The reason Council members gave for rejecting this recommendation was that developers could build more quickly and cheaply in Blair Park. I doubt Piedmonters endorse putting children at risk of injury just to lower costs for developers.
