articles.text: About 40 Piedmont residents and friends gathered at the Exedra on Oct. 18 to participate in the nationwide “No Kings” protest. The local gathering began when Piedmont resident Jane Cullinan posted on Nextdoor that she and her husband planned to be at the Exedra around 11:30 a.m. “because we’re ancient and can’t walk far enough to join one of the main protest marches,” she wrote in her post. Cullinan said she initially expected just three participants - herself, her husband, and friend Dr. Steve Sidney -when she made the post. However, it drew more than 300 likes and responses on Nextdoor, and about 40 people ultimately came out to stand along Highland Avenue holding signs and waving to passing cars. Some attendees told Cullinan they had seen her post, while others appeared to have organized independently. The group gathered for about an hour, drawing supportive honks from drivers and friendly conversation among neighbors. “Anyway, it was great to be there,” Cullinan said.
articles.title: Piedmonters Join “No Kings” Rally at the Exedra

articles.text: The City of Piedmont is inviting residents to share their views on upcoming updates to its “Reach Codes” — local energy-efficiency standards that go beyond California’s minimum building requirements. These codes, designed to reduce fossil fuel use by integrating energy-saving measures into home renovations, are reviewed every three years alongside statewide building code updates. So far, the city has received 14 responses to its community survey and hopes to hear from more residents before proposed updates go to the City Council later this year. The brief survey, available at piedmont.ca.gov/ReachCodeSurvey, takes less than five minutes to complete. “Piedmont was one of the first cities in California to pass energy efficiency reach codes for existing homes,” said Sustainability Program Manager Deniz Ergun. “Every three years, the statewide building code update provides an opportunity to check in with the community and look for ways to make them work better. We appreciate everyone who’s completed the survey already, and encourage all residents to do so in the coming days – it only takes a minute or two!” The survey asks residents whether they are aware of existing Reach Codes, what their experience has been with related projects, and how they would prioritize improvements from a menu of energy-efficiency options. Piedmont’s Reach Codes, first adopted in 2021, require features such as solar panels on new second stories or expanded roofs, EV-charging circuits in major garage remodels, and electrical panel upgrades that support future electrification. Staff are considering 2025 updates that would make the requirements easier to meet, including adjusting cost thresholds to reflect inflation, incentivizing higher-impact measures, and expanding the list of choices for homeowners. Proposed Reach Code updates are expected to come before the City Council later this year. articles.title: City Seeks Resident Input on Green Building Updates

The brief survey, available at piedmont.ca.gov/ReachCodeSurvey, takes less than five minutes to complete. “Piedmont was one of the first cities in California to pass energy efficiency reach codes for existing homes,” said Sustainability Program Manager Deniz Ergun. “Every three years, the statewide building code update provides an opportunity to check in with the community and look for ways to make them work better. We appreciate everyone who’s completed the survey already, and encourage all residents to do so in the coming days – it only takes a minute or two!” The survey asks residents whether they are aware of existing Reach Codes, what their experience has been with related projects, and how they would prioritize improvements from a menu of energy-efficiency options. Piedmont’s Reach Codes, first adopted in 2021, require features such as solar panels on new second stories or expanded roofs, EV-charging circuits in major garage remodels, and electrical panel upgrades that support future electrification. Staff are considering 2025 updates that would make the requirements easier to meet, including adjusting cost thresholds to reflect inflation, incentivizing higher-impact measures, and expanding the list of choices for homeowners. Proposed Reach Code updates are expected to come before the City Council later this year. articles.text: Frances is a gentle 14-yearold torbie who moves through the world with quiet dignity and endless charm. Her foster says, “She’s a whisper of grace in a noisy world,” and it’s easy to understand why. She spends her days napping peacefully, slowly stretching awake, and taking unhurried strolls around the room, her soft, steady steps radiating calm. Although she’s blind and hard of hearing, Frances explores confidently and loves the comforting presence of people nearby. When you pet her, she leans in with the sweetest meows and a soft, steady purr. Her foster adds, “There’s something incredibly endearing about her quiet presence; she doesn’t need to do much to steal your heart.” Frances has early-stage kidney disease and arthritis, both managed with a special diet and a monthly injection that helps her stay comfortable. Adopt Frances through Cat Town. She’s tolerant of gentle handling and deeply enjoys soft affection from those she trusts. She would do well in a calm, indoor-only home with a loving adopter who values the peace she brings—and she may be comfortable with another mellow cat or respectful teen. Frances is spayed, vaccinated, microchipped, and negative for FeLV and FIV. Learn more at www.cattownoakland.org or email adopt@ cattownoakland.org.

articles.text: Dear PUSD Families & Staff: It was great to see Matt and the Wildwood Dads’ Club at the Pumpkin Patch this weekend. There really are no better or fascinating pumpkins than at this pumpkin patch. Who knew there were so many strange and beautiful pumpkins, including the creamy giant behind me in the photo – and yes, it is real! The pumpkin patch is open through 10/30. Enjoy! In Partnership, Jennifer Hawn, Ed.D. Superintendent PUSD and College Admissions Today [Oct. 20] Since our last Board meeting, I have had the opportunity to explore recent research and guidance on college admissions—specifically, what makes students truly competitive in today’s landscape. Interviews with admissions leaders at several of the nation’s most selective universities, including Dartmouth, Brandeis, and Yale, offer valuable insight into what colleges are genuinely looking for in applicants. Across institutions, one message is clear: intentional choices, curiosity, and growth of character matter far more in telling a student’s story than overloaded schedules or endless lists of advanced courses. [Interviews from “Data Dive into the Transcript and Testing” episode of the “Admissions Beat” Podcast] Intentional Choices Over Overload “If you overload yourself, you risk losing the curiosity, balance, and humanity that make you stand out.” Admissions officers are encouraging students to find balance between healthy challenge and well-being. The goal is not to take every rigorous course available, but to choose those that align with a student’s authentic interests and intellectual curiosity. Depth Over Quantity “We’re not going to say, ‘Your high school had 28 AP classes— Jennifer Hawn picks out a pumpkin in front of Giant Jack at the Wildwood Dads Club Pumpkin Patch. you should have taken all 28.’ That’s bananas, and it would make you a not interesting person.” Admissions officers review each student’s transcript in context, considering what courses were available and how a student made thoughtful choices. Taking a smaller number of courses that inspire purpose and joy in an area of study is more impressive than an overloaded schedule without direction. Growth Over Perfection “We are not trying to admit masterpieces… We’re looking for growth.” Colleges and universities are not seeking students who appear “finished.” They are looking for learners who are still growing on their academic journey. Students who demonstrate curiosity, reflection, and adaptability to change stand out as those who are ready to thrive in college and beyond Next Steps: Community Education Last week, I also spoke with an admissions reader for Stanford University who echoed these same ideas. The notion that “if a course is offered, a student must take it” is false logic, and it can do a disservice to our students as they pursue both academic excellence and a personalized, meaningful college admissions experience. Our counselors already do tremendous work guiding students according to the key ideas above, and through the college admission process, overall. However, it’s clear that continued community education is essential. To this end, we are planning a series of parent workshops focused on the facts of college admissions and the importance of student well-being: • An Additional College Admissions Workshop: November 17, 6:00 p.m. at PHS (location TBD) • Mental Health and Student Stress Workshop: January 26, 6:00 p.m. Details to follow. We also invite you to read last week’s letter [see page 1] from the Board and Superintendent outlining next steps following the October 8th Board meeting.

As PEF celebrates its 50th anniversary, it’s time to take a look back at how it all began—when a group of parents and community members came together to help sustain and enrich Piedmont’s public schools. Over five decades, PEF has grown and evolved, but its mission has remained the same: to support excellence in education and strengthen the community for generations to come. In the 1960s, property taxes in California were distributed in proportion to local collections— affluent communities paid more and received more. Amid the uncertainty that followed, Piedmont residents moved to safeguard local schools. articles.text: The community is invited to the Consent Assembly Preview Night on Tuesday, October 28, at 7:00 p.m. in the Alan Harvey Theater at Piedmont High School. The Consent Assembly features dramatic presentations based on real accounts of sexual violence and consent shared by Bay Area high school students. The assembly is designed to foster empathy and critical thinking by presenting a variety of perspectives, including those of survivors, perpetrators, and bystanders. It promotes a culture of inclusion by exploring diverse relationships and inspiring students to embrace the values of affirmative consent, allyship, effective communication, and healthy relationships. Healthy communities and relationships depend on both belonging and consent, ensuring that each person’s boundaries are respected and everyone feels included. While the assembly is an important component of consent education, it is also potentially triggering for survivors of sexual harm. This event is a full, identical performance of the Consent Assembly that all freshmen and seniors at PHS and MHS will attend the next day. During Wednesday’s school-day Consent assembly, Wellness Center counselors will be available, and the library will be open as a safe space for students. The Consent Assembly has been an important part of education in the Piedmont community since 2007. During the past five years, the Consent Assembly has traveled to other schools, including Bishop O’Dowd, Menlo-Atherton, Head Royce, Lick Wilmerding, and El Cerrito High School, to supplement their consent education. Parents, students, and all interested community members are invited to the Preview Night on October 28, at 7:00 p.m. to encourage dialogue across families while fostering a supportive and safe community for everyone. Photo by Anna Gotto In 2022 Piedmont and Millennium High School students performed the Consent Assembly in San Francisco for Lick-Wilmerding High School students. Bruno Banuelos shares his experiences with the crowd.

articles.text: For high school seniors applying to the University of California (UC) system, writing strong responses to the Personal Insight Questions (PIQs) depends less on having perfect essays and more on communicating who they are. The PIQs offer applicants a chance to express their accomplishments, experiences, interests, and background. The UC application offers eight PIQs from which first‑year applicants respond to four. No question is inherently better than another in the eyes of admissions officers. By selecting prompts tied to their authentic experiences, students give themselves the best chance to write meaningful answers. The goal of the PIQs is to show admissions readers who you are. It is not advisable to write what you think they want to hear; instead, lean into what matters to you. Remember, these are “insight” questions, so capturing voice is critical. AI cannot capture a student’s insight or voice! Give yourself plenty of time to brainstorm, draft through multiple revisions, and polish each of the four responses. The UC Admissions website offers worksheets and writing tips to help students brainstorm and refine thorough responses. While each PIQ response is a maximum of 350 words, students should use concrete examples and brief stories to illustrate their qualities or growth, rather than just stating traits. That said, these are not narrative essays. Admissions officers instruct students to think of the PIQs as a formal written interview, emphasizing lessons learned and quantifying impact made. While the PIQs are not a writing test, typos, grammar mistakes, and careless writing can distract the reader and weaken the message. Consider having a trusted teacher, advisor, or peer review responses for clarity and consistency. Remember that no admission decision is based solely on the PIQ essays. So while they are important, they’re only one part of the 13-point holistic review process used by all UC campuses. fit life experiences, writing with authenticity, writing with enough time to revise, and focusing on precise, illustrative storytelling, students will be able to craft responses that meaningfully reflect who they are and what they offer the UC community. Karen Shopoff Rooff is Director of College Consulting at Study Smarter. Study Smarter has been providing individualized academic tutoring, test preparation, and college counseling to Piedmont families since 1997. Karen is a former college professor and an experienced coach. For more information please visit www.studysmarter. com, email info@studysmarter. com, or call (510) 350-8444. articles.text: Piedmont High School junior Brynne Jones recently completed the National Security Language Initiative for Youth (NSLI-Y), a seven-week immersive program funded by the U.S. State Department. The initiative places students in countries where the U.S. has limited diplomatic engagement and teaches critical languages for diplomacy. With a competitive 10–11% acceptance rate, a minimum GPA of 2.5, and required essays on intercultural communication, the program attracts motivated students ready for challenge. For Brynne, the program marked her first extended time away from home. “I’ve never been away from my parents for that long,” she said. She lived with a host family in Taipei, Taiwan, attended Tam Kang University, and navigated daily life independently, including commuting on the metro alone. The experience combined intensive language learning with cultural immersion. Brynne learned about the Taiwanese dialect and visited sites like Beitou, Zhongshan, and the National Art Museum. She attended puppet shows at the National Center for Traditional Arts in Yilan, explored a local onion farm, visited the Tea Museum, and toured the semiconductor museum. Adapting to her host family was initially challenging, but forming bonds with her house siblings and fellow program participants helped her adjust. Unlike some programs, NSLI-Y did not require a strict “language pledge,” which Brynne appreciated. “I’m really glad we didn’t have that, because I don’t think I could have made friends,” Brynne Jones with her host family brother (7), sister (8), grandma, mother, and father making scarecrows during the fall harvest festival in the New Taipei City rice paddy fields. she said. The program also offered opportunities to meet U.S. State Department representatives and international university students, expanding her perspective on global engagement. The experience influenced Brynne’s academic and career goals. Originally considering business, she is now interested in International Business or International Relations, and she is currently taking a course in the field. “Intercultural connection is definitely really important to me now,” she explained. “Language is important to ease conflict. Finding similarities between cultures helps in today’s global climate.” Her first impressions of Taipei highlighted its unique blend of modern and traditional elements. “Taipei is a mix of industrial and traditional architecture. Even compared to China, Taipei seemed more integrated. Everyone was super polite, and the public transportation system was really convenient. Being by the shore, I thought the integration of both industrial and natural beauty was amazing,” Brynne recalled. Despite homework and the demands of independence, Brynne found the program rewarding. With limits to her Mandarin skills, tools like Google Translate helped her communicate, while friendships with program peers and her host siblings provided support. Brynne’s NSLI-Y experience demonstrates how immersive language programs can foster cultural fluency, independence, and academic curiosity. For students interested in diplomacy, international relations, or global business, her journey shows the profound impact of combining language learning, cultural exploration, and personal growth. Evolette Mak is a senior at Piedmont High School and a writing intern with the Piedmont Post.
articles.title: Brynne Jones’ 7-week program in Taiwan

Brynne Jones’ 7-week program in Taiwan By Evolette Mak Piedmont High School junior Brynne Jones recently completed the National Security Language Initiative for Youth (NSLI-Y), a seven-week immersive program funded by the U.S. State Department. The initiative places students in countries where the U.S. has limited diplomatic engagement and teaches critical languages for diplomacy. With a competitive 10–11% acceptance rate, a minimum GPA of 2.5, and required essays on intercultural communication, the program attracts motivated students ready for challenge. For Brynne, the program marked her first extended time away from home. “I’ve never been away from my parents for that long,” she said. She lived with a host family in Taipei, Taiwan, attended Tam Kang University, and navigated daily life independently, including commuting on the metro alone. The experience combined intensive language learning with cultural immersion. Brynne learned about the Taiwanese dialect and visited sites like Beitou, Zhongshan, and the National Art Museum. She attended puppet shows at the National Center for Traditional Arts in Yilan, explored a local onion farm, visited the Tea Museum, and toured the semiconductor museum. Adapting to her host family was initially challenging, but forming bonds with her house siblings and fellow program participants helped her adjust. Unlike some programs, NSLI-Y did not require a strict “language pledge,” which Brynne appreciated. “I’m really glad we didn’t have that, because I don’t think I could have made friends,” Brynne Jones with her host family brother (7), sister (8), grandma, mother, and father making scarecrows during the fall harvest festival in the New Taipei City rice paddy fields. she said. The program also offered opportunities to meet U.S. State Department representatives and international university students, expanding her perspective on global engagement. The experience influenced Brynne’s academic and career goals. Originally considering business, she is now interested in International Business or International Relations, and she is currently taking a course in the field. “Intercultural connection is definitely really important to me now,” she explained. “Language is important to ease conflict. Finding similarities between cultures helps in today’s global climate.” Her first impressions of Taipei highlighted its unique blend of modern and traditional elements. “Taipei is a mix of industrial and traditional architecture. Even compared to China, Taipei seemed more integrated. Everyone was super polite, and the public transportation system was really convenient. Being by the shore, I thought the integration of both industrial and natural beauty was amazing,” Brynne recalled. Despite homework and the demands of independence, Brynne found the program rewarding. With limits to her Mandarin skills, tools like Google Translate helped her communicate, while friendships with program peers and her host siblings provided support. Brynne’s NSLI-Y experience demonstrates how immersive language programs can foster cultural fluency, independence, and academic curiosity. For students interested in diplomacy, international relations, or global business, her journey shows the profound impact of combining language learning, cultural exploration, and personal growth. Evolette Mak is a senior at Piedmont High School and a writing intern with the Piedmont Post. Thinking Outside the Classroom Tips for writing strong PIQs By Karen Shopoff Rooff For high school seniors applying to the University of California (UC) system, writing strong responses to the Personal Insight Questions (PIQs) depends less on having perfect essays and more on communicating who they are. The PIQs offer applicants a chance to express their accomplishments, experiences, interests, and background. The UC application offers eight PIQs from which first‑year applicants respond to four. No question is inherently better than another in the eyes of admissions officers. By selecting prompts tied to their authentic experiences, students give themselves the best chance to write meaningful answers. The goal of the PIQs is to show admissions readers who you are. It is not advisable to write what you think they want to hear; instead, lean into what matters to you. Remember, these are “insight” questions, so capturing voice is critical. AI cannot capture a student’s insight or voice! Give yourself plenty of time to brainstorm, draft through multiple revisions, and polish each of the four responses. The UC Admissions website offers worksheets and writing tips to help students brainstorm and refine thorough responses. While each PIQ response is a maximum of 350 words, students should use concrete examples and brief stories to illustrate their qualities or growth, rather than just stating traits. That said, these are not narrative essays. Admissions officers instruct students to think of the PIQs as a formal written interview, emphasizing lessons learned and quantifying impact made. While the PIQs are not a writing test, typos, grammar mistakes, and careless writing can distract the reader and weaken the message. Consider having a trusted teacher, advisor, or peer review responses for clarity and consistency. Remember that no admission decision is based solely on the PIQ essays. So while they are important, they’re only one part of the 13-point holistic review process used by all UC campuses. By choosing PIQ prompts that fit life experiences, writing with authenticity, writing with enough time to revise, and focusing on precise, illustrative storytelling, students will be able to craft responses that meaningfully reflect who they are and what they offer the UC community. articles.text: Piedmont Play School (PPS) is a play-based cooperative preschool that has been serving the community since 1948. At PPS, we believe children learn best through play, exploration, and joyful interaction with their environment. The program emphasizes social-emotional development, helping children understand and manage their emotions while building positive relationships with peers. The curriculum blends art, music, science, cooking, building, sensory exploration, pretend play, and outdoor adventures. Activities are open-ended and hands-on, encouraging curiosity, imagination, and confidence while supporting social and emotional growth. Above all, PPS values creativity as a process rather than a product—nurturing each child’s individuality and fostering a love of learning that lasts well beyond preschool. A typical day includes supervised free play, circle time with songs and stories, and plenty of outdoor exploration. Children might ride tricycles, dig in the sandbox, or investigate a science corner—all designed to spark discovery and connection. PPS welcomes children beginning at age two, with enrollment designed as a two-year experience that prepares them for Transitional Kindergarten or Kindergarten. The school year follows the Piedmont Unified School District calendar, running from mid-August through late May. Classes are held from 9:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m., with extended care options available. What sets PPS apart is its strong sense of community. As a cooperative school, parents take part in their child’s early learning journey through meaningful classroom shifts (about two hours per month) and by sharing their talents in school roles. Together, families build lasting friendships and a true sense of belonging, making PPS a vibrant and welcoming place for children to grow. articles.text: Beach 5th graders and their families embarked on another fun group camping trip over the weekend of October 18, this time to Samuel P. Taylor State Park. Organized by the 5th Grade special events coordinators, 18 families gathered at a beautiful, forested campground nestled beneath towering redwoods in Marin County to reconnect with nature en masse. With perfect fall weather setting the tone, the group spent the weekend hiking, playing, and enjoying the great outdoors. Kids roamed freely, exploring the trails, splashing in the creek, and climbing trees, while parents hung out and enjoyed the peaceful surroundings. Former Beach Padre Grande Peter Jaeschke led communal meals including quesadillas, barbeque chicken, vegan chili and pancakes using the Padre’s traditional pancake recipe. The evening capped with the classic camping tradition of roasting s’mores around the fire. The group camp site is super kid friendly and easy to get to, making participants eager to highly recommend Samuel P. Taylor campsites for all families. These outdoor adventures remain a cherished tradition for the Beach 5th grade class. Campers display fall festive and kitten camping plates. articles.text: On Sunday, October 26 (11am-2pm), families are invited to Rockridge for Trick-or-Treating at over 40 district businesses and to join in a host of activities and special offers to celebrate Halloween. The largest event of the year and an annual tradition, the Halloween Parade is fun and free for all ages. Local businesses are bringing the Halloween fun with a spooky haunted Rockridge Market Hall-oween, mini soda floats at Ben ‘N Nick’s, community ofrenda building at Xocolate & Confections, craft tables at multiple locations, along with a host of sales and promotions. That is in addition to the two fun hubs where kids can get crafty and musical. The Oakland Public Library - Rockridge Branch (5366 College Avenue) is the starting point for the day where kids can pick up a free, commemorative tote bag for trick-or-treating. While there, they can enjoy crafts hosted by MOCHA, music by Asheba, a puppet show by Ricky Roo & Friends, and slightly spooky story times by librarians. This area includes a pop up community picnic zone where attendees can order takeout from Rockridge restaurants and enjoy their meals together. Bike valet and stroller parking are also at this location. From 12p.m. - 2 p.m., the outdoor courtyard at College Avenue Presbyterian Church (5951 College Avenue) transforms into a Halloween party with DJ Danny Santos dropping beats, mini-pumpkin decorating, temporary tattoos, and more. For a full event schedule and details, visit www.RockridgeDistrict.com. The annual Halloween Parade is made possible by a collaboration between the Rockridge District Association, Rockridge Community Planning Council, Oakland Public Library, Friends of the Rockridge Library, and College Avenue Presbyterian Church. Sponsors include Kelly S Wright State Farm, Ben ‘N Nick’s, Body Fit Training, East Bay Book Sellers, Saffron Kitchen, JCC East Bay, Rockridge Market Hall, 1st United Credit Union, and Market. Families will enjoy the Halloween festivities in the Rockridge business district this year on October 26.

articles.text: Homegrown triathlon celebration for Oakland kids The Oakland Triathlon Club (OTC) will host its third annual Youth Splash and Dash on Sunday, October 26, at the Mills at Northeastern campus in Oakland. The event pairs a short pool swim with a campus run, giving children an upbeat introduction to multisport competition in a safe, supportive setting. The Splash and Dash is a celebration of Oakland’s youth and community spirit. Every participant receives an OTC swim cap, goodie bag, and USA Triathlon finisher medal. Volunteers from across the East Bay help create the fun, inclusive atmosphere that defines the event. Directed by longtime Oakland resident Betsy Block, the family-friendly race continues her effort to revive multisport events in the city, not just for kids, but eventually for adults as well. “This event is both low-key Kids 6-10 partake in a 100-yard swim and 11-15 go for 200 yards. and deeply joyful,” said Block. “It’s about Oakland kids discovering the fun of multisport without pressure, and it’s about building community. My dream is that this becomes the seed for bringing back a full-scale Oakland triathlon for adults, too.” Started as a grassroots effort to give Oakland youth an easy first step into triathlon, the Splash and Dash earned national attention last year when USA TriathYoung triathletes speedily change clothes between the splash and dash elements of the race.

Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. articles.text: Piedmont’s football team got back in the win column on Friday, October 17 under the lights of Witter Field, beating Western Alameda County Conference Mission Division foes Irvington in a one-sided 40-15 victory. The result improves Piedmont’s record to 3-4 overall and 1-1 against league competition. It was a big return to the starting lineup for running back and linebacker Xavier Henderson, who had 108 rushing yards and four touchdowns. It marked his second four-touchdown game of the season. Piedmont’s pass defense was key to the victory with interceptions by George Saunders and Cash Panico, and Saunders returning one for a 79-yard touchdown. Irvington opened the game with a 47-yard kickoff return of an onside kick for a touchdown, but the Highlanders ran off 26 unanswered points to take a 26-7 lead in the third quarter before the Vikings’ next score. PHS then finished the game with another 14 unanswered points. The Highlanders play at Washington in Fremont this Friday, October 24 for their third league match. Last year, Piedmont beat the Huskies 56-20, but this year’s Washington team is currently 4-2. They lost to Irvington 21-16 earlier this month. Game Recap To open the game, Irvington returned an onside kick 47 yards for a touchdown when their central blocker quickly jumped on a bouncing ball and ran past Piedmont’s coverage unit to take a quick 7-0 lead just seven seconds into the game. Irvington then intercepted a pass at their own 43, but committed a turnover on downs following sacks by Max Fujimoto and John Bunje. Piedmont got on the board with an eight-play drive, where Henderson patiently found a rushing lane to score on a 13-yard carry. Earlier in the drive, he had a 10-yard touchdown called off Staff Photos Xavier Henderson had 120 total yards and four rushing touchdowns against Irvington. Jack Meyjes had four receptions for 95 yards and a touchdown. due to a penalty. A missed extra point made it 7-6 Irvington with 1:35 left in the first quarter. After a couple trades of possession, Saunders nabbed an interception after an initial deflection by Mateo Long, sprinting down the sideline for a 79-yard return for a touchdown with 7:35 left in the second—bringing the score to 12-7 after a failed 2-point conversion. PHS had its next drive stall out at the Irvington 24. But on first down of the Vikings’ next series, Henderson came up with a strip and fumble recovery at the 31. The Highlanders then scored on four plays on 4th-and-6 at the 27, where Jimmy Lagios found Jack Meyjes, who made a great contested catch over his defender. The extra point by Matias Seelenberger made it 19-7 with 2:43 left in the half. In the third quarter, Rehan Mumtaz turned a reverse 54 yards to the Irvington two, which set up a 1-yard touchdown by Henderson with 11:09 left—now 26-7. Then, Irvington finally got back on the board with a threeplay series with 10:06 left, 26-15 after a two-point conversion. PHS punted on its next possession, which led to Panico jumping on a seam route by Irvington’s tight end, returning it 32 yards to the Vikings 37. That set up a seven-play touchdown series by the Highlanders, resulting in a five-yard Henderson touchdown—33-15 with 9:48 left in the fourth quarter. Piedmont scored its final touchdown with 4:22 left in the game, this time on a five-play series where Henderson broke a tackle on a 32-yard carry to the house. Final stats: Lagios completed 10 of 19 passes for 190 yards and a touchdown. Henderson had 120 total yards on 15 carries and two reception, four touchdowns, and a forced fumble and fumble recovery. Meyjes had four receptions for 95 yards and a touchdown. Panico and Saunders had interceptions, while Saunders scored a defensive touchdown. NEXT UP Piedmont (3-4 overall, 1-1 league) visits Washington in Fremont on Friday, October 24 at 7:00 p.m. Cash Panico had an interception in the third quarter.
articles.title: Highlanders back in win column; 40-15 over Irvington

articles.text: Piedmont High’s cross country team traveled to Quarry Lakes Regional Recreation Area in Fremont on Saturday, October 18 to compete in the 42nd annual P. Wilder Mariner Cross Country Invitational. The girls’ team came away with a ninth-place finish out of 15 schools, while the boys were 11th of 16. Piedmont had some illnesses, and top runners Leighton Mand, Amalia Gray, Cora Brozowski Schrader, Nikita Gorelik and Kelsey Coleman were not able to compete. The boys’ team was missing Alex Shleuning and Noah Sohn. “We brought a small contingent to the Wilder Invitational this year because we had several runners sick and unable to run,” coach Steve Zirkelbach said. Skylar Best led the way for the Highlanders’ girls’ team finishing 11th of 112 runners with a time of 20:18.7 on the 5,000-meter course. Next in for Piedmont was Cora Chun, placing 38th with a time of 21:54. Mara Kemp-Malone followed her in 45th in 22:10.8, while they were rounded out by Quincy Antaya and Gladwin Horseley in 83rd and 84th with respective times of 24:48 and 25:00.3. The boys’ team was led by Ian Chung who placed 31st of 112 runners with a time of 17:27. Freshman Dylan Wallway was next at 41st in 17:37.3. Sophomore Aaron Bennett Photos by Jenni Tsoi-Best Skylar Best led the way for Piedmont, placing 11th in a field of 112 runners. placed 46th with a time of 17:41.3, Devon Thai was 62nd in 18:02.8, while Dresden Schultte-Sasse rounded out the top five in 92nd, 19:48.3. Piedmont has three events left in its regular season before the Western Alameda County Conference Cross Country Championship on Saturday, November 8 at Hayward High. Ian Chung led Piedmont’s boys’ team in 31st of 112.

articles.text: Stella Wilk had nine kills in Piedmont’s win against Encinal. Lucia Dorsey had eight kills against the Jets. Vora to go up 23-18. Encinal chipped away to a 23-21 deficit, but Piedmont closed with a kill by Vora and an offensive error. Final stats: Wilk led with nine kills, two aces, and 12 digs. Ting had eight kills and three digs. Dorsey had eight kills, three blocks and four digs. Dando had eight kills. Sachs had seven kills, two blocks and one dig. Huynh had three kills, four aces, 16 digs and 20 assists. Fiona Olsen finished with one kill and one block. Vora had one kill, four aces, three digs and 14 assists. Skye Prata Baack recorded two aces and three digs. Panico had one ace and six digs. Olivia Stevens had 19 digs, one ace and six assists. NEXT UP Piedmont (9-9 overall, 2-6 league) hosts Castro Valley tonight, October 22, at 6:30 p.m. They also visit Bishop O’Dowd on Thursday, October 24 at the same time. Piedmont High’s girls’ volleyball team posted a satisfying 3-1 victory over Encinal on Thursday, October 16 at Binks Rawlings Gym, snapping a four-match losing streak. The win improves PHS’ record to 9-9 overall and 2-6 in the difficult Western Alameda County Conference’s Foothill Division. “All the teams are really hard and it challenges us to move around and make blocks. Encinal is a school most comparable to how we are; they are younger and trying to figure out their groove,” coach Mariah Cardenas said. The Highlanders have two matches left in their regular season, hosting Castro Valley on October 22 before visiting Bishop O’Dowd two days later. They must finish with a .500 winning percentage to automatically qualify for North Coast Section. Piedmont last faced CV on October 2, and although they lost 3-0, each set was separated by less than five points at 25-20, 25-22, 25-22. Against Encinal, Piedmont split the first two sets until winning the final two by 25-21 scores. PHS attackers started landing their shots, including nine kills by Stella Wilk, and eight kills for three different players: Maika Ting, Lucia Dorsey, and Izara Dando. “It’s definitely been good to get out of that funk. If we bring this energy into the next two games, we have a huge chance at winning,” Wilk mentioned. It was a strong end to the match for recent freshman call-up Carina Vora, who had three straight aces and a kill to win the final set as a setter. “Carina is a freshman and I moved her up from JV. I tell our setters that they need to be aggressive, and setter-dumping every eight to 10 sets to keep the other team humble,” Cardenas said. Match Recap Piedmont won 3-1 by scores of 25-18, 18-25, 25-21, 25-21. In Piedmont’s first-set win, Maika Ting led the charge with four kills while Lucia Dorsey added three. As for the second-set loss, Piedmont fell behind in the middle stages before the Jets closed the set by gaining points by way of two offensive errors before landing a winning kill. Piedmont opened the third set with a 5-2 lead thanks to two kills by Mira Sachs and one by Wilk. Encinal battled back to tie 8-8 and eventually took a 12-11 lead. But the Jets’ lead was shortlived, taking the next three points to lead 13-11 by way of a kill by Wilk, and offensive error, and a block by Sachs. Encinal tied 15-15, but PHS scored five of the next seven points with two kills by Izara Dando, one by Ting, and one by Allyson Huynh. Holding a 22-21 lead, Piedmont got the final three points of the set with a kill by Sachs and two Jets’ errors. In the final set, Piedmont trailed 5-3, but went on a seven-point scoring run to take an 11-5 lead, including two kills by Wilk and Lucia Dorsey, one kill by Huynh, and an ace by Charli Panico. However, the Jets powered their way back to the front at 18-17. After that, PHS scored six straight, including three consecutive aces by freshman Carina Staff Photos Freshman Carina Vora helped win the final set with three straight aces and a kill.
articles.title: Piedmont volleyball team beats Encinal 3-1

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team dominated in its final Western Alameda County Conference match, beating Castro Valley 6-1 at the Trojans’ home courts on Thursday, October 16. It marked the second time Piedmont beat CV by a 6-1 score this season. “Our depth was on full display: despite missing two doubles players we won the match 6-1, the same score as the first time we played,” said assistant coach Corey Reich. The wins improves Piedmont’s record to 10-8 overall and 4-1 against league opponents. They have just three matches left in their regular season before the start of the league’s individual tournament at Chabot College on November 7-8. Piedmont hosts Alameda today, October 22, visits Berkeley the following day, and closes the season hosting Bishop O’Dowd on October 28. “We have a massive week ahead. I know ecologically, that pollinators are extremely important, but I hope to squash the Hornets and Yellow Jackets on Wednesday and Thursday,” Reich said. Match Recap Piedmont won three of four matches at singles and all three doubles matches, with each set finishing in straight sets. At singles, Kate Jumper won 6-4, 6-2 at the No. 2 spot. Faith Chin won 6-1, 6-3 at No. 3, while Arianna Kortum won cleanly 6-1, 6-1 at No. 4. Ella Ruthven lost 6-1, 6-0 against Castro Valley’s top starter at No. 1. “Kate got off to a slow start losing the first three games but quickly settled in, winning 12 of the next 15 games. Faith and Arianna were both a level above their opponents and won convincingly. Ella R. played Isabella Huskik, a highly ranked tournament player,” Reich said. At doubles, Emma Chan and Samantha Huyhn won 6-2, 6-2 at the No. 1 spot. Inara Mehta and Chiara Silvo won 6-2, 6-4 at No. 2, while Ella Thomasson and Lila Rosen won 7-5, 7-5 at No. 3. “Sam and Emma are really hitting their stride and dominated a good doubles team from Castro Valley. Inara and Chiara played well, both hitting beautiful groundstrokes with Inara being a menace at net. The roller coaster match of the day came at three doubles with Lila and Ella T prevailing 7-5, 7-5. They went up, they went down, they saved a set point, and won a dramatic 6-5 deuce point to win the first set,” Reich said. NEXT UP Piedmont (10-8 overall, 4-1 league) hosts Alameda today, October 22, at 3:30 p.m. They visit Berkeley at the Berkeley Tennis Club the next day, October 23, at the same time. pages.text: Wednesday, October 22, 2025 13 Tennis team dominates Castro Valley 6-1 By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team dominated in its final Western Alameda County Conference match, beating Castro Valley 6-1 at the Trojans’ home courts on Thursday, October 16. It marked the second time Piedmont beat CV by a 6-1 score this season. “Our depth was on full display: despite missing two doubles players we won the match 6-1, the same score as the first time we played,” said assistant coach Corey Reich. The wins improves Piedmont’s record to 10-8 overall and 4-1 against league opponents. They have just three matches left in their regular season before the start of the league’s individual tournament at Chabot College on November 7-8. Piedmont hosts Alameda today, October 22, visits Berkeley the following day, and closes the season hosting Bishop O’Dowd on October 28. “We have a massive week ahead. I know ecologically, that pollinators are extremely important, but I hope to squash the Hornets and Yellow Jackets on Wednesday and Thursday,” Reich said. Match Recap Piedmont won three of four matches at singles and all three doubles matches, with each set finishing in straight sets. At singles, Kate Jumper won 6-4, 6-2 at the No. 2 spot. Faith Chin won 6-1, 6-3 at No. 3, while Arianna Kortum won cleanly 6-1, 6-1 at No. 4. Ella Ruthven lost 6-1, 6-0 against Castro Valley’s top starter at No. 1. “Kate got off to a slow start losing the first three games but quickly settled in, winning 12 of the next 15 games. Faith and Arianna were both a level above their opponents and won convincingly. Ella R. played Isabella Huskik, a highly ranked tournament player,” Reich said. At doubles, Emma Chan and Samantha Huyhn won 6-2, 6-2 at the No. 1 spot. Inara Mehta and Chiara Silvo won 6-2, 6-4 at No. 2, while Ella Thomasson and Lila Rosen won 7-5, 7-5 at No. 3. “Sam and Emma are really hitting their stride and dominated a good doubles team from Castro Valley. Inara and Chiara played well, both hitting beautiful groundstrokes with Inara being a menace at net. The roller coaster match of the day came at three doubles with Lila and Ella T prevailing 7-5, 7-5. They went up, they went down, they saved a set point, and won a dramatic 6-5 deuce point to win the first set,” Reich said. Piedmont volleyball team beats Encinal 3-1 By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s girls’ volleyball team posted a satisfying 3-1 victory over Encinal on Thursday, October 16 at Binks Rawlings Gym, snapping a four-match losing streak. The win improves PHS’ record to 9-9 overall and 2-6 in the difficult Western Alameda County Conference’s Foothill Division. “All the teams are really hard and it challenges us to move around and make blocks. Encinal is a school most comparable to how we are; they are younger and trying to figure out their groove,” coach Mariah Cardenas said. The Highlanders have two matches left in their regular season, hosting Castro Valley on October 22 before visiting Bishop O’Dowd two days later. They must finish with a .500 winning percentage to automatically qualify for North Coast Section. Piedmont last faced CV on October 2, and although they lost 3-0, each set was separated by less than five points at 25-20, 25-22, 25-22. Against Encinal, Piedmont split the first two sets until winning the final two by 25-21 scores. PHS attackers started landing their shots, including nine kills by Stella Wilk, and eight kills for three different players: Maika Ting, Lucia Dorsey, and Izara Dando. “It’s definitely been good to get out of that funk. If we bring this energy into the next two games, we have a huge chance at winning,” Wilk mentioned. It was a strong end to the match for recent freshman call-up Carina Vora, who had three straight aces and a kill to win the final set as a setter. “Carina is a freshman and I moved her up from JV. I tell our setters that they need to be aggressive, and setter-dumping every eight to 10 sets to keep the other team humble,” Cardenas said. Match Recap Piedmont won 3-1 by scores of 25-18, 18-25, 25-21, 25-21. In Piedmont’s first-set win, Maika Ting led the charge with four kills while Lucia Dorsey added three. As for the second-set loss, Piedmont fell behind in the middle stages before the Jets closed the set by gaining points by way of two offensive errors before landing a winning kill. Piedmont opened the third set with a 5-2 lead thanks to two kills by Mira Sachs and one by Wilk. Encinal battled back to tie 8-8 and eventually took a 12-11 lead. But the Jets’ lead was shortlived, taking the next three points to lead 13-11 by way of a kill by Wilk, and offensive error, and a block by Sachs. Encinal tied 15-15, but PHS scored five of the next seven points with two kills by Izara Dando, one by Ting, and one by Allyson Huynh. Holding a 22-21 lead, Piedmont got the final three points of the set with a kill by Sachs and two Jets’ errors. In the final set, Piedmont trailed 5-3, but went on a seven-point scoring run to take an 11-5 lead, including two kills by Wilk and Lucia Dorsey, one kill by Huynh, and an ace by Charli Panico. However, the Jets powered their way back to the front at 18-17. articles.text: The Piedmont Fencing Team is back for its 2025-26 campaign, getting started at the Air Force ROC, RJCC in Colorado Springs on Saturday and Sunday, September 13-14. Piedmont Middle School seventh grader Oliver Lê competed in the Division 1 Cadet Men’s Foil at the Air Force ROC, RJCC, finishing 15th of 24. He won two of six matches in the Pool Play stage, beating Niko Messenger of South Denver Fencing Academy 5-1 and Max Mandrioli of the same academy 5-3. In the knockout stages, Lê defeated Maddox Nguyen of Denver Dencing Center 15-12 in the Round of 32. He fell 15-4 in the Round of 16. “Oliver finished 15th in Cadet Mens Foil and is closer to qualifying for US Summer Nationals and Junior Olympics. It was an excellent result,” coach David Sinkkonen said. Favianna Brown, a sophomore at Piedmont High, competed in the Junior Women’s Foil, Division I-A Women’s Foil and the Cadet Women’s Foil category. She won her first ever match in at Junior Women’s Foil, finishing 25th overall. Brown defeated Alexandra Vorobiev 5-4 during Pool Play. Vorobiev was rated as a “very hard” opponent and was the No. 18 seed of 27 players. “Favianna Brown won her first preliminary bout/match ever in her preliminary pool. She looked much improved and looking forward to a great year,” Sinkkonen said. Leading the charge for Piedmont Fencing Team was Nathaniel Goff, a junior who resides in Piedmont Middle School seventh-grader Oliver Lê competed in the Division 1 Cadet Men’s Foil category. Harrow, London but represents the team internationally. He finished fifth of 30 in the Division II Men’s Foil, sixth of 28 in the Junior Men’s Foil category and eighth of 28 in the Division 1-A Men’s Foil. In his fifth-place run, Goff won four of five Pool Play matches, including a shutout 5-0 win over a “hard” rated opponent. He won 15-5 in the Round of 32, followed up with a dominant 15-4 win in the Round of 16, but lost 15-8 in the Round of 8. To finish sixth in the Junior Men’s Foil, he won five of six Pool Play matches, including a 5-4 win over “hard” rated opponent. He also won 15-8 in the Round of 16, but lost 15-9 in the Round of 8. In the Division 1-A Men’s Foil, he won three of six Pool Play matches, including a “hard” rated win 5-4. He won 15-11 in the Round of 32 and 15-10 in the Round of 16. He fell in the Round of 8, 15-10. Also competing from Piedmont was PMS seventh-grade student Preston Guidi and Piedmont High sophomore Spencer Tsai. It marked both athlete’s first-ever tournaments. “It was their first ever tournament, so it’s expected to have some struggles,” Sinkkonen said. Tsai had some good moments. He had a narrow 5-3 loss in pool play to a “very hard” rated opponent in the Cadet Men’s Foil, and a 5-3 loss to a “hard” opponent in Division II Men’s Foil. Guidi, meanwhile, took points against two “very hard” opponents in the Cadet Men’s Foil. Piedmont Fencing Team’s next significant event with be the AFM Super Regional in Santa Clara on Friday and Saturday, October 31-November 1. pages.text: 16 16 Wednesday, October 22, 2025 Piedmont Avenue HALLOWEEN CELEBRATION By Paisley Strellis The Piedmont Avenue Halloween Parade was started in 1987 by a number of Piedmont Avenue merchants who “wanted to give kids a safe place to trick-or-treat,” recalled the late Richard Stone, owner of Continental Hearing. In its early years, Stone says just two or three blocks of the street were closed to traffic for an afternoon and kids were invited to wear their costumes and trick-or-treat at various participating merchants. Stone, who was a member of the Lions Club, used the opportunity to raise money for Children’s Hospital and the Lions Center for the Blind in Oakland. Piedmont Ave. Halloween Celebration a very sweet tradition “We sold all-beef hot dogs for a dollar and gave the proceeds to those charities,” he said. articles.text: Photo courtesy of OMCA Celebrate Dia de los Muertos at OMCA with music, dance, food and art. Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) will host its 31st annual Dia de los Muertos Celebration this Sunday, October 26. The museum, in collaboration with OMCA’s El Día de Muertos Volunteer Community Committee, explores the culture and heritage of Latin America through music, dance, food, and art. Dia de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, is a celebration and appreciation of life and death observed in Mexico and Latin American countries. Festivities begin at 11 a.m. with a procession to the museum garden led by the Día de los Muertos Committee for the dedication of the central ofrenda. Performances throughout the day include a poetry reading by Oakland Youth Poet Laureates Myra Estrada and Cael Dueñas-Lara, and concerts performed by a student-run mariachi band, Danza artists, Ballet Folklorico Mexicano and more. Visitors may view community-placed offerings at the ofrenda (altar) and explore the art of repujado (embossing), and are invited to visit the onsite mercado (market) to support local artisans offering handmade goods, altar items, and Día de los Muertos– inspired art. articles.text: A San Francisco holiday tradition returns to Union Square this fall. The Holiday Ice Rink, presented by Kaiser Permanente, opens for its 18th season on Wednesday, November 5 with an opening celebration featuring on-ice performances, special guests, and complimentary admission for the first 100 skaters during the 5:30 p.m. and 7 p.m. sessions. Located in the heart of San Francisco’s shopping and arts district, the rink offers a seasonal destination for residents and visitors alike. The outdoor rink will remain open throughout the holiday season. “We are proud to welcome back the ice rink to Union Square, which continues to bring our community together and support our local economy,” Marisa Rodriguez, chief executive officer of the Union Square Alliance, said in a press release. “It’s a joyful tradition that celebrates the holiday season and everything Union Square has to offer.” This year’s programming includes a mix of returning favorites and new experiences. Signature events include: • Flashback Fridays (Nov. 21, Dec. 26, Jan. 16), featuring 1980s music spun live by Classic Hits 103.7; • Drag on Ice (Dec. 4), showcasing performances by local drag artists; • Silent Skate (Dec. 11), an iceside silent disco with wireless headphones and live DJs; • Polar Bear Skate (Jan. 1), inviting guests to wear swimwear on the ice in celebration of the new year. Weekend skating lessons will also be offered through the Learn to Skate program on a firstcome, first-served basis. Lessons are free with advance registration and taught by professional instructors. “Kaiser Permanente is proud to support an event that promotes wellness and togetherness during the holidays,” said Chris Boyd, senior vice president and area manager for Kaiser Permanente’s Golden Gate service area. The rink will operate daily from 10 a.m. to 11 p.m., closing at 9:30 p.m. on New Year’s Eve. Tickets are $22 for general admission and $17 for children ages 8 and under, including skate rental. All tickets must be purchased in advance at unionsquareicerink. com. A portion of proceeds will benefit the San Francisco Recreation and Park Department. The outdoor rink is located in the heart of San Francisco’s shopping and arts district.

articles.text: The San Francisco Conservatory of Flowers is hosting its annual Halloween-themed fundraiser this Friday, October 24. The event, titled “Boo-tiful Boo-tanicals,” will run from 6 to 9 p.m., with final entry at 8:30 p.m. Visitors of all ages are welcome, though programming is best suited for ages 10 and up. Guests can explore the darker side of the plant kingdom through the conservatory’s own exhibits on poisonous, carnivorous and razorsharp flora. Staff rotate specimens into the exhibits from greenhouses routinely, and will highlight carnivorous and poisonous species throughout the evening. The botanical garden is home to an intriguing collection of carnivorous plants within its Aquatic Plants Gallery, including tropical pitcher plants (genus Nepenthes) and sundews (genus Drosera). Special programming includes a talk on carnivorous plant conservation by botanist Barry Rice at 6:30 p.m., followed by “Wicked Plant Trivia” at 8 p.m. Each program requires a $5 add-on ticket. At 7:30 p.m., attendees can gather outside for the “Photosynthesis Light Show,” a live projection display featuring vibrant visuals and music cast onto the historic Victorian greenhouse. The conservatory’s galleries will be open for drop-in tours, and guests are encouraged to dress in “plant-themed” costumes. “Boo-tiful Boo-tanicals” and other annual fundraisers are part of the Conservatory of Flowers’ effort to engage the community with educational and entertaining plant-based experiences. The Conservatory of Flowers is located at 100 John F. Kennedy Drive in Golden Gate Park. For tickets and more information, visit gggp.org. “Photosynthesis Light Show.”
articles.title: SF Conservatory of Flowers hosts Halloween-themed fundraiser this Friday

articles.text: Vienna Boys Choir The world-renowned Vienna Boys Choir returns to UC Berkeley for a special performance celebrating the 200th birthday of composer Johann Strauss Jr. The concert, titled “Strauss For Ever,” takes place Sunday, November 16 at 3 p.m. at Zellerbach Hall. Presented by Cal Performances as part of its “Vocal Celebration / Family” series, the event showcases Strauss Jr.’s timeless compositions through the pure, soaring voices of one of the world’s oldest and most prestigious boys’ choirs. The program includes familiar favorites such as The Blue Danube, Tales from the Vienna Woods, and a lively mix of polkas. Founded in 1498, the Vienna Boys Choir has performed across the globe, preserving Austria’s rich musical heritage. The group, made up of boys aged 9 to 14 from various countries, is known for its crystal-clear tone, precision, and spirited performances. The choir has been singing choral arrangements of Strauss’s music since the 1920s. “Strauss For Ever” offers audiences a unique opportunity to hear the signature waltz and polka sounds of Vienna reimagined through youthful voices, serving as an homage to a composer who helped define his city’s cultural identity. Tickets are available at calperformances.org, by phone at (510) 642-9988, or in person at the Ticket Office at Zellerbach Hall, Tuesday through Friday, 12 p.m. to 5:30 p.m. and Saturday through Sunday, 1 p.m. to 5 p.m.
articles.title: Vienna Boys Choir performs at UC Berkeley Nov. 16

The season-launch program draws connections between 19th-century composers and contemporary voices through themes of memory, time and reflection, and features Gustav Mahler’s Rückert-Lieder, arranged by David Hefti, alongside Sillage, a contemporary piece by composer Artur Akshelyan. Sillage, which sets a poem by 20th-century Armenian writer Z. Melkonian, was the winner of LCCE’s 2024 Composition Contest. “Based on the text choices, I settled on a philosophically charged poem in which emotions embody a certain nostalgia, as if fragments of life and death coexist in collective memory, shaped by both past and future,” Akshelyan said in a press release. to explore not only change, but the things which remain constant: time, memory, endings and beginnings, the pursuit of happiness, and our connection to the world around us,” Hofman said. Performers include violinists Anna Presler and Liana Bérubé, violist Phyllis Kamrin, cellists Tanya Tomkins and Leighton Fong, pianist Allegra Chapman, guitarist Michael Goldberg, and soprano Nikki Einfeld as lead vocalist. Founded in 1992, Left Coast Chamber Ensemble is a collective of 17 musicians based in the San Francisco Bay Area. Known for thematic programs that pair contemporary and historical repertoire, the ensemble regularly commissions new works and engages in collaborations across disciplines. Its members perform in a range of settings, from chamber and orchestral concerts to multi-media and operatic productions. LCCE also runs an annual composition contest and offers a music education program. More information is available at leftcoastensemble.org or by calling (415) 617-5223. articles.text: The Branford Marsalis Quartet, one of the longest-running and most acclaimed ensembles in modern jazz, performs four concerts at Miner Auditorium in San Francisco tomorrow, October 23 through Sunday, October 26. The quartet returns to San Francisco to perform a range of music including a selection of the Keith Jarrett compositions that make up his 2025 Blue Note debut Belonging. Led by saxophonist Branford Marsalis, a Grammy-winning saxophonist and national Jazz Master, the quartet currently includes pianist Joey Calderazzo, bassist Eric Revis and drummer Justin Faulkner. Calderazzo and Revis joined the group in the 1990s, while Faulkner became the newest member in 2009. Marsalis, the group’s founder, Branford Marsalis is a highly regarded composer and jazz tenor saxophonist who comes from a lineage of jazz greats hailing from New Orleans. He is the eldest son of pianist and educator Ellis Marsalis, and his brothers Wynton, Jason and Delfeayo are all well-known musicians in the genre. Marsalis’ vast repertoire includes works by Copland, Debussy, Glazunov, Ibert, Mahler, Milhaud, Rorem, Vaughn Williams, Villa-Lobos and Sally Beamish. He is often a guest with leading symphony orchestras including those in Chicago, Detroit, Dusseldorf and North Carolina as well as the New York Philharmonic. Formed in 1986, the Branford Marsalis Quartet has remained a central outlet for Marsalis’ artistic vision, blending post-bop traditions with innovative improvisation and modern sensibilities. The group’s discography includes Braggtown (2006), Four MFs Playin’ Tunes (2012), and The Secret Between the Shadow and the Soul (2019). The Branford Marsalis Quartet performs at Miner Auditorium, presented by SFJAZZ, Thursday, October 23 through Sunday, October 26. All concerts begin at 7:30 p.m. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfjazz.org/. in for good reason. Gallegos’ conducting technique is crystal clear and musically superior. It sure would be wise for one of the area’s major orchestras to invite him to guest conduct. (Hint, hint.) Schumann’s early “overture, scherzo, and finale” was played with affection. Sure it was a challenge for the orchestra, but they responded with an enthusiastic finesse. Amateurs love what they do. The conductor provided eloquent, spoken program notes. He knows what to say, and how to say it. Composer Dwight Stone also spoke a few words about his piece. The result was a double treat. “The Quantum Effect“ proved to be a fine work with a surprising and beautiful melodic line. The Orchestra played this new work with a warmth of tone. It proves that modern music need not be pugnacious. Bravo, Maestro Stone. In a conversation I had with Geoffrey Gallegos, he told me that he was “afraid of the large venue.” That was not a musical problem for the Orchestra. Their tone filled the large concert space. The problem was a shamefully small audience. Gallegos and his Orchestra deserve more support from the community. They really deserve it.

articles.text: Friday, October 24, 5:30 – 7:30 p.m. 13th Annual Brewing Artisanal Competition A major community fundraiser for PCA, this year’s event once again presents the best of local brewers with tastings and a souvenir glass, combined with a delectable Oktoberfest hot meal generously donated by Dave Larson and Piedmont Grocery. Live music will be provided by a jazz trio from PHS. The lawn portion of this event is open to all, but the tasting inside Hall is limited to adults over 21. A panel of five judges will award prizes in several categories, including Best Pale Ale, Best Lager, Best Porter, and Best in Show. Save time in line by buying advance tickets at https://www. tinyurl.com/ymf8mz7c. Saturday, November 1, 4:00 – 6:00 p.m. Artist’s Opening Reception Piedmont native Michael Stehr opens his annual exhibition of new work at PCA with a curated wine and cheese reception. This year’s exhibit is entitled Love at First Sight: Considering the Nature of Inspiration. The exhibition includes 40 new works framed in gilt moldings made by the artist. Please visit the Fine Art section of his website at www.mstehr.com for an online preview of the exhibit, which will be open for viewing in person from 11 a.m.–2 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays November 2-16. E-mail Michael at mstehrart@gmail.com to RSVP for the reception Sunday, November 2, 4:00 p.m. Piedmont Chamber Orchestra Piedmont’s popular local chamber orchestra returns with an intriguing program of smaller works featuring soloists Kate Juliana, soprano, Susanne Rublein, flute, and pianist Hadley McCarroll, in popular works by W.A. Mozart. Conductors Martha Stoddard and Andrew O’Donnell will lead the orchestra in Bay Area Artists’ Showcase … Mostly Mozart, with selections from Don Giovanni, the Rondo from Piano Concerto No. 20 in D minor, and Andante for Flute in C Major. The program also includes movements from Mozart’s Symphony No. 39 and Joachim Raff’s Sinfonietta for winds and horns. Admission is free, but reservations are strongly recommended, at https://www.eventbrite. com/e/1758819669979. articles.text: What is the purpose of an orchestra conductor? This question has perplexed music lovers for ages. It has been the consternation of musicians since the first conductor ascended the podium. The usual feeling is a power struggle between the conductor versus the Orchestra while both entities attempt to realize the intentions of the composer. These days it is the conductor who is referred to as “Maestro.” Originally “Maestro” referred to a composer. How things have changed. Generally speaking, conductors fall into three divisions. There are 1) the ruthless dictators, 2) the benevolent inspirers and, 3) the incompetent fools. At the forefront of category number one was Arturo Toscanini who was famous for his uncontrolled temper tantrums. But he was a temperamental musical genius when on the podium and a modest man in private life. In category number two was the benevolent genius of Bruno Walter. His musicians loved him. Seeing the busy Geoffrey Gallegos, conductor of the Contra Costa Chamber Orchestra, reminds one of Bruno Walter. He encourages the best from an orchestra comprised mainly of amateur musicians. … and they respond enthusiastically. There are very few pros in the ranks. Some might observe that the orchestra lacks “professional aplomb,” but they make up in great measure with a love for what they do. Their concert on Sunday afternoon was a fearless program of Schumann and Beethoven, with a modern premiere (The Quantum Effect by Dwight Stone) thrown Composer Dwight Stone on the left, and conductor Geoffrey Gallegos on the right, taking curtain calls with the Contra Costa chamber Orchestra. The concert deserved a bigger audience.

pages.text: 20 Wednesday, October 22, 2025 By Allyson Aleksey The Branford Marsalis Quartet, one of the longest-running and most acclaimed ensembles in modern jazz, performs four concerts at Miner Auditorium in San Francisco tomorrow, October 23 through Sunday, October 26. The quartet returns to San Francisco to perform a range of music including a selection of the Keith Jarrett compositions that make up his 2025 Blue Note debut Belonging. Led by saxophonist Branford Marsalis, a Grammy-winning saxophonist and national Jazz Master, the quartet currently includes pianist Joey Calderazzo, bassist Eric Revis and drummer Justin Faulkner. Calderazzo and Revis joined the group in the 1990s, while Faulkner became the newest member in 2009. Marsalis, the group’s founder, Branford Marsalis Quartet performs at SFJAZZ October 23–26 Branford Marsalis is a highly regarded composer and jazz tenor saxophonist who comes from a lineage of jazz greats hailing from New Orleans. He is the eldest son of pianist and educator Ellis Marsalis, and his brothers Wynton, Jason and Delfeayo are all well-known musicians in the genre. Marsalis’ vast repertoire includes works by Copland, Debussy, Glazunov, Ibert, Mahler, Milhaud, Rorem, Vaughn Williams, Villa-Lobos and Sally Beamish. He is often a guest with leading symphony orchestras including those in Chicago, Detroit, Dusseldorf and North Carolina as well as the New York Philharmonic. Formed in 1986, the Branford Marsalis Quartet has remained a central outlet for Marsalis’ artistic vision, blending post-bop traditions with innovative improvisation and modern sensibilities. The group’s discography includes Braggtown (2006), Four MFs Playin’ Tunes (2012), and The Secret Between the Shadow and the Soul (2019). The Branford Marsalis Quartet performs at Miner Auditorium, presented by SFJAZZ, Thursday, October 23 through Sunday, October 26. pages.text: Wednesday, October 22, 2025 27 Features Walking on Wednesday Wed. Walkers explore improvements on Grand Ave. By Dick Carter The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group got lucky with the weather again last week. After two days of steady rain, skies cleared just in time for the group’s weekly outing on October 15. Last week a total of 46 walkers and four canine companions gathered for a tour of improvements on Grand Avenue. The intersections of Grand and Linda and Grand and Greenbank were identified as priority locations for pedestrian safety enhancement in 2021. In 2022, Piedmont received a $500,000 grant from Alameda County Transportation Commission to fund pedestrian safety improvements along Grand Avenue. The project, which included a new bioswale and bulb-outs, began this year. According to Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales, including a bioswale “is a great example of how these types of projects can simultaneously enhance safety while improving the aesthetics of the neighborhood.” A bioswale is a landscaped, vegetated channel that collects stormwater runoff from roofs, driveways, and lawns. The soil and plants absorb and filter rainwater, reduce flooding by slowing its flow into storm drains, and improve water quality by minimizing sediment and chemical runoff. Their deep-rooted plants and porous soil allow more rainwater to soak into the ground, helping recharge groundwater and protect creeks and bays. Park Commissioner and walker Jack Fischrup noted that Piedmont’s new bioswale was designed primarily as a water-retention area. It temporarily holds rainwater before gradually channeling it into the existing drainage system. One nearby resident who passed by told the group that during the week’s heavy rain, the bioswale filled and overflowed within about 30 minutes—but drained completely soon after. The curved sidewalk surrounding it provided a perfect place for the walkers’ traditional group photo. The group turned on Jerome Avenue to explore the seldom-visited Hill Lane, a short dead-end street serving garages of nearby homes. The walkers continued along Grand Avenue, sharing research from Piedmont Historical Society president Gail Lombardi about the area’s early zoning. In 1929, the City Council allowed commercial businesses from the Oakland border to Linda Avenue on the west side of Grand and to Fairview Avenue on the east. Seven months later, voters rejected an effort to extend the business district to Oakland Avenue – a boundary that remains unchanged to this day. On their return route via Wildwood Avenue, Palm Drive, and the upper trail of Piedmont Park, the group noted that Bushy Dell Creek’s water level had already returned to normal after the rain. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at 10:30 a.m. at the Exedra at Highland and Magnolia Avenues. Everyone is welcome to join and there is no charge Register at tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. The group was pleased to have Gill and Ron Day in from England visiting family, and longtime walker Christine Calliste in town from Granada visiting her family. articles.text: • AP Research: recommended for grades 11+, AP Seminar is a prerequisite; • Honors Art & Honors Ceramics: Although few students are eligible to take these courses, they would be third year art courses for grades 11+ embedded within existing sections; and • Honors 10th grade English: see below. We had initially discussed allowing AP Seminar, a class the Board approved last year, to fulfill the 10th grade English requirement as a number of other districts do. After hearing valid concerns from members of our English department, we instead approved a 10th grade honors English class designed by one of our esteemed English teachers. Similarly, after hearing concerns about the possibility of offering AP World History from members of our history department, we agreed to pause on that course to allow time for the history department to finalize the design of an honors world history course and hold a community meeting to discuss the merits of honors versus AP world history. The approval of these courses has resurfaced a conversation that our community had in 2013, 2016, and again in December 2019 regarding honors and AP courses, student stress, and college admissions. The most recent December 2019 conversation was thorough and yielded some valuable insights. Unfortunately, the Covid pandemic occurred and thwarted the next steps that came out of that Board workshop. As we have reviewed the materials from the 2019 workshop it is apparent that many of the concerns and questions that were the premise for holding that workshop are the same ones that are resurfacing today. We believe that it is time for our community to once again come together to discuss these concerns. In the coming weeks we will do the following: • Organize a parent education night featuring mental health professionals to discuss student stress and effective techniques to address it; • Solicit information from college admissions officers regarding how admissions decisions are made, including the importance of weighted or AP courses in admissions; • Research the policies and safeguards, if any, comparable districts put on weighted courses. There is an incredible amount of knowledge in this community. We are committed to doing our research, bringing in experts, engaging in this conversation with open minds, and listening to our community members. As a Board we are confident in the ability of our community to come together, have difficult discussions, and reach conclusions that represent our community’s priorities. articles.text: Editor: The informative article in last week’s Post did not mention that the Piedmont Beautification Foundation is providing $100,000 for the major renovation of the Linda Beach Tot Lot, now under construction. This represents 25% of the $400,000 cost of the project. The $100,000 contribution follows a long history of PBF support for Piedmont’s tot lots, including the Lower Dracena Park Tot Lot (1979), Wildwood School Tot Lot (1989), and Piedmont Park Tot Lot (1991). This legacy continues with the current project as well as their upcoming Fall 2025 Campaign, which will raise funds to support replacing the Piedmont Park swing set. I fear that history will judge the Council’s delegation of authority as consistent with Piedmont’s record of discrimination. I hope Piedmonters will hold the Council accountable for this dangerous, implicitly discriminatory scheme devised to please, and hide behind, developers. –Ralph Catalano, Ph.D. Distinguished Emeritus Professor of Public Health, University of California, Berkeley In support of school board decision Editor: I am writing to express support for the School Board and Administration’s decision to add an honors Humanities course to the high school curriculum. Establishing high level courses in the Humanities is critical to maintaining diverse opportunities for our students. I know this firsthand. In my senior year at Piedmont High School in 1989, I took a class called “Humanities” with Ms. Stone. I was brand new to Piedmont, having moved here from Whitefish Bay, Wisconsin, a suburb of Milwaukee similar to Piedmont, though more conservative in its politics. At the time, I was a product of my community upbringing, and outspoken about it. In Humanities, we studied philosophy, religion, art, and culture. Ms. Stone arranged field trips to highlight real-world examples of what we were studying, including a trip to the University Art Museum in Berkeley to see an exhibit displaying the work of Robert Mapplethorpe. Ms. Stone explained that Mapplethorpe’s photography was controversial for being explicit, sexual, and even homoerotic. She was not wrong. I still remember the images of, and my aversion to, the exhibit vividly. Ms. Stone asked students to write an essay about censorship referencing our Mapplethorpe experience for context. I passionately wrote several pages detailing why there should be no place in our society for exhibits like these, and I’m certain I said as much in our classroom discussions. Ms. Stone, who I knew felt very different than I, gave me a 10/10 on my essay. Using Humanities as the backdrop, Ms. Stone taught tolerance, perspective, and balance, qualities that I, frankly, did not exhibit much as a youngster. But I did develop these and other values with time. I attribute much of my growth to life experience and the occasional seminal moment, like this particular field trip. Our education system must offer a range of diverse options so each of our students has an opportunity to have a Mapplethorpe moment, whether in physics, calculus, or world history, or humanities, yearbook, and art. Let’s continue to support the breadth of our curriculum and challenge our students. If we do not, we deny them the chance to explore, potentially closing doors to personal and professional growth. I occasionally revisit my personal “baselines”, political and otherwise, and recall my Robert Mapplethorpe experience while doing so. Let’s ensure we offer similar opportunities to our students. And thank you Ms. Stone. –Jonathan Essner Piedmont High School, Class of 1990 Beautification donates $100,000 for Linda Beach Tot Lot Editor: The informative article in last week’s Post did not mention that the Piedmont Beautification Foundation is providing $100,000 for the major renovation of the Linda Beach Tot Lot, now under construction.
