This legacy continues with the current project as well as their upcoming Fall 2025 Campaign, which will raise funds to support replacing the Piedmont Park swing set. The former swing set was removed in September 2024 due to structural damage. Replacement of the Piedmont Park swings is a funded project in the City’s 2025-26 budget. PBF’s contributions will offset and supplement this funding. This project responds to many requests that PBF has received to see that the Tot Lot includes a swing set. For more information about the Piedmont Beautification Foundation, visit its website www.PiedmontBeautificationFoundation.org –Cameron Wolfe, Jr. Post your ad in the Call (510) 626-2468 nancy@cmc-ads.com GOOD THROUGH NOVEMBER 2025 GOOD THROUGH NOVEMBER 2025 GOOD THROUGH NOVEMBER 2025 GOOD THROUGH NOVEMBER 2025 Oct. 14th Pulse Continued from page 1 • AP Research: recommended for grades 11+, AP Seminar is a prerequisite; • Honors Art & Honors Ceramics: Although few students are eligible to take these courses, they would be third year art courses for grades 11+ embedded within existing sections; and • Honors 10th grade English: see below. We had initially discussed allowing AP Seminar, a class the Board approved last year, to fulfill the 10th grade English requirement as a number of other districts do. After hearing valid concerns from members of our English department, we instead approved a 10th grade honors English class designed by one of our esteemed English teachers. Similarly, after hearing concerns about the possibility of offering AP World History from members of our history department, we agreed to pause on that course to allow time for the history department to finalize the design of an honors world history course and hold a community meeting to discuss the merits of honors versus AP world history. The approval of these courses has resurfaced a conversation that our community had in 2013, 2016, and again in December 2019 regarding honors and AP courses, student stress, and college admissions. The most recent December 2019 conversation was thorough and yielded some valuable insights. Unfortunately, the Covid pandemic occurred and thwarted the next steps that came out of that Board workshop. As we have reviewed the materials from the 2019 workshop it is apparent that many of the concerns and questions that were the premise for holding that workshop are the same ones that are resurfacing today. We believe that it is time for our community to once again come together to discuss these concerns. In the coming weeks we will do the following: • Organize a parent education night featuring mental health professionals to discuss student stress and effective techniques to address it; • Solicit information from college admissions officers regarding how admissions decisions are made, including the importance of weighted or AP courses in admissions; • Research the policies and safeguards, if any, comparable districts put on weighted courses. There is an incredible amount of knowledge in this community. We are committed to doing our research, bringing in experts, engaging in this conversation with open minds, and listening to our community members. As a Board we are confident in the ability of our community to come together, have difficult discussions, and reach conclusions that represent our community’s priorities. articles.text: The 13th annual Piedmont Artisanal Brewing Competition at the Piedmont Center for the Arts will include music on the front lawn while guests enjoy their freshly made German dinner. A trio of Piedmont High musicians – Deniz Radzik, Eric Verner and Maxim Miller – will perform jazz standards during the Deniz Radzik’s father was a musician, and Deniz started playing violin in 4th grade, and ended up playing percussion and drums in the middle school concert and jazz band. As he entered high school he played with several California jazz conservatory bands. Eric Venner also comes from a musical family. His mother sang in the choir at Boston University where she met Eric’s father, who sang in the Stanford A Capela group. Eric started playing classical guitar at age eight. articles.text: During the August 8 school board meeting the board approved five new honors or AP classes for next year’s master schedule. AP Business with Personal Finance, AP Research, Honors Sophomore English, Honors Ceramics 3 and Honors Art 3 were all approved by the board. The meeting eclipsed the four hour mark with much discussion in favor and against the new additions. AP Cybersecurity, and AP World History were not approved; the district says they are exploring other options with the history teachers and will wait until changing the technology programming. PHS Principal David Yoshihara and Assistant Supt. Ariel Dolowich presented the rationale for the additions and information on the new classes. “I have had very fruitful conversations, I have also had some very mixed and uneven responses when it comes to consideration of new courses. Hopefully this allows us to grow closer and be able to engage and sometimes philosophically, we agree to disagree, but I think it’s fruitful for us to come together and build a common vision,” said Dolowich. Teachers Union President Elise Marks noted that most teachers had no idea about the changes until the board packet of background documents was released Friday. “In the past, when new courses were proposed, they went through a rigorous two-year process,” said Marks. “We have been told by our current Board that that protocol is no longer in effect.” New Courses Approved AP Business with Personal Finance is a personal finance course mixed with a college level introduction to Business. Yoshihara projected the class would be popular enough to require more than one class period. AP Research, a grade 11 and 12 course, builds on a current PHS course AP Seminar which has grown in popularity. Students largely do research that is assigned to them in Seminar. “In AP Research, you will do your own authentic research, and you will dive deep into that. It’s sort of like a mini thesis,” Yoshihara explained. Eight sophomores and 10 juniors would be eligible next year to take the course, meaning it will only have one period offered and at most will have 18 students. “You’ve got to feed the pipe to get into Research, it’s not a first year course,” said Yoshihara. For 10th grade Honors English, the course and the regular variety are both feeder classes into the same junior level course. However, Marks, the AP English teacher, provided a grave warning about the impact of this offering, because it will split the grade in half. “Bifurcating the sophomore class into the ‘AP kids’ and the ‘other kids’ will do real damage to those who take what will be perceived as the ‘lower path’,” said Marks. The additions of the new Arts classes received the least pushback during the meeting, the two additional offerings will not require stand alone sections. Ceramics 3 Honors and Art 3 Honors, will not require additional teachers; the honors students will be in the same classroom as students enrolled in the non-honors variety. For the art track after students take Art 1, a yearlong course, students can take another year of Art 2, or semesters of digital photography or digital design. From there, students can enter the Art levels with Honors options. In Art 3 there is a wide variety of options, in the existing AP Art classes students are building towards one portfolio the whole year. The Honors 3 options offer more flexibility than the more stringent AP class. Commentary Student Representative Hunter Fasteau asked Principal Yoshihara what the changes would do for the difficulty in scheduling classes. Fasteau made the comment two and half hours into the four-plus hour meeting. Student Reps are not required to sit through the duration of the meetings and were given the option to leave at 9.00 p.m. “Adding classes means there’s additional choice, but it also means that students aren’t going to get every single class they request,” said Board President Lindsay Thomasson. articles.text: After years of community input and planning, the Linda Beach Tot Lot by Beach School will soon reopen with fresh play equipment, safer surfacing and a bright, inviting look designed for the youngest residents. The tot lot has always been more than a playground. It is where new parents meet, grandparents linger on sunny benches, and toddlers take their first wobbly steps toward the slide. Families can look forward to swings, slides and low climbing features sized for ages two to five, along with interactive panels and balance elements that encourage imagination and movement. The new rubber play surface is designed as a cheerful path for little explorers, with color blocks and gentle curves that make even a short loop feel like an adventure. Fencing and pathways will provide easier access for strollers. Neighbors helped shape the upgrade through months of outreach and surveys, with parents, caregivers and even tots weighing in on favorite features. Top requests included an enclosed layout, a welcoming theme, and classic play elements like climbing and sliding. The result is a cozy, modern take on a neighborhood playground that still feels New Linda Beach Tot Lot is coming soon

articles.text: Editor: We are writing to express our support and gratitude to the School Board and administration for their recent decision to add a new Honors English class for 10th graders at Piedmont High School. This is an important step toward addressing a long-standing equity gap between STEM and humanities course offerings at the secondary level. Piedmont students with interests and talents in STEM have had early access to advanced coursework beginning in 6th grade with compression math and continuing in 10th grade with advanced science courses. By contrast, students whose strengths lie in the humanities (reading, writing, history, and the arts) have had to wait until their junior year for comparable rigor and depth in their PHS classes. The addition of an Honors English course for 10th graders begins to correct this imbalance. We are encouraged by ongoing conversations between district administrators and teachers about adding an advanced history option, such as AP Modern World History, for 10th graders. We sincerely hope that an accelerated history course can be added for the 2026/27 school year. While we share concerns about our high school students feeling pressure to take too many advanced classes to be competitive for college admissions, the current proposal is about choice and equity - ensuring that humanities-focused students have some earlier access to advanced coursework that STEM students have long enjoyed. Thank you for your thoughtful leadership on this important issue and for your continued dedication to all of our students. articles.text: Editor: I voted for our school board members because I was excited about the policies and approaches that I believed they all would bring to the district. At the October 8th board meeting there was a rigorous and honest discussion about our curriculum at the high school level and I wanted to publicly thank the board for taking the positions that they did. Piedmont went through a period where we drifted away from rigorous academic standards and having high expectations for our kids. I am glad to see us shifting back in the other direction and I believe the last board vote was an important step in the right direction. As echoed by many of our board members — and very appropriately named by Max Roman, Ruchi Medhekar and Lindsay Thomasson — we should work hard to push against the soft bigotry of low expectations, believe that our kids can do hard things, and help them prepare for a competitive and (unfortunately) unforgiving adult world. If we don’t, they’ll be significantly disadvantaged when they get to college and when they get into the workforce. Just ask anyone who teaches college students or hires recent grads and you will hear them lament the general unpreparedness of these young adults. I also wanted to say that Ruchi’s comments at the end were some of the most thoughtful, cogent and authentic commentary that I’ve heard from a public figure (especially an unpaid, volunteer). Her point about stress and challenge growing over time is one I wholeheartedly support. We should let our kids experience manageable stress and challenge now when the stakes are significantly lower than they ever will be in their lives. I have never been more excited about the direction our district is headed. The decisions, leadership and community outreach from Dr. Hawn and Ariel Dolowich demonstrate they are a team that is seeking the best for our students, our families, and trying to make it work with our teachers. I know these positions are often difficult to take because there are so many constituents to balance in the district so a big thank you to them for taking a principled, logical and appropriate approach to our kids’ futures. Above all else I appreciate the swiftness with which they make decisions and the humility they have to understand if those decisions need to be reversed or changed. It is clear that these are not universally popular decisions. Nothing worth deciding ever is. There are a myriad of ways we can address concerns such as caps on APs or limiting the weighted grades. But denying choice is not the right solution. I stand by the board’s vote on Wednesday. Adam Fishman

With appreciation, Abha Kothari & Arvind Seshan Alan & Allison Hampton Alissa & John Welch Amy Vallerie Angela & Joe Anastasi Benjamin Strub & Sabrina Seal Blair & Kevin Paige Corey McCarthy Courtney & Mark Azad Diana Lee & Roger Tsai Erick & Allie Rasmus Dean Esti Iturralde & Will Rogan Evren & Jonathan Essner Jake Sorensen & Anne Hawkins Katie & Dirk Van Den Bos Laura Maestrelli & Dustin Frazier Linda & Andrew Wendel Liz Cha Meredith Fowlie Michele Kwok & Albert Tong Michelle Yang & Ray Guo Naomi Edelson & CJ Evans Sarah Bell Sara Ironside Yulia Rozen and Daniel Levinsohn A return to excellence by School Board Editor: I voted for our school board members because I was excited about the policies and approaches that I believed they all would bring to the district. At the October 8th board meeting there was a rigorous and honest discussion about our curriculum at the high school level and I wanted to publicly thank the board for taking the positions that they did. Piedmont went through a period where we drifted away from rigorous academic standards and having high expectations for our kids. I am glad to see us shifting back in the other direction and I believe the last board vote was an important step in the right direction. As echoed by many of our board members — and very appropriately named by Max Roman, Ruchi Medhekar and Lindsay Thomasson — we should work hard to push against the soft bigotry of low expectations, believe that our kids can do hard things, and help them prepare for a competitive and (unfortunately) unforgiving adult world. If we don’t, they’ll be significantly disadvantaged when they get to college and when they get into the workforce. Just ask anyone who teaches college students or hires recent grads and you will hear them lament the general unpreparedness of these young adults. I also wanted to say that Ruchi’s comments at the end were some of the most thoughtful, cogent and authentic commentary that I’ve heard from a public figure (especially an unpaid, volunteer). Her point about stress and challenge growing over time is one I wholeheartedly support. We should let our kids experience manageable stress and challenge now when the stakes are significantly lower than they ever will be in their lives. I have never been more excited about the direction our district is headed. The decisions, leadership and community outreach from Dr. Hawn and Ariel Dolowich demonstrate they are a team that is seeking the best for our students, our families, and trying to make it work with our teachers. I know these positions are often difficult to take because there are so many constituents to balance in the district so a big thank you to them for taking a principled, logical and appropriate approach to our kids’ futures. Above all else I appreciate the swiftness with which they make decisions and the humility they have to understand if those decisions need to be reversed or changed. It is clear that these are not universally popular decisions. Nothing worth deciding ever is. There are a myriad of ways we can address concerns such as caps on APs or limiting the weighted grades. But denying choice is not the right solution. I stand by the board’s vote on Wednesday. Adam Fishman

articles.text: Morton and Aquarius are a charming pair who balance each other beautifully. Morton, a 3-year-old tuxedo with bright green eyes and extra toes, is confident, social, and full of personality. articles.text: Annual ShakeOut drill is a reminder to be ready for earthquakes Pause what you are doing at 10:16 a.m. on Thursday, Oct. 16, and practice what to do during an earthquake as part of the Great California ShakeOut. Anytime you feel shaking or receive an alert, take these three steps immediately if you are able: • Drop to your hands and knees. This position helps prevent a fall and reduces the chance of being hit by falling or flying objects. • Cover under a sturdy desk or table. Stay on your knees, bend over to protect vital organs, and cover your head and neck with one arm. If no shelter is nearby, crawl next to an interior wall. • Hold on until the shaking stops. If you are under furniture, hold it with one hand and be ready to move with it if it shifts. If not, hold your head and neck with both arms and hands. If you use a wheelchair or walker: • Lock the wheels of your device. • Cover your head with your hands and arms. • Hold on until the shaking stops. Living near the Hayward Fault means earthquakes are part of our future. Learning and practicing “drop, cover, and hold on” can significantly reduce the chance of injury during the initial shaking. The Piedmont Fire Department encourages everyone to join the drill. After practicing, take a few more steps to prepare: • Sign up for AC Alert emergency notifications at acalert. org • Check and refresh your disaster supply kit • Make a plan for how you will notify loved ones of your status after an emergency International ShakeOut Day is held each year on the third Thursday of October to help communities protect themselves during earthquakes. Register at shakeout.org for tips on planning your own drill and talking with others about preparedness.

articles.text: Health Class teacher Lael McAuliffe MHS student representative to the school board Saniyah Johnson Piedmont’s School Board conducted a first reading at its meeting on October 8 concerning its plan to update Piedmont’s graduation requirements. The changes align with the University of California’s A-G requirements for UC admissions. The planned changes would eliminate the requirements for graduation of semesters of computer science, health education and ethnic studies; those classes would still be offered but would be electives. The plan would also change the math requirement from two to three years, eliminates the option for visual and performing arts to count for foreign language study and requires students to have two years of foreign language. A waiver is proposed for students unable to meet these new requirements to still graduate. “We believe that offering A-G requirement, which almost 97% of our students currently meet, raises the floor and allows our students to maximize what they are taking as they proceed through their high school career,” said Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich. “I want to be abundantly clear that the purpose of this policy is to allow students to make more choices in determining what courses make sense for them. We are not taking anything away. I hear the narrative that we are eliminating Health to add APs, that is inaccurate,” said Thomasson. Public comments, limited to two minutes and 30 seconds each, were largely against the proposed changes. “I fear that students that do not choose a third year of math [will] find themselves at risk of not graduating,” said math teacher Sam Colburn. Among others, Counselor Chris Hartford and Health Science teacher Lael McAuliffe spoke about removing the requirement for students to take the Health Class. “The Health class, by nature, [helps] the most vulnerable kids who need the most. [Those students] hang out with the teacher, it’s like [the class acts] as a Wellness Center. I basically fear that without that class we are going to miss [supporting] those kids,” said Hartford. “Health is not an elective topic, it is a life skill,” said McAuliffe. “The CDC reports that nearly one in three teens experiences persistent sadness or hopelessness.” “I thought long and hard about [the Health class] as well, it really does matter, we are all deeply invested in the social emotional health of kids,” said board member Susy Struble. “Again, the class is not going away, I know that feels like small comfort.” “The second that we saw any issues with our student health and wellbeing that we could tie back to the lack of having this as a requirement at sophomore year we would change it right back,” said Struble. Ethnic Studies teacher Gabby Kashani reminded the board that she fought to get the Ethnic Studies class into PHS despite the disfavor of former Asst. Superintendent Cheryl Wozniak. Kashani recalled how once the class was offered, the board in 2020 then thanked her for bringing the class to Piedmont one year before the state mandate. “I took Ethnic Studies and I feel like it really helps broaden kid’s perspectives and outlooks on different things and cultures,” said junior Saniyah Johnson Millennium High student rep to the board. “Things are not always as it is in your own bubble and community.” For teachers and counselors speaking at the meeting, there was a definite connection between adding more AP classes, which was next on the agenda, and making room by removing requirements of health and ethnic studies. “I know and I have seen the stress of students, even now currently coming into my office, just to ask me a question, I feel like they are nervous,” said Counselor Stefanie Manalo-Leclair. “I want us to pay attention to our students mental and emotional health, if there is an increase in APs and honors, that will not be a choice, they will sign up for it.” PHS student representative to the board Hunter Fasteau also wore his heart on his sleeve, makEthnic Studies teacher Gabby Kashani ing comments with Johnson, two hours into the meeting at around 9:00 p.m. “There is an indescribable feeling of inadequacy amongst students when they cannot achieve their best,” said Fasteau. “I know in myself that I have to go home and study for 2-3 more hours for homework due tomorrow, while also dedicating time to being here, to doing something that I care about.” “We can’t lose sight that human beings have to grow and mature and develop outside of the classroom,” added Fasteau. The board did not vote on the item, as it was a first reading.
articles.title: PHS plans to change graduation requirements

articles.text: At the October 8 School Board meeting, several new courses were approved for Piedmont High School, including AP Business with Personal Finance, AP Research, Honors English for sophomores, Honors Ceramics, and Honors Art. At the same time, Health was removed as a required course, and Ethnic Studies, another unweighted class, was no longer mandatory. While the changes were intended to broaden academic opportunities, many students worry they will increase stress and competition. Freshman Dario Banuelos voiced concern about removing Health. “I believe the removal of health as a required course was a mistake as it is one of the most applicable classes and helps greatly to stay mentally and physically healthy. Doing this while also adding a number of more stressful classes doesn’t do much except hurt the environment at PHS.” Many students said the decision felt rushed and disconnected from actual student needs. Senior Kalyani Spieckerman explained, “Parents and adults keep arguing that it’s important to have weighted humanities classes to balance out the STEM ones, but it’s harmful to have that many weighted classes at all. It will make kids feel immense pressure to take the harder option, even if it’s not right for them.” Spieckerman added that Piedmont’s culture already promotes the idea that unweighted classes are “less than,” pressuring students to take more rigorous tracks. “With more weighted classes, we’re going to see kids opting into courses they probably shouldn’t take just to avoid social consequences,” she said. Sophomore Stella Joseph argued, “I feel like introducing these classes will only put more pressure on the students to take them at a younger age or only pursue the courses with weighted options rather than pursuing something they are more interested in.” This pressure is amplified by how colleges evaluate course rigor: colleges consider the total number of APs a student could have taken, not just those they actually enroll in. If a school adds more AP options, a student who takes only a portion, say ten out of 20, may appear less ambitious, even if those ten already represent a significant challenge. As a result, students feel compelled to overload themselves, prioritizing transcript appearance over genuine learning or well-being. Sophomore Cory Minor said, “Adding more weighted classes would make Piedmont’s already super competitive atmosphere ten times more competitive.” Junior Heiko Sexton-Boer, who spoke at the meeting, expressed his frustration about how the adults went about it. “I talked with some of the board members after the meeting and was told their ultimate goal was to create weighted classes for sophomores. They met that goal, but they could’ve taken more steps and avoided all this backlash,” he said. Sexton-Boer said he was not diametrically opposed to adding more weighted classes, but suggested the issue lies more in how and why decisions were made than in the courses themselves. Not all students oppose the changes. Sophomore Lukas Bekele said, “I like that they’re adding more weighted classes that are interesting. I think Business with Personal Finance sounds great.” Freshman Danilo Titterton acknowledged both sides, “I think that the new additions of APs have benefits and downsides.” Many students argue that the focus should be on meaningful learning and emotional well-being, not just the number of weighted courses on a transcript. Parents often fail to recognize how much academic pressure has changed. Unlike a decade ago, students must balance APs, extracurriculars, leadership roles, and community service just to remain competitive for college. As colleges increasingly value balance, curiosity, and emotional health, students fear these curriculum changes push them toward burnout and away from genuine learning. Seniors, amid college applications, feel these changes entrench a culture where success is measured by grades rather than personal growth. Senior Athena Li summed up the sentiment: “I wish there was more of a way for [PHS] seniors to express our opinions, feedback, and experience. Even if we won’t be affected, we care. We’ve been here the longest, taken the most APs, seen the most changes, and truly know best what it’s like to be a student at PHS, so it’s really a disservice to the underclassmen and juniors that this experience is essentially lost.” Many students also feel powerless, as their concerns are often met with dismissal or negativity from the adults who hold decision-making power, a reality made clear when students and teachers voiced opposition to the additions, yet the changes still passed. This highlights the frustration of being constantly told to advocate while seeing the very adults in their community undermine their voices. Evolette Mak is an intern with the Piedmont Post and a senior at Piedmont High School.
articles.title: More APs, more pressure: student perspective on PHS curriculum changes

Public comments, limited to two minutes and 30 seconds each, were largely against the proposed changes. “I fear that students that do not choose a third year of math [will] find themselves at risk of not graduating,” said math teacher Sam Colburn. Among others, Counselor Chris Hartford and Health Science teacher Lael McAuliffe spoke about removing the requirement for students to take the Health Class. “The Health class, by nature, [helps] the most vulnerable kids who need the most. [Those students] hang out with the teacher, it’s like [the class acts] as a Wellness Center. I basically fear that without that class we are going to miss [supporting] those kids,” said Hartford. “Health is not an elective topic, it is a life skill,” said McAuliffe. “The CDC reports that nearly one in three teens experiences persistent sadness or hopelessness.” “I thought long and hard about [the Health class] as well, it really does matter, we are all deeply invested in the social emotional health of kids,” said board member Susy Struble. “Again, the class is not going away, I know that feels like small comfort.” “The second that we saw any issues with our student health and wellbeing that we could tie back to the lack of having this as a requirement at sophomore year we would change it right back,” said Struble. Ethnic Studies teacher Gabby Kashani reminded the board that she fought to get the Ethnic Studies class into PHS despite the disfavor of former Asst. Superintendent Cheryl Wozniak. Kashani recalled how once the class was offered, the board in 2020 then thanked her for bringing the class to Piedmont one year before the state mandate. “I took Ethnic Studies and I feel like it really helps broaden kid’s perspectives and outlooks on different things and cultures,” said junior Saniyah Johnson Millennium High student rep to the board. “Things are not always as it is in your own bubble and community.” For teachers and counselors speaking at the meeting, there was a definite connection between adding more AP classes, which was next on the agenda, and making room by removing requirements of health and ethnic studies. “I know and I have seen the stress of students, even now currently coming into my office, just to ask me a question, I feel like they are nervous,” said Counselor Stefanie Manalo-Leclair. “I want us to pay attention to our students mental and emotional health, if there is an increase in APs and honors, that will not be a choice, they will sign up for it.” PHS student representative to the board Hunter Fasteau also wore his heart on his sleeve, makEthnic Studies teacher Gabby Kashani ing comments with Johnson, two hours into the meeting at around 9:00 p.m. “There is an indescribable feeling of inadequacy amongst students when they cannot achieve their best,” said Fasteau. “I know in myself that I have to go home and study for 2-3 more hours for homework due tomorrow, while also dedicating time to being here, to doing something that I care about.” “We can’t lose sight that human beings have to grow and mature and develop outside of the classroom,” added Fasteau. The board did not vote on the item, as it was a first reading. Democracy is not a spectator sport! More APs, more pressure: student perspective on PHS curriculum changes By Evolette Mak At the October 8 School Board meeting, several new courses were approved for Piedmont High School, including AP Business with Personal Finance, AP Research, Honors English for sophomores, Honors Ceramics, and Honors Art. At the same time, Health was removed as a required course, and Ethnic Studies, another unweighted class, was no longer mandatory. While the changes were intended to broaden academic opportunities, many students worry they will increase stress and competition. Freshman Dario Banuelos voiced concern about removing Health. “I believe the removal of health as a required course was a mistake as it is one of the most applicable classes and helps greatly to stay mentally and physically healthy. Doing this while also adding a number of more stressful classes doesn’t do much except hurt the environment at PHS.” Many students said the decision felt rushed and disconnected from actual student needs. Senior Kalyani Spieckerman explained, “Parents and adults keep arguing that it’s important to have weighted humanities classes to balance out the STEM ones, but it’s harmful to have that many weighted classes at all. It will make kids feel immense pressure to take the harder option, even if it’s not right for them.” Spieckerman added that Piedmont’s culture already promotes the idea that unweighted classes are “less than,” pressuring students to take more rigorous tracks. “With more weighted classes, we’re going to see kids opting into courses they probably shouldn’t take just to avoid social consequences,” she said. Sophomore Stella Joseph argued, “I feel like introducing these classes will only put more pressure on the students to take them at a younger age or only pursue the courses with weighted options rather than pursuing something they are more interested in.” This pressure is amplified by how colleges evaluate course rigor: colleges consider the total number of APs a student could have taken, not just those they actually enroll in. If a school adds more AP options, a student who takes only a portion, say ten out of 20, may appear less ambitious, even if those ten already represent a significant challenge. As a result, students feel compelled to overload themselves, prioritizing transcript appearance over genuine learning or well-being. Sophomore Cory Minor said, “Adding more weighted classes would make Piedmont’s already super competitive atmosphere ten times more competitive.” Junior Heiko Sexton-Boer, who spoke at the meeting, expressed his frustration about how the adults went about it. “I talked with some of the board members after the meeting and was told their ultimate goal was to create weighted classes for sophomores. They met that goal, but they could’ve taken more steps and avoided all this backlash,” he said. Sexton-Boer said he was not diametrically opposed to adding more weighted classes, but suggested the issue lies more in how and why decisions were made than in the courses themselves. Not all students oppose the changes. Sophomore Lukas Bekele said, “I like that they’re adding more weighted classes that are interesting. I think Business with Personal Finance sounds great.” Freshman Danilo Titterton acknowledged both sides, “I think that the new additions of APs have benefits and downsides.” Many students argue that the focus should be on meaningful learning and emotional well-being, not just the number of weighted courses on a transcript. Parents often fail to recognize how much academic pressure has changed. Unlike a decade ago, students must balance APs, extracurriculars, leadership roles, and community service just to remain competitive for college. As colleges increasingly value balance, curiosity, and emotional health, students fear these curriculum changes push them toward burnout and away from genuine learning. Seniors, amid college applications, feel these changes entrench a culture where success is measured by grades rather than personal growth. Senior Athena Li summed up the sentiment: “I wish there was more of a way for [PHS] seniors to express our opinions, feedback, and experience. Even if we won’t be affected, we care. We’ve been here the longest, taken the most APs, seen the most changes, and truly know best what it’s like to be a student at PHS, so it’s really a disservice to the underclassmen and juniors that this experience is essentially lost.” Many students also feel powerless, as their concerns are often met with dismissal or negativity from the adults who hold decision-making power, a reality made clear when students and teachers voiced opposition to the additions, yet the changes still passed. This highlights the frustration of being constantly told to advocate while seeing the very adults in their community undermine their voices. Evolette Mak is an intern with the Piedmont Post and a senior at Piedmont High School. READ IT IN THE POST

articles.text: On Thursday, October 9, more than 70 donors and supporters of the Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) Wellness Center gathered at the home of Liz and Gregor Watson for a sponsor appreciation event. This year’s Wellness Center campaign raised a record $67,200 to support the mental health of Piedmont students. The PUSD Wellness Center serves students at Piedmont High School, Piedmont Middle School and Millennium High School. It provides a familiar space on campus where trained staff connect teens to the right level of counseling support. The model of on-site counseling paired with mental health education strengthens the safety net for students navigating academic, social and life stressors. “Your generosity equals counseling hours and a safe space for the kids in our community,” said Wellness Center Support Committee co-chair Martha Joerger. “I hope everyone here feels an immense amount of pride in the fact that they’re part of something that is so impactful for our children.” Photos by Wellness Center Support Committee Millennium High School Principal Irma Muñoz Daniels (left), Wellness Center Directors Sari Sanghvi and Alisa Crovetti and PUSD Superintendent Dr. Jennifer Hawn A highlight of the evening was a panel moderated by digital safety expert Rita Fabi and featuring teen mental health specialists. Panelists included clinical psychologist Dr. Naomi Edelson, who discussed teen anxiety and stress; adolescent medicine specialist Dr. Lauren Hartman, who spoke about body image and eating disorders; and licensed marriage and family therapist Martin Wellness Center Support Committee Co-Chairs Amelie Kappes (left), Martha Joerger, and Sarah Meyjes Diller, who addressed parent-teen dynamics. Dr. Edelson, who treats anxiety and related conditions in teens, outlined what to watch for and how to respond. “Avoidance is really the hallmark of anxiety,” she said, noting indicators such as school refusal, withdrawing from friends or frequent physical complaints. She advised parents to offer “calm confidence,” acknowledging teens’ struggles while reinforcing their capability. Dr. Hartman, a nationally recognized leader in eating-disorder care, emphasized early detection and de-stigmatizing conversations, and encouraged parents to model body-positive language and behavior. “Whether it’s an eating disorder or a struggle with body image, it’s not parents’ fault,” she said. Therapist Martin Diller, who works primarily with adolescent and young adult males, underscored the value of clear communication at home and noted that early conversations can help teens build coping skills. “Parents should preemptively negotiate limits, expectations and rules,” he said. Attendees left with a clear takeaway: when communities and families prioritize youth mental health alongside academics, arts and athletics, students are better equipped to thrive—today and long after graduation. For more information about the PUSD Wellness Center, or to donate, visit Piedmontwellness.org. Event Hosts Gregor and Liz Watson Wellness Center co-founders and former PUSD teachers Sue Smegal (left) and Brooke Zimmerman
articles.title: PUSD Wellness Center hosts mental health forum

articles.text: Have you ever seen a dog shake someone’s hand or sit on command? Believe it or not, keepers at Oakland Zoo work with our animals to train them to behave similarly. If you are at the Zoo at the right time, you might see a bear standing up with front paws on the fence, a macaw being asked to put its wing out, or other interesting behaviors from the Zoo animal residents. Our animals are trained to exhibit different behaviors to help us better care for them. For example, a bear standing up with paws on the fence allows Keepers to check their belly and feet for injuries. This helps ensure the animals are happy and healthy in a safer, more frequent, and less stressful manner. Animal Training Game Using a “bridge” signal during training helps animals understand what action is rewarded, reducing confusion. This signal, such as a whistle or clicker, bridges the gap between the desired action and the reward, which is usually a yummy treat. For this game you will “train” another person to act. First, send the person who will be the trainee into another room, so the person guiding them can decide on a task. Once the trainer chooses the action, the trainee re-enters the room, and the people guiding use claps to direct the trainee. The claps are slow at first and then speed up as the person gets closer and closer to the correct action. The clapping acts as your “bridge” guiding the person to the proper action. Nathaniel Landers is Manager of Teen Outreach at Oakland Zoo. Got a burning question for an animal expert? Submit questions to education@oaklandzoo.org with “Piedmont Post” as the subject for a chance to be featured. Keeper Jessie Sayre asks one of Oakland Zoo’s resident brown bears for a “focus behavior” to steady himself during training.
articles.title: Animal training Is more than just tricks

articles.text: Local high school students from The Next Gen Soccer scored a big win for the community during the Oakland Roots Youth Soccer Night on October 7. The youth-led nonprofit, started by local teens, is dedicated to keeping gently used soccer gear out of landfills and into the hands of kids who need it most. The group spent the night cheering on the Roots and spreading awareness about their mission: making soccer more accessible and sustainable for our local community. Following this event, The Next Gen Soccer is expanding its outreach this fall. Throughout November the group is offering free home pick-up service in Piedmont for families who want to donate used soccer gear. Items accepted include: • Gently used pinnies • Cleats • Shin guards • Soccer balls • Portable pop-up soccer goals “Our goal is simple, to give every kid the chance to play,” said Aidan and Nathan, at The Next Gen Soccer. “If your kids have outgrown their gear, we’ll make sure it finds a new home where it’s needed.” Families interested in donating can schedule a pickup or learn more by visiting www.thenextgensoccer.org or emailing info@ thenextgensoccer.com.
articles.title: Local teens kick off campaign to recycle soccer equipment

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, free compostable bags are available at City Hall to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. Compostable bags are also available from Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) for a fee. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. The Highlanders’ girls team came away with the first-place medal in the Division 6 race, winning the title over 19 other schools. They topped the second-place school, Hughson, by 19 points. articles.text: Staff Photos Rylan Patty scored 13 goals at the Monterey Invitational, including seven in a 13-8 win over Willow Glen. Piedmont High’s boys’ water polo team won two of three matches at the Monterey Invitational on Friday and Saturday, October 10-11. They opened with a 12-8 win over Willow Glen on Friday before losing narrowly 12-11 to Aptos later in the day. They returned on Saturday to beat the host school, Monterey HS, 14-4. Sophomore Rylan Patty had a huge tournament with 13 goals throughout the tournament, and senior captain Elles Kreickhaus added 10 goals. Sophomore Henry Stein filled the stat sheets with a total of five goals, 10 assists, and six steals. The matches bring Piedmont’s record to 10-7. Piedmont now has just three matches left in their regular season before the start of the Western Alameda County Conference tournament on October 28-30. 13-8 win vs. Willow Glen Both teams remained deadlocked 3-3 through the first quarter, but Willow Glen wound up taking a 6-5 lead going into halftime. That’s when Piedmont took things over, outscoring Willow Glen 4-2 in the third quarter to take a 9-8 lead. PHS then added four goals in the fourth while keeping their opposition scoreless. It was a huge performance by Patty, logging a team-leading seven goals. Senior leader Elles Kreickhaus also had four goals and two assists, while sophomore Henry Stein was critical on the defensive side with four steals. Piedmont’s backup goalie Dylan Jerez actually entered in the third quarter and was a critical part of the win with four saves in the third. Final stats: Patty had seven goals, one assist, and three steals. Kreickhaus had four goals and two assists. Stein had a goal, three assists, and four steals. Wilson Walker scored once. Zach Dupree had three steals. Luke McAuliffe had five saves, while Jerez had four. 12-11 loss to Aptos Piedmont trailed 4-3 by the end of the first quarter while stayed one goal back by halftime, 7-6. Aptos outscored the Highlanders 4-2 in the third quarter to make it 11-8, while PHS made things close in the final going with three goals while conceding just one. Final stats: Stein led with four goals, three assists, and one steal. Patty logged three goals. Kappas had one goal, assist, and three steals. Kreickhaus had one goal and assist. Dupree scored once. Nick Riordan had one steal. McAuliffe had nine saves and four steals. 13-4 over Monterey Piedmont took a commanding 5-1 lead in the first quarter and limited Monterey to no goals in the second, leading 8-1 going into the break. Piedmont added three goals in the third while conceding two, and then scored twice more in the fourth while giving away one. PHS finished the game with five different scorers. Final stats: Kreickhaus led with five goals and two steals. Patty scored three goals. Kappas had two goals and a steal. Colin Amen and Henry Van Den Bos scored once. Stein had four Elles Kreickhaus had 10 goals throughout the three matches at the Monterey Invitational.

articles.text: Piedmont suffered a 3-0 loss to league foes Alameda, but kept the scores close. Piedmont High’s girls’ volleyball team traveled to Alameda for a Western Alameda County Conference match on Thursday, October 9, falling by a 3-0 score. Despite the sweep, the Highlanders held tight at different points in each set, losing by scores of 25-15, 25-23, and 25-23. “I give them the formula and sometimes it takes them a couple of sets to apply it. When they execute, they realize what’s going wrong early,” coach Mariah Cardenas said. The result brings Piedmont’s record to 8-8 with four matches remaining on their schedule. PHS must attain a .500 winning percentage to qualify for the North Coast Section postseason, but could still be eligible for an at-large bid. PHS has remained competitive in all of their eight losses. In fact, 13 of their total losing sets were separated by just five points or less. With eight sophomores, five juniors, and just two seniors, Piedmont has shown great potential. “I think we know what we have to do, but we make bad errors at bad times. There are some high intensity moments, and you notice some anxiety out there. This league is tough, and Staff Photos we are small from a stature standpoint. We’re really young, but we’re gaining knowledge. There are definitely growing pains,” Cardenas said. Match Recap In the first set, Alameda opened to a 7-1 lead, but Piedmont stormed back with five straight points to make it a 7-6 deficit. From there, Piedmont kept the set within a three points deficit, including a four-point run to make it 15-13 Alameda, but couldn’t pull ahead. Trailing 17-14, Alameda closed the set with eight of nine points to win 25-15. Maika Ting logged 14 kills against Alameda. Stella Wilk had six kills in the match with he Hornets.
articles.title: Piedmont falls in battle with Alameda

articles.text: In a rivalry match for Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis team the Highlanders beat the Bishop O’Dowd Dragons 5-2 on Thursday, October 9 at Merritt College in Oakland. The result improves PHS’ record to 9-8 overall and 3-1 in the Western Alameda County Conference. Clinching Thursday’s match day was the No. 2 doubles team of Maddie Tran and Inara Mehta with an exciting three sets, 7-5, 3-6, 6-3. “We were warming up in the first set and then cooled off in the second. Our coaches gave us good advice after that. One of their girls kept hitting down the line, so I had to adapt to that,” Tran said. “We were down in the first set and then we came back. The second set was a little rougher than we would’ve liked. I was missing some shots and volleys, but then we pulled it all together in the third set,” Mehta added. The duo has played alongside each other all season as Piedmont’s second doubles team. It marks their first time playing together after Tran combined with Emma Chan last season at No. 2 doubles and Mehta paired with graduate Abigail Call at No. 3 doubles. Mehta won Thursday’s match with a powerful overhand at the net. “I think we’ve gotten better at setting up our points in terms of winning at the net. Maddie is really good at lobbing and that sets me up well. It’s important to set up those points and win those points,” Mehta said. “We’ve definitely gotten better working with each other, especially at the net. She angles the ball really well when I’m at the net, where the other team is forced to hit it up or to me. I’ll be able to end the point like that,” Tran said. Thursday’s victory featured freshman Ella Ruthven defeating O’Dowd’s No. 1, junior Ayla Akcaoglu, in straight sets, 6-4, 6-4. It was a critical win for Ruthven, a new varsity starter playing Staff Photos Maddie Tran at No. 2 doubles helped clinch Piedmont’s victory over Bishop O’Dowd. Inara Mehta was the other half of Piedmont’s win at No. 2 doubles.

By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s girls’ volleyball team traveled to Alameda for a Western Alameda County Conference match on Thursday, October 9, falling by a 3-0 score. Despite the sweep, the Highlanders held tight at different points in each set, losing by scores of 25-15, 25-23, and 25-23. “I give them the formula and sometimes it takes them a couple of sets to apply it. When they execute, they realize what’s going wrong early,” coach Mariah Cardenas said. The result brings Piedmont’s record to 8-8 with four matches remaining on their schedule. PHS must attain a .500 winning percentage to qualify for the North Coast Section postseason, but could still be eligible for an at-large bid. PHS has remained competitive in all of their eight losses. In fact, 13 of their total losing sets were separated by just five points or less. With eight sophomores, five juniors, and just two seniors, Piedmont has shown great potential. “I think we know what we have to do, but we make bad errors at bad times. There are some high intensity moments, and you notice some anxiety out there. This league is tough, and Staff Photos we are small from a stature standpoint. We’re really young, but we’re gaining knowledge. There are definitely growing pains,” Cardenas said. Match Recap In the first set, Alameda opened to a 7-1 lead, but Piedmont stormed back with five straight points to make it a 7-6 deficit. From there, Piedmont kept the set within a three points deficit, including a four-point run to make it 15-13 Alameda, but couldn’t pull ahead. Trailing 17-14, Alameda closed the set with eight of nine points to win 25-15. See Girls’ Volleyball on page 27 Maika Ting logged 14 kills against Alameda. The result improves PHS’ record to 9-8 overall and 3-1 in the Western Alameda County Conference. Clinching Thursday’s match day was the No. 2 doubles team of Maddie Tran and Inara Mehta with an exciting three sets, 7-5, 3-6, 6-3. “We were warming up in the first set and then cooled off in the second. Our coaches gave us good advice after that. One of their girls kept hitting down the line, so I had to adapt to that,” Tran said. “We were down in the first set and then we came back. The second set was a little rougher than we would’ve liked. I was missing some shots and volleys, but then we pulled it all together in the third set,” Mehta added. The duo has played alongside each other all season as Piedmont’s second doubles team. It marks their first time playing together after Tran combined with Emma Chan last season at No. 2 doubles and Mehta paired with graduate Abigail Call at No. 3 doubles. Mehta won Thursday’s match with a powerful overhand at the net. “I think we’ve gotten better at setting up our points in terms of winning at the net. Maddie is really good at lobbing and that sets me up well. It’s important to set up those points and win those points,” Mehta said. “We’ve definitely gotten better working with each other, especially at the net. She angles the ball really well when I’m at the net, where the other team is forced to hit it up or to me. I’ll be able to end the point like that,” Tran said. Thursday’s victory featured freshman Ella Ruthven defeating O’Dowd’s No. 1, junior Ayla Akcaoglu, in straight sets, 6-4, 6-4. It was a critical win for Ruthven, a new varsity starter playing See Girls’ Tennis on page 28 Staff Photos Maddie Tran at No. 2 doubles helped clinch Piedmont’s victory over Bishop O’Dowd. Inara Mehta was the other half of Piedmont’s win at No. 2 doubles.

articles.text: It was a difficult way to start their Western Alameda County Conference Mission Division schedule for the Piedmont High football team, suffering a onesided 63-7 loss to the visiting Hayward Farmers at Witter Field on Friday, October 10. Piedmont held a 7-6 lead with two minutes left in the first quarter, but things began to unravel after Hayward returned the ensuing kickoff for a touchdown. “It’s 0-1, the message is its just one game and it’s not going to make or break our season. Our goals aren’t changing. We knew it would be a learning year, we’re not physical enough just yet, that’s the hump we have to get over,” said coach Jordan Seiden. The Farmers’ offense ran play after play, using their speed and athleticism to switch the field Hayward’s offense had their way the entire game. Jimmy Lagios rolls out as he avoids pressure from Hayward. 4020 Piedmont Avenue Oakland, CA 94611 Hours: Tuesday-Saturday: 11 a.m. – 5:30 p.m. Sunday: 1 p.m – 5 p.m. Donations accepted at 2501 Harrison Street Tuesday & Wednesday: 9 a.m. – 12:00 p.m. Saturdays: 10 a.m. – 12:00 p.m. Piedmont looks to regroup after a loss to Hayward. Staff Photos on numerous occasions to create huge gains. Piedmont, with its young roster, struggled to adjust. It marks the Highlanders’ second consecutive sizeable defeat after falling to Arroyo 40-26 the previous week. PHS notably was without star running back and linebacker Xavier Henderson, who won our Athlete of the Month award in September. Starting offensive and defensive lineman Bill Ashton was also out, creating a void in the interior lines. “As soon as I found out X wasn’t going to play, a lot of things changed. He suffered a concussion and just wasn’t ready to go. Bill was out and had to piece things together on the line,” Seiden said. Piedmont looks to turn the page on the difficult night and prepares for its second Mission Division game of the season when hosting Irvington on October 17. The Vikings are currently 5-1, while PHS dominated last year’s game in a 49-7 victory. Game Recap After two trades of possession to start the first quarter, Hayward got on the board first with around 5:45 left in the quarter on a 12-yard pass to the back corner of the end zone. Piedmont contested that the reception was out of bounds, but the officials ruled the receiver in. The Farmers failed on a two-point conversion, giving them a 6-0 initial lead. But Piedmont answered on their next drive, scoring on an eight-play, 69 yard series. During the drive, Rehan Mumtaz started things with a 12-yard carry, while Dash Waters-Worthen had a 14-yard reception where he nearly broke through for a long run after the catch, but was tripped up. The Highlanders scored on a 17-yard pass, where Jimmy Lagios found Waters-Worthen on a flat route after bluffing a run block, turning it up field for the score. A converted extra point by Mattias Seelenberger gave his team a 7-6 lead, but that was it for Piedmont. Hayward came back with a 73-yard kickoff return for a touchdown with 1:58 left in the first, and then padded their lead after a 40yard punt return to the 28— leading to a 5-yard touchdown carry to give HHS a 20-7 lead at the start of the second quarter. From there, Hayward scored three more touchdowns before halftime to take a commanding 41-7 lead going into the break. The Farmers scored again a couple of minutes into the third quarter, going up 48-7 and activating the running clock. They scored once more in the third, and once in the fourth. NEXT UP Piedmont (2-4 overall, 0-1 league) hosts Irvington on Friday, October 17 at 7:00 p.m.

articles.text: Honorable Mentions: Kelsey Coleman, Henry Stein We’re awarding this week’s Athlete of the Week honors to Amalia Gray of the girls’ cross-country team and water polo player Rylan Patty. Honorable mentions go to Kelsey Coleman of girls’ cross country and Henry Stein of the water polo team. Gray had a marquee performance at the 2025 Asics Clovis Invitational, helping Piedmont win the Division 6 championship. She was the Highlanders’ fastest runner, clocking a time of 20:24.20 on the 5,000 meter course to finish 15th of 153 runners. Patty came away from the Monterey Invitational as Piedmont’s leading scorer in their three matches. Photo by Jenni Tsoi Best Amalia Gray is the Post’s Athlete of the Week after leading the girls’ cross country team to the D6 title at the Clovis Invitational. 13-4 win over Monterey, and another three goals in their 12-11 loss to Aptos. Honorable Mentions Coleman had a breakout performance as a freshman on the girls’ cross country team’s Clovis Invitational win. She notched Piedmont’s fifth-fastest time to help solidify the title, finishing 34th in 21:07.10. Stein was another main part of Piedmont’s performance at the Monterey Invitational, filling the stat sheet in several categories in each match. He had a goal and three assists in their 13-8 win over Willow Glen, four assists and a steal in their 13-4 win over Monterey, and four goals, three assists, and a steal in their 12-11 loss to Aptos. The “Blue Lady” is a story from over 70 years ago, where a young woman had an affair with a handsome piano player at the restaurant, falling in love with him. The lady in blue was said to have been murdered by her betrayed fiancé while walking on the beach below the restaurant. Hayward Plunge, Hayward Allegedly, a swimming instructor back in the 1960s at the Hayward Plunge indoor pool led his entire class up the trail and left them in Ward Creek, telling them to wait until he returned. The children stayed there until the night; the coach returned and murdered them, leaving each of them in the creek. Many locals claim strange sightings, like voices of children around them—sometimes laughter or cries, sounds of footsteps pitter pattering, cold spots, and dark shadows. This writer even had a strange sighting of children in all-white garb from head-to-toe during the day as a teenager. Starting at Memorial Park, the initial portion of the Hayward Plunge Trail starts in the back of the park past the bandstand. It travels for 1.3 miles slightly uphill alongside Ward Creek until intersecting with Campus Drive and Oaks Drive. Continue up Oaks Drive to continue the Hayward Plunge Trail. From there, the trail goes for another 1.6 miles to Durham Way and gains 600 feet in the process through the hills of Green Belt Park. Redwood Road Preschool, Oakland Hills This one is very peculiar. Slightly past the intersection of Pinehurst and Redwood Road, there is a former preschool with a gruesome history. Legend has it, a knife wielding murder in the early 80s slayed an entire class of preschoolers at the school. Other reports from the Gasden Times indicated a man, Alan Robert Baer, was shot by police on the preschool property in 1981. All that is left of the school is the foundation and a lone swing set, while people have reported paranormal experiences of children’s laughter, voices, and swings in full-motion as if the school yard was bustling. Black Diamond Mines, Antioch The Black Diamond Mines is a location of the White Witch or Wailing Witch, per urban legend. The story goes that a nanny was expelled from town in the 1870s for practicing witchcraft, only to turn up dead in the mines under suspicious circumstances. Other legend says a nanny, named Mary, was executed after being accused of witchcraft when all of the children under her watch died of illnesses. Niles Canyon, Fremont The Niles Canyon ghost is an urban legend about young woman who died in a horse carriage accident over 100 years ago, said to have occurred specifically on February 28 when horses were spooked by two oncoming automobiles—throwing her from the carried. articles.text: Musical runs through Dec. 21 Cara Impallomeni will perform in Berkeley Playhouse’s production of Annie as the titular character. Berkeley Playhouse premieres the beloved musical Annie on November 7. The musical will be performed onstage through December 21. Annie is a classic Broadway musical based on the comic strip Little Orphan Annie by Harold Gray, with original music by Charles Strouse and lyrics by Martin Charnin. The show premiered in 1977 and won seven Tony Awards including Best Musical. Set during the Great Depression, it follows the optimistic orphan Annie as she escapes a harsh orphanage run by Miss Hannigan and finds a new home with billionaire Oliver Warbucks. Featuring iconic songs like “Tomorrow” and “It’s the Hard Knock Life,” Annie has become a timeless classic celebrated around the world. “This classic musical is very near and dear to my heart,” Director Megan McGrath said, adding that one of her first experiences performing was playing Tessie when she was eight years old. “I got to revisit the show again as a Boylan Sister when the Berkeley Playhouse last produced the show in 2017, and it was such a fun production to be a part of,” McGrath said. “Getting to direct and choreograph Annie at the Playhouse is a full circle moment for me, and now as a mom, I get to rediscover this story of a spirited young girl through my daughter’s eyes.” The cast includes Brendan Simon as Oliver Warbucks, Melinda Meeng as Grace Farrell, Sarah Bylsma as Miss Hannigan, Diella Wottrich as Sophie, Adam Saville as Franklin Delano Roosevelt, Milo Mee as Bert Healy, and Melody Payne Alonzo as Cecille. Cara Impallomeni will perform in Berkeley Playhouse’s production of Annie as the star character. McGrath said that despite the show taking place during the depression era, the show “positively beams with light, love, found family, and hope for a better tomorrow.” The musical is appropriate for all ages. For tickets or more information, call the box office at (510) 845-8542 x351 or visit berkeleyplayhouse.org. ®
articles.title: Berkeley Playhouse premieres Annie on Nov. 7

articles.text: The Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO), the oldest independent youth orchestra in California, opens its 89th season with a fall concert on Saturday, Nov. 8, at 7:30 p.m. at First Church Berkeley. The performance features a dynamic program that includes Hector Berlioz’s Le Corsaire Overture, Maurice Ravel’s Rapsodie Espagnole, and Antonín Dvořák’s Symphony No. 8. “This concert highlights the talents of our young musicians and introduces YPSO’s new season,” said Executive Director Nadia Liu. “As we look ahead to our international tour, we are excited to share these performances with our community.” The evening opens with Berlioz’s Le Corsaire, an energetic overture known for its dramatic flair and vivid orchestration. Ravel’s Rapsodie Espagnole follows, showcasing Spanish-inspired rhythms and textures. The concert concludes with Dvořák’s Symphony No. 8, celebrated for its pastoral warmth and expressive melodies. The orchestra, composed of musicians aged 12 to 22, continues its tradition of offering professional-level performance opportunities while fostering musical education and growth. YPSO enters the new season with a focus on musical excellence and community engagement. The 2025-26 season includes a celebration of the upcoming 250th anniversary of the United States and culminates in an international tour scheduled for June 2026. Music Director David Ramadanoff has led YPSO for over three decades. He studied at the Cleveland Institute of Music and The Juilliard School, before serving as Assistant Conductor of the San Francisco Symphony. Maestro Ramadanoff chooses programs that “highlight diverse eras and composers while fostering each student’s musical growth.” Tickets for the Nov. 8 concert are available through YPSO’s website and at the door. For more information, visit ypso.org.
articles.title: YPSO opens season on Nov. 8 featuring Berlioz, Ravel and Dvořák

Sam Hyland, known by stagename Ouida, will perform alongside her nine-piece band blending UK-inspired R&B and soul with warm jazz and pop melodies this Friday, October 17. The concert is free and will begin at 6 p.m. on the museum lawn. DJ Dailo Mac will spin music in the museum amphitheater throughout the evening. “Friday Nights” occur every Friday evening beginning at 5 p.m. The museum offers free live music and hands-on activities on OMCA’s outdoor lawn space. Use your museum ticket to gain afterhours access to the museum, or bring a blanket and enjoy music on the lawn for free. Visitors may bring their own food or visit one of the many food trucks that offer a variety of local cuisine. Beer, wine, mixed and non-alcoholic drinks are available for sale. The performance features a dynamic program that includes Hector Berlioz’s Le Corsaire Overture, Maurice Ravel’s Rapsodie Espagnole, and Antonín Dvořák’s Symphony No. 8. “This concert highlights the talents of our young musicians and introduces YPSO’s new season,” said Executive Director Nadia Liu. “As we look ahead to our international tour, we are excited to share these performances with our community.” The evening opens with Berlioz’s Le Corsaire, an energetic overture known for its dramatic flair and vivid orchestration. Ravel’s Rapsodie Espagnole follows, showcasing Spanish-inspired rhythms and textures. The concert concludes with Dvořák’s Symphony No. 8, celebrated for its pastoral warmth and expressive melodies. The orchestra, composed of musicians aged 12 to 22, continues its tradition of offering professional-level performance opportunities while fostering musical education and growth. YPSO enters the new season with a focus on musical excellence and community engagement. The 2025-26 season includes a celebration of the upcoming 250th anniversary of the United States and culminates in an international tour scheduled for June 2026. Music Director David Ramadanoff has led YPSO for over three decades. He studied at the Cleveland Institute of Music and The Juilliard School, before serving as Assistant Conductor of the San Francisco Symphony. Maestro Ramadanoff chooses programs that “highlight diverse eras and composers while fostering each student’s musical growth.” Tickets for the Nov. 8 concert are available through YPSO’s website and at the door. articles.text: Visit San Francisco’s Exploratorium every Thursday evening to experience the science museum “after hours.” After Dark is a recurring adults‑only event that transforms the museum into a late‑night playground of science, art and sensory exploration from 6 to 10 p.m. Guests aged 18 and up are invited to wander through 700+ interactive exhibits focused on science, technology, engineering and more. With the lights dimmed, guests can explore the museum’s classic galleries, a live DJ set, themed programs and alcoholic and nonalcoholic drink options at cash bars. “It’s kind of like an adult playground,” Sam Sharkland, senior program developer at the Exploratorium, told ABC7. “It’s 18+, we have cocktails available and lots of extra programming, so you can almost be a kid or scratch that scientific curiosity that you may have lost.” Each Thursday features a different theme or special programming. Previous nights have included Sexplorations, talks tied to science and culture, live performances, and temporary exhibits. On November 6, the museum will host After Dark: Soundscapes, inviting guests to explore acoustics, rhythm and vibration through the museum’s many hands‑on galleries. Tickets are required and “After Dark Membership” offers are available for frequent visitors. For more information, visit https://www.exploratorium.edu. articles.text: The San Francisco Public Library is teaming up with de Young to offer an expert-led discussion on the fine arts museum’s newest exhibition. The de Young’s Manga as Art exhibition celebrates Manga, a type of image-driven narrative storytelling in Japan. The de Young is the first North American museum to highlight in a major exhibition the contemporary Japanese art form, and features well-known artists including Chiba Tetsuya, Akatsuka Fujio, Takahashi Rumiko, Taniguchi Jiro, Yamazaki Mari, Araki Hirohiko, Yamashita Kazumi, Tagame Gengoroh, Yoshinaga Fumi, Oda Eiichiro, and Tanaami Keiichi. “Captivating millions around the world with dynamic graphic narratives, manga is one of the most significant visual mediums of our time,” said Thomas Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “San Francisco has long been a gateway for Japanese cultural exchange in the United States, and we are delighted to honor this legacy by showcasing the artistry and power of contemporary Japanese narrative art in Art of Manga.” San Francisco State University humanities professor Hanako Asakura and manga author and anime expert Gilles Poitras will discuss the popularity boom of Japanese manga literature as well as elements of its vibrant storytelling through illustrations. The event is held at the Koret Auditorium at the Main Library in San Francisco, from 2 p.m. to 4 p.m. on Sunday, October 26. All San Francisco Public Library programs are free and open to all. For more information, visit https://sfpl.org/events. Photo courtesy of The Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco A young museum patron views an installation at de Young’s newest exhibition, Manga as Art.
articles.title: SF Library and de Young host free Manga as Art discussion on Oct. 26

articles.text: The Randall Museum in San Francisco invites families to celebrate the spooky season in style at its beloved Family Halloween Day, held this Saturday, October 18, from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. The free annual event transforms the museum inside and out with Halloween-themed games, crafts, and hands-on activities designed to delight kids and grown-ups alike. Young visitors are encouraged to arrive in costume and join in the festive fun, which includes a costume showcase, “creepy critters,” and interactive stations to spark imagination and seasonal spirit. Designed for kids from infancy to age 12 and their families, the event promises something for every little ghoul and goblin. Highlights include live musical entertainment from the Luke Schwartz Trio and spellbinding performances by magician Brian Scott. Admission is free, with many activities offered at no or low cost. “This is one of our most joyful and community-focused events,” said a Randall Museum spokesperson. “We love seeing the museum filled with kids in costume, learning, playing, and celebrating Halloween in a creative, safe, and nature-friendly environment.” The Randall Museum is operated by the San Francisco Recreation and Parks Department and the non-profit organization Randall Museum Friends and provides a unique experience for Bay Area kids of all ages, from science, engineering and art activities to bird-watching and live animal exhibits. The museum traditionally hosts seasonal-themed community events, and Family Halloween Day continues that tradition with a playful twist. The event will be held at the Randall Museum, located at 199 Museum Way in San Francisco in the city’s Twin Peaks neighborhood. Children under 8 must be accompanied by an adult. For more information, call (415) 554-9600 or visit www.randallmuseum.org.
articles.title: Randall Museum hosts free family Halloween Day this Saturday
