articles.text: In anticipation of the annual Artisanal Beer Festival, organizers at the Piedmont Center for the Arts have once again reached out to their community of craft brewers. Each year, they invite both returning favorites and newcomers to share their latest creations — and, of course, their inventive names. You might think that after so many festivals, the brewers would start running out of clever ideas. Not so. As in previous years, the list of names submitted for the upcoming festival proves that creativity remains one of the core ingredients in Piedmont’s brewing scene. Past festivals have featured memorable names such as Jazzman, Stub Your Toe-in-theDark Ale, Mashing Pumpkins, Cognitive Dissonance, Paul the Pilsner, Saison Du Poe, Sake to Me, and Ah, Bitter Dregs. Beyond their puns and wordplay, the brewers delight in explaining how each name ties back to the flavor and character of the beer itself. This year’s lineup promises to be just as inventive. Longtime participant Matt Gearhart will return with Rye-T-Oh! and Nothing Special Ale, while fellow veteran Aaron Bagnell will present a cream ale aptly titled Hops on Pops. Twenty-year brewer Michael Fedor will offer a pale ale brewed with hops grown right here in town — The Piedmont Pala Ave Pale. Kyle Killion has been brewing for more than fifteen years. Piedmont City Vice Mayor and 2024 judge Conna McCarthy with brewer Aaron Bagnell This year he is presenting Crimes of Passion (fruit), a Belgian Wit with passion fruit and Mr. Prickles, a prickly pear IPA. Local duo Jon and Maureen Rhodin, who have been brewing together for nine years, plan to unveil something “dank and hoppy” — though they haven’t yet settled on a name. “You know it must be good if it doesn’t even have a name yet,” joked one organizer. The festival will also feature the “People’s Choice” award, introduced last year to allow attendees to vote for their favorite beer. The inaugural winner, Trevor Fleshman, took the honor with Nipple Confusion, a single-batch American IPA inspired by his new fatherhood. New faces will also join the mix. Piedmont resident Wes Blummer, a craft brewer of four years, will make his festival debut with three beers: Grapeful Dead, a Saison titled Every Villain Is Lemons, and a Vienna lager called Big Arnold. “There’s no limit to the creativity of our brewers — in what they make or what they call it,” said festival co-organizer Carter Dunlap, who helps coordinate the event each year. Admission to this year’s festival includes a custom tasting glass and unlimited sampling for $15. An Oktoberfest-style meal of grilled bratwurst, sauerkraut and potato salad will also be available for $15. Tickets can be purchased online at tinyurl.com/ymf8mz7c or at the door via credit card or cash. For more information, contact Carter Dunlap at carter@ dunlapclan.net.
articles.title: Artisanal brewers tap into creativity for this year’s festival

articles.text: Saturday, October 18, 7:30 p.m. Benicia Chamber Players Concert Enjoy the quartet of violinists Alicia Choi and Patrick Galvin, violist Luis Eduardo Bellorín, and cellist Brady Anderson, as Benicia Chamber Players kick off their 2025–26 season with a playful, thought-provoking program that asks how composers can stay rooted in tradition while creating something entirely new? In Carrots and Counterpoint, three composers from different eras explore that question in bold, unexpected ways through the string quartet. Florence Price blends American folksongs and African spirituals with classical technique in her Five Folksongs in Counterpoint. Schubert’s Rosamunde Quartet fuses his love of song and chamber music, reworking melodies from earlier vocal pieces, including music from the play Rosamunde. Inspired by Cézanne’s quote, “The day will come when a single, freshly observed carrot will start a revolution,” Gabriella Smith’s Carrot Revolution reimagines the string quartet with wild textures and fresh perspective. Come for the counterpoint, stay for the carrots. Advance tickets, $25, at https:// www.eventbrite.com/e/1736096845399, or $30 at the door. Friday, October 24, 5:30 – 7:30 p.m. 13th Annual Brewing Competition A major community fundraiser for PCA, this year’s event once again presents the best of our local brewers with tastings for the $15 cost of a souvenir glass, combined once more with a delectable Oktoberfest hot meal (also $15) on the lawn, very generously donated by Piedmont Grocery Co., all enjoyed with family-friendly live music provided by a jazz trio from PHS! The lawn portion of this event is open to all, but the tasting, in our Hall, is limited to adults over 21. A panel of five judges will award prizes in four categories – Best Pale Ale, Best Lager, Best Porter, and Best in Show. Save time in line by buying advance tickets at https://www.tinyurl.com/ymf8mz7c. Saturday, November 1, 4:00 – 6:00 p.m. Michael Stehr Art Exhibit Piedmont native Michael Stehr opens his annual exhibition of new work at PCA with a curated wine and cheese reception. This year’s exhibit is entitled Love at First Sight: Considering the Nature of Inspiration, a title appropriate for this artist and art historian who spends his time being inspired and inspiring others. The exhibition will include 40 new works framed in gilt moldings made by the artist. Visit the Fine Art section of his website at www.mstehr.com for an online preview of the exhibit, which will be open for viewing in person from 11 a.m.–2 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays November 2-16. Please email mstehrart@gmail.com to RSVP for the reception. Sunday, November 2, 4:00 p.m. Piedmont Chamber Orchestra Concert Piedmont’s popular local chamber orchestra returns with an intriguing program of smaller works featuring soloists Kate Juliana, soprano, Susanne Rublein, flute, and pianist Hadley McCarroll, in works by Mozart. Conductors Martha Stoddard and Andrew O’Donnell will lead the orchestra in a Bay Area Artists’ Showcase … Mostly Mozart, with selections from Don Giovanni, the Rondo from Piano Concerto No. 20 in D minor, and Andante for Flute in C Major. The program also includes movements from Mozart’s Symphony No. 39 and Joachim Raff’s Sinfonietta for winds and horns. Admission is free, but reservations are strongly recommended, at https://www.eventbrite. com/e/1758819669979. Saturday, November 8, 3:00 p.m. Ravel’s Complete Solo Piano Works To celebrate the 150th birthday of French composer Maurice Ravel, renowned pianist Dr. Gwendolyn Mok has gathered a group of pianists to perform the complete repertoire of Ravel’s solo piano works at Piedmont Center for the Arts. The concert begins with early works such as Menuet antique, Jeux d’eau, Sonatine, and Miroirs. The second part consists of Ravel’s later solo piano compositions, structurally more complex and virtuosic. The 13 pianists come mostly from the Bay Area, with guests from Toronto and Tokyo; many have competed in prestigious international piano competitions for amateur pianists and are top prize winners. Note that the organizer will donate proceeds from the event to a major international charity. Get tickets at https://www.brownpapertickets.com/e/6716987.

articles.text: Hello from Germany. The year is 2025. It feels like a picture of America at its best — and in some ways, like the best parts of the Weimar Republic. People of all nations are everywhere and, for the most part, welcomed and appreciated. Native Germans share their country with Africans, Indians, Asians and people from across the Middle East. Schools are full, thanks to a new baby boom. Elementary education begins with first grade — there is no kindergarten — and all instruction is in German. Yet, as in America, many immigrants continue to speak their native languages at home. Every student studies a foreign language, with English the most common choice, followed by French and Russian. Music remains a core part of education. Singing begins in classrooms, and private music schools offer instrumental training. Youth orchestras thrive, often touring internationally. Traveling across the country, I’ve noticed that prices are much lower than in the Bay Area. Restaurant meals cost about half as much, and portions are large, even with a 19% tax. Traditional German restaurants are less common now, replaced by international cuisine. Turkish eateries dominate, followed by a wide range of Asian options. It feels like a picture of America at its best — and in some ways, like the best parts of the Weimar Republic. People of all nations are everywhere and, for the most part, welcomed and appreciated. Native Germans share their country with Africans, Indians, Asians and people from across the Middle East. Schools are full, thanks to a new baby boom. Elementary education begins with first grade — there is no kindergarten — and all instruction is in German. Yet, as in America, many immigrants continue to speak their native languages at home. Every student studies a foreign language, with English the most common choice, followed by French and Russian. Music remains a core part of education. Singing begins in classrooms, and private music schools offer instrumental training. Youth orchestras thrive, often touring internationally. Traveling across the country, I’ve noticed that prices are much lower than in the Bay Area. Restaurant meals cost about half as much, and portions are large, even with a 19% tax. Traditional German restaurants are less common now, replaced by international cuisine. Turkish eateries dominate, followed by a wide range of Asian options. Despite A German vegetable counter. Note the different manner of display. Germany’s large African population, African restaurants are rare. Food markets resemble those in the United States, featuring both national and regional specialties alongside international fare. Sausages — a regional dish — come in countless varieties. Meat counters are immense, with wild game such as deer and boar available year-round. Every street seems to have a bakery offering fresh breads and rolls, beautifully displayed. Germany’s musical life is A photo of three outstanding musicians just prior to a concert in a German castle. On the left is Bulgaria’s most important musician. He is composer/pianist/administrator Filip Pavlov. In the middle is violinist/conductor Barbara Stanzeleit and on the right is her husband Dieter Stanzeleit who was one of Germany‘s most important orchestral violinists. Here is an example of dining at its finest. These examples of Ukrainian food were better than anything I ever had in the Ukraine. You can see Ukrainian style borscht and a platter of fish with a fabulous cream sauce, decorated with vegetables. vibrant. Schools introduce students to music, but it’s the conservatories that produce professional talent. Many orchestra positions are now held by foreign musicians. One of the country’s best traditions is school concerts — something I wish America would revive. Recently, I performed in a concert held in a castle for an old friend, once a leading orchestral violinist, who now lives in a fantasy world where he imagines himself the uncrowned king of Romania. Joining me was violinist and conductor Barbara Stanzeleit, a beloved local teacher, and pianist Filip Pavlov, who flew in from Bulgaria. Pavlov is virtually unknown in the U.S., yet he is one of Bulgaria’s great musical figures — a superb composer, pianist and national arts administrator. Both he and Stanzeleit are also gifted writers. Still, all is not idyllic. While Germany has grown more tolerant, some immigrant communities have become less so. Open-mindedness meets resistance from a small but troubling resurgence of extremist thought — echoes of darker times. As a historian, I cannot help but notice the parallels. The shadows of the Weimar Republic linger still. And into this house of mirrors we go. How shall we proceed?

articles.text: George MacKay in 1917 Before discussing writer/ director Sam Mendes’ film 1917, I feel I would be remiss not to mention Peter Jackson’s extraordinary They Will Not Grow Old. Jackson was given access to hundreds of archival WWI news footage from Britain’s Imperial War Museum – scratched, grainy, and hand cranked film that he, using stateof-the-art restorative technology, not only colorized but literally brought back to life. It’s as if he opened a portal in time and we see young Brits gathered on a battlefield, waiting, some, breaking the fourth wall, staring into the camera, smiling, their youthful faces filled with an optimistic eagerness that would soon be devastatingly transformed. WWI, which began in July 1914 and lasted until November 1918, was one of the deadliest wars in history. Nine million combatants and seven million civilians were killed as a direct result. Indirectly, 50 to 100 million deaths occurred worldwide, attributed to what was referred to as the “Spanish Flu,” the pandemic thought to have begun in the damp, muddy, disease-ridden trenches, conditions that were almost as lethal as the withering machinegun fire, shelling and chlorine gas faced by the troops. WWI was an extraordinary display of nationalistic hubris, bordering on a collective insanity in which millions of men, on all sides, were sacrificed for mere yards of soil. It was a nightmare of the awful, a killing field of stasis that continued beyond all reason. This is the context for Mendes’ most remarkable film, 1917, set in northern France, at the height of the war. Freddie Highmore portrays Evan Taylor/August Rush, an 11-year-old orphan residing in a boys’ home. He is tormented by the older boys, who consider him a “freak” because he insists he is able to hear music everywhere, even in a field of wind-swept wheat. In an early scene, Evan is asked by a social worker, Richard Jefferies (Terrance Howard), “If you could have just one thing, what would it be?” Evan looks at Richard and says, “to be found.” The story reveals that his parents — Louis Connelly (Jonathan Rhys-Meyers), an Irish band rocker, and his mother, Lyla Novacek (Keri Russell), a gifted cellist — are unaware of his existence. She was told by her self-serving father that Evan had died at birth. Believing that if he follows the music, this intangible, surreal sound, he will find his parents. And so Evan runs away from the boys’ home, making his way to New York City where he is overwhelmed by a cascading orchestra of urban “noise.” And it’s there that the journey of Evan Taylor begins. He is soon given the stage name August Rush by a vagrant opportunist called” “Wizard (Robin Williams), who recognizes Evan’s musical genius and sends him, along with a collection of homeless kids, out on the streets to busker. articles.text: Special to the Post They say St. Andrews is a small, relatively quiet, rainy seaside town. They say the students who attend the university are some of the smartest in the United Kingdom and beyond. They say St. Andrews is a bubble, isolated from the rest of the world past the rolling green hills of the Scottish countryside and across the frigid waters of the North Sea. They say nothing has changed in the almost 700 years since the town was founded. I have found almost all of these claims to be true – except for the one about the town being quiet. Every street you travel, every pub you pass or store you enter, there is some kind of noise. Whether it’s a group of friends passionately talking on their way to a lecture, the clatter of a construction site and its crew, or the laughter of older Scottish men nursing a pint as the sun goes down. Whatever the sound, St. Andrews is filled with it in a way that makes it seem as if the air and ground are humming along. My first week at university – orientation – consisted of walking an average of 10,000 steps a day, exploring a town that for the most part still lives in the 15th century, going to a polo match on the beach, and discovering the Tesco meal deal (a genuine lifesaver in times of need). Now, after writing that sentence, I can’t believe this is my life. That the clatter of hoofbeats on the wet sand of West Sands Beach, the loud chatter of students watching the polo match unfold, and the pop of a champagne bottle could all combine into something considered normal. But even then, my attention kept turning toward the view to my right – the outline of the historic town against the gray clouds, with the sound of hoofbeats and mallet whacks to accompany it. It still feels like something straight out of a movie. As the days went on, I found that my two closest friends so far were both juniors on exchange, an Australian from Canberra and an American from Minnesota. I met the Minnesotan while I was lost and desperately trying to find IT, and with true Midwestern hospitality she immediately helped me. We parted ways, but later that night at a dorm bonding event I saw her again and she introduced me to the girl from Australia. The three of us live on the same floor, so most nights, when we aren’t drowning in assignments and readings, we’re in one of our rooms watching a show in the background while we talk about everything and anything. And while I’m acutely aware that both of them will be leaving after the first semester, that’s a problem for me to handle in December. Not to worry, I have plenty of other friends: a Scot and an Italian I walk with every Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday morning to our International Relations class. We once got into quite a debate about driving licenses and the legitimacy of an American one, because apparently it’s too easy to be considered a test. I was offended, but they weren’t entirely wrong. I have a German friend to get coffee with, another Australian to play tennis with, a Brit to discuss shows we’ve both watched and their insanely bad plot points. Too many nationalities, but that is the point: St. Andrews is truly international. When classes started, I found it surreal to walk through buildings and quads that are centuries old. As an American, our history mostly dates to 1776. While that’s a decent chunk of time, it’s nothing like living in the first dorm ever built at St. Andrews and walking down the same hallways people 200 years ago walked down. Or even studying in a library whose floor creaks with every step because the wood is older than everyone there combined. It’s strange that in Scotland, this kind of history is so… normal. That’s honestly the only way I can put it. In the same breath you can look at a Pret a Manger and see the remains of what once was Scotland’s oldest and largest abbey before it was destroyed by Henry the Eighth. Since being here, I’ve taken a day trip to Edinburgh, started exploring local pubs with friends, snuck into the postgraduate library because it’s built in a church (the stained glass sets the mood for reading history), and helped a friend beachcomb for seashells for a biology class. Every day seems to bring something new – running through the rain back to my dorm after medieval history, helping a friend hunt down her stolen package, sitting by the sea with takeaway fish and chips. The possibilities feel endless. They say the rain is an inconvenience. They say the cigarette butts between the cobblestones are just garbage. They say the smell of the old buildings isn’t pleasant. But I say the rain blurs the edges of reality, shrouding St. Andrews in mystery. I say the cigarette butts unite the students and locals. I say the smell of the old buildings is a reminder of the generations of students who came before us. St. Andrews is more than it seems. It’s not just a town that houses the oldest university in Scotland. It’s a town for anyone to enjoy whether playing a round of golf with the North Sea to your right, wandering through narrow alleyways, or sitting in a coffee shop with a cup of tea while storm clouds roll in. It doesn’t matter who you are or what you like; St. Andrews may be small, but it has a bit of everything. Larissa Edel is a Piedmont resident and former Post intern who is now a first-year student at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland. St. Andrews University in Fife, Scotland

articles.text: An increasing number of couples are choosing to include their furry friends in their wedding day, and it’s easy to see why! Your dog is a beloved member of the family, and having them by your side on your special day can make it even more unforgettable. However, incorporating your pup can add an extra layer of chaos to an already stressful event. Luckily, with some careful planning and simple tips, you can include your pawsome partner in your wedding day stress-free. First, be sure to plan your schedule carefully for the days leading up to the ceremony. Does your dog need a grooming appointment? Schedule it with enough time for touch-ups. Also make sure it is close enough to the big day that you can ensure your pooch remains perfectly coiffed. If you’re purchasing accessories like a custom flower girl collar or ring bearer pillow to attach to your pup’s harness, make sure to order items way ahead of time and do a dress rehearsal to avoid last-minute issues. If your dog is joining you at a destination wedding, make sure to pack their essentials including food, medication, waste bags, and a crate. The crate will provide a safe space for your dog to decompress during the festivities, ensuring Fluffy is alert and smiling in her photos. One of the most important things to plan for is assigning someone the role of designated dog attendant. This is one more way to greatly reduce stress on your wedding day. This person will be in charge of holding your fur baby during the ceremony, bringing them to photos, and caring for them during the reception. Finally, if you’re incorporating your dog into the ceremony, make extra time to rehearse in order to teach your dog where to go, and who to go to. Make sure someone at either end of the aisle has a leash handy. And remember, if your dog doesn’t behave exactly as planned on the wedding day, this often makes for a memorable and hilarious moment rather than an embarrassing one. can ensure a stress-free and enjoyable wedding day experience for both you and your furry friend. Remember, your wedding day is about celebrating your love, and with a little planning, your dog can be a happy and integral part of it. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland. She helped to launch the service dog and facility dog training organization Alpha Dog Assist in Mill Valley consultation. pages.text: 20 Wednesday, October 15, 2025 Features A Yank discreetly invades Scotland By Larissa Edel Special to the Post They say St. Andrews is a small, relatively quiet, rainy seaside town. They say the students who attend the university are some of the smartest in the United Kingdom and beyond. They say St. Andrews is a bubble, isolated from the rest of the world past the rolling green hills of the Scottish countryside and across the frigid waters of the North Sea. They say nothing has changed in the almost 700 years since the town was founded. I have found almost all of these claims to be true – except for the one about the town being quiet. Every street you travel, every pub you pass or store you enter, there is some kind of noise. Whether it’s a group of friends passionately talking on their way to a lecture, the clatter of a construction site and its crew, or the laughter of older Scottish men nursing a pint as the sun goes down. Whatever the sound, St. Andrews is filled with it in a way that makes it seem as if the air and ground are humming along. My first week at university – orientation – consisted of walking an average of 10,000 steps a day, exploring a town that for the most part still lives in the 15th century, going to a polo match on the beach, and discovering the Tesco meal deal (a genuine lifesaver in times of need). Now, after writing that sentence, I can’t believe this is my life. That the clatter of hoofbeats on the wet sand of West Sands Beach, the loud chatter of students watching the polo match unfold, and the pop of a champagne bottle could all combine into something considered normal. But even then, my attention kept turning toward the view to my right – the outline of the historic town against the gray clouds, with the sound of hoofbeats and mallet whacks to accompany it. It still feels like something straight out of a movie. As the days went on, I found that my two closest friends so far were both juniors on exchange, an Australian from Canberra and an American from Minnesota. I met the Minnesotan while I was lost and desperately trying to find IT, and with true Midwestern hospitality she immediately helped me. We parted ways, but later that night at a dorm bonding event I saw her again and she introduced me to the girl from Australia. The three of us live on the same floor, so most nights, when we aren’t drowning in assignments and readings, we’re in one of our rooms watching a show in the background while we talk about everything and anything. And while I’m acutely aware that both of them will be leaving after the first semester, that’s a problem for me to handle in December. Not to worry, I have plenty of other friends: a Scot and an Italian I walk with every Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday morning to our International Relations class. We once got into quite a debate about driving licenses and the legitimacy of an American one, because apparently it’s too easy to be considered a test. I was offended, but they weren’t entirely wrong. I have a German friend to get coffee with, another Australian to play tennis with, a Brit to discuss shows we’ve both watched and their insanely bad plot points. Too many nationalities, but that is the point: St. Andrews is truly international. When classes started, I found it surreal to walk through buildings and quads that are centuries old. As an American, our history mostly dates to 1776. While that’s a decent chunk of time, it’s nothing like living in the first dorm ever built at St. Andrews and walking down the same hallways people 200 years ago walked down. Or even studying in a library whose floor creaks with every step because the wood is older than everyone there combined. It’s strange that in Scotland, this kind of history is so… normal. That’s honestly the only way I can put it. In the same breath you can look at a Pret a Manger and see the remains of what once was Scotland’s oldest and largest abbey before it was destroyed by Henry the Eighth. Since being here, I’ve taken a day trip to Edinburgh, started exploring local pubs with friends, snuck into the postgraduate library because it’s built in a church (the stained glass sets the mood for reading history), and helped a friend beachcomb for seashells for a biology class. Every day seems to bring something new – running through the rain back to my dorm after medieval history, helping a friend hunt down her stolen package, sitting by the sea with takeaway fish and chips. The possibilities feel endless. They say the rain is an inconvenience. They say the cigarette butts between the cobblestones are just garbage. They say the smell of the old buildings isn’t pleasant. But I say the rain blurs the edges of reality, shrouding St. Andrews in mystery. I say the cigarette butts unite the students and locals. I say the smell of the old buildings is a reminder of the generations of students who came before us. St. Andrews is more than it seems. It’s not just a town that houses the oldest university in Scotland. It’s a town for anyone to enjoy whether playing a round of golf with the North Sea to your right, wandering through narrow alleyways, or sitting in a coffee shop with a cup of tea while storm clouds roll in. It doesn’t matter who you are or what you like; St. Andrews may be small, but it has a bit of everything. Larissa Edel is a Piedmont resident and former Post intern who is now a first-year student at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland. Tips for making your dog part of your wedding day By Sierra Berrick An increasing number of couples are choosing to include their furry friends in their wedding day, and it’s easy to see why! Your dog is a beloved member of the family, and having them by your side on your special day can make it even more unforgettable. However, incorporating your pup can add an extra layer of chaos to an already stressful event. Luckily, with some careful planning and simple tips, you can include your pawsome partner in your wedding day stress-free. First, be sure to plan your schedule carefully for the days leading up to the ceremony. Does your dog need a grooming appointment? Schedule it with enough time for touch-ups. Also make sure it is close enough to the big day that you can ensure your pooch remains perfectly coiffed. If you’re purchasing accessories like a custom flower girl collar or ring bearer pillow to attach to your pup’s harness, make sure to order items way ahead of time and do a dress rehearsal to avoid last-minute issues. If your dog is joining you at a destination wedding, make sure to pack their essentials including food, medication, waste bags, and a crate. The crate will provide a safe space for your dog to decompress during the festivities, ensuring Fluffy is alert and smiling in her photos. One of the most important things to plan for is assigning someone the role of designated dog attendant. This is one more way to greatly reduce stress on your wedding day. This person will be in charge of holding your fur baby during the ceremony, bringing them to photos, and caring for them during the reception. Finally, if you’re incorporating your dog into the ceremony, make extra time to rehearse in order to teach your dog where to go, and who to go to. Make sure someone at either end of the aisle has a leash handy. And remember, if your dog doesn’t behave exactly as planned on the wedding day, this often makes for a memorable and hilarious moment rather than an embarrassing one. By following these tips, you can ensure a stress-free and enjoyable wedding day experience for both you and your furry friend. Remember, your wedding day is about celebrating your love, and with a little planning, your dog can be a happy and integral part of it. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland. She helped to launch the service dog and facility dog training organization Alpha Dog Assist in Mill Valley consultation. To contact her call 507–2017, email Sierra109@gmail.com, or visit her website at www.oakhillsdogtraining.weebly.com. ADVERTISE IN THE POST St. Andrews University in Fife, Scotland

articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group enjoyed a special walk last week led by walker and architect Jim Kellogg. The outing, titled Piedmont Heritage Trees and Architectural Heritage, combined a tour of the city’s distinctive trees with a look at how Piedmont’s architectural character first took shape in the late 19th century. A strong turnout of about 40 walkers and three canine companions gathered at the Exedra on a crisp fall morning. From there, the group followed a loop that took them past City Hall, along Bonita Avenue and Park Way to Dracena Park, and back to the Recreation Department Building by way of Jerome and Magnolia Avenues. Along the route, walkers learned about the origins of Piedmont’s architectural styles, the city’s Heritage Tree program, and even received a preview of the soon-to-open Piedmont Community Pool. Kellogg began by describing the Piedmont Heritage Tree program, launched in 2018 and coordinated by parks and project manager Nancy Kent. The program’s goal is to recognize distinctive trees notable for their size, species, location, or historical importance in Piedmont’s parks and open spaces. Since its inception, the Park Commission has designated 28 Heritage Trees. A full list, with photos and an interactive map, can be found at piedmont.ca.gov. Just steps from the Exedra are six examples of these designated trees. They include the Highland Poplar grove encircling the Exedra itself, two majestic Coast Live Oaks, the tall Coastal Redwood used for Piedmont’s holiday tree lighting, the Yulan Magnolia gracing the front of Community Hall, and the Akebono Cherry grove that surrounds the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. From there, Kellogg guided the walkers to Vista Avenue, where two “Mountain Moon” evergreen magnolias stand prominently in front of City Hall. The group then paused at the Wetmore House on Vista and Bonita Avenues, built in 1878. Kellogg explained that the home, the oldest in Piedmont, is an excellent example of French Colonial–Plantation style architecture. Across the street, City Hall, designed in 1910 by architect Albert Farr, represents the Spanish Mission Revival style that would influence many of Piedmont’s later civic buildings, including Frank C. Havens Elementary School. Continuing down Bonita Avenue, walkers viewed several homes that capture the transition between architectural eras. The Bekenfeld House at 227 Bonita, built in 1895, remains Piedmont’s finest Queen Anne Victorian, complete with spindle detailing and a whimsical carved gargoyle in its front gable. Next door, the Esty House at 231 Bonita, built just a year later, reflects an entirely different vision—a shingle-sided Berkeley Craftsman with multiple gables, dormers, and handcrafted redwood interiors. As Kellogg noted, Piedmont’s style shifted quickly at the turn of the century from ornate Victorian to the simpler, nature-inspired Craftsman aesthetic. pages.text: Wednesday, October 15, 2025 21 Walking on Wednesday Walking on Wednesdays explores Piedmont’s heritage trees and architecture By Jim Kellogg The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group enjoyed a special walk last week led by walker and architect Jim Kellogg. The outing, titled Piedmont Heritage Trees and Architectural Heritage, combined a tour of the city’s distinctive trees with a look at how Piedmont’s architectural character first took shape in the late 19th century. A strong turnout of about 40 walkers and three canine companions gathered at the Exedra on a crisp fall morning. From there, the group followed a loop that took them past City Hall, along Bonita Avenue and Park Way to Dracena Park, and back to the Recreation Department Building by way of Jerome and Magnolia Avenues. Along the route, walkers learned about the origins of Piedmont’s architectural styles, the city’s Heritage Tree program, and even received a preview of the soon-to-open Piedmont Community Pool. Kellogg began by describing the Piedmont Heritage Tree program, launched in 2018 and coordinated by parks and project manager Nancy Kent. The program’s goal is to recognize distinctive trees notable for their size, species, location, or historical importance in Piedmont’s parks and open spaces. Since its inception, the Park Commission has designated 28 Heritage Trees. A full list, with photos and an interactive map, can be found at piedmont.ca.gov. Just steps from the Exedra are six examples of these designated trees. They include the Highland Poplar grove encircling the Exedra itself, two majestic Coast Live Oaks, the tall Coastal Redwood used for Piedmont’s holiday tree lighting, the Yulan Magnolia gracing the front of Community Hall, and the Akebono Cherry grove that surrounds the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. From there, Kellogg guided the walkers to Vista Avenue, where two “Mountain Moon” evergreen magnolias stand prominently in front of City Hall. The group then paused at the Wetmore House on Vista and Bonita Avenues, built in 1878. Kellogg explained that the home, the oldest in Piedmont, is an excellent example of French Colonial–Plantation style architecture. Across the street, City Hall, designed in 1910 by architect Albert Farr, represents the Spanish Mission Revival style that would influence many of Piedmont’s later civic buildings, including Frank C. Havens Elementary School. Continuing down Bonita Avenue, walkers viewed several homes that capture the transition between architectural eras. The Bekenfeld House at 227 Bonita, built in 1895, remains Piedmont’s finest Queen Anne Victorian, complete with spindle detailing and a whimsical carved gargoyle in its front gable. Next door, the Esty House at 231 Bonita, built just a year later, reflects an entirely different vision—a shingle-sided Berkeley Craftsman with multiple gables, dormers, and handcrafted redwood interiors. As Kellogg noted, Piedmont’s style shifted quickly at the turn of the century from ornate Victorian to the simpler, nature-inspired Craftsman aesthetic. Another highlight was the Harold Farr House at 127 Bonita, built in 1907. Designed by Albert Farr for his brother, it was the architect’s first project in Piedmont and showcases his early Craftsman design with a cedar shingle exterior and multiple gabled roofs. Farr’s later works, like City Hall, revealed his adaptability as he embraced the Mission Revival look that became his hallmark. The group continued down Park Way to Dracena Park, where they encountered four more Heritage Trees. These included a mature Coastal Live Oak, a California Buckeye recently nominated for Heritage status by residents Jack and Sharona Fischrup, a native Bigleaf Maple, and a grove of six Dawn Redwoods in the old quarry area. Kellogg shared that Dawn Redwoods were once thought extinct—known only from fossils—until living specimens were rediscovered in central China in 1948. Today they are thriving again and stand as one of only three remaining redwood species alongside the Coastal Redwood and the Giant Sequoia. From Dracena Park, the walkers proceeded along Latham Street to Jerome and Fairview Avenues, where they viewed a contemporary remodeled home showcasing modernist, sustainable design. With horizontal redwood siding and brightly colored stucco accents, the home draws inspiration from Mexican architect Luis Barragán, whose modernist approach celebrated color, light, and simplicity. Kellogg noted that several new Piedmont homes now feature modernist or sustainable elements, representing a broader interpretation of architectural heritage than the city’s early-20th-century roots. The tour concluded at the Piedmont Community Pool complex, where Hadley Clegg, the Recreation Department’s aquatic coordinator, greeted the group. Clegg described the nearly completed facility, now in its commissioning phase, which will soon open for community use. The complex includes a 27-meter, 12-lane competition pool; a large multi-depth family pool; locker and restroom facilities; a multipurpose community room for small events; and an outdoor rooftop pavilion with panoramic views of the grounds. Both pools will feature year-round heated water, and programs will include swim training, lap swimming, water polo, and rental options for group activities. The walkers were impressed by the design and the promise of expanded recreation opportunities for residents. “It’s wonderful to see how the city is blending heritage with the future,” one participant remarked. The Walking on Wednesdays group continues to meet each week at 10:30 a.m. at the Exedra, at the corner of Highland and Magnolia Avenues. Everyone is welcome to join, including friendly dogs. There is no cost to participate, though registration is required. To register, visit tinyurl.com/3ethkehu or call (510) 420-3070 for more information. articles.text: Piedmont opened the second set with a pair of points thinks to a serving error and an ace by Allyson Hunyh, but Alameda went back ahead. The Highlanders got back to the front at 9-8 following a kill by Nora Trombi and an ace by Skye Prata Baack, but the Hornets regained the lead at 11-10 and never relinquished. Both teams traded points until Piedmont tied the match at 22-22 after two kills by Stella Wilk and 23-23 after an AHS offensive error, but that was the closest it got. Alameda closed the set with a pair of kills to win it 25-23. In the third set, PHS opened with four straight points with two kills by Maika Ting and two aces by Huyhn. Piedmont pushed their lead to 12-4 following kills by Wilk, two aces by Carina Vora, and a kill by Trombi. However, Alameda chipped away at the lead to take over at 16-15. From there, Ting logged three straight kills to keep things close at 23-22 Alameda, but the Hornets won the set with a final kill. Final stats: Ting had 14 kills and five digs. Wilk had six kills, two digs, and an assist. Trombi had four kills. Izara Dando had three kills and one block. Sofia Meyer had two kills. Huyhn had two aces, two digs, and 13 assists. Community members are advised to avoid the area and use alternate routes whenever possible. Paving will take place between 7 p.m. and 7 a.m. During this period: • The intersection will remain open, with alternating lane closures. • Loud work will begin at 7 p.m. and should end by 10 p.m. • Moderate construction noise will continue overnight until 7 a.m. • The work area will be brightly lit. The City of Piedmont and the contractor, Rapid Grading Services, say they are taking steps to minimize impacts on nearby residents. Conducting the work at night is expected to reduce the total number of workdays and help avoid major daytime traffic disruptions. Grand Avenue Project Nears Completion Paving at the Oakland and Grand intersection is among the final steps of a $1.5 million roadway improvement and bicycle/ pedestrian safety project along Grand Avenue. The project includes: • Pedestrian safety enhancements, such as bulb-outs, flashing beacons, and high-visibility striping, at the Grand/ Linda and Grand/Greenbank intersections. • A bicycle turn box with flashing beacon push button at Grand and Linda. • ADA-compliant curb ramps at all street crossings. • Bulb-out islands and a landscaped bioswale at Grand and Fairview — Piedmont’s first “green infrastructure.” These improvements are part of the City’s 2021 Safer Streets Plan, which identified the Grand/ Linda and Grand/Greenbank intersections as two of the top ten priority locations for pedestrian safety improvements citywide. Heavy paving trucks and equipment will make their way to the intersection of Oakland and Grand Avenues starting this Wednesday night.

pages.text: 2 2 Wednesday, October 8, 2025 Opinion By Jay Russell QUESTION: What do you most enjoy about the changing of the seasons to fall? Asked on Friday, October 11, 2024. Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on October 16, 2024. DAWN ROUNSAVILLE, Grand Avenue I like the cooler temps, but not too cool. I’m heading to Virginia where the changing colors are just gorgeous. JEN ANZENBERG, La Salle Avenue The cooler weather, especially after two weeks of the heat wave. Firefighters’ Contract Continued from page 1 Department, particularly with the retaining and recruitment of Firefighter-Paramedics.” According to Gidney, the Fire Department has made progress toward full staffing, but still remains understaffed by two firefighter positions, with additional vacancies expected in the coming year. “Other Fire Departments are actively recruiting our members,” said Gidney, “and we lack sufficiently competitive pay and benefits to compete.” Gidney cited the recent loss of one of Piedmont’s firefighters to such recruiting, as well as seven union members already eligible to retire. The union advocated for solutions to retiree healthcare and longevity pay. According to the union, by rejecting their recommendations, the Council missed out on the opportunity to demonstrate real interest in the longterm employment of the City’s firefighters. The proposal would ensure that when young firefighters retire, they would have medical insurance to tide them over between retirement and Medicare eligibility. Firefighters would fund the “lion’s share” of the cost and be required to serve the entirety of their career with the City of Piedmont. The City’s commitment would be to manage the fund and ensure that premiums are paid. According to Gidney, the response from the City Council through their negotiator suggested that they were “not interested in discussing retiree medical insurance,” a response that the union found “regrettably offensive and disrespectful.” The second proposal was to provide modest additional compensation, or “longevity pay,” to firefighters who obtained certain service milestones. Common through the fire prevention industry, the practice is meant to provide incentives based upon experience, leading to better performance and ultimately enhanced service to the public. “Our further attempts to negotiate fell on deaf ears and our only option is the contract we have tonight,” said Gidney. “[The contract] makes no progress to ensure a high quality workforce, no progress to ensure the service levels that the residents of Piedmont deserve, no progress to care for the people who care for the city.” “To be clear,” Gidney added, “we are open to solutions, but so far the Council has offered none and disregarded ours.” ROBERT BOSTICK, PHS grad The obvious things are the leaves changing, and it’s cooler. I have to say I don’t like the shorter days though. PIPER GUIDI, 2nd grade We are excited to decorate for Halloween. BOBBY GRIBBEN, Wildwood Avenue I have to say football. The City reassures residents that regional communication networks will remain strong in the event of disaster. “As your police department, we’ll continue to work with our regional partners to pre-plan traffic control points, integrate live data through traffic cameras, AC Alerts and 911 Systems for realtime situational awareness,” said Police Chief Frederick Shavies. “We will conduct joint evacuation drills, like we have done in the past and continue to do, with residents to ensure familiarity and confidence. The City reassures residents that regional communication networks will remain strong in the event of disaster. “As your police department, we’ll continue to work with our regional partners to pre-plan traffic control points, integrate live data through traffic cameras, AC Alerts and 911 Systems for realtime situational awareness,” said Police Chief Frederick Shavies. “We will conduct joint evacuation drills, like we have done in the past and continue to do, with residents to ensure familiarity and confidence. Public Response A total of 23 speakers were in line to speak during public comment on the Specific Plan, with representation in favor and against the plan. “I fear that regardless of your true intentions, history will judge your endorsement of the scheme before you tonight as consistent with Piedmont’s record of exclusionary practices,” said one resident. “Please do not settle prematurely for the dangerous, implicitly discriminatory scheme just to please developers.” “It is going to be different,” said resident Andy Madera. “Moraga Avenue is going to look much different with apartment buildings there and we are going to have people living in our community that could not otherwise afford to live there, and so it will be different.” I think we should have some homes there,” said resident Vincent Fisher. “I think 132 is an appropriate number – I think 199 is ridiculous. I also think locating all the low-income housing on the far edge of Piedmont is not very good to those folks either.” Read the Draft Moraga Canyon Specific Plan and view video and materials from past meetings and events at piedmont.ca.gov/ MCSP. articles.text: Dear PUSD Families & Staff: It was great seeing so many parents and staff at this year’s Oktoberfest on Saturday. Thank you to Boosters for hosting this event, which provides critical funds for our athletics programs. And, a special thanks to all of the volunteers and sponsors who made this event happen, including our students who helped serve. And, I have to say that this year’s Oktoberfest fashion was fabulous, with more lederhosen and dirndl dresses than I have seen in a long time. Nicely done! In Partnership, Jennifer Hawn, Ed.D. Superintendent High School Courses Throughout the last month, I have written [at Smore.com/n/ gt0zk] about our efforts to align high school course offerings with students interests and needs. To this end, we have reviewed other high-performing high schools to compare course catalogs, we have surveyed students to better understand their course preferences, we have met with high school students to gather informal feedback, and we have discussed at a 9/12 Board Workshop and the 9/22 Board meeting. We have also discussed changes with administrators, teachers, and counselors to broaden our perspective on how the proposed changes may impact students’ high school experience and future college and career opportunities. One point we hear from staff is the concern about student well-being related to the number of AP courses a student may take. That is, if we offer more AP courses, students will feel compelled to take them in order to maximize a student’s effort to take the most rigorous course load available. This is an important point and one we should consider carefully. Will students take all of the APs made available, and will that impact their stress and overall well-being? Given our college-going community, I would acknowledge that the answer is likely yes to both questions. However, the issue [at Go.collegewise.com/school-limits-apclasses#limits] is more complex than whether to offer versus limit APs to ensure student wellness. Local context matters. A key factor to consider is the variety of offerings for students at all grade levels. I would argue that we have done a wonderful job of providing students with a smooth transition from 8th grade to 9th and 10th grade related to rigor. Where we have room for growth is in our non-STEM offerings at all grade levels. This year, we added AP Seminar and opened it up to grade 10 and above. What a wonderful course addition for all grades. Even better, 10th grade students have an AP option in addition to AP Computer Science Principles (another outstanding course, by the way). In order to further open up opportunities for students, at next week’s Board meeting, we will be looking at our high school graduation requirements to eliminate requirements that are not essential to meet the UC A-G requirements. We will also consider additional honors and AP offerings in a variety of subjects. The goal is to expand opportunities for students to explore their interests. One subject that we have few AP options for is History/Social Studies. We currently offer AP US History. Years ago, we offered AP European History; however, after the teacher left, so did the course. A review of similar high schools shows that we are alone in offering only one History/Social Studies AP. Moreover, student survey results indicate a strong desire for AP World History, which we are proposing to the Board as an offering for next fall. Finally, meetings with members of the History/Social Studies department indicate a desire to explore other options for students, including Honors and AP courses. We are excited to continue these conversations. Ultimately, the goal is to enhance student opportunities through course offerings that align with students interests and needs. We are grateful to our staff, students, and parents for their input on our course proposals that we are recommending for approval at Wednesday’s Board meeting. Green Space Opportunities The Board’s development and approval of a Strategic Plan in March 2023 included four strategic priorities, including “Creating an Environment to Thrive.” This priority includes the following: “Cultivate a culture of caring, belonging, and trust that will provide students and staff with the support they need to foster connections and truly engage in meaningful learning. Provide green, open spaces for students and staff to unplug and recharge in a welcoming and natural setting.” To these ends, the identification and development of a plan to cultivate green spaces throughout our campuses is presented in this green space report, prioritized according to two categories: first, locations that are or could be used by students and staff, and second, locations that are perimeter or adjacent spaces that are high traffic and highly visible. For groups who wish to sponsor or volunteer, please contact Pete Palmer at ppalmer@piedmont.k12.ca.us. A special thanks to Pete, our groundskeeping team, and our custodial team for ensuring our schools are wonderful green spaces for our students and staff to thrive. Green Space Sponsors will have a gratitude sign posted at the Green Space location. PMS Parents...your sign is in the works!

articles.text: We all can carry impossibly high standards for ourselves and others. At work, we want to be the leader who always has the right answer. At home, the parent who never loses patience. In community, the friend who shows up flawlessly every time. But here’s the truth: we’re all just humans human-ing — messy, imperfect, trying, failing, learning, and trying again. The sooner we admit that, the freer we become. Imperfection Is a Gift When we drop the myth of perfection, something beautiful happens: people exhale. The meeting that was stiff becomes honest. The team that was afraid to speak up starts sharing bold ideas. The child who thought they had to get it all right suddenly feels safe to experiment. Imperfection doesn’t lower the bar; it creates the trust that makes excellence possible. Giving Ourselves Permission It starts with us. How often do we replay in our heads, over and over again, the awkward moment, the misstep, the thing we should’ve said differently? That loop of self-criticism serves no purpose. So, what if instead we replaced the script with: “I’m just a human human-ing.” We’re all generally trying our best, and that’s all we can ask for. Extending Permission to Others The second step is grace outward. The colleague who missed a deadline. The houseguest who needed more than you expected. The friend who forgot to call. When we remember they’re just human-ing too, it softens our reaction. Compassion doesn’t mean ignoring accountability; it means recognizing that accountability lands best in a culture where mistakes aren’t met with shame, blame, or criticism. Closing Thought Next time you stumble, catch yourself, or catch someone else stumbling, remember: we’re all just humans human-ing. Give yourself and others permission to be imperfect, to learn, to keep going. In the end, we’re never going to reach the bar of “perfect,” so let’s not try. Instead, let’s celebrate the wins, the mistakes, and the in-betweens. articles.text: During the September 24 School Board Meeting Piedmont board trustees, students and teachers met to discuss education in Piedmont, including the State of the School report on Piedmont High School (PHS). Superintendent Jennifer Hawn noted that PHS Principal David Yoshihara sent out the first alumni newsletter, and the negotiations between the district and labor groups, teachers and CSEA unions, began on September 23. On negotiations, this time around, teachers are not negotiating salaries, but are questioning work conditions. The most urgent issue for Piedmont teachers is class size. “Our contract language is unusually weak [in that area],” said APT President Elise Marks about class size. In teacher contracts nothing is specified as to the maximum amount of students in each class, class size maximums are calculated per site, as an average. Nowadays, 5th grade classes average 27 or 28, up from 25 or 26 before the pandemic. Class sizes, when averaged with every class, get under the 28 student on average mark because some classes with unusually small enrollment bring the average under the watermark minimum. Public Comment During the public comment segment of the meeting, PHS senior Elspeth Grippando brought up the absence of a PHS math teacher following a firing. Grippando mentioned that retired teacher Doyle O’Reagan did well in his place but cannot continue. Math Analysis classes have been effected. Grippando explained that a new substitute, Ms. Hook, will take O’Reagan’s place and that Ms. Bailey, PHS art teacher, has been subbing for Math Analysis and plans to until the end of winter break. PHS Math teacher Olesia Parasiuk-Zasun is providing lessons for the substitutes, but not teaching. “These new substitute teachers are disrupting our learning pathways,” said Grippando. “Students need a real math teacher to learn,” she added. Another senior, Malia Williams, addressed the school board to talk about how PHS students don’t have off-campus privileges during the brunch period. Williams proposed offering it as a privilege for students with perfect attendance. Next to the microphone was PHS student, Stella Wilk, whom spoke to the unreliable parking around campus and proposed a student designated parking area. Wilk spoke about the difficulty in student parking directly leading to tardies. Recent changes in parking in the city’s civic center near the pool and police station are factors as well. Mira Sachs, last year’s student representative to the school board, spoke about the usage of Artificial Intelligence, requesting more guidance from the district on policies. “What we don’t have is directed guidance for how AI can be used positively for learning,” said Sachs. Sachs reported to the board there’s no set guidelines, and that students want to work efficiently but don’t know where the line is crossed. Next up for the school board will be a regularly scheduled meeting tonight, October 8, in City Hall at 7:00 p.m.
articles.title: Keeping up with the School Board: Sept. 24 recap

articles.text: When the bell rings at Piedmont High School, students’ phones are supposed to be tucked away. Under the current cell phone policy, phones must remain in backpacks or designated holders during class time, and they’re not to be seen during passing periods or brunch. This change follows Governor Gavin Newsom’s signing of the PhoneFree School Act, which requires every school district, charter school, and county office of education to adopt a policy limiting or prohibiting smartphone use by July 1, 2026. Last year, the rule was simpler: phones had to stay out of sight during class, but students could use them freely during short breaks. Now, students caught with their phones risk having them confiscated for the rest of the day, a shift many, especially juniors and seniors, are still adjusting to. While the policy is meant to improve focus and reduce distractions, its effect on students’ daily lives has been met with an overwhelmingly negative response. “I understand that some people are on their phones too much,” said sophomore Zoya Schulze, “but I feel that texting someone in the hallway shouldn’t get your phone taken away.” Senior Elias Reed-Miguel shared a similar view: “I think we should go back to the policy from last year. There were no problems with it, and if teachers want fewer phones, they could just be stricter about using the cell hotel.” Senior Olive Reining agreed, adding, “I don’t see how the new policy is an improvement from last year. I think kids should be able to use their phones as it’s our time.” The new rules have also changed how students manage stress and downtime. “The phone policy makes us less focused because we’re eager to use our phones more,” said junior Lukas Kim. Most students agree that the cell phone policy is frustrating, but some question whether it actually supports their personal growth. Rather than serving as a teaching tool, many feel it functions more as a punishment, removing the chance for students to learn responsibility and time management on their own. “I think students need to learn how to manage their phone use independently,” said senior Luke McAuliffe. “What works for one person might not work for another.” When asked what they’d like to see moving forward, most students agreed on one thing: they want to be part of the conversation. Despite student board representatives and even some teachers voicing opposition to the new rules last year, those concerns appear to have gone unheard. The policy may aim to reduce screen time and classroom distractions to ease teachers’ workloads, but it could also have the opposite effect. If this rule remains in place throughout high school for current freshmen, it might do more harm than good, limiting students’ ability to self-regulate and prepare for real-world expectations. In a society where technology is deeply woven into everyday life, learning how to use phones responsibly may be more valuable than banning them altogether. Whether the phone policy changes or stays the same, one thing is clear: the current approach feels more like a bandage over a toothache than a real solution. Evolette Mak is a student writer with the Piedmont Post.

So, what if instead we replaced the script with: “I’m just a human human-ing.” We’re all generally trying our best, and that’s all we can ask for. Extending Permission to Others The second step is grace outward. The colleague who missed a deadline. The houseguest who needed more than you expected. The friend who forgot to call. When we remember they’re just human-ing too, it softens our reaction. Compassion doesn’t mean ignoring accountability; it means recognizing that accountability lands best in a culture where mistakes aren’t met with shame, blame, or criticism. Closing Thought Next time you stumble, catch yourself, or catch someone else stumbling, remember: we’re all just humans human-ing. Give yourself and others permission to be imperfect, to learn, to keep going. In the end, we’re never going to reach the bar of “perfect,” so let’s not try. Instead, let’s celebrate the wins, the mistakes, and the in-betweens. Nina Meehan is a Communication and Creativity Speaker and Coach. https://ninameehan.com/ SPECIAL EVENT! articles.text: Attention bird paparazzi: The Moraga bald eagles are not the only draw in town. Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) reports that a flock of flamingos escaped their offices last week and are now tree-hopping in Piedmont. PEF is offering $25 Mulberry’s gift cards to the first five photojournalists who post pictures of the fugitive flamingos on Instagram and tag @piedmonteducationfund. “Every photo helps,” says Catie Osborn, Giving Campaign co-chair. “They can’t go far, they’re plastic.” In addition to helping them locate the flamingos, PEF hopes the Instagram posts will rally the community around the 2025/26 Giving Campaign, which kicked off earlier this month with a goal to raise $5,000,000 for district schools. This year, PEF is aiming for 100 percent participation from Piedmont families. “Our main goal is to create a strong community of proud donors,” says PEF Director Heather Frank. “Participation is vital to supporting our schools and signals a united commitment to bettering the education system for all students. When families and the broader community show up, it reinforces that we’re all in this together for the long haul.” One hundred percent participation may seem like a stretch goal, but with contributions of any amount, the PEF believes it’s well within reach. “Every dollar helps,” says Catie Osborn. “It’s not about the donation amount, it’s about working together to better the education for all our students.” PEF wishes all Piedmont pet detectives happy hunting for the purple birds around town. articles.text: PIE presents Understanding Sensory Regulation in Neurodivergent Children Piedmonters for Inclusive Education (PIE) kick off their annual Neurodiversity Speaker Series with a session on Understanding Sensory Regulation in Neurodivergent Children. The virtual event will be held on Tuesday, October 28 from 7:00 to 8:30 p.m. RSVP at Uclawsf.zoom. us/meeting/register/4aJnivLMSDOux50lIeMF0Q#/registration to receive the Zoom link. About the event: When children show big behaviors such as throwing things, leaving the group, or struggling to sit at dinner, it’s often a sign of being overwhelmed, not defiance. This talk will reframe behavior as communication and explore how sensory differences can impact regulation at home and in school. Parents will learn how to become “sensory detectives,” spotting cues of overwhelm, building trust through connection, and using practical tools, from sensory breaks to emotional regulation strategies to support children to thrive. The event will discuss ways to set loving limits, foster resilience, and create environments where kids can meet their full potential. About the speaker: Lee-Anne Bloom, MS, OTR/L is the founder of Oak Bloom OT in Oakland. She helps children thrive through a strengths-based approach that blends play, creativity, interest exploration, and mindful awareness. With expertise in ADHD, Autism, and Sensory Processing differences, she supports kids in building skills, resilience, and confidence while adapting environments for sensory and emotional needs. As both a professional and a parent of a neurodivergent child, she is passionate about de-stigmatizing neurodiversity. About PIE: Founded in 1999, PIE is a volunteer-run community of parents committed to advancing equity and inclusion for children with disabilities and learning differences in Piedmont schools. PIE works alongside families, educators, and the school district to strengthen the schools, foster understanding and acceptance, and provide a supportive network for families. Visit www.piedmontie.org to learn more.
articles.title: Neurodiversity speaker series opens Oct. 28

articles.text: This fall, six seniors from Piedmont High School were recognized as National Merit Semifinalists, an honor awarded to the top one percent of high school juniors nationwide based on their PSAT/NMSQT scores. “I felt pretty good coming out of the test, so I was just happy when I saw I got semifinalist,” said Nathan Tuan. “I prepared by doing Khan Academy and the Blue Book tests, and some College Board problems that you can find on their website.” Another semifinalist, Athena Li, reflected on her preparation with a casual approach. “I did the two practice PSATs on College Board a little while beforehand. I honestly wasn’t aiming for it, I just thought I’d take the test and see how I’d do.” The National Merit Scholarship Program recognizes academic excellence and gives students the opportunity to advance to the finalist stage, where they can compete for scholarships totaling more than $30 million nationwide. However, beyond the prestige, the financial reward is not as significant as many might assume. “Being a semifinalist does not affect my college plans at all. They don’t really give that much money,” said Maddox Ma. “It’s like $2,500 one time, so not enough to make an impact.” Given the sheer difficulty and rarity of becoming a semifinalist, many find it surprising that such an achievement yields a relatively modest monetary reward, especially considering the soaring cost of college tuitions today. The $2,500 scholarship, while symbolic of academic excellence, barely makes a dent in the financial reality of higher education, where a single semester’s tuition can easily exceed twenty times that amount. Still, the recognition carries value beyond numbers. Earning a spot among the top one percent of test takers nationwide is less a financial victory than a reflection of persistence, preparation, and curiosity. In an academic world often driven by outcomes, the National Merit distinction reminds students that the pursuit of knowledge still holds meaning on its own. Out of 3,500,000 PSAT test takers, around 16,000 students are named National Merit Semifinalists. 35 years of experience in architectural design www.kaplanarchitects.com (510) 361-0223

articles.text: The Piedmont High School Class of 1960 held its 65th reunion on September 20 at the Moraga Country Club. There were 49 attendees, 35 of whom were from the class, and five who still make their home in Piedmont. The event began at noon with a number of people arriving early. The camaraderie started immediately with a warm greeting of “it’s so good to see you,” followed by hugs. The event was to be from noon to four and included a lovely buffet of salmon, chicken, and delicious salads. There was no planned program except a short introduction by Matt Lifschiz, the “Chairman of the Reunion Committee”. The latter is a group of 18 classmates who have enjoyed getting together for many years to plan the event. This class is a little unusual as they don’t seem to wait every 5 years, as is customary. In fact, they had a reunion last year at the same venue, and everyone had such a good time that they said to do it again in 2025. Since their 50th reunion in 2010, this group has had at least six “reunions”. A couple were in a private home, and the others were at various restaurants, including Trader Vic’s. The latter was also the site of a special birthday tribute to one of their favorite teachers, Jim Killian, and included members from the classes of ‘59 and ‘61. Besides residents of Southern and Northern California, guests came from Oregon, Idaho, Nevada and Pennsylvania. As the afternoon started to wind down, the quiet buzz around the room was that this was probably going to be the last reunion, as the committee is getting tired. The buzz got louder, and the wishes were heard that the majority would love another get-together, even if it could be something simple in a private home. This Class of ‘60 loves being together and sharing what’s happening, where they are living, and what they are doing. So, who knows? It might happen again next year or if not, surely in two years. PHS 1960 classmates still living in Piedmont include Gage Lund Herman (left), Liz Land Silverman, Stan Silverman, Fran Bishopric Wolfe, and Matt Lifschiz.
articles.title: PHS Class of ’60 celebrates 65th reunion

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, free compostable bags are available at City Hall to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. Compostable bags are also available from Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) for a fee. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: Photos by Jenni Tsoi Best Ian Chung (1494) and Noah Sohn (1518) leading things for the boys’ team out the gate at the Artichoke Invitational. Piedmont Cross Country Teams Strong in Early Meets Piedmont High’s cross country teams competed in two events over the past week, including their first Western Alameda County Conference meet of the season at Point Pinole Regional Park on Wednesday, Oct. 1, and the Artichoke Invitational at Half Moon Bay High School on Saturday, Oct. 4. The Highlander boys won the WACC meet in a field of nine schools, while the girls finished fourth of nine. At the Artichoke Invitational, Piedmont’s girls placed fourth of 19 teams in the small schools division, and the boys were seventh of 27. “The varsity girls’ team had a very good team performance again on Saturday,” coach Steve Zirkelbach said. Filling in for Zirkelbach at the league meet was assistant coach Leighton Mand charges her way up a hill at the Artichoke Invitational. and PHS alum Sophia Mills. “This one is always a fun one with some added challenges like the massive hill and a few hay bales to hurdle,” Mills said. “A highlight for me once again was the tight spread of the varsity boys squad, about 30 seconds from first to fifth runner.” The Highlanders now look ahead to the Asics Clovis Invitational at Woodward Park, which is also the site of the CIF State Championships, on Oct. 10-11. The long-running event, now in its 46th year, will bring together hundreds of athletes from across California. Artichoke Invitational Junior Leighton Mand led the girls with a 16th-place finish among 158 runners, clocking 15:11 on the 2.3-mile course. Senior Skylar Best followed in 20th at 15:26, and junior Amalia Gray was close behind in 22nd at 15:35. Sophomore Nikita Gorelik placed 33rd (15:58), and sophomore Viviane Oesterer rounded out Piedmont’s top five in 55th (16:34). Skylar Best (1488) in the middle of a huge pack at the Artichoke Invitational.
articles.title: Boys win WACC Meet, girls place fourth at Artichoke Invitational

articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis team reeled in two wins over the past week to improve their record to 8-8 overall. They recently defeated Western Alameda County Conference foe, Berkeley, in a clean 7-0 sweep at the Corey Reich Tennis Center on Thursday, October 2, while they beat Marin Catholic 5-2 on Tuesday, September 30. The Highlanders’ win over Berkeley improved their league record to 2-1 with five WACC matches left in the regular season before the league’s individual tournament on November 7-8. In their win over the Yellowjackets, freshman Ella Ruthven had a dominant 6-1, 6-1 win at No. 1 singles. Ruthven has been Piedmont’s top singles starter for the season, a rarity for a freshman newcomer. “It’s really fun playing singles. The team has been really fun and super supportive. I’m getting a lot of great tips to win my matches,” Ruthven said. As the No. 1 singles starter, Ruthven has had her share of difficult matches, including g a narrow loss to Marin Catholic, 7-6 (10-8), 6-4. Despite taking on some of the best competition throughout the North Coast Section, Ruthven is keeping a positive perspective. “It’s definitely pushing me harder because a lot of my competition is older and bigger than me, but it just pushes to use my strengths and work on the things I need to work on. I just try to forget bad points and move on from the matches I lose, so I just try Staff Photos Ella Ruthven romped past Berkeley’s No. 1 singles player, 6-1, 6-1. Kate Jumper won her matches against Berkeley and Marin Catholic.
articles.title: Tennis team rolls past Berkeley, Marin Catholic

articles.text: It was a defensive battle for Piedmont, falling in a narrow 13-0 battle to Berkeley. Piedmont High’s flag football team traveled to Berkeley High on Monday, Oct. 6, falling 13-0 in a tough defensive matchup. The loss brings the Highlanders’ record to 4-8 overall, with four games remaining in the season. “Their coach came over and said our defense figured us out. We held them scoreless through three quarters, so that was impressive,” coach Beth Black said. “We made a lot of adjustments from our last game, and the players are applying them. It’s a bummer it’s not turning into wins.” The game marked quarterback Edie Elmquist’s return to the position after an injury forced her out for the previous two games. It was also Piedmont’s third straight contest without scoring points. “Edie had a sore arm, so she Staff Photos Kate Tong had an interception in the third quarter. didn’t throw before, but she threw well tonight and was connecting on more passes,” Black said. It was also a strong night for receiver Stephanie Lee, who caught eight passes. “Stephanie was making plays. She made good turns on the flat and really dipped her hips to avoid flag pulls. She’s good on both sides of the ball,” Black said. Stephanie Lee led the team with eight receptions.
articles.title: Piedmont falls to Berkeley in defensive battle

articles.text: Piedmont girls split league matches Piedmont High’s girls’ volleyball team split a pair of Western Alameda County Conference road matches last week, beating Encinal 3–1 on Sept. 30 before falling 3–0 to Castro Valley on Oct. 2. Maiki Ting and Stella Wilk powered the Highlanders past Encinal, combining for 30 kills: 17 from Ting and 13 from Wilk. Against league champion Castro Valley, sophomore Olivia Stevens led the team with 12 kills. She also anchored the defense versus Encinal with 25 digs. The Highlanders now stand at 8–6 overall and 1–3 in league play. With five matches left in the regular season, they need two more wins to automatically clinch a North Coast Section playoff berth, their first since 2018. 3–1 over Encinal All four sets were tight, each decided by five points or fewer. After dropping the opener 25–23, Piedmont won the next three, 25–20, 25–22, 25–23. Wilk opened strong with five kills and a block in the first set. Ting and Wilk each had four kills in the second, and Mira Sachs added two kills and a block. Ting led the way down the stretch with six kills in the third set and seven more in the fourth. Final stats: Ting 17 kills, one assist, two digs; Wilk 13 kills, three aces, one block, 18 digs, four assists; Dando six kills, one block, two digs; Allyson Huynh three kills, three aces, eight digs, 21 assists. 3–0 to Castro Valley The loss to Castro Valley was close throughout, with sets ending 25–20, 25–22, 25–22. Final stats: Wilk one kill, 14 digs, one ace; Ting two assists, 10 digs, three aces; Huynh 17 assists, 14 digs, one ace; Stevens 12 kills, two digs; Fiona Olsen and Jasmine Houlder one kill each; Trombi three kills, three digs; Dando three kills, one dig, one block; Meyer three kills, two digs, one assist. Next up: Piedmont (8–6, 1–3) visits Alameda on Thursday, Oct. 9, at 6:30 p.m. Maika Ting led with 17 kills against Encinal. Staff Photos Stella Wilk had 13 kills on Encinal, along with 18 digs. Olivia Stevens had 12 kills on Castro Valley.
