articles.text: Mark Kliszewski is known in Piedmont by two very different titles: Judge and Coach. By profession, he has spent four decades in the law, serving since 1985 as a Juvenile Court Referee for the Alameda Superior Court. His guiding principle is simple but powerful: young people deserve guidance, not just punishment. a volunteer who has devoted thousands of hours to coaching youth sports, including football, basketball, baseball, softball, and soccer. His players know him not only as a coach but as a mentor who builds discipline, confidence, and teamwork. Born in Overton, Wales, in 1949 to Polish parents who were liberated from Nazi concentration camps, Coach K came to the United States as a child. In Los Angeles, his parents became leaders in the Polish community, especially in Scouting and education, leaving a lasting impression of service that shaped his life. His impact has been widely recognized. In 1986, the City of Piedmont named him Outstanding Volunteer for his service to youth, and in 1991, he received the Service to Youth Award from the Piedmont Council of the Boy Scouts of America and the Sidney C. Singer family. These honors reflect not only his dedication to the law and the playing field, but also his lifelong devotion to helping young people succeed. Q: How did you first get involved with Piedmont High School football, and what was the program like when you started? Coach K: My son entered Piedmont Middle School as a pretty good football player. The head of the Rec Dept saw that, and, since a coach was needed for their teams, asked me to take on the 7th and then 8th grade teams. I did that for three years. Then Mark Kliszewski, known as “Coach K”, pictured in 2008. every season, and freshman players who had never played before entering high school. And we beat the cream of the crop around the Bay Area. It was truly wonderful and eventually led to some terrific varsity teams. Q: How has the role of student-athletes changed at Piedmont, especially when it comes to balancing academics and athletics? Coach K: I don’t believe that the student athlete has changed much. Piedmont students have always done very well academically, with many on the honor roll and having great success in school and in life. There are always some knuckleheads, but no one has been extraordinarily Coach K in 1969. Coach [Mike] Humphries, who was a good friend, asked that I join him in coaching the Freshman team at Piedmont High. I’ve stayed with one of the high school teams pretty much ever since. Q: What major changes have you seen in the football program over the decades—in terms of culture, coaching style, or player development? Coach K: When I began, football was a big deal in Piedmont. We played in a very tough league, and always did well. We had 3 teams of up to 40 players on each. Varsity and JV practiced on the big field and frosh were on the baseball outfield. It was great for development, as kids would come in with virtually no knowledge or ability, and would be ready for varsity before junior year. The culture was great. Witter was pretty much packed every Friday home night, and a band and cheerleaders were always there. On Homecoming there’d be a parade around the field, a contest between classes for best float, announcement of homecoming king and queen, a huge rally in the gym, etc. Generally, Piedmont was the same over summers, with coaches trying to get players to come to practices, and Piedmont families travelling all over the place. Coaching went from very good to pretty bad, as coaches were paid very little, and some just weren’t into it after a while. Our frosh program was great, because Mike Humphries stayed 48 years and I tagged along for 24. Q: How has the community’s involvement or support for the football program changed over the years? Coach K: Football has always been popular in Piedmont. There are fans, and they like to come out Friday nights and enjoy games. Teams were up and down most years, but community support has been pretty solid. Unfortunately, it has become difficult to get players to join the program. In the seventies and eighties, football was king. Since about 2010 there has been a slide. That can be attributed to several factors. Water polo and cross country have taken kids out of football to join their high school teams. Other season sports like basketball, lacrosse, swimming, baseball, etc. have attracted potential players to outside club teams who have insisted that they come to daily practices after school, thus eliminating them from football. Additionally, kids themselves, and oftentimes parents, have become very concerned about football injuries, and have opted not to play. And, of course, when COVID came along, football was very affected by the “no nearness” rules and barely hung on for three or four years. This is all exacerbated by the fact that there just aren’t enough students at PHS to fill all the teams. Luckily, the program has made a big comeback in the last 2 years and there is good hope for a future rebound. Q: Are there any particular seasons or games that stand out to you as especially meaningful or memorable? Why? Coach K: When I coached the frosh with Mike Humphries, we had an incredible run. We actually won 36 straight games over 5 years. This with a new class bad, and many have been very successful. Q: What are some of the biggest challenges the program has faced, and how did the team overcome them? Coach K: The COVID crisis of 2019-21 was very difficult. We were unable to play football. We could line up and run plays with our masks on, but we couldn’t get close to each other, or even use a ball. Practices were pretty ridiculous and players began to stop coming. We only had about 15-18 players on varsity so games were almost impossible to play. JV had about the same numbers. After 5 games varsity had to give up its season. Luckily, many of the varsity players were sophomores, so they were placed on JV and we managed to complete the JV season. That kept kids playing and did a lot to save football in Piedmont. Q: What values or lessons do you hope players take away from being part of the Piedmont football program? Coach K: Football is a pretty unique sport. All 11 players on the field have to be in sync for there to be success. If one player does the wrong thing, a play falls apart. This is a great lesson for life. Coordinating with other people, helping when someone needs help, working together towards a common goal, befriending others whom you may not know, all qualities that are begun in, and carried forward, from football. Also, hard work is learned and hopefully continued after football ends. Q: Have there been any traditions, rituals, or team habits that have stuck with the program across generations? Coach K: Each team has its own personality. Players between 14 and 18 years old have quirks and differences, but it’s pretty clear that almost everyone wants to better himself, get stronger, and win games. That never changes. Q: If you could leave future players with one piece of advice or one story that represents what Piedmont football is about, what would it be? Coach K: No matter how much you try, or even fail, stick with it. You can always make yourself better. You can always learn more. You can always challenge yourself to achieve the next goal. This interview is part of Jason Shum’s Eagle Scout Project with Troop 15, documenting the history of Piedmont High School football for the Piedmont Football Archive (PiedmontGridiron. club). Mark Kliszewski pictured in 1995.
articles.title: An Interview with Mark Kliszewski (Coach K)

articles.text: The Piedmont Middle School 8th grade girls’ volleyball team is rolling at 10-0 as the end of their season approaches. Piedmont Middle School’s 8th Grade Girls Volleyball team continues its regular season win streak. The Scots, who went undefeated in 7th grade regular-season play last year, have kept the momentum going this fall as 8th graders. Piedmont now stands at 10-0 with two regular-season games remaining. Their final home match was Monday, Oct. 6, at 4 p.m. in Morrison Gym against Willard, which had taken a set from them earlier this season. The Scots will finish the regular season on the road against Albany. Coached by Nikkola Yuen, the team is led by setters and defensive specialists Sarina Hill and Madelyn Huynh; libero Siena Botero; outside hitters Sofie Bechtel and Juliana Pouzo; middles Charlotte Bailey, Campbell Miller, Jane Saunders, and Ava Ubaka; and defenders Simone Tornatore and Abby Walsh-Poole. The team has dropped only two sets across its 10 matches, competing against Head-Royce (twice), Longfellow (twice), King (twice), Willard, Albany, Benicia, and Bentley. Their strong record secures them a spot in the upcoming East Bay Middle School Tournament in Lafayette later this month, where they will face other top programs. pages.text: 12 Wednesday, October 8, 2025 By Jason Shum Mark Kliszewski is known in Piedmont by two very different titles: Judge and Coach. By profession, he has spent four decades in the law, serving since 1985 as a Juvenile Court Referee for the Alameda Superior Court. His guiding principle is simple but powerful: young people deserve guidance, not just punishment. By passion, he is “Coach K,” a volunteer who has devoted thousands of hours to coaching youth sports, including football, basketball, baseball, softball, and soccer. His players know him not only as a coach but as a mentor who builds discipline, confidence, and teamwork. Born in Overton, Wales, in 1949 to Polish parents who were liberated from Nazi concentration camps, Coach K came to the United States as a child. In Los Angeles, his parents became leaders in the Polish community, especially in Scouting and education, leaving a lasting impression of service that shaped his life. His impact has been widely recognized. In 1986, the City of Piedmont named him Outstanding Volunteer for his service to youth, and in 1991, he received the Service to Youth Award from the Piedmont Council of the Boy Scouts of America and the Sidney C. Singer family. These honors reflect not only his dedication to the law and the playing field, but also his lifelong devotion to helping young people succeed. Q: How did you first get involved with Piedmont High School football, and what was the program like when you started? Coach K: My son entered Piedmont Middle School as a pretty good football player. The head of the Rec Dept saw that, and, since a coach was needed for their teams, asked me to take on the 7th and then 8th grade teams. I did that for three years. Then Mark Kliszewski, known as “Coach K”, pictured in 2008. every season, and freshman players who had never played before entering high school. And we beat the cream of the crop around the Bay Area. It was truly wonderful and eventually led to some terrific varsity teams. Q: How has the role of student-athletes changed at Piedmont, especially when it comes to balancing academics and athletics? Coach K: I don’t believe that the student athlete has changed much. Piedmont students have always done very well academically, with many on the honor roll and having great success in school and in life. There are always some knuckleheads, but no one has been extraordinarily Coach K in 1969. An Interview with Mark Kliszewski (Coach K) Coach [Mike] Humphries, who was a good friend, asked that I join him in coaching the Freshman team at Piedmont High. I’ve stayed with one of the high school teams pretty much ever since. Q: What major changes have you seen in the football program over the decades—in terms of culture, coaching style, or player development? Coach K: When I began, football was a big deal in Piedmont. We played in a very tough league, and always did well. We had 3 teams of up to 40 players on each. Varsity and JV practiced on the big field and frosh were on the baseball outfield. It was great for development, as kids would come in with virtually no knowledge or ability, and would be ready for varsity before junior year. The culture was great. Witter was pretty much packed every Friday home night, and a band and cheerleaders were always there. On Homecoming there’d be a parade around the field, a contest between classes for best float, announcement of homecoming king and queen, a huge rally in the gym, etc. Generally, Piedmont was the same over summers, with coaches trying to get players to come to practices, and Piedmont families travelling all over the place. Coaching went from very good to pretty bad, as coaches were paid very little, and some just weren’t into it after a while. Our frosh program was great, because Mike Humphries stayed 48 years and I tagged along for 24. Q: How has the community’s involvement or support for the football program changed over the years? Coach K: Football has always been popular in Piedmont. There are fans, and they like to come out Friday nights and enjoy games. Teams were up and down most years, but community support has been pretty solid. Unfortunately, it has become difficult to get players to join the program. In the seventies and eighties, football was king. Since about 2010 there has been a slide. That can be attributed to several factors. Water polo and cross country have taken kids out of football to join their high school teams. Other season sports like basketball, lacrosse, swimming, baseball, etc. have attracted potential players to outside club teams who have insisted that they come to daily practices after school, thus eliminating them from football. Additionally, kids themselves, and oftentimes parents, have become very concerned about football injuries, and have opted not to play. And, of course, when COVID came along, football was very affected by the “no nearness” rules and barely hung on for three or four years. This is all exacerbated by the fact that there just aren’t enough students at PHS to fill all the teams. Luckily, the program has made a big comeback in the last 2 years and there is good hope for a future rebound. Q: Are there any particular seasons or games that stand out to you as especially meaningful or memorable? Why? Coach K: When I coached the frosh with Mike Humphries, we had an incredible run. We actually won 36 straight games over 5 years. This with a new class bad, and many have been very successful. Q: What are some of the biggest challenges the program has faced, and how did the team overcome them? Coach K: The COVID crisis of 2019-21 was very difficult. We were unable to play football. We could line up and run plays with our masks on, but we couldn’t get close to each other, or even use a ball. Practices were pretty ridiculous and players began to stop coming. We only had about 15-18 players on varsity so games were almost impossible to play. JV had about the same numbers. After 5 games varsity had to give up its season. Luckily, many of the varsity players were sophomores, so they were placed on JV and we managed to complete the JV season. That kept kids playing and did a lot to save football in Piedmont. Q: What values or lessons do you hope players take away from being part of the Piedmont football program? Coach K: Football is a pretty unique sport. All 11 players on the field have to be in sync for there to be success. If one player does the wrong thing, a play falls apart. This is a great lesson for life. Coordinating with other people, helping when someone needs help, working together towards a common goal, befriending others whom you may not know, all qualities that are begun in, and carried forward, from football. Also, hard work is learned and hopefully continued after football ends. Q: Have there been any traditions, rituals, or team habits that have stuck with the program across generations? Coach K: Each team has its own personality. Players between 14 and 18 years old have quirks and differences, but it’s pretty clear that almost everyone wants to better himself, get stronger, and win games. That never changes. Q: If you could leave future players with one piece of advice or one story that represents what Piedmont football is about, what would it be? Coach K: No matter how much you try, or even fail, stick with it. You can always make yourself better. You can always learn more. You can always challenge yourself to achieve the next goal. This interview is part of Jason Shum’s Eagle Scout Project with Troop 15, documenting the history of Piedmont High School football for the Piedmont Football Archive (PiedmontGridiron. club). Mark Kliszewski pictured in 1995. Piedmont Middle School 8th Grade Girls Volleyball continues undefeated run The Piedmont Middle School 8th grade girls’ volleyball team is rolling at 10-0 as the end of their season approaches. By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont Middle School’s 8th Grade Girls Volleyball team continues its regular season win streak. The Scots, who went undefeated in 7th grade regular-season play last year, have kept the momentum going this fall as 8th graders. Piedmont now stands at 10-0 with two regular-season games remaining. Their final home match was Monday, Oct. 6, at 4 p.m. in Morrison Gym against Willard, which had taken a set from them earlier this season. The Scots will finish the regular season on the road against Albany. Coached by Nikkola Yuen, the team is led by setters and defensive specialists Sarina Hill and Madelyn Huynh; libero Siena Botero; outside hitters Sofie Bechtel and Juliana Pouzo; middles Charlotte Bailey, Campbell Miller, Jane Saunders, and Ava Ubaka; and defenders Simone Tornatore and Abby Walsh-Poole. The team has dropped only two sets across its 10 matches, competing against Head-Royce (twice), Longfellow (twice), King (twice), Willard, Albany, Benicia, and Bentley. Their strong record secures them a spot in the upcoming East Bay Middle School Tournament in Lafayette later this month, where they will face other top programs. Middle school girls volleyball is a fall sport managed through the Piedmont Recreation Department. A development program is also available, and teams are formed for both 7th- and 8th-grade players.

articles.text: Branford Marsalis Quartet The Branford Marsalis Quartet, one of the longest-running and most acclaimed ensembles in modern jazz, performs four concerts at Miner Auditorium in San Francisco October 23 through 26. The quartet returns to San Francisco to perform a range of music including a selection of the Keith Jarrett compositions that make up his 2025 Blue Note debut Belonging. Led by saxophonist Branford Marsalis, a Grammy-winning saxophonist and national Jazz Master, the quartet currently includes pianist Joey Calderazzo, bassist Eric Revis and drummer Justin Faulkner. Calderazzo and Revis joined the group in the 1990s, while Faulkner became the newest member in 2009. Marsalis, the group’s founder, is a highly regarded composer and jazz tenor saxophonist who comes from a lineage of jazz greats hailing from New Orleans. He is the eldest son of pianist and educator Ellis Marsalis, and his brothers Wynton, Jason and Delfeayo are all well-known musicians in the genre. Marsalis’ vast repertoire includes works by Copland, Debussy, Glazunov, Ibert, Mahler, Milhaud, Rorem, Vaughn Williams, Villa-Lobos and Sally Beamish. He is often a guest with leading symphony orchestras including those in Chicago, Detroit, Dusseldorf and North Carolina as well as the New York Philharmonic. Formed in 1986, the Branford Marsalis Quartet has remained a central outlet for Marsalis’ artistic vision, blending post-bop traditions with innovative improvisation and modern sensibilities. The group’s discography includes Braggtown (2006), Four MFs Playin’ Tunes (2012), and The Secret Between the Shadow and the Soul (2019). The Branford Marsalis Quartet performs at Miner Auditorium, presented by SFJAZZ, Thursday, October 23 through Sunday, October 26. All concerts begin at 7:30 p.m. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfjazz.org/.
articles.title: Branford Marsalis Quartet performs at Miner Auditorium Oct. 23 - 26

articles.text: Mezzo-soprano Daniela Mack joins the San Francisco Opera to perform a program of Manuel de Falla songs and Ludwig van Beethoven’s Fifth Symphony on Saturday, November 1, at the War Memorial Opera House. This one-night only concert begins with Manuel de Falla’s music from Siete Canciones Populares Españolas, inspired by his home country of Spain, and an arrangement of the second orchestral suite from his ballet El Sombrero de Tres Picos (The Three-Cornered Hat) (1917). The orchestra will perform Beethoven’s iconic Fifth Symphony after intermission. “The San Francisco Opera Orchestra and I customarily work together in the orchestra pit, but these musicians, due to their vast experience, can also command the stage. In our fall concert, the Orchestra will do just that in Beethoven’s Fifth Symphony,” Music Director Eun Sun Kim said in a press release. Kim added that Manuel de Falla “absorbed Beethoven’s influence, even citing the famous ‘fate’ motif from the Fifth SymDaniela Mack phony in his ballet.” Falla’s song cycle will feature mezzo-soprano Mack, a native of Buenos Aires who has gained critical acclaim as a classic soloist. She starred as Frida Kahlo in San Francisco Opera’s first Spanish-language opera, Gabriela Lena Frank and Nilo Cruz’s El último sueño de Frida y Diego (The Last Dream of Frida and Diego), in June 2023. The concert begins at 7:30 p.m. For tickets and more information, contact the San Francisco Opera Box Office at 301 Van Ness Avenue, call (415) 864-3330 or visit at sfopera.com.
articles.title: SF Opera presents Beethoven and Falla concert Nov. 1

articles.text: Musical runs from Nov. 15 - Dec. 30 at Ashby Stage Shotgun Players closes out its 2025 season with a new production of Sunday in the Park with George, the Pulitzer Prize–winning musical by Stephen Sondheim and James Lapine, showing November 15 through December 30 at the Ashby Stage in Berkeley. Directed by Susannah Martin with music direction by David Möschler, the show is inspired by Georges Seurat’s pointillist painting A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte. The musical explores the artist’s obsessive creative process and its impact on his relationships. The production features immersive on-stage seating and an expanded bar menu. “This musical captures the questioning, fear, joy, and obsession that go into making art and the toll it takes on the people we love,” Director Susannah Martin said in a press release. “I’ve never experienced a musical which gets so deeply into the experience of being an artist and the process of making art.” “The sound-world of the show is just as daring, provocative, interesting, and non-traditional as the type of art that the character of George Seurat was striving to create,” added Möschler. “It’s not book scenes followed by songs belted out ad nauseum; it’s a score that is interwoven through dialogue and comes together more like a film score that helps create a strong sense of narrative and dramatic continuity from beginning to end.” Kevin Singer stars as George, with Marah Sotelo as Dot. The cast includes Alex Rodriguez, Laura Domingo, Jill Slyter and a 16-member ensemble. Artistic Director Patrick Dooley called the work a “legitimate masterpiece,” adding, “Sondheim captures the tension between artist and muse, beautifully and tragically.” Tickets and performance details are available at shotgunplayers.org.
articles.title: Shotgun Players closes season with Sondheim’s Sunday in the Park with George

articles.text: Left Coast Chamber Ensemble (LCCE) opens its 33rd season with Midnight Memories: Mendelssohn, Mahler, Moderns, on Saturday, November 1 at Noe Valley Ministry in San Francisco, and Sunday, November 2 at First Church of Christ, Scientist in Berkeley. The season-launch program draws connections between 19th-century composers and contemporary voices through themes of memory, time and reflection, and features Gustav Mahler’s Rückert-Lieder, arranged by David Hefti, alongside Sillage, a contemporary piece by composer Artur Akshelyan. Sillage, which sets a poem by 20th-century Armenian writer Z. Melkonian, was the winner of LCCE’s 2024 Composition Contest. “Based on the text choices, I settled on a philosophically charged poem in which emotions embody a certain nostalgia, as if fragments of life and death coexist in collective memory, shaped by both past and future,” Akshelyan said in a press release. the things which remain constant: time, memory, endings and beginnings, the pursuit of happiness, and our connection to the world around us,” Hofman said. Performers include violinists Anna Presler and Liana Bérubé, violist Phyllis Kamrin, cellists Tanya Tomkins and Leighton Fong, pianist Allegra Chapman, guitarist Michael Goldberg, and soprano Nikki Einfeld as lead vocalist. Founded in 1992, Left Coast Chamber Ensemble is a collective of 17 musicians based in the San Francisco Bay Area. Known for thematic programs that pair contemporary and historical repertoire, the ensemble regularly commissions new works and engages in collaborations across disciplines. Its members perform in a range of settings, from chamber and orchestral concerts to multi-media and operatic productions. LCCE also runs an annual composition contest and offers a music education program. More information is available at leftcoastensemble.org or by calling (415) 617-5223. Soprano Nikki Einfeld is the featured soloist in LCCE’s upcoming Midnight Memories concerts. Also featured is music by Fanny Mendelssohn, part of the ensemble’s ongoing effort to connect 19th-century works with modern perspectives. articles.text: The Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) in San Francisco’s newest exhibition, UNBOUND: Art, Blackness, and the Universe, is now on view. UNBOUND is a unique group exhibition that explores connections between Blackness and spiritual cosmologies. Organized by Key Jo Lee, MoAD Chief of Curatorial Affairs and Public Programs, the community retrospective highlights the similarities between the Black existence and “cosmic Blackness,” or Afrofuturism. UNBOUND includes paintings, glass sculptures, and installations celebrating the modern artistic genre. The exhibition features artists David Alabo, Renee Cox, Oasa DuVerney, Torkwase Dyson, Allison Janae Hamilton, Barkley L. Hendricks, Cullen B. Washington Jr., M. Carmen Lane and Sidra Bell, Michi Meko, Gustavo Nazareno, Rashaad Newsome, Chris Ofili, Mikael Owunna, Harmonia Rosales, Lorna Simpson, Didier William, and Fred Wilson. “For the past twenty years, MoAD has proudly embarked on a journey to ensure that Black creative expression is embraced, elevated, and seen by international visitors and those that call the Bay Area home,” said Monetta White, Executive Director and CEO. “The artistic depth of UNBOUND will bring intergenerational African Diasporic voices together under an innovative curatorial framework that shifts the focus through which we understand and appreciate contemporary art.” “This exhibition is a celebration of the vast conceptual capacity of Blackness, and treats Black existence with the same imaginative and intellectual openness we apply to thinking through metaphysics and the cosmos,” Lee added. “In doing so, it makes a radical claim that Blackness is not marginal, but central to how we comprehend being, time, and the universe itself.” For more information, visit https://www.moadsf.org. Allison Janae Hamilton is one of over a dozen Black artists featured in MoAD’s UNBOUND.
articles.title: UNBOUND: Art, Blackness and the Universe now on view at MoAD

articles.text: Last Weekend! to Oct. 13, 11–2 p.m. Slavic Arts Exhibition The Center for Slavic Arts and Culture is proud to present its very first exhibition, KALEIDOSCOPE. The show brings together 17 artists from five Slavic countries, including a photographer and a jewelry designer, each sharing their talent and creative vision. In challenging and uncertain times, art reminds us of beauty, resilience, and the strength of our community. Kaleidoscope is a celebration of creativity, and a reminder of how art can connect, uplift, and inspire us all. This exhibition will be open weekend days from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. until mid-October. CSAC celebrates Slavic culture’s rich heritage and vibrant traditions, and works to preserve and promote the art, history, and unique identities of the twelve Slavic nations, fostering understanding and appreciation across diverse communities. Come to explore a world of creativity, tradition, and inspiration. Saturday, October 11, 6:00 p.m. Rebecca & Gary Parks Album Release Concert Rebecca Parks writes award-winning songs that set scenes, tell stories, and dramatize conversations. She has introspective vulnerability and a folk-rock sensibility with a theatrical touch. Her lyrics are sharp, her melodies memorable. She’s not afraid of controversial subjects, but she also doesn’t take herself too seriously. Brimming with gratitude, hard fought self-knowledge, and wry wit, Rebecca’s new album, Secret Stage, is a defining artistic statement. It proudly displays her prowess as a fingerstyle guitarist and pianist, and her sumptuous vocals and harmonies alongside her husband, the gifted vocalist, Gary Parks. Secret Stage explores maturity and personal themes of social justice, and comes with two bonus albums: Adventures with Amy is solo guitar work, and Dyad is a mix of folk and rock covers, with Gary singing lead on most of them and Rebecca contributing arrangements. Tickets at www.brownpapertickets.com/e/6712938, free for under-18! All paid attendees will receive a 3-CD set. Sunday, October 12, 4:30 p.m. In the Tradition Jazz & Pop Piano Trio The In the Tradition Piano Trio – Bill Jackman, Michael Jones, and Albert Brooks – will pay tribute to Jimmy Van Heusen, who composed nearly 1000 songs between 1930 and 1970, of which fifty or more have become American standards.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Gardens of Golden Gate Park Visit the museum for free on the second Tuesday of the month during regular operating hours. Admission to The San Francisco Botanical Garden (SFBG) is free on Tuesday, October 14, for all visitors including nonresidents. The 55-acre garden is located in the heart of Golden Gate Park, showcasing more than 8,000 different plant species from around the world making it one of the most diverse and botanically significant gardens in the United States. pages.text: Wednesday, October 8, 2025 15 UNBOUND: Art, Blackness and the Universe now on view at MoAD By Allyson Aleksey The Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) in San Francisco’s newest exhibition, UNBOUND: Art, Blackness, and the Universe, is now on view. UNBOUND is a unique group exhibition that explores connections between Blackness and spiritual cosmologies. Organized by Key Jo Lee, MoAD Chief of Curatorial Affairs and Public Programs, the community retrospective highlights the similarities between the Black existence and “cosmic Blackness,” or Afrofuturism. UNBOUND includes paintings, glass sculptures, and installations celebrating the modern artistic genre. The exhibition features artists David Alabo, Renee Cox, Oasa DuVerney, Torkwase Dyson, Allison Janae Hamilton, Barkley L. Hendricks, Cullen B. Washington Jr., M. Carmen Lane and Sidra Bell, Michi Meko, Gustavo Nazareno, Rashaad Newsome, Chris Ofili, Mikael Owunna, Harmonia Rosales, Lorna Simpson, Didier William, and Fred Wilson. “For the past twenty years, MoAD has proudly embarked on a journey to ensure that Black creative expression is embraced, elevated, and seen by international visitors and those that call the Bay Area home,” said Monetta White, Executive Director and CEO. “The artistic depth of UNBOUND will bring intergenerational African Diasporic voices together under an innovative curatorial framework that shifts the focus through which we understand and appreciate contemporary art.” “This exhibition is a celebration of the vast conceptual capacity of Blackness, and treats Black existence with the same imaginative and intellectual openness we apply to thinking through metaphysics and the cosmos,” Lee added. “In doing so, it makes a radical claim that Blackness is not marginal, but central to how we comprehend being, time, and the universe itself.” For more information, visit https://www.moadsf.org. pages.text: 16 16 Wednesday, October 8, 2025 The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet Festivities in Germany and a salute to the Bamberg Orchestra By Joseph Gold October 3 is a festive day in Germany because it is the celebration of the reunification of western Germany and eastern Germany after the war. In many ways, it is much like our Fourth of July. By coincidence, October 3 was the opening concert of the Bamberg Symphony. To put things into perspective, Bamberg and Santa Monica are relatively the same in size. Bamberg’s history goes back into the depths of antiquity. The Orchestra is much more recent. I think it was founded soon after the Second World War. What is interesting to note is that the Bamberg Symphony established itself as a very important Orchestra through recordings and impressive concerts. I want to extend thanks to their excellent organization and in particular to two ladies of the administration, Ms. Kahl and Ms. Mueller. My wife and I walked a long distance from our hotel to the Symphony Hall. As we approached there was a clearing, and we saw an extraordinarily beautiful building in front of us. We arrived about an hour early in order to get our tickets. The foyer of the auditorium was already filled with people enjoying a variety of liquid refreshments and other things to nibble on. It was obvious that everyone was having a good time. That’s the way things are in Germany these days. The interior of the concert hall is beautiful to look at. Is intelligently decorated and is comprised of blonde colored wood all around. The stage was empty, and at the appointed time the Orchestra assembled on the stage, All aspects of music at the Bamberg Symphony’s opening concert. The cartoons on the pamphlet prepared the audience for everything that came later. faced the audience and took their bows. I wish American orchestras would do it this way. The conductor, Manfred Honeck, walked to the podium energetically. It was obvious from the very start that the program was going to be out of the ordinary – and It was. One of the most famous concerts in the musical world is the New Year’s concert in Vienna performed by the Vienna Philharmonic. Well… Move over Vienna Philharmonic. This concert in Bamberg was every bit as good. The Orchestra plays in a most inspired fashion. The conductor is also an inspiring influence. It would be interesting to know whether the orchestra would play just as well with another The impressive concert hall in Bamberg conductor. All I can tell you is that everybody performed with inspiration. Musicianship was at a high level as were all aspects of profound concert performance. The Orchestra can play super softly and then make a huge crescendo. Everything is always in perfect proportion. It was as if everyone on stage was the reincarnation of the great singer Richard Tauber. Lovely soprano Jasmin Delfs was the soloist, and the Bamberg youth choir added to the program. There was inspiration at every turn. Of special interest The Bamberg Symphony is a very important part of this fine city. Let me quote from the beautiful printed program that was handed out. “We are the Bamberg Symphony. An orchestra with a hometown like no other. We are a UNESCO world heritage site with 1000 years of history. Bamberg‘s serenity and beauty inspire our unique characteristically, somber and warm sound. With this Bamberg sound, we captivate our audience with joy, passion, and dedication… And we bring it to the world.” The printed program is certainly a “keeper” and the concert was memorable in every aspect. When the concert ended, the audience stood up en mass and applauded enthusiastically. All of the performers stood up, faced the audience and took their bows. Bravi to all the performers and thanks for the experience. The concert hall in Bamberg is highly impressive. Everyone taking curtain calls at the Bamberg Symphony opening concert.

articles.text: “Suspension of disbelief” is a term often invoked when discussing certain genres of literature, film, or art. Coined by poet Samuel Taylor Coleridge in 1817, it originally referred to “poetic faith”—the idea that audiences willingly set aside skepticism to engage with a story’s imaginative world. Over time, the phrase has evolved to encompass a wide range of creative expressions. As defined today, it is the audience’s conscious decision to overlook logical inconsistencies and accept the impossible—whether in fantasy, fiction, or science fiction— so they can become emotionally immersed in an artist’s reality-bending vision. In short, it’s the act of believing there is something beyond the evidence. E.M. Forster captured this idea beautifully when he wrote: “For human intercourse, as soon as we look at it for its own sake and not as a social adjunct, is seen to be haunted by a specter… what we call intimacy is only a makeshift, perfect knowledge is an illusion. But in the novel we can know people perfectly… Fiction is truer than history for it goes beyond the evidence.” Children, of course, are natural masters of this art. Because their understanding of logic and physics is still forming, the line between reality and imagination remains soft. Their ability to believe, to accept the fantastic without hesitation, is what allows them to connect so deeply with stories of wonder. This is the foundation on which studios like Pixar, Ghibli, Disney, DreamWorks, and Warner Bros. have built their magic. Their films rely on anthropomorphism, imbuing animals or objects with human qualities, and on the limitless possibilities of animation and CGI. From the Marvel Universe to post-apocalyptic fiction, from The Time Traveler’s Wife to The Age of Adaline, audiences routinely embrace the impossible: superheroes, ghosts, aliens, spirits, and worlds that bend the laws of time and nature. For adults, grounded in science and logic, it can be tempting to dismiss such imaginative leaps. But encouraging children to suspend disbelief—to believe in Santa Claus and his flying reindeer, in elves at the North Pole, in worlds unseen—nurtures more than just creativity. Some psychologists suggest that imagination itself is linked to empathy: the capacity to share and understand the feelings of others. In that sense, the willingness to believe in something beyond the evidence may not only enrich art—it may also deepen our humanity. Set in West Texas—a desolate, wind-blown stretch of the Lone Star State where boarded-up storefronts and rusting farm equipment mark the landscape—Hell or High Water opens with two brothers robbing a small Midlands Bank branch. Their first attempt goes sideways when they arrive before the cash drawers are filled. Undeterred, they hit another branch, taking only small, untraceable bills before making their getaway and burying the car. Toby Howard (Chris Pine) and his ex-con brother Tanner (Ben Foster) are trying to steal just enough money to pay off the reverse mortgage on their late mother’s ranch—ironically held by the very bank they’re robbing. Toby, divorced and desperate to provide a better life for his two sons, has learned the property

articles.text: sits on oil-rich land, a fact not yet noticed by Midlands. Their robberies attract the attention of two Texas Rangers— Marcus Hamilton (Jeff Bridges), a grizzled veteran on the brink of retirement, and his partner Alberto Parker (Gil Birmingham). As they track the brothers from dusty town to dusty town, they trade dry banter and weary insights about the changing world around them. If you’re a fan of the Coen brothers’ No Country for Old Men, you’ll find much to admire here. Written by Taylor Sheridan (Sicario), the film is a taut neo-western and a richly drawn character study of four men bound by duty, family, and circumstance. The brothers’ love and resentment play out with a mix of grit and tenderness, while the Rangers’ easy-going ribbing masks affection forged through years on the road. Beyond its sharp dialogue and tense pacing, Hell or High Water offers a pointed look at rural America’s economic despair. Behind the faded façades of these small towns lies a quiet anger— ordinary people trying to keep their heads above water as the system fails them. The final act delivers both a satisfying twist and a somber inevitability. Every performance shines—Bridges once again proves his mastery, Pine brings quiet depth, and Foster delivers a live-wire unpredictability that keeps the film pulsing to the end. Hell or High Water. articles.text: Disney’s Lilo & Stitch, nominated for an Academy Award at the 75th Oscars, remains one of the studio’s most heartfelt and imaginative hand-drawn features. With its lush watercolor palette and Hawaiian setting, it’s a story that’s both whimsical and deeply human—family-friendly, poignant, and occasionally beguiling. Like E.T., it captures the loneliness of an outsider who discovers love and belonging in unexpected places. Set on the island of Kauai, the film follows Lilo (Daveigh Chase), a spirited 7-year-old girl struggling to cope after the death of her parents. Her older sister, Nani (Tia Carrere), works hard to care for her, but the two clash often—Lilo’s mischievous behavior and boundless imagination make things difficult. Hoping a pet might help, Nani takes Lilo to an animal shelter, where she chooses a strange blue “dog” she names Stitch. Unbeknownst to her, Stitch is actually a genetically engineered alien experiment designed to wreak havoc. Meanwhile, the Galactic Federation has dispatched Stitch’s mad scientist creator, Dr. Jumba Jookiba (David Ogden Stiers), A scene from Disney Animation’s Lilo & Stitch

articles.text: J.R. Villarreal and Keke Palmer in Akeelah and the Bee Akeelah and the Bee is a heartwarming and inspiring story that will captivate older kids and early teens alike. It centers on 11-yearold Akeelah Anderson (Keke Palmer), an African-American girl from South Los Angeles who discovers an extraordinary gift for spelling. Akeelah attends Crenshaw Junior High, a tough inner-city school where skipping class is common. She lives with her hardworking mother, Tanya (Angela Bassett), and her siblings; her father has passed away. When the school principal, Mr. Welch (Curtis Armstrong), recognizes Akeelah’s remarkable memory and her talent for spelling difficult, often obscure words, he encourages her to enter the school spelling bee. Though reluctant at first, Akeelah wins—and soon finds herself advancing through local and regional competitions, ultimately earning a spot at the prestigious Scripps National Spelling Bee. To prepare, she trains under Professor Joshua Larabee (Laurence Fishburne), a stern but caring academic on leave from his university. Her mother initially resists, believing that Akeelah’s focus should remain on school and family. Yet, with persistence from both the principal and Professor Larabee, Tanya comes to see her daughter’s gift for what it is—something rare and worth nurturing. As Akeelah’s journey continues, her siblings, friends, and even her community rally behind her. What began as a solitary pursuit transforms into a collective mission of pride and hope. pages.text: 18 Wednesday, October 8, 2025 MOVIES FOR KIDS Akeelah and the Bee Lilo & Stitch By Chris Honoré Disney’s Lilo & Stitch, nominated for an Academy Award at the 75th Oscars, remains one of the studio’s most heartfelt and imaginative hand-drawn features. With its lush watercolor palette and Hawaiian setting, it’s a story that’s both whimsical and deeply human—family-friendly, poignant, and occasionally beguiling. Like E.T., it captures the loneliness of an outsider who discovers love and belonging in unexpected places. Set on the island of Kauai, the film follows Lilo (Daveigh Chase), a spirited 7-year-old girl struggling to cope after the death of her parents. Her older sister, Nani (Tia Carrere), works hard to care for her, but the two clash often—Lilo’s mischievous behavior and boundless imagination make things difficult. Hoping a pet might help, Nani takes Lilo to an animal shelter, where she chooses a strange blue “dog” she names Stitch. Unbeknownst to her, Stitch is actually a genetically engineered alien experiment designed to wreak havoc. Meanwhile, the Galactic Federation has dispatched Stitch’s mad scientist creator, Dr. Jumba Jookiba (David Ogden Stiers), J.R. Villarreal and Keke Palmer in Akeelah and the Bee By Chris Honoré Akeelah and the Bee is a heartwarming and inspiring story that will captivate older kids and early teens alike. pages.text: Wednesday, October 8, 2025 19 AMERICANS IN PARIS By Patricia Forsyth Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on November 2, 2022 In France Toussaint, or All Saints, is a national celebration with emphasis on cultural and education for families during a two-week school closure. Toussaint is as major a holiday-break as Christmas, Winter-Ski, or Easter. The time off from school envelops three weekends where 2-3 days to explore châteaux can be indulged for a family getaway, or peut-être a longer trip to the South of France. The French schedule of eight weeks for school breaks, followed by an early July summer recess lasting seven weeks, with back to school on September 1st, could be better for family life-balance than in the U.S. Toussaint encourages families to spend time together and soak up the rich cultural history of their heritage. Long ago the remembrances were rooted in religious rituals and hocus-pocus, but today’s children are happily unaware of its origin. November 1st is All Saints to honor the dead, especially loved ones who have passed. Much earlier in France’s long history of Catholicism, prayers and blessings were intoned for the Martyrs, so numerous that they lacked their own feast day. Whether pagans or early Christians, the ancients feared the coming of the dark days of winter after the last harvest. Toussaint was a politic time to lobby the spirits that be. The iconography of Halloween is the same here as in the U.S., where dressed-up children cadge candy from their neighbors. articles.text: The Historic Pardee Home Museum and the National Women’s History Alliance (NWHA) are inviting community members to join them in recognizing the 114th Anniversary of the triumph of California suffragists winning passage of the pivotal Suffrage Amendment to the State Constitution in the 1919 election. This community event will be held at Oakland’s Pardee Home Museum in downtown Oakland, 672 11th Street, on October 4th at 1:00 p.m. The program will feature presentations, refreshments and a rousing California Women’s Suffrage Campaign Readers’ Theatre. Several local volunteers, representing individual suffragists, female and male, will briefly present the dramatic story of the challenges and campaigns women endured from their defeat in 1896 to their victory on October 10, 1911. As part of the celebration there will be a Tour of the Pardee Home Museum, one of California’s architectural and historical treasures. The beauty of the home museum and its gardens is striking. The stunning interior of the house showcases artifacts from throughout the world. Featured in the collection is a classic particularly relevant to this celebration: a unique First Edition of “The History of the Woman Suffrage” distinguished by a special lengthy inscription by Susan B. Anthony herself lobbying Governor Pardee to support California women’s right to vote. It’s only one thing to savor and enjoy at this special event. Admission to this California Suffrage Celebration is $25 and supports the Pardee Home Museum and the NWHA’s work. Tickets are available on Eventbrite or by calling Richelle Lieberman of Pardee Home at 510-381-1973. The Historic Pardee Home Museum

articles.text: World adventurer and coach of disabled and able-bodied athletes, Terry Cotter passed away on September 14, 2025. He was 84. Ralph Evans Cotter III, always known as Terry, passed away peacefully on Sunday, September 14 at Stanford Hospital. Terry was born on September 12, 1941 as the son of Mr. and Mrs. Ralph E. Cotter, Jr., of Oakland, and grandson of Major and Mrs. Winfield S. Overton of Piedmont and Mr. and Mrs. Ralph E. Cotter, Sr., of Oakland. Terry attended Montclair Elementary School, then Piedmont Jr. and Sr. High School. He then studied at Menlo College and graduated from Arizona State University with a major in journalism. He also served in the California National Guard. His life-long passion for Africa and animal conservation developed in high school when he first traveled to Africa with his aunt, uncle and cousins. After college, he went back on a solo motorcycle journey riding from Germany to the southernmost part of Africa. This adventure turned his interest from journalism to travel and he opened the International Travel Guild in San Francisco where he specialized in African tours and treks. Later in his life, his great love for African animals led him to meaningful work with Safari West in Sonoma County, California, and White Oak, the internationally recognized conservation center in Yulee, Florida. Terry dedicated his life to coaching disabled and able-bodied athletes across the globe. An avid cyclist, he helped lead charitable rides such as Best Buddies, Sea to Shining Sea, and Face Across America, each dedicated to improving the lives of people with intellectual and developmental disabilities. He served as a Team Leader for The Vietnam Challenge, a transformative bicycle journey that brought together able-bodied and disabled American and Vietnamese veterans riding from Hanoi to Ho Chi Minh City. His leadership also extended to AXA Worldride 1995, a 13,000- mile global bicycle journey with 10,000 participants-disabled and able-bodied-riding together across continents. It was during Worldride that he met his beloved wife, Eliza Cotter, who matched his energy and enthusiasm for so many wonderful adventures. He guided and encouraged athletes on some of the most inspiring stages, including carrying the Olympic Torch for the 1984 Los Angeles Games and the Paralympic Torch at the 1996 Atlanta Paralympics, where he also coached the Afghan Paralympic Bicycling Team. He coached Special Olympics track and field in Marin County for over 30 years and taught adaptive skiing at Achieve Tahoe in Lake Tahoe for six seasons. He climbed Mt. Kilimanjaro five times, twice leading Special Olympic athletes on the trek. He is survived by his wife Eliza Cotter, his sister Susan Johnson, and his daughter Hannah Cotter. He is also survived by his step-children, grandchildren, and many nieces, nephews and their children, all of whom he loved dearly. To honor Terry’s legacy, the family kindly requests that donations be made to the Safari West Wildlife Fountain at safariwestwildlifefoundation.org.
articles.title: Terry Cotter dies on September 14

articles.text: In the last few years, the Piedmont Center for the Arts Artisanal Beer Festival organizers noticed that more guests were enjoying the late Fall vibe on PCA’s front lawn. In fact, more than a few patrons brought blankets. So last year PCA decided to include a trio of Piedmont High students playing some cool jazz. And as the evening wore on, the front lawn scene drew more patrons and started to look like an outdoor music festival. Organizers even learned that some patrons just came to enjoy the music. Jazz lovers are in for another treat this year. After rave reviews from last year’s crowd, the PCA is pleased to announce that last year’s jazz combo will return this year – Deniz Radzik, Eric Verner and Maxim Miller. While they are all PHS students, each has been playing music for some time. Deniz Radzik’s father was a musician, and Deniz started playing violin in 4th grade. However, he ended up playing percussion and drums in the middle school concert and jazz band. As he entered high school, he played with several California jazz conservatory bands. Eric Venner also comes from a musical family. His mother sang in the choir at Boston University where she met Eric’s father, who sang in the Stanford A Capella group. Eric started playing classical guitar at age eight and switched to blues, jazz, and funk guitar at age 12, He is now part of the PHS jazz combo. Maximo Miller started playing piano at age seven with the encouragement of his parents and switched to jazz when he was 12. He plays in the PHS jazz band, and gigs around the area with the sophomore combo. This year’s Beer Festival takes place on Friday, October 23 from 5:30-7:30 p.m. The beer tasting takes place inside the center. Admission is $15 and includes a custom PCA beer glass. The traditional Oktoberfest meal, donated by Piedmont Grocery, is also $15 and is served of the PCA lawn. Credit cards and cash only. Attendees are encouraged to purchase tickets in advance at https:// tinyurl.com/ymf8mz7c Beer Festival attendees enjoy listening to PHS jazz musicians on the PCA lawn.

articles.text: There was a large turnout of 25 readers on the patio inside Piedmont Community Hall on Oct. 6 for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s monthly First Mondays Reading Group discussion. The group gathered to talk about their October nonfiction selection, The Wright Brothers by David McCullough. Published in 2015, the book chronicles the lives and achievements of American inventors and aviation pioneers Orville and Wilbur Wright. It spent seven weeks on The New York Times Nonfiction Best Sellers list and was widely praised by critics and historians. Janet Maslin of The New York Times described it as a “concise, exciting and fact-packed book [that] sees the easy segue between bicycling and aerial locomotion, which at that point was mostly a topic for bird fanciers and dreamers.” The biography tells of the brothers’ childhoods, their entrepreneurial spirit as bicycle shop owners, and their pursuit of manned flight. It also describes their challenges, the legal issues tied to protecting their patents, and their eventual global recognition. One reader compared the book to a Ken Burns documentary. The readers were universally impressed by the Wright brothers’ genius, ingenuity, curiosity, and perseverance. Their risk tolerance and careful study of how birds fly were especially striking. The brothers ran a bicycle shop to earn a living, but their focus— and likely obsession—was achieving flight. Readers noted it was unsurprising that they never married or seemed to have lives outside their work. Many were disappointed by the lack of early U.S. government support for the brothers’ efforts, noting that the French showed greater interest in flight. The discussion reflected on how the late 19th and early 20th centuries were an age of innovation, with the telephone, automobiles, and other transformative inventions emerging. Several readers commented on the pace of technological change then and drew parallels to the present day. The group agreed that human flight was transformative for civilization. Some wondered why it had taken so long to achieve, while others noted both the positive and negative consequences of flight, particularly in warfare. The readers also compared the Wright brothers’ accomplishments to those of J. Robert Oppenheimer and expressed surprise that the brothers’ full lives have not received more historical attention. Participants appreciated learning about the Wrights’ sister, Katharine, whose significant contributions to their success have often been overlooked. The trio’s accomplishments were contrasted with the more ordinary lives of their other siblings, which several readers found both interesting and familiar in family dynamics. The group generally enjoyed McCullough’s writing style, though some felt the book could have used tighter editing. One participant summed it up as “liked but not loved.” A few found parts repetitive, especially in the second half, but agreed the middle section describing the first flights was the book’s high point. The later chapters, focusing on legal battles over patents, were less exciting but showed the brothers’ business acumen. Everyone agreed it had been a The Wright Brothers by David McCullough lively discussion. Several noted they might not have picked up the book on their own and were glad the group had chosen it. Members also appreciated the diversity of life experiences within the group, which adds richness to their discussions. The readers had previously selected Euphoria by Lily King for November and Differ We Must by Steve Inskeep for December. After Bob Hall’s presentation of three fiction options, they chose Cry, the Beloved Country by Alan Paton for January. With their business concluded, the group took a photo together in the circle outside the Community Hall. The group will meet on the patio outside the Community Hall for their next discussion that will be on November 3rd at 1:30 PM. New readers are welcome. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required. Go to https:// bit.ly/3R86PP4, or call the Recreation Department at 510 420- 3070, to register. pages.text: 24 Wednesday, October 8, 2025 Walking on Wednesday Wednesday Walkers learn about Moraga Canyon Housing Plan Walking with Kevin Jackson, the city’s planning and building director By Dick Carter The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group had a special guest and topic last week. Kevin Jackson, the city’s planning and building director, met the walkers at Coaches Field to discuss the city’s Moraga Canyon Specific Plan for future housing development and to answer questions about what it could mean for Piedmont. Before the group set off, three surprise visitors greeted them at the Exedra. Police Chief Frederick Shavies, Captain Chris Monahan, and Commander Brandy Marvin-Morris stopped by to introduce themselves and invite the walkers to tour the Police Department’s new dispatch center on Nov. 5. The group gladly accepted the invitation. About 50 walkers and five dogs gathered for the morning walk. They made their way down Highland Avenue and up Moraga Avenue, following the boardwalk along the canyon’s edge to Coaches Field, which was dedicated in 1994. Longtime walkers know this route well. In 1884, Walter Blair built “Blair Park” here on 40 acres between Moraga Avenue and Mountain View Cemetery as a picnic attraction for guests of his Piedmont Springs Hotel, then located where the Exedra stands today. What is now called Blair Park lies farther up Moraga Avenue. Before Coaches Field was created, that part of the canyon served as a city landfill. Above the field sits the Kennelly Skate Park, opened in 2001 with help from the Kennelly family’s donation. At Coaches Field, Jackson outlined the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan, a key part of Piedmont’s state-required Housing Element. The plan guides how the city could meet Sacramento’s mandate of 587 new homes by 2031 — a major jump from the previous goal of 60. It identifies areas near Grand Avenue and in Moraga Canyon as “priority development areas.” The city aims to adopt the plan by year’s end. It envisions up to 199 new multifamily units, including 60 reserved for lower-income households. The plan does not authorize immediate construction; rather, it sets design and safety standards for future developers. Two main development options are under review. One would locate housing on the current Blair Park open space while keeping Coaches Field and the Corporation Yard in place. The other would build hillside housing above Coaches Field and relocate the Corporation Yard to Blair Park. In both cases, the plan calls for improved parking, transit access, and wildfire safety. All housing — affordable and market-rate — must be built on the same side of Moraga Avenue, with buildings up to 60 feet (four to six stories) tall. Two single-family homes could also be added on Abbott Way and Maxwelton Road. Jackson emphasized that the city itself will not build the housing. After the plan’s adoption, private developers will be invited to submit proposals that make financial and design sense for both the city and potential builders. Several have already expressed interest. He also described the two years of public meetings, study sessions, and outreach that shaped the plan, and reminded the group that the next City Council hearing is scheduled for Monday, Oct. 6, at 6 p.m. in City Hall. Afterward, Jackson led the walkers through the Corporation Yard, pointing out where housing might be located and noting features such as the new wireless tower that provides better cell coverage and rental income from AT&T and T-Mobile. At the top near the skate park, walkers paused to admire the sweeping view of San Francisco Bay — a view, Jackson noted, that future residents would surely appreciate. When it was time to return to the Exedra, the group thanked Jackson for his time and clear explanations. They walked back with a much better understanding of the city’s housing plans — and with appreciation for the opportunity to learn directly from the official guiding them. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 AM. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required. Those interested should go to https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu to register or contact the Piedmont Recreation Department at (510) 420-3070 for more information. articles.text: In the 1960s Hollywood was dishing up pap like Doris Day and Rock Hudson in Pillow Talk, while much tastier fare was simmering abroad, in France and Italy and England and Sweden and Poland and Japan, where innovative artists such as Ingmar Bergman and Akira Kurosawa and Federico Fellini were looking at life in a more complex, exciting way and putting their vision of it on the screen. American audiences began to take notice, especially of a French director named Francois Truffaut, whose The 400 Blows, about a resilient young street kid, became an art house hit. And then Truffaut’s Jules and Jim arrived. One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends and then chatting about it when the lights come up. That’s just what the Piedmont Flix Fest, which meets on the second Thursday of each month, offers: a great movie in a comfortable setting, and then a lively discussion of it afterward. The Flix Fest’s next showing is indeed the 1962 Truffaut film, Jules and Jim. There’s nothing quite like this luminous tragicomedy. It sets out in the deceptively carefree days before World War I, when a soft-spoken Austrian author Jules (Oskar Werner) strikes up a friendship with an exuberant Frenchman, Jim (Henri Serre). Both men fall for the same bohemian force of nature, Catherine (Jeanne Moreau). Seeming to have come out of nowhere, she entrances them with her beauty and wild freedom, and Jim instantly starts writing a novel about the intensity of their threeway romance. Jules wins her hand—but not all her heart. After the war, Jim visits her and Jules and their daughter in their Austrian home and discovers not only that his feelings for Catherine are unchanged, but also that they’re reciprocated. All this plays out in a fresh, inventive style that entranced critics and audiences alike, though not everyone loved the movie – it was condemned by the Catholic Legion of Decency when it opened in the U.S. Jules and Jim will be screened on Thursday, October 9th at 1:00 p.m. at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. Doors will open at 12:45. The movie is free and available to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, and everyone is welcome to bring snacks or lunch. The next movie in the Piedmont series is the James Stewart western, Bend of the River, to be screened on November 13th.

PIEDMONT FLIX FEST French New Wave classic plays Piedmont By Bob Hall In the 1960s Hollywood was dishing up pap like Doris Day and Rock Hudson in Pillow Talk, while much tastier fare was simmering abroad, in France and Italy and England and Sweden and Poland and Japan, where innovative artists such as Ingmar Bergman and Akira Kurosawa and Federico Fellini were looking at life in a more complex, exciting way and putting their vision of it on the screen. American audiences began to take notice, especially of a French director named Francois Truffaut, whose The 400 Blows, about a resilient young street kid, became an art house hit. And then Truffaut’s Jules and Jim arrived. One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends and then chatting about it when the lights come up. That’s just what the Piedmont Flix Fest, which meets on the second Thursday of each month, offers: a great movie in a comfortable setting, and then a lively discussion of it afterward. The Flix Fest’s next showing is indeed the 1962 Truffaut film, Jules and Jim. There’s nothing quite like this luminous tragicomedy. It sets out in the deceptively carefree days before World War I, when a soft-spoken Austrian author Jules (Oskar Werner) strikes up a friendship with an exuberant Frenchman, Jim (Henri Serre). Both men fall for the same bohemian force of nature, Catherine (Jeanne Moreau). Seeming to have come out of nowhere, she entrances them with her beauty and wild freedom, and Jim instantly starts writing a novel about the intensity of their threeway romance. Jules wins her hand—but not all her heart. After the war, Jim visits her and Jules and their daughter in their Austrian home and discovers not only that his feelings for Catherine are unchanged, but also that they’re reciprocated. All this plays out in a fresh, inventive style that entranced critics and audiences alike, though not everyone loved the movie – it was condemned by the Catholic Legion of Decency when it opened in the U.S. Jules and Jim will be screened on Thursday, October 9th at 1:00 p.m. at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. Doors will open at 12:45. The movie is free and available to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, and everyone is welcome to bring snacks or lunch. The drive began at its own 15-yard line. The Highlanders converted a fourth-and-6 at their 34 with an eight-yard pass, then a key third-and-2 at the Berkeley 22 with a three-yard completion to Corey Minor. A four-yard pass to Lee on first-and-goal advanced the ball to the 15, but incompletions on third and fourth down ended the drive. Both teams traded possessions for the rest of the first half. Early in the third quarter, Berkeley drove to the Piedmont 38 before Kate Tong intercepted a deep pass. The Highlanders went three-and-out on the next series. Piedmont’s defense then came up big again, forcing a turnover on downs at its own 11. Senior safety Dahlia Osman broke up a pass in the end zone on fourth down to stop the drive. Berkeley finally broke through with 7:36 left in the fourth quarter, capping a six-play series with a 10-yard touchdown pass and a successful one-point conversion for a 7-0 lead. After another Piedmont punt, the Yellowjackets scored again on a four-play, 44-yard drive to make it 13-0 with 2:10 remaining. Beatrice Nackley broke up their extra-point attempt. articles.text: Shell Corp. has withdrawn its conditional use permit to convert the former Shell Service Station at 29 Wildwood Avenue into an Electric Vehicle (EV) Charging Station. Shell will re-apply with a new application that uses state laws to remove local discretion over EV charging station permits. The original permit, approved by Piedmont City Council on November 18, 2024, included 45 conditions that Shell would have to meet before the proposed charging station could open for business. These conditions included signage and design reviews, the requirement of a security plan, restriction of operating hours, noise mitigation measures and a plan for regularly scheduled maintenance. The new application under California Government Code Sections 65850.7 and 65850.71 circumvents the approved conditions, removing local discretion over EV charging station permits. “It is important to be clear: the City has no discretion in this matter,” read a notice signed by Planning Director Kevin Jackson. “We are carrying out what state law requires.” The California Office of the Attorney General issued a legal alert in March 2025 reiterating local jurisdictions’ obligations under the state laws in question. A copy of this alert is available at piedmont.ca.gov/29Wildwood, along with the revised site plan. articles.text: Piedmont High School students and staff gathered for a school-wide Homecoming Rally in Binks Rawlings Gym on Friday, September 26. Students rallied to show school spirit with contests and chants while getting pumped up for the big football game that night. Purple black-lights on the far side of the gym lit up the court in purple for the gathering. Students and staff showed remarkable coordination with their outfits, with purple tutus and Piedmont jerseys well represented. Rallies include competition among the four classes, so there is some rivalry. Mostly it was an opportunity for the entire student body to rally together while celebrating time-honored traditions. articles.text: Paul Peterson, Catherine Rongey, & Pamela Strike Fullerton Over its 75-year history, Piedmont Play School (PPS), a parent co-operative preschool, has prepared hundreds of children to thrive in kindergarten. In 1999, PPS families and donors raised funds to build 401 Hampton Road – intended to be PPS’s permanent home. Now, despite many requests by PPS for discussion or collaboration, the City of Piedmont is terminating Piedmont Play School’s use of the building to ostensibly replace PPS with a Recreation Department program. This violates the trust of the community that built 401 Hampton, and could end this treasured institution while discouraging donors from supporting future City projects. The irony of this decision is that PPS needs so little: just four hours each weekday morning during the school year. The Piedmont Recreation Department (PRD) already has full use of the building for afternoon, evening, and weekend programming, and has exclusive use all summer for camps. The City also has other options for space. Several rooms at 358 Hillside Avenue, previously occupied by PRD preschool programs, currently sit unused. Should the City displace a nonprofit community program like PPS from the home that donors built for it, if this is the case? History and intent should matter in public decisions. Donors funded and constructed 401 Hampton expressly as Piedmont Play School’s home. As Mark Becker – the designer and builder of the PPS building – wrote in a July 31, 2025, email to the City: “We firmly believe that the spirit of the agreement was for PPS to stay there in perpetuity.” This is not a zero-sum choice; it’s a values test. articles.text: Council to consider adoption of housing plan on Oct. 6 The City of Piedmont has released two new informational videos with individuals answering questions about traffic on Moraga Avenue and wildfire evacuation in connection with the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan – a housing plan for developing City-owned land in Moraga Canyon into a new neighborhood of up to 199 multi-family housing units. Two new short videos feature technical experts answering common community questions about traffic on Moraga Avenue and wildfire evacuation in connection with the Draft Moraga Canyon Specific Plan. The controversial housing plan would provide space to develop buildings as six stories either in the Blair Park area or on the hillside near Coaches Field. The plan includes 139 market-rate housing units and 60 low-income housing units, as well as road safety improvements and an expansion of Coaches Field. The videos provide information on key issues ahead of the City Council’s October 6 meeting, when they will consider adoption of the Specific Plan. The Piedmont Planning Commission voted to recommend the Council adopt the Specific Plan at a public hearing on September 8. Traffic & Road Safety In the first video, Sam Tabibnia of Fehr & Peers, the transportation consultant in charge of traffic engineering work on the Specific Plan, explains what traffic counts and industry-standard models show about Moraga Avenue today and projections with development. The video covers: • How traffic counts and nationally recognized trip generation models project daily trips on Moraga Avenue to rise about 5% – within the day-to-day fluctuations we already experience • How proposed roadway improvements – sidewalks, a buffered uphill bike lane, and a new traffic signal with A Piedmont resident reviews information on the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan on display at the Harvest Festival. pedestrian refuge island at Red Rock Road – would slow vehicle speeds and improve safety for everyone • How the Specific Plan would require future development proposals to demonstrate that each driveway meets Caltrans stopping sight distance standards before approval “The conclusion is clear,” said Tabibnia in the video. “Not only does Moraga Avenue have the capacity to handle new traffic, but the improvements in the Specific Plan will slow down traffic and make this area more accessible for everyone – whether you’re traveling by vehicle, by bike, or on foot.” Watch the traffic video at: bit. ly/MCSPtraffic. Wildfire evacuation In the second video, Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan explains how evacuations are planned, managed, and regionally coordinated today, as well as how the Draft Moraga Canyon Specific Plan supports community safety. The video explains: • Why evacuation planning looks at an entire regional network, not a single street • How alerting, real-time monitoring, and multi-agency coordination make evacuations today very different from 1991 • How the Specific Plan includes fire-safe construction standards and vegetation management requirements that reduce wildfire risk • How evacuation modeling that includes new housing was completed as part of the City’s 2023 Housing Element Watch the wildfire evacuation video at: bit.ly/MCSPwildfire. “Evacuation is never about a single street,” said Brannigan. “It’s about an entire network – and more importantly, how we manage that network together with our regional partners.” Public Information The Draft Moraga Canyon Specific Plan details development locations, site improvements, and infrastructure requirements for the construction of an anticipated 199 units of new housing on Cityowned land in Moraga Canyon, 60 of which would be affordable to lower income households. The Draft Specific Plan is available for download and review at piedmont.ca.gov/MCSP, along with presentation materials, reports, and video from past meetings and events. Community members may submit comments online at piedmont.ca.gov/MCSPComments, by email to MoragaCanyonNews@piedmont.ca.gov, or by mail to: Kevin Jackson, Planning & Building Director, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611. Comments submitted by October 2 will be included in the agenda packet for the City Council public hearing on October 6. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: The Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF) recently received a generous six-figure bequest from a donor’s IRA — a gift that underscores the lasting impact of thoughtful estate planOrdinarily, distributions from an IRA are taxed as income to the account owner, and after death, they may be taxed again as part of the estate. By designating PBF, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit, as a beneficiary, this donor avoided both layers of taxation. As a result, the full value of the gift will go directly to supporting PBF’s work Although the donor left no specific instructions, the Trustees reviewed the donor’s giving history and considered the Foundation’s needs. They voted to allocate half of the gift to the Endowment Fund, ensuring future stability, and half to the General Fund, where it can be put At their September meeting, the Trustees also adopted a new policy to guide future bequests. Donor preferences for specific projects will be honored whenever feasible. If no preference is expressed, the Trustees will make an allocation after reviewing the donor’s history and PBF’s priorities. Similarly, if publicity directions are not provided, the Trustees will use their best judgment in deciding how to share the news. Today, PBF is leading two major campaigns — Reforest Piedmont and the Dearing Memorial — while maintaining both the General Endowment and the Sports Facilities Endowment. At the same September meeting, Trustees also voted to support a major renovation of the Piedmont Park Play Area, including new swings and safety matting. This project will appear in PBF’s fall brochure and follows closely on the heels of PBF’s support for the Beach Tot Lot, where work is set to begin. With these projects moving forward, PBF extends its heartfelt thanks for both current gifts and future bequests. Every contribution, large or small, strengthens the Foundation’s ability to invest in Piedmont’s beauty and vitality for generations to come. Contributions may be mailed to: Piedmont Beautification Foundation, City Hall, 120 Vista Ave. Piedmont, CA 94611
