articles.text: Last night, while most were asleep in the Bay, around 103,000 birds f lew across Alameda County. From now until the end of November, thousands and thousands of birds will touch down in San Francisco Bay, home to the largest estuary on the West Coast. Twice a year migratory birds return to the San Francisco Bay Estuary — an important midpoint and endpoint during their journey along the Pacific Flyway to find food, shelter and a place to rest. While fall migration is a blessing for Bay Area residents it’s also a great reminder to keep the Bay Area bird-friendly as our feathered neighbors continue to face threats of climate change, habitat loss, building collisions, and feral cats. The Golden Gate Bird Alliance and the California Institute for Community Art and Nature (California I CAN), are proud to once again bring the 4th Annual Berkeley Bird Festival back to the Bay Area on Sunday, October 19, this year under the theme — Safe Travels. The Berkeley Bird Festival will continue to give Bay Area residents and visitors alike the opportunity to learn about, celebrate, and help protect the region’s birdlife through a range of free, family-friendly activities. The festival will take place all day, with field trips starting as early as 8:00 a.m. and others ending as late as 3:00 p.m. A full program of events at the David Brower Center will run from 12:00-5:00 p.m. Birding field trips occur throughout Berkeley at sites including; Berkeley Meadow, Tilden Park, UC Botanical Garden at Berkeley, Aquatic Park, Live Oak Park and Shorebird Nature Center. The local student-led Bears for Birds Club will take groups birding on the hour (12:00-5:00 p.m.) from the David Brower Center to the UC Berkeley campus. Behind the Scenes tours of the UC Berkeley Museum of Vertebrate Zoology (MVZ) will also be coordinated throughout the day. On the street in front of the David Brower Center, attendees will find beautiful bird-themed chalk art and tabling community orgs. Inside the David Brower Center will be more local exhibitors, bird-expert talks in the Goldman Theater, a children’s storytime corner with local author Harmony Yu. Berkeley Public Library will offer arts and craft activities on the terrace, and a special in-person program will be held in the Tamalpais Room with bird-related stories, images, poems, songs, and demonstrations by writers, poets, birders, scientists, activists, artists, and bird-lovers. New programs this year include a screening of the award-winning documentary “Lights Out Texas”, a Q&A with the film director; a bird-safe glass demo and activity station; an information booth on birding apps eBird and Merlin; and a video footage showing the entire nesting season of a pair of osprey in Richmond on GGBA’s Osprey Nest Cam. There will also be a field trip at Strawberry Creek on campus specifically for BIPOC birders, and a trip to Berkeley Aquatic Park led entirely in Spanish. The Berkeley Bird Festival is made possible by the financial support of the City of Berkeley Civic Arts Commission, the Wood Foundation, the David Brower Center, and by our following partners: the UC Berkeley Museum of Vertebrate Zoology, Berkeley Public Library, Bears for Birds, International Bird Rescue, Raptors Are The Solution, Palomacy, Folding for Justice, Heyday, Nature Sounds Society, Bay Nature, Pegasus Books, Wholly H20 and more. Founded in 1917, Golden Gate Bird Alliance (GGBA) is one of the oldest conservation organizations in Northern California. Its membership area includes San Francisco and East Bay cities such as Berkeley, Oakland, and Alameda. The California Institute for Community, Art, & Nature was founded in 2016 by Malcolm Margolin. Its programs focus on three areas: California Indian Cultural Preservation and Revival, Art and the Environment, and recognizing and maintaining the City of Berkeley as a center for social, political, and cultural innovation. For more information on California I CAN, visit https://californiaican.org/. For more information, visit Berkeleybirdfestival.org.
articles.title: 4th Annual Berkeley Bird Festival takes flight on Sunday, Oct. 19

articles.text: On September 14 and 21 the Bay Area swimming community came together for two annual fundraising swims for UCSF School of Medicine. The first swim was Josh Bernstein’s annual Golden Gate Invitational, an open water event in which swimmers go the length of the Golden Gate Bridge at dawn. It raised thousands of dollars for the UCSF Cardiology Council for research and treatment. The second swim was the huge Swim Across America event for UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital, which raised hundreds of thousands of dollars for pediatric Josh Bernstein cancer research and treatment. Dr. Bernstein, PHS Class of ‘75, has been involved in both events for many years. Josh Bernstein and son Jack jumping into the Bay at the Golden Gate Bridge. Swim Across America benefactor Rob McLaren (left), longtime SAA Director Susan Helmrich, Ph.D., and Josh Bernstein, DDS requirements related to design, landscaping, hours of operation, or amenities. • As a ministerial project, the building permit application is statutorily exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA Guidelines section 15268). As a result, the new project will differ significantly from what had been previously approved. It will not include canopies, fencing, landscaping, benches, or an air compressor, and there will be no restrictions on allowed hours of operation. Work Notice This news coincides with a work notice from the Alameda County Environmental Health Department (ACEHD), notifying neighbors of removal of lead and asbestos and building demolition at the former Shell service station. Work is scheduled to begin on Wednesday, October 1, and is expected to take about two weeks. Building abatement and demolition activities include: Removal of asbestos-containing material from the roof and lead-containing paint from inside and outside the building using hand tools to minimize the release of lead and asbestos fibers from material being removed. Assessment of the building’s stability and determination of safe demolition methods. Demolition of the above grade portion of the building following completion of the abatement activities. According to the notice, all materials will be placed in sealed containers and transported offsite to licensed disposal facilities. articles.text: In the education literature, the term “productive struggle” refers to the process of effortful learning that develops grit and creative problem solving. And neuroscience research shows that deep, lasting learning is achieved through productive struggle. To tap into this learning phenomenon we need to emphasize the effort over the correct answer. Smart brains are efficient brains. When a student learns a skill or concept, myelin is produced, making brain signals faster and stronger. Challenging tasks which require cognitive struggle increase the production of myelin. Although challenge and struggle may make the learning feel more difficult in the moment, it is a difficulty that pays off in the long run. We can think about learning as a continuum, with surface learning at one end, and deep learning at the other. An example of surface learning would be a fact that is memorized for a test the next day. This can create an illusion of knowledge, yet this surface learning tends to dissipate, and may not be able to be retrieved for a future application to a new situation. On the other end of the continuum, we have deep learning, or mastery. Deep learning is enhanced by productive struggle, and results in conceptual understanding and procedural fluency with the new skill that is transferrable across situations and persists over time. For example, by adding some heavy lifting such as “show/discuss/explain your work,” rather than simply produce a correct answer, the element of struggle and effort required can led to more durable learning. Both educators and parents can respond to incorrect answers by asking back questions which narrow the area of struggle, but do not entirely remove the struggle by giving the correct answer. Techniques to enhance productive struggle can be included in the classroom as well as at home. In the class setting, students can be called on who may not have the correct answer. Within a safe and supportive environment, students can be given time to explore and tinker with their ideas, alone or in a pair or group. Assessments can include expression and discussion of ideas and reasoning, the challenge/ struggle of which will contribute to enhanced knowledge and retrieval, as opposed to a more passive multiple-choice format which tests a student’s ability to simply recognize a correct answer. At home, praise can be given for perseverance, or being able to express, discuss or explain a concept. Parents can encourage the child to apply curricular items to personal, meaningful experiences. Mixed practice can be encouraged at home, which may seem counterproductive, but due to the productive struggle which it creates, significantly improves long term performance. Simply highlighting and modeling our own reasoning process can also be educational. ronments which value the “productive struggle,” in additional to enhancing specific learning, we are also teaching our children the life skill of embracing, rather than being made uncomfortable by, a challenge. We are teaching our children to enjoy the effort, starting with being intrigued by and learning from our mistakes. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of Speech, Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language reading and writing. She can be reached at pengilly.katie@gmail.com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com.
articles.title: Thinking Outside the Classroom “Productive Struggle” makes better learners

pages.text: 6 Wednesday, October 1, 2025 SchOOLs Thinking Outside the Classroom By Katie Pengilly In the education literature, the term “productive struggle” refers to the process of effortful learning that develops grit and creative problem solving. And neuroscience research shows that deep, lasting learning is achieved through productive struggle. To tap into this learning phenomenon we need to emphasize the effort over the correct answer. Smart brains are efficient brains. When a student learns a skill or concept, myelin is produced, making brain signals faster and stronger. Challenging tasks which require cognitive struggle increase the production of myelin. Although challenge and struggle may make the learning feel more difficult in the moment, it is a difficulty that pays off in the long run. We can think about learning as a continuum, with surface learning at one end, and deep learning at the other. An example of surface learning would be a fact that is memorized for a test the next day. This can create an illusion of knowledge, yet this surface learning tends to dissipate, and may not be able to be retrieved for a future application to a new situation. On the other end of the continuum, we have deep learning, “Productive Struggle” makes better learners or mastery. Deep learning is enhanced by productive struggle, and results in conceptual understanding and procedural fluency with the new skill that is transferrable across situations and persists over time. For example, by adding some heavy lifting such as “show/discuss/explain your work,” rather than simply produce a correct answer, the element of struggle and effort required can led to more durable learning. Both educators and parents can respond to incorrect answers by asking back questions which narrow the area of struggle, but do not entirely remove the struggle by giving the correct answer. Techniques to enhance productive struggle can be included in the classroom as well as at home. In the class setting, students can be called on who may not have the correct answer. Within a safe and supportive environment, students can be given time to explore and tinker with their ideas, alone or in a pair or group. Assessments can include expression and discussion of ideas and reasoning, the challenge/ struggle of which will contribute to enhanced knowledge and retrieval, as opposed to a more passive multiple-choice format which tests a student’s ability to simply recognize a correct answer. At home, praise can be given for perseverance, or being able to express, discuss or explain a concept. Parents can encourage the child to apply curricular items to personal, meaningful experiences. Mixed practice can be encouraged at home, which may seem counterproductive, but due to the productive struggle which it creates, significantly improves long term performance. Simply highlighting and modeling our own reasoning process can also be educational. By making learning environments which value the “productive struggle,” in additional to enhancing specific learning, we are also teaching our children the life skill of embracing, rather than being made uncomfortable by, a challenge. We are teaching our children to enjoy the effort, starting with being intrigued by and learning from our mistakes. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of Speech, Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language reading and writing. She can be reached at pengilly.katie@gmail.com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com. articles.text: In conjunction with the launch of this year’s Giving Campaign and to mark Piedmont Education Foundation’s 50th anniversary, Dress Best For Less (DBFL) granted the Foundation $50,000 on September 16. DBFL board president Nagisa Yamamoto presented the check to Giving Campaign co-chairs Kim Hunter and Catie Osborn, and PEF executive director Heather Frank. “The mission of Dress Best for Less is to support the children of Piedmont. We are excited to be able to do that in a way that also helps the environment,” said Yamamoto. Formed by a group of Piedmont moms in 1982, Dress Best for Less sells unused clothing and household items to raise money for local schools. They donate the lion’s share of their profits to the Education Foundation and have given more than one million dollars to date. “DBFL’s support is an important part of PEF’s long history,” said Frank. “Their early collaboration helped bolster a fledgling PEF and their ongoing investment has played a key role in the growth of PEF and improvement of our schools.” PEF was established in 1975 by a group of Piedmont community members who wanted to build a better future for their children. Their mission is to provide sustained financial support to Piedmont schools through fundraising and community engagement. PEF’s Giving Campaign is in full swing. To make a gift, visit PiedmontEdFoundation.org/ donate. Community members that give before November 2 will receive a purple sign of appreciation for their front yard. DBFL accepts donations of lightly used designer shoes and clothing. In addition to the donation center at 2501 Harrison Street in Oakland, a donation bin is located at Mulberry’s Market. The Dress Best for Less retail store is located at 4020 Piedmont Ave. Photo by Amy Cordani Kim Hunter (left), Nagisa Yamamoto, Heather Frank, and Catie Osborn
articles.title: Education Foundation receives $50,000 grant from Dress Best for Less

articles.text: The spotlight was on Piedmont High School’s 2025 Homecoming Court as students packed Binks Rawlings Gym on September 26 for the annual Homecoming Rally. The event wrapped up a spirited week of dress-up days and activities leading into Friday night’s Homecoming game with Arroyo High School. This year’s court featured seniors and juniors from both Piedmont High School and Millennium High School. Representing PHS were seniors Sadie Shoop and Peter Murdock, along with juniors Faith Chin and Diego Cabello-Boyd. From MHS, the nominees were seniors Saniyah Johnson and Angela Enkh, and juniors Cea’naiya Alexander and Alex Lee. As each name was announced, the gym erupted in cheers, with students proudly celebrating their classmates. “It was exciting and interesting being on junior court for the first time,” said PHS junior Faith Chin. Continuing the tradition, English teacher Eduardo Wolbert was selected as this year’s grand marshal. Games including mattress sliding, musical chairs, and a staff-versus-student tug-of-war kept the energy high. The celebration continued later that night, when the court was honored at Witter Field during halftime at the football game. The role of the Homecoming Court has shifted over time. While the introductions remain a highlight of the rally, the fanfare isn’t quite what it once was. Even just a few years ago, the crowning of the Homecoming King and Queen carried more weight and was a centerpiece of Homecoming week. Decades earlier, the court rode through town on elaborate floats in a parade through town, and again during halftime of the football game. It was a time when Homecoming was treated as an important community event for more than just the high school. Today, the tradition continues in a more scaled-down form but still reflects a shared sense of pride and recognition. Though times have changed, the excitement surrounding the court remains a reminder of the long history of school spirit at Piedmont. ®
articles.title: Homecoming week takes center stage at Piedmont

articles.text: Staff Photos Xavier Henderson runs in one of his three touchdowns against Arroyo. Piedmont High’s homecoming night on Friday, September 26 didn’t result in the celebration imagined by the football team, losing 40-26 to the visiting Arroyo Dons. For the Highlanders, it was a game where what could go wrong, did go wrong. And with a young team, the mistakes were too much to overcome. “It wasn’t a great week of practice, and you practice how you play. Again, this is a young team, and they don’t understand that you can’t just turn it off and on,” said coach Jordan Seiden. Despite the two-touchdown loss, Piedmont put itself in position to take control of the game but struggled to capitalize. The Highlanders recovered a fumble at the Arroyo 14 in the first quarter, but relinquished a fumble of its own two plays later. At 12-12 near midfield in the second, PHS committed a costly interception returned for a touchdown. They gave away another fumble with 30 seconds left in the first half when at Arroyo’s 34. Piedmont failed to convert eight third downs, while committing eight penalties on the night. “We didn’t necessarily lay down, but if we played closer to our quality, it’s a different game. False starts, jumping offside, not getting stops. We couldn’t get them off the field on fourth downs, said Seiden. Although it was a disappointing loss, Arroyo looks like the class of the Western Alameda County Conference’s Shoreline Division. It marked their second win over an upper Mission Division team after the Dons opened the season with a 48-14 win over Washington. Piedmont now enters a bye week and looks ahead to opening its Mission Division schedule on Friday, October 10 when hosting Hayward. Regardless of the recent result, the Highlanders have a good chance to contend for their third straight league title. Game Recap After the Dons scored on their opening drive, Piedmont scored on a quick five-play drive where Rehan Mumtaz took a carry 32 yards to the Arroyo 36, while Cash Panico scored on a 31-yard reception—making it 6-6 after a missed point after attempt with 6:46 left in the first quarter. Piedmont’s Henderson recovered a fumbled snap on Arroyo’s Cash Panico makes a 31-yard touchdown reception in the first quarter. next drive at their 44, but they eventually punted. After pinning the Dons at their own 12, George Saunders recovered a fumble at the 14, but PHS did nothing with it after a false start and relinquishing a fumble at the 22 near the end of the first quarter. PHS then forced a punt, turning it into a six-play touchdown series, which included Jack Meyjes converting a 4th-and-6, while Henderson scored on a 19-yard carry with 9:12 left in the second. Piedmont led 12-6 after a missed extra point. Arroyo tied the game on a 13-play drive, making it 12-12 with 2:46 left in the half. PHS started their next series at the 48, resulting in a pick-6 on their first play after the Dons read Piedmont’s wide receiver screen—taking a 19-12 lead with 2:37 remaining. The Highlanders drove to the Arroyo 34 with 30 seconds left, but gave away another fumble. Coming out of halftime, Piedmont tied the game at 19-19 on a nine-play drive, finishing with a 22-yard touchdown run by Henderson. On defense, Saunders grabbed a critical interception with Arroyo driving to Piedmont’s four, returning it to the 35. However, PHS failed to convert a 4th-and-1 at Arroyo’s 46 on the next drive. That turned into a 48 yard touchdown run by the Dons, taking a 26-19 lead. After throwing another interception, Arroyo scored on the very first play on a 53-yard carry up the gut—33-19 with 1:33 left in the third. After trades of possession, Piedmont forced Arroyo to punt within its on 10, and a bad snap enabled PHS to take over at the Dons’ three, leading to a two-yard touchdown by Henderson with 8:51 left in the fourth—33-26 Arroyo, but that was the closest it got. Arroyo scored on an exhaustive 12-play drive, converting three third-downs in the process, 40-26 with 2:23 left. NEXT UP Piedmont (2-3 overall) hosts Hayward on Friday, October 10 at 7:00 p.m. It was a packed house at Witter Field for Homecoming Night.
articles.title: Arroyo spoils Piedmont’s homecoming night

articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team pulled off a big 14-10 win over Western Alameda County Conference rival Castro Valley on Thursday, September 25 at Chabot College in Hayward. The result brings the Highlanders’ early league record to 2-0 after beating Berkeley 17-12 the previous week. They have now defeated both of last year’s WACC Tournament finalists. “It means a lot. They are both really good programs, but it shows where we are. The boys played incredible and we executed everything we wanted to,” said coach Rik Krumins. It was a strong game by both sophomores Rylan Patty and Henry Stein, with Patty scoring five goals and Stein netting four goals and three assists. Freshman Ben Kappas also had a goal and two assists. “They are some of the more talented guys I’ve played with. They are making huge jumps from last year, are more mature, and getting stronger. The talent is all there and they are just going to keep getting better,” senior Elles Kreickhaus said of the underclassmen Henry Stein logged four goals and three assists in Piedmont’s win vs. Castro Valley. Luke McAuliffe ranges for a big save against Castro Valley. Rylan Patty scored five goals against Castro Valley. Staff Photos “Henry, Rylan and Ben are great and just getting better. We’re lucky to have them,” senior goalie Luke McAuliffe added. McAuliffe’s performance was key to the win with 10 saves and a steal. “Luke is incredible. He always steps up in big games and this is one we wanted. It was a measuring stick kind of game,” Krumins said. Piedmont is 9-5 with five matches left in the final month of the regular season before the WACC Tournament on October 28-30. Match Recap Piedmont opened to a 6-2 lead in the first quarter and kept a four-goal lead up 10-6 through the second. PHS made it 13-8 in the third quarter, while the Trojans inched closer to make it 14-10 in the fourth. Patty scored the game’s first goal 40 seconds into the action, but Castro Valley tied two minutes later. PHS then scored three straight with Kappas, Nick Riordan, and Kreickhaus—pushing their advantage to 4-1 with 1:37 left. CV got one back quickly on the next possession, but then Kreickhaus assisted Stein at 1:01, while Kappas stole a ball at midpool, finding Zach Dupree with 45 seconds left. In the second quarter, Kappas assisted Stein for a goal 45 seconds in, then Kreickhaus threw an assist to Patty with 4:48 left. Castro Valley scored on a 5-meter penalty and added another goal with 3:58 left, making it 8-4. Stein found Kreickhaus for a goal with three minutes left, but CV added two goals before Patty landed a shot with a second left—10-6. Patty scored again 30 seconds into the third, but CV responded with two goals of its own. Stein scored the quarter’s final two goals with 1:51 and 1:15 left—13-8. CV scored with 4:22 left in the fourth, while Stein found Patty for a goal a little over a minute later. CV scored the game’s final goal with 1:25 left. Final stats: Patty scored five goals and two steals. Stein scored four goals, three assists, and two steals. Kreickhaus had two goals, an assist and a steal. articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ water polo team dropped two matches last week, falling 11-8 at Mission San Jose on Sept. 26 and 16-5 to Castro Valley on Sept. 25. Esme Krumins and Abigail Jacoby led the Highlanders against Mission San Jose, each scoring three goals. Krumins added three more against Castro Valley. The results bring Piedmont’s record to 4-6 overall and 0-2 in the Western Alameda County Conference. 11-8 vs. Mission San Jose The game stayed tied 2-2 after the first quarter, before Mission SJ took a 5-4 lead on a last-second goal before halftime. The one-goal deficit held through the third, 8-7, but the Warriors pulled away with three goals in the final quarter while Piedmont managed just one. Mission struck first, 45 seconds into the game, but Krumins answered a minute later. After Mission regained the lead, Jacoby tied it with two seconds left in the opening quarter. In the second, Mission scored twice to go up 4-2, but goals from Krumins and Brooke Paten tied it again at 4-4. Mission then scored as time expired to lead at the break. The Warriors extended their lead to 7-4 early in the third. Jacoby scored twice in quick succession to cut it to 7-6, then Vivian Burke beat the buzzer to make it 8-7 heading into the fourth. Mission scored early, Krumins answered, but the Highlanders couldn’t close the gap as Mission added two more. The Trojans led 4-0 after the first quarter and 10-3 at halftime. They added four more in the third and two in the fourth while Piedmont scored just twice in the second half. pages.text: Wednesday, October 1, 2025 13 Piedmont beats Castro Valley 14-10 By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team pulled off a big 14-10 win over Western Alameda County Conference rival Castro Valley on Thursday, September 25 at Chabot College in Hayward. The result brings the Highlanders’ early league record to 2-0 after beating Berkeley 17-12 the previous week. They have now defeated both of last year’s WACC Tournament finalists. “It means a lot. They are both really good programs, but it shows where we are. The boys played incredible and we executed everything we wanted to,” said coach Rik Krumins. It was a strong game by both sophomores Rylan Patty and Henry Stein, with Patty scoring five goals and Stein netting four goals and three assists. Freshman Ben Kappas also had a goal and two assists. “They are some of the more talented guys I’ve played with. They are making huge jumps from last year, are more mature, and getting stronger. The talent is all there and they are just going to keep getting better,” senior Elles Kreickhaus said of the underclassmen Henry Stein logged four goals and three assists in Piedmont’s win vs. Castro Valley. Luke McAuliffe ranges for a big save against Castro Valley. Rylan Patty scored five goals against Castro Valley. Staff Photos “Henry, Rylan and Ben are great and just getting better. We’re lucky to have them,” senior goalie Luke McAuliffe added. McAuliffe’s performance was key to the win with 10 saves and a steal. “Luke is incredible. He always steps up in big games and this is one we wanted. It was a measuring stick kind of game,” Krumins said. Piedmont is 9-5 with five matches left in the final month of the regular season before the WACC Tournament on October 28-30. Castro Valley scored on a 5-meter penalty and added another goal with 3:58 left, making it 8-4. Patty scored again 30 seconds into the third, but CV responded with two goals of its own. Stein scored the quarter’s final two goals with 1:51 and 1:15 left—13-8. CV scored with 4:22 left in the fourth, while Stein found Patty for a goal a little over a minute later. CV scored the game’s final goal with 1:25 left. articles.text: Coach Dick Carter’s devotion to Piedmont football began in 1961 when he first suited up for the Highlanders as a freshman. A graduate of the Class of 1965, he returned to the program as a coach, starting with Piedmont Middle School flag football in 2004 and 2005 before becoming Freshman and JV Football Coach at Piedmont High School in 2006. It is a role he continues today. A lifelong Piedmonter, he passed on his love for the game to his twin sons boys who also played for Piedmont. Coach Carter’s impact reaches far beyond the sidelines. He has served as Chair of the Piedmont Recreation Commission, co-founded the popular Walking on Wednesdays program that brings neighbors together for weekly exercise and community connection, and continues to support seniors through local recreation programs. Known as a steady and thoughtful leader, he has strengthened community ties across generations and helped make recreation and athletics a central part of Piedmont life. Outside of his civic and coaching roles, Coach Carter built a distinguished career in marketing and business leadership. He earned a BA in History and an MBA in Marketing from the University of California, Berkeley, where he also served as the Varsity Boxing Coach while completing his graduate studies. His career spans leadership roles at Procter & Gamble, Ralston Purina, and No Nonsense Fashions, as well as executive positions in marketing agencies. As an entrepreneur, he owned and operated four Wendy’s restaurants before launching Carter Marketing Group. He later served as Chief Marketing Officer of the California Alumni Association, where he revitalized membership, expanded partnerships, and generated significant new revenue. Coach Carter has also served as a member of University Senior Living Partners LLC, developing senior living communities connected to colleges and universities. Today, Coach Carter remains a cornerstone of both Piedmont athletics and community life, embodying the tradition, continuity, and civic spirit that make Piedmont special. Q: How has Piedmont Football changed over the years? Dick Carter, PHS Class of 1965, has been a part of the Piedmont High football program since 2006. get to play on grass very often today. That’s a change too. Q: What do you think your sons gained from playing football at Piedmont? Coach Carter: My twin sons played football all four years while they were at Piedmont and I think it was helpful in establishing the importance of doing something hard in its entirety and not quitting. Things in life are hard at times, but you have to have the mental strength and discipline to stick with challenges and work through them. I think football helped my boys understand this. It also provided some confidence that they could handle difficult things in their lives. Additionally, I think the need for every player on the field to perform his job correctly for a play to be successful reinforced the importance of teamwork for my sons. Q: What traditions or rituals have stayed consistent over the years? Coach Carter: Friday night lights at Witter are an important one. I remember being in elementary school at Havens and coming to the high school football games. We sat in the stands at the south end of the field. It was fun and exciting. (We tried to get the players to give us their chin straps at the end of the games.) The players doing Piedmont victory jacks in front of the stands after a win is a great tradition. It’s a rightful celebration for everyone. We’ve been doing it for a while now. Coach Carter: I look at Piedmont High football from two different time perspectives. First, I think back over 60 years ago when I was a student at PHS and played football, and second from 20 years ago when I first started coaching the freshman team in the fall of 2006. From both perspectives there has been a dramatic increase in commitment required to play high school football. This is especially the case compared to playing Piedmont football in the early 1960s. Back then, we showed up in August for “double days” and started the season. There were no off-season weight training and conditioning. Twenty years ago, there was an understanding that this work was needed, but the follow-through by the coaches and boys was inconsistent. The “arms war” of high school football has escalated very significantly over the recent years and what is required to play football is much greater today for players and coaches. With the increased commitment and effort required to play high school football, players have gotten bigger, stronger, faster, and more athletic. A “big player” in the 1960s was 200+ pounds. The idea of a high school player being 300 pounds or more was almost unimaginable. You certainly see this sized player today. High school football coaching and the level of playbook sophistication today is much greater today. It is probably greater than that of many college football teams in the 1960s. I can only remember the PHS head varsity, JV, and freshmen coaches when I played. I’m not sure if there were assistants. In the 1960s the coaches were usually PE or other PHS teachers. This was less common 20 years ago and today. That brings up another important difference between now and both 60 and 20 years ago. We had three levels, varsity, JV, and freshman at both of these times. The varsity had over 30 players and the JV and freshmen teams each had between 30 and 40. So, there were almost 100 boys playing football each year. It was almost a right-of-passage for a 9th grade boy to play freshman football. Unfortunately, the much smaller number of boys participating required the merging of the freshman and JV teams about ten years ago. A positive recent change has been the importance given to coaching safe techniques. When I played, you were taught to tackle with your “head across the bow” (i.e., in front of the direction of the ballcarrier). It wasn’t until the last five or so years that it has become recognized that rugby tackling with your head out of the tackle can be just as effective and can reduce concussions and neck injuries. Equipment is better today too. I was small in high school and it seemed my helmet and shoulder and other pads weighed almost as much as I did. Pads are lighter today and this along with higher levels of conditioning make the game faster. Witter Field got converted from grass to turf around 1999. (Turf could make the game faster too.) The grass in the middle of the field was destroyed during the season, which made for a hard surface, but it was fun playing in mud when it rained. Boys don’t Q: Who are some standout players or teams from the past that you think deserve to be remembered? Coach Carter: I didn’t coach them, but Mike Humphries’ frosh teams went undefeated for something like three seasons in a row in the early 2000s. Coach Kliszewski coached these teams too and can provide more information. It is an impressive accomplishment. Our 2018 JV team went 10 and 0 and is memorable one for me. It was team that was made up primarily of a large, strong sophomore class. As freshmen they took their lumps and gained experience, but as sophomores they excelled. Two years later I believe these same boys went undefeated, 5 and 0, as seniors in a shortened 2020 season. There have been many excellent Piedmont players over the years. Drew Olsen was an outstanding quarterback who played at UCLA and in the NFL. He started on the PHS Varsity as a freshman, but I didn’t have any coaching experience with him. I did coach Gabe Watson and he stands out in my memory as the best Piedmont running back that I ever experienced. Sadly, Gabe tore his ACL in a playoff game at the end of his senior season. He worked hard to rehab and had some excellent college football accomplishments. He finished his career at the University of Texas. Gabe was an outstanding athlete and a fine young man. He was the best player on all his PHS teams and he was also the hardest worker. There was a correlation. Q: What do you think sets Piedmont’s football program apart from others in the area? Coach Carter: Piedmont doesn’t have the biggest or most athletic players in the area and often in its games. I think our boys realize that in order to win they have to be in excellent physical condition and play with better technique and skill than their opponents. This means Piedmont players have to work very hard before and during the season, and they do. Other schools’ players work hard too, but we are almost always competitive because of our hard work and the pride and confidence that comes with it. Q: What inspired you to become a football coach, and what keeps you motivated each season? Coach Carter: Since I had two sons playing middle school f lag football with practices at 6:30 a.m. I felt I should be down on Witter with them in the morning dark. It turned out to be the best decision I’ve ever made. Helping boys develop into better football players and young men during their time in the PHS football program has been a joy for me. I particularly enjoy working with freshmen and watching them develop over their four years. They become “our boys.” It especially gratifying to see them after they graduate and come back as grown men for visits. Q: How has support from the school or local community changed over the years? Coach Carter: Unfortunately, the cost of conducting the football program has increased dramatically over the recent years and not all of it can be borne by the school. This has necessitated parents and the community stepping up and providing more financial support for the program. JV Coach Greg Dietrick, who is also the father of Piedmont boys and future PHS players, has done a wonderful job of organizing some of this support. I would also note that players’ mothers have provided needed team support in recent years as “team parents.” This was not part of the program when I was in school and it is very beneficial today. I believe the Piedmont Boosters have been active in the supporting the team since at least the 1990s. Their contributions have also been consistent and very important. Q: What are some of the toughest moments the team has faced, and how did they overcome them? Coach Carter: I think the toughest moments were when the numbers of players dropped to levels that did not allow for fielding full teams. About 10 years ago, we had to combine the freshmen and JV teams. This means less opportunity for younger boys to play and develop. It also means that sometimes our freshmen are playing against juniors on the other teams, but our players have Coach Carter as a member of the Piedmont Freshman Football Team in 1961

articles.text: Piedmont’s JV boys’ water polo team reeled off league wins over Encinal and Berkeley. Piedmont High School’s JV water polo team, led by coaches Rik Krumins, Lennie, Chris Sazo and John Savage, beat Encinal on Sept. 16 by a score of 12-5. It was a strong turnaround after losing 10-4 to the same team earlier this season in the Novice Tournament. The JV squad followed up with an 8-7 win over Berkeley on Sept. 23. Their play reflected the hard work the players and coaches are putting in to build skills and confidence. This year’s team includes several athletes with years of swimming, baseball, or basketball experience but no prior water polo background. They are putting in great effort, learning quickly, and enjoying the season. Some of Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team. JV players include Alex Wolff, August Collins, Ben Gitter, Chase Mellers, Dev Nabizadeh, Dylan Jerez, Ethan Wong, Graham Smith, Henry Van Den Bos, Jack Dahling, Jude Franco, Leo Maltz, Oliver Hurwitz, Rory Hull and Walker Wilson. Piedmont responded to a 10-4 loss to Encinal with a resounding 12-5 victory.
articles.title: JV boys’ water polo team tops Encinal & Berkeley

articles.text: It was a tough week for Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis team, dropping back-to-back 4-3 road matches to Alameda on Sept. 23 and Head-Royce on Sept. 24. “Both matches were 4-3 and could’ve gone our way with a few points making the difference,” coach Jim Landes said. The losses leave Piedmont at 6-8 overall and 1-1 in the Western Alameda County Conference. articles.text: Play ends Oct. 12 Berkeley Playhouse’s production of The Addams Family, based on the macabre 1964 television series and The New Yorker cartoon that inspired it, has been extended due to popular demand. The play is currently running at the Julia Morgan Theater in Berkeley now through October 12. Directed by Mel Martinez, with music direction by Erika Oba and choreography by Cat Delos Santos Reyes, The Addams Family is a comedic musical that’s fun for the whole family with themes of family dysfunction, being true to oneself, and celebrating love in all its forms. In Martinez’s rendition, Wednesday Addams, the family’s whip-smart and devious daughter, is grown up and in love with a “normal” young man from a respectable family. The ghoulish Addams’ family dynamic is challenged when they host a dinner for her boyfriend and his parents. Christian Arteaga stars as patriarch Gomez Addams with Tielle Baker playing the great Morticia Addams, supported by Serene Hammami as the mischievous Wednesday and Keenan Moran and William Spitz playing Pugsley. “The Addams Family is a musical that at its core is about love, family, and being true to who you are, and our Addams Family truly embraces their Latin Culture with nods to the Mexican Gothic aesthetic in our design,” said Director Mel Martinez. “Much like me, our Gomez is both Spanish and Mexican and we wanted to lean into the Mexican representation. It is important to me to show that brown is beautiful, and joyful, and full of heart,” he added. “The heart of the show is how close this family is. Every decision they make is because they love each other.” Performances run Friday through Sunday, and select weekday evenings, through October 12. The play is appropriate for all ages. For tickets, call the box office at (510) 845-8542 x351 or visit berkeleyplayhouse.org. Photo courtesy of Berkeley Playhouse Cast in Berkeley Playhouse’s The Addams Family.
articles.title: Last chance to see Berkeley Playhouse’s The Addams Family

articles.text: American indie rock band The Decemberists perform alongside the San Francisco Symphony at Davies Symphony Hall one-night only, on Friday, October 10. Formed in Portland, Oregon, in 2000, The Decemberists are known for their narrative lyrics and folk-infused sound. The band is led by singer-songwriter Colin Meloy, with Chris Funk, Jenny Conlee, Nate Query, and John Moen. Their music blends indie rock with elements of folk, baroque pop, and Americana, often weaving complex narratives inspired by mythology, history, and 19th-century literature. The Decemberists join forces with the San Francisco Symphony for a one-night-only performance playing lush symphonic arrangements of selections from their expansive catalog, reimagining the band’s popular music in a bold new light. The Decemberists gained critical acclaim with albums like Picaresque (2005), The Crane Wife (2006), and The Hazards of Love (2009). Their 2011 release The King is Dead marked a shift toward a more stripped-down, rootsy sound and included the hit single “Down by the Water.” The concert begins at 7:30 p.m. A lobby exhibit in Davies Symphony Hall, entitled Gaïa, will be accessible before and after the show. Gaïa is the latest project from cellist Gautier Capuçon, featuring newly commissioned works by 16 composers. To purchase tickets, visit https:// www.sfsymphony.org/Buy-Tickets/2025-26/Decemberists.
articles.title: The Decemberists perform with SF Symphony Oct. 10

articles.text: Oakland Ballet Company performs Luna Mexicana, a ballet celebrating Dia de los Muertos and traditional Mexican dance, on Saturday, November 1, at the Paramount Theatre in Oakland. Luna Mexicana is an original work by Oakland Ballet Company’s Artistic Director Graham Lustig and is one of the Bay Area’s most celebrated events honoring Dia de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, a holiday celebrated and observed mostly in Mexico and Latin America. Lustig’s production features a young woman whose ancestors “dance” back to life in the form of teetering skeletons, skirt-swishing ladies and a bride and groom duet. In 2018, Oakland Ballet Company premiered Viva la Vida, co-choreographed by Lustig and Martín Romero of Ballet Folklorico Mexico Danza. The dance celebrates the life and artistry of iconic Mexican artist Frida Kahlo, and is now included in annual presentations of Luna Mexicana. The program is presented in two acts with an intermission, and features a selection of Mexican contemporary and folkloric dance as well as music curated by Lustig. Past performances have included the Aztec ensemble Nahui-Ehekatl and Co. and dancers from Ballet Folklorico Mexico Danza. Light bites and refreshments will be served. Audience members of all ages are encouraged to attend in Day of the Dead costume. Luna Mexicana is a family-friendly event and ideal for audience members ages 7 and up. Tickets are available online now. Visit https://oaklandballet. org to purchase tickets. Ramona Kelley in Oakland Ballet’s performance Luna Mexicana Photo courtesy of Oakland Ballet

articles.text: Concert is Oct. 17 at Paramount Theatre The Oakland Symphony launches its 2025-26 season with “THE FIREBIRD!,” performed at the Paramount Theatre on October 17. The season begins with Anna Clyne’s This Midnight Hour, a short orchestral piece by the British composer known for creating vivid, emotional music. Critics describe the work as a musical painting or dream sequence, moving through different moods, scenes, and images. Kendrick Armstrong, Oakland Symphony Music Director, said the piece “is an absolute showcase for the orchestra.” “It is based on poetry that Clyne wanted to create of perseverance and determination, [and] what it means to perverse through a dark period of time of your own personal life and historical context. It conveys a ‘midnight hour’ that leads to a hopeful and bright ending,” he said. The program includes Maurice Ravel’s Piano Concerto in G, influenced by Jazz music and performed by pianist Sara Davis Buechner, who returns to the Oakland Symphony for its season opener. “I’m excited to have Sara return to the symphony,” Armstrong said. “When I took on the post as [music director], I was waiting for the right opportunity to bring her back to the Oakland Symphony. I’m ecstatic to have her back to perform the Ravel Kendrick Armstrong Piano Concerto in G.” “THE FIREBIRD!” also includes Adolphus Hailstork’s Symphony No. 1, and ends with Igor Stravinsky’s The Firebird suite, lending the season launch its title. “[The Firebird] is one of those pieces that’s imperative for a conductor to do with [their] orchestra,” Armstrong said. “It’s a whirlwind of a piece. It will be a dynamic way for us to end our first concert of the season.” A pre-concert talk by John Kendall Bailey begins at 7 p.m. Bailey is an experienced oboe and piano player based in the Bay Area who works with the Oakland Symphony and various youth and community ensembles. The concert begins at 8 p.m. To purchase tickets, visit h t t p s: // w w w.o a k l a n d s y m - phony.org/event/season-opening-the-firebird/.
articles.title: Oakland Symphony opens new season with THE FIREBIRD!

articles.text: Autumn Lights Festival, an art-filled and family-friendly fundraising event for the Friends of the Gardens at Lake Merritt (FGLM), returns this year on Thursday, October 16. The festival has drawn more than 12,000 art and nature enthusiasts to Lake Merritt since 2012 and celebrates its 13th anniversary over three nights on October 16 through 18. Patrons will experience more than 50 locally-produced illuminated art displays, some of which were presented at Burning Man music festivals, throughout Oakland’s seven-acre municipal gardens. Filma Collective, a coworking artists’ space based in Berkeley, is one of over a dozen featured artist organizations this year. “This is a very special show for us as it’s the only botanical installation we do, a fusion of art and nature,” Filma Collective artists wrote in a statement. “The festival is a yearly fundraiser for the public gardens in Oakland’s Lake Merritt which are a beloved pillar of the local community. We’ve been in love with the gardens for years and feel blessed we’re able to participate in helping it remain available to all our friends in the community.” Ticket purchases benefit the Friends of the Gardens at Lake Merritt, a volunteer organization formed in 2004. FGLM volunteers provide much needed maintenance assistance as the City of Oakland’s gardening staff has been dramatically reduced over time. The nonprofit partners with the City of Oakland to support the maintenance, revitalization, and programming of the seven-acre collection of themed gardens within Lakeside Park on the shores of Lake Merritt, including a bonsai garden, a Sensory Garden, a Toddler Garden, an Urban Edible Garden, and more. The Autumn Lights festival is FGLM’s biggest annual fundraiser. Tickets are on sale now and can be purchased by visiting https://gardensatlakemerritt.org/ autumn-lights-festival-2025/.
articles.title: Lake Merritt Gardens nonprofit launches Autumn Lights Festival on Oct. 16

articles.text: The de Young Museum’s most anticipated exhibition of 2025, Art of Manga, is now on view. Art of Manga features over 600 drawings by more than a dozen iconic Japanese artists, comics and novelists who specialize in the genre, which has become widely popular in the United States and in Western culture. Manga is a type of imagedriven narrative storytelling in Japan, the word manga originated literally translating as “pictures run riot.” The de Young, one of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, is the first North American museum to highlight in a major exhibition the contemporary Japanese art form. Featured artists include Chiba Tetsuya, Akatsuka Fujio, Takahashi Rumiko, Taniguchi Jiro, Yamazaki Mari, Araki Hirohiko, Yamashita Kazumi, Tagame Gengoroh, Yoshinaga Fumi, Oda Eiichiro, and Tanaami Keiichi. “Captivating millions around the world with dynamic graphic narratives, manga is one of the most significant visual mediums of our time,” said Thomas Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “San Francisco has long been a gateway for Japanese cultural exchange in the United States, and we are delighted to honor this legacy by showcasing the artistry and power of contemporary Japanese narrative art in Art of Manga.” Art of Manga organizing curator Nicole Coolidge Rousmaniere said the genre cultivates “an ease of visceral understanding that enables readership from around the world.” “We are living in a time when the narrative shift from text to images is increasingly becoming a reality,” she added. “Readers become invested in characters and their stories, and manga publishers and artists take their letters and social media comments into account and adapt the ongoing story or create new manga, which often then becomes a forerunner to greater cultural shifts.” Art of Manga will be on view at the de Young museum now through January 25, 2026. For more information, visit https://www.famsf.org/. Art of Manga exhibition opening at de Young. Photo by Gary Sexton
articles.title: Art of Manga on view now at de Young

articles.text: Berkeley Symphony invites community members to the second concert in its Symphonic Series, Refracted Light, on Sunday, Oct. 5, at 4 p.m. at the First Congregational Church of Berkeley. Guest conductor Edwin Outwater of the San Francisco Conservatory of Music will cross the bay to lead the program, presenting Berkeley Symphony as it hasn’t quite been heard before. The concert opens with Berkeley composer Samuel Adams’ virHelen Kim Edwin Outwater tuosic Chamber Concerto, featuring violinist Helen Kim. The piece expands the traditional concerto into a five-movement dialogue between soloist and orchestra. Experimental artist Yaz Lancaster follows with Gender Envy, a layered, textural work that invites audiences to expand definitions of identity. The evening closes with Joseph Haydn’s grand Symphony No. 100, imposing and percussive. Tickets start at just $15, available now at https://purchase. berkeleysymphony.org/ChooseSeats/801.
articles.title: Berkeley Symphony presents Refracted Light

articles.text: Paul Newman and Robert Redford in Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid and the Gun (2018), which was acknowledged as his last film, decades had passed. He was not exempt from the gravity of aging or the passage of time. I reflected on the film, on his casual and comfortable portrayal of the character Forest Tucker, a serial bank robber, always well-mannered, whose gun was a mere prop, as was his ever-present, stylish fedora. Was the film a metaphor? Was it Redford’s smiling farewell, captured in his portrayal of this elderly gentleman who simply loved robbing banks, and, when caught, managed to escape something like 17 times. Or was The Old Man and the Gun simply a final tip of that classic hat? His filmography is stunning, the variety and number of roles beyond impressive. In recognition of his contribution to the film arts, the Academy presented him with an honorary award for his work as actor, director, narrator (voice over) and producer, as well as the creation of Sundance (in 1981), which annually nurtured and screened the work of independent filmmakers. There isn’t space to list the many films in which he portrayed a leading character, so permit me to select those films that I judge to be memorable. Let’s start with Barefoot in the Part (1967) which was soon followed by his signature role as Sundance in Butch Cassidy and the Sundance kid (1969); then Jeremiah Johnson (1972); The Sting (1973); The Way We Were (1975); Three Days of the Condor (1975); All the President’s Men (1978); The Natural (1984); Out of Africa (1985); Indecent Proposal (1993); The Horse Whisperer (1998); Spy Games (2001); An Unfinished Life (2005); All Is Lost (2013); and, as mentioned above, with grace and class, The Old Man and the Gun (2018). When not appearing on the Robert Redford in The Horse Whisperer screen, Redford stood behind the camera as director /producer, winning his only Oscar as the director of Ordinary People (1988). He directed and produced A River Runs Through It and was nominated for a Golden Globe for Best Director. He acted, directed and produced The Horse Whisperer; directed and produced The Legend of Baggar Vance; and directed and produced Lions For Lambs. pages.text: 18 18 Wednesday, October 1, 2025 By Chris Honoré Hearing the news that Robert Redford, at the age of 89, had died gave me pause and a saddened sense of disbelief. articles.text: Alicia Vikander as Ava in Ex Machina When the film Ex Machina was released (2014), artificial intelligence aka A.I. was still the stuff of the future, imagined only by Sci-Fi novelists and screenwriters and serious techies. Recall the extraordinary Stanley Kubrick hit film 2001: A Space Odyssey (now streaming), based on a short story by the revered sci-fi author Arthur C. Clarke. On board the starship is the passive-aggressive A.I. computer named HAL (9000), programmed to navigate the craft, which is headed into the distant reaches of outer space. The crew consists of five astronauts, three in suspended animation. Their journey proves to be harrowing. Since Kubrick’s stunning movie, countless films have been added to the futuristic/sci-fi genre, many imagining the integration of sophisticated A.I. computers as part of their narratives. Be prepared to be captivated (or puzzled or creepily moved) by Ex Machina, a stylish film, released in 2014, that not only constructs a compelling glimpse into the future but asks some big questions along the way. What does it mean to be fully human? Can edgy, idiosyncratic computer geeks/engineers ever create A.I. machines (call them animatronics) that possess a brain that doesn’t just store information, no matter how sophisticated, but can respond to questions Alicia Choi, violin 7:30 PM Friday October 17, 2025 1305 W 2nd Street Benicia, CA P Pi ie ed dm mo on nt t C Ce 801 Magnolia Avenue Piedmont, CA

articles.text: Lightyear is a kid-friendly, action-adventure spin-off from Disney-Pixar’s Toy Story. And parents might consider the following: if your little guys have not been introduced to the Toy Story franchise, well, begin there before introducing them to Lightyear. In preparation, here is some backstory: in 1995, the year that the first Toy Story was released, it began with Andy, a boy who had a bevy of plastic toy-figures in his room. Buzz Lightyear was not one of them. What happened was that Andy went to the movies and watched a sci-fi action adventure film starring Buzz Lightyear, and he was smitten. Loved the character, which became an action figure. For Christmas, of course, under the tree was Buzz Lightyear. What Lightyear is not is a film about how Buzz ends up in Andy’s room, joining the gang of figures that come to life, so to speak. Instead, Lightyear is the film that captured Andy’s imagination. In other words, it’s sort of an origin tale that stands alone and is only referenced in Toy Story. The question then begged is, what was there about this animated story that so captured Andy’s imagination? First, the tale unfolds with Buzz (Chris Evans), a charismatic, all-American, lantern-jawed space ranger and a crew of hundreds on board a Star Trek-like deep space star A scene from Disney-Pixar’s Lightyear ship, akin to the iconic Enterprise. In command is Alisha Hawthorne (Uzo Aduba). The ship is 4.2 million light years from Earth on a deep space mission; all have been in deep hibernation. Awakened, they decide to explore an unfamiliar planet named T’Kani Prime. Of course, stuff happens that provides excitement. The planet has breathable air; however the ship is damaged on landing, plus there are hostile, voracious insect-like creatures that threaten the crew. What allows the ship to travel at warp speed is a hyperspeed crystal that is also in need of repair. Of course, Buzz is the obvious choice to be the test pilot. This is when time travel comes into play and the story does get a bit convoluted. Buzz takes the crystal out for a very short test; however, when he returns he discovers that four years have passed on the planet. There’s also an evil emperor, Zurg (James Brolin), who threatens the new colony now established on T’Kani Prime. He has an army of robotic soldiers. There is also a scene-stealing robotic cat named Sox (Peter Sohn) who is Buzz’s close companion. Think of the critter as Buzz’s feline wingman and advisor. It’s all wonderfully animated, filled with lots of action and adventure, and a great introduction to Buzz Lightyear, a swaggering daredevil, dedicated to the mission no matter the breathtaking risk. Lightyear. Directed by Angus MacLane. Disney-Pixar animation. Voiced by Chris Evans, Taika Waititi, Keke Palmer. 1 hr., 40 min. Rated PG. Released in 2022. Streaming on Disney=/ Prime/Apple/Fandango.

articles.text: Sunday, Sep. 7 – Oct. 13, 11–2 p.m. Slavic Arts Exhibition The Center for Slavic Arts and Culture is proud to present its very first exhibition, KALEIDOSCOPE. The show brings together 17 artists from five Slavic countries, including a photographer and a jewelry designer, each sharing their talent and creative vision. In challenging and uncertain times, art reminds us of beauty, resilience, and the strength of our community. Kaleidoscope is a celebration of creativity, and a reminder of how art can connect, uplift, and inspire us all. This exhibition will be open weekend days from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. until mid-October. CSAC celebrates Slavic culture’s rich heritage and vibrant traditions, and works to preserve and promote the art, history, and unique identities of the twelve Slavic nations, fostering understanding and appreciation across diverse communities. Come to explore a world of creativity, tradition, and inspiration. Sunday, October 5, 5:00 p.m. Spruce Ritual Ensemble Concert Experiencing Lucian Balmer’s ensemble Spruce Ritual is to feel a greater depth of humanness, heart, and soul. Through sublime melodies and intricate compositions, they take the listener on a heartfelt musical journey, mixing the wisdom, knowledge, and spirit of two great ancient cultures: eastern Hindustani music and western classical music, and infusing their own sacred spirit to create music that is achingly beautiful, human and transformational. Accompanying Lucian will be: Charith Premawardhana (viola), Robin Reynolds (cello), Will Marsh (sitar), Souryadeep Bhattacharyya (sarod), Srishti Biyani Oswal (bansuri/vocals), and Josh Mellinger (tabla). Experience an immersive evening where music and motion converge – the unique sound of Spruce Ritual intertwined with the storytelling grace of kathak dancer Karishma, a Bay Area-based performer and dance educator with over 20 years of experience, weaving ancestral roots with contemporary ritual. Buy advance tickets for In Sacred Motion at https:// www.viewcy.com/e/spruce_ritual_in_sac. Raga-inspired original chamber music! Saturday, October 11, 6:00 p.m. Rebecca & Gary Parks Album Release Concert Rebecca Parks writes award-winning songs that set scenes, tell stories, and dramatize conversations. She has introspective vulnerability and a folk-rock sensibility with a theatrical touch. Her lyrics are sharp, her melodies memorable. She’s not afraid of controversial subjects, but she also doesn’t take herself too seriously. Brimming with gratitude, hard fought self-knowledge, and wry wit, Rebecca’s new album, Secret Stage, is a defining artistic statement. It proudly displays her prowess as a fingerstyle guitarist and pianist, and her sumptuous vocals and harmonies alongside her husband, the gifted vocalist, Gary Parks. Secret Stage explores maturity and personal themes of social justice, and comes with two bonus albums: Adventures with Amy is solo guitar work, and Dyad is a mix of folk and rock covers, with Gary singing lead on most of them and Rebecca contributing arrangements. Tickets at www.brownpapertickets.com/e/6712938, free for under-18! All paid attendees will receive a 3-CD set. Sunday, October 12, 4:30 p.m. In the Tradition Jazz & Pop Piano Trio The In the Tradition Piano Trio – Bill Jackman, Michael Jones, and Albert Brooks – will pay tribute to Jimmy Van Heusen, who composed nearly 1000 songs between 1930 and 1970, of which fifty or more have become American standards. Van Heusen, although less well-remembered amongst the general public, certainly is known among jazz musicians, who continue to record the many great tunes he composed. These tunes include jazz standards such as: Like Someone in Love (1944) and Polka Dots and Moonbeams (1940). Van Heusen wrote popular music mainly for film, but also for stage, yet his rich use of melody, harmony, and the bass line in popular music made his tunes ideal vehicles for jazz musicians. Don’t miss the relaxed pleasure of an afternoon in the Classic Jazz Club with the trio. Doors open at 4:15 PM. Tickets $30, cash/check ONLY, at the door, or $25 in advance at https://www.brownpapertickets.com/e/6214927. As you look at the old section of the city, it’s hard to believe that it was virtually destroyed. German food is not held in high regard. This is unfortunate because there is much that is delicious. The Germans are a very practical people and because of that their culinary tastes are practical also. A very typical German style potato soup contains large cubes of potatoes within a creamy potato broth. Even better is the smooth carrot soup which is enhanced by thin strips of ginger. Many of the restaurants in the old part of the city date from the 1200s the 1300s and as late as the 1400s. It’s a lot of fun eating in places like this. There are many local specialties, but sausage (of all kinds) is the traditional cuisine. Be sure to top your sausage sandwich with some sauerkraut. When it comes to music, Nurnberg is famous… thanks to Richard Wagner and his opera Der Meistersingers of Nuernberg. The local Orchestra presented a concert which I was excited to attend on a recent trip to Germany. The first thing that I noticed was that they perform in an extraordinarily beautiful concert hall. It looks similar to the big concert hall at UC Berkeley. When we arrived in the auditorium, no one was on stage. The orchestra arrives on stage en masse. They seat themselves in a very orderly fashion, and the concert master tunes the Orchestra. They are ready in a few seconds. No time is wasted and everything is elegantly “in order”. The conductor arrives and away they go. It was obvious almost from the start that the Nuremberg Symphony is not one of the fine orchestras of the world. articles.text: Etude Winery is south of Napa in the Carneros region. On a recent visit to the Carneros region in southern Napa I had the opportunity to visit and taste the new releases of Etude Winery. I have heard about this famed estate for many years but never had the chance to visit. Etude was founded in 1982 by Tony Soter. His goal was to produce world-class Pinot Noir from cool-climate regions. The name “Etude” comes from the musical term for a piece designed to focus on technical mastery. Etude applies that idea to winemaking – striving for precision, letting terroir show, minimizing unnecessary intervention in the cellar. The winery’s vision emphasizes that winemaking begins in the vineyard. Soil, vine health, clone selection, microclimates – all these are very deliberately managed. Etude is on Cuttings Wharf Road on the Napa side of the Carneros AVA. Carneros is known for cooler temperatures and fog influence, which is especially good for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Their flagship estate vineyard is Grace Benoist Ranch. It includes many blocks, lots of different Pinot Noir clones (some heirloom) planted in soils that include volcanic origin (less common in much of Carneros). Although Pinot Noir is their star, they also produce Cabernet Sauvignon from notable Napa sites (Rutherford, Oakville, Coombsville), plus white varietals (Pinot Gris, Pinot Blanc, sometimes Chardonnay in small quantities). In 2000, the brand Kenny Griess is Assistant Winemaker at Etude.

The current winemaker is Jon Priest, who continues the philosophy of letting vineyard expression show in the wine. While Napa is more famous for Cabernet, Etude’s consistent focus on Pinot Noir sets it apart. The willingness to experiment with many clones and vineyard blocks gives nuance to the wines. The winery has ample outdoor and indoor tasting space and the tasting room is airy and light. 2022 Etude Chardonnay Estate The Etude Chardonnay opens with wafts of vanilla and honeysuckle that give way to lemon and orange peel, saline and almonds. The medium-bodied palate is lush and inviting and the racy acidity adds an irresistible tautness. It has a long dynamic finish and should last 5 to 6 years in the cellar. 2022 Etude Pinot Noir Grace Benoist Ranch This hails from the volcanic soils of the Grace Benoist Vineyard. The medium-hued Pinot Noir exhibits abundant aromas of plums, allspice, and sweet cherries. Medium to full-bodied and fleshy with silky tannins as well as a luscious finish this lovely wine would make a great partner to grilled salmon. 2022 Etude Pinot Noir Hallberg Vineyard Sourced from a vineyard in the cool Sonoma Coast AVA the Hallberg Pinot has beautifully sweet currant, plum, black cherry, and floral notes that emerge from this dark ruby-colored wine. Rita Hills AVA for this wine. It shows layers of beautifully articulated red fruit, flowers and spices meld together in this seamless, intensely perfumed Pinot Noir. Sweet candied and floral notes linger on the close. 2022 Etude Pinot Noir Heirloom This was my favorite wine of the tasting and the most Burgundian in style. articles.text: As the weather shifts cooler, we realize that fall is just around the corner. While we must be ready to say goodbye to summer, it means many of our favorite fall events are fast approaching. This year, like the last twelve, that means the Piedmont Center for the Arts Artisanal Beer Fest. This year’s event takes place on Friday, October 24, from 5:30- 7:30 p.m. at the PCA, 801 Magnolia Ave. at Bonita. Each year, preparation for this popular event begins earlier in the summer with invitations to brewers from Piedmont and the greater Bay Area. As most beers take weeks, if not months to create, brewers need to begin their creations well in advance. The forecast for the variety of beers presented this year is excellent. As several brewers are planning to present more than one entry, the variety of beers to be tasted should please any palette. The list of brewers is made up of many who have participated in the past years along with the addition of experienced brewers who are entering their first festival. The festival is meant to support and enjoy local home brewers’ efforts, and as in the past, the top beers selected by the judges will be announced during the event, This year’s judges will be Dave Larson, owner of Piedmont Grocery; Lorrel Plimier, Matt Gerhardt shows off his Best Specialty winner “Jazzman” to PCA Beer Festival judge and current Councilwoman Jennifer Long at last year’s PCA Beer Festival. Piedmont City Council Member; Nancy Kent, Piedmont Parks Manager; Steve Roland, Devoted Community Volunteer; and Liam Kelly, Piedmont Recreation Department. Returning this year by popular demand, will be the addition of the “Peoples’ Choice” vote, which allows each patron to vote for their overall favorite entry. Last year, the addition of a threepiece jazz combo added to the festival ambiance on the front lawn. These three Piedmont High musicians have agreed to perform again this year. In addition to sampling many beers, the festival also features a German Oktoberfest meal on the lawn in front of the Center. Grilled bratwurst and German mustard, red cabbage, and potato salad will be provided by longtime supporter Dave Larson of Piedmont Grocery. Tickets for beer tastings are $15, which includes a keepsake Center for the Arts Beer Glass. The Oktoberfest meal is also $15. articles.text: One of the most common dog training concerns today is leash reactivity. You’ve likely seen it: a person walking their dog says “Be nice, Sparky!” in a warning tone as you pass by, and their dog suddenly becomes a lunging, barking menace. This concerning behavior can instigate fights and lead to safety concerns for owners on both ends. Fortunately, this problem is quite avoidable, and with dedication, even very reactive dogs can learn to walk nicely on a leash. Leash reactivity is a form of barrier frustration. Dogs are social creatures, and when repeatedly denied interaction with their peers combined with frequent tension on the leash, this builds frustration. Over time, they learn to associate this frustration with other dogs, taking it out on their peers. To prevent leash reactivity, ensure you always walk your dog on a loose leash. The leash should become completely slack unless you’re actively offering a correction for poor behavior. This means that if your dog pulls on the leash frequently it might be time to change your training equipment or consult a trainer. When encountering other dogs, allow a loose leash if you want your dog to greet, or make the decision ahead of time to not greet and keep a brisk pace. Proper implementation and training of the “off” or “leave it” command is key. But what if your dog is already leash reactive? Fortunately, this can also be addressed. The first thing to do is to positively reinforce training of the “off” or “leave it” command so that you have a way to reliably get your dog’s attention. Begin using this command every time you approach another dog, and start well before you pass them. If your dog looks away from you toward them after initially responding, use your command again and give a verbal negative marker (“uh uh“) if your dog does not turn their eyes back to you. If the verbal negative marker does not work, offer a quick leash correction to let your dog know that your commands are not optional. Immediately reward with treats every time your dog brings their eyes to you. While every dog is unique and may need different training equipment, this is the first step to overcoming leash reactivity. Positively reinforcing the dog’s ability to focus on you reduces the need to put any pressure on the leash. Over time, this will decrease the dog’s associated frustration, as well as the stress you experience on walks. With consistency and patience, even very reactive dogs can learn to walk nicely on a leash. Take the time to work with your dog every day to decrease their frustration and increase your own confidence. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland, California. She helped to launch the service dog and facility dog training organization Alpha Dog Assist in Mill Valley in 2021 and currently offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. To contact her, please call 510–507– 2017, email Sierra109@gmail. com, or visit her website at www. oakhillsdogtraining.weebly.com.

pages.text: 24 24 Wednesday, October 1, 2025 13th Annual Artisanal Brewing Fest returns Oct. 24 at PCA As the weather shifts cooler, we realize that fall is just around the corner. While we must be ready to say goodbye to summer, it means many of our favorite fall events are fast approaching. This year, like the last twelve, that means the Piedmont Center for the Arts Artisanal Beer Fest. This year’s event takes place on Friday, October 24, from 5:30- 7:30 p.m. at the PCA, 801 Magnolia Ave. at Bonita. Each year, preparation for this popular event begins earlier in the summer with invitations to brewers from Piedmont and the greater Bay Area. As most beers take weeks, if not months to create, brewers need to begin their creations well in advance. The forecast for the variety of beers presented this year is excellent. As several brewers are planning to present more than one entry, the variety of beers to be tasted should please any palette. The list of brewers is made up of many who have participated in the past years along with the addition of experienced brewers who are entering their first festival. The festival is meant to support and enjoy local home brewers’ efforts, and as in the past, the top beers selected by the judges will be announced during the event, This year’s judges will be Dave Larson, owner of Piedmont Grocery; Lorrel Plimier, Matt Gerhardt shows off his Best Specialty winner “Jazzman” to PCA Beer Festival judge and current Councilwoman Jennifer Long at last year’s PCA Beer Festival. Piedmont City Council Member; Nancy Kent, Piedmont Parks Manager; Steve Roland, Devoted Community Volunteer; and Liam Kelly, Piedmont Recreation Department. Returning this year by popular demand, will be the addition of the “Peoples’ Choice” vote, which allows each patron to vote for their overall favorite entry. Last year, the addition of a threepiece jazz combo added to the festival ambiance on the front lawn. These three Piedmont High musicians have agreed to perform again this year. In addition to sampling many beers, the festival also features a German Oktoberfest meal on the lawn in front of the Center. Grilled bratwurst and German mustard, red cabbage, and potato salad will be provided by longtime supporter Dave Larson of Piedmont Grocery. Tickets for beer tastings are $15, which includes a keepsake Center for the Arts Beer Glass. The Oktoberfest meal is also $15. More information can be found by visiting the PCA website at www.piedmontcenterforthearts. org. Tickets can be purchased at the door via credit card or cash. PCA recommends purchasing your tickets ahead of the event at https://tinyurl.com/ymf8mz7c 13th Annual Artisanal PIEDMONT BEER FESTIV AL A fundraiser for the Piedmont Center for the Arts Walking with Confidence: Managing Leash Reactivity in Dogs By Sierra Berrick One of the most common dog training concerns today is leash reactivity. You’ve likely seen it: a person walking their dog says “Be nice, Sparky!” in a warning tone as you pass by, and their dog suddenly becomes a lunging, barking menace. This concerning behavior can instigate fights and lead to safety concerns for owners on both ends. Fortunately, this problem is quite avoidable, and with dedication, even very reactive dogs can learn to walk nicely on a leash. Leash reactivity is a form of barrier frustration. Dogs are social creatures, and when repeatedly denied interaction with their peers combined with frequent tension on the leash, this builds frustration. Over time, they learn to associate this frustration with other dogs, taking it out on their peers. To prevent leash reactivity, ensure you always walk your dog on a loose leash. The leash should become completely slack unless you’re actively offering a correction for poor behavior. This means that if your dog pulls on the leash frequently it might be time to change your training equipment or consult a trainer. When encountering other dogs, allow a loose leash if you want your dog to greet, or make the decision ahead of time to not greet and keep a brisk pace. Proper implementation and training of the “off” or “leave it” command is key. But what if your dog is already leash reactive? Fortunately, this can also be addressed. The first thing to do is to positively reinforce training of the “off” or “leave it” command so that you have a way to reliably get your dog’s attention. Begin using this command every time you approach another dog, and start well before you pass them. If your dog looks away from you toward them after initially responding, use your command again and give a verbal negative marker (“uh uh“) if your dog does not turn their eyes back to you. If the verbal negative marker does not work, offer a quick leash correction to let your dog know that your commands are not optional. Immediately reward with treats every time your dog brings their eyes to you. While every dog is unique and may need different training equipment, this is the first step to overcoming leash reactivity. Positively reinforcing the dog’s ability to focus on you reduces the need to put any pressure on the leash. Over time, this will decrease the dog’s associated frustration, as well as the stress you experience on walks. With consistency and patience, even very reactive dogs can learn to walk nicely on a leash. Take the time to work with your dog every day to decrease their frustration and increase your own confidence. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland, California. She helped to launch the service dog and facility dog training organization Alpha Dog Assist in Mill Valley in 2021 and currently offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. To contact her, please call 510–507– 2017, email Sierra109@gmail. com, or visit her website at www. oakhillsdogtraining.weebly.com.
